  14. i, j, k = low, mid + 1, low — teen pointers: i = left half mein (buffer ke andar), j = right half mein (buffer ke andar), k = jahan likhna hai (arr ke andar). Dhyaan do ki i aur j buffer padhte hain aur k arr likhta hai. Agar dono ek hi array par hote to hum abhi tak na padhe hue elements ko overwrite kar dete.

  15. while i <= mid and j <= high — dono halves mein elements bache hon. <= kyunki dono bounds inclusive hain.

  16. if buffer[i] <= buffer[j] — wahi stability wala <=.

17-18. Left ka element arr[k] par, i aage.

19-21. Warna right ka element, j aage.

  1. k += 1 — dono branches ke baad, ek hi baar. Isliye if/else ke bahar likha hai. Agar dono branches mein alag alag likhte to code duplicate hota; galat nahi, bas gandaa.

  2. while i <= mid — left half ke bache hue elements copy karo.

24-26. Copy aur pointers.

Right half ke bache hue elements ke liye loop kyun nahi likha? Ye ek sundar trick hai. Agar left half khatam ho gaya aur right mein elements bache hain, to wo bache hue elements buffer mein j se high tak hain — aur unhe arr[k] se arr[high] tak jaana hai. Par kyunki har step mein j aur k dono ek saath badhe hain, aur shuruaat mein k = low, j = mid+1... jab left khatam hua to k aur j ka farak exactly wahi hai jitne left ke elements copy hue. Actually k == j ho jata hai us waqt! Aur buffer[j..high] hi arr[j..high] hai (line 12-13 ne copy kiya tha aur unhe abhi tak overwrite nahi kiya). To wo elements pehle se sahi jagah par hain. Isliye kuchh karne ki zaroorat nahi.

Ye subtle hai — interview mein agar aap ye samjha do to bahut strong lagta hai. Agar aap sure nahi ho, to safety ke liye doosra drain loop bhi likh do; galat nahi hoga, bas fizool copies.

docs.title: Complexity derive karke
docs.text:
Recurrence relation likho:

T(n) = 2 * T(n/2)  +  O(n)
       ^^^^^^^^^^     ^^^^
       do halves      merge (linear)
       recursively

T(1) = O(1)

Recursion tree se solve karo — ye sabse intuitive tareeka hai:

Level 0:   1 problem of size n         ->  merge cost = n
              |
Level 1:   2 problems of size n/2      ->  merge cost = 2 * (n/2) = n
              |
Level 2:   4 problems of size n/4      ->  merge cost = 4 * (n/4) = n
              |
Level 3:   8 problems of size n/8      ->  merge cost = 8 * (n/8) = n
              |
             ...
              |
Level k:   2^k problems of size n/2^k  ->  merge cost = 2^k * (n/2^k) = n
              |
Last level: problems of size 1  ->  n/2^k = 1  ->  2^k = n  ->  k = log2(n)

TOTAL = (cost per level) * (number of levels)
      = n * (log2(n) + 1)
      = O(n log n)

Har level par cost exactly n kyun hai? Kyunki har level par saare subproblems mil kar poore array ko exactly ek baar cover karte hain. Level 2 par 4 subarrays hain, har ek n/4 size ka — total n. Merging linear hai, to us level ka total merging cost n.

Levels exactly log2(n) kyun hain? Kyunki har level par size aadha hota hai:

n -> n/2 -> n/4 -> n/8 -> ... -> 1

Kitni baar aadha karna pada?  n / 2^k = 1  =>  2^k = n  =>  k = log2(n)

n = 8:    8 -> 4 -> 2 -> 1     3 halvings  = log2(8) = 3  ✓
n = 1024: 1024 -> ... -> 1     10 halvings = log2(1024) = 10  ✓
n = 10^6: ~20 halvings         log2(10^6) ~ 20  ✓

Ye number kitna chhota hai — feel karo: n = 10 lakh par log2(n) ~ 20. Yaani merge sort ~2 crore operations karega. Insertion sort ~5 kharab (5 × 10^11). 25,000 guna farak.

Best, average, worst — sab same kyun?

Merge sort ka split hamesha exactly beech se hota hai, chahe data kaisa bhi ho. Wo data dekh kar decide nahi karta (jaisa quicksort pivot par karta hai). Isliye recursion tree hamesha exactly wahi shape ki hoti hai:

Best case  (sorted):        T(n) = 2T(n/2) + O(n)  ->  O(n log n)
Average    (random):        T(n) = 2T(n/2) + O(n)  ->  O(n log n)
Worst      (reverse):       T(n) = 2T(n/2) + O(n)  ->  O(n log n)

Ye guarantee merge sort ki sabse badi taakat hai. Quicksort average mein tez hai par worst case O(n²). Merge sort kabhi surprise nahi deta.

Comparisons exactly kitne? Merge of size n mein at most n-1 comparisons (best case mein sirf min(len(L), len(R)) — jab ek list poori pehle khatam ho jaye).

Worst case total comparisons ~ n*log2(n) - n + 1
n = 1000:  ~9,000 comparisons
n = 10^6:  ~19,000,000 comparisons

Space derive karo — ye interview mein galat bola jata hai:

Top-down slicing version: 

Har recursive call arr[:mid] aur arr[mid:] se DO NAYI lists banata hai.
Ek waqt mein (call stack ki depth par) kitni lists zinda hain?

Level 0: n elements ka input
Level 1: n elements (do halves)
Level 2: n elements (chaar quarters)
...
Har level par n elements zinda hain, aur log n levels hain.

Peak memory: O(n log n)   <- ye Python ke naive slicing version ki sacchai hai

Hmm — par actually Python mein depth-first execution hoti hai, to ek waqt mein poore log n levels ke saare slices zinda nahi hote. Jo zinda hote hain: current path par har level ka left result + abhi ban rahi slices. Wo n/2 + n/4 + n/8 + ... = n hai, plus result list n — to peak ~O(n), par allocations total O(n log n) hote hain. Practically ye version buffer version se ~2-3x dheema hai isi allocation churn ki wajah se.

Buffer version (line 1 wala): 

buffer:           O(n)   <- ek hi baar allocate
recursion stack:  O(log n)  <- depth log n, har frame O(1)

Total auxiliary space: O(n)

Ye correct answer hai jo interview mein bolna chahiye: O(n) auxiliary space, jisme O(log n) recursion stack shamil hai.

Case Time Space Best Theta(n log n) O(n) Average Theta(n log n) O(n) Worst Theta(n log n) O(n) Recursion depth — O(log n) Linked list version Theta(n log n) O(log n) — stack only

docs.title: Stability, in-place, adaptive
docs.text:
Property Value Kyun Stable Haan merge mein left[i] <= right[j] — tie par left (jo original mein pehle tha) pehle jata hai In-place Nahi O(n) auxiliary buffer chahiye Adaptive Nahi (plain version) Har haal mein same recursion tree, same merges. arr[mid] <= arr[mid+1] wala check thodi adaptivity deta hai; Timsort ise poori tarah exploit karta hai

Stability ka trace:

Input: [ 3, 1a, 1b, 2 ]
Split: left = [3, 1a],  right = [1b, 2]

left sort:   [3] + [1a]  ->  merge: 3 <= 1a? No  ->  [1a, 3]
right sort:  [1b] + [2]  ->  merge: 1b <= 2? Yes ->  [1b, 2]

final merge:  L = [1a, 3],  R = [1b, 2]
  1a <= 1b ?  EQUAL -> `<=` True  ->  1a pehle  ->  [1a]
  3  <= 1b ?  No                  ->  1b        ->  [1a, 1b]   ORDER BACHA ✓
  3  <= 2  ?  No                  ->  2         ->  [1a, 1b, 2]
  L drain                         ->  3         ->  [1a, 1b, 2, 3]

Agar line 10 mein `<` hota:
  1a < 1b ?  EQUAL -> False  ->  else branch  ->  1b pehle  ->  [1b, ...]
  Result: [1b, 1a, 2, 3]  ->  UNSTABLE

docs.title: Kab use karna hai / kab nahi
docs.text:
Use karo jab: - Guaranteed O(n log n) chahiye. Real-time systems, SLA-bound services jahan worst case matter karta hai. Quicksort ka O(n²) risk acceptable nahi. - Stability chahiye. Multi-key sorting, records, objects. - Linked lists sort karni hain. Merge sort linked list ke liye best algorithm hai — O(1) extra space (sirf pointer manipulation), aur random access ki zaroorat nahi. Quicksort linked list par bekaar hai kyunki partitioning ko random access chahiye. - External sorting — data RAM mein nahi samaata. Merge sort natural fit hai: chunks sort karo, disk par likho, phir k-way merge. - Parallel / distributed sorting — dono halves poori tarah independent hain, alag threads ya machines par chal sakte hain.

Mat use karo jab: - Memory tight hai. O(n) buffer chahiye. In-place merge sort exist karta hai par uske constants itne kharab hain ki wo bekar hai. - Chhota array (n < 32). Insertion sort tez hai — recursion overhead merge sort ko maar deta hai. Isiliye production implementations chhote subarrays par switch karti hain. - Cache-sensitive code aur array bahut bada. Quicksort ka memory access pattern zyada cache-friendly hai (partitioning ek hi array par hoti hai), isliye quicksort practically merge sort se ~2x tez hota hai same asymptotic class hote hue bhi.

docs.title: Kitne tareeke se optimize
docs.text:
# Optimisation Kya deta hai Kya leta hai 1 Chhote subarrays par insertion sort (cutoff ~16-32) 10-15% speedup — recursion overhead khatam Ek if aur insertion sort ka code 2 arr[mid] <= arr[mid+1] check Already-sorted ranges par merge skip. Nearly-sorted data par bada fayda Ek comparison per merge — free 3 Ek hi buffer reuse karo (allocate mat karo har call par) 2-3x speedup, allocator pressure khatam Ek extra parameter pass karna 4 Buffer aur array ke roles alternate karo (ping-pong) Har merge par copy-back bach jata hai, ~20% Code complicated, aakhir mein result kis array mein hai wo track karna padta hai 5 Bottom-up (iterative) merge sort Recursion khatam, stack overflow ka risk nahi Code thoda kam readable, arr[mid] <= arr[mid+1] optimisation lagana mushkil 6 Natural merge sort — pehle se sorted "runs" detect karo Nearly-sorted data par O(n) Run detection ka overhead 7 Timsort — natural runs + galloping + insertion sort + merge invariants Real data par sabse tez stable sort Bahut complicated (CPython mein ~2000 lines C) 8 Parallel merge sort Multi-core par ~linear speedup Thread overhead; chhote arrays par ulta dheema

Bottom-up (iterative) version — recursion ke bina:

def merge_sort_bottom_up(arr):
    """Iterative merge sort. Koi recursion nahi, koi stack risk nahi."""
    n = len(arr)                                        # 1
    buffer = [0] * n                                    # 2
    width = 1                                           # 3
    while width < n:                                    # 4
        for low in range(0, n, 2 * width):              # 5
            mid = min(low + width - 1, n - 1)           # 6
            high = min(low + 2 * width - 1, n - 1)      # 7
            if mid < high:                              # 8
                _merge(arr, buffer, low, mid, high)     # 9
        width *= 2                                      # 10
    return arr                                          # 11
  1. Length.
  2. Ek hi buffer, poore algorithm ke liye.
  3. width = 1 — shuruaat mein hum size-1 ke subarrays ko merge karte hain (jo already sorted hain). Ye recursion ke "bottom" se shuru karne jaisa hai.
  4. while width < n — jab tak ek hi subarray poore array ko cover na kar le. < n hai <= n nahi — agar width >= n ho gaya to poora array ek hi sorted block hai, kaam khatam. <= likhne se ek fizool iteration chalti.
  5. for low in range(0, n, 2 * width) — array par 2*width ke jumps mein chalo. Har jump ek jodi ko cover karta hai: [low, low+width-1] aur [low+width, low+2*width-1]. Step 2*width hai width nahi — kyunki hum jodiyaan merge kar rahe hain, ek-ek nahi.
  6. mid = min(low + width - 1, n - 1) — pehle block ka end. min ke saath clamp kyunki array ki length 2*width ka multiple nahi ho sakti — aakhri jodi adhoori ho sakti hai. Bina min ke _merge mein out-of-range indices aate.
  7. high = min(low + 2*width - 1, n - 1) — doosre block ka end, wahi clamping.
  8. if mid < high — agar mid == high, iska matlab doosra block khali hai (aakhri adhoori jodi mein sirf pehla block hai). Us case mein merge karne ko kuchh nahi. <= likhte to mid == high par bhi merge call hoti jo galat range de kar bug create karti (ya no-op karti, implementation par depend).
  9. Merge — wahi function jo upar likha tha.
  10. width *= 2 — agla level: 1, 2, 4, 8, 16... Ye exactly recursion tree ke levels hain, bas neeche se upar.
  11. Return.

Bottom-up ka trace — [5, 2, 4, 6, 1, 3], n = 6:

width Jodiyaan merge hui Array baad mein 1 [5]+[2], [4]+[6], [1]+[3] [2,5, 4,6, 1,3] 2 [2,5]+[4,6], [1,3]+[] (skip) [2,4,5,6, 1,3] 4 [2,4,5,6]+[1,3] [1,2,3,4,5,6]

3 levels = ceil(log2(6)) = 3. ✓

Interview answer: Merge sort is the classic divide and conquer sort. Split the array at the midpoint, recursively sort both halves, then merge the two sorted halves in linear time. The merge is the interesting part: because both inputs are sorted, comparing only their front elements is enough to decide which element is globally next, so merging n elements costs O(n) comparisons, not O(n²).

The recurrence is T(n) = 2T(n/2) + O(n). Drawing the recursion tree, each level does a total of O(n) work — the subproblems at any level partition the whole array — and the depth is log2(n) because the size halves each level. So the total is O(n log n), and critically that's the same in the best, average and worst case, because the split point never depends on the data.

It's stable, provided the merge uses left[i] <= right[j] — on a tie it must take from the left half, which came earlier in the original array. Changing that to a strict < silently makes the sort unstable. It is not in-place: it needs O(n) auxiliary space, plus O(log n) for the recursion stack.

Where it really wins is linked lists — merging is pure pointer manipulation, so you get O(n log n) with only O(log n) stack and no random access — and external sorting, where the data doesn't fit in memory: sort chunks, spill them to disk, then do a k-way merge.

Cross-question: "Quicksort and merge sort are both O(n log n) on average, but quicksort is usually faster in practice. Why?"

Two reasons. Memory: quicksort partitions in place, so it touches one array with a sequential access pattern that's very cache friendly, while merge sort constantly copies between the array and an auxiliary buffer, doubling memory traffic. And constant factors: quicksort's inner loop is a comparison plus a pointer increment, which is tighter than merge sort's inner loop with its bounds checks and copies. Merge sort wins when you need the worst-case guarantee, stability, or you're sorting a linked list.

Cross-question: "What's the actual space complexity of merge sort? I've seen O(n), O(n log n) and O(log n) quoted."

All three appear, and it depends on the implementation. A naive version that slices new lists at every recursive call allocates O(n log n) in total, though the live peak is closer to O(n). A proper implementation allocates a single O(n) buffer once and reuses it, plus O(log n) for the recursion stack — so O(n). And for linked lists you need no buffer at all, just pointer rewiring, so it's O(log n) for the stack alone. The answer I'd give unqualified is O(n) auxiliary space for arrays.

Cross-question: "How would you sort a 100 GB file on a machine with 8 GB of RAM?"

External merge sort. Read the file in chunks that fit in memory — say 4 GB — sort each chunk with an in-memory sort, and write each sorted chunk back to disk as a run. That gives you 25 sorted runs. Then do a k-way merge: open all 25 runs, keep a min-heap of their current heads, repeatedly pop the smallest and write it to the output while pulling the next element from that run. The heap makes each output element cost O(log k). Total I/O is 2 passes over the data, which is close to optimal.

docs.title: Kya hai
docs.text:
Wahi merge sort, par array ki jagah singly linked list par — aur yahan ye array wale version se behtar ho jata hai, kyunki merging ke liye koi extra array nahi chahiye, sirf pointers rewire karne hote hain.

Real-world analogy: Train ke dabbe (coaches). Aap unhe reorder karna chahte ho. Array wale case mein aapko har dabbe ka saamaan doosre dabbe mein shift karna padta (copy). Linked list mein aap sirf couplings (jodne wale hook) badal dete ho — dabbe wahin khade rehte hain, bas order badal jata hai. Isliye O(1) extra space.

docs.title: Kyu hai
docs.text:
Linked list par baaki sorts kyun fail karte hain:

Algorithm Linked list par problem Quick sort Partitioning ko arr[i], arr[j] random access chahiye. Linked list par arr[i] O(i) hai → poora algorithm O(n²) Heap sort Heap ko parent/child index arithmetic (2i+1) chahiye — linked list par O(n) per access Shell sort Gap-h par arr[j - gap] chahiye — O(gap) traversal Insertion sort Chalta hai, par O(n²) Merge sort ✓ Sirf sequential access chahiye. Merge ke liye do heads dekhne hain, bas

Merge sort sirf aage ki taraf chalta hai — wahi ek cheez linked list de sakti hai. Isliye ye linked list ke liye canonical sort hai. Java ka Collections.sort LinkedList par merge sort hi karta hai (haalanki wo pehle array mein copy karta hai).

Doosra fayda: array version O(n) buffer maangta tha. Linked list version mein merge ka output wahi nodes hain jo input mein the — bas next pointers badle. O(1) extra space (plus O(log n) recursion stack).

docs.title: Kaise kaam karta hai
docs.text:
Teen kadam:

1. SPLIT: list ko beech se do halves mein todo
   -> Middle dhoondhne ke liye "slow/fast pointer" (tortoise and hare)

   slow ek kadam, fast do kadam:
   1 -> 2 -> 3 -> 4 -> 5 -> None
   s    
   f    

   1 -> 2 -> 3 -> 4 -> 5 -> None
        s         
             f    

   1 -> 2 -> 3 -> 4 -> 5 -> None
             s              
                       f    (f.next is None -> ruko)

   slow = 3 -> ye middle hai

2. RECURSE: dono halves ko sort karo

3. MERGE: do sorted lists ko pointers rewire karke jodo

Split ke liye slow/fast trick kyun? Kyunki linked list ki length pata karne ke liye ek poora traversal (O(n)) lagega, phir n/2 tak jaane ke liye aur O(n/2). Slow/fast ek hi traversal mein kaam kar deta hai. Dono ka asymptotic same hai (O(n)), par slow/fast idiom interviews mein bahut common hai aur isko jaanana zaroori hai.

Ek critical detail: split karte waqt pehle half ka last node ka next None set karna padta hai, warna dono halves ek doosre se jude rehte hain aur infinite recursion ho jati hai.

docs.title: Poora dry run
docs.text:
Input list: 4 -> 2 -> 1 -> 3 -> None

Call 1: sort(4->2->1->3)

Split — slow/fast:

Step prev slow fast fast.next init None 4 4 2 1 4 2 1 3 2 2 1 None — (loop ruk gaya, fast is None)

prev = 2, to prev.next = None → left = 4 -> 2 -> None, right = 1 -> 3 -> None.

Call 2: sort(4->2)

Split: init prev=None, slow=4, fast=4. fast.next = 2, fast.next.next = None → loop condition fail after one step. prev = 4, slow = 2. prev.next = None → left = 4 -> None, right = 2 -> None.

  • sort(4) → base case (single node) → 4
  • sort(2) → base case → 2
  • merge(4, 2):
Step L R L.val <= R.val? Chuna Output so far 1 4 2 4 <= 2? No R (2) 2 2 4 None R khatam attach L 2 -> 4

Result: 2 -> 4 -> None

Call 3: sort(1->3)

Split → left = 1, right = 3. Merge:

Step L R L.val <= R.val? Chuna Output 1 1 3 1 <= 3? Yes L (1) 1 2 None 3 L khatam attach R 1 -> 3

Result: 1 -> 3 -> None

Back in Call 1: merge(2->4, 1->3)

Step L R L.val <= R.val? Chuna Output so far 1 2 1 2 <= 1? No R (1) 1 2 2 3 2 <= 3? Yes L (2) 1 -> 2 3 4 3 4 <= 3? No R (3) 1 -> 2 -> 3 4 4 None R khatam attach L 1 -> 2 -> 3 -> 4

Final: 1 -> 2 -> 3 -> 4 -> None ✓

docs.title: Code
docs.text:
class ListNode:
    def __init__(self, val=0, nxt=None):          # 1
        self.val = val                            # 2
        self.next = nxt                           # 3


def sort_list(head):
    """Singly linked list ko merge sort se sort karta hai. O(1) extra space (stack chhod kar)."""
    if head is None or head.next is None:         # 4
        return head                               # 5

    prev, slow, fast = None, head, head           # 6
    while fast is not None and fast.next is not None:   # 7
        prev = slow                               # 8
        slow = slow.next                          # 9
        fast = fast.next.next                     # 10
    prev.next = None                              # 11

    left = sort_list(head)                        # 12
    right = sort_list(slow)                       # 13
    return merge_lists(left, right)               # 14


def merge_lists(a, b):
    """Do sorted linked lists ko jodta hai. Naye nodes nahi banata, sirf rewire karta hai."""
    dummy = ListNode()                            # 15
    tail = dummy                                  # 16
    while a is not None and b is not None:        # 17
        if a.val <= b.val:                        # 18
            tail.next = a                         # 19
            a = a.next                            # 20
        else:                                     # 21
            tail.next = b                         # 22
            b = b.next                            # 23
        tail = tail.next                          # 24
    tail.next = a if a is not None else b         # 25
    return dummy.next                             # 26

Line-by-line — kya aur kyun:

  1. Constructor. nxt naam rakha hai next nahi — next Python ka builtin function hai (next(iterator)), use parameter naam banane se builtin shadow ho jata hai us scope mein. Attribute ka naam self.next rakhna theek hai kyunki wo alag namespace hai.
  2. Node ki value.

  3. Agle node ka pointer, default None.

  4. if head is None or head.next is None — base case. Do situations:

  5. head is None — khali list.

  6. head.next is None — ek hi node, already sorted. or ka order matter karta hai: head is None pehle check hona chahiye, warna head.next par AttributeError aayega jab head None ho. Python ka or short-circuit karta hai, isliye ye safe hai. Ulta likhne se crash. Aur is None use kiya hai, == None nahi — is identity check hai (tez aur correct); == custom __eq__ call kar sakta hai.

  7. Return.

  8. prev, slow, fast = None, head, head — teen pointers ek line mein.

  9. slow middle dhoondhega.
  10. fast do guna speed se chalega.

  11. prev sabse important hai — ye slow se ek peeche rehta hai, taaki hum list ko prev aur slow ke beech kaat sakein. Bina prev ke aap slow par pahunch to jaoge par pehle half ko terminate nahi kar paoge. Dono slow aur fast head se shuru — agar fast = head.next se shuru karte to middle ki definition badal jati (thoda left ki taraf), jo 2-node list par infinite recursion de sakti hai. Ye ek asli trap hai; neeche detail.

  12. while fast is not None and fast.next is not None — do checks:

  13. fast is not None — odd-length list mein fast exactly None par pahunchta hai.

  14. fast.next is not None — even-length list mein fast last node par ruk jata hai, aur fast.next.next par AttributeError aata. Dono chahiye, aur is order mein — fast.next check karne se pehle fast ka None na hona confirm karna zaroori hai.

  15. prev = slow — slow aage badhne se pehle uski current position bacha lo.

  16. slow = slow.next — ek kadam.

  17. fast = fast.next.next — do kadam. Jab fast end par pahunchega, slow exactly beech mein hoga (kyunki wo aadhi speed se chala).

  18. prev.next = None — list ko do hisson mein kaato. Ye line sabse critical hai. Iske bina left list right ke through poori original list ko point karti rahegi, aur sort_list(head) wahi list dobara sort karne ki koshish karega — infinite recursion, RecursionError. Ye linked-list merge sort ka #1 bug hai. prev guaranteed non-None hai kyunki line 4 ne 0 aur 1 node ke cases pehle hi return kar diye, to list mein kam se kam 2 nodes hain aur loop kam se kam ek baar chala.

  19. left = sort_list(head) — pehla half. head abhi bhi pehle node ko point karta hai, aur ab uski chain prev par khatam ho jati hai (line 11 ki wajah se).

  20. right = sort_list(slow) — doosra half slow se shuru hota hai.

  21. Merge.

  22. dummy = ListNode() — dummy / sentinel node. Ye ek khali node hai jo asli list ka hissa nahi banega. Iska poora maqsad: "pehla node kaun hai" wala special case hatana. Bina dummy ke aapko har append par check karna padta: "kya ye pehla node hai? agar haan to head = node, warna tail.next = node". Dummy ke saath ye branch khatam ho jati hai — hum hamesha tail.next likhte hain. Ye idiom linked list ke har problem mein kaam aata hai.

  23. tail = dummy — tail hamesha output list ka aakhri node hai. Shuruaat mein wo dummy hai.

  24. while a is not None and b is not None — dono lists mein nodes bache hon. and hai or nahi — or hone se ek list khatam hone par bhi loop chalta aur a.val par AttributeError.

  25. if a.val <= b.val — <= — stability. Tie par a (jo original mein pehle tha) chuna jata hai. < likhne se unstable.

  26. tail.next = a — output list ke end mein a ko jod diya. Dhyaan do: naya node nahi banaya, wahi node reuse kiya. Yahi O(1) space ka raaz hai. Agar aap ListNode(a.val) likh kar naya node banate, to space O(n) ho jata aur koi fayda nahi.

  27. a = a.next — a ko aage. Note: a.next abhi bhi purani chain ko point karta hai, par hum us par kabhi wapas nahi jayenge — agli iteration mein tail.next use overwrite kar dega ya line 25 ka drain use sahi jagah jod dega.

21-23. Warna b wala.

  1. tail = tail.next — tail ko naye aakhri node par le jao. if/else ke bahar kyunki dono cases mein karna hai.

  2. tail.next = a if a is not None else b — drain. Ek list khatam ho chuki hai, doosri mein nodes bache ho sakte hain. Kyunki bachi hui list already sorted hai aur uske saare elements output ke last element se bade hain, hum poori bachi hui chain ko ek hi pointer assignment se jod sakte hain — element by element copy karne ki zaroorat nahi. Ye array version se behtar hai, jahan extend O(k) copies karta tha; yahan ye O(1) hai. Agar dono None hain to tail.next = None set hota hai — jo bilkul sahi hai (list terminate honi chahiye).

  3. return dummy.next — dummy nahi, dummy.next. dummy ek fake node hai; asli list uske baad shuru hoti hai. dummy return karne se output mein ek extra garbage node aa jayega — classic bug.

Do-node list par infinite recursion ka trap (line 6 ki wajah):

List: 1 -> 2 -> None

Agar humne  slow = head, fast = head  kiya (jo humne kiya):
  init:  prev=None, slow=1, fast=1
  loop check: fast(1) not None ✓, fast.next(2) not None ✓ -> chalo
    prev = 1
    slow = 2
    fast = fast.next.next = None
  loop check: fast is None -> ruko
  prev.next = None  ->  left = [1], right = [2]     ✓ SAHI

Agar humne  slow = head, fast = head.next  kiya:
  init:  prev=None, slow=1, fast=2
  loop check: fast(2) not None ✓, fast.next(None) is None -> RUKO turant
    prev abhi bhi None hai!
  prev.next = None  ->  AttributeError: 'NoneType' object has no attribute 'next'

Isliye fast = head se shuru karna zaroori hai is particular implementation mein.

docs.title: Complexity derive karke
docs.text:
T(n) = 2*T(n/2)  +  O(n)
                    ^^^^
       split (O(n) slow/fast traversal) + merge (O(n) pointer rewiring)

Same recurrence as array merge sort  ->  O(n log n)

Split ka cost O(n) hai — array version mein split O(1) tha (bas mid calculate karo, slicing ko chhod kar). Linked list par middle dhoondhne ke liye traverse karna padta hai. Par ye recurrence ko badalta nahi kyunki merge bhi O(n) hai — dono mil kar O(n) per level.

Space:

Merge ka extra space:  O(1)  <- sirf dummy, tail, a, b pointers
Recursion stack depth: O(log n)  <- balanced split ki wajah se

Total auxiliary: O(log n)

Compare karo array version se, jahan O(n) buffer chahiye tha. Linked list version asymptotically kam memory leta hai.

Case Time Space Best Theta(n log n) O(log n) Average Theta(n log n) O(log n) Worst Theta(n log n) O(log n)

Bottom-up version se O(1) space: Agar recursion hi hata do (bottom-up iterative merge), to space poora O(1) ho jata hai. Ye LeetCode "Sort List" ka follow-up hai: "sort in O(n log n) time and O(1) space".

docs.title: Stability, in-place, adaptive
docs.text: Property Value Kyun Stable Haan a.val <= b.val — tie par left/pehla wala In-place Haan (linked list ke context mein) Koi naya node nahi banta, sirf pointers badalte hain. O(log n) stack Adaptive Nahi Har haal mein same splits aur merges

docs.title: Kab use karna hai / kab nahi
docs.text:
Use karo jab: - Aapke paas linked list hai aur usse sort karna hai. Ye best available option hai. - Interview mein "Sort a linked list in O(n log n) time" poochha jaye — ye standard answer hai. - Data structure ko convert nahi kar sakte (jaise memory-constrained embedded list).

Mat use karo jab: - Aapke paas array hai — array par quicksort/Timsort cache locality ki wajah se kaafi tez hain. - List chhoti hai (< 50 nodes) — insertion sort simpler aur practically tez hai. - Aap list ko array mein copy kar sakte ho aur wapas — ye kabhi kabhi practically tez hota hai (O(n) copy + fast array sort), haalanki O(n) extra space leta hai.

docs.title: Kitne tareeke se optimize
docs.text:
# Optimisation Kya deta hai Kya leta hai 1 Bottom-up iterative Space O(log n) → O(1), koi stack overflow risk nahi Code kaafi lamba (list ko manually chunks mein kaatna padta hai) 2 Length ek baar calculate karo, phir split ke liye counting use karo Har call mein slow/fast traversal ki jagah simple counter Ek extra parameter, mamooli fayda 3 Chhoti lists par insertion sort (< 8 nodes) Recursion overhead bachta Cutoff tune karna padta hai 4 Natural runs detect karo Nearly-sorted lists par O(n) Extra pass 5 List ko array mein copy karo, array sort karo, wapas likho Practically tez (cache locality) O(n) space — asli fayda khatam 6 Doubly linked list — prev pointer se split O(1) mein Split sasta Extra memory per node

Interview answer: Merge sort is the natural algorithm for linked lists, and it's actually better there than on arrays. There are three steps: find the middle with the slow/fast pointer technique, cut the list in two, recursively sort both halves, then merge by rewiring next pointers. Merging allocates nothing — it reuses the existing nodes — so the extra space is just O(log n) for the recursion stack, versus O(n) for the array version.

The two details that make or break it: first, after finding the middle you must set the previous node's next to None, otherwise the first half still runs through the whole original list and you get infinite recursion. Second, use a dummy head node in the merge so you don't need a special case for "is this the first node" on every append — you always write to tail.next.

Quicksort is a poor fit for linked lists because partitioning wants random access, and heapsort needs index arithmetic for parent and child positions. Merge sort only needs sequential forward traversal, which is exactly what a singly linked list gives you. That's why Java's Collections.sort and most standard library list sorts are merge-based.

Cross-question: "Can you do it in O(1) space?"

Yes, with a bottom-up iterative version. Instead of recursing, you make passes with a run width that doubles each pass — 1, 2, 4, 8 — splitting off runs of that width from the front of the list, merging pairs of them, and appending to an output list. No recursion, so no stack, and merging is still pure pointer rewiring. It's noticeably more code because you have to manually detach runs of a given length, but it's the standard answer to that follow-up.

Cross-question: "Why does the slow/fast split start both pointers at head rather than fast at head.next?"

Because we also need the node before slow so we can cut the list. If fast starts at head.next, then on a two-node list the loop exits immediately with prev still None, and prev.next = None throws AttributeError. Starting both at head guarantees at least one loop iteration whenever the list has two or more nodes, which the base case has already ensured.

docs.title: Kya hai
docs.text:
Quick sort ek pivot element chunta hai, array ko is tarah rearrange karta hai ki pivot se chhote sab left mein aur bade sab right mein aa jayen (partition), aur phir dono sides ko recursively sort karta hai.

Real-world analogy: Ek badi class ke 100 students ko roll number order mein khada karna hai. Aap kehte ho: "Jinka roll number 50 se kam hai wo is taraf, baaki us taraf." Ek hi kadam mein class do groups mein bant gayi, aur ab 50 khud apni sahi jagah par hai — uske left mein 49 log hain, right mein 50. Ab har group ke andar wahi tareeka dohrao. Dhyaan do ki aapne kabhi "poore group ko sort" nahi kiya — aapne bas baant diya, aur baantne se hi sorting apne aap ho gayi.

Merge sort se ulta: Merge sort mein todna aasan tha (bas beech se) aur jodna mehnat (merge). Quick sort mein todna mehnat hai (partition) aur jodna free hai — kyunki partition ke baad left, pivot, right pehle se sahi order mein hain, unhe jodne ke liye kuchh karna hi nahi.

docs.title: Kyu hai
docs.text:
Merge sort ne guaranteed O(n log n) de diya tha. To quicksort kyun?

Do wajah:

1. Memory. Merge sort ko O(n) auxiliary buffer chahiye. Quick sort in-place partition karta hai — sirf O(log n) recursion stack. Jab aap 8 GB array sort kar rahe ho aur RAM 10 GB hai, ye farak zindagi aur maut ka hai.

2. Speed — constant factors. Dono O(n log n) hain, par quicksort practically 2-3x tez hota hai. Kyun?

Merge sort ka inner loop:
    - buffer se padho
    - array mein likho
    - do bounds check
    - do pointers manage karo
    => har element par ~2 memory operations (ek read + ek write) alag alag arrays mein

Quick sort ka inner loop (Lomuto):
    - array se padho
    - ek comparison
    - kabhi kabhi swap
    => ek hi array par sequential access -> CPU cache mein sab kuchh

CPU cache line 64 bytes ki hoti hai. Quicksort ek hi array par aage-peeche chalta hai, to prefetcher use predict kar leta hai. Merge sort do arrays ke beech kood-ta hai, to cache misses zyada hote hain. Yahi wajah hai ki C ka qsort, C++ ka std::sort, Java ka primitive-array sort — sab quicksort family se hain.

Quicksort ki kharabi: Agar pivot hamesha kharab chuna jaye (jaise hamesha sabse chhota element), to partition balanced nahi hota aur recursion depth n ho jati hai → O(n²). Aur ye sirf theoretical nahi — already-sorted array par naive quicksort exactly yahi karta hai, jo ki real world mein bahut common input hai. Isi problem ke solutions (randomisation, median-of-three, introsort) is section ka bada hissa hain.

docs.title: Kaise kaam karta hai — Lomuto partition
docs.text:
Idea: array ko chaar zones mein rakho jab tak scan chal raha hai:

   [ <= pivot | > pivot | abhi nahi dekha | pivot ]
              ^         ^                 ^
              i+1       j                 high

   i  = "chhote wale zone" ka aakhri index
   j  = current scanner
   pivot = arr[high] (last element)

Har step par:
   agar arr[j] <= pivot:  i++ ; swap(arr[i], arr[j])   <- element ko chhote zone mein daalo
   j++

Scan khatam hone par:
   swap(arr[i+1], arr[high])   <- pivot ko apni sahi jagah par
   return i+1                   <- pivot ka final index

ASCII trace of the invariant:

Shuru mein:  i = low - 1,  j = low

  low                              high
   |                                |
  [ ? ? ? ? ? ? ? ? ? ? ? ? ? ? ? | P ]
  ^
  j
 (i yahan se ek peeche, "khali zone")

Beech mein:

  [ <=P <=P <=P | >P >P >P >P | ? ? ? ? | P ]
                ^              ^
                i              j

Ant mein (j == high):

  [ <=P <=P <=P | >P >P >P >P >P >P | P ]
                ^                     ^
                i                     high

  swap(arr[i+1], arr[high]):

  [ <=P <=P <=P | P | >P >P >P >P >P ]
                  ^
                  i+1 = pivot ki final jagah, PAKKI

Sabse important insight: partition ke baad pivot apni final position par hai — wo kabhi dobara nahi hilega. Isliye recursion mein use include nahi karte: qs(low, p-1) aur qs(p+1, high). Agar aap p ko include kar dete (qs(low, p)), to subproblem chhota nahi hota aur infinite recursion ho sakti hai.

docs.title: Poora dry run
docs.text:
Input: [10, 80, 30, 90, 40, 50, 70], low = 0, high = 6.

Partition call 1 — pivot = arr[6] = 70, i = -1:

j arr[j] arr[j] <= 70? i (naya) Swap Array 0 10 Yes 0 arr[0]↔arr[0] (self) [10,80,30,90,40,50,70] 1 80 No 0 — [10,80,30,90,40,50,70] 2 30 Yes 1 arr[1]↔arr[2] [10,30,80,90,40,50,70] 3 90 No 1 — [10,30,80,90,40,50,70] 4 40 Yes 2 arr[2]↔arr[4] [10,30,40,90,80,50,70] 5 50 Yes 3 arr[3]↔arr[5] [10,30,40,50,80,90,70]

Loop khatam (j high tak nahi jata). Ab final swap: arr[i+1] ↔ arr[high] = arr[4] ↔ arr[6]:

[10, 30, 40, 50, **70**, 90, 80] — pivot index 4 return hua.

Verify: index 4 se pehle [10,30,40,50] sab <= 70 ✓. Index 4 ke baad [90,80] sab > 70 ✓.

Recursion: qs(0, 3) aur qs(5, 6).

Partition call 2 — qs(0, 3) par [10, 30, 40, 50], pivot = arr[3] = 50, i = -1:

j arr[j] <= 50? i Swap Array (0..3 hissa) 0 10 Yes 0 self [10,30,40,50] 1 30 Yes 1 self [10,30,40,50] 2 40 Yes 2 self [10,30,40,50]

Final swap: arr[3] ↔ arr[3] — self. Pivot index 3.

Dhyaan do: ye WORST CASE partition hai — pivot sabse bada nikla, to left mein 3 elements aur right mein 0. Aisa isliye hua kyunki ye sub-array already sorted hai aur hum last element ko pivot chunte hain. Yahi naive quicksort ki bimari hai.

Recursion: qs(0, 2) aur qs(4, 3) (khali, turant return).

Partition call 3 — qs(0, 2) par [10, 30, 40], pivot = 40:

j arr[j] <= 40? i Array 0 10 Yes 0 [10,30,40] 1 30 Yes 1 [10,30,40]

Pivot index 2. Recursion: qs(0,1), qs(3,2) (khali).

Partition call 4 — qs(0, 1) par [10, 30], pivot = 30:

j arr[j] <= 30? i Array 0 10 Yes 0 [10,30]

Pivot index 1. Recursion: qs(0,0) (single, return), qs(2,1) (khali, return).

Partition call 5 — qs(5, 6) par [90, 80], pivot = arr[6] = 80, i = 4:

j arr[j] <= 80? i Swap Array (5..6) 5 90 No 4 — [90,80]

Final swap: arr[i+1] ↔ arr[high] = arr[5] ↔ arr[6] → [80, 90]. Pivot index 5.

Recursion: qs(5,4) (khali), qs(6,6) (single).

Final array: [10, 30, 40, 50, 70, 80, 90] ✓

Recursion tree — ye complexity samajhne ke liye:

                  qs(0,6)  n=7, pivot=70 at idx 4
                 /                        \
        qs(0,3) n=4                     qs(5,6) n=2
        pivot=50 at idx 3               pivot=80 at idx 5
        /            \                  /          \
   qs(0,2) n=3    qs(4,3) empty    qs(5,4) empty  qs(6,6) n=1
   pivot=40 idx 2
   /        \
qs(0,1) n=2  qs(3,2) empty
pivot=30 idx 1
 /      \
qs(0,0) qs(2,1)
 n=1    empty

Depth = 4 for n = 7.  log2(7) ~ 2.8, so we're deeper than ideal
kyunki left side ke saare partitions unbalanced the.

docs.title: Code
docs.text:
import random                                       # 1


def quick_sort(arr, low=0, high=None):
    """Lomuto partition ke saath quick sort. In-place."""
    if high is None:                                # 2
        high = len(arr) - 1                         # 3
    if low < high:                                  # 4
        p = lomuto_partition(arr, low, high)        # 5
        quick_sort(arr, low, p - 1)                 # 6
        quick_sort(arr, p + 1, high)                # 7
    return arr                                      # 8


def lomuto_partition(arr, low, high):
    """arr[low..high] ko pivot ke around partition karta hai. Pivot ka final index return karta hai."""
    r = random.randint(low, high)                   # 9
    arr[r], arr[high] = arr[high], arr[r]           # 10
    pivot = arr[high]                               # 11
    i = low - 1                                     # 12
    for j in range(low, high):                      # 13
        if arr[j] <= pivot:                         # 14
            i += 1                                  # 15
            arr[i], arr[j] = arr[j], arr[i]         # 16
    arr[i + 1], arr[high] = arr[high], arr[i + 1]   # 17
    return i + 1                                    # 18

Line-by-line — kya aur kyun:

  1. import random — pivot randomisation ke liye. Ye O(n²) worst case se bachne ka sabse practical tareeka hai.

  2. if high is None — default argument trick, taaki caller sirf quick_sort(arr) likh sake. high=None default rakha hai, high=len(arr)-1 nahi — kyunki Python ke default arguments function define hone ke waqt ek baar evaluate hote hain, aur us waqt arr exist hi nahi karta. def f(arr, high=len(arr)-1) NameError dega. Ye Python ka important rule hai.

  3. high = len(arr) - 1 — last valid index. len(arr) nahi — high inclusive hai is code ke convention mein.

  4. if low < high — base case ka ulta. Agar low >= high to range mein 0 ya 1 element hai — already sorted, kuchh nahi karna. < hai <= nahi: agar <= likh dete to low == high (single element) par bhi partition call hoti; lomuto_partition(arr, 5, 5) chalta, range(5,5) khali, final swap self-swap, return 5, phir quick_sort(arr, 5, 4) aur quick_sort(arr, 6, 5) — dono base case hit karte. Yaani galat nahi, bas fizool calls. Par if True (koi check hi nahi) likhne se infinite recursion.

  5. p = lomuto_partition(...) — partition karo, pivot ka final index lo.

  6. quick_sort(arr, low, p - 1) — left side, pivot ko chhod kar. p - 1 hai p nahi. Ye sabse critical line hai. Agar aap quick_sort(arr, low, p) likh dete to:

  7. Pivot dobara subproblem mein aa jata.
  8. Agar pivot sabse chhota tha (p == low), to subproblem (low, low) hota — theek hai.

  9. Par agar p == high (pivot sabse bada), to quick_sort(arr, low, high) = same call → infinite recursion, stack overflow. Pivot ka final position par hona hi wo guarantee hai jo subproblem ko strictly chhota banati hai.

  10. quick_sort(arr, p + 1, high) — right side, pivot ko chhod kar. Wahi logic.

  11. Return.

  12. r = random.randint(low, high) — random pivot chuno. randint dono ends inclusive deta hai (randrange exclusive deta hai — dhyaan rakhna). Kyun? Kyunki fixed pivot (jaise hamesha arr[high]) par ek adversary aisa input bana sakta hai jo hamesha worst case hit kare. Sorted array par last-element pivot hamesha sabse bada nikalta hai → har partition mein ek taraf 0 elements → depth n → O(n²). Randomisation ke saath koi bhi fixed input worst case guarantee nahi kar sakta — worst case ki probability n! ke inverse jaisi ho jati hai. Expected time O(n log n) har input par. Ye "expected" hai "guaranteed" nahi — theoretically worst case abhi bhi O(n²) hai, par uski probability itni kam hai ki practically nahi hota.

  13. arr[r], arr[high] = arr[high], arr[r] — random pivot ko high par le aao. Ye chhota sa step is liye hai ki baaki ka algorithm bilkul waise hi chal sake jaise wo last element ko pivot maan kar likha gaya tha. Agar aap ye swap na karte aur direct pivot = arr[r] likhte, to partition logic mein r ko special-case karna padta — bahut zyada complexity. Ek swap se poori problem gayab.

  14. pivot = arr[high] — pivot ki value copy kar li. Value copy karna zaroori hai kyunki line 16 ke swaps arr[high] ko badal sakte hain... actually nahi, j kabhi high tak nahi jata (line 13 range(low, high) hai). Par phir bhi value copy karna clearer hai aur har comparison mein array access bachata hai.

  15. i = low - 1 — low - 1, low nahi. i "chhote-zone ka aakhri index" hai. Shuru mein chhota zone khali hai, to i low se ek peeche hona chahiye. Agar i = low likh dete, to pehla element bina check kiye chhote zone ka hissa maan liya jata, aur line 15 ka i += 1 ek extra jagah aage kar deta → galat answer aur kabhi kabhi IndexError. Ye ek classic off-by-one hai.

  16. for j in range(low, high) — low se high - 1 tak. high include nahi kyunki arr[high] pivot hai, use khud se compare karna bekaar hai (aur usse swap karne se logic toot jayega).

  17. if arr[j] <= pivot — <= hai < nahi. Kyun? Socho agar array mein saare elements barabar hain ([5,5,5,5,5]):

    • <= ke saath: har element chhote zone mein jayega → i har baar badhega → pivot end mein high par hi rahega → partition point = high → ek taraf n-1, doosri taraf 0 → O(n²). Bura!
    • < ke saath: koi element chhote zone mein nahi jayega → i low-1 par hi rahega → pivot low par jayega → ek taraf 0, doosri taraf n-1 → bhi O(n²). Bhi bura! Yaani dono choices duplicates par O(n²) deti hain — isliye Lomuto duplicates ke liye kharab hai. Iska asli solution 3-way partitioning hai (alag section). <= conventionally use hota hai. Note: <= ke saath Lomuto unstable hai (neeche).

  18. i += 1 — chhota zone ek badhao. Line 16 se pehle, kyunki i ab wo naya slot hai jahan chhota element rakhna hai.

  19. arr[i], arr[j] = arr[j], arr[i] — chhote element ko chhote zone ke end mein le aao, aur jo wahan tha (jo pakka > pivot tha, ya i == j par khud hi) use j par bhej do. i == j par ye self-swap hai — waste, par harmless. Chaho to if i != j guard laga do; typically fayda kam hai.

  20. arr[i + 1], arr[high] = arr[high], arr[i + 1] — pivot ko apni final jagah par. i + 1 kyun? i chhote zone ka aakhri index hai, to i + 1 pehla index hai jahan > pivot wale elements shuru hote hain. Pivot ko wahin jaana chahiye — uske left mein sab chhote, right mein sab bade. Agar aap arr[i] par swap karte to ek chhota element pivot ke right mein chala jata — galat answer.

  21. return i + 1 — pivot ka final index. Yahi quick_sort mein p banta hai.

docs.title: Complexity derive karke
docs.text:
Best case — pivot hamesha exact median:

T(n) = 2 * T(n/2) + O(n)        <- partition O(n), do halves barabar

Recursion tree:
  Level 0:  n            work = n
  Level 1:  n/2, n/2     work = n
  Level 2:  4 x n/4      work = n
  ...
  Depth = log2(n)

Total = n * log2(n)  ->  O(n log n)

Worst case — pivot hamesha sabse chhota ya sabse bada:

T(n) = T(n-1) + T(0) + O(n)
     = T(n-1) + O(n)

Expand karo:
T(n) = n + T(n-1)
     = n + (n-1) + T(n-2)
     = n + (n-1) + (n-2) + ... + 1
     = n(n+1)/2
     ->  O(n²)

Recursion tree:
  n
  |
  n-1
  |
  n-2
  |
  ...
  |
  1
  Depth = n  ->  STACK OVERFLOW bhi ho sakta hai!

Kab hota hai? Naive (last-element) pivot ke saath: already sorted array, reverse sorted array, ya saare elements barabar. Ye teenon real world mein bahut common hain — yahi naive quicksort ka danger hai.

Average case — ye derivation interview mein bahut impress karti hai:

Random pivot ke saath, pivot equally likely hai kisi bhi rank k (1 se n) ka hona:

T(n) = O(n) + (1/n) * sum over k=1..n of [ T(k-1) + T(n-k) ]

Ise solve karna algebra-heavy hai. Ek intuitive shortcut:

"Achha" pivot wo hai jo array ko 25%-75% se behtar baante.
Kitne pivots achhe hain? Jo middle 50% mein aate hain -> aadhe pivots achhe hain.
Yaani har partition par 50% chance ki hum "achha" split payein.

Achha split ke baad bada hissa <= 0.75n hota hai.
Kitne achhe splits ke baad size 1 par pahunchenge?

  n * (0.75)^d = 1
  d = log(n) / log(4/3)  ~  2.4 * log2(n)

Aur kyunki aadhe pivots achhe hain, expected total levels ~ 2 * 2.4 * log2(n) ~ 4.8 log2(n)

Har level par O(n) kaam  ->  Expected total = O(n log n)  ✓

Ye argument yaad rakho — "half the pivots give at least a 25-75 split, and you only need log base 4/3 of n such splits" — interview mein bahut clean lagta hai.

Precise result: Expected comparisons = 2n ln(n) ~ 1.39 n log2(n). Yaani merge sort se ~39% zyada comparisons, par swaps kam aur cache behtar — net practically tez.

Space:

Auxiliary data:      O(1)  <- in-place partition
Recursion stack:     depth par depend

  Best/average depth: O(log n)
  Worst case depth:   O(n)      <- stack overflow ka risk!

Total space: O(log n) average, O(n) worst

Tail-call optimisation se worst-case stack O(log n) ho sakta hai — chhote side ko recurse karo, bade side par loop karo. Neeche code hai.

Case Time Space (stack) Kab Best Theta(n log n) O(log n) Pivot hamesha median Average Theta(n log n), ~1.39n log n comparisons O(log n) Random data / random pivot Worst Theta(n²) O(n) Sorted input + last-element pivot; ya saare elements equal

docs.title: Stability, in-place, adaptive
docs.text:
Property Value Kyun Stable Nahi Partition mein door ke swaps equal elements ko ek doosre ke aar paar phenk dete hain In-place Haan O(1) auxiliary data. (Stack O(log n) hai, jo "in-place" ki common definition mein allowed hai) Adaptive Nahi — ulta, sorted input par worst case hit hota hai naive pivot ke saath Partition data ki sortedness ka fayda nahi uthata

Instability ka counterexample:

Input: [ 3a, 3b, 1 ],  pivot = arr[high] = 1

i = -1
j=0: arr[0]=3a <= 1 ? No   -> i stays -1
j=1: arr[1]=3b <= 1 ? No   -> i stays -1
final swap: arr[i+1] = arr[0]  <->  arr[high] = arr[2]
   [3a, 3b, 1]  ->  [1, 3b, 3a]
                        ^^  ^^
                        3b ab 3a se pehle -> ORDER TOOTA

Quicksort ko stable banaya ja sakta hai? Haan, par O(n) extra space chahiye (do temporary lists banao, <=pivot aur >pivot, phir jodo) — us case mein aap basically merge sort jaisa memory profile le rahe ho aur quicksort ka main fayda kho rahe ho.

docs.title: Kab use karna hai / kab nahi
docs.text:
Use karo jab: - Arrays sort karni hain aur average-case speed chahiye. C ka qsort, C++ ka std::sort (introsort), Java ka primitive sort — sab quicksort family. - Memory constrained — merge sort ka O(n) buffer afford nahi kar sakte. - Quickselect chahiye — k-th smallest element O(n) average mein. Ye quicksort ka hi partition step hai, sirf ek side par recurse karke.

Mat use karo jab: - Worst-case guarantee chahiye — real-time systems, security-sensitive code (attacker crafted input se DoS ho sakta hai — ye ek asli attack hai, "algorithmic complexity attack"). Merge sort ya heap sort use karo, ya introsort. - Stability chahiye — quicksort de nahi sakta. - Linked list — random access nahi hai. - Bahut saare duplicates — Lomuto/Hoare dono O(n²) ho jate hain. 3-way partition use karo.

docs.title: Kitne tareeke se optimize
docs.text:
# Optimisation Kya deta hai Kya leta hai 1 Random pivot Adversarial input ka danger khatam, expected O(n log n) har input par RNG call per partition (~5% overhead) 2 Median-of-three (first, mid, last ka median) Sorted/reverse-sorted par perfect split, RNG ka overhead nahi Craft kiye gaye "median-of-3 killer" inputs par abhi bhi O(n²) 3 Median-of-medians (BFPRT) Guaranteed O(n log n) Constants itne bade ki practically dheema; theoretical interest 4 Chhote subarrays par insertion sort (cutoff 10-32) 10-20% speedup Ek if 5 Tail recursion elimination — chhote side par recurse, bade par loop Stack O(n) → O(log n) guaranteed 3 lines 6 3-way partition (Dutch flag) Duplicates par O(n²) → O(n) Thoda extra comparison work 7 Hoare partition Lomuto se ~3x kam swaps Pivot final position par nahi hota — recursion boundaries alag 8 Dual-pivot quicksort ~10% kam comparisons; Java 7+ mein default Code kaafi complicated 9 Introsort — quicksort + depth limit, limit paar hone par heapsort Guaranteed O(n log n) + quicksort ki speed. C++ std::sort yahi hai Ek depth counter 10 Parallel quicksort Multi-core speedup Thread overhead

Optimised production-quality version (5, 4, 1 ek saath):

import random                                       # 1

INSERTION_CUTOFF = 16                               # 2


def quick_sort_optimised(arr, low=0, high=None):
    if high is None:                                # 3
        high = len(arr) - 1                         # 4
    while low < high:                               # 5
        if high - low + 1 <= INSERTION_CUTOFF:      # 6
            _insertion_range(arr, low, high)        # 7
            return arr                              # 8
        p = lomuto_partition(arr, low, high)        # 9
        if p - low < high - p:                      # 10
            quick_sort_optimised(arr, low, p - 1)   # 11
            low = p + 1                             # 12
        else:                                       # 13
            quick_sort_optimised(arr, p + 1, high)  # 14
            high = p - 1                            # 15
    return arr                                      # 16


def _insertion_range(arr, low, high):
    for i in range(low + 1, high + 1):              # 17
        key = arr[i]                                # 18
        j = i - 1                                   # 19
        while j >= low and arr[j] > key:            # 20
            arr[j + 1] = arr[j]                     # 21
            j -= 1                                  # 22
        arr[j + 1] = key                            # 23
  1. RNG import.
  2. INSERTION_CUTOFF = 16 — module-level constant. 16 typical hai; 10 se 32 tak sab reasonable. Ye number measure karke chuna jata hai, theory se nahi — ye CPU cache size aur branch predictor par depend karta hai. 3-4. Default high.
  3. while hai if nahi — yahi tail-call elimination ka core hai. if hota to hume dono sides par recurse karna padta. while ke saath, ek side par recurse karte hain aur doosre side ke liye low/high update karke loop dobara chalate hain — bina stack frame use kiye.
  4. if high - low + 1 <= INSERTION_CUTOFF — range ka size. +1 kyunki dono ends inclusive hain (low=0, high=15 mein 16 elements). Agar +1 bhool jao to cutoff effectively 17 ho jayega — bug to nahi, par intent galat.
  5. Chhoti range par insertion sort — recursion overhead se sasta.
  6. return, break nahi — insertion sort ne poori range sort kar di, ab is call mein aur kuchh nahi karna.
  7. Partition.
  8. if p - low < high - p — konsa side chhota hai? p - low = left side ka size, high - p = right side ka size (approx; exact hai p-1 - low + 1 aur high - (p+1) + 1, par comparison ke liye ye kaafi hai).
  9. Chhote side par recurse. Recursion depth chhote side ke size se bandhi hoti hai, aur chhota side hamesha <= n/2 hota hai → depth guaranteed O(log n), chahe pivot kitna bhi kharab ho. Ye stack overflow ka risk poori tarah khatam kar deta hai.
  10. low = p + 1 — bade (right) side ko loop se handle karo, recursion se nahi. 13-15. Ulta case: right chhota hai to right par recurse, left par loop.
  11. Return.
  12. range(low + 1, high + 1) — insertion sort par ek sub-range mein. low + 1 se kyunki arr[low] akela sorted hai. high + 1 kyunki high inclusive hai. 18-23. Standard insertion sort, bas 0 ki jagah low bound. Line 20 mein j >= low hai j >= 0 nahi — critical, warna insertion sort apni range se bahar nikal kar pehle se sorted elements ko kharab kar deta.

Median-of-three partition:

def median_of_three(arr, low, high):
    mid = low + (high - low) // 2                   # 1
    a, b, c = arr[low], arr[mid], arr[high]         # 2
    if a > b:                                       # 3
        a, b = b, a                                 # 4
    if b > c:                                       # 5
        b, c = c, b                                 # 6
    if a > b:                                       # 7
        a, b = b, a                                 # 8
    return b                                        # 9
  1. Middle index, overflow-safe formula.
  2. Teen candidate values. 3-8. Sorting network — teen comparisons se teen values sort. Har if ek "compare and swap" hai. Teesri comparison (line 7) zaroori hai: pehle do comparisons ke baad c sabse bada hai, par a aur b ka order pakka nahi. Agar aap line 7-8 hata dete to [3,1,2] par galat median milta.
  3. b ab median hai.

Median-of-three sorted input par perfect kaam karta hai: [1,2,3,4,5,6,7] par first=1, mid=4, last=7 → median = 4 = exact median. Isliye sorted input ka worst case poori tarah khatam ho jata hai. Par ek adversary "median-of-3 killer" input bana sakta hai — isliye production code (Introsort) depth limit bhi rakhta hai.

Interview answer: Quicksort picks a pivot, partitions the array so everything less than or equal to the pivot is on the left and everything greater is on the right, then recurses on the two sides. The key property is that after partitioning, the pivot is in its final sorted position, so it's excluded from both recursive calls — that's what guarantees the subproblems shrink.

With a good pivot the recurrence is T(n) = 2T(n/2) + O(n), giving O(n log n). With a bad pivot — one that always lands at an extreme — it degenerates to T(n) = T(n-1) + O(n), which is O(n²) and, worse, O(n) recursion depth, so you can blow the stack. Naive last-element pivot hits that worst case on already-sorted input, which is very common in practice.

The fix is randomising the pivot. Then no fixed input can force the worst case; the expected time is O(n log n) for every input. Intuitively, half of all pivots split the array no worse than 25-75, and you only need log base 4/3 of n such splits to reach size one, so the expected depth is a constant multiple of log n.

It's in-place with O(log n) stack, but not stable — partitioning does long-distance swaps that reorder equal elements. In production I'd use introsort: quicksort with a recursion depth limit of about 2·log2(n), falling back to heapsort when the limit is exceeded, plus insertion sort below about 16 elements. That gives you quicksort's speed with a hard O(n log n) guarantee, and it's exactly what C++'s std::sort does.

Cross-question: "Why is quicksort faster than merge sort in practice when both are O(n log n)?"

Cache behaviour and constant factors. Quicksort partitions in place — one array, sequential access in both directions, which the hardware prefetcher handles well. Merge sort copies between the array and an auxiliary buffer, so it does roughly twice the memory traffic and gets more cache misses. Quicksort's inner loop is also tighter: a compare and an index increment, versus merge sort's bounds checks and copies. Merge sort does fewer comparisons — about n log n versus quicksort's 1.39 n log n — but comparisons on primitives are cheap and memory traffic isn't.

Cross-question: "How do you guarantee O(log n) stack depth even in the worst case?"

Recurse into the smaller partition and loop on the larger one. The smaller partition is always at most half the range, so each recursive call at least halves the problem size, which bounds the depth at log2(n) regardless of how unbalanced the partitions are. The larger side is handled by updating low or high and going round the while loop again, which uses no stack frame at all.

Cross-question: "What happens on an array where every element is equal?"

With Lomuto partitioning it's the worst case, O(n²), regardless of whether you use <= or < in the comparison — one of the two sides always ends up empty. Hoare partitioning handles it much better because both pointers stop on equal elements, so it splits near the middle. The proper fix is 3-way partitioning — Dutch national flag — which groups all elements equal to the pivot in the middle and excludes them from both recursive calls, making an all-equal array O(n).

docs.title: Kya hai
docs.text:
Hoare partition (jo C.A.R. Hoare ne 1959 mein original quicksort ke saath likha tha) array ke dono ends se andar ki taraf chalta hai: left pointer bade element ka intezaar karta hai, right pointer chhote ka, aur jab dono ruk jayen to unhe swap kar deta hai.

Real-world analogy: Do teachers ek line ke do sirey se chalte hain. Left wali teacher aage chalti hai jab tak koi "lamba" bachcha na mil jaye. Right wali peeche se chalti hai jab tak koi "chhota" bachcha na mil jaye. Dono ruk jaayen to bas dono bachchon ki jagah badal do — ek hi swap mein do elements sahi taraf pahunch gaye. Lomuto mein har chhota element ek alag swap maangta tha.

docs.title: Kyu hai
docs.text:
Lomuto ki teen kharabiyaan:

1. Bahut zyada swaps. Lomuto har <= pivot element par ek swap karta hai. Random data par ~n/2 swaps per partition. Hoare sirf tab swap karta hai jab dono taraf galat element mile — average ~n/6 swaps. ~3x kam memory writes.

2. Duplicates par bilkul mar jata hai. [5,5,5,5,5] par Lomuto ka partition point hamesha ek extreme par hota hai → O(n²). Hoare mein dono pointers equal elements par ruk jate hain aur swap karte hain, jisse partition beech mein hota hai → O(n log n). Ye bada practical farak hai.

3. Pehle aur aakhri element ke saath asymmetry. Lomuto ka high element special hai.

Hoare ki apni kharabi: pivot apni final position par nahi hota. Ye recursion boundaries ko badal deta hai, aur agar aap Lomuto ki aadat se qs(low, p-1) aur qs(p+1, high) likh dein to infinite recursion ho jati hai. Ye is section ka sabse important trap hai.

docs.title: Kaise kaam karta hai
docs.text:
pivot = arr[low]   (ya median-of-three)

  i shuru: low - 1        j shuru: high + 1
       (do..while style, isliye ek step bahar se)

Loop:
  i ko aage badhao jab tak arr[i] < pivot ho
     -> ruk jao jab arr[i] >= pivot   (yaani "ye element right side ka hai")
  j ko peeche laao jab tak arr[j] > pivot ho
     -> ruk jao jab arr[j] <= pivot   (yaani "ye element left side ka hai")

  agar i >= j:  return j    <- pointers cross ho gaye, partition ho gaya
  swap(arr[i], arr[j])      <- dono galat taraf the, ab sahi taraf


Diagram:

  [ < pivot ...... | ...... > pivot ]
                 ^ ^
                 j i     <- cross hone ke baad

  return j  ->  "left partition [low..j], right partition [j+1..high]"

Sabse important baat — Hoare j return karta hai aur boundaries hain [low, j] aur [j+1, high], [low, j-1] aur [j+1, high] NAHI. Kyunki pivot kahin bhi ho sakta hai — wo j par bhi ho sakta hai. Agar aap j ko exclude kar dein to wo element kabhi sort nahi hoga.

docs.title: Poora dry run
docs.text:
Input: [3, 7, 8, 5, 2, 1, 9, 5, 4], low = 0, high = 8. Pivot = arr[low] = 3.

Shuruaat: i = -1, j = 9.

Iteration 1:

Pointer Steps Ruk gaya i i=0: arr[0]=3, 3 < 3? No → ruko i = 0 (val 3) j j=8: arr[8]=4, 4 > 3? Yes → j=7: arr[7]=5, 5>3? Yes → j=6: 9>3? Yes → j=5: arr[5]=1, 1>3? No → ruko j = 5 (val 1)

i (0) >= j (5)? No. Swap arr[0] ↔ arr[5]:

[**1**, 7, 8, 5, 2, **3**, 9, 5, 4]

Iteration 2:

Pointer Steps Ruk gaya i i=1: arr[1]=7, 7 < 3? No → ruko i = 1 (val 7) j j=4: arr[4]=2, 2 > 3? No → ruko j = 4 (val 2)

i (1) >= j (4)? No. Swap arr[1] ↔ arr[4]:

[1, **2**, 8, 5, **7**, 3, 9, 5, 4]

Iteration 3:

Pointer Steps Ruk gaya i i=2: arr[2]=8, 8 < 3? No → ruko i = 2 (val 8) j j=3: arr[3]=5, 5 > 3? Yes → j=2: arr[2]=8, 8>3? Yes → j=1: arr[1]=2, 2>3? No → ruko j = 1 (val 2)

i (2) >= j (1)? Yes → return j = 1.

Result: [1, 2, 8, 5, 7, 3, 9, 5, 4], partition point j = 1.

Verify: arr[0..1] = [1, 2] — dono <= 3 ✓. arr[2..8] = [8,5,7,3,9,5,4] — sab >= 3 ✓.

Dhyaan do: pivot ki value 3 ab index 5 par hai — apni final position par nahi. Isliye recursion qs(0, 1) aur qs(2, 8) hoti hai — j left side mein include hai.

Full recursion:

Call Range Array (relevant hissa) Pivot Return j Naye calls 1 0..8 [3,7,8,5,2,1,9,5,4] 3 1 (0,1), (2,8) 2 0..1 [1,2] 1 0 (0,0) base, (1,1) base 3 2..8 [8,5,7,3,9,5,4] 8 see below

Call 3: pivot = arr[2] = 8. i = 1, j = 9. - i: i=2: 8 < 8? No → ruko at i=2. - j: j=8: 4 > 8? No → ruko at j=8. - i(2) >= j(8)? No → swap arr[2] ↔ arr[8] → [1,2,**4**,5,7,3,9,5,**8**] - i: i=3: 5<8? Yes → i=4: 7<8? Yes → i=5: 3<8? Yes → i=6: 9<8? No → ruko at i=6. - j: j=7: 5>8? No → ruko at j=7. - i(6) >= j(7)? No → swap arr[6] ↔ arr[7] → [1,2,4,5,7,3,**5**,**9**,8] - i: i=7: 9<8? No → ruko at i=7. - j: j=6: 5>8? No → ruko at j=6. - i(7) >= j(6)? Yes → return 6.

Calls: (2, 6) on [4,5,7,3,5] and (7, 8) on [9,8].

Ye chalta rahega. Final: [1,2,3,4,5,5,7,8,9].

Iteration count comparison: is input par Hoare ne 3 swaps kiye pehle partition mein. Lomuto ne kitne kiye hote? Pivot 4 (last element) ke saath: elements <= 4 hain 3,2,1,4 — yaani 4 swaps + 1 final swap = 5 swaps. Hoare consistently kam swaps karta hai.

docs.title: Code
docs.text:
def quick_sort_hoare(arr, low=0, high=None):
    """Hoare partition ke saath quick sort."""
    if high is None:                                # 1
        high = len(arr) - 1                         # 2
    if low < high:                                  # 3
        p = hoare_partition(arr, low, high)         # 4
        quick_sort_hoare(arr, low, p)               # 5
        quick_sort_hoare(arr, p + 1, high)          # 6
    return arr                                      # 7


def hoare_partition(arr, low, high):
    """arr[low..high] ko partition karta hai. Ek index j return karta hai jahan
    arr[low..j] sab <= pivot aur arr[j+1..high] sab >= pivot."""
    pivot = arr[low]                                # 8
    i = low - 1                                     # 9
    j = high + 1                                    # 10
    while True:                                     # 11
        i += 1                                      # 12
        while arr[i] < pivot:                       # 13
            i += 1                                  # 14
        j -= 1                                      # 15
        while arr[j] > pivot:                       # 16
            j -= 1                                  # 17
        if i >= j:                                  # 18
            return j                                # 19
        arr[i], arr[j] = arr[j], arr[i]             # 20

Line-by-line — kya aur kyun:

1-2. Default high.

  1. if low < high — base case guard.

  2. Partition.

  3. quick_sort_hoare(arr, low, p) — p, p - 1 NAHI. Ye Hoare ka sabse bada gotcha hai. Lomuto mein pivot p par apni final jagah par tha, isliye use exclude karte the. Hoare mein p sirf ek boundary hai — arr[p] kis side ka hai wo guarantee nahi. Agar aap p - 1 likh dein, to arr[p] kabhi kisi recursive call mein include nahi hoga aur wo unsorted reh jayega. Wrong output.

  4. quick_sort_hoare(arr, p + 1, high) — right side p+1 se. Ye Lomuto jaisa hi hai.

Progress guarantee: Hoare hamesha j < high return karta hai (jab pivot arr[low] ho), isliye (low, p) strictly chhota hai (low, high) se, aur (p+1, high) bhi. Agar aap pivot arr[high] chunte to j == high ho sakta hai aur infinite recursion! Isliye Hoare ke saath pivot arr[low] ya arr[mid] chuno, arr[high] kabhi nahi. Ye ek real, dhoondhne mein mushkil bug hai.

  1. Return.

  2. pivot = arr[low] — value copy, index nahi. Value copy karna zaroori hai kyunki line 20 ke swaps arr[low] ki value badal denge. Agar aap pivot_idx = low rakh kar har baar arr[pivot_idx] padhte, to pivot ki value beech mein badal jati aur algorithm galat ho jata.

  3. i = low - 1 — ek step peeche. Kyunki line 12 pehle i += 1 karti hai (do-while pattern). Agar i = low rakhte to pehla element skip ho jata... nahi, ulta — line 12 use low+1 par le jati, aur arr[low] (jo pivot hai) kabhi check nahi hota. Yaani hum ek element chhod dete.

  4. j = high + 1 — same reason, line 15 pehle j -= 1 karti hai.

  5. while True — infinite loop, exit sirf line 19 se. Ye "do-while" ka Python equivalent hai (Python mein do-while nahi hota). Structure zaroori hai: har iteration mein dono pointers kam se kam ek kadam chalne chahiye, warna agar arr[i] == arr[j] == pivot ho to dono ruk jate hain, swap hota hai (jo kuchh nahi badalta), aur agla iteration bhi wahi karta hai → infinite loop. Lines 12 aur 15 ka forced increment/decrement ye guarantee deta hai.

  6. i += 1 — forced step, condition check karne se pehle.

  7. while arr[i] < pivot — strict <. Yaani i ruk jata hai jab arr[i] >= pivot ho — equal elements par bhi ruk jata hai. Yahi wo cheez hai jo duplicates ko handle karti hai. Agar <= likh dete to i saare equal elements ko paar kar jata; aur j bhi (agar >= likhte) — dono poore array ko paar kar jate aur arr[i] par IndexError aata (array ke bahar). Aur agar sirf ek side <= hota to partition hamesha ek extreme par hota → O(n²). Equal elements par dono pointers ka rukna hi Hoare ka duplicates-friendly hone ka raaz hai.

  8. i aage.

  9. j -= 1 — forced step.

  10. while arr[j] > pivot — strict >, symmetric reason.

  11. j peeche.

  12. if i >= j — pointers cross ho gaye ya mil gaye → partition complete. >= hai > nahi. Agar > likh dete to i == j par loop continue karta, line 20 self-swap karta (no-op), aur agla iteration i ko j se aage aur j ko i se peeche le jata — chalta rahega, par ek extra fizool round. Actually i == j par > ke saath: swap no-op, phir i += 1 (ab i > j), arr[i] < pivot check... ye out-of-bounds ja sakta hai. Isliye >= zaroori hai.

  13. return j — j, i nahi. Ye Hoare ka classic confusion hai. j return karne se boundary aisi banti hai ki arr[low..j] sab <= pivot aur arr[j+1..high] sab >= pivot. i return karne se ye invariant nahi banta (kyunki cross hone par i j+1 ya usse aage ho sakta hai) aur recursion galat ho jati hai.

  14. Swap — dono galat taraf ke elements ki adla badli.

Bounds safety — ye kaise guaranteed hai ki arr[i] aur arr[j] kabhi out of range nahi jate?

pivot = arr[low] hai.

i ka loop:  `while arr[i] < pivot`
  i badhta jayega, par jab wo kisi element par pahunche jo >= pivot ho, ruk jayega.
  Kya aisa element pakka milega? Haan -- arr[low] khud pivot hai, aur pivot < pivot False hai.
  Par i to low se aage ja chuka hai...
  Sochne ka sahi tareeka: pehli iteration mein i = low par ruk jayega (kyunki arr[low] = pivot,
  pivot < pivot False). Baad ki iterations mein, pichhle swap ne arr[j] par ek element rakha
  hai jo >= pivot tha... nahi, arr[i] par jo rakha wo <= pivot tha.

  Asli guarantee: j hamesha ek aisa element chhod kar aata hai jo <= pivot hai (yaani i ke
  liye rukne ki jagah), aur i hamesha aisa element chhod kar aata hai jo >= pivot hai (j ke
  liye rukne ki jagah). Isliye dono ek doosre ke liye "sentinel" ka kaam karte hain.

Ye reasoning subtle hai. Practical baat: Hoare partition ko exactly is form mein likho (pivot = arr[low], i = low-1, j = high+1, while True ke andar forced steps). Isme se kuchh bhi badalne se bounds ya termination toot sakti hai. Ye code CLRS aur Sedgewick dono mein isi form mein hai.

docs.title: Complexity derive karke
docs.text:
Same recurrences as Lomuto quicksort:

Best:     T(n) = 2T(n/2) + O(n)     ->  O(n log n)
Average:  Expected O(n log n)
Worst:    T(n) = T(n-1) + O(n)      ->  O(n²)

Constant factors mein farak — swaps ginte hain:

Lomuto:  har element jo <= pivot hai, uspar ek swap.
         Random data par ~n/2 elements <= pivot  ->  ~n/2 swaps per partition

Hoare:   swap sirf tab jab dono taraf galat element mile.
         Probability ki ek particular pair swap-worthy ho: analysis se ~n/6
         ->  ~n/6 swaps per partition

Ratio:   n/2 : n/6  =  3 : 1

Yaani Hoare ~3x kam swaps karta hai.

Comparisons: Hoare thodi zyada comparisons karta hai (dono pointers alag alag chalte hain, kabhi kabhi overlap), par swaps memory writes hain jo comparisons se mehngi hoti hain.

Duplicates par farak — ye sabse bada practical antar hai:

Input: [5, 5, 5, 5, 5, 5, 5, 5]  (n = 8, sab equal)

Lomuto (pivot = arr[high] = 5, condition arr[j] <= pivot):
  har j par 5 <= 5 True  ->  i har baar badhta  ->  i = high-1 end mein
  final swap arr[high] <-> arr[high]  ->  p = high
  recursion: (low, high-1) aur (high+1, high)
  ->  ek side mein n-1, doosri mein 0  ->  T(n) = T(n-1) + O(n)  ->  O(n²) ✗

Hoare (pivot = arr[low] = 5):
  i: arr[0]=5 < 5? No -> ruko at i=0
  j: arr[7]=5 > 5? No -> ruko at j=7
  i(0) >= j(7)? No -> swap (no-op)
  i: i=1, arr[1]=5 < 5? No -> ruko at i=1
  j: j=6, arr[6]=5 > 5? No -> ruko at j=6
  swap (no-op)
  ... yeh chalta rahega jab tak i aur j beech mein na milen
  i=3, j=4:  i >= j? No -> swap
  i=4, j=3:  i >= j? Yes -> return 3

  Partition beech mein!  ->  T(n) = 2T(n/2) + O(n)  ->  O(n log n) ✓

Ye ek asli, measurable farak hai. Real datasets mein duplicates bahut common hote hain (status codes, categories, boolean flags) — isliye Hoare ya 3-way partition zaroori ho jata hai.

Space: O(1) auxiliary + O(log n) average recursion stack (O(n) worst).

Metric Lomuto Hoare Swaps (average) ~n/2 per partition ~n/6 per partition Comparisons ~n ~n (thodi zyada) All-equal array O(n²) O(n log n) Pivot final position par? Haan Nahi Recursion boundaries (low, p-1), (p+1, high) (low, p), (p+1, high) Code likhne mein Aasan Trickier (bounds, while True) Quickselect ke liye Achha (pivot index pata hai) Thoda awkward

docs.title: Kab use karna hai / kab nahi
docs.text:
Use karo jab: - Aap quicksort likh rahe ho aur data mein duplicates ka chance hai. - Memory writes mehngi hain (Lomuto se 3x kam swaps). - Aap classic/reference implementation follow kar rahe ho (CLRS, Sedgewick).

Mat use karo jab: - Aapko quickselect chahiye (k-th smallest) — Lomuto behtar hai kyunki wo pivot ka exact final index deta hai, jisse aap seedha compare kar sakte ho k se. Hoare ke saath extra logic chahiye. - Aap pehli baar likh rahe ho aur bugs ka risk nahi le sakte — Lomuto forgiving hai. - Duplicates bahut zyada hain (>30%) — 3-way partition dono se behtar hai.

docs.title: Kitne tareeke se optimize
docs.text:
# Optimisation Kya deta hai Kya leta hai 1 Random pivot (arr[low] se pehle arr[low] aur random index swap) Adversarial input ka fix RNG cost 2 Median-of-three Sorted input par balanced split 3 comparisons per partition 3 Insertion sort cutoff 10-20% speedup Ek if 4 Tail recursion elimination Stack O(log n) guaranteed 3 lines 5 Dual-pivot (Yaroslavskiy) — do pivots, teen partitions ~10% kam comparisons; Java 7+ ka default primitive sort Kaafi complicated code 6 3-way partition Duplicates par O(n) Extra pointer management 7 Introsort — depth limit + heapsort fallback Guaranteed O(n log n) Depth counter

Random pivot Hoare ke saath — sahi tareeka:

import random

def hoare_partition_random(arr, low, high):
    r = random.randint(low, high)                   # 1
    arr[low], arr[r] = arr[r], arr[low]             # 2
    pivot = arr[low]                                # 3
    i, j = low - 1, high + 1                        # 4
    while True:                                     # 5
        i += 1                                      # 6
        while arr[i] < pivot:                       # 7
            i += 1
        j -= 1                                      # 8
        while arr[j] > pivot:                       # 9
            j -= 1
        if i >= j:                                  # 10
            return j                                # 11
        arr[i], arr[j] = arr[j], arr[i]             # 12
  1. Random index chuno, dono ends inclusive.
  2. Random element ko low par le aao — high par nahi! Ye Hoare ke liye critical hai. Agar aap pivot arr[high] banate to j == high return ho sakta hai, jisse quick_sort(arr, low, high) = same call = infinite recursion. Lomuto mein high par le jana sahi tha; Hoare mein low par. Ye ek line hai jo do algorithms ke beech ulti hoti hai aur interview mein pooch li jati hai.
  3. Pivot value copy.
  4. Sentinel positions. 5-12. Same as before.

Interview answer: Hoare partitioning works from both ends inward. The left pointer advances while elements are strictly less than the pivot, the right pointer retreats while elements are strictly greater, and when both stop we swap them — so one swap fixes two misplaced elements at once. When the pointers cross we return the right pointer as the partition boundary.

Compared to Lomuto it does roughly three times fewer swaps, because Lomuto swaps on every element that's less than or equal to the pivot while Hoare only swaps on genuinely crossed pairs. More importantly, it handles duplicates well: both pointers stop on elements equal to the pivot, so an all-equal array splits near the middle and stays O(n log n), whereas Lomuto degenerates to O(n²) there.

The trap is that the pivot does not end up in its final position, so the recursive calls are quicksort(low, p) and quicksort(p+1, high) — including p in the left side, not excluding it. If you copy Lomuto's p-1 boundary, the element at p is never sorted. And the pivot must be taken from arr[low] or the middle, never arr[high], because with arr[high] the partition can return high itself and you get infinite recursion.

Cross-question: "Why does the inner loop use strict less-than rather than less-than-or- equal?"

Two reasons. Termination: if both pointers skipped over equal elements, then on an array where everything equals the pivot, both would run off the ends of the array and index out of bounds. Balance: stopping on equal elements is what makes both pointers meet near the middle on duplicate-heavy input, which is exactly why Hoare beats Lomuto there.

Cross-question: "Which would you use for quickselect?"

Lomuto, because it returns the pivot's exact final index. Quickselect needs to compare that index against k to decide which side to recurse into, and Lomuto gives it directly. Hoare returns a boundary, not a placed element, so you have to reason about whether k falls in [low, j] or [j+1, high] and you don't get the "found it exactly" early exit for free.

docs.title: Kya hai
docs.text:
3-way partition array ko teen hisson mein baantta hai — < pivot, == pivot, > pivot — aur beech wale hisse ko recursion se poori tarah exclude kar deta hai, kyunki wo saare elements already apni final positions par hain.

Real-world analogy: Ek bade box mein hazaaron marbles hain teen rangon ke — laal, safed, neela — aur unhe rang ke hisaab se alag karna hai. Aap ek hi baar mein saare marbles ko teen dher mein daal dete ho. Ab safed wale dher ko aap dobara chhoote hi nahi — wo done hai. Bas laal aur neele dhero par kaam bacha hai. Isi ko Dutch National Flag problem kehte hain (Netherlands ke jhande ke teen rang), aur ise Edsger Dijkstra ne formulate kiya tha.

docs.title: Kyu hai
docs.text:
Lomuto aur Hoare dono ki duplicates par problem hai:

Input: [3, 1, 3, 3, 2, 3, 3, 3, 3, 3]   (10 elements, 7 teen ke)

Lomuto (pivot 3): saare 3s ek side mein  ->  unbalanced  ->  O(n²)

Hoare (pivot 3):  beech mein split hota hai  ->  O(n log n)
                  PAR: 3s dono sides mein bant gaye hain, aur
                  har recursive call unhe DOBARA compare karegi
                  ->  bekaar kaam, log n levels tak

2-way (dono):  saare 3s ko log n levels tak baar baar compare karna padta hai
3-way:         saare 3s ek hi partition step mein settle ho jate hain, phir kabhi nahi chhue

Concrete example: Ek array jisme sirf k distinct values hain (jaise HTTP status codes: 200, 301, 404, 500 — k = 4), par n = 10 lakh elements.

Algorithm Comparisons Lomuto / Hoare O(n log n) = 10^6 × 20 = 2 crore 3-way O(n log k) = 10^6 × 2 = 20 lakh

10x farak. Aur agar sab elements same hon (k = 1): 3-way O(n) hai — ek hi pass.

QA context mein ye bahut relevant hai: aap aksar aisa data sort karte ho jisme distinct values kam hain — test status (pass/fail/skip), severity levels, environment names, browser names.

docs.title: Kaise kaam karta hai
docs.text:
Teen pointers, teen zones:

  [ < pivot | == pivot | abhi nahi dekha | > pivot ]
             ^          ^                 ^
             lt         i                gt

  lt = pehla index jahan pivot ke barabar wale shuru hote hain
  i  = current scanner
  gt = aakhri index jahan pivot ke barabar wale khatam hote hain (se ek aage bada zone)

Invariants (ye hamesha true rehte hain):
  arr[low .. lt-1]   <  pivot
  arr[lt  .. i-1]    == pivot
  arr[i   .. gt]     = abhi nahi dekha
  arr[gt+1 .. high]  >  pivot

Har step par arr[i] dekho:
  arr[i] <  pivot:  swap(arr[lt], arr[i]);  lt++;  i++
  arr[i] == pivot:  i++                              <- kuchh swap nahi
  arr[i] >  pivot:  swap(arr[i], arr[gt]);  gt--     <- i NAHI badhta!

Loop tab tak jab tak i <= gt

Ant mein:
  [ < pivot | == pivot | > pivot ]
              ^         ^
              lt       gt+1

  Recursion: qs(low, lt-1)  aur  qs(gt+1, high)
  Beech ka hissa [lt..gt] — DONE, kabhi nahi chhua jayega

Sabse important line: arr[i] > pivot case mein i kyun nahi badhta?

Kyunki jo element gt se aaya hai, wo abhi tak dekha nahi gaya — hume nahi pata wo pivot se chhota hai, barabar hai, ya bada. Isliye use bhi check karna padega, aur wo ab i par hai. Agar aap i += 1 kar dete to wo element bina check ke chhoot jata → wrong answer.

Ulta, arr[i] < pivot case mein i badhta hai kyunki jo element lt se aaya hai wo pehle hi dekha ja chuka tha (wo == pivot zone ka element tha), to use dobara check karne ki zaroorat nahi.
