docs.title: Code
docs.text:
Variant A — fully sorted matrix:

def search_matrix_fully_sorted(matrix, target):
    """Har row sorted AUR row i ka last < row i+1 ka first. O(log(m*n))."""
    if not matrix or not matrix[0]:                 # 1
        return False                                # 2
    m, n = len(matrix), len(matrix[0])              # 3
    lo, hi = 0, m * n - 1                           # 4
    while lo <= hi:                                 # 5
        mid = lo + (hi - lo) // 2                   # 6
        value = matrix[mid // n][mid % n]           # 7
        if value == target:                         # 8
            return True                             # 9
        elif value < target:                        # 10
            lo = mid + 1                            # 11
        else:                                       # 12
            hi = mid - 1                            # 13
    return False                                    # 14

Line-by-line:

  1. if not matrix or not matrix[0] — do checks:
  2. not matrix — khali list [].

  3. not matrix[0] — [[]] case, yaani ek khali row. Bina doosre check ke line 3 ka len(matrix[0]) 0 deta aur line 4 ka m*n-1 = -1 hota; loop chalta hi nahi, to actually crash nahi hoga. Par explicit rakhna clearer hai. or ka order matter karta hai — not matrix pehle, warna khali list par matrix[0] IndexError.

  4. False.

  5. Dimensions.
  6. lo, hi = 0, m * n - 1 — virtual 1D array ke bounds.
  7. Template A loop.
  8. Overflow-safe mid.
  9. matrix[mid // n][mid % n] — 1D index ko 2D mein convert.
  10. mid // n = row (kitni poori rows paar ho gayi).
  11. mid % n = column (us row mein kahan). n (columns) se divide karo, m (rows) se NAHI. Ye sabse common bug hai. Socho: ek row mein n elements hain, to n elements ke baad agli row shuru hoti hai. Verify: 3×4 matrix, mid = 6 → row = 6//4 = 1, col = 6%4 = 2 → element #7 (0-indexed #6) = matrix[1][2] ✓ 8-13. Standard binary search.
  12. Not found.

Variant B — staircase search:

def search_matrix_staircase(matrix, target):
    """Har row AUR har column sorted. O(m + n)."""
    if not matrix or not matrix[0]:                 # 1
        return False                                # 2
    m, n = len(matrix), len(matrix[0])              # 3
    row, col = 0, n - 1                             # 4
    while row < m and col >= 0:                     # 5
        value = matrix[row][col]                    # 6
        if value == target:                         # 7
            return True                             # 8
        elif value > target:                        # 9
            col -= 1                                # 10
        else:                                       # 11
            row += 1                                # 12
    return False                                    # 13

Line-by-line — kya aur kyun:

1-3. Guards aur dimensions.

  1. row, col = 0, n - 1 — TOP-RIGHT corner. Ye choice hi poore algorithm ka core hai. 0, 0 (top-left) se shuru karte to right aur down dono directions mein values badhti, aur decide nahi kar pate kis taraf jaana hai.

  2. while row < m and col >= 0 — dono bounds.

  3. row < m — neeche jate jate matrix se bahar nikal sakte hain.

  4. col >= 0 — left jate jate bahar nikal sakte hain. Note ki hum kabhi row < 0 ya col >= n nahi hote, kyunki hum sirf row++ aur col-- karte hain. Isliye sirf do bound checks chahiye, chaar nahi.

  5. Current value.

7-8. Match.

9-10. value > target → column hatao. Kyunki column sorted hai, matrix[row][col] se neeche sab aur bade honge. To poore column ka bacha hua hissa useless hai. col -= 1, row += 1 nahi.

11-12. value < target → row hatao. Kyunki row sorted hai, matrix[row][col] ke left sab aur chhote honge. To poore row ka bacha hua hissa useless hai. row += 1.

  1. Not found.

Ye 13 lines ka function bahut elegant hai — har step exactly ek poori row ya poora column eliminate karta hai.

Index bhi chahiye to:

def search_matrix_staircase_pos(matrix, target):
    """Position (row, col) return karta hai, na milne par (-1, -1)."""
    if not matrix or not matrix[0]:
        return (-1, -1)
    m, n = len(matrix), len(matrix[0])
    row, col = 0, n - 1
    while row < m and col >= 0:
        v = matrix[row][col]
        if v == target:
            return (row, col)
        elif v > target:
            col -= 1
        else:
            row += 1
    return (-1, -1)

Variant B ke liye binary-search-per-row (alternative):

import bisect

def search_matrix_binary_per_row(matrix, target):
    """Har row par binary search. O(m log n). Staircase se dheema par simpler."""
    if not matrix or not matrix[0]:                 # 1
        return False                                # 2
    for row in matrix:                              # 3
        if row[0] > target:                         # 4
            break                                   # 5
        if row[-1] < target:                        # 6
            continue                                # 7
        i = bisect.bisect_left(row, target)         # 8
        if i < len(row) and row[i] == target:       # 9
            return True                             # 10
    return False                                    # 11

1-2. Guards. 3. Har row par. 4-5. row[0] > target → break. Kyunki columns sorted hain, agle rows ka pehla element aur bada hoga. Poore baaki rows skip. Ye pruning O(m log n) ko practically bahut tez bana deti hai. 6-7. row[-1] < target → is row mein target nahi ho sakta, agli row par jao. continue, break nahi — agle rows mein bade elements ho sakte hain. 8. Binary search us row par. 9-10. Bounds check + match check. 11. Not found.

Ye version staircase se dheema hai (O(m log n) vs O(m+n)) par: - Simpler hai samajhne mein. - Agar m << n ho to actually tez ho sakta hai: m log n vs m + n. Jaise m=5, n=10^6: 5 * 20 = 100 vs 5 + 10^6 ≈ 10^6. Binary-per-row jeet gaya!

Iska ulta bhi sach hai: agar m >> n to staircase behtar hai.

docs.title: Complexity derive karke
docs.text:
Variant A (fully sorted):

Binary search on m*n elements:
   T = O(log(m*n)) = O(log m + log n)

1000 x 1000 matrix:  log2(10^6) ≈ 20 steps

Variant B (staircase):

Har step mein ya to row++ ya col--
   row: 0 se m-1 tak badh sakta hai  ->  zyada se zyada m steps
   col: n-1 se 0 tak ghat sakta hai  ->  zyada se zyada n steps

Maximum total steps = m + n - 1

T = O(m + n)

1000 x 1000 matrix:  2000 steps

Variant B (binary per row):

m rows, har row par O(log n) binary search
T = O(m log n)

1000 x 1000 matrix:  1000 * 10 = 10,000 steps

Comparison table:

Approach Complexity 1000×1000 5×10^6 10^6×5 Brute force O(m·n) 10^6 5×10^6 5×10^6 Binary per row O(m log n) 10,000 100 2×10^6 Staircase O(m + n) 2,000 10^6 10^6 Flattened binary (variant A only) O(log(m·n)) 20 23 23

Ye table important hai — "sabse tez algorithm" matrix ki shape par depend karta hai: - Square matrix: staircase best (O(m+n)). - Bahut kam rows, bahut zyada columns: binary-per-row best (O(m log n)). - Fully sorted (variant A): flattened binary search always best.

Kya Variant B mein O(log(m·n)) possible hai? Nahi — ye ek proven lower bound hai. Intuition: matrix mein ek "anti-diagonal" ho sakti hai jahan values target ke aas paas hain, aur aapko us poori diagonal ko check karna pad sakta hai. Diagonal ki length min(m,n) hai, aur adversary argument se Omega(m + n) lower bound nikalta hai.

Space: O(1) sab approaches mein.

Variant Best Average Worst Space A: Flattened binary O(1) O(log(mn)) O(log(mn)) O(1) B: Staircase O(1) O(m+n) O(m+n) O(1) B: Binary per row O(log n) O(m log n) O(m log n) O(1)

docs.title: Kab use karna hai / kab nahi
docs.text:
Use karo jab: - Sorted 2D data — spreadsheets, price matrices, distance tables, image intensity maps. - Young tableau structures (row-column sorted matrices ka formal naam). - Multiplication table type problems — "k-th smallest in a m×n multiplication table". - Interview — LeetCode 74, 240 dono top-100 questions hain.

Mat use karo jab: - Matrix sorted nahi hai — poora scan chahiye. - Data ko flatten karke ek baar sort karna better hai (agar multiple searches hain). - Aapko range queries chahiye — 2D segment tree / BIT better.

Related problems jo isi technique se solve hote hain:

def count_less_equal(matrix, target):
    """Kitne elements target se chhote ya barabar hain. O(m + n)."""
    m, n = len(matrix), len(matrix[0])              # 1
    count = 0                                       # 2
    row, col = m - 1, 0                             # 3
    while row >= 0 and col < n:                     # 4
        if matrix[row][col] <= target:              # 5
            count += row + 1                        # 6
            col += 1                                # 7
        else:                                       # 8
            row -= 1                                # 9
    return count                                    # 10

1-2. Setup. 3. BOTTOM-LEFT se shuru — is problem ke liye ye corner behtar hai. 4. Bounds. 5. matrix[row][col] <= target? 6. count += row + 1 — is column mein row se upar ke saare elements bhi <= target hain (column sorted hai). To ek hi step mein row + 1 elements count ho gaye. Yahi efficiency hai. 7. Agle column par. 8-9. Warna upar jao. 10. Total count.

Ye function "k-th smallest element in sorted matrix" ke liye binary search ka core hai — aap value par binary search karte ho aur har candidate value ke liye ye count nikaalte ho.

docs.title: Kitne tareeke se optimize
docs.text:
# Optimisation Kya deta hai Kya leta hai 1 Staircase (top-right ya bottom-left) O(m·n) → O(m+n) Corner sahi chunna 2 Flattened binary search (variant A) O(m+n) → O(log(mn)) Extra precondition chahiye 3 Row pruning — row[0] > target par break Practically bahut tez Ek check 4 Shape ke hisaab se algorithm chuno — m << n to binary-per-row Best of both Ek if 5 Divide and conquer — matrix ko 4 quadrants mein baanto, do reject karo O(n^1.58) — theoretically interesting Practically staircase se dheema 6 Diagonal binary search — pehle diagonal par binary search se region narrow karo Kuchh cases mein tez Complicated 7 Preprocess — flatten aur sort agar bahut saari searches hain Har search O(log(mn)) O(mn log(mn)) one-time + O(mn) space

Interview answer: There are two different problems here and they need different solutions.

If the matrix is fully sorted — each row sorted and each row's first element greater than the previous row's last — then it's just a flattened sorted array, and I do a single binary search over indices 0 to m·n - 1, converting index i to matrix[i // n][i % n]. Note it's divide by n, the number of columns, not m. That's O(log(m·n)).

If only the rows and columns are individually sorted, with no relationship across rows, then the flattening doesn't work and the right approach is staircase search. Start at the top-right corner. Everything to its left in that row is smaller and everything below it in that column is larger, so a single comparison lets you eliminate an entire row or an entire column: if the current value is greater than the target, decrement the column; if it's less, increment the row. Each step removes a full row or column, so it's O(m + n) with O(1) space.

The corner matters. Top-left doesn't work because moving right and moving down both increase the value, so you can't decide which way to go. Only top-right and bottom-left give you two directions with opposite effects.

One nuance worth mentioning: binary searching each row is O(m log n), which is asymptotically worse than O(m + n) for a square matrix but better for a very wide, short matrix — five rows and a million columns gives 100 operations versus a million. So I'd pick based on the shape.

Cross-question: "Can the row-and-column-sorted version be done in O(log(m·n))?"

No, and that's provable, not just a limitation of the algorithm. There can be an anti-diagonal of values straddling the target, and an adversary can force you to examine essentially all of it, which gives an Omega(m + n) lower bound. Staircase search matches that bound, so it's optimal.

docs.title: Kya hai
docs.text:
Ye binary search ka sabse powerful aur sabse kam samjha jaane wala application hai. Yahan aap array par binary search nahi karte — aap answer ki possible values ki range par binary search karte ho.

Real-world analogy: Aapko pata karna hai ki ek lift mein maximum kitna weight le ja sakte ho bina alarm baje. Aap har possible weight try nahi karoge. Aap 500 kg try karoge — alarm baja? Haan → 250 try karo. Nahi baja? → 750 try karo. Aap "weight" ki value par binary search kar rahe ho, kisi array par nahi.

docs.title: Kyu hai
docs.text:
Bahut saari optimisation problems aisi hoti hain jahan:

  1. Answer ek number hai ek known range mein (jaise 1 se 10^9).
  2. Answer verify karna aasan hai — "kya X possible hai?" ka jawab O(n) mein mil jata hai.
  3. Answer monotonic hai — agar X possible hai to X se aasan sab possible hain (ya ulta).

Aise cases mein poori range par search karna O(range) hai, par binary search se O(log(range) × verify_cost) ho jata hai.

Problem: "Minimum X dhoondho jisse condition satisfy ho"

Brute force:  X = 1, 2, 3, ... try karo  ->  O(range * verify)
Binary search: O(log(range) * verify)

range = 10^9, verify = O(n) = 10^5:
   Brute force:   10^9 * 10^5 = 10^14   -> IMPOSSIBLE
   Binary search: 30 * 10^5   = 3*10^6  -> milliseconds

Ye technique ka naam alag alag hai — "binary search on answer", "parametric search", "binary search the result". Competitive programming mein bahut common hai, aur system design mein bhi (capacity planning, rate limiting).

docs.title: Kaise kaam karta hai
docs.text:
Recognition pattern:

Kya problem ka answer ek NUMBER hai?
   |
   +-- Kya answer ki range pata hai (ya bound kar sakte ho)?
       |
       +-- Kya "kya X kaam karta hai?" O(n) ya O(n log n) mein check kar sakte ho?
           |
           +-- Kya wo check MONOTONIC hai?
               (yaani agar X kaam karta hai to X+1 bhi karega, ya ulta)
               |
               +-- HAAN  ->  BINARY SEARCH ON ANSWER

Monotonicity ka matlab:

"can(X)" ek boolean function hai.

Pattern 1 (minimum dhoondhna):
   can:  F F F F F T T T T T
                   ^
                   answer (pehla T)

Pattern 2 (maximum dhoondhna):
   can:  T T T T T F F F F F
                 ^
                 answer (aakhri T)

Agar pattern aisa ho:  F T F T T F  ->  BINARY SEARCH LAG HI NAHI SAKTI

Template:

def binary_search_answer_min(lo, hi, can):
    """Sabse chhota X dhoondho [lo, hi] mein jahan can(X) True ho.
    Assumes: can ka pattern F F F T T T hai."""
    while lo < hi:
        mid = lo + (hi - lo) // 2
        if can(mid):
            hi = mid          # mid khud answer ho sakta hai
        else:
            lo = mid + 1      # mid kaam nahi karta, aage dekho
    return lo

Ye Template B hai (half-open, hi = mid), jo humne "Binary Search Boundary Conditions" mein derive kiya tha. Har binary-search-on-answer problem isi template se solve hoti hai.

docs.title: Poora dry run
docs.text:
Problem: Koko Eating Bananas (LeetCode 875)

Koko ke paas piles = [3, 6, 7, 11] kele ke dher hain aur h = 8 ghante hain. Wo har ghante ek dher se k kele khati hai (agar dher mein k se kam hain to poora dher khaake ruk jati hai, agla ghanta doosre dher se). Minimum k kya hai jisse wo h ghanton mein sab kha le?

Recognition: - Answer ek number hai: k. ✓ - Range: 1 se max(piles) = 11. ✓ (k > 11 ka koi fayda nahi — 11 se hi har dher ek ghante mein khatam) - Verify: "kya k speed se h ghanton mein ho jayega?" → har dher ke liye ceil(pile / k) ghante, sabka sum. O(n). ✓ - Monotonic: agar k kaam karta hai to k+1 bhi karega (zyada speed = kam time). ✓ Pattern: F F F T T T ✓

Verify function ka trace:

hours_needed(k) = sum(ceil(p / k) for p in piles)

k ceil(3/k) ceil(6/k) ceil(7/k) ceil(11/k) Total <= 8? 1 3 6 7 11 27 No 2 2 3 4 6 15 No 3 1 2 3 4 10 No 4 1 2 2 3 8 Yes 5 1 2 2 3 8 Yes 6 1 1 2 2 6 Yes 11 1 1 1 1 4 Yes

Answer = 4. Aur dekho pattern: F F F T T T T — perfectly monotonic ✓

Binary search trace (lo = 1, hi = 11):

Step lo hi mid hours_needed(mid) <= 8? Action 1 1 11 6 6 Yes hi = 6 2 1 6 3 10 No lo = 4 3 4 6 5 8 Yes hi = 5 4 4 5 4 8 Yes hi = 4 5 — — — — lo(4) == hi(4) return 4 ✓

4 steps + 4 verify calls. Brute force 4 verify calls leta (k=1,2,3,4) — is chhote example mein similar. Par agar max(piles) = 10^9 hota to brute force 10^9 calls leta, binary search sirf 30.

Doosra example — Split Array Largest Sum (LeetCode 410)

nums = [7, 2, 5, 10, 8] ko m = 2 contiguous subarrays mein baanto taaki subarrays ke sums mein se maximum minimum ho.

Recognition: - Answer ek number hai: minimum possible "largest sum". ✓ - Range: max(nums) = 10 (kam se kam) se sum(nums) = 32 (zyada se zyada, agar m=1). ✓ - Verify: "kya har subarray ka sum <= X rakhte hue m ya kam subarrays mein baant sakte hain?" → greedy: jitna daal sakte ho ek subarray mein daalo, phir naya. O(n). ✓ - Monotonic: bada X = zyada aasan = kam subarrays chahiye. F F F T T T ✓

Verify function trace: parts_needed(X) = greedy se kitne subarrays chahiye.

X Greedy split Parts <= 2? 10 [7,2] [5,10] [8] — 7+2=9<=10, +5=14>10 so new; 5+10=15>10 so 5 alone then 10 alone... let me redo

Careful trace of parts_needed(10): 

current = 0, parts = 1
7:  0+7 = 7 <= 10   -> current = 7
2:  7+2 = 9 <= 10   -> current = 9
5:  9+5 = 14 > 10   -> parts = 2, current = 5
10: 5+10 = 15 > 10  -> parts = 3, current = 10
8:  10+8 = 18 > 10  -> parts = 4, current = 8
parts = 4

X parts_needed(X) <= 2? 10 4 No 15 3 ([7,2,5]=14, [10], [8]) No 18 2 ([7,2,5]=14, [10,8]=18) Yes 20 2 Yes 32 1 Yes

Answer = 18.

Binary search trace (lo = max(nums) = 10, hi = sum(nums) = 32):

Step lo hi mid parts_needed(mid) <= 2? Action 1 10 32 21 2 Yes hi = 21 2 10 21 15 3 No lo = 16 3 16 21 18 2 Yes hi = 18 4 16 18 17 3 ([7,2,5]=14, [10], [8]) No lo = 18 5 — — — — lo(18) == hi(18) return 18 ✓

docs.title: Code
docs.text:
Universal template:

def bs_answer_min(lo, hi, can):
    """Sabse chhota X in [lo, hi] jahan can(X) True. Pattern: F...F T...T"""
    while lo < hi:                                  # 1
        mid = lo + (hi - lo) // 2                   # 2
        if can(mid):                                # 3
            hi = mid                                # 4
        else:                                       # 5
            lo = mid + 1                            # 6
    return lo                                       # 7


def bs_answer_max(lo, hi, can):
    """Sabse bada X in [lo, hi] jahan can(X) True. Pattern: T...T F...F"""
    while lo < hi:                                  # 8
        mid = lo + (hi - lo + 1) // 2               # 9
        if can(mid):                                # 10
            lo = mid                                # 11
        else:                                       # 12
            hi = mid - 1                            # 13
    return lo                                       # 14

Line-by-line:

  1. while lo < hi — Template B.
  2. Left-biased mid — (hi - lo) // 2.
  3. can(mid) — verify function.
  4. hi = mid — mid khud answer ho sakta hai, isliye mid - 1 nahi. 5-6. lo = mid + 1 — mid definitely answer nahi, aage dekho.

  5. lo == hi par ruka.

  6. Same loop.

  7. mid = lo + (hi - lo + 1) // 2 — RIGHT-BIASED! +1 par dhyaan do. Kyun zaroori hai? Kyunki line 11 mein lo = mid hai. Agar mid left-biased hota to lo = 0, hi = 1 par mid = 0, lo = mid = 0 — state nahi badla → INFINITE LOOP. Right-biased mid lo = 0, hi = 1 par mid = 1 deta, lo = 1 — progress ✓ Rule: lo = mid ke saath right-biased mid, hi = mid ke saath left-biased mid. 10-11. mid kaam karta hai → answer mid ya aage. 12-13. mid kaam nahi karta → mid - 1 tak.
  8. Answer.

Koko Eating Bananas — poora solution:

import math

def min_eating_speed(piles, h):
    """Minimum k jisse Koko h ghanton mein sab kele kha le."""
    def hours_needed(k):                            # 1
        return sum(math.ceil(p / k) for p in piles) # 2

    lo, hi = 1, max(piles)                          # 3
    while lo < hi:                                  # 4
        mid = lo + (hi - lo) // 2                   # 5
        if hours_needed(mid) <= h:                  # 6
            hi = mid                                # 7
        else:                                       # 8
            lo = mid + 1                            # 9
    return lo                                       # 10
  1. Nested verify function — closure se piles access karta hai.
  2. math.ceil(p / k) — har dher ke liye kitne ghante. ceil zaroori hai — 7 kele, speed 3 → 7/3 = 2.33 → 3 ghante chahiye (2 ghante mein 6, teesre ghante mein 1). Integer arithmetic version (float precision se bachne ke liye): (p + k - 1) // k. Ye ceil(p/k) ka exact integer equivalent hai aur bade numbers par float rounding errors se bacha hai. Production mein ye behtar hai.
  3. lo, hi = 1, max(piles) — bounds ki reasoning:
  4. lo = 1 — minimum possible speed (0 se kam nahi kha sakte, aur 0 se kabhi khatam nahi hoga).
  5. hi = max(piles) — isse zyada speed ka koi fayda nahi. Speed max(piles) par har dher exactly ek ghante mein khatam ho jata hai, jo minimum possible time hai. Isse zyada speed same result degi. Bounds ko tight rakhna important hai — hi = 10^9 bhi kaam karta par 30 steps ki jagah ~4 steps mein kaam ho jata hi = max(piles) ke saath (chhote inputs par). 4-9. Standard bs_answer_min template.
  6. Answer.

Split Array Largest Sum — poora solution:

def split_array_min_largest_sum(nums, m):
    """nums ko m subarrays mein baanto, maximum subarray sum ko minimise karo."""
    def parts_needed(limit):                        # 1
        parts, current = 1, 0                       # 2
        for x in nums:                              # 3
            if current + x <= limit:                # 4
                current += x                        # 5
            else:                                   # 6
                parts += 1                          # 7
                current = x                         # 8
        return parts                                # 9

    lo, hi = max(nums), sum(nums)                   # 10
    while lo < hi:                                  # 11
        mid = lo + (hi - lo) // 2                   # 12
        if parts_needed(mid) <= m:                  # 13
            hi = mid                                # 14
        else:                                       # 15
            lo = mid + 1                            # 16
    return lo                                       # 17
  1. Verify function.
  2. parts = 1 — 1 se shuru, 0 se nahi. Kyunki ek non-empty array kam se kam ek part banata hai. 0 se shuru karne par answer ek kam aata.
  3. Har element. 4-5. Current part mein fit ho jata hai → add. 6-8. Nahi fit hota → naya part shuru karo, current element usme daalo. Ye greedy hai — "jitna daal sakte ho daalo". Ye greedy optimal kyun hai? Kyunki har element ko current part mein daalne se kabhi nuksaan nahi hota — agar aap use naye part mein daalte to future ke liye kam jagah bachti. Exchange argument se prove hota hai.
  4. Parts count.
  5. lo = max(nums), hi = sum(nums) — bounds ki reasoning:
  6. lo = max(nums) — koi bhi split mein, sabse bada element apne aap ek subarray mein hoga (kam se kam), to answer max(nums) se kam ho hi nahi sakta.
  7. hi = sum(nums) — agar m = 1 to poora array ek subarray hai, sum = sum(nums). Isse zyada kabhi nahi. Bounds ko sahi derive karna is technique ka aadha kaam hai. Galat bounds = galat answer ya infinite loop. 11-16. Template.
  8. Answer.

Aur bahut saari problems isi pattern par:

def min_days_to_ship(weights, days):
    """LeetCode 1011: Capacity To Ship Packages Within D Days."""
    def days_needed(cap):                           # 1
        d, current = 1, 0                           # 2
        for w in weights:                           # 3
            if current + w <= cap:                  # 4
                current += w                        # 5
            else:                                   # 6
                d += 1                              # 7
                current = w                         # 8
        return d                                    # 9

    lo, hi = max(weights), sum(weights)             # 10
    while lo < hi:                                  # 11
        mid = lo + (hi - lo) // 2                   # 12
        if days_needed(mid) <= days:                # 13
            hi = mid                                # 14
        else:                                       # 15
            lo = mid + 1                            # 16
    return lo                                       # 17


def max_min_distance(positions, m):
    """LeetCode 1552: Magnetic Force Between Two Balls.
    m balls ko positions mein rakho taaki minimum gap MAXIMUM ho."""
    positions.sort()                                # 18
    def can_place(gap):                             # 19
        count, last = 1, positions[0]               # 20
        for p in positions[1:]:                     # 21
            if p - last >= gap:                     # 22
                count += 1                          # 23
                last = p                            # 24
        return count >= m                           # 25

    lo, hi = 1, positions[-1] - positions[0]        # 26
    while lo < hi:                                  # 27
        mid = lo + (hi - lo + 1) // 2               # 28
        if can_place(mid):                          # 29
            lo = mid                                # 30
        else:                                       # 31
            hi = mid - 1                            # 32
    return lo                                       # 33

1-9. days_needed — bilkul parts_needed jaisa. Ye do problems structurally identical hain, sirf naming alag hai. Ye pattern recognition ki value dikhata hai. 10-17. Same template.

  1. Sort zaroori hai — gaps ka matlab hi tabhi hai jab positions ordered hon. 19-25. can_place(gap) — greedy: pehli ball position[0] par, phir jab bhi gap ya zyada doori mile to agli ball rakho. Ye maximum balls place karta hai given gap ke saath. Ye greedy optimal hai — pehli opportunity par ball rakhne se future ke liye maximum jagah bachti hai.
  2. Bounds: lo = 1 (minimum meaningful gap), hi = positions[-1] - positions[0] (maximum possible gap, jab sirf 2 balls hon). 27-32. bs_answer_max template — kyunki hum minimum gap ko maximise kar rahe hain. Line 28 par right-biased mid (+1), line 30 par lo = mid. Ye combination zaroori hai, warna infinite loop.
  3. Answer.

docs.title: Complexity derive karke
docs.text:
Binary search steps:  O(log(hi - lo))
Har step mein verify: O(V)   jahan V = verify function ki cost

Total:  O(V * log(range))

Examples:

Problem Range Verify cost Total Koko bananas max(piles) ≈ 10^9 O(n) O(n log(10^9)) = O(30n) Split array sum(nums) ≈ 10^9 O(n) O(30n) Ship packages sum(weights) O(n) O(30n) Magnetic force max_pos ≈ 10^9 O(n) O(n log n) sort + O(30n) Median of 2 arrays — O(1) O(log(min(m,n)))

Brute force se comparison:

Brute force:  O(range * V)
Binary search: O(log(range) * V)

Speedup factor = range / log(range)

range = 10^9:  10^9 / 30 ≈ 33 million times faster

Space: O(1) beyond the verify function's needs.

docs.title: Stability, in-place, adaptive
docs.text:
Property Value Kyun Precondition Verify function monotonic honi chahiye Ye sabse critical requirement hai Answer exact hai? Haan, integer domains par Float domains par epsilon ke andar Modifies data Verify function par depend Template khud nahi karta

Monotonicity kaise verify karo? Ek chhota test likho:

def check_monotonic(can, lo, hi, samples=100):
    """Verify karo ki can() monotonic hai (F...F T...T pattern)."""
    import random
    values = sorted(random.sample(range(lo, hi + 1), min(samples, hi - lo + 1)))
    results = [can(v) for v in values]
    seen_true = False
    for r in results:
        if r:
            seen_true = True
        elif seen_true:
            return False        # True ke baad False aaya -> NOT monotonic
    return True

Ye check debugging mein bahut kaam aata hai — agar aapka binary search galat answer de raha hai, pehle ye check karo ki verify function sach mein monotonic hai ya nahi.

docs.title: Kab use karna hai / kab nahi
docs.text:
Use karo jab: - "Minimum X dhoondho jisse..." ya "Maximum X dhoondho jisse..." — ye phrasing hi signal hai. - "Minimise the maximum" ya "maximise the minimum" — ye phrases lagbhag hamesha binary search on answer signal karti hain. - Answer ki range pata hai ya bound ki ja sakti hai. - Verify O(n) ya O(n log n) mein ho jata hai.

Mat use karo jab: - Verify monotonic nahi hai — algorithm galat answer dega, silently. - Answer ek number nahi hai (jaise ek path, ek subset). - Direct formula ya greedy solution exist karta hai — wo O(n) hoga, ye O(n log range). - Range bahut chhoti hai — brute force simpler.

Signal phrases jo binary-search-on-answer indicate karti hain:

Phrase Example problem "minimum X such that..." Koko bananas "maximum X such that..." Magnetic force "minimise the maximum" Split array largest sum "maximise the minimum" Magnetic force, aggressive cows "at least/at most k ... within limit" Ship packages in D days "smallest capacity/speed/size" Capacity to ship "k-th smallest in sorted matrix" Binary search on value + count

docs.title: Kitne tareeke se optimize
docs.text:
# Optimisation Kya deta hai Kya leta hai 1 Tight bounds — lo aur hi ko carefully derive karo Kam iterations. lo = max(nums) vs lo = 1 bahut farak Sochne ka waqt 2 Verify function optimise karo Ye log(range) baar chalta hai — ek constant factor bhi matter karta hai 3 Early exit verify mein — agar parts > m ho gaya to turant False return Verify O(n) → often O(k) Ek check 4 Integer ceil ((a + b - 1) // b) instead of math.ceil(a / b) Float precision bugs khatam, thoda tez Formula yaad rakhna 5 Float domain par iteration cap Infinite loop se safety Ek counter 6 Verify ke results cache karo agar mehngi hai Repeated calls free Memory 7 Parallel verify agar independent hai Wall-clock kam Complexity

Early exit optimisation (#3):

def parts_needed_early_exit(nums, limit, max_parts):
    """Agar parts max_parts se zyada ho gaye to turant ruk jao."""
    parts, current = 1, 0                           # 1
    for x in nums:                                  # 2
        if x > limit:                               # 3
            return max_parts + 1                    # 4
        if current + x <= limit:                    # 5
            current += x                            # 6
        else:                                       # 7
            parts += 1                              # 8
            if parts > max_parts:                   # 9
                return parts                        # 10
            current = x                             # 11
    return parts                                    # 12

1-2. Setup aur loop. 3-4. x > limit — ek single element hi limit se bada hai → impossible. Turant return. Ye check bina, code galat parts count karta (ya infinite loop mein ja sakta agar logic thodi alag hoti). 5-8. Normal greedy. 9-10. Early exit — parts pehle hi max_parts se zyada ho gaya, aur aage sirf badhega. Baaki array scan karne ka koi matlab nahi. Bade arrays par ye kaafi time bachata hai. 11-12. Continue aur return.

Float domain par binary search:

def bs_answer_float(lo, hi, can, eps=1e-9, max_iter=200):
    """Continuous domain par minimum X jahan can(X) True."""
    for _ in range(max_iter):                       # 1
        if hi - lo < eps:                           # 2
            break                                   # 3
        mid = (lo + hi) / 2                         # 4
        if can(mid):                                # 5
            hi = mid                                # 6
        else:                                       # 7
            lo = mid                                # 8
    return hi                                       # 9
  1. for with iteration cap, while nahi. Float mein hi - lo rounding ki wajah se eps se neeche nahi aa sakta → infinite loop. Cap ek hard safety hai. 200 iterations mein range 2^-200 guna chhoti — kisi bhi practical precision se zyada. 2-3. Precision check.
  2. (lo + hi) / 2 — float division. Overflow ka issue nahi (Python floats). 5-6. hi = mid — mid answer ho sakta hai. 7-8. lo = mid, lo = mid + 1 NAHI — float domain mein "next value" ka koi matlab nahi.
  3. hi return karo, lo nahi — kyunki hi par can hamesha True raha hai (ya initial value), aur hum minimum "True" chahte hain. Actually dono almost equal hain (eps ke andar), to koi bhi chalega — par hi semantically sahi hai.

Interview answer: Binary search on the answer flips the usual setup: instead of searching an array for a value, you search the space of possible answers for the optimum. It applies when three things hold — the answer is a number in a boundable range, you can check "is X feasible?" efficiently, and that feasibility check is monotonic, so once X works every larger X works too, or vice versa.

The recognition signals are phrases like "minimise the maximum", "maximise the minimum", or "smallest capacity such that". Koko eating bananas, splitting an array to minimise the largest subarray sum, capacity to ship packages in D days, placing balls to maximise the minimum gap — those are all the same problem with different stories.

The complexity is O(V · log(range)) where V is the cost of the feasibility check. With a range of a billion and an O(n) check, that's thirty passes over the data instead of a billion, which turns an impossible brute force into milliseconds.

The two things I'm careful about: deriving tight bounds, because they're part of the correctness argument — for split-array, lo must be max(nums), since the largest element always forms at least one subarray by itself, and hi is sum(nums) — and matching the midpoint bias to the update. If the update is lo = mid I must bias the midpoint upward with (hi - lo + 1) // 2, otherwise with lo and hi adjacent nothing changes and it loops forever.

Cross-question: "How do you know your feasibility check is monotonic?"

I argue it from the problem semantics: for Koko, a higher eating speed can never require more hours, so if speed k finishes in time, so does k+1. If I can't argue it cleanly, that's a warning sign that binary search doesn't apply. In practice, when debugging a wrong answer, the first thing I do is sample the feasibility function across the range and check the pattern really is all-false-then-all-true — a non-monotonic check makes binary search return an arbitrary wrong answer with no error.

Cross-question: "Why does the greedy feasibility check for split-array give the true minimum number of parts?"

Exchange argument. Suppose an optimal split puts element x into a new part while the greedy would have fit it into the current part. Moving x back into the current part keeps that part within the limit, by assumption, and leaves the next part with strictly fewer elements, so it can only be easier to complete. Repeating that transformation converts any optimal solution into the greedy one without increasing the part count, so greedy is optimal.

docs.title: Part 3: Recursion and Divide and Conquer
docs.text:
Merge sort aur quick sort mein humne recursion use ki, par uske mechanics ko detail mein nahi dekha. Ye part wahi karta hai: call stack ko concretely trace karna, recursion trees se complexity nikalna, Master Theorem ko sach mein usable banana, aur ye samajhna ki recursion kab galat tool hai.

Agar aapko recursion "jaadu" lagti hai, to iska matlab hai ki aapne kabhi call stack ko step-by-step nahi dekha. Wo hum sabse pehle karenge.

docs.title: Kya hai
docs.text:
Call stack ek data structure hai jo program ke andar har active function call ko track karta hai — kaunsa function chal raha hai, uske local variables kya hain, aur wo khatam hone par kahan wapas jaana hai.

Real-world analogy: Aap ek kitaab padh rahe ho. Page 50 par ek footnote hai jo kehta hai "details ke liye Appendix A dekho". Aap page 50 par ungli rakh kar Appendix A par jaate ho. Wahan ek aur reference milta hai — ab aap do jagah ungli rakh chuke ho. Appendix padh kar aap wapas aate ho, ungli hataate ho, aur page 50 se continue karte ho. Aapki ungliyaan hi call stack hain, aur "jahan wapas aana hai" wo return address hai.

docs.title: Kyu hai
docs.text:
Recursion tabhi samajh mein aati hai jab aapko pata ho ki har recursive call ka apna alag "copy" hota hai local variables ka. Ye wo cheez hai jo log confuse karte hain:

def f(n):
    x = n * 2
    if n > 0:
        f(n - 1)
    print(x)     # <- kaunsi x?

Har call ki apni x hai. f(3) ki x = 6, f(2) ki x = 4, f(1) ki x = 2, f(0) ki x = 0. Wo ek doosre ko touch nahi karti. Isliye output 0, 2, 4, 6 hai — ulta order mein, kyunki print recursive call ke baad hai.

Bina stack ko samjhe, ye output "jaadu" lagta hai. Stack ke saath, ye obvious hai.

docs.title: Kaise kaam karta hai
docs.text:
Stack frame — har function call ke liye ek "box":

Ek stack frame mein kya hota hai:

  +---------------------------+
  | Return address            |  <- khatam hone par kahan wapas jaana hai
  | Parameters                |  <- n = 3
  | Local variables           |  <- x = 6
  | Saved registers           |  <- CPU state
  +---------------------------+

Stack grow karta hai jab call hoti hai, shrink karta hai jab return hota hai.
LIFO — Last In, First Out.

Do phases har recursion mein:

WINDING (neeche jaate hue) — calls stack par push hoti hain
UNWINDING (wapas aate hue) — calls pop hoti hain, values return hoti hain

Ye do phases yaad rakhna sabse zaroori hai:

def f(n):
    # ---- ye code WINDING phase mein chalta hai ----
    if base_case: return
    f(n-1)
    # ---- ye code UNWINDING phase mein chalta hai ----

docs.title: Poora dry run
docs.text:
Example 1 — Factorial. factorial(4)

def factorial(n):
    if n <= 1:
        return 1
    return n * factorial(n - 1)

Winding phase (stack build hota hai):

Step Action Stack (bottom → top) 1 factorial(4) called [f(4): n=4] 2 4 <= 1? No → needs factorial(3) [f(4): n=4] 3 factorial(3) called [f(4): n=4] [f(3): n=3] 4 3 <= 1? No → needs factorial(2) [f(4)] [f(3)] 5 factorial(2) called [f(4)] [f(3)] [f(2): n=2] 6 2 <= 1? No → needs factorial(1) [f(4)] [f(3)] [f(2)] 7 factorial(1) called [f(4)] [f(3)] [f(2)] [f(1): n=1] 8 1 <= 1? Yes → return 1 Maximum depth = 4

Unwinding phase (stack collapse hota hai):

Step Action Return value Stack 9 f(1) returns 1 1 [f(4)] [f(3)] [f(2)] 10 f(2) computes 2 * 1 = 2, returns 2 [f(4)] [f(3)] 11 f(3) computes 3 * 2 = 6, returns 6 [f(4)] 12 f(4) computes 4 * 6 = 24, returns 24 []

Visual:

WINDING (calls jaate hue)              UNWINDING (values wapas aate hue)

f(4) = 4 * f(3)                        f(4) = 4 * 6 = 24     <- FINAL
        |                                      ^
        v                                      |
      f(3) = 3 * f(2)                        f(3) = 3 * 2 = 6
              |                                      ^
              v                                      |
            f(2) = 2 * f(1)                        f(2) = 2 * 1 = 2
                    |                                      ^
                    v                                      |
                  f(1) = 1  <- BASE CASE                  f(1) = 1

Example 2 — Winding vs unwinding print order.

def trace(n):
    if n == 0:                              # 1
        return                              # 2
    print(f"WINDING:   entering trace({n})")     # 3
    trace(n - 1)                            # 4
    print(f"UNWINDING: leaving trace({n})")      # 5

trace(3) ka output:

WINDING:   entering trace(3)      <- f(3) ka line 3
WINDING:   entering trace(2)      <- f(2) ka line 3
WINDING:   entering trace(1)      <- f(1) ka line 3
                                  <- f(0) base case, kuchh print nahi
UNWINDING: leaving trace(1)       <- f(1) ka line 5
UNWINDING: leaving trace(2)       <- f(2) ka line 5
UNWINDING: leaving trace(3)       <- f(3) ka line 5

Dhyaan do ki UNWINDING order ulta hai. Kyunki stack LIFO hai — jo call sabse baad mein push hui, wo sabse pehle pop hoti hai.

Ye pattern bahut kaam ka hai: - Preorder tree traversal = winding mein kaam karo. - Postorder tree traversal = unwinding mein kaam karo. - Linked list ko ulta print karna = unwinding mein print karo.

Example 3 — Do recursive calls (binary recursion). fib(4)

def fib(n):
    if n <= 1:
        return n
    return fib(n - 1) + fib(n - 2)

Call order (depth-first, left pehle):

# Call Depth Stack at that moment Returns 1 fib(4) 1 [4] pending 2 fib(3) 2 [4,3] pending 3 fib(2) 3 [4,3,2] pending 4 fib(1) 4 [4,3,2,1] 1 5 fib(0) 4 [4,3,2,0] 0 6 fib(2) returns 3 [4,3] 1 (=1+0) 7 fib(1) 3 [4,3,1] 1 8 fib(3) returns 2 [4] 2 (=1+1) 9 fib(2) 2 [4,2] pending 10 fib(1) 3 [4,2,1] 1 11 fib(0) 3 [4,2,0] 0 12 fib(2) returns 2 [4] 1 13 fib(4) returns 1 [] 3 (=2+1)

Total calls: 9. Maximum stack depth: 4.

Important observation: fib(2) do baar compute hua (steps 3-6 aur 9-12). Ye duplicate work hi exponential blowup ki wajah hai, aur memoisation ka motivation.

Tree:

                 fib(4)
                /      \
          fib(3)        fib(2)      <- fib(2) yahan DOBARA
          /    \        /    \
     fib(2)  fib(1)  fib(1) fib(0)
     /    \
 fib(1)  fib(0)

Total nodes = 9 calls
Maximum depth = 4  (fib(4) -> fib(3) -> fib(2) -> fib(1))

Space: Maximum depth = 4 frames, 9 nahi. Kyunki jab fib(3) ki subtree khatam hoti hai, uske frames pop ho jate hain aur fib(2) ki subtree unhi ki jagah use karti hai.

Ye distinction critical hai: total calls = time. Maximum depth = space.

docs.title: Code — stack ko explicitly dekhna
docs.text:
import sys                                          # 1
import traceback                                    # 2


def factorial_with_trace(n, depth=0):
    indent = "  " * depth                           # 3
    print(f"{indent}-> factorial({n})  [stack depth: {len(traceback.extract_stack())}]")  # 4
    if n <= 1:                                      # 5
        print(f"{indent}<- base case, return 1")    # 6
        return 1                                    # 7
    result = n * factorial_with_trace(n - 1, depth + 1)    # 8
    print(f"{indent}<- factorial({n}) = {result}")  # 9
    return result                                   # 10


print(f"Python's recursion limit: {sys.getrecursionlimit()}")   # 11

Line-by-line:

1-2. sys recursion limit ke liye, traceback stack inspect karne ke liye. 3. indent — visual depth. depth parameter manually track kar rahe hain. 4. traceback.extract_stack() — actual Python call stack ki list. Uski length se pata chalta hai ki hum kitne deep hain. Ye debugging ke liye bahut useful hai. 5-7. Base case — winding rukti hai. 8. Recursive call. depth + 1 pass kiya (naya value, depth khud nahi badla — ye important hai, depth immutable integer hai aur har frame ki apni copy hai). 9. Unwinding phase ka print. 10. Return. 11. sys.getrecursionlimit() — default 1000 CPython mein.

Stack overflow demonstrate karna:

import sys

def infinite_recursion(n):
    return infinite_recursion(n + 1)                # 1

def safe_deep_recursion(n):
    if n == 0:                                      # 2
        return 0                                    # 3
    return 1 + safe_deep_recursion(n - 1)           # 4

# infinite_recursion(0)
#   -> RecursionError: maximum recursion depth exceeded

# safe_deep_recursion(999)   -> works
# safe_deep_recursion(5000)  -> RecursionError

sys.setrecursionlimit(10000)                        # 5
# safe_deep_recursion(5000)  -> ab kaam karta hai (par risky)
  1. Koi base case nahi → RecursionError. Python ne ise crash se bacha liya — C mein ye segmentation fault deta. 2-4. Proper base case.
  2. setrecursionlimit(10000) — limit badha sakte ho par SAVDHAAN. Python ka limit CPU stack overflow se bachane ke liye hai. Agar aap use bahut bada kar do to Python interpreter segfault kar sakta hai — jo se recover nahi kar sakte (RecursionError se kar sakte ho). Practically 10,000-50,000 tak safe hai typical systems par, par behtar solution hai recursion ko iteration mein badalna.

Recursion ko iteration mein badalna — explicit stack se:

def factorial_iterative_stack(n):
    """Recursion ko manually stack se simulate karna."""
    stack = []                                      # 1
    while n > 1:                                    # 2
        stack.append(n)                             # 3
        n -= 1                                      # 4
    result = 1                                      # 5
    while stack:                                    # 6
        result *= stack.pop()                       # 7
    return result                                   # 8
  1. Explicit stack — call stack ki jagah heap par ek list. Heap ki koi 1000 ki limit nahi hai, sirf available RAM. 2-4. Winding phase simulate — jo values baad mein multiply karni hain, unhe push karo.
  2. Base case ka value. 6-7. Unwinding phase simulate — pop karke multiply.
  3. Result.

Ye pattern har recursion ko iteration mein badal sakta hai, aur wo tab zaroori hai jab depth bahut zyada ho.

docs.title: Complexity derive karke
docs.text:
Time = total number of calls:

Linear recursion (ek call per level):
   factorial(n):  n calls  ->  O(n)

Binary recursion (do calls per level):
   fib(n):  T(n) = T(n-1) + T(n-2) + O(1)
            ~ 1.618^n (golden ratio)  ->  O(1.618^n), exponential

Divide and conquer (do calls par input aadha):
   merge_sort(n):  T(n) = 2T(n/2) + O(n)  ->  O(n log n)

Space = maximum stack depth × frame size:

factorial(n):    depth n       ->  O(n) space
fib(n):          depth n       ->  O(n) space (calls exponential hain PAR depth linear)
merge_sort(n):   depth log n   ->  O(log n) stack space
quick_sort(n):   depth log n average, n worst  ->  O(log n) / O(n)

Ye distinction interview mein bahut poochha jata hai:

"fib(n) O(2^n) time leta hai. Kya wo O(2^n) space bhi leta hai?"

Nahi. Space maximum depth ke barabar hai, jo n hai — kyunki har waqt sirf ek path stack par hota hai, poora tree nahi.

Ek frame ka size: typically 50-100 bytes Python mein (parameters, locals, bookkeeping). 1000 deep recursion ≈ 50-100 KB. Ye bahut nahi hai — Python ki limit safety ke liye hai, memory ke liye nahi.

Recursion type Time Space (stack depth) Example Linear O(n) O(n) factorial, linked list traversal Tail recursion O(n) O(n) in Python, O(1) with TCO sum of list Binary (no memo) O(2^n) O(n) naive fibonacci Divide & conquer O(n log n) O(log n) merge sort Backtracking O(b^d) O(d) N-queens, permutations

docs.title: Kab recursion theek hai / kab nahi
docs.text:
Recursion accha hai jab: - Problem ka structure hi recursive hai — trees, graphs, nested JSON, filesystem. - Depth logarithmic hai — divide and conquer. - Code bahut zyada clear ho jata hai iteration se.

Recursion bura hai jab: - Depth linear aur bada hai — Python mein 1000 ki limit hit ho jayegi. - Overlapping subproblems hain bina memoisation ke — exponential blowup. - Tail recursion hai — Python TCO nahi karta, to loop hi likh do. - Performance critical — har call mein frame setup ka overhead hai.

Interview answer: The call stack holds one frame per active function call, and each frame has its own copy of the parameters and locals. That's the whole mental model — recursion isn't magic, it's just many independent frames of the same function.

Every recursive function has two phases. Code before the recursive call runs on the way down — the winding phase — and code after it runs on the way back up — unwinding. That's why printing before the call gives you preorder and printing after gives you postorder, and why unwinding output appears in reverse order: the stack is LIFO.

The distinction I'm careful about is time versus space. Naive fibonacci makes exponentially many calls, so it's O(2^n) time, but its stack depth is only n, because at any moment only one root-to-leaf path is live — the rest have already returned and their frames popped. So it's O(n) space, not O(2^n).

In Python the practical constraint is the recursion limit, which defaults to 1000. Raising it with sys.setrecursionlimit works but is risky, because past a point you segfault the interpreter instead of getting a catchable RecursionError. The real fix for deep recursion is to convert to iteration with an explicit stack on the heap, which has no such limit.

docs.title: Kya hai
docs.text:
Recursion tree ek diagram hai jo har recursive call ko ek node ki tarah dikhata hai, aur har node par kitna kaam ho raha hai wo likhta hai. Us tree ko level-by-level jod kar aap complexity derive kar lete ho.

Real-world analogy: Ek company mein CEO ne ek project 2 VPs ko baanta. Har VP ne apna hissa 2 directors ko baanta. Har director ne 2 managers ko. Aap poori company ka total effort jaanna chahte ho. Aap har level par total effort jodte ho (5 CEO-hours + 2×3 VP-hours + 4×2 director-hours...) aur phir levels ka total nikaalte ho. Yahi recursion tree analysis hai.

docs.title: Kyu hai
docs.text:
Recurrence relations (T(n) = 2T(n/2) + n) ko solve karne ke teen tareeke hain:

  1. Substitution — guess karo aur induction se prove karo. Guess karna mushkil.
  2. Master Theorem — formula lagao. Fast, par sirf specific forms par kaam karta hai.
  3. Recursion tree — draw karo aur ginn lo. Sabse intuitive, hamesha kaam karta hai.

Recursion tree sabse valuable hai kyunki wo aapko kyun bhi batata hai, sirf kya nahi. Aur jab Master Theorem apply nahi hota (jaise T(n) = T(n/3) + T(2n/3) + n), tab recursion tree hi bachata hai.

docs.title: Kaise kaam karta hai
docs.text:
Teen kadam:

1. Tree DRAW karo:
   - Root par original problem (size n)
   - Har node ke children = recursive calls
   - Har node par likho: "is call mein KITNA kaam hua" (recursive calls ko chhod kar)

2. HAR LEVEL ka total kaam nikaalo:
   - Level k par kitne nodes hain?
   - Har node ka size kya hai?
   - Har node par kitna kaam?
   - Multiply karo

3. LEVELS ka total jodo:
   - Kitne levels hain? (depth)
   - Sab levels ka sum

docs.title: Poora dry run
docs.text:
Example 1 — Merge sort: T(n) = 2T(n/2) + n

Level 0:                  n                          <- 1 node, size n, work n
                       /     \
Level 1:            n/2       n/2                    <- 2 nodes, size n/2, work n/2 each
                   /   \     /   \
Level 2:        n/4   n/4  n/4   n/4                 <- 4 nodes, size n/4, work n/4 each
                 ...
Level k:      2^k nodes, each of size n/2^k
                 ...
Level log n:  n nodes of size 1                      <- leaves

Table:

Level Nodes Size per node Work per node Total work at level 0 1 = 2^0 n n n 1 2 = 2^1 n/2 n/2 2 × n/2 = n 2 4 = 2^2 n/4 n/4 4 × n/4 = n 3 8 = 2^3 n/8 n/8 8 × n/8 = n k 2^k n/2^k n/2^k 2^k × n/2^k = n log₂n n 1 1 n × 1 = n

Depth: size n/2^k = 1 par leaves → 2^k = n → k = log₂n.

Total: n × (log₂n + 1) = O(n log n) ✓

Key observation: har level par kaam same hai (n). Ye "balanced" case hai.

Example 2 — Binary search: T(n) = T(n/2) + 1

Level 0:    n         work 1
            |
Level 1:   n/2        work 1
            |
Level 2:   n/4        work 1
            |
           ...
Level log n: 1        work 1
Level Nodes Work per node Total work 0 1 1 1 1 1 1 1 k 1 1 1 log n 1 1 1

Total: 1 × (log₂n + 1) = O(log n) ✓

Example 3 — Naive fibonacci: T(n) = T(n-1) + T(n-2) + 1

Level 0:                    n                        1 node
                          /   \
Level 1:              n-1       n-2                  2 nodes
                     /   \     /   \
Level 2:          n-2   n-3  n-3   n-4               4 nodes
                  /  \  ...
Level 3:       n-3  n-4 ...                          up to 8 nodes

Ye tree UNBALANCED hai — left branch n-1 jata hai, right n-2. Left subtree deeper hai.

Level Nodes (max) Work per node Total 0 1 1 1 1 2 1 2 2 4 1 4 k ≤ 2^k 1 ≤ 2^k

Depth: shortest path n-2, n-4, n-6... → depth n/2. Longest path n-1, n-2, n-3... → depth n.

Bounds: 

Lower bound: complete tree of depth n/2  ->  2^(n/2) nodes  ->  Omega(1.41^n)
Upper bound: complete tree of depth n    ->  2^n nodes      ->  O(2^n)

Actual: exactly fib(n+1) - 1 leaf nodes, and fib(n) ~ phi^n / sqrt(5)
        where phi = 1.618 (golden ratio)

T(n) = Theta(1.618^n)

Numbers: fib(40) naive → 331 million calls (~30 seconds Python mein). fib(50) → 40 billion calls (~hours). Yahi memoisation ka motivation hai.

Example 4 — Unbalanced but nice: T(n) = T(n/3) + T(2n/3) + n

(Ye wo case hai jahan Master Theorem apply NAHI hota.)

Level 0:                    n                     work n
                         /     \
Level 1:              n/3       2n/3              work n/3 + 2n/3 = n
                     /   \      /    \
Level 2:          n/9  2n/9  2n/9   4n/9          work n/9+2n/9+2n/9+4n/9 = n
                  ...
Level Total work 0 n 1 n/3 + 2n/3 = n 2 n/9 + 2n/9 + 2n/9 + 4n/9 = 9n/9 = n k n (jab tak koi branch leaf tak na pahunche)

Har level par work n hai — merge sort jaisa. Par depth alag hai:

Shortest path (hamesha n/3 branch):  n -> n/3 -> n/9 -> ... -> 1
   n/3^k = 1  ->  k = log_3(n)

Longest path (hamesha 2n/3 branch):  n -> 2n/3 -> 4n/9 -> ... -> 1
   n * (2/3)^k = 1  ->  (3/2)^k = n  ->  k = log_{3/2}(n) = log(n)/log(1.5)

Total work bounds:
   Lower: n * log_3(n)      = n * log(n)/log(3)     ~ 0.63 n log2(n)
   Upper: n * log_{3/2}(n)  = n * log(n)/log(1.5)   ~ 1.71 n log2(n)

Both are Theta(n log n)  ->  T(n) = Theta(n log n)  ✓

Ye derivation kyun important hai? Quicksort ka average case analysis exactly aisa hi hai — splits perfectly balanced nahi hote par "reasonably balanced" hote hain, aur phir bhi O(n log n) nikalta hai.

Example 5 — Kaam ghatta hai: T(n) = 2T(n/2) + 1

Level Nodes Work per node Total 0 1 1 1 1 2 1 2 2 4 1 4 k 2^k 1 2^k log n n 1 n

Total: 1 + 2 + 4 + ... + n = 2n - 1 = O(n)

Yahan LEAVES dominate karti hain — poora kaam bottom level par hai. Ye "leaf-heavy" case hai. (Example: binary tree ka size count karna.)

Example 6 — Root dominates: T(n) = 2T(n/2) + n²

Level Nodes Work per node Total 0 1 n² n² 1 2 (n/2)² = n²/4 2 × n²/4 = n²/2 2 4 n²/16 4 × n²/16 = n²/4 k 2^k n²/4^k n²/2^k

Total: n² × (1 + 1/2 + 1/4 + 1/8 + ...) = n² × 2 = O(n²)

Yahan ROOT dominate karta hai — geometric series converge kar jati hai, to top level ka kaam hi total hai.

docs.title: Teen patterns — ye yaad rakho
docs.text:
PATTERN 1: Har level par SAME kaam (balanced)
   T(n) = 2T(n/2) + n     ->  n per level, log n levels  ->  O(n log n)
   Ye tab hota hai jab work function "critical exponent" par ho

PATTERN 2: LEAVES dominate (bottom-heavy)
   T(n) = 2T(n/2) + 1     ->  1, 2, 4, ..., n  ->  O(n)
   Ye tab jab recursive calls ka multiplication work se tez badhe

PATTERN 3: ROOT dominates (top-heavy)
   T(n) = 2T(n/2) + n²    ->  n², n²/2, n²/4, ...  ->  O(n²)
   Ye tab jab work bahut mehnga ho recursion ke muqable

Ye teen patterns hi Master Theorem ke teen cases hain — bas Master Theorem inhe formula mein likh deta hai. Agar aap tree draw kar sakte ho, aapko Master Theorem yaad rakhne ki zaroorat hi nahi.

docs.title: Code — recursion tree ko count karke verify karna
docs.text:
def count_calls(func):
    """Decorator jo recursive calls ginn leta hai."""
    def wrapper(*args, **kwargs):                   # 1
        wrapper.calls += 1                          # 2
        wrapper.depth += 1                          # 3
        wrapper.max_depth = max(wrapper.max_depth, wrapper.depth)   # 4
        try:                                        # 5
            return func(*args, **kwargs)            # 6
        finally:                                    # 7
            wrapper.depth -= 1                      # 8
    wrapper.calls = 0                               # 9
    wrapper.depth = 0                               # 10
    wrapper.max_depth = 0                           # 11
    return wrapper                                  # 12


@count_calls                                        # 13
def fib(n):
    if n <= 1:                                      # 14
        return n                                    # 15
    return fib(n - 1) + fib(n - 2)                  # 16


fib(20)
print(f"Total calls: {fib.calls}")        # 21891
print(f"Max depth:   {fib.max_depth}")    # 20

Line-by-line:

  1. *args, **kwargs — kisi bhi signature wale function ko wrap kar sakta hai.
  2. wrapper.calls += 1 — total calls counter. Ye function object par attribute hai (Python mein functions objects hain), global variable se cleaner.
  3. wrapper.depth += 1 — current depth badhao (winding).
  4. max_depth update — peak stack usage. 5-6. try ke andar actual call. 7-8. finally mein depth ghatao (unwinding). finally isliye ki agar exception aa jaye to bhi depth sahi rahe. Bina finally ke, ek exception depth ko permanently galat kar deta. 9-11. Counters initialise. Wrapper define hone ke BAAD — kyunki wrapper object line 9 se pehle exist nahi karta.
  5. Wrapper return.
  6. Decorator apply. 14-16. Naive fibonacci.

Output verify karta hai theory:

fib(20):  Total calls = 21,891
          Theory: ~2 * fib(21) - 1 = 2 * 10946 - 1 = 21,891  ✓
          Ya: 1.618^20 ≈ 15,127 (same order)  ✓

          Max depth = 20
          Theory: longest path n-1, n-2, ..., 1  ->  depth n = 20  ✓

Time vs space clearly dikh raha hai: 21,891 calls (time) par sirf 20 depth (space).

docs.title: Kitne tareeke se optimize (recursion trees ka use)
docs.text:
# Insight from tree Optimisation Example 1 Same subtree baar baar Memoisation fib: O(2^n) → O(n) 2 Tree unbalanced hai Balance karo (better pivot) quicksort worst → average 3 Leaves dominate karti hain Base case ko bada karo (cutoff) merge sort + insertion sort 4 Root dominates Divide step ko sasta karo Better partitioning 5 Ek branch useless hai Prune karo Backtracking, alpha-beta 6 Depth linear hai Iteration mein badlo Tail recursion → loop

Interview answer: A recursion tree makes a recurrence concrete: draw one node per call, label each with the non-recursive work it does, sum across each level, then sum the levels. It's the most reliable way to solve a recurrence because it shows you where the time actually goes, not just the answer.

For merge sort's T(n) = 2T(n/2) + n, level k has 2^k nodes of size n/2^k, so every level does exactly n work, and the depth is log n because the size halves each level — hence n log n. For T(n) = 2T(n/2) + 1, each level does 2^k work, so the leaves dominate and the total is the geometric sum 1 + 2 + 4 + ... + n, which is O(n). For T(n) = 2T(n/2) + n², the root dominates — the levels form a converging geometric series n², n²/2, n²/4, which sums to 2n², so O(n²).

Those three shapes — level-balanced, leaf-heavy, root-heavy — are exactly the three cases of the Master Theorem. If you can draw the tree you don't need to memorise the theorem, and the tree also handles recurrences the theorem can't, like T(n) = T(n/3) + T(2n/3) + n, where the levels still do n work each but the depth ranges between log₃n and log₁.₅n, both Theta(log n), so the answer is Theta(n log n). That's essentially quicksort's average-case argument.

Trees also surface optimisations directly. Seeing the same subtree repeated in fibonacci's tree is what tells you memoisation collapses it from exponential to linear.

docs.title: Kya hai
docs.text:
Master Theorem ek formula hai jo T(n) = a·T(n/b) + f(n) form ki recurrences ko turant solve kar deta hai, bina tree draw kiye.

Real-world analogy: Recursion tree draw karna = har baar zameen naap kar area nikaalna. Master Theorem = area = length × width formula. Formula tez hai, par sirf rectangles par kaam karta hai. Agar shape weird hai to naapna hi padega.

docs.title: Kyu hai
docs.text:
Recursion tree accurate hai par har baar draw karna slow hai. Master Theorem un common cases ko formula bana deta hai jo divide-and-conquer mein baar baar aate hain.

Aur ye interview mein directly poochha jata hai: "What's the complexity of T(n) = 3T(n/2) + n?" — Master Theorem se 10 second mein jawab. Tree se 2 minute.

docs.title: Kaise kaam karta hai
docs.text:
Standard form:

T(n) = a · T(n/b) + f(n)

   a = kitne subproblems banate hain   (a >= 1)
   b = har subproblem kitna chhota hai (b > 1)
   f(n) = divide + combine ka cost (recursion ke bahar ka kaam)

Critical exponent:

c = log_b(a)

Iska matlab: "leaves ki sankhya n^c hai"

Kyun? Tree mein:
   depth = log_b(n)
   leaves = a^depth = a^(log_b n) = n^(log_b a) = n^c

Ab teen cases — compare karo f(n) ko n^c se:

CASE 1: f(n) = O(n^(c - epsilon))     -- f CHHOTA hai, leaves dominate
        T(n) = Theta(n^c)

CASE 2: f(n) = Theta(n^c · log^k n)   -- BARABAR hai, har level same kaam
        T(n) = Theta(n^c · log^(k+1) n)
        (sabse common: k=0, to T(n) = Theta(n^c log n))

CASE 3: f(n) = Omega(n^(c + epsilon))  -- f BADA hai, root dominates
        AND regularity condition: a·f(n/b) <= k·f(n) for some k < 1
        T(n) = Theta(f(n))

Practical mental shortcut — teen cases ko yaad rakhne ka tareeka:

Compare:  f(n)  vs  n^(log_b a)

   f chhota  ->  answer = n^(log_b a)         (leaves ka kaam)
   f barabar ->  answer = f(n) · log n        (ek extra log)
   f bada    ->  answer = f(n)                (root ka kaam)

"JO BADA HAI WAHI ANSWER HAI, AUR BARABAR PAR EK LOG LAG JATA HAI"

docs.title: Poora dry run
docs.text:
Example 1 — Merge sort: T(n) = 2T(n/2) + n

a = 2, b = 2, f(n) = n

c = log_b(a) = log_2(2) = 1
n^c = n^1 = n

Compare f(n) = n  vs  n^c = n
   BARABAR  ->  CASE 2 with k = 0

T(n) = Theta(n^1 · log^1 n) = Theta(n log n)   ✓

Verify with tree: har level par n kaam, log n levels → n log n ✓

Example 2 — Binary search: T(n) = T(n/2) + 1

a = 1, b = 2, f(n) = 1 = n^0

c = log_2(1) = 0
n^c = n^0 = 1

Compare f(n) = 1  vs  n^c = 1
   BARABAR  ->  CASE 2 with k = 0

T(n) = Theta(n^0 · log n) = Theta(log n)   ✓

Example 3 — Binary tree traversal: T(n) = 2T(n/2) + 1

a = 2, b = 2, f(n) = 1

c = log_2(2) = 1
n^c = n

Compare f(n) = 1  vs  n^c = n
   f CHHOTA hai (1 = O(n^(1-epsilon)) for epsilon = 1)  ->  CASE 1

T(n) = Theta(n^1) = Theta(n)   ✓

Verify with tree: leaves n hain, har leaf par O(1) → O(n) ✓

Example 4 — Root-dominated: T(n) = 2T(n/2) + n²

a = 2, b = 2, f(n) = n²

c = log_2(2) = 1
n^c = n

Compare f(n) = n²  vs  n^c = n
   f BADA hai (n² = Omega(n^(1+epsilon)) for epsilon = 1)  ->  CASE 3 candidate

Regularity check:  a·f(n/b) <= k·f(n) for some k < 1?
   2 · (n/2)² = 2 · n²/4 = n²/2
   Is n²/2 <= k·n² for some k < 1?  Haan, k = 1/2  ✓
   REGULARITY SATISFIED

T(n) = Theta(f(n)) = Theta(n²)   ✓

Example 5 — Strassen's matrix multiplication: T(n) = 7T(n/2) + n²

a = 7, b = 2, f(n) = n²

c = log_2(7) ≈ 2.807
n^c = n^2.807

Compare f(n) = n²  vs  n^2.807
   f CHHOTA hai  ->  CASE 1

T(n) = Theta(n^2.807)   ✓

Ye famous result hai — naive matrix multiplication O(n³) hai, Strassen O(n^2.807). 7 subproblems (naive 8 karta) hone se exponent gir gaya.

Compare: agar a = 8 hota (naive divide and conquer): 

c = log_2(8) = 3
f(n) = n² is O(n^(3-epsilon))  ->  CASE 1
T(n) = Theta(n³)   <- naive se koi fayda nahi

Strassen ka poora insight yahi hai: 8 se 7 multiplications par jao.

Example 6 — Karatsuba multiplication: T(n) = 3T(n/2) + n

a = 3, b = 2, f(n) = n

c = log_2(3) ≈ 1.585
n^c = n^1.585

Compare f(n) = n  vs  n^1.585
   f CHHOTA  ->  CASE 1

T(n) = Theta(n^1.585)   ✓

Naive multiplication O(n²) hai; Karatsuba O(n^1.585). Bade numbers ke liye ye real speedup hai.

Example 7 — Case 3 with regularity FAILURE (kab Master Theorem fail hota hai):

T(n) = 2T(n/2) + n·log(n)

a = 2, b = 2, f(n) = n log n
c = log_2(2) = 1,  n^c = n

Compare: n log n  vs  n
   n log n bada hai, PAR  n log n = Omega(n^(1+epsilon))?
   Kya n log n >= n^1.0001 for large n?
   NAHI -- log n polynomially chhota hai kisi bhi n^epsilon se.

   To ye NA Case 2 hai (kyunki exactly n nahi hai)
   NA Case 3 hai (kyunki polynomially bada nahi hai)

   MASTER THEOREM APPLY NAHI HOTA (basic version).

Extended Master Theorem (Case 2 generalised) se: 

f(n) = Theta(n^c · log^k n)  with k = 1
T(n) = Theta(n^c · log^(k+1) n) = Theta(n · log² n)

Ye "gap" Master Theorem ki sabse important limitation hai — n^c aur n^(c+epsilon) ke beech ki functions (jaise n^c log n) basic version handle nahi karta.

Example 8 — a ka format wrong: T(n) = T(n-1) + n

Ye a·T(n/b) form mein HAI HI NAHI -- yahan subproblem n-1 hai, n/b nahi.

MASTER THEOREM APPLY NAHI HOTA.

Tree se solve karo:
   n + (n-1) + (n-2) + ... + 1 = n(n+1)/2  ->  Theta(n²)

Ye quicksort ke worst case ka recurrence hai. Master Theorem n/b form maangta hai (divide), n-k form (decrease) nahi.
