docs.title: Code — Master Theorem ka calculator
docs.text:
import math                                         # 1


def master_theorem(a, b, f_exponent, f_log_power=0):
    """T(n) = a*T(n/b) + n^f_exponent * log^f_log_power(n)
    Return: (case, description)"""
    if a < 1 or b <= 1:                             # 2
        return (None, "Invalid: need a >= 1 and b > 1")   # 3
    c = math.log(a) / math.log(b)                   # 4
    eps = 1e-9                                      # 5
    if f_exponent < c - eps:                        # 6
        return (1, f"Theta(n^{c:.4f})")             # 7
    elif abs(f_exponent - c) < eps:                 # 8
        k = f_log_power                             # 9
        return (2, f"Theta(n^{c:.4f} * log^{k + 1}(n))")   # 10
    else:                                           # 11
        reg = a * (1 / b) ** f_exponent             # 12
        if reg < 1 - eps:                           # 13
            return (3, f"Theta(n^{f_exponent} * log^{f_log_power}(n))")   # 14
        return (None, "Case 3 candidate but regularity condition fails")   # 15


print(master_theorem(2, 2, 1))      # (2, 'Theta(n^1.0000 * log^1(n))')  merge sort
print(master_theorem(2, 2, 0))      # (1, 'Theta(n^1.0000)')             tree traversal
print(master_theorem(2, 2, 2))      # (3, 'Theta(n^2 * log^0(n))')       root-dominated
print(master_theorem(7, 2, 2))      # (1, 'Theta(n^2.8074)')             Strassen
print(master_theorem(3, 2, 1))      # (1, 'Theta(n^1.5850)')             Karatsuba

Line-by-line:

  1. math for log. 2-3. Validity check. a >= 1 (kam se kam ek subproblem) aur b > 1 (subproblem strictly chhota hona chahiye, warna recursion khatam hi nahi hoti). b = 1 par infinite recursion.
  2. c = log(a)/log(b) — change of base formula, kyunki Python ka math.log natural log deta hai. math.log(a, b) bhi likh sakte the — same cheez, thodi cleaner.
  3. eps — floating point comparison ke liye tolerance. log_2(8) = 3.0000000000000004 jaisi values aati hain, to == 3 fail ho jata. Ye float comparison ka standard fix hai. 6-7. Case 1 — f ka exponent c se chhota. 8-10. Case 2 — barabar. log^(k+1) — ek extra log. 11-15. Case 3 candidate — f bada.
  4. reg = a * (1/b)^f_exponent — regularity condition ka check. Condition hai: a·f(n/b) <= k·f(n) for some k < 1. Agar f(n) = n^p to f(n/b) = (n/b)^p = n^p / b^p. a · n^p / b^p <= k · n^p → a / b^p <= k. To k = a / b^p = a * (1/b)^p. Agar ye < 1 hai to condition satisfied. 13-14. Regularity OK → Case 3.
  5. Regularity fail — ye rare hai par possible (jaise f(n) = n²·sin²(n) type oscillating functions). Us case mein Master Theorem apply nahi hota, tree/substitution use karo.

docs.title: Complexity derive karke — Master Theorem ka proof sketch
docs.text:
Case 2 ka proof (sabse common case):

T(n) = a·T(n/b) + f(n)   with f(n) = Theta(n^c), c = log_b(a)

Recursion tree:
   Level i:  a^i nodes, each of size n/b^i
             work per node = f(n/b^i) = (n/b^i)^c
             total work at level i = a^i · (n/b^i)^c
                                   = a^i · n^c / b^(ic)
                                   = n^c · (a / b^c)^i

   Ab: b^c = b^(log_b a) = a
       To (a / b^c) = (a / a) = 1

   Total work at level i = n^c · 1^i = n^c    <- HAR LEVEL PAR SAME!

Depth = log_b(n)

Total = n^c · log_b(n) = Theta(n^c log n)   ✓

Case 1 ka proof:

f(n) = O(n^(c-eps)), yaani f chhota hai

Total work at level i = a^i · f(n/b^i)
                      <= a^i · (n/b^i)^(c-eps)
                      = n^(c-eps) · (a / b^(c-eps))^i
                      = n^(c-eps) · (a / (b^c · b^(-eps)))^i
                      = n^(c-eps) · (b^eps)^i          [kyunki b^c = a]

   Ye GEOMETRIC SERIES hai ratio b^eps > 1 ke saath -> INCREASING
   -> LAST level (leaves) dominate karta hai

Leaves ki sankhya = a^(log_b n) = n^(log_b a) = n^c
Har leaf par O(1) kaam

Total = Theta(n^c)   ✓

Case 3 ka proof:

f(n) = Omega(n^(c+eps)), yaani f bada hai

Total work at level i = n^(c+eps) · (a / b^(c+eps))^i
                      = n^(c+eps) · (b^(-eps))^i

   GEOMETRIC SERIES ratio b^(-eps) < 1 ke saath -> DECREASING
   -> FIRST level (root) dominate karta hai

Total = Theta(f(n))   ✓

Regularity condition ye ensure karti hai ki series sach mein converge kare
aur recursion niche ki taraf shrink ho.

docs.title: Kab use karna hai / kab nahi
docs.text:
Use karo jab: - Recurrence exactly a·T(n/b) + f(n) form mein hai. - Sab subproblems same size ke hain. - f(n) polynomial hai (n^p ya n^p log^k n). - Aapko fast answer chahiye interview mein.

Mat use karo (ya use nahi kar sakte) jab: - Subproblems alag size ke hain — T(n) = T(n/3) + T(2n/3) + n. Tree use karo. - Decrease-and-conquer hai — T(n) = T(n-1) + f(n). Ye n/b form nahi hai. - f(n) polynomially compare nahi hoti — T(n) = 2T(n/2) + n log n. Extended version chahiye. - Regularity condition fail — rare, par oscillating f par hota hai. - a ya b n par depend karte hain — T(n) = nT(n/2) + n. Ye Master Theorem ka scope nahi.

Alternatives:

Situation Method Standard divide & conquer Master Theorem Unequal splits Recursion tree T(n) = T(n-1) + f(n) Direct summation — sum of f(i) Complicated / unknown Substitution — guess + induction Multiple recursive terms Akra-Bazzi theorem (advanced)

Akra-Bazzi ka ek line summary: wo Master Theorem ka generalisation hai jo unequal splits handle karta hai. Formula involved hai, par jaanana ki wo exist karta hai — ye depth dikhata hai.

docs.title: Kitne tareeke se use karo (Master Theorem se algorithm design)
docs.text:
Master Theorem sirf analysis ka tool nahi hai — wo DESIGN ka tool bhi hai:

Sawaal: "Kya main matrix multiplication ko n^3 se tez kar sakta hoon?"

T(n) = a·T(n/2) + n²  ke saath, c = log_2(a)
   Result: Theta(n^log_2(a))  (Case 1, jab log_2(a) > 2, yaani a > 4)

Ab: n^3 se tez chahiye  ->  log_2(a) < 3  ->  a < 8

Naive divide-and-conquer a = 8 use karta hai (8 sub-multiplications).
Agar hum a = 7 kar sakein  ->  n^2.807  <- STRASSEN
Agar a = 6  ->  n^2.585
Agar a = 5  ->  n^2.322

Ye SAWAAL ne research direction di, aur Strassen ne 1969 mein a=7 achieve kiya.
Aaj ka best (Coppersmith-Winograd family) ~n^2.37 hai.

Yahi soch general design mein bhi lagti hai:

Aap kya control kar sakte ho Effect a ghatao (kam subproblems) Exponent log_b(a) girta — sabse bada impact b badhao (chhote subproblems) Exponent girta f(n) sasta karo Sirf Case 3 mein matter karta hai

Rule: agar aap Case 1 mein ho (leaves dominate), to f(n) optimise karna bekaar hai — a ya b badalna padega. Agar Case 3 mein ho (root dominates), to f(n) optimise karo. Master Theorem batata hai kahan effort lagana hai.

Interview answer: The Master Theorem solves recurrences of the form T(n) = a·T(n/b) + f(n), where a is the number of subproblems, b is the shrink factor, and f is the divide-and-combine cost. You compute the critical exponent c = log_b(a) — that's the exponent of the number of leaves, since there are a^(log_b n) = n^(log_b a) of them — and compare f(n) to n^c.

If f is polynomially smaller, the leaves dominate and T(n) = Theta(n^c). If they're the same order, every level does equal work and you get an extra log: T(n) = Theta(n^c log n). If f is polynomially larger and satisfies a regularity condition, the root dominates and T(n) = Theta(f(n)). The one-line version is: whichever is bigger wins, and a tie costs you a log factor.

Merge sort is a = 2, b = 2, f = n, so c = 1 and f matches n^1 — case 2, n log n. Strassen is a = 7, b = 2, f = n², so c = log2(7) ≈ 2.807, and f is smaller — case 1, n^2.807. That last one shows the theorem as a design tool, not just an analysis tool: naive divide-and-conquer matrix multiplication uses eight subproblems, giving log2(8) = 3, and Strassen's entire contribution was reducing eight to seven, which dropped the exponent below 3.

The important limitation is the word "polynomially". T(n) = 2T(n/2) + n log n falls in the gap: n log n is bigger than n but not bigger by any n^epsilon factor, so neither case 2 nor case 3 applies in the basic form. And T(n) = T(n-1) + n isn't of the right shape at all — that's decrease-and-conquer, not divide-and-conquer, and you solve it by direct summation to get n²/2. When the theorem doesn't apply I fall back to drawing the recursion tree, which always works.

docs.title: Kya hai
docs.text:
Divide and conquer ek problem-solving template hai: problem ko chhote independent hisson mein todo, har hisse ko recursively solve karo, aur results ko jodo.

Real-world analogy: Ek 500-page report ka proofreading. Aap akele nahi karte — aap use 5 logon mein 100-100 pages baant dete ho. Har koi apna hissa independently karta hai. Phir sab apne corrections ek jagah jama karte hain. Teen kadam: divide, conquer, combine.

docs.title: Kyu hai
docs.text:
Bahut saari problems ka naive solution O(n²) ya usse bura hota hai. Divide and conquer aksar use O(n log n) mein le aata hai, do wajah se:

  1. Subproblems independent hain — parallelise ho sakte hain.
  2. Combine step aksar linear hota hai — aur n linear kaam × log n levels = n log n.

Kab ye kaam karta hai?

Problem P ko chhote instances P1, P2, ..., Pk mein tod sakte ho?
   AUR
P1...Pk ke solutions se P ka solution bana sakte ho?
   AUR
Wo combining step recursion se sasta hai?

   HAAN -> Divide and conquer

Kab kaam NAHI karta: jab subproblems overlap karte hain (fibonacci) — us case mein dynamic programming chahiye. Ye do techniques ka sabse bada farak hai:

Divide and conquer:  subproblems INDEPENDENT hain (merge sort ke halves)
Dynamic programming: subproblems OVERLAP karte hain (fib(n-1) aur fib(n-2) dono fib(n-3) use karte hain)

docs.title: Kaise kaam karta hai
docs.text:
Universal template:

def divide_and_conquer(problem):

    # 1. BASE CASE
    if problem is small enough:
        return solve_directly(problem)

    # 2. DIVIDE
    subproblems = split(problem)

    # 3. CONQUER (recurse)
    sub_solutions = [divide_and_conquer(sp) for sp in subproblems]

    # 4. COMBINE
    return merge(sub_solutions)

Char parts, aur har ek mein design decisions:

Part Sawaal poochhna hai Merge sort ka jawab Quick sort ka jawab Base case Kitna chhota "chhota kaafi" hai? 1 element (ya cutoff 32) 1 element (ya cutoff 16) Divide Kaise todein? Kitna cost? Beech se, O(1) Pivot ke around, O(n) Conquer Kitne subproblems? 2, each n/2 2, sizes variable Combine Kaise jodein? Kitna cost? Merge, O(n) Kuchh nahi, O(1)

Merge sort aur quick sort ek doosre ke ulte hain:

Merge sort:   sasta divide (O(1)),  mehnga combine (O(n))
Quick sort:   mehnga divide (O(n)), sasta combine (O(1))

Dono ka total: O(n) per level  ->  O(n log n)

Ye "hard work kahan karein" ka classic trade-off hai.

docs.title: Poora dry run
docs.text:
Problem: Maximum Subarray Sum (divide and conquer se)

Array mein aisa contiguous subarray dhoondho jiska sum maximum ho.

Array: [-2, 1, -3, 4, -1, 2, 1, -5, 4], n = 9.

Divide and conquer ka idea:

Beech se todo. Maximum subarray teen jagah ho sakta hai:
   1. Poori tarah LEFT half mein
   2. Poori tarah RIGHT half mein
   3. Beech ko CROSS karta hua

Pehle do recursively solve honge. Teesra alag se calculate karna padega.

Cross-sum kaise nikaalein?

mid se LEFT ki taraf chalte hue best sum:
   arr[mid], arr[mid]+arr[mid-1], arr[mid]+arr[mid-1]+arr[mid-2], ... ka maximum

mid+1 se RIGHT ki taraf chalte hue best sum:
   arr[mid+1], arr[mid+1]+arr[mid+2], ... ka maximum

Cross sum = left_best + right_best

Ye O(n) hai (ek left scan + ek right scan)

Trace — top level call: solve(0, 8), mid = 4.

Left half [-2, 1, -3, 4, -1], indices 0-4:

solve(0, 4), mid = 2: - solve(0, 2) on [-2, 1, -3], mid = 1: - solve(0, 1) on [-2, 1], mid = 0: - solve(0,0) → -2 - solve(1,1) → 1 - cross: left from 0 = -2, right from 1 = 1, cross = -1 - max(-2, 1, -1) = 1 - solve(2, 2) → -3 - cross around mid=1: left from 1 going left: arr[1]=1, arr[1]+arr[0]=-1 → best 1. right from 2: arr[2]=-3 → best -3. cross = 1 + (-3) = -2 - max(1, -3, -2) = 1 - solve(3, 4) on [4, -1], mid = 3: - solve(3,3) → 4; solve(4,4) → -1 - cross: left from 3 = 4, right from 4 = -1, cross = 3 - max(4, -1, 3) = 4 - cross around mid=2 (range 0-4): left from 2 going left: arr[2]=-3, +arr[1]=-2, +arr[0]=-4 → best -2. right from 3: arr[3]=4, +arr[4]=3 → best 4. cross = -2 + 4 = 2 - max(1, 4, 2) = 4

Right half [2, 1, -5, 4], indices 5-8:

solve(5, 8), mid = 6: - solve(5, 6) on [2, 1]: max = 3 (both together) - solve(7, 8) on [-5, 4]: solve(7,7)=-5, solve(8,8)=4, cross=-1 → max = 4 - cross around mid=6: left from 6: arr[6]=1, +arr[5]=3 → best 3. right from 7: arr[7]=-5, +arr[8]=-1 → best -1. cross = 3 + (-1) = 2 - max(3, 4, 2) = 4

Top-level cross around mid=4 (range 0-8): - left from 4: arr[4]=-1, +arr[3]=3, +arr[2]=0, +arr[1]=1, +arr[0]=-1 → best 3 - right from 5: arr[5]=2, +arr[6]=3, +arr[7]=-2, +arr[8]=2 → best 3 - cross = 3 + 3 = 6

Final: max(left=4, right=4, cross=6) = 6 ✓

Verify: subarray [4, -1, 2, 1] = 4 - 1 + 2 + 1 = 6 ✓

Summary table:

Call Range Left result Right result Cross result Max solve(0,0) [-2] — — — -2 solve(1,1) [1] — — — 1 solve(0,1) [-2,1] -2 1 -1 1 solve(2,2) [-3] — — — -3 solve(0,2) [-2,1,-3] 1 -3 -2 1 solve(3,3) [4] — — — 4 solve(4,4) [-1] — — — -1 solve(3,4) [4,-1] 4 -1 3 4 solve(0,4) left half 1 4 2 4 solve(5,6) [2,1] 2 1 3 3 solve(7,8) [-5,4] -5 4 -1 4 solve(5,8) right half 3 4 2 4 solve(0,8) full 4 4 6 6 ✓

docs.title: Code
docs.text:
def max_subarray_dc(arr):
    """Maximum subarray sum, divide and conquer se. O(n log n)."""
    if not arr:                                     # 1
        return 0                                    # 2
    return _mss(arr, 0, len(arr) - 1)               # 3


def _mss(arr, lo, hi):
    if lo == hi:                                    # 4
        return arr[lo]                              # 5
    mid = lo + (hi - lo) // 2                       # 6
    left_max = _mss(arr, lo, mid)                   # 7
    right_max = _mss(arr, mid + 1, hi)              # 8
    cross_max = _cross_sum(arr, lo, mid, hi)        # 9
    return max(left_max, right_max, cross_max)      # 10


def _cross_sum(arr, lo, mid, hi):
    """Best sum jo mid aur mid+1 dono ko include kare."""
    left_best = float('-inf')                       # 11
    total = 0                                       # 12
    for i in range(mid, lo - 1, -1):                # 13
        total += arr[i]                             # 14
        left_best = max(left_best, total)           # 15
    right_best = float('-inf')                      # 16
    total = 0                                       # 17
    for i in range(mid + 1, hi + 1):                # 18
        total += arr[i]                             # 19
        right_best = max(right_best, total)         # 20
    return left_best + right_best                   # 21

Line-by-line:

1-2. Khali guard. 0 return karna debatable hai (kuchh definitions kehti hain empty subarray allowed nahi, to -inf ya exception behtar) — problem statement par depend. 3. Helper call, inclusive bounds.

4-5. Base case: ek element. Uska sum wahi element hai. Note: negative bhi ho sakta hai — hum "at least one element" wali definition use kar rahe hain.

  1. Mid.
  2. Left half ka best.
  3. Right half mid + 1 se — mid left mein hai.
  4. Cross sum — ye woh case hai jo recursion cover nahi karti.

  5. Teenon ka max.

  6. left_best = float('-inf') — 0 se initialise NAHI karna. Agar saare elements negative hon ([-5, -3, -8]) to 0 se initialise karne par answer 0 aata, jo galat hai (kyunki hume kam se kam ek element lena hai). -inf correct hai.

  7. Running sum.
  8. for i in range(mid, lo - 1, -1) — mid se lo tak ULTA. lo - 1 (exclusive end) isliye ki lo include ho. range(mid, lo, -1) lo ko chhod deta. Ulta kyun? Kyunki cross-sum ko mid zaroor include karna hai (definition se). Hum mid se shuru karke left ki taraf extend karte hain aur best point yaad rakhte hain. 14-15. Running sum aur best track. max ke saath, kyunki extend karna hamesha behtar nahi hota (negative numbers aa sakte hain). 16-20. Same right side ke liye, mid+1 se hi tak seedha.
  9. Dono ka sum. Ye guaranteed contiguous hai kyunki left mid par khatam hota hai aur right mid+1 se shuru.

Comparison — Kadane's algorithm (DP, O(n)):

def max_subarray_kadane(arr):
    """Maximum subarray sum, O(n) — divide and conquer se behtar."""
    if not arr:                                     # 1
        return 0                                    # 2
    best = current = arr[0]                         # 3
    for x in arr[1:]:                               # 4
        current = max(x, current + x)               # 5
        best = max(best, current)                   # 6
    return best                                     # 7

1-2. Guard. 3. best = ab tak ka global best. current = is index par khatam hone wala best subarray. Dono arr[0] se — pehla element hi pehla candidate hai. 4. Baaki elements. 5. current = max(x, current + x) — ye poora algorithm hai. Do choices: - current + x — pichhle subarray ko extend karo. - x — naya subarray yahin se shuru karo. Jo bada ho wahi. current negative ho gaya to use extend karna kabhi faayde ka nahi — naya shuru karna behtar. 6. Global best update. 7. Result.

Ye O(n) hai — divide and conquer ke O(n log n) se behtar. Ye ek important lesson hai: divide and conquer hamesha best nahi hota. Agar problem mein "optimal substructure" hai aur ek linear DP scan kaam kar sakta hai, to wo behtar hai.

Doosra example — Closest Pair of Points (yahan D&C sach mein zaroori hai):

import math

def closest_pair(points):
    """2D plane mein sabse nazdeek do points ki doori. O(n log n)."""
    px = sorted(points, key=lambda p: p[0])         # 1
    py = sorted(points, key=lambda p: p[1])         # 2
    return _cp(px, py)                              # 3


def _cp(px, py):
    n = len(px)                                     # 4
    if n <= 3:                                      # 5
        return _brute_force(px)                     # 6
    mid = n // 2                                    # 7
    mid_x = px[mid][0]                              # 8
    left_px, right_px = px[:mid], px[mid:]          # 9
    left_set = set(map(tuple, left_px))             # 10
    left_py = [p for p in py if tuple(p) in left_set]     # 11
    right_py = [p for p in py if tuple(p) not in left_set]   # 12
    d_left = _cp(left_px, left_py)                  # 13
    d_right = _cp(right_px, right_py)               # 14
    d = min(d_left, d_right)                        # 15
    strip = [p for p in py if abs(p[0] - mid_x) < d]      # 16
    return min(d, _strip_closest(strip, d))         # 17


def _strip_closest(strip, d):
    best = d                                        # 18
    for i in range(len(strip)):                     # 19
        for j in range(i + 1, min(i + 8, len(strip))):    # 20
            dist = _dist(strip[i], strip[j])        # 21
            if dist < best:                         # 22
                best = dist                         # 23
    return best                                     # 24


def _dist(a, b):
    return math.hypot(a[0] - b[0], a[1] - b[1])     # 25


def _brute_force(pts):
    best = float('inf')                             # 26
    for i in range(len(pts)):                       # 27
        for j in range(i + 1, len(pts)):            # 28
            best = min(best, _dist(pts[i], pts[j])) # 29
    return best                                     # 30

Line-by-line:

1-2. Do pre-sorted copies — ek x se, ek y se. Ye ek baar sort hoti hain (O(n log n)), phir recursion unhe reuse karti hai. Agar aap har recursive call mein sort karte to T(n) = 2T(n/2) + n log n = O(n log² n) ho jata. Ye pre-sorting hi O(n log n) achieve karti hai. 3. Recurse. 4. Size. 5-6. Base case: 3 ya kam points → brute force (3 pairs max). Bade base case use kiya kyunki chhote inputs par recursion ka overhead brute force se zyada hai, aur n <= 3 par mid split degenerate ho sakta hai. 7-8. Mid point aur uski x-coordinate — ye "dividing line" hai. 9. x-sorted arrays ko split. 10. set bana liya left points ka — O(1) membership test ke liye. map(tuple, ...) isliye ki lists hashable nahi hoti, tuples hoti hain. 11-12. y-sorted array ko bhi split karo, PAR y-order maintain rakhte hue. Ye O(n) filter hai, sort nahi — isliye recurrence 2T(n/2) + O(n) rehta hai. 13-14. Recursive calls. 15. Dono halves ka minimum. 16. strip — dividing line ke d ke andar wale points. Kyunki agar closest pair halves ke aar paar hai, to dono points line se d se kam door hone chahiye (warna unki doori d se zyada hogi). Ye already y-sorted hai (kyunki py se filter kiya). 17. Strip ka best aur d ka min.

18-24. _strip_closest — yahan jaadu hai. 19-20. min(i + 8, len(strip)) — sirf agle 7 points check karo! Kyun sirf 7? Ye ek geometric proof hai: 

Strip 2d wide hai (line ke dono taraf d).
Agar aap strip ko d x d ke squares mein baanto, to har square mein
ZYADA SE ZYADA ek point ho sakta hai (kyunki har half ke andar
koi do points d se kam door nahi hain -- wo hum already jaan chuke hain).

Ek point ke liye, jo points uske y-coordinate se d ke andar hain,
wo ek 2d x d rectangle mein hain, jisme zyada se zyada 8 squares hain
(2 x 4 grid of d/2 sized cells in the tighter version).

To har point ke liye zyada se zyada 7 aur points check karne hain.
Isliye ye double loop O(n) hai, O(n²) nahi. Ye poore algorithm ka critical insight hai. 21-23. Distance aur best update. 24. Result. 25. math.hypot(dx, dy) — sqrt(dx² + dy²), par overflow-safe aur zyada accurate. Manually math.sqrt(dx**2 + dy**2) likhne se bade values par overflow ho sakta hai. 26-30. Brute force base case.

Complexity: 

Pre-sorting:  O(n log n)  -- ek baar
Recursion:    T(n) = 2T(n/2) + O(n)   [split O(n), strip build O(n), strip scan O(n)]
              = O(n log n)

Total: O(n log n)

Brute force O(n²) hai. n = 10,000 par: 10^8 vs 1.3×10^5. ~800x tez.

docs.title: Complexity derive karke — general D&C
docs.text:
Generic:  T(n) = a·T(n/b) + D(n) + C(n)

   a = subproblems
   b = shrink factor
   D(n) = divide ka cost
   C(n) = combine ka cost

f(n) = D(n) + C(n)  ->  Master Theorem lagao

Common patterns:

Algorithm a b D(n) C(n) T(n) Binary search 1 2 O(1) O(1) O(log n) Merge sort 2 2 O(1) O(n) O(n log n) Quick sort (avg) 2 2 O(n) O(1) O(n log n) Max subarray 2 2 O(1) O(n) O(n log n) Closest pair 2 2 O(n) O(n) O(n log n) Karatsuba 3 2 O(n) O(n) O(n^1.585) Strassen 7 2 O(n²) O(n²) O(n^2.807) Tree traversal 2 2 O(1) O(1) O(n)

Space: 

Recursion stack:  O(log n) balanced, O(n) unbalanced
Auxiliary data:   algorithm-specific (merge sort O(n), quicksort O(1))

docs.title: Kab use karna hai / kab nahi
docs.text:
Use karo jab: - Problem naturally splits hoti hai — sorting, searching, geometry, matrices. - Subproblems independent hain (overlap nahi karte). - Combine step sasta hai recursion ke muqable. - Parallelism chahiye — independent subproblems alag cores par.

Mat use karo jab: - Subproblems overlap karte hain → DP use karo (fibonacci, LCS, knapsack). - Linear solution exist karta hai → Kadane's, prefix sums, two pointers. D&C ka log n factor waste hai. - Combine step recursion se mehnga hai → Case 3 mein aa jaoge, koi fayda nahi. - Recursion depth bahut zyada — Python ki 1000 limit.

Divide and conquer vs Dynamic programming — ye farak interview mein poochha jata hai:

Aspect Divide & Conquer Dynamic Programming Subproblems Independent Overlapping Same subproblem dobara? Nahi Haan, kai baar Storage Zaroori nahi Zaroori (memo/table) Direction Top-down (usually) Top-down ya bottom-up Example Merge sort, binary search Fibonacci, LCS, knapsack Complexity source Recursion tree ki shape Distinct states ki sankhya

docs.title: Kitne tareeke se optimize
docs.text:
# Optimisation Kya deta hai Kya leta hai 1 Bada base case (cutoff) Chhote inputs par brute force tez — recursion overhead khatam Cutoff tune karna 2 a ghatao — kam subproblems (Strassen, Karatsuba) Exponent girta — sabse bada impact Bahut clever algebra chahiye 3 Pre-processing — ek baar sort karo, recursion mein reuse n log² n → n log n (closest pair) Extra memory 4 Memoise agar overlaps hain Exponential → polynomial Ab wo DP hai 5 Parallelise — independent subproblems alag threads par Multi-core linear speedup Thread overhead; chhote inputs par ulta 6 Tail call elimination Stack O(n) → O(log n) Sirf ek recursive call wale cases mein 7 Iterative bottom-up Recursion overhead khatam, stack risk khatam Code kam readable

Parallel divide and conquer:

from concurrent.futures import ThreadPoolExecutor    # 1

PARALLEL_CUTOFF = 10000                             # 2

def parallel_merge_sort(arr, executor=None, depth=0):
    if len(arr) <= 1:                               # 3
        return arr                                  # 4
    if len(arr) < PARALLEL_CUTOFF or depth > 3:     # 5
        return _sequential_merge_sort(arr)          # 6
    mid = len(arr) // 2                             # 7
    own = executor is None                          # 8
    if own:                                         # 9
        executor = ThreadPoolExecutor(max_workers=4)      # 10
    try:                                            # 11
        fut_left = executor.submit(parallel_merge_sort, arr[:mid], executor, depth + 1)   # 12
        right = parallel_merge_sort(arr[mid:], executor, depth + 1)     # 13
        left = fut_left.result()                    # 14
        return merge(left, right)                   # 15
    finally:                                        # 16
        if own:                                     # 17
            executor.shutdown()                     # 18
  1. Thread pool.
  2. Cutoff — isse chhote arrays par parallelism ka overhead fayde se zyada hai. 3-4. Base case. 5-6. Do conditions: array chhota hai, ya depth zyada ho gayi. Depth limit zaroori hai warna aap hazaaron threads bana doge — har ek ka creation cost ~50 microseconds, jo poora fayda kha jayega. depth > 3 matlab maximum 2^3 = 8 parallel branches.
  3. Mid. 8-10. Agar caller ne executor nahi diya to khud banao (aur baad mein shutdown karo).
  4. Left half ko background thread par submit karo.
  5. Right half ko IS thread par karo — ek naya thread banane ki jagah current thread ko use karna zyada efficient hai. Ye "work stealing" ka simple version hai.
  6. Left ka result wait karo.
  7. Merge — ye sequential hona chahiye, dono halves chahiye. 16-18. Cleanup.

Note: Python mein GIL ki wajah se CPU-bound work threads se parallelise nahi hota. Asli parallelism ke liye ProcessPoolExecutor chahiye — par uska data serialisation cost zyada hai. Ye Python ki ek genuine limitation hai jo interview mein mention karna acha lagta hai.

Interview answer: Divide and conquer has four parts: a base case, a divide step, recursive conquest of the subproblems, and a combine step. The design question is where you put the work. Merge sort has a trivial divide — just take the midpoint — and an O(n) combine. Quicksort is the mirror image: an O(n) divide via partitioning and a free combine, because after partitioning the pieces are already in the right relative order. Both end up doing O(n) per level, so both are O(n log n).

The precondition is that the subproblems are independent. If they overlap — the same subproblem arising in multiple branches, like fibonacci — then plain divide and conquer recomputes it exponentially many times, and the fix is dynamic programming, which is divide and conquer plus memoisation.

Two things I watch for. First, divide and conquer isn't automatically the best approach: maximum subarray sum has a clean O(n log n) divide and conquer solution, but Kadane's algorithm solves it in O(n) with a single linear scan. Second, preprocessing matters: in closest-pair-of-points, if you re-sort inside every recursive call you get O(n log² n), but sorting once up front and filtering the sorted arrays in linear time inside the recursion gives O(n log n).

Cross-question: "What's the difference between divide and conquer and dynamic programming?"

Whether the subproblems overlap. In divide and conquer each subproblem appears once, so there's nothing to cache and no table needed. In dynamic programming the same subproblem is reached from multiple paths, so you store results and reuse them. Structurally, DP is divide and conquer with memoisation — and in fact the usual way to derive a DP solution is to write the naive recursion first and then observe the repeated subproblems.

docs.title: Kya hai
docs.text:
Memoisation ka matlab hai: jo answer ek baar compute kar liya, use yaad rakh lo, aur agli baar wahi input aane par dobara compute mat karo — bas yaad kiya hua answer de do.

Real-world analogy: Aap calculator par sqrt(2) nikaalte ho aur uska result ek diary mein likh lete ho. Agle 50 baar jab sqrt(2) chahiye ho, aap calculator nahi uthate — diary dekh lete ho. Diary hi memo table hai.

docs.title: Kyu hai
docs.text:
Recursion tree wale section mein humne dekha tha ki fib(4) mein fib(2) do baar compute hota hai. Bade n par ye duplication catastrophic ho jati hai:

fib(30):  ~2.7 million calls   (~1 second Python mein)
fib(40):  ~331 million calls   (~2 minutes)
fib(50):  ~40 billion calls    (~4 ghante)
fib(100): ~10^21 calls         (universe ki umar se zyada waqt)

Par DISTINCT subproblems kitne hain?
fib(0), fib(1), fib(2), ..., fib(n)  ->  sirf n+1

fib(100) ke liye sirf 101 distinct values compute karni hain!
Baaki sab REPEATS hain.

Memoisation ka poora idea: O(2^n) calls mein se sirf O(n) unique hain. Baaki sab lookup ho sakte hain.

Bina memo:  O(1.618^n) time
Ke saath:   O(n) time, O(n) space

fib(100):  10^21 operations  ->  100 operations

Ye Dynamic Programming ka pehla kadam hai — actually memoisation hi DP hai, bas top-down form mein.

docs.title: Kaise kaam karta hai
docs.text:
def f(x):
    if x in memo:                 # <- CACHE HIT: pehle compute kar chuke hain
        return memo[x]

    if base_case(x):              # <- BASE CASE
        result = base_value

    else:
        result = combine(f(smaller), f(smaller))    # <- RECURSE

    memo[x] = result              # <- CACHE MEIN SAVE karo
    return result

Teen requirements memoisation ke liye:

  1. Pure function — same input hamesha same output de. Agar function mein randomness ya external state hai to memoisation galat answers dega.
  2. Hashable inputs — cache ki key banani hai. Lists hashable nahi hain (tuples hain).
  3. Overlapping subproblems — warna cache kabhi hit hi nahi hoga, sirf memory waste.

Recursion tree par memoisation ka effect:

Bina memo (fib(5)):

                  5
              /       \
            4           3
          /   \       /   \
        3      2     2     1
      /  \    / \   / \
     2    1  1   0 1   0
    / \
   1   0

15 nodes


Memo ke saath (fib(5)):

                  5
              /       \
            4           [3]     <- CACHE HIT, subtree cut
          /   \
        3      [2]      <- CACHE HIT
      /   \
    2      [1]
   / \
  1   0

9 nodes, par unme se 3 cache hits (O(1))
Effectively: 6 real computations = n+1

Ye "subtree cutting" hi memoisation ka visual hai.

docs.text:
fib(6) with memoisation. Memo shuru mein khali {}.

Step Call Memo mein hai? Action Memo ke baad 1 fib(6) No needs fib(5), fib(4) {} 2 fib(5) No needs fib(4), fib(3) {} 3 fib(4) No needs fib(3), fib(2) {} 4 fib(3) No needs fib(2), fib(1) {} 5 fib(2) No needs fib(1), fib(0) {} 6 fib(1) No base case → 1 {1:1} 7 fib(0) No base case → 0 {0:0, 1:1} 8 fib(2) returns — 1 + 0 = 1 {0:0, 1:1, 2:1} 9 fib(1) YES CACHE HIT → 1 unchanged 10 fib(3) returns — 1 + 1 = 2 {0:0,1:1,2:1,3:2} 11 fib(2) YES CACHE HIT → 1 unchanged 12 fib(4) returns — 2 + 1 = 3 {...,4:3} 13 fib(3) YES CACHE HIT → 2 unchanged 14 fib(5) returns — 3 + 2 = 5 {...,5:5} 15 fib(4) YES CACHE HIT → 3 unchanged 16 fib(6) returns — 5 + 3 = 8 {...,6:8}

docs.title: Code
docs.text:
Manual memoisation:

def fib_memo(n, memo=None):
    """Memoised fibonacci. O(n) time, O(n) space."""
    if memo is None:                                # 1
        memo = {}                                   # 2
    if n in memo:                                   # 3
        return memo[n]                              # 4
    if n <= 1:                                      # 5
        return n                                    # 6
    result = fib_memo(n - 1, memo) + fib_memo(n - 2, memo)   # 7
    memo[n] = result                                # 8
    return result                                   # 9

Line-by-line — kya aur kyun:

1-2. if memo is None: memo = {} — ye Python ka SABSE IMPORTANT gotcha hai. Agar aap def fib_memo(n, memo={}): likhte to: - Default argument function definition ke waqt EK BAAR evaluate hota hai. - Wo ek hi dictionary har call mein share hoti hai. - Ye yahan accidentally kaam kar jata hai (kyunki fibonacci deterministic hai aur cache persist karna faayde ka hai) par ye ek time bomb hai: agar function ka logic kabhi badle, ya alag parameters aayein, to stale results mil sakte hain. - Aur wo memory kabhi free nahi hoti. Rule: mutable defaults ([], {}, set()) kabhi mat use karo. Hamesha None sentinel.

3-4. Cache check SABSE PEHLE — base case se bhi pehle. Kyunki cache lookup O(1) hai aur base case check bhi O(1), to order performance ke liye matter nahi karta — par conceptually cache check pehle hona chahiye taaki ye clear rahe ki "pehle dekho pata hai ya nahi".

5-6. Base case. Note: hum base case ko memo mein store NAHI kar rahe. Ye theek hai kyunki base case ka computation already O(1) hai. Store karna bhi galat nahi, bas fizool.

  1. Recursive calls, memo ko pass karte hue. Ye pass karna zaroori hai — agar aap fib_memo(n-1) likhte (bina memo ke) to har recursive call apna naya khali memo banati aur poori memoisation bekaar ho jati. Ye ek silent performance bug hai — code sahi answer deta hai, bas exponentially slow rehta hai.

  2. Result ko cache karo. Ye line recursion se pehle nahi ho sakti (result to abhi compute hi nahi hua).

  3. Return.

functools.lru_cache — Pythonic tareeka:

from functools import lru_cache                     # 1

@lru_cache(maxsize=None)                            # 2
def fib_lru(n):
    if n <= 1:                                      # 3
        return n                                    # 4
    return fib_lru(n - 1) + fib_lru(n - 2)          # 5


print(fib_lru(100))                                 # 6
print(fib_lru.cache_info())                         # 7
fib_lru.cache_clear()                               # 8
  1. Import.
  2. @lru_cache(maxsize=None) — unbounded cache.
  3. maxsize=None — koi limit nahi, sab yaad rakho. DP ke liye ye chahiye.
  4. maxsize=128 (default) — sirf 128 recent entries. DP ke liye ye KHATARNAK hai — agar aapko purane values chahiye aur wo evict ho gaye to recompute hoga, aur worst case mein exponential blowup wapas aa sakta hai.
  5. Python 3.9+ mein @cache bhi hai, jo @lru_cache(maxsize=None) ka shortcut hai. 3-5. Bilkul naive recursion — koi memo logic nahi likhna pada.
  6. fib_lru(100) — instant. Bina cache ke ye universe ki umar se zyada leta.
  7. cache_info() → CacheInfo(hits=98, misses=101, maxsize=None, currsize=101). Debugging ke liye bahut useful — hits/misses ratio batata hai ki cache kaam kar raha hai ya nahi.
  8. cache_clear() — memory free karne ke liye, ya tests ke beech state reset karne ke liye.

lru_cache ki limitations — ye interview mein poochhi jaati hain:

# 1. Arguments HASHABLE hone chahiye
@lru_cache(maxsize=None)
def f(lst):
    return sum(lst)

# f([1,2,3])  ->  TypeError: unhashable type: 'list'
# Fix: tuple use karo
# f((1,2,3))  ->  works


# 2. Keyword vs positional args ALAG keys banate hain
@lru_cache(maxsize=None)
def g(a, b=2):
    return a + b

g(1, 2)      # miss, computes
g(1, b=2)    # ANOTHER miss! alag cache key
g(a=1, b=2)  # TEESRA miss!
# Teen alag cache entries same result ke liye


# 3. Memory leak ka risk with maxsize=None on methods
class Analyzer:
    @lru_cache(maxsize=None)                        # KHATARNAK
    def compute(self, x):
        return x * 2
# Cache `self` ko bhi key ka hissa banata hai
# ->  har Analyzer instance cache mein permanently reference hota hai
# ->  instances kabhi garbage collect nahi hote  ->  MEMORY LEAK
# Fix: functools.cached_property, ya instance-level cache dict


# 4. Recursion limit abhi bhi lagti hai
# fib_lru(3000)  ->  RecursionError, kyunki depth 3000 hai
# Fix: iterative (bottom-up) version, ya pehle chhote values compute karo:
#   for i in range(0, 3000, 500): fib_lru(i)
#   fib_lru(3000)   -> ab kaam karega, kyunki har call chhoti depth ki hai

Custom memoisation decorator (jab lru_cache kaam na kare):

import functools                                    # 1

def memoize(key_func=None):
    """Decorator jo custom key function support karta hai."""
    def decorator(func):                            # 2
        cache = {}                                  # 3
        @functools.wraps(func)                      # 4
        def wrapper(*args, **kwargs):               # 5
            if key_func is not None:                # 6
                key = key_func(*args, **kwargs)     # 7
            else:                                   # 8
                key = (args, tuple(sorted(kwargs.items())))   # 9
            if key not in cache:                    # 10
                cache[key] = func(*args, **kwargs)  # 11
            return cache[key]                       # 12
        wrapper.cache = cache                       # 13
        wrapper.cache_clear = cache.clear           # 14
        return wrapper                              # 15
    return decorator                                # 16


@memoize(key_func=lambda grid, r, c: (r, c))        # 17
def unique_paths(grid, r, c):
    """grid ko key mein include nahi karte (wo constant hai)."""
    if r == 0 or c == 0:                            # 18
        return 1                                    # 19
    return unique_paths(grid, r - 1, c) + unique_paths(grid, r, c - 1)   # 20
  1. functools.
  2. Teen-level nesting — decorator factory (memoize) → decorator → wrapper. Ye pattern tab chahiye jab decorator khud arguments leta hai.
  3. cache = {} — closure mein, har decorated function ka apna cache.
  4. @functools.wraps(func) — zaroori hai. Ye original function ka __name__, __doc__, __module__ wrapper par copy karta hai. Bina iske, help(), debugging, aur introspection sab galat naam dikhate hain (wrapper instead of unique_paths).
  5. Wrapper. 6-7. Custom key function — jab default key theek na ho. 8-9. Default key: (args, sorted kwargs). tuple(sorted(...)) isliye ki dict hashable nahi hai, aur sorted se f(a=1,b=2) aur f(b=2,a=1) same key banayein. lru_cache ye normalisation nahi karta — ye is custom version ka fayda hai. 10-11. Cache miss par compute.
  6. Result. 13-14. Cache introspection aur clearing expose ki. 15-16. Return.
  7. key_func=lambda grid, r, c: (r, c) — grid ko key se exclude kiya, kyunki:
  8. grid ek list of lists hai — unhashable, lru_cache crash karta.
  9. Aur wo poore recursion mein constant hai — use key mein daalna fizool. Ye custom memoize ka main use case hai. 18-20. Grid paths recursion.

docs.title: Complexity derive karke
docs.text:
General rule:

Memoised recursion ki complexity =

   (number of DISTINCT states)  x  (work per state, recursive calls ko chhod kar)


Kyun? Kyunki:
   - Har distinct state EXACTLY EK BAAR compute hoti hai (baaki baar cache hit)
   - Cache hit O(1) hai (dict lookup)
   - To total = states x per-state work

Examples:

Problem States Work per state Time Space fib(n) n+1 (values of n) O(1) O(n) O(n) Grid paths (m×n) m·n O(1) O(mn) O(mn) LCS(s1, s2) \|s1\|·\|s2\| O(1) O(mn) O(mn) 0/1 Knapsack n·W O(1) O(nW) O(nW) Coin change amount O(coins) O(amount·coins) O(amount) Edit distance m·n O(1) O(mn) O(mn) TSP (bitmask DP) 2^n · n O(n) O(2^n · n²) O(2^n · n)

Ye formula memoisation analysis ka poora kaam hai. State space ginn lo, per-state work ginn lo, multiply karo.

Space complexity ke do parts:

Memo table:       O(number of states)
Recursion stack:  O(maximum recursion depth)

Total: O(states + depth)

fib(n):  memo O(n) + stack O(n) = O(n)
LCS:     memo O(mn) + stack O(m+n) = O(mn)

Time-space trade-off:

Bina memo:  O(2^n) time,  O(n) space
Ke saath:   O(n) time,    O(n) space

Time exponentially kam, space same order  ->  CLEAR WIN

Par hamesha nahi:

0/1 Knapsack:
   Bina memo:  O(2^n) time,  O(n) space
   Ke saath:   O(nW) time,   O(nW) space

Agar W bahut bada hai (say 10^9), to memo table 10^9 entries ka hoga -> MEMORY CRASH
Us case mein memoisation ULTA nuksaan hai.

Ye "pseudo-polynomial" ka concept hai — O(nW) polynomial dikhta hai par W input ki value hai, size nahi. Value exponential ho sakti hai input ke bits mein.

docs.title: Kab use karna hai / kab nahi
docs.text:
Use karo jab: - Overlapping subproblems hain — recursion tree mein same node baar baar dikhta hai. - Function pure hai (deterministic, no side effects). - Arguments hashable hain (ya bana sakte ho). - State space manageable hai memory mein.

Mat use karo jab: - Koi overlap nahi — merge sort, quicksort, binary search. Memo sirf memory waste karega, kabhi hit nahi hoga. - State space bahut bada — memory crash. - Function impure hai — random, time-dependent, I/O. Galat answers milenge. - Bottom-up (tabulation) simpler hai — us case mein wo behtar hai (no recursion limit, better cache locality).

Memoisation vs Tabulation:

Aspect Memoisation (top-down) Tabulation (bottom-up) Style Recursive Iterative Kaunse states compute hote hain Sirf zaroori wale Sab Recursion limit Problem Nahi Code likhna Aasan (naive recursion + decorator) Order sochna padta hai Cache locality Kharab (dict, random access) Acchi (array, sequential) Space optimisation Mushkil Aasan (rolling arrays) Speed Function call overhead Tez

Kab memoisation behtar hai? Jab state space sparse hai — yaani sab states reachable nahi hain. Tabulation sab compute karta hai (waste), memoisation sirf zaroori wale.

docs.title: Kitne tareeke se optimize
docs.text:
# Optimisation Kya deta hai Kya leta hai 1 @lru_cache(maxsize=None) use karo Zero-effort memoisation Hashable args ki requirement 2 State ko chhota karo — sirf zaroori parameters key mein Kam memory, zyada cache hits Sochna padta hai 3 dict ki jagah array agar states dense integers hain 2-3x tez (hashing nahi), kam memory Sirf integer keys 4 Tabulation par switch Recursion limit khatam, cache locality behtar Order sochna padta hai 5 Rolling array — sirf recent states rakho O(n²) space → O(n) Sirf tabulation mein aasan 6 maxsize set karo agar memory bounded hai Memory cap Cache misses ka risk 7 Immutable args — tuples, frozensets Hashable ban jate hain Conversion cost

Optimisation #2 — state minimisation ka example:

# BURA: poori list state mein
@lru_cache(maxsize=None)
def solve_bad(remaining_items_tuple, capacity):     # 1
    ...

# ACCHA: sirf index aur capacity
@lru_cache(maxsize=None)
def solve_good(index, capacity):                    # 2
    ...
  1. remaining_items_tuple — har alag combination ek naya state. Agar 20 items hain to 2^20 = 10 lakh possible tuples. State space explode.
  2. index — sirf "kahan tak pahunche hain". Items ki list ek global/closure variable hai. States: n × capacity. Bahut chhota.

Ye ek asli, bahut common mistake hai — state mein zyada information daal dena. Rule: state mein sirf wo daalo jo future decisions ko affect karta hai.

Optimisation #3 — array vs dict:

# Dict version
memo = {}
def f(i, j):
    if (i, j) in memo:
        return memo[(i, j)]
    ...

# Array version (states dense integers hon to)
memo = [[-1] * (n + 1) for _ in range(m + 1)]       # 1
def f(i, j):
    if memo[i][j] != -1:                            # 2
        return memo[i][j]
    ...
  1. 2D array pre-allocated, -1 sentinel "not computed" ke liye. [[-1] * (n+1)] * (m+1) NAHI likhna — wo m+1 references banata ek hi list ke. List comprehension zaroori hai.
  2. != -1 check. Sentinel value aisi honi chahiye jo valid answer na ho. Agar -1 valid answer ho sakta hai (jaise minimum cost problems mein) to None use karo ya alag visited array.

Array version 2-3x tez hai kyunki: - Koi hashing nahi (tuple hash karna mehnga hai). - Contiguous memory → cache friendly. - Koi collision handling nahi.

Interview answer: Memoisation caches the result of each distinct subproblem so it's computed once and looked up thereafter. It converts naive fibonacci from O(1.618^n) to O(n), because although the recursion tree has exponentially many nodes, there are only n+1 distinct values of the argument — every other node is a repeat.

The complexity rule is simple: memoised recursion costs (number of distinct states) × (work per state, excluding the recursive calls). That's how I analyse every DP problem — grid paths have m·n states with O(1) work, so O(mn); coin change has amount states with O(coins) work per state, so O(amount · coins).

In Python I use functools.lru_cache with maxsize=None, or @cache in 3.9+. Three things to watch: arguments must be hashable, so lists have to become tuples; a bounded maxsize is dangerous for DP because evicting an entry you still need can reintroduce exponential blowup; and putting lru_cache on a method keeps self as part of the key, so instances never get garbage collected — a real memory leak.

The most common design mistake is putting too much in the state. If the state is the whole remaining item list, you get 2^n states and gain nothing; if it's just an index plus the remaining capacity, you get n·W states. The rule is: the state should contain only what actually affects future decisions.

Cross-question: "When would memoisation be worse than tabulation?"

When recursion depth is a problem — Python's 1000-frame limit kills memoised solutions on large inputs while a bottom-up loop is fine. When cache locality matters — a bottom-up table is a contiguous array scanned in order, while a memo dict is random access with hashing. And when you want to space-optimise: rolling arrays that keep only the last one or two rows are natural bottom-up and awkward top-down. Memoisation wins when the state space is sparse, because it only computes the states actually reachable, while tabulation fills the whole table.

Cross-question: "Why is def f(n, memo={}) dangerous?"

Default arguments are evaluated once, at function definition time, so every call shares the same dict. For pure fibonacci that happens to be beneficial — the cache persists across calls — but it's a landmine: the cache never gets freed, it can't be reset, and if the function's semantics ever depend on anything outside its arguments, stale entries produce wrong answers silently. The safe pattern is a None sentinel and creating the dict inside.

docs.title: Kya hai
docs.text:
Backtracking ek systematic trial-and-error hai: ek choice karo, aage badho, aur agar wo raasta fail ho jaye to wapas aakar (backtrack) doosri choice try karo.

Real-world analogy: Ek maze (bhool-bhulaiya) mein raasta dhoondhna. Har junction par aap ek direction chunte ho aur ek chalk se nishaan banate ho. Agar dead end aa jaye, to aap wapas aate ho, apna nishaan mitate ho, aur doosri direction try karte ho. Wo "nishaan mitaana" hi undo/backtrack step hai — aur wahi is technique ka naam hai.

docs.title: Kyu hai
docs.text:
Kuchh problems mein aapko saare valid solutions chahiye hote hain, ya koi ek valid solution, aur unhe direct compute karne ka koi formula nahi hai:

  • N-Queens: 8 queens ko chessboard par rakho taaki koi ek doosre ko attack na kare.
  • Sudoku solve karna.
  • Ek set ke saare subsets / permutations generate karna.
  • Graph coloring.
  • Word search in a grid.

Brute force in sabko solve kar sakta hai — saare possibilities generate karo, phir valid wale filter karo. Par:

N-Queens (n=8): brute force = 64 choose 8 = 4.4 billion positions
                backtracking = ~2,057 positions explored

Sudoku: brute force = 9^81 ≈ 10^77 grids
        backtracking = typically thousands of states

Permutations of 10 items: brute force generate-and-filter = 10^10 if done naively
                          backtracking = exactly 10! = 3.6 million

Backtracking ka poora fayda "pruning" hai — jaise hi pata chale ki current partial solution kabhi valid nahi ban sakta, us poore subtree ko abhi cut kar do.

Bina pruning:  poora tree explore karo, phir check karo
Pruning ke saath: invalid branch pehle hi cut  ->  exponentially kam kaam

docs.title: Kaise kaam karta hai
docs.text:
Universal template:

def backtrack(state, choices):

    if is_complete(state):              # 1. GOAL TEST
        record(state)
        return

    for choice in choices:              # 2. HAR CHOICE TRY KARO
        if is_valid(state, choice):     # 3. PRUNE — invalid ko skip karo
            make(state, choice)         # 4. CHOOSE
            backtrack(state, next_choices)   # 5. EXPLORE
            undo(state, choice)         # 6. UNCHOOSE (BACKTRACK)

Choose → Explore → Unchoose — ye teen shabd poora template hain.

Sabse critical line: undo. Bina uske: - Agar aap shared mutable state (list, set, board) use kar rahe ho, to ek branch ka effect agli branch mein leak ho jayega. - Result poori tarah galat hoga.

Decision tree visualisation:

Subsets of [1, 2, 3]:

                        []
                    /        \
             include 1      skip 1
                  /              \
              [1]                []
             /   \              /   \
       incl 2   skip 2     incl 2   skip 2
          /        \          /        \
      [1,2]       [1]      [2]        []
      /   \       /  \     /  \       /  \
  [1,2,3][1,2] [1,3][1] [2,3][2]  [3]   []

8 leaves = 2^3 subsets  ✓

Har level par ek decision: "is element ko lein ya na lein"

Board 4×4, har row mein ek queen.

SOLUTION!

Solution mila:

Q . . .
