Pruning ka fayda: Brute force 4^4 = 256 placements try karta (har row mein 4 choices). Backtracking ne ~24 states explore kiye. 10x kam. n=8 par: brute force 8^8 = 16.7 million vs backtracking ~2,057. 8000x kam.

docs.title: Code
docs.text:
Subsets:

def subsets(nums):
    """Saare subsets. O(2^n) results, O(n·2^n) total time."""
    result = []                                     # 1
    current = []                                    # 2

    def backtrack(start):                           # 3
        result.append(current[:])                   # 4
        for i in range(start, len(nums)):           # 5
            current.append(nums[i])                 # 6
            backtrack(i + 1)                        # 7
            current.pop()                           # 8

    backtrack(0)                                    # 9
    return result                                   # 10

Line-by-line — kya aur kyun:

  1. result — saare subsets.
  2. current — shared mutable state, abhi tak ka partial subset.
  3. Nested function — nums, result, current closure se access karta hai.
  4. result.append(current[:]) — current[:] — COPY! current nahi. Ye sabse critical line hai. Agar aap result.append(current) likhte to:
  5. result mein same list object ke references jate.
  6. Line 6/8 usi list ko modify karti rehti.
  7. Aakhir mein result mein saari entries khali lists hoti (kyunki current end mein khali ho jati hai). current[:], list(current), ya current.copy() — teeno same, koi bhi chalega.
  8. for i in range(start, len(nums)) — start se, 0 se NAHI. Ye duplicates rokta hai: [1,2] aur [2,1] same subset hain, hum sirf ek chahte hain. start se shuru karke hum hamesha increasing order mein elements lete hain.
  9. CHOOSE.
  10. EXPLORE — i + 1, start + 1 NAHI. Kyunki hum abhi nums[i] use kar chuke hain, agle level par i ke baad se dekhna hai. start + 1 likhne se same element dobara aa sakta.
  11. UNCHOOSE. pop() line 6 ke append() ko exactly undo karta hai. Bina iske: current badhti rehti aur kabhi shrink nahi hoti — poore results galat.
  12. Shuruaat.
  13. Return.

Permutations:

def permutations(nums):
    """Saare permutations. n! results."""
    result = []                                     # 1
    current = []                                    # 2
    used = [False] * len(nums)                      # 3

    def backtrack():                                # 4
        if len(current) == len(nums):               # 5
            result.append(current[:])               # 6
            return                                  # 7
        for i in range(len(nums)):                  # 8
            if used[i]:                             # 9
                continue                            # 10
            used[i] = True                          # 11
            current.append(nums[i])                 # 12
            backtrack()                             # 13
            current.pop()                           # 14
            used[i] = False                         # 15

    backtrack()                                     # 16
    return result                                   # 17

1-2. Result aur current. 3. used — kaunse indices already permutation mein hain. Permutations mein har element exactly ek baar aata hai. 4. Nested. 5-7. Goal test: current poori length ka ho gaya → record aur return. Subsets mein har state record hoti thi; yahan sirf complete states. 8. for i in range(len(nums)) — 0 se, start se NAHI. Ye subsets se bada farak hai: permutations mein order matter karta hai, to har position par har unused element aa sakta hai. 9-10. Already used → skip. 11-12. CHOOSE — do cheezein mark karni hain: used aur current. 13. EXPLORE. 14-15. UNCHOOSE — dono undo karo, ULTA order mein. Order technically matter nahi karta yahan (dono independent hain), par convention hai ki undo ko choose ka mirror image rakho — isse bugs kam hote hain jab state complicated ho. 16-17. Run aur return.

N-Queens (optimised, sets se O(1) validity check):

def solve_n_queens(n):
    """N-Queens ke saare solutions."""
    result = []                                     # 1
    cols = set()                                    # 2
    diag1 = set()                                   # 3
    diag2 = set()                                   # 4
    placement = []                                  # 5

    def backtrack(row):                             # 6
        if row == n:                                # 7
            result.append(_render(placement, n))    # 8
            return                                  # 9
        for col in range(n):                        # 10
            d1 = row - col                          # 11
            d2 = row + col                          # 12
            if col in cols or d1 in diag1 or d2 in diag2:   # 13
                continue                            # 14
            cols.add(col)                           # 15
            diag1.add(d1)                           # 16
            diag2.add(d2)                           # 17
            placement.append(col)                   # 18
            backtrack(row + 1)                      # 19
            placement.pop()                         # 20
            diag2.discard(d2)                       # 21
            diag1.discard(d1)                       # 22
            cols.discard(col)                       # 23

    backtrack(0)                                    # 24
    return result                                   # 25


def _render(placement, n):
    return ["." * c + "Q" + "." * (n - c - 1) for c in placement]
  1. Results.
  2. cols — occupied columns. 3-4. diag1, diag2 — occupied diagonals. Ye trick key insight hai:
  3. row - col har \ (top-left to bottom-right) diagonal par CONSTANT hai. (0,0): 0; (1,1): 0; (2,2): 0 — same diagonal, same value ✓
  4. row + col har / (top-right to bottom-left) diagonal par CONSTANT hai. (0,2): 2; (1,1): 2; (2,0): 2 — same diagonal ✓ Isse validity check O(1) ho jata hai, O(n) nahi (jo naive "har pehle wali queen se compare karo" hota).
  5. placement[row] = col — har row mein queen ka column.
  6. Recursion by row. Row-by-row jaana automatic constraint hai — har row mein exactly ek queen, to "same row" ki check ki zaroorat hi nahi. 7-9. Goal: saari n rows fill ho gayi → solution record.
  7. Har column try karo. 11-12. Diagonal identifiers. 13-14. PRUNE — teen O(1) set lookups. Agar koi conflict hai to ye branch poori tarah skip. Ye pruning hi exponential savings deti hai. 15-18. CHOOSE — chaar state updates.
  8. EXPLORE — agli row. 20-23. UNCHOOSE — chaaron undo, exact reverse order mein. discard use kiya remove ki jagah — discard element na hone par error nahi deta (defensive), remove KeyError phenkta. Yahan element hamesha hoga to dono theek hain, par discard safer hai. 24-25. Run.

docs.title: Complexity derive karke
docs.text:
General formula:

Time = O(branching_factor ^ depth × work_per_node)

   branching_factor = har node par kitni choices
   depth = solution kitna deep hai
   work_per_node = validity check + state update ka cost

Examples:

Problem Branching Depth Work/node Time Space Subsets 2 (take/skip) n O(n) copy O(n·2^n) O(n) Permutations n → n-1 → ... n O(n) copy O(n·n!) O(n) N-Queens n n O(1) with sets O(n!) upper bound O(n) Sudoku 9 81 O(1) O(9^81) worst, practically fast O(1) Combinations C(n,k) n k O(k) copy O(k·C(n,k)) O(k) Word search (grid) 4 word length L O(1) O(m·n·4^L) O(L)

Subsets ka derivation: 

Har element ke liye 2 choices (lo ya na lo)
   -> 2^n total subsets
Har subset ko copy karne mein O(n)
   -> O(n · 2^n) total time

Space: recursion depth n + current list n = O(n)
       (result ko output maante hain, space mein nahi ginte)

Permutations ka derivation: 

Level 0: n choices
Level 1: n-1 choices (ek used ho gaya)
Level 2: n-2
...
Total leaves = n × (n-1) × ... × 1 = n!

Har complete permutation ko copy karne mein O(n)
   -> O(n · n!)

n=10:  10! × 10 = 36 million operations   (theek hai)
n=12:  12! × 12 = 5.7 billion             (minutes)
n=15:  15! × 15 = 2 × 10^13               (bhool jao)

N-Queens ka actual behaviour (pruning ka effect):

n Solutions Nodes explored (with pruning) Brute force (n^n) 4 2 60 256 6 4 894 46,656 8 92 15,720 16.7 million 10 724 348,150 10^10 12 14,200 10 million 8.9 × 10^12

Pruning ka fayda n ke saath exponentially badhta hai — n=8 par 1000x, n=12 par ~900,000x.

Space: 

Recursion stack: O(depth)
Current state:   O(depth) typically

Total: O(depth)

NOTE: `result` list ka size output ka hissa hai, auxiliary space nahi.
Agar interviewer poochhe "space complexity", to O(depth) bolo aur mention karo
ki output ko alag se ginte hain.

docs.title: Kab use karna hai / kab nahi
docs.text:
Use karo jab: - Saare solutions chahiye (subsets, permutations, combinations). - Koi ek valid solution chahiye aur constraints hain (Sudoku, N-Queens, maze). - Constraint satisfaction problem hai. - Solution ko incrementally build kar sakte ho aur partial solutions ko validate kar sakte ho.

Mat use karo jab: - Optimisation problem hai aur DP kaam kar sakta hai — DP polynomial hai, backtracking exponential. - Greedy solution exist karta hai — O(n log n) vs O(2^n). - Search space bahut bada hai aur pruning weak hai — practically infeasible. - Sirf count chahiye, actual solutions nahi — aksar closed-form formula ya DP hoti hai.

docs.title: Kitne tareeke se optimize
docs.text:
# Optimisation Kya deta hai Kya leta hai 1 Early pruning — jitna jaldi invalid detect karo Exponentially kam nodes. Sabse bada impact Validity check likhna 2 Constraint propagation — ek choice ke baad doosri choices ko narrow karo Sudoku mein 100x+ Complexity 3 Ordering heuristics — sabse constrained variable pehle (MRV) Aksar 10-100x Sorting/priority overhead 4 Symmetry breaking — symmetric solutions ko skip karo N-Queens mein ~2-8x Symmetry identify karna 5 O(1) validity check (sets/bitmasks) O(n) → O(1) per check Extra state maintain 6 Bitmask state integers mein Bahut tez, kam memory Readability 7 Memoise agar states repeat hoti hain Exponential → polynomial Ab wo DP hai 8 Iterative deepening Memory O(depth), aur shallow solutions jaldi milte hain Repeated work

Bitmask N-Queens (sabse tez known approach):

def total_n_queens_bitmask(n):
    """N-Queens solutions ki COUNT, bitmasks se. Bahut tez."""
    count = 0                                       # 1
    full = (1 << n) - 1                             # 2

    def backtrack(row_mask, ld, rd):                # 3
        nonlocal count                              # 4
        if row_mask == full:                        # 5
            count += 1                              # 6
            return                                  # 7
        available = ~(row_mask | ld | rd) & full    # 8
        while available:                            # 9
            bit = available & (-available)          # 10
            available -= bit                        # 11
            backtrack(row_mask | bit,               # 12
                      ((ld | bit) << 1) & full,     # 13
                      (rd | bit) >> 1)              # 14

    backtrack(0, 0, 0)                              # 15
    return count                                    # 16
  1. Counter.
  2. full = (1 << n) - 1 — n ones. n=4 → 0b1111 = 15. Ye "saare columns bhare" ka mask.
  3. Teen bitmasks: row_mask = occupied columns, ld = left diagonals ka threat, rd = right diagonals ka threat.
  4. nonlocal — nested function se outer variable modify karne ke liye zaroori. Bina iske Python count ko local samajhta aur UnboundLocalError deta. 5-7. Sab columns bhar gaye → ek solution.
  5. ~(row_mask | ld | rd) & full — available positions.
  6. row_mask | ld | rd — saare threatened positions.
  7. ~ — invert (available positions).
  8. & full — sirf n bits rakho (Python ke unbounded integers mein ~ infinite ones deta hai, & full clamp karta hai). Ye & full zaroori hai, bina uske infinite loop.
  9. Jab tak koi available position hai.
  10. available & (-available) — lowest set bit isolate karo. Ye ek classic bit trick hai: two's complement mein -x = ~x + 1, aur x & -x exactly lowest set bit deta hai. 0b1010 & -0b1010 = 0b0010 ✓
  11. Us bit ko available se hatao (- ya ^ dono chalega).
  12. Naya row_mask — ye column ab occupied.
  13. ((ld | bit) << 1) & full — left diagonal threat ek column left shift. Kyunki agli row mein, is queen ka left-diagonal threat ek position left hoga. & full overflow clamp.
  14. (rd | bit) >> 1 — right diagonal threat, right shift. Ye shifting hi poore diagonal tracking ko O(1) bana deti hai — koi set, koi arithmetic, bas bit shifts. 15-16. Run.

Ye version standard version se ~5-10x tez hai kyunki saare operations single CPU instructions hain.

Interview answer: Backtracking is systematic trial and error. You build a solution incrementally, and whenever a partial solution can't possibly extend to a valid one, you abandon that branch immediately and back up. The template is three steps: choose, explore, unchoose.

The unchoose step is what people get wrong. If the state is a shared mutable structure — a list, a set, a board — every modification made on the way down must be exactly reversed on the way back up, or the next branch inherits corrupted state. And when recording a solution, you must append a copy, not the live list, or every entry in your results ends up pointing at the same object that gets emptied by the time you return.

The value over brute force is pruning. For N-Queens with n = 8, brute force is 8^8 — about 16 million placements — while backtracking explores around 16,000 nodes because it rejects a column the moment it conflicts. That gap widens exponentially with n. The validity check itself should be O(1): track occupied columns in a set, and use row - col and row + col as diagonal identifiers, since those are constant along each diagonal.

Complexity is branching factor to the depth, times the per-node work. Subsets is O(n·2^n), permutations is O(n·n!). Space is O(depth) for the stack and current state — the output list is usually counted separately.

Cross-question: "When is backtracking the wrong choice?"

When the problem is optimisation rather than enumeration and has overlapping subproblems, because then dynamic programming solves it in polynomial time while backtracking is exponential. Coin change is the clean example: backtracking explores every combination, DP solves it in O(amount × coins). The signal is whether you need all solutions — enumeration, so backtracking — or the best one — optimisation, so try DP or greedy first.

docs.title: When Recursion Is the Wrong Tool
Kya hai
docs.text:
Ye section un cases ke baare mein hai jahan recursion technically kaam karti hai par galat choice hai — aur unhe kaise pehchaanein aur kaise fix karein.

Real-world analogy: Hathoda ek achha tool hai. Par agar aapko peench (screw) lagani hai to hathoda peench ko theek se lagayega hi nahi — aur agar lag bhi gayi to deewar kharab ho jayegi. Recursion bhi aisa hi hai: kuchh problems ke liye perfect, kuchh ke liye actively nuksaandeh.

docs.title: Kyu hai
docs.text:
Recursion ki teen practical costs hain jo log ignore kar dete hain:

1. Stack depth ki hard limit

import sys
print(sys.getrecursionlimit())   # 1000 (CPython default)

Ek linear recursion n = 5000 par RecursionError deti hai. Ek loop n = 10^9 par bhi chalti hai. Ye ek hard wall hai, performance issue nahi.

2. Function call overhead

Har call mein: - Stack frame allocate karo - Arguments copy karo - Return address save karo - Return par sab restore karo

Python mein ye ~1 microsecond per call hai. 10 lakh calls = 1 second sirf overhead. Ek loop iteration ~50 nanoseconds hai — 20x tez.

3. Exponential blowup bina memoisation ke

fib(50) naive recursion se 4 ghante, loop se microseconds.

docs.title: Kaise pehchaanein — chaar red flags
docs.text:
Red flag 1 — Tail recursion (recursive call last statement hai)

def sum_list_bad(lst, i=0, total=0):
    if i == len(lst):                               # 1
        return total                                # 2
    return sum_list_bad(lst, i + 1, total + lst[i]) # 3  <- TAIL CALL
  1. Recursive call function ka aakhri operation hai — uske baad kuchh nahi hota, bas result pass through hota hai. Ye ek loop hai jo recursion ka bhes badal kar aaya hai.

Kuchh languages (Scheme, Scala, Haskell) mein compiler ise loop mein badal deta hai (tail call optimisation, TCO). Python ye NAHI karta — Guido van Rossum ne deliberately reject kiya, kyunki wo stack traces ko useless bana deta (debugging mushkil ho jati).

Fix — loop likh do:

def sum_list_good(lst):
    total = 0                                       # 1
    for x in lst:                                   # 2
        total += x                                  # 3
    return total                                    # 4

1-4. Simple, fast, koi depth limit nahi. Aur ye zyada readable bhi hai. (Aur practically sum(lst) likho — wo C mein hai.)

Red flag 2 — Linear depth on large input

def process_log_lines_bad(lines, i=0):
    if i >= len(lines):                             # 1
        return []                                   # 2
    return [transform(lines[i])] + process_log_lines_bad(lines, i + 1)   # 3
  1. Do problems:
  2. Depth = len(lines). 10,000 log lines → RecursionError.
  3. [x] + rest har level par naya list banata — O(n) per level, O(n²) total.

Fix: 

def process_log_lines_good(lines):
    return [transform(line) for line in lines]      # 1
1. O(n), no stack, no intermediate lists. 50x tez.

Red flag 3 — Overlapping subproblems bina memo ke

def count_ways_bad(n):
    if n < 0: return 0                              # 1
    if n == 0: return 1                             # 2
    return count_ways_bad(n-1) + count_ways_bad(n-2) + count_ways_bad(n-3)   # 3
  1. Har call teen aur calls banati hai, aur bahut overlap hai. count_ways_bad(30) → ~10 crore calls, ~1 minute.

Fix 1 — memoise: 

from functools import lru_cache
@lru_cache(maxsize=None)
def count_ways_memo(n):
    if n < 0: return 0
    if n == 0: return 1
    return count_ways_memo(n-1) + count_ways_memo(n-2) + count_ways_memo(n-3)
O(n) time. n=30 → microseconds.

Fix 2 — bottom-up (behtar, koi recursion limit nahi): 

def count_ways_dp(n):
    if n < 0: return 0                              # 1
    dp = [0] * (n + 1)                              # 2
    dp[0] = 1                                       # 3
    for i in range(1, n + 1):                       # 4
        dp[i] = dp[i-1] + (dp[i-2] if i >= 2 else 0) + (dp[i-3] if i >= 3 else 0)   # 5
    return dp[n]                                    # 6
1-2. Guard aur table. 3. Base case. 4-5. Bottom-up fill. Conditional expressions negative indices se bachate hain — Python mein dp[-1] last element deta hai, error nahi, to ye guards zaroori hain. 6. Answer. O(n) time, O(n) space, no recursion, n = 10^6 bhi chalta hai.

Red flag 4 — Deep tree/graph traversal

def dfs_bad(node, visited):
    visited.add(node)                               # 1
    for nb in graph[node]:                          # 2
        if nb not in visited:                       # 3
            dfs_bad(nb, visited)                    # 4
  1. Ek linked-list-shaped graph (1 → 2 → 3 → ... → 100000) par depth 100,000 → RecursionError.

Fix — explicit stack: 

def dfs_iterative(start, graph):
    visited = set()                                 # 1
    stack = [start]                                 # 2
    while stack:                                    # 3
        node = stack.pop()                          # 4
        if node in visited:                         # 5
            continue                                # 6
        visited.add(node)                           # 7
        for nb in graph[node]:                      # 8
            if nb not in visited:                   # 9
                stack.append(nb)                    # 10
    return visited                                  # 11

1-2. Visited set aur explicit stack (heap par, koi limit nahi). 3. Jab tak kuchh bacha hai. 4. pop() — LIFO, isliye ye DFS hai. pop(0) karte to BFS hota (par O(n) — deque use karo). 5-6. Visited check pop ke BAAD bhi — kyunki ek node stack mein kai baar push ho sakti hai (line 10 push karta hai, par wo node beech mein visit ho sakti hai). Bina is check ke duplicate processing. 7. Mark visited. 8-10. Neighbours push. 11. Result.

Ye version n = 10^7 tak scale karta hai (memory allow kare to).

docs.title: Poora dry run — recursion vs iteration ka concrete comparison
docs.text:
Problem: n tak ka sum.

n Recursive time Iterative time Recursive result 100 0.00003 s 0.000004 s 5050 1,000 0.0003 s 0.00004 s 500500 5,000 — 0.0002 s RecursionError 100,000 — 0.004 s RecursionError 10,000,000 — 0.4 s RecursionError

Iterative ~8x tez hai aur unbounded scale karta hai.

Problem: Fibonacci.

n Naive recursion Memoised Iterative 20 0.002 s 0.00002 s 0.000003 s 30 0.25 s 0.00003 s 0.000004 s 40 30 s 0.00004 s 0.000005 s 50 ~4 hours 0.00005 s 0.000006 s 1000 never RecursionError 0.0001 s 100,000 never RecursionError 0.5 s

Iterative version har case mein jeet ta hai. Memoised version bhi recursion limit par mar jata hai.

docs.title: Code — recursion ko iteration mein badalne ke patterns
docs.text:
Pattern 1 — Tail recursion → while loop:

# RECURSIVE (tail)
def gcd_rec(a, b):
    if b == 0:                                      # 1
        return a                                    # 2
    return gcd_rec(b, a % b)                        # 3

# ITERATIVE
def gcd_iter(a, b):
    while b != 0:                                   # 4
        a, b = b, a % b                             # 5
    return a                                        # 6

1-2. Base case. 3. Tail call — parameters badal kar wapas. 4. Base case ki condition ULTI — if b == 0: return → while b != 0: continue. 5. Parameters ko wahi assign karo jo recursive call mein pass hote the. Tuple assignment se simultaneous update. 6. Return.

Ye mechanical transformation hai — har tail recursion aise badal sakti hai: 

def f(params):              def f(params):
    if base: return X   =>      while not base:
    return f(new_params)            params = new_params
                                return X

Pattern 2 — Linear recursion with post-processing → loop with accumulator:

# RECURSIVE
def factorial_rec(n):
    if n <= 1: return 1                             # 1
    return n * factorial_rec(n - 1)                 # 2

# ITERATIVE
def factorial_iter(n):
    result = 1                                      # 3
    for i in range(2, n + 1):                       # 4
        result *= i                                 # 5
    return result                                   # 6

1-2. Ye tail recursion NAHI hai — n * recursive call ke baad hota hai. 3. Accumulator — wo variable jo unwinding phase ka kaam karega. 4-5. Loop direction ULTI — recursion n se 1 tak jati thi, loop 2 se n tak jata hai. Kyunki multiplication commutative hai, order matter nahi karta. Agar operation commutative na hota (jaise string concatenation), to order maintain karna padta ya explicit stack use karna padta. 6. Return.

Pattern 3 — Tree recursion → explicit stack:

# RECURSIVE
def inorder_rec(node, out):
    if node is None: return                         # 1
    inorder_rec(node.left, out)                     # 2
    out.append(node.val)                            # 3
    inorder_rec(node.right, out)                    # 4

# ITERATIVE
def inorder_iter(root):
    out = []                                        # 5
    stack = []                                      # 6
    node = root                                     # 7
    while node is not None or stack:                # 8
        while node is not None:                     # 9
            stack.append(node)                      # 10
            node = node.left                        # 11
        node = stack.pop()                          # 12
        out.append(node.val)                        # 13
        node = node.right                           # 14
    return out                                      # 15

1-4. Standard inorder. 5-7. Output, explicit stack, current pointer. 8. node is not None or stack — do conditions: - node is not None — abhi bhi left jaana hai. - stack — abhi bhi pending nodes hain. or hai and nahi — dono conditions independently loop continue karne ki wajah hain. 9-11. Jitna left ja sakte ho jao, sab push karte hue. Ye recursion ka line 2 hai (winding phase). 12. Pop — ye recursion ka "line 2 se wapas aana" hai. 13. Visit — recursion ka line 3. 14. Right subtree par jao — recursion ka line 4. Agli loop iteration line 9 se uske left chain ko push karegi. 15. Result.

Ye conversion har tree recursion ke liye kaam karti hai, bas stack par kya push karna hai wo problem par depend karta hai.

Pattern 4 — Manual stack with state (general case):

def factorial_manual_stack(n):
    """Poori general technique — call stack ko manually simulate karna."""
    stack = [(n, 'compute')]                        # 1
    result = 1                                      # 2
    while stack:                                    # 3
        value, action = stack.pop()                 # 4
        if action == 'compute':                     # 5
            if value <= 1:                          # 6
                continue                            # 7
            stack.append((value, 'multiply'))       # 8
            stack.append((value - 1, 'compute'))    # 9
        else:                                       # 10
            result *= value                         # 11
    return result                                   # 12
  1. Stack mein (value, action) tuples — action batata hai ki is frame ka kaunsa hissa execute karna hai (winding ya unwinding).
  2. Accumulator. 3-4. Stack machine loop.
  3. Winding phase. 6-7. Base case.
  4. Unwinding step ko pehle push karo — kyunki stack LIFO hai, ye baad mein pop hoga.
  5. Recursive call ko baad mein push karo — ye pehle pop hoga. Ye order critical hai — reverse karne se galat sequence. 10-11. Unwinding phase — actual multiplication.
  6. Result.

Ye technique har recursion par kaam karti hai, chahe kitni bhi complicated ho. Compilers exactly yahi karte hain.

docs.title: Complexity comparison
docs.text: Aspect Recursion Iteration Time (per operation) ~1 microsecond (Python) ~50 nanoseconds Space O(depth) stack O(1) ya O(n) explicit Max depth 1000 (Python default) Unbounded (RAM tak) Readability Better for tree/graph problems Better for linear problems Debugging Stack traces confusing Straightforward Cache locality Poor (stack frames scattered) Better

docs.title: Kab recursion sahi hai — decision guide
docs.text:
RECURSION USE KARO jab:
   ✓ Problem ka structure recursive hai (tree, graph, nested data)
   ✓ Depth logarithmic hai (divide and conquer)
   ✓ Depth chhoti aur bounded hai (< 1000)
   ✓ Code iteration se BAHUT clear hai
   ✓ Backtracking / constraint satisfaction hai

ITERATION USE KARO jab:
   ✗ Tail recursion hai (Python TCO nahi karta)
   ✗ Depth linear aur unbounded hai
   ✗ Simple accumulation hai (sum, count, product)
   ✗ Performance critical hai
   ✗ Depth 1000 se zyada ho sakti hai

MEMOISATION ADD KARO jab:
   ✓ Overlapping subproblems hain
   ✓ Function pure hai
   ✓ State space manageable hai

BOTTOM-UP DP USE KARO jab:
   ✓ Overlapping subproblems AUR depth bahut zyada
   ✓ Space optimisation chahiye (rolling arrays)

docs.title: Kitne tareeke se fix karo
docs.text:
# Problem Fix 1 Tail recursion While loop — mechanical transformation 2 Linear depth on big input Loop with accumulator 3 Overlapping subproblems @lru_cache ya bottom-up DP 4 Deep tree/graph Explicit stack (heap par, no limit) 5 Depth thodi zyada hai (2000-5000) sys.setrecursionlimit() — temporary fix, risky 6 List building via [x] + rest List comprehension ya append — O(n²) → O(n) 7 Complicated recursion Manual stack with (state, action) tuples 8 Deep recursion but need recursion Trampolining — recursion ko iterative driver se chalao

Trampolining (advanced technique):

def trampoline(f, *args):
    """Tail-recursive function ko bina stack growth ke chalao."""
    result = f(*args)                               # 1
    while callable(result):                         # 2
        result = result()                           # 3
    return result                                   # 4


def sum_to_trampolined(n, acc=0):
    if n == 0:                                      # 5
        return acc                                  # 6
    return lambda: sum_to_trampolined(n - 1, acc + n)   # 7


print(trampoline(sum_to_trampolined, 1000000))      # 8
  1. Pehli call. 2-3. Jab tak result ek function hai, use call karte raho. Har call PICHHLI call ke return hone ke BAAD hoti hai — to stack kabhi grow nahi karta. Depth hamesha 1-2 frames.
  2. Actual value. 5-6. Base case — real value return karta hai.
  3. Recursive call ko lambda mein wrap kiya — yaani call turant nahi hoti, wo ek "thunk" (deferred computation) return karti hai. Ye stack growth rok deta hai.
  4. n = 10^6 par bhi chalta hai — koi RecursionError nahi.

Ye technique functional programming se aati hai. Python mein rare hai (loop simpler hai), par ye dikhata hai ki recursion aur iteration fundamentally ek hi cheez hain.

Interview answer: Recursion is the wrong tool in four situations. First, tail recursion — where the recursive call is the last thing the function does. Python has no tail call optimisation, deliberately, because it would destroy stack traces, so a tail-recursive function is just a loop that also burns a stack frame per iteration. Rewrite it as a while loop.

Second, linear depth on large input. Python's recursion limit is 1000 by default, so a recursive sum over a 10,000-element list is a hard failure, not a slowdown. Raising the limit works up to a point but eventually segfaults the interpreter instead of raising a catchable error.

Third, overlapping subproblems without memoisation — naive fibonacci at n=50 takes hours. Add lru_cache and it's microseconds, or better, write it bottom-up so there's no recursion limit at all.

Fourth, deep graph traversal. A DFS on a path-shaped graph with a hundred thousand nodes has depth a hundred thousand. The fix is an explicit stack — a list on the heap, which has no depth limit beyond available RAM.

Where recursion genuinely wins is when the data itself is recursive — trees, nested JSON, filesystems — or when the depth is logarithmic, like divide and conquer, or in backtracking, where the choose-explore-unchoose pattern is dramatically clearer than manual stack management. Even then, there's a mechanical conversion available: push (state, action) pairs onto an explicit stack, where the action tells you whether you're in the winding or unwinding phase. That's exactly what compilers do.

docs.title: Part 4: Graph Algorithms
docs.text:
Graph ek aisa data structure hai jo relationships ko model karta hai — kaun kisse juda hai. Aur ye itna general hai ki bahut saari problems jo graph jaisi nahi dikhtin, wo actually graph problems hain: dependency resolution, state machines, test flow coverage, network routing, social connections, compiler passes, build systems.

Is part mein hum har algorithm ko poore trace ke saath dekhenge, aur end mein ek table hogi jo "problem ki property → sahi algorithm" map karti hai.

docs.title: Kya hai
docs.text:
Graph = vertices (nodes) + edges (connections). Representation ka matlab hai: ise memory mein kaise store karein.

Real-world analogy: Ek city ka road network. Aap use do tareeke se likh sakte ho: 1. Ek table jisme har jodi shehron ke liye likha ho "road hai ya nahi" — 100 shehron ke liye 10,000 entries, jisme zyadatar "nahi" hongi. (Adjacency matrix) 2. Har shehar ke liye ek list jisme sirf uske padosi shehar likhe hon. (Adjacency list)

Agar roads kam hain (jo real mein hota hai), to list bahut kam jagah leti hai.

docs.title: Kyu hai
docs.text:
Representation ka choice poore algorithm ki complexity badal deta hai:

V = vertices, E = edges

Adjacency matrix:  O(V²) space,  edge check O(1),  neighbours O(V)
Adjacency list:    O(V+E) space, edge check O(deg), neighbours O(deg)

Sparse graph (E ~ V):
   Matrix: 10^6 space for V=1000       <- 1 MB, mostly zeros
   List:   ~2000 entries               <- 8 KB
   500x farak

Dense graph (E ~ V²):
   Dono similar

Real-world graphs almost hamesha sparse hote hain. Facebook: 3 billion users, average ~350 friends → E ≈ 10^12, par V² = 9 × 10^18. Matrix impossible, list feasible.

docs.title: Kaise kaam karta hai
docs.text:
Example graph:

        1 ---- 2
        |    / |
        |   /  |
        |  /   |
        3 ---- 4
        |
        5

Edges: (1,2), (1,3), (2,3), (2,4), (3,4), (3,5)
V = 5, E = 6, undirected

Adjacency Matrix:

      1  2  3  4  5
   1 [0, 1, 1, 0, 0]
   2 [1, 0, 1, 1, 0]
   3 [1, 1, 0, 1, 1]
   4 [0, 1, 1, 0, 0]
   5 [0, 0, 1, 0, 0]

matrix[i][j] = 1 agar edge hai
Undirected mein matrix SYMMETRIC hota hai (matrix[i][j] == matrix[j][i])

Adjacency List:

   1: [2, 3]
   2: [1, 3, 4]
   3: [1, 2, 4, 5]
   4: [2, 3]

Total entries = 2E = 12 (har edge do baar, undirected hone ki wajah se)

Edge List:

   [(1,2), (1,3), (2,3), (2,4), (3,4), (3,5)]

Simplest. Kruskal ke liye perfect (edges ko sort karna hota hai).

docs.title: Poora dry run — teenon representations par same operations
docs.text:
Graph upar wala. Operations compare karte hain.

Operation 1: "Kya 2 aur 4 ke beech edge hai?"

Representation Steps Cost Matrix matrix[2][4] → direct lookup O(1) Adj list 4 in adj[2] → [1,3,4] scan → position 2 par mila O(deg(2)) = O(3) Edge list poori list scan → (2,4) position 3 par O(E) = O(6)

Operation 2: "Vertex 3 ke saare neighbours do"

Representation Steps Cost Matrix row 3 ka poora scan: [1,1,0,1,1] → indices 1,2,4,5 O(V) = O(5) Adj list adj[3] → [1,2,4,5] direct O(deg(3)) = O(4) Edge list poori list scan, 3 wale edges nikalo O(E) = O(6)

Operation 3: "Poora graph traverse karo (BFS/DFS)"

Representation Total work Cost Matrix har vertex ke liye poori row scan: V × V O(V²) = 25 Adj list har vertex ke liye uske neighbours: sum of degrees = 2E O(V + E) = 11 Edge list har vertex ke liye poori edge list: V × E O(V·E) = 30

Sparse graph par (V=1000, E=3000):

Operation Matrix Adj list Space 10^6 6,000 Traversal 10^6 4,000 Edge check 1 ~3

Adj list traversal mein 250x tez hai.

docs.title: Code
docs.text:
from collections import defaultdict, deque          # 1


class GraphMatrix:
    """Adjacency matrix representation. Dense graphs ke liye."""

    def __init__(self, n, directed=False):
        self.n = n                                  # 2
        self.directed = directed                    # 3
        self.m = [[0] * n for _ in range(n)]        # 4

    def add_edge(self, u, v, w=1):
        self.m[u][v] = w                            # 5
        if not self.directed:                       # 6
            self.m[v][u] = w                        # 7

    def has_edge(self, u, v):
        return self.m[u][v] != 0                    # 8

    def neighbours(self, u):
        return [v for v in range(self.n) if self.m[u][v] != 0]   # 9


class GraphList:
    """Adjacency list representation. Sparse graphs ke liye — default choice."""

    def __init__(self, directed=False):
        self.adj = defaultdict(list)                # 10
        self.directed = directed                    # 11
        self.vertices = set()                       # 12

    def add_edge(self, u, v, w=1):
        self.adj[u].append((v, w))                  # 13
        self.vertices.add(u)                        # 14
        self.vertices.add(v)                        # 15
        if not self.directed:                       # 16
            self.adj[v].append((u, w))              # 17

    def has_edge(self, u, v):
        return any(nb == v for nb, _ in self.adj[u])    # 18

    def neighbours(self, u):
        return [nb for nb, _ in self.adj[u]]        # 19

    def degree(self, u):
        return len(self.adj[u])                     # 20

Line-by-line — kya aur kyun:

  1. defaultdict aur deque — graph code mein ye do sabse zyada use hote hain.

2-3. Size aur directedness store.

  1. [[0] * n for _ in range(n)] — list comprehension, [[0]*n]*n NAHI. [[0]*n]*n n references banata ek hi row ke — m[0][0] = 1 karne se saari rows mein change dikhta. Ye 2D array ka #1 Python bug hai. [0] * n andar wala theek hai kyunki integers immutable hain.

  2. Edge set. w=1 default weight — 0 weight edge aur "no edge" mein confusion ho jata, isliye 0-weight edges ke liye alag sentinel (jaise float('inf') for "no edge") chahiye. 6-7. Undirected mein dono directions.

  3. != 0 — non-zero matlab edge hai. Agar 0-weight edges chahiye to ye tootega — us case mein None ya float('inf') sentinel use karo.

  4. Poori row scan — O(V). Ye matrix ki main weakness hai traversal ke liye.

  5. defaultdict(list) — key na hone par khali list automatically banati hai. Bina iske har add_edge mein if u not in adj: adj[u] = [] likhna padta. Savdhaan: defaultdict par read karne se bhi key ban jati hai — len(g.adj) unexpected badh sakta hai agar aap g.adj[nonexistent] padhte ho.

  6. Directedness.

  7. vertices set — isolated vertices (jinki koi edge nahi) track karne ke liye. Sirf adj se wo dikhte hi nahi.

  8. self.adj[u].append((v, w)) — tuple (neighbour, weight) store kar rahe hain. Agar weights nahi chahiye to sirf v store kar sakte the — simpler. Par weighted version general hai aur Dijkstra/Prim/Kruskal ke liye chahiye. 14-15. Vertices track — dono endpoints, kyunki v ka apna koi outgoing edge na ho. 16-17. Undirected mein reverse edge.

  9. any(nb == v for nb, _ in self.adj[u]) — generator expression, list nahi banati. O(deg(u)) worst case par early exit karti hai jaise hi mil jaye. Agar has_edge bahut frequently call hoti hai to adjacency list ki jagah dict of dicts ya set use karo — O(1) ho jayega.

  10. Neighbours (weights ke bina).

  11. Degree — len() O(1) hai.

Teesra option — dict of dicts (dono ka best):

class GraphDict:
    """Dict of dicts — O(1) edge lookup AUR O(deg) neighbour iteration."""

    def __init__(self, directed=False):
        self.adj = defaultdict(dict)                # 1
        self.directed = directed                    # 2

    def add_edge(self, u, v, w=1):
        self.adj[u][v] = w                          # 3
        if not self.directed:                       # 4
            self.adj[v][u] = w                      # 5

    def has_edge(self, u, v):
        return v in self.adj[u]                     # 6

    def weight(self, u, v):
        return self.adj[u].get(v)                   # 7

    def neighbours(self, u):
        return self.adj[u].keys()                   # 8
  1. defaultdict(dict) — har vertex ke liye ek dict {neighbour: weight}.
  2. Directedness.
  3. Edge — dict assignment, list append nahi. Isse duplicate edges automatically overwrite ho jate hain (jo aksar desired hai). 4-5. Reverse.
  4. v in self.adj[u] — O(1) hash lookup. Matrix ka fayda, list ke space ke saath.
  5. Weight lookup, None agar edge nahi.
  6. .keys() — view object, list nahi. Memory-efficient iteration.

Ye representation practically best hai zyadatar cases mein — space O(V+E), edge check O(1), neighbour iteration O(deg). NetworkX library exactly yahi use karti hai.

QA context — test dependency graph:

def build_test_dependency_graph(test_configs):
    """Test dependencies ka DAG banao. QA mein test ordering ke liye."""
    g = defaultdict(list)                           # 1
    all_tests = set()                               # 2
    for test_name, config in test_configs.items():  # 3
        all_tests.add(test_name)                    # 4
        for dep in config.get('depends_on', []):    # 5
            g[dep].append(test_name)                # 6
            all_tests.add(dep)                      # 7
    return g, all_tests                             # 8

1-2. Graph aur vertex set. 3. Har test config par. 4. Test ko vertices mein. 5. config.get('depends_on', []) — .get with default, config['depends_on'] nahi. Agar key na ho to KeyError; .get khali list deti hai. Defensive. 6. g[dep].append(test_name) — direction: dependency → dependent. Yaani "dep ke baad test_name chal sakta hai". Ye direction topological sort ke liye sahi hai. Agar aap ulta likhte (g[test_name].append(dep)) to topological sort ulta order deta. 7. Dependency ko bhi vertices mein — wo khud shayad configs mein na ho. 8. Return.
