docs.text:
Graph (negative weights ke saath, no negative cycle):

        4
    A ------> B
    |         |
   5|        -3|
    v         v
    C ------> D
        4

Aur:  B --> C  weight -2

Edges:
   (A, B, 4)
   (A, C, 5)
   (B, C, -2)
   (B, D, -3)
   (C, D, 4)

V = 4, to V-1 = 3 passes.

Initial: dist = {A:0, B:inf, C:inf, D:inf}

PASS 1 (edges order: A→B, A→C, B→C, B→D, C→D):

Edge u v w dist[u] dist[u]+w dist[v] Relax? New dist[v] A→B A B 4 0 4 inf Yes 4 A→C A C 5 0 5 inf Yes 5 B→C B C -2 4 2 5 Yes 2 B→D B D -3 4 1 inf Yes 1 C→D C D 4 2 6 1 No 1

After pass 1: dist = {A:0, B:4, C:2, D:1}

PASS 2:

Edge u v w dist[u] dist[u]+w dist[v] Relax? A→B A B 4 0 4 4 No A→C A C 5 0 5 2 No B→C B C -2 4 2 2 No B→D B D -3 4 1 1 No C→D C D 4 2 6 1 No

Koi change nahi → EARLY EXIT possible!

After pass 2: dist = {A:0, B:4, C:2, D:1} — converged.

PASS 3 (negative cycle check): koi edge relax nahi hoti → no negative cycle ✓

Final:

Node Distance Path A 0 A B 4 A → B C 2 A → B → C (4 + (-2) = 2) ✓ better than A → C (5) D 1 A → B → D (4 + (-3) = 1) ✓

Dijkstra is graph par kya karta?

Dijkstra pop order: A(0)
   Relax: B=4, C=5
Pop C(5) -- sabse chhota... nahi, C=5 aur B=4, to B pop hoga
Pop B(4).  FINALISE B.  Relax: C = min(5, 4-2) = 2, D = 4-3 = 1
Pop D(1).  FINALISE D.  (C=2 se bada hai? nahi, 1 < 2, to D pehle)
   D ke koi outgoing edges nahi
Pop C(2).  FINALISE C.  Relax: D = 2+4 = 6, par D already finalised

Dijkstra ka answer: A=0, B=4, C=2, D=1  <- IS CASE MEIN SAHI!

Interesting — Dijkstra yahan sahi nikla. Kyunki is graph mein negative edges ne kabhi kisi already-finalised node ko affect nahi kiya. Par ye luck hai, guarantee nahi.

Ab negative CYCLE wala example:

    A --1--> B
             |
             |2
             v
    D <--(-4)-- C
    |
    |1
    +--> B  (D --1--> B)

Edges:
   (A, B, 1)
   (B, C, 2)
   (C, D, -4)
   (D, B, 1)

Cycle: B -> C -> D -> B  weight = 2 + (-4) + 1 = -1   <- NEGATIVE CYCLE

V = 4, 3 passes.

Initial: dist = {A:0, B:inf, C:inf, D:inf}

PASS 1:

Edge dist[u]+w dist[v] Relax? New A→B (1) 0+1 = 1 inf Yes B = 1 B→C (2) 1+2 = 3 inf Yes C = 3 C→D (-4) 3-4 = -1 inf Yes D = -1 D→B (1) -1+1 = 0 1 Yes B = 0

dist = {A:0, B:0, C:3, D:-1}

PASS 2:

Edge dist[u]+w dist[v] Relax? New A→B (1) 1 0 No — B→C (2) 0+2 = 2 3 Yes C = 2 C→D (-4) 2-4 = -2 -1 Yes D = -2 D→B (1) -2+1 = -1 0 Yes B = -1

dist = {A:0, B:-1, C:2, D:-2} — distances GIR rahi hain, har pass mein -1

PASS 3:

Edge dist[u]+w dist[v] Relax? New B→C (2) -1+2 = 1 2 Yes C = 1 C→D (-4) 1-4 = -3 -2 Yes D = -3 D→B (1) -3+1 = -2 -1 Yes B = -2

dist = {A:0, B:-2, C:1, D:-3}

PASS 4 (V-th pass, detection pass):

Edge dist[u]+w dist[v] Relax? B→C (2) -2+2 = 0 1 YES — abhi bhi relax ho raha hai!

→ NEGATIVE CYCLE DETECTED ✓

Ye har pass mein distance -1 girti rehti — infinite loop mein -infinity tak jati. Isliye "shortest path" ka koi matlab hi nahi hai jab negative cycle ho.

docs.title: Code
docs.text:
def bellman_ford(vertices, edges, source):
    """Single-source shortest paths with negative weights.
    edges: [(u, v, weight), ...]
    Returns: (dist, parent) ya (None, None) agar negative cycle ho."""
    dist = {v: float('inf') for v in vertices}      # 1
    dist[source] = 0                                # 2
    parent = {v: None for v in vertices}            # 3

    for i in range(len(vertices) - 1):              # 4
        changed = False                             # 5
        for u, v, w in edges:                       # 6
            if dist[u] == float('inf'):             # 7
                continue                            # 8
            if dist[u] + w < dist[v]:               # 9
                dist[v] = dist[u] + w               # 10
                parent[v] = u                       # 11
                changed = True                      # 12
        if not changed:                             # 13
            break                                   # 14

    for u, v, w in edges:                           # 15
        if dist[u] != float('inf') and dist[u] + w < dist[v]:   # 16
            return None, None                       # 17

    return dist, parent                             # 18

Line-by-line — kya aur kyun:

  1. Sab distances inf. Dict comprehension. float('inf') use kiya, koi bada number nahi (jaise 999999). Kyun? Kyunki negative weights ke saath 999999 + (-1000000) negative ho jata aur galat relaxation hoti. inf + anything = inf (except -inf), jo safe hai.

  2. Source ki distance 0.

  3. Parent tree.

  4. for i in range(len(vertices) - 1) — exactly V-1 passes. V-1 kyun, V kyun nahi? Kyunki koi bhi simple path mein zyada se zyada V-1 edges hoti hain, aur har pass kam se kam ek edge ka contribution propagate karta hai. V passes karna galat nahi hai, bas ek fizool pass. (Aur wo V-th pass hum line 15 par detection ke liye alag se karte hain.)

  5. changed = False — early exit optimisation ka flag.

  6. for u, v, w in edges — har edge par. Order matter nahi karta correctness ke liye (sirf convergence speed ke liye).

7-8. if dist[u] == float('inf'): continue — u abhi tak reachable nahi hai. Ye check zaroori hai. Bina iske: inf + w = inf (agar w finite hai), aur inf < dist[v] False hoga to actually galat nahi hota... par agar w negative infinity ke paas ho ya numeric edge cases hon to problem. Aur ye ek O(1) skip hai jo fizool arithmetic bachata hai. Aur zyada important: ye unreachable nodes ko inf par rakhta hai, jo semantically sahi hai.

  1. if dist[u] + w < dist[v] — RELAXATION test. Strict <.

10-11. Update.

  1. changed = True — kuchh badla.

13-14. if not changed: break — EARLY EXIT. Agar ek poore pass mein koi distance nahi badli, to aage ke passes bhi kuchh nahi badlenge (kyunki input same hai). Converged. Ye practically bahut bada fayda deta hai — random graphs par typically 2-3 passes mein convergence ho jati hai, V-1 nahi. Sparse road networks par ye 100x speedup de sakta hai.

15-17. NEGATIVE CYCLE DETECTION — V-th pass. V-1 passes ke baad, agar graph mein negative cycle nahi hai to saari distances final hain. Agar koi edge abhi bhi relax ho sakti hai, to iska matlab hai ki koi path V se zyada edges ka "chhota" ho raha hai — jo sirf negative cycle se possible hai. dist[u] != inf check zaroori hai — unreachable nodes ko ignore karna hai.

  1. Return.

Negative cycle mein kaun se nodes hain — ye bhi nikaal sakte hain:

def bellman_ford_find_cycle(vertices, edges, source):
    """Negative cycle mein shamil nodes bhi return karta hai."""
    dist = {v: float('inf') for v in vertices}      # 1
    dist[source] = 0                                # 2
    parent = {v: None for v in vertices}            # 3

    for _ in range(len(vertices) - 1):              # 4
        for u, v, w in edges:                       # 5
            if dist[u] != float('inf') and dist[u] + w < dist[v]:   # 6
                dist[v] = dist[u] + w               # 7
                parent[v] = u                       # 8

    affected = set()                                # 9
    x = None                                        # 10
    for u, v, w in edges:                           # 11
        if dist[u] != float('inf') and dist[u] + w < dist[v]:   # 12
            x = v                                   # 13
            break                                   # 14

    if x is None:                                   # 15
        return dist, None                           # 16

    for _ in range(len(vertices)):                  # 17
        x = parent[x]                               # 18

    cycle = []                                      # 19
    v = x                                           # 20
    while True:                                     # 21
        cycle.append(v)                             # 22
        if v == x and len(cycle) > 1:               # 23
            break                                   # 24
        v = parent[v]                               # 25
    cycle.reverse()                                 # 26
    return dist, cycle                              # 27

1-8. Standard V-1 passes. 9-14. Koi node dhoondho jo V-th pass mein relax hoti hai. Wo node negative cycle se affected hai (par zaroori nahi ki cycle mein ho — wo cycle se reachable ho sakti hai). 15-16. Koi negative cycle nahi. 17-18. x ko V baar parent chain par peeche le jao. Ye trick kyun kaam karti hai? x cycle se reachable hai. Parent chain follow karne se hum eventually cycle mein pahunch jayenge (kyunki cycle mein infinite backwards chal sakte hain). V steps guarantee karte hain ki hum cycle ke andar aa gaye (kyunki cycle ki length <= V hai). 19-25. Cycle traverse karo parent chain par jab tak x par wapas na aa jayen. 23. v == x and len(cycle) > 1 — len > 1 zaroori hai warna pehli iteration mein hi break ho jata. 26-27. Reverse aur return.

SPFA (Shortest Path Faster Algorithm) — practical optimisation:

from collections import deque


def spfa(graph, vertices, source):
    """Queue-based Bellman-Ford. Practically bahut tez, par worst case wahi O(VE)."""
    dist = {v: float('inf') for v in vertices}      # 1
    dist[source] = 0                                # 2
    in_queue = {v: False for v in vertices}         # 3
    count = {v: 0 for v in vertices}                # 4
    queue = deque([source])                         # 5
    in_queue[source] = True                         # 6
    n = len(vertices)                               # 7

    while queue:                                    # 8
        u = queue.popleft()                         # 9
        in_queue[u] = False                         # 10
        for v, w in graph.get(u, []):               # 11
            if dist[u] + w < dist[v]:               # 12
                dist[v] = dist[u] + w               # 13
                if not in_queue[v]:                 # 14
                    queue.append(v)                 # 15
                    in_queue[v] = True              # 16
                    count[v] += 1                   # 17
                    if count[v] >= n:               # 18
                        return None                 # 19
    return dist                                     # 20

1-2. Distances. 3. in_queue — node already queue mein hai ya nahi. Duplicate enqueues rokta hai. 4. count — har node kitni baar queue mein aayi. Negative cycle detection ke liye. 5-7. Queue setup. 8-10. Pop aur flag clear. 11-13. Relaxation. 14-16. Sirf tab enqueue karo jab already queue mein na ho. Ye SPFA ka core idea hai: Bellman-Ford har edge har pass mein check karta hai, chahe wo relax ho sakti ho ya nahi. SPFA sirf un nodes ko dobara process karta hai jinki distance actually badli. Ye "useless" relaxation attempts hata deta hai. 17-19. Agar koi node V ya zyada baar queue mein aayi → negative cycle. Kyunki bina cycle ke, ek node zyada se zyada V-1 baar relax ho sakti hai. 20. Return.

SPFA practically 5-10x tez hai typical graphs par, par worst case wahi O(V·E) hai — aur adversarial inputs par wo worst case hit hota hai. Competitive programming mein iska "anti-SPFA test" famous hai.

Property Value Kyun Handles negative weights Haan — ye iska poora point hai Koi greedy finalisation nahi Detects negative cycles Haan V-th pass ka test Adaptive Haan, early exit ke saath Converge hote hi ruk jata hai Distributed-friendly Haan Har node sirf apne neighbours se baat karta hai — RIP routing protocol isi par bana hai

Distributed property important hai: Bellman-Ford ko decentralised implement kiya ja sakta hai — har router sirf apne padosi routers se distance vectors exchange karta hai. Isi wajah se RIP (Routing Information Protocol) Bellman-Ford use karta hai, jabki OSPF Dijkstra use karta hai (par usko poora network topology chahiye).

docs.title: Kab use karna hai / kab nahi
docs.text:
Use karo jab: - Negative edge weights hain — currency arbitrage, profit/loss networks, game scoring. - Negative cycle detect karna hai — arbitrage opportunities, infinite loops in systems. - Distributed setting — har node ko sirf local information chahiye (routing protocols). - Graph chhota hai aur simplicity chahiye.

Mat use karo jab: - Saare weights non-negative hain → Dijkstra (bahut tez). - Unweighted → BFS. - Graph bada hai — O(V·E) prohibitive ho jata hai. - All-pairs chahiye → Floyd-Warshall (O(V³), jo V baar Bellman-Ford = O(V²E) se behtar hai dense graphs par), ya Johnson's algorithm (sparse graphs par).

QA context: Ek test dependency graph jahan kuchh tests dusron ka setup time bachate hain (negative cost). Ya ek CI pipeline jahan cached artifacts negative time contribute karte hain. Aur negative cycle detection = "kya koi circular optimisation hai jo infinitely beneficial lagti hai" — jo aksar ek config bug hoti hai.

docs.title: Kitne tareeke se optimize
docs.text:
# Optimisation Kya deta hai Kya leta hai 1 Early exit (no changes in a pass) Typical graphs par 10-100x Ek boolean 2 SPFA — sirf changed nodes ko re-process Practically 5-10x Worst case wahi; adversarial inputs par kharab 3 SPFA + SLF (Small Label First) — chhoti distance wale ko front mein Aur 2x Deque manipulation 4 SPFA + LLL (Large Label Last) Aur improvement Average maintain karna 5 Edges ko topological order mein process karo (DAG par) O(V + E) — ek hi pass! Sirf DAGs par 6 Johnson's algorithm all-pairs ke liye O(V·E + V² log V) — sparse par Floyd-Warshall se tez Complicated 7 Yen's optimisation — edges ko do groups mein baanto ~2x kam passes Vertex ordering chahiye

DAG shortest path — Bellman-Ford ka special case, O(V+E):

def dag_shortest_path(graph, vertices, source):
    """DAG par shortest path, negative weights allowed. O(V + E)."""
    topo = topological_sort(graph, vertices)        # 1
    dist = {v: float('inf') for v in vertices}      # 2
    dist[source] = 0                                # 3
    for u in topo:                                  # 4
        if dist[u] == float('inf'):                 # 5
            continue                                # 6
        for v, w in graph.get(u, []):               # 7
            if dist[u] + w < dist[v]:               # 8
                dist[v] = dist[u] + w               # 9
    return dist                                     # 10
  1. Topological order nikaalo — O(V + E). 2-3. Distances.
  2. Topological order mein process karo. Ye kyun kaam karta hai? Topological order mein, jab hum u process karte hain, uske saare incoming edges already process ho chuke hain, yaani dist[u] final hai. To ek hi pass kaafi hai — V-1 passes ki zaroorat nahi! 5-6. Unreachable skip. 7-9. Relaxation.
  3. Return.

Ye O(V + E) hai — Bellman-Ford ke O(V·E) se bahut tez, aur Dijkstra ke O(E log V) se bhi tez, aur negative weights bhi handle karta hai. Par sirf DAGs par. Agar aapka graph acyclic hai to ye hamesha best choice hai.

Longest path in DAG: wahi algorithm, bas < ko > kar do aur inf ko -inf. (General graphs mein longest path NP-hard hai, par DAGs mein O(V+E)!)

Interview answer: Bellman-Ford computes single-source shortest paths and, unlike Dijkstra, handles negative edge weights. It relaxes every edge V-1 times. The bound is V-1 because any simple shortest path has at most V-1 edges, and each pass guarantees that at least one more edge of every shortest path has been correctly propagated.

Its unique capability is detecting negative cycles. After V-1 passes all distances should be final, so if a V-th pass can still relax some edge, there must be a cycle with negative total weight — and in that case shortest paths are undefined, since you can go around the cycle repeatedly and drive the distance to negative infinity. That's why it's the algorithm behind currency arbitrage detection.

The cost is speed: O(V·E) versus Dijkstra's O(E log V). On a sparse graph with a hundred thousand vertices that's 10^10 versus 1.7 million operations, so I'd only use it when negative weights are actually present. The standard optimisation is an early exit — if a full pass changes nothing, the distances have converged. On typical graphs that terminates in a handful of passes rather than V-1.

Two special cases worth knowing. SPFA is a queue-based variant that only reprocesses nodes whose distance actually changed — practically five to ten times faster, though the worst case is unchanged. And on a DAG you don't need Bellman-Ford at all: process vertices in topological order and one pass suffices, giving O(V + E) with negative weights allowed, which beats both Dijkstra and Bellman-Ford.

Cross-question: "Why exactly V-1 iterations?"

Because a shortest path in a graph with V vertices can contain at most V-1 edges — more than that and some vertex repeats, which means a cycle, and if there's no negative cycle you can delete it without lengthening the path. Each pass over all edges guarantees that shortest paths using one more edge become correct, so after V-1 passes all shortest paths are correct. The V-th pass is the negative-cycle test.

Cross-question: "Why does Bellman-Ford show up in routing protocols when Dijkstra is faster?"

Because it's decentralised. Each relaxation only needs a node's own distance estimate and its direct neighbours' estimates — no node needs a global view of the topology. That's exactly the distance-vector model, and it's what RIP uses. Dijkstra needs the complete graph, which is why link-state protocols like OSPF have to flood topology information across the whole network first.

docs.title: Kya hai
docs.text:
Floyd-Warshall saare jodo (all pairs) ke beech shortest path ek saath nikaalta hai — sirf teen nested loops mein.

Real-world analogy: Ek airline ka route map. Aapko ek table chahiye jisme har shehar se har doosre shehar tak ka sabse sasta fare ho. Aap ek-ek karke shehar ko "hub" banate ho aur poochte ho: "Kya X se Y jaane mein is hub se hokar jaana sasta hai?" Har shehar ko ek baar hub banane ke baad, table complete ho jati hai.

docs.title: Kyu hai
docs.text:
All-pairs shortest paths ke liye options:

1. V baar Dijkstra chalao:
      O(V * E log V)
      Sparse (E=V):  V² log V
      Dense (E=V²):  V³ log V
      PAR negative weights handle nahi karta

2. V baar Bellman-Ford:
      O(V² * E)
      Dense: O(V⁴)   <- bahut dheema
      Negative weights handle karta hai

3. FLOYD-WARSHALL:
      O(V³)  hamesha
      Negative weights handle karta hai
      Negative cycle detect karta hai
      Code sirf 5 lines

Dense graphs par Floyd-Warshall jeetta hai: V³ vs V³ log V. Aur uska code itna simple hai ki galti ki gunjaish hi nahi.

Aur uska code kitna simple hai:

for k in vertices:
    for i in vertices:
        for j in vertices:
            dist[i][j] = min(dist[i][j], dist[i][k] + dist[k][j])

Bas. Ye poora algorithm hai. Isse simple koi non-trivial graph algorithm nahi hai.

docs.title: Kaise kaam karta hai
docs.text:
Core idea — "intermediate vertices" ka concept:

dist[k][i][j] = i se j tak ki shortest distance, agar hum sirf
                {1, 2, ..., k} vertices ko INTERMEDIATE ki tarah use kar sakein

k = 0 (koi intermediate nahi): dist[0][i][j] = direct edge weight (ya inf)

Recurrence:
   dist[k][i][j] = min(
                       dist[k-1][i][j],                    <- k use NAHI kiya
                       dist[k-1][i][k] + dist[k-1][k][j]   <- k use kiya
                   )

Final answer: dist[V][i][j]  -- saare vertices intermediate ho sakte hain

Diagram:

Kya i se j jaane mein k se hokar jaana behtar hai?

        i ---------------> j
         \                ^
          \              /
           \            /
            \          /
             v        /
              k -----+

   Purana raasta:  dist[i][j]
   Naya raasta:    dist[i][k] + dist[k][j]

   Jo chhota ho wahi lo.

Loop order kyun k bahar hai — ye SABSE IMPORTANT baat hai:

SAHI:
   for k:       <- intermediate vertex BAHAR
      for i:
         for j:

GALAT:
   for i:
      for j:
         for k:    <- k andar

Kyun?  Kyunki recurrence ka structure hai "dist[k-1] se dist[k] banao".
       Jab hum k ka loop chalate hain, hum ye guarantee karte hain ki
       dist[i][k] aur dist[k][j] dono PICHHLE k values ke saath already
       optimal ho chuke hain.

       Agar k andar hoga, to hum dist[i][k] use karenge jo abhi tak
       compute hi nahi hua -> GALAT ANSWERS.

Ye ek line ka farak hai jo poore algorithm ko todta hai, aur interview mein
poochha jata hai.

Space optimisation — 3D se 2D:

Recurrence mein dist[k] sirf dist[k-1] par depend karta hai.
To hum 3D array ki jagah 2D use kar sakte hain, in-place update karte hue.

Kya ye safe hai?  Yaani kya dist[i][k] ya dist[k][j] is iteration mein badal sakte hain?

   dist[i][k] = min(dist[i][k], dist[i][k] + dist[k][k])
   dist[k][k] hamesha 0 hai (ya negative agar negative cycle ho)
   To dist[i][k] apne aap se update nahi hota  ->  SAFE  ✓

   Similarly dist[k][j]  ->  SAFE  ✓

Isliye 2D in-place kaam karta hai.  ->  O(V²) space

docs.title: Code
docs.text:
def floyd_warshall(n, edges):
    """All-pairs shortest paths. O(V³) time, O(V²) space.
    n = vertices ki sankhya (0 se n-1)
    edges = [(u, v, weight), ...]"""
    INF = float('inf')                              # 1
    dist = [[INF] * n for _ in range(n)]            # 2
    for i in range(n):                              # 3
        dist[i][i] = 0                              # 4
    for u, v, w in edges:                           # 5
        dist[u][v] = min(dist[u][v], w)             # 6

    for k in range(n):                              # 7
        dk = dist[k]                                # 8
        for i in range(n):                          # 9
            dik = dist[i][k]                        # 10
            if dik == INF:                          # 11
                continue                            # 12
            di = dist[i]                            # 13
            for j in range(n):                      # 14
                nd = dik + dk[j]                    # 15
                if nd < di[j]:                      # 16
                    di[j] = nd                      # 17
    return dist                                     # 18


def has_negative_cycle(dist, n):
    """Diagonal par negative value = negative cycle."""
    return any(dist[i][i] < 0 for i in range(n))    # 19

Line-by-line — kya aur kyun:

  1. INF = float('inf') — ek variable mein, kyunki baar baar use hoga.

  2. [[INF] * n for _ in range(n)] — list comprehension, [[INF]*n]*n NAHI. Wahi 2D array trap — *n n references banata ek hi row ke.

3-4. Diagonal 0. Har vertex se khud tak ki distance 0. Ye zaroori hai — warna line 15 mein dist[i][k] + dist[k][j] mein jab i == k ho to inf + something = inf aata aur koi path nahi milta.

5-6. Direct edges. min(dist[u][v], w) use kiya, direct assignment nahi — kyunki parallel edges ho sakte hain (do vertices ke beech kai edges). Sabse chhoti chahiye. Agar aap dist[u][v] = w likhte to aakhri edge jeet jata, sabse chhota nahi.

  1. for k in range(n) — OUTER LOOP, intermediate vertex. Ye order critical hai — k bahar, i aur j andar.

  2. dk = dist[k] — row k ko ek local variable mein cache kar liya. Python mein dist[k][j] do lookups hai (dist[k] phir [j]). dk[j] sirf ek. Ye ~20-30% speedup deta hai — inner loop n³ baar chalti hai, to har micro-optimisation matter karti hai.

  3. for i in range(n) — source vertex.

  4. dik = dist[i][k] — ye value inner loop mein constant hai, to bahar nikal li. n³ se n² lookups.

11-12. if dik == INF: continue — BAHUT bada optimisation. Agar i se k tak koi path hi nahi hai, to k ke through koi bhi path exist nahi karta. Poora inner j loop skip. Sparse graphs par ye 10x tak speedup de sakta hai.

  1. di = dist[i] — row i cache.

  2. for j in range(n) — destination vertex.

  3. nd = dik + dk[j] — i → k → j ka total.

16-17. if nd < di[j]: di[j] = nd — relaxation. if check use kiya, min() nahi. di[j] = min(di[j], nd) bhi sahi hai par: - min() ek function call hai (Python mein overhead). - if version sirf tab write karta hai jab zaroorat ho. Inner loop mein ye ~15% farak deta hai.

  1. Return.

  2. Negative cycle detection: dist[i][i] < 0. Kyun kaam karta hai? dist[i][i] ka matlab hai "i se i tak wapas aane ki shortest distance". Normally wo 0 hai (kahin jaao hi mat). Agar wo negative hai, to iska matlab hai ki ek cycle exist karta hai jo i se shuru hokar i par wapas aata hai aur uska total weight negative hai — negative cycle.

Path reconstruction ke saath:

def floyd_warshall_with_paths(n, edges):
    """Distances + next-hop matrix path reconstruction ke liye."""
    INF = float('inf')                              # 1
    dist = [[INF] * n for _ in range(n)]            # 2
    nxt = [[None] * n for _ in range(n)]            # 3
    for i in range(n):                              # 4
        dist[i][i] = 0                              # 5
    for u, v, w in edges:                           # 6
        if w < dist[u][v]:                          # 7
            dist[u][v] = w                          # 8
            nxt[u][v] = v                           # 9

    for k in range(n):                              # 10
        for i in range(n):                          # 11
            if dist[i][k] == INF:                   # 12
                continue                            # 13
            for j in range(n):                      # 14
                nd = dist[i][k] + dist[k][j]        # 15
                if nd < dist[i][j]:                 # 16
                    dist[i][j] = nd                 # 17
                    nxt[i][j] = nxt[i][k]           # 18
    return dist, nxt                                # 19


def reconstruct(nxt, u, v):
    """u se v tak ka path."""
    if nxt[u][v] is None:                           # 20
        return []                                   # 21
    path = [u]                                      # 22
    while u != v:                                   # 23
        u = nxt[u][v]                               # 24
        path.append(u)                              # 25
    return path                                     # 26

1-5. Setup. 6-9. Direct edges. nxt[u][v] = v — "u se v jaane ke liye agla hop v hai" (direct edge). 10-17. Standard triple loop. 18. nxt[i][j] = nxt[i][k] — k NAHI, nxt[i][k]. Kyun? Kyunki nxt[i][j] "i se j jaane ke liye pehla hop" store karta hai, poora path nahi. Naya path i → ... → k → ... → j hai, aur uska pehla hop wahi hai jo i → ... → k ka pehla hop tha. Yaani nxt[i][k]. Agar aap nxt[i][j] = k likhte to reconstruction galat hoti — wo k ko direct hop maan leti jabki i se k tak bhi ek raasta hai. 19. Return. 20-21. No path. 22-25. Next-hop chain follow karo. 26. Path.

Transitive closure (reachability) — Floyd-Warshall ka boolean version:

def transitive_closure(n, edges):
    """Kaun se node se kaun sa node reachable hai. O(V³)."""
    reach = [[False] * n for _ in range(n)]         # 1
    for i in range(n):                              # 2
        reach[i][i] = True                          # 3
    for u, v in edges:                              # 4
        reach[u][v] = True                          # 5
    for k in range(n):                              # 6
        for i in range(n):                          # 7
            if not reach[i][k]:                     # 8
                continue                            # 9
            for j in range(n):                      # 10
                if reach[k][j]:                     # 11
                    reach[i][j] = True              # 12
    return reach                                    # 13

1-5. Boolean matrix, direct edges. 6-12. Same triple loop, par min ki jagah OR. reach[i][j] = reach[i][j] OR (reach[i][k] AND reach[k][j]) 8-9. k se i reachable nahi → skip poora inner loop. 13. Return.

Ye "Warshall's algorithm" hai (Floyd ne shortest paths mein extend kiya). Iska use: - Dependency closure — "A par kya kya depend karta hai, indirectly bhi". - QA: "is module ko badalne se kaun se tests affect honge?"

Bitset optimisation: Boolean version mein har row ko ek integer bana kar bitwise OR use kar sakte ho — 64x speedup:

def transitive_closure_bitset(n, edges):
    """Bitset version — har row ek integer. ~64x tez."""
    reach = [1 << i for i in range(n)]              # 1
    for u, v in edges:                              # 2
        reach[u] |= 1 << v                          # 3
    for k in range(n):                              # 4
        bit_k = 1 << k                              # 5
        rk = reach[k]                               # 6
        for i in range(n):                          # 7
            if reach[i] & bit_k:                    # 8
                reach[i] |= rk                      # 9
    return reach                                    # 10
  1. Har row ek integer jisme bit j set hai agar j reachable hai. 1 << i = self-loop. 2-3. Direct edges — bit set karo. 4-6. k loop. 7-8. reach[i] & bit_k — kya i se k reachable hai? Ek bitwise AND, O(1).
  2. reach[i] |= rk — POORI ROW ek operation mein! Ye for j in range(n) loop ko ek single OR mein replace kar deta hai. Inner loop poori tarah gayab.
  3. Return.

Complexity: O(V³/64) effectively — kyunki har OR 64 bits ek saath process karta hai (Python mein arbitrary precision integers hain to aur bhi zyada). n = 1000 par ye 100x+ tez hai.

docs.title: Complexity derive karke
docs.text:
Teen nested loops, har ek n iterations:
   n * n * n = n³

TIME: O(V³)   -- hamesha, koi best/worst case nahi

Comparison:

Approach Sparse (E=V) Dense (E=V²) Negative weights? V × Dijkstra (heap) O(V² log V) O(V³ log V) Nahi V × Dijkstra (array) O(V³) O(V³) Nahi V × Bellman-Ford O(V³) O(V⁴) Haan Floyd-Warshall O(V³) O(V³) Haan Johnson's algorithm O(V² log V + VE) O(V³ log V) Haan

Conclusion: - Sparse graph + negative weights → Johnson's (Bellman-Ford se reweight karo, phir V baar Dijkstra). - Dense graph → Floyd-Warshall. - Sparse + non-negative → V × Dijkstra.

Practical numbers:

V Floyd-Warshall ops Feasible? 100 10^6 Instant 500 1.25 × 10^8 ~10 seconds Python mein 1000 10^9 ~2 minutes Python, ~1 second C++ 5000 1.25 × 10^11 Bhool jao

Python mein Floyd-Warshall ki practical limit ~400-600 vertices hai. Numpy ke saath ye 2000+ tak ja sakta hai.

Space: 

dist matrix:  O(V²)
nxt matrix:   O(V²) agar paths chahiye

TOTAL: O(V²)

V = 1000 par: 10^6 floats = ~8 MB. Theek hai. V = 10,000 par: 10^8 floats = 800 MB. Problem.

Metric Value Time Theta(V³) — hamesha Space Theta(V²) Negative weights Haan Negative cycle detection Haan (diagonal) Path reconstruction Haan (next-hop matrix)

docs.title: Stability, in-place, adaptive
docs.text:
Property Value Kyun Adaptive Nahi Hamesha V³, chahe graph khali ho ya complete In-place Haan (2D array par) 3D recurrence ko 2D mein collapse kar sakte hain Handles negative weights Haan Koi greedy assumption nahi Detects negative cycles Haan dist[i][i] < 0 Parallelisable Haan, achhe se i aur j loops independent hain given k

Negative cycle ke saath results: Agar negative cycle hai to dist values meaningless hain (un pairs ke liye jo cycle se guzarte hain). Sirf detect karo aur error return karo.

docs.title: Kab use karna hai / kab nahi
docs.text:
Use karo jab: - All-pairs shortest paths chahiye aur graph dense hai. - V chhota hai (< 500 Python mein, < 2000 C++ mein). - Negative weights hain. - Transitive closure / reachability chahiye. - Code simplicity matter karti hai — 5 lines ka algorithm galat likhna mushkil hai.

Mat use karo jab: - V bada hai — V³ prohibitive. - Sirf ek source chahiye → Dijkstra/Bellman-Ford. - Sparse graph → Johnson's algorithm (V² log V + VE). - Memory tight — O(V²) matrix.

Kuchh interesting uses:

Problem Floyd-Warshall variant Shortest paths min(d[i][j], d[i][k] + d[k][j]) Transitive closure d[i][j] OR (d[i][k] AND d[k][j]) Maximum bottleneck path (widest path) max(d[i][j], min(d[i][k], d[k][j])) Minimum bottleneck (minimax path) min(d[i][j], max(d[i][k], d[k][j])) Path counting d[i][j] += d[i][k] * d[k][j] Most reliable path (probabilities) max(d[i][j], d[i][k] * d[k][j])

Widest path ka example (QA context): "Ek data pipeline mein har jodi services ke beech maximum throughput kya hai?" — jahan path ka throughput uske sabse patle link se decide hota hai.

def widest_path(n, edges):
    """Har jodi ke beech maximum bottleneck capacity."""
    cap = [[0] * n for _ in range(n)]               # 1
    for i in range(n):                              # 2
        cap[i][i] = float('inf')                    # 3
    for u, v, c in edges:                           # 4
        cap[u][v] = max(cap[u][v], c)               # 5
    for k in range(n):                              # 6
        for i in range(n):                          # 7
            for j in range(n):                      # 8
                through_k = min(cap[i][k], cap[k][j])   # 9
                if through_k > cap[i][j]:           # 10
                    cap[i][j] = through_k           # 11
    return cap                                      # 12

1-3. Initial: 0 capacity (no path), diagonal inf (khud tak unlimited). 4-5. Direct edges, max kyunki parallel edges mein sabse mota chahiye. 6-8. Same triple loop. 9. min(cap[i][k], cap[k][j]) — path ka bottleneck uske sabse patle segment se decide hota hai. 10-11. > comparison, < nahi — hum maximise kar rahe hain. 12. Return.

Dhyaan do ki structure bilkul same hai — bas min/+ ki jagah max/min. Ye Floyd- Warshall ki generality dikhata hai: wo kisi bhi semiring par kaam karta hai.

docs.title: Kitne tareeke se optimize
docs.text:
# Optimisation Kya deta hai Kya leta hai 1 if dist[i][k] == INF: continue Sparse graphs par 5-10x Ek check 2 Row caching (dk = dist[k], di = dist[i]) Python mein 20-30% Do variables 3 if instead of min() 10-15% Python mein — 4 Numpy vectorisation — inner loop ko array operation banao 50-100x Python mein Numpy dependency 5 Bitset for boolean (transitive closure) 64x+ Sirf boolean version 6 Blocked / tiled version Cache-friendly, 2-3x Complicated 7 Parallel (i, j loops) Linear multi-core speedup Threading 8 Johnson's algorithm sparse graphs par O(V² log V + VE) Complicated 9 Skip if dist[k][j] == INF bhi Aur pruning Ek aur check

Numpy version — Python mein sabse practical optimisation:

import numpy as np                                  # 1


def floyd_warshall_numpy(n, edges):
    """Vectorised Floyd-Warshall. Pure Python se 50-100x tez."""
    INF = np.inf                                    # 2
    dist = np.full((n, n), INF, dtype=np.float64)   # 3
    np.fill_diagonal(dist, 0)                       # 4
    for u, v, w in edges:                           # 5
        dist[u, v] = min(dist[u, v], w)             # 6
    for k in range(n):                              # 7
        dist = np.minimum(dist,                     # 8
                          dist[:, k, None] + dist[None, k, :])   # 9
    return dist                                     # 10
  1. numpy. 2-4. Matrix setup. fill_diagonal in-place hai. 5-6. Edges.
  2. Sirf k ka loop bacha — i aur j loops vectorised ho gaye. 8-9. Ye ek line poore i aur j loops ko replace karti hai:
  3. dist[:, k, None] — column k, shape (n, 1). Ye dist[i][k] for all i.
  4. dist[None, k, :] — row k, shape (1, n). Ye dist[k][j] for all j.
  5. Broadcasting se (n,1) + (1,n) = (n,n) matrix ban jati hai jisme result[i][j] = dist[i][k] + dist[k][j].
  6. np.minimum element-wise minimum. Ye n² operations ko ek single vectorised call mein kar deta hai, jo C level par SIMD instructions se chalti hai.
  7. Return.

Speedup: V = 500 par pure Python ~10 seconds, numpy ~0.15 seconds. ~65x.

Interview answer: Floyd-Warshall computes all-pairs shortest paths with three nested loops. The outer loop k iterates over "allowed intermediate vertices": after iteration k, dist[i][j] holds the shortest path from i to j using only vertices 0 through k as intermediates. The update is dist[i][j] = min(dist[i][j], dist[i][k] + dist[k][j]) — either you don't route through k, or you do.

The critical detail is that k must be the outermost loop. The recurrence builds layer k from layer k-1, so when you use dist[i][k] and dist[k][j] they must already be finalised for all smaller intermediates. Putting k innermost reads values that haven't been computed yet and gives wrong answers — and it looks almost identical, so it's a classic bug.

It's O(V³) time and O(V²) space, always — no best or worst case. That makes it the right choice for dense graphs, where running Dijkstra V times would be O(V³ log V), and it handles negative weights, which Dijkstra can't. Negative cycles show up as a negative value on the diagonal, since dist[i][i] would otherwise be zero.

It also generalises beyond shortest paths. Replace min and plus with OR and AND and you get transitive closure; with max and min you get the widest-path or bottleneck problem — for example, maximum throughput between every pair of services in a pipeline. In Python I'd vectorise the inner two loops with numpy broadcasting, which is about 65 times faster than the pure loops, or use bitsets for the boolean version, which gives roughly 64x.

Cross-question: "For all-pairs shortest paths on a sparse graph with negative weights, is Floyd-Warshall the best choice?"

No — Johnson's algorithm is. It runs Bellman-Ford once from a virtual source to compute a potential function, reweights all edges so they're non-negative while preserving shortest-path ordering, then runs Dijkstra from every vertex. That's O(VE + V² log V), which on a sparse graph with E ≈ V is O(V² log V) versus Floyd-Warshall's O(V³). Floyd-Warshall wins on dense graphs and on simplicity — it's five lines and hard to get wrong.

docs.title: Kya hai
docs.text:
A (A-star) Dijkstra ka guided version hai: wo har node ko sirf "source se kitna door hai" nahi, balki "source se kitna door hai + target tak kitna aur lagega (anumaan)"* ke hisaab se priority deta hai.

Real-world analogy: Aap Delhi se Mumbai jaa rahe ho aur raaste mein har junction par decide karna hai kis taraf jaana hai. Dijkstra poore India mein saare directions mein barabar failta jayega — Kashmir ki taraf bhi utna hi explore karega jitna Rajasthan ki taraf. A* ke paas ek compass hai: wo jaanta hai Mumbai dakshin-pashchim mein hai, to wo Kashmir wale raaste ko kam priority deta hai. Wo compass hi "heuristic" hai.

docs.title: Kyu hai
docs.text:
Dijkstra sahi answer deta hai, par wo saare directions mein equally explore karta hai:

Dijkstra ka exploration pattern (target T ki taraf):

           . . . . . . .
         . . . . . . . . .
       . . . . . . . . . . .
     . . . . . S . . . . . . .        S = source
       . . . . . . . . . . .          T = target
         . . . . . . . . .
           . . . . . . .        T

   Ek CIRCLE (ya ellipse) mein failta hai. T ki taraf koi extra preference nahi.
   Nodes explored ~ pi * d²   (d = distance to target)


A* ka exploration pattern:

                    . . .
                 . . . . .
              . . . . . .
           . S . . . . . . . T
              . . . . . .
                 . . . . .
                    . . .

   T ki taraf ELONGATED. Peeche wale directions almost ignore.
   Nodes explored ~ proportional to d (good heuristic ke saath)

Real numbers (road network, 1 million nodes):

Algorithm Nodes explored Time Dijkstra ~500,000 2.5 s A* (straight-line heuristic) ~15,000 0.08 s Speedup 33x 31x

Yahi wajah hai ki Google Maps, game AI, aur robotics sab A* use karte hain.

docs.title: Kaise kaam karta hai
docs.text:
Teen values har node ke liye:

g(n) = source se n tak ki ACTUAL cost (jo humne abhi tak dekhi hai)
h(n) = n se target tak ki ESTIMATED cost (heuristic)
f(n) = g(n) + h(n)  = total estimated cost of path through n

Priority queue f(n) par order karti hai, g(n) par nahi.

Dijkstra:  priority = g(n)         <- sirf peeche ki taraf dekhta hai
A*:        priority = g(n) + h(n)  <- aage ki taraf bhi

Dijkstra A* ka special case hai jahan h(n) = 0 for all n.

ADMISSIBILITY — sabse important concept:

Ek heuristic h ADMISSIBLE hai agar:

   h(n) <= actual_cost(n to target)   for every n

Yaani wo KABHI OVER-ESTIMATE nahi karta.

Agar h admissible hai  ->  A* GUARANTEED optimal path deta hai.
Agar h over-estimate karta hai  ->  A* SUB-OPTIMAL path de sakta hai (par tez hoga).

Kyun admissibility zaroori hai:

Maan lo h(n) over-estimate karta hai. Ek node n jo OPTIMAL path par hai:
   f(n) = g(n) + h(n)  <- ye BADA ho jayega actual se

   To n heap mein neeche chala jayega.
   Ek doosra node m (sub-optimal path par) jiska h(m) accurate hai:
   f(m) = g(m) + h(m)  <- ye chhota lag sakta hai

   A* m ko pehle explore karega, aur target par sub-optimal path se pahunch jayega.
   -> GALAT ANSWER

CONSISTENCY (monotonicity) — aur strong property:

Ek heuristic CONSISTENT hai agar har edge (n, m) ke liye:

   h(n) <= cost(n, m) + h(m)

Ye "triangle inequality" hai heuristic par.

Consistent  ->  Admissible  (par ulta zaroori nahi)

Consistent heuristic ke saath:
   - f values monotonically increase hoti hain path par
   - Ek node ko dobara re-open karne ki zaroorat NAHI padti
   - A* Dijkstra jaisa behave karta hai (har node ek baar finalise)

Isliye practical implementations consistent heuristics prefer karti hain.

Common heuristics:

Domain Heuristic Admissible? Note Grid (4-directional) Manhattan distance: \|dx\| + \|dy\| Haan Perfect for 4-dir Grid (8-directional) Chebyshev: max(\|dx\|, \|dy\|) Haan Diagonals allowed Grid (any angle) Euclidean: sqrt(dx² + dy²) Haan Kabhi kabhi weak (under-estimates) Road network Straight-line (great-circle) distance Haan Roads seedhe nahi hote to under-estimate Puzzle (15-puzzle) Misplaced tiles count Haan Weak Puzzle (15-puzzle) Sum of Manhattan distances Haan Bahut behtar Any h = 0 Haan Ye Dijkstra hai Any h = actual distance Haan (barely) Perfect — sirf optimal path explore hoga

Heuristic ki quality ka trade-off:

h = 0:            Dijkstra. Optimal, par slow.
h = weak:         Optimal, thoda tez.
h = strong:       Optimal, bahut tez.
h = perfect:      Optimal, sirf optimal path explore hota hai.
h > actual:       TEZ, par SUB-OPTIMAL answer.

"Jitna h actual ke kareeb, utna tez -- par usse UPAR gaye to correctness gayi."

Step Pop (f, g, node) h Neighbours explored Pushed (f=g+h) 1 (8, 0, (0,0)) 8 (0,1) g=1 h=7; (1,0) g=1 h=7 (8,1,(0,1)), (8,1,(1,0)) 2 (8, 1, (0,1)) 7 (0,2) g=2 h=6 (8,2,(0,2)) 3 (8, 2, (0,2)) 6 (0,3) g=3 h=5 (8,3,(0,3)) 4 (8, 3, (0,3)) 5 (0,4) g=4 h=4 (8,4,(0,4)) 5 (8, 4, (0,4)) 4 (1,4) g=5 h=3 (8,5,(1,4)) 6 (8, 5, (1,4)) 3 (2,4) g=6 h=2 (8,6,(2,4)) 7 (8, 6, (2,4)) 2 (3,4) g=7 h=1 (8,7,(3,4)) 8 (8, 7, (3,4)) 1 (4,4) g=8 h=0 (8,8,(4,4)) 9 (8, 8, (4,4)) 0 TARGET! return 8

Dhyaan do ki har node ka f = 8 hai — kyunki Manhattan heuristic is grid par (walls ke alawa) perfect hai us path ke liye. Jab heuristic perfect hoti hai, A* koi bhi extra node explore nahi karta.

Ab Dijkstra ka comparison (same grid):

Step Pop (g, node) Explored 1 (0, (0,0)) (0,1), (1,0) 2 (1, (0,1)) (0,2) 3 (1, (1,0)) (2,0) 4 (2, (0,2)) (0,3) 5 (2, (2,0)) (2,1) 6 (3, (0,3)) (0,4) 7 (3, (2,1)) (2,2) 8 (4, (0,4)) (1,4) 9 (4, (2,2)) (3,2) 10 (5, (1,4)) (2,4) 11 (5, (3,2)) (4,2) 12 (6, (2,4)) (3,4) 13 (6, (4,2)) (4,1), (4,3) 14 (7, (3,4)) (4,4) 15 (7, (4,1)) (4,0) 16 (7, (4,3)) (4,4) already 17 (8, (4,4)) TARGET

Dijkstra ne 17 nodes explore kiye. A ne 9. Chhote grid par bhi ~2x farak.*

Bade grids par ye farak dramatic ho jata hai: 1000×1000 grid par Dijkstra ~500,000 nodes explore karega, A* ~2,000.

docs.title: Code
docs.text:
import heapq                                        # 1


def a_star(graph, start, goal, heuristic):
    """A* search. graph: {node: [(neighbour, cost), ...]}
    heuristic(node, goal) -> estimated remaining cost (admissible hona chahiye)"""
    g_score = {start: 0}                            # 2
    parent = {start: None}                          # 3
    open_heap = [(heuristic(start, goal), 0, start)]    # 4
    closed = set()                                  # 5

    while open_heap:                                # 6
        f, g, node = heapq.heappop(open_heap)       # 7
        if node == goal:                            # 8
            return g, _rebuild(parent, goal)        # 9
        if node in closed:                          # 10
            continue                                # 11
        closed.add(node)                            # 12
        for nb, cost in graph.get(node, []):        # 13
            if nb in closed:                        # 14
                continue                            # 15
            tentative_g = g + cost                  # 16
            if nb in g_score and tentative_g >= g_score[nb]:   # 17
                continue                            # 18
            g_score[nb] = tentative_g               # 19
            parent[nb] = node                       # 20
            f_new = tentative_g + heuristic(nb, goal)          # 21
            heapq.heappush(open_heap, (f_new, tentative_g, nb))   # 22

    return float('inf'), None                       # 23


def _rebuild(parent, goal):
    path = []                                       # 24
    node = goal                                     # 25
    while node is not None:                         # 26
        path.append(node)                           # 27
        node = parent[node]                         # 28
    path.reverse()                                  # 29
    return path                                     # 30

Line-by-line — kya aur kyun:

  1. heapq.

  2. g_score — actual cost from start. Ye Dijkstra ke dist jaisa hai.

  3. Parent tree.

  4. open_heap = [(heuristic(start, goal), 0, start)] — tuple (f, g, node).

  5. f pehle — heap isi par order karta hai. Yahi Dijkstra se farak hai.
  6. g doosre — hume g chahiye jab node pop ho (taaki neighbours ka g calculate kar sakein). Isse g_score dict lookup bach jata hai.

  7. node teesre. Note: agar f aur g dono tie ho jayein to Python node compare karega — agar nodes comparable nahi hain to TypeError. Tuples of ints (grid coordinates) comparable hain, to grids par safe hai. Custom objects ke liye counter add karo. Ek aur cheez: g ko tiebreaker rakhne se f tie par CHHOTA g wala pehle aata, jo aksar behtar hai (kam explored path prefer karo)... actually zyadatar implementations BADA g prefer karti hain (yaani -g use karti hain) kyunki wo goal ke zyada kareeb hai. Dono valid hain, thoda performance farak.

  8. closed — finalised nodes.

6-7. Heap pop.

8-9. Goal check pop par, push par NAHI. Ye critical hai. Agar aap goal ko push karte waqt check karte, to aapko pehla mila hua path milta, jo shortest nahi ho sakta. Pop par check karne se guarantee hai ki uska f minimum hai, aur admissible h ke saath h(goal) = 0 to f = g = shortest distance.

10-11. Lazy deletion — stale heap entries skip.

  1. Finalise.

  2. Neighbours.

14-15. nb in closed → skip. Consistent heuristic ke saath ye safe hai — ek closed node ka g_score final hai. Agar heuristic sirf admissible hai (consistent nahi), to ye check galat ho sakta hai — us case mein closed nodes ko "re-open" karna padta hai. Practically zyadatar heuristics (Manhattan, Euclidean) consistent hoti hain, to ye check theek hai.

  1. tentative_g = g + cost — is path se nb tak ka cost.

17-18. if nb in g_score and tentative_g >= g_score[nb]: continue — already behtar path mil chuka hai. >= use kiya, > nahi — equal cost par bhi skip, kyunki koi improvement nahi. nb in g_score check pehle — warna KeyError.

19-20. Better path — update.

  1. f_new = tentative_g + heuristic(nb, goal) — A* ka core formula: f = g + h.

  2. Push.

  3. Goal unreachable.

24-30. Path reconstruction.

Grid A* — practical version:

import heapq


def a_star_grid(grid, start, goal):
    """4-directional grid pathfinding. 0 = passable, 1 = wall."""
    rows, cols = len(grid), len(grid[0])            # 1

    def h(node):                                    # 2
        return abs(node[0] - goal[0]) + abs(node[1] - goal[1])   # 3

    g_score = {start: 0}                            # 4
    parent = {start: None}                          # 5
    heap = [(h(start), 0, start)]                   # 6
    closed = set()                                  # 7
    dirs = [(0, 1), (1, 0), (0, -1), (-1, 0)]       # 8

    while heap:                                     # 9
        f, g, (r, c) = heapq.heappop(heap)          # 10
        if (r, c) == goal:                          # 11
            return g                                # 12
        if (r, c) in closed:                        # 13
            continue                                # 14
        closed.add((r, c))                          # 15
        for dr, dc in dirs:                         # 16
            nr, nc = r + dr, c + dc                 # 17
            if not (0 <= nr < rows and 0 <= nc < cols):   # 18
                continue                            # 19
            if grid[nr][nc] == 1:                   # 20
                continue                            # 21
            if (nr, nc) in closed:                  # 22
                continue                            # 23
            ng = g + 1                              # 24
            if (nr, nc) in g_score and ng >= g_score[(nr, nc)]:   # 25
                continue                            # 26
            g_score[(nr, nc)] = ng                  # 27
            parent[(nr, nc)] = (r, c)               # 28
            heapq.heappush(heap, (ng + h((nr, nc)), ng, (nr, nc)))   # 29
    return -1                                       # 30
  1. Dimensions. 2-3. Manhattan distance heuristic. 4-directional movement ke liye ye exactly admissible aur consistent hai — kyunki har move exactly ek coordinate ko 1 se badalta hai, to minimum moves = Manhattan distance. Agar diagonals allowed hote to Manhattan over-estimate karta (diagonal ek move mein dono coordinates badalta) → inadmissible → galat answer. Us case mein Chebyshev (max(|dr|, |dc|)) chahiye. 4-8. Setup. dirs — 4 directions. 9-10. Pop. Tuple unpacking (r, c) directly heap entry se. 11-12. Goal. 13-15. Lazy deletion. 16-23. Neighbours with bounds, wall, aur closed checks. Order matter karta hai — bounds pehle.
  2. New g. 25-26. Better path check. 27-29. Update aur push.
  3. Unreachable.

Weighted A* (speed ke liye optimality trade karo):

def a_star_weighted(graph, start, goal, heuristic, weight=1.5):
    """f = g + weight*h. weight > 1 se tez par sub-optimal (bounded by weight)."""
    g_score = {start: 0}                            # 1
    heap = [(weight * heuristic(start, goal), 0, start)]    # 2
    closed = set()                                  # 3
    while heap:                                     # 4
        f, g, node = heapq.heappop(heap)            # 5
        if node == goal:                            # 6
            return g                                # 7
        if node in closed:                          # 8
            continue                                # 9
        closed.add(node)                            # 10
        for nb, cost in graph.get(node, []):        # 11
            ng = g + cost                           # 12
            if nb in g_score and ng >= g_score[nb]: # 13
                continue                            # 14
            g_score[nb] = ng                        # 15
            heapq.heappush(heap, (ng + weight * heuristic(nb, goal), ng, nb))   # 16
    return float('inf')                             # 17

1-2. weight * heuristic(...) — heuristic ko amplify kiya. 16. Same amplification.

Ye kya karta hai: weight > 1 se heuristic inadmissible ho jati hai (over-estimate), to A target ki taraf aur aggressively jata hai. Result: bahut tez, par path sub-optimal ho sakta hai.*

Guarantee: found path ka cost <= weight × optimal_cost. Yaani weight = 1.5 par path zyada se zyada 50% lamba hoga.

Practical numbers:

weight Nodes explored Path quality Use case 1.0 15,000 Optimal Jab optimality zaroori hai 1.2 4,000 ≤ 20% worse Good balance 1.5 1,500 ≤ 50% worse Real-time games 3.0 400 ≤ 200% worse Very fast, rough path ∞ ~d Any path Pure greedy best-first

Game AI mein weight = 1.2 se 2.0 common hai — player ko pata nahi chalta ki path 5% lamba hai, par CPU 4x bach jata hai.

docs.title: Complexity derive karke
docs.text:
Worst case (h = 0, yaani Dijkstra):
   TIME:  O(E log V)
   SPACE: O(V)

Best case (h = perfect):
   Sirf optimal path explore hota hai
   TIME:  O(d log d)   where d = path length
   SPACE: O(d)

Practical (good heuristic):
   Nodes explored ~ b^(epsilon * d)
   where b = branching factor
         d = solution depth
         epsilon = "relative error" of heuristic = (h* - h) / h*

   Agar h perfect (epsilon = 0):  O(d) nodes
   Agar h = 0 (epsilon = 1):      O(b^d) nodes  <- Dijkstra

Ye formula bahut insightful hai: heuristic ki quality exponent mein aati hai, base mein nahi. Isliye thodi si behtar heuristic bhi bahut bada farak karti hai.

Space complexity ki practical problem:

A* SAARE generated nodes memory mein rakhta hai (open + closed sets).
Bade search spaces mein ye MEMORY EXHAUSTION deta hai.

15-puzzle: ~10^13 states  ->  A* memory se marega, chahe heuristic kitni bhi acchi ho.

Solutions:
   IDA* (Iterative Deepening A*)  ->  O(d) memory
   SMA* (Simplified Memory-bounded A*)  ->  fixed memory budget
   Beam search  ->  har level par sirf top-k rakho (par optimality gayi)
Metric Value Time (worst) O(E log V) — Dijkstra jaisa Time (good heuristic) Practically 10-100x kam nodes Space O(V) — ye main limitation hai Optimality Guaranteed agar h admissible Completeness Haan (agar solution exist karta hai to milega)

docs.title: Kab use karna hai / kab nahi
docs.text:
Use karo jab: - Single source, single target aur target ki location ka kuchh andaaza hai. - Pathfinding — games, robotics, GPS. - Puzzle solving — 15-puzzle, Rubik's cube (IDA ke saath). - Aapke paas ek achhi admissible heuristic* hai.

Mat use karo jab: - Koi achhi heuristic nahi hai — h = 0 se ye Dijkstra hi ban jata hai, bas extra overhead ke saath. - All-pairs ya single-source-all-targets chahiye — heuristic ka koi matlab hi nahi (target hi nahi hai). Dijkstra use karo. - Memory tight hai aur search space bada — IDA use karo. - Graph mein negative weights hain — A Dijkstra jaisa hi fail karega.

docs.title: Kitne tareeke se optimize
docs.text:
# Optimisation Kya deta hai Kya leta hai 1 Behtar heuristic Exponentially kam nodes. Sabse bada impact Domain knowledge 2 Weighted A* (f = g + w·h) 4-10x tez Path ≤ w× optimal 3 Tie-breaking — equal f par bada g prefer karo 10-30% kam nodes Ek sign change 4 Bidirectional A* ~2x Complicated (meeting condition subtle) 5 IDA* — iterative deepening with f-limit O(d) memory Repeated work 6 Jump Point Search (uniform grids) 10-40x grids par Sirf uniform-cost grids 7 Precomputed landmarks (ALT) Road networks par 10-100x Heavy preprocessing 8 Contraction hierarchies Road networks par 1000x+ Bahut heavy preprocessing 9 Hierarchical A* — abstract levels Bade maps par bahut tez Multiple map levels

Tie-breaking optimisation (#3) — chhota change, bada fayda:

heapq.heappush(heap, (f_new, -tentative_g, nb))     # 1
  1. -tentative_g — negative! Isse equal f par bada g wala pehle aata hai. Kyun behtar hai? Bada g matlab hum goal ke zyada kareeb hain (aur h chhota hai). Un nodes ko pehle explore karna goal tak jaldi pahunchata hai. Ye ek character (minus sign) ka change hai jo typically 10-30% nodes bachata hai.

IDA* — memory-bounded A*:

def ida_star(start, goal, successors, heuristic):
    """Iterative Deepening A*. O(d) memory instead of O(b^d)."""
    threshold = heuristic(start, goal)              # 1
    path = [start]                                  # 2
    while True:                                     # 3
        result = _search(path, 0, threshold, goal, successors, heuristic)   # 4
        if result == 'FOUND':                       # 5
            return path                             # 6
        if result == float('inf'):                  # 7
            return None                             # 8
        threshold = result                          # 9


def _search(path, g, threshold, goal, successors, heuristic):
    node = path[-1]                                 # 10
    f = g + heuristic(node, goal)                   # 11
    if f > threshold:                               # 12
        return f                                    # 13
    if node == goal:                                # 14
        return 'FOUND'                              # 15
    minimum = float('inf')                          # 16
    for nb, cost in successors(node):               # 17
        if nb in path:                              # 18
            continue                                # 19
        path.append(nb)                             # 20
        t = _search(path, g + cost, threshold, goal, successors, heuristic)   # 21
        if t == 'FOUND':                            # 22
            return 'FOUND'                          # 23
        if t < minimum:                             # 24
            minimum = t                             # 25
        path.pop()                                  # 26
    return minimum                                  # 27
  1. Initial threshold = heuristic value — kyunki koi bhi path kam se kam itna to lagega.
  2. Current path (stack ki tarah).
  3. Iterative deepening loop.
  4. Depth-limited search with f <= threshold. 5-6. Mil gaya. 7-8. Koi path nahi (saare branches inf return kiye).
  5. threshold = result — result wo minimum f value hai jo threshold se bahar gayi. Agli iteration mein us tak explore karo. Ye ensures ki hum minimum possible increment karte hain, jisse optimality bani rehti hai.

10-11. Current node aur uska f. 12-13. f > threshold → is branch par ruk jao, aur f return karo (taaki caller minimum track kar sake). 14-15. Goal. 16. Minimum f jo threshold cross kiya. 17-19. Successors, cycle check (nb in path — O(depth), par depth chhoti hoti hai). 20. Path extend. 21. Recurse. 22-23. Found propagate. 24-25. Minimum track. 26. BACKTRACK — path se pop. 27. Return minimum.

IDA* ka memory: O(depth) — sirf current path. A* ka O(b^d). 15-puzzle jaise problems mein ye difference between "solvable" aur "out of memory" hai.

Repeated work: IDA* har threshold par poora search dohrata hai. Par kyunki har iteration mein nodes exponentially badhte hain, total work sirf ~2x hota hai (fibonacci-like growth).

Interview answer: A* is Dijkstra with a heuristic. Instead of prioritising nodes by g — the cost from the start — it prioritises by f = g + h, where h estimates the remaining cost to the goal. That biases the search toward the target instead of expanding uniformly in all directions. On a road network that typically cuts explored nodes by an order of magnitude or more.

The correctness condition is admissibility: h must never overestimate the true remaining cost. If it does, a node on the optimal path can get pushed down the queue behind a node on a suboptimal path, and you return a suboptimal answer. A stronger property, consistency — h(n) ≤ cost(n,m) + h(m) for every edge — additionally guarantees that once a node is closed its distance is final, so you never have to reopen it. Manhattan distance on a 4-directional grid, Chebyshev on an 8-directional one, and straight-line distance on road networks are all consistent.

Dijkstra is exactly A* with h = 0, and the quality of h determines where you sit between the two: a perfect heuristic explores only the optimal path, a zero heuristic explores everything.

The main limitation is memory — A keeps every generated node, so on huge state spaces like the 15-puzzle it exhausts RAM regardless of how good the heuristic is. IDA fixes that: iterative deepening on the f value, using O(depth) memory at the cost of about twice the work. And when optimality isn't strictly required, weighted A* with f = g + 1.5h explores maybe ten times fewer nodes while guaranteeing the path is at most 50% longer than optimal — that's the standard trade-off in game AI.

Cross-question: "What happens if your heuristic overestimates?"

You lose the optimality guarantee, but you don't lose completeness — you'll still find a path, just possibly a longer one. If the overestimate is bounded by a factor w, as in weighted A*, the path you find is guaranteed to be within w times optimal. That's a deliberate and useful trade when speed matters more than perfect paths.

docs.title: Kya hai
docs.text:
Union-Find (ya Disjoint Set Union, DSU) ek data structure hai jo elements ko groups mein rakhta hai aur do operations bahut tez karta hai: "ye do elements ek hi group mein hain?" (find) aur "in do groups ko mila do" (union).

Real-world analogy: Ek school mein bachche alag alag clubs mein hain. Har club ka ek captain hai. Kisi bachche se poochho "tumhara captain kaun hai?" — wo apne senior se poochhega, wo apne se, jab tak captain tak na pahunche. Do bachche same club mein hain agar unka captain same ho. Do clubs merge karne ke liye, ek captain doosre captain ko apna captain maan leta hai — ek hi assignment.

docs.title: Kyu hai
docs.text:
"Kya A aur B connected hain?" ye sawaal graph mein DFS/BFS se O(V+E) mein solve hota hai. Par agar aapko hazaaron aise sawaal poochne hon, ya edges dynamically add ho rahe hon, to har baar poora traversal bekaar hai.

Naive (har query par DFS):     Q queries x O(V+E)  =  O(Q(V+E))
Union-Find:                    O((V+E) * alpha(V)) ~ O(V+E)  practically LINEAR

Aur union-find ka asli power: wo incremental hai. Edges add hote jate hain aur connectivity information automatically maintain hoti hai. DFS ko har edge addition par poora dobara chalana padta.

Iska use kahan hota hai: - Kruskal's MST — "kya ye edge cycle banayegi?" - Connected components dynamically. - Cycle detection undirected graphs mein. - Percolation simulations. - Image segmentation — same-colour regions merge karna. - QA: test flakiness clustering — "kaun se tests aapas mein correlated failures dikhate hain".

docs.title: Kaise kaam karta hai
docs.text:
Basic structure — forest of trees:

Har element ka ek "parent" hota hai.
Root (jiska parent khud hai) us group ka REPRESENTATIVE hai.

parent = [0, 0, 1, 3, 3]
          0  1  2  3  4

Trees:
      0           3
      |          / \
      1         4   (kuchh aur)
      |
      2

find(2):  2 -> 1 -> 0  ->  root = 0
find(4):  4 -> 3       ->  root = 3
find(2) != find(4)  ->  alag groups

Do optimisations jo isse fast banate hain:

1. Path Compression (find ke dauraan)

find(2) call karne par:
   Before:  0 <- 1 <- 2
   After:   0 <- 1
            ^
            +---- 2      <- 2 ko SEEDHA root se joda

Agli baar find(2) O(1) hoga.

2. Union by Rank/Size (union ke dauraan)

Do trees merge karte waqt, CHHOTE tree ko BADE tree ke neeche lagao.

GALAT (bina rank ke):
   Har baar A ko B ke neeche lagate raho
   ->  ek lambi chain ban jati hai  ->  find O(n)

SAHI (rank ke saath):
   Chhota tree bade ke neeche
   ->  height logarithmic rehti hai  ->  find O(log n)

Dono optimisations SAATH mein:  O(alpha(n))  --  practically constant

alpha(n) — inverse Ackermann function:

alpha(n) itna dheere badhta hai ki:
   alpha(n) <= 4  for all n < 2^65536

Yaani universe mein jitne atoms hain (10^80) usse bhi bade n ke liye alpha(n) <= 4.

PRACTICALLY CONSTANT.
