docs.text:
Elements 0-5, operations:

Initial: parent = [0,1,2,3,4,5], rank = [0,0,0,0,0,0] (har element apna group)

   0    1    2    3    4    5      (6 separate groups)

Op 1: union(0, 1)

Step Detail find(0) parent[0] = 0 → root 0 find(1) parent[1] = 1 → root 1 Different roots Union karo rank[0] == rank[1] == 0 Equal → 1 ko 0 ke neeche, rank[0] += 1

parent = [0,0,2,3,4,5], rank = [1,0,0,0,0,0]

   0        2    3    4    5
   |
   1

Op 2: union(2, 3)

Same logic: parent = [0,0,2,2,4,5], rank = [1,0,1,0,0,0]

   0        2        4    5
   |        |
   1        3

Op 3: union(0, 2)

Step Detail find(0) = 0, find(2) = 2 Different rank[0] = 1, rank[2] = 1 Equal → 2 ko 0 ke neeche, rank[0] += 1

parent = [0,0,0,2,4,5], rank = [2,0,1,0,0,0]

      0          4    5
     / \
    1   2
        |
        3

Op 4: find(3) with path compression

Step Path Action 1 3 → 2 parent[3] = 2 2 2 → 0 parent[2] = 0, root found Compression Path [3, 2] parent[3] = 0, parent[2] = 0

parent = [0,0,0,0,4,5]

      0             4    5
    / | \
   1  2  3          <- 3 ab SEEDHA root se juda

Ab find(3) O(1) hai.

Op 5: union(4, 5)

parent = [0,0,0,0,4,4], rank = [2,0,1,0,1,0]

      0             4
    / | \           |
   1  2  3          5

Op 6: connected(1, 3)?

find(1) = 0, find(3) = 0 → same root → TRUE ✓

Op 7: connected(1, 5)?

find(1) = 0, find(5) = 4 → different → FALSE ✓

Op 8: union(3, 5)

Step Detail find(3) = 0, find(5) = 4 Different rank[0] = 2, rank[4] = 1 rank[0] > rank[4] → 4 ko 0 ke neeche, rank unchanged

parent = [0,0,0,0,0,4], rank = [2,0,1,0,1,0]

       0
    / | | \
   1  2 3  4
            |
            5

Sab ek group mein. components = 1.

docs.title: Code
docs.text:
class UnionFind:
    """Disjoint Set Union with path compression + union by rank.
    Practically O(1) amortised per operation."""

    def __init__(self, n):
        self.parent = list(range(n))                # 1
        self.rank = [0] * n                         # 2
        self.size = [1] * n                         # 3
        self.components = n                         # 4

    def find(self, x):
        """x ka root, path compression ke saath."""
        root = x                                    # 5
        while self.parent[root] != root:            # 6
            root = self.parent[root]                # 7
        while self.parent[x] != root:               # 8
            nxt = self.parent[x]                    # 9
            self.parent[x] = root                   # 10
            x = nxt                                 # 11
        return root                                 # 12

    def union(self, a, b):
        """Do groups merge karo. True agar merge hua, False agar already same."""
        ra, rb = self.find(a), self.find(b)         # 13
        if ra == rb:                                # 14
            return False                            # 15
        if self.rank[ra] < self.rank[rb]:           # 16
            ra, rb = rb, ra                         # 17
        self.parent[rb] = ra                        # 18
        self.size[ra] += self.size[rb]              # 19
        if self.rank[ra] == self.rank[rb]:          # 20
            self.rank[ra] += 1                      # 21
        self.components -= 1                        # 22
        return True                                 # 23

    def connected(self, a, b):
        return self.find(a) == self.find(b)         # 24

    def group_size(self, x):
        return self.size[self.find(x)]              # 25

Line-by-line — kya aur kyun:

  1. list(range(n)) — har element apna parent (yaani apna group). [0]*n likhna galat hoga — sab ka parent 0 ho jata, yaani sab ek group mein.

  2. rank — tree ki approximate height. Height, size nahi — rank sirf upper bound hai height ka (path compression ke baad actual height kam ho sakti hai, par rank update nahi hota).

  3. size — group mein kitne elements. Alag se maintain kiya, kyunki rank size nahi batata.

  4. components — kitne separate groups. Connected components count ke liye ye free hai.

5-7. Root dhoondho — parent chain follow karo jab tak parent[root] == root na ho.

8-11. PATH COMPRESSION — two-pass version. Pehle pass (5-7) ne root dhoondh liya. Ab doosra pass (8-11) poore path ke har node ka parent seedha root kar deta hai. - Line 9: nxt = self.parent[x] — agla node bachao PEHLE, kyunki line 10 use overwrite kar degi. Bina is line ke aap chain kho dete ho. - Line 10: parent[x] = root — direct link. - Line 11: x = nxt — aage. Ye "two-pass" version hai. Ek "one-pass" recursive version bhi hai: 

def find(self, x):
    if self.parent[x] != x:
        self.parent[x] = self.find(self.parent[x])
    return self.parent[x]
Recursive version chhota hai par recursion limit ka risk hai bade n par (agar path lamba ho — jo union-by-rank ke saath nahi hona chahiye, par defensive rehna behtar hai). Iterative version production ke liye behtar hai.

  1. Root return.

  2. Dono roots.

14-15. Already same group → False. Ye return value bahut useful hai: Kruskal mein "kya ye edge cycle banayegi?" ka jawab exactly yahi hai. False = cycle.

16-17. UNION BY RANK — chhote ko bade ke neeche. if rank[ra] < rank[rb]: swap — isse ra hamesha bada (ya barabar) rank wala hota hai. Swap karke code simplify ho jata hai — neeche sirf ek case handle karna padta hai. Bina union-by-rank ke: worst case mein ek lambi chain ban sakti hai (union(0,1), union(1,2), union(2,3), ...) → find O(n).

  1. parent[rb] = ra — chhota tree bade ke neeche.

  2. Size update — ra ka size badha, kyunki rb uske andar aa gaya. rb ka size update karne ki zaroorat nahi — wo ab root nahi raha, uska size meaningless hai. (Par usko stale chhodna theek hai, kyunki hum hamesha size[find(x)] padhte hain.)

20-21. if rank[ra] == rank[rb]: rank[ra] += 1 Rank sirf tab badhta hai jab dono trees ki height same ho. Kyun? - Agar rank[ra] > rank[rb]: rb ko ra ke neeche lagane se ra ki height nahi badhti (kyunki rb ka subtree ra ki existing height se chhota hai). - Agar equal: naya tree ki height ek badh jati hai. Ye rule hi logarithmic height guarantee karta hai.

  1. Component count kam.

  2. Merge hua.

  3. Connectivity check.

  4. size[find(x)] — root ka size, size[x] nahi. Non-root elements ka size stale hota hai.

Union by size (rank ka alternative):

def union_by_size(self, a, b):
    ra, rb = self.find(a), self.find(b)             # 1
    if ra == rb:                                    # 2
        return False                                # 3
    if self.size[ra] < self.size[rb]:               # 4
        ra, rb = rb, ra                             # 5
    self.parent[rb] = ra                            # 6
    self.size[ra] += self.size[rb]                  # 7
    self.components -= 1                            # 8
    return True                                     # 9

1-3. Same. 4-5. Size par compare, rank par nahi. 6-7. Merge. 8-9. Same.

Rank vs size — kaunsa behtar? - Same asymptotic complexity — dono O(log n) height guarantee dete hain (path compression ke saath dono O(alpha(n))). - Size zyada intuitive hai aur size array waise bhi chahiye hota hai aksar. - Rank thoda kam memory (chhote integers). - Practically size thoda behtar hota hai — kyunki wo actual tree ke baare mein zyada information rakhta hai.

Weighted Union-Find (with relationships) — advanced:

class WeightedUnionFind:
    """Union-Find jo elements ke beech RELATIVE values track karta hai.
    Use case: 'A, B se 5 zyada hai' type constraints."""

    def __init__(self, n):
        self.parent = list(range(n))                # 1
        self.rank = [0] * n                         # 2
        self.weight = [0] * n                       # 3

    def find(self, x):
        if self.parent[x] != x:                     # 4
            root = self.find(self.parent[x])        # 5
            self.weight[x] += self.weight[self.parent[x]]   # 6
            self.parent[x] = root                   # 7
        return self.parent[x]                       # 8

    def union(self, a, b, diff):
        """b - a = diff set karo."""
        ra, rb = self.find(a), self.find(b)         # 9
        if ra == rb:                                # 10
            return self.weight[b] - self.weight[a] == diff   # 11
        if self.rank[ra] < self.rank[rb]:           # 12
            ra, rb = rb, ra                         # 13
            a, b = b, a                             # 14
            diff = -diff                            # 15
        self.parent[rb] = ra                        # 16
        self.weight[rb] = self.weight[a] + diff - self.weight[b]   # 17
        if self.rank[ra] == self.rank[rb]:          # 18
            self.rank[ra] += 1                      # 19
        return True                                 # 20

1-3. weight[x] = x ki value minus uske parent ki value. 4-8. Recursive find with weight accumulation. Line 6: weight[x] += weight[parent[x]] — jab hum x ko seedha root se jodte hain, uska weight poore path ka cumulative ho jana chahiye. Line 5 (recursive call) pehle chalti hai, jisse weight[parent[x]] already root-relative ho chuka hota hai. Order critical hai — line 6 line 7 se pehle, warna parent[x] badal jata hai. 9-11. Same group → consistency check. Ye constraint satisfaction ke liye use hota hai. 12-15. Rank-based swap. diff ko bhi negate karna zaroori hai kyunki a aur b swap ho gaye. 16-17. Merge with weight adjustment. 18-20. Rank.

Use case: "Evaluate Division" (LeetCode 399) — a/b = 2, b/c = 3, a/c = ?. Ya "constraints check" problems.

docs.title: Complexity derive karke
docs.text:
Bina kisi optimisation ke: 

find:  O(n)  worst case (lambi chain)
union: O(n)  (find dominates)

Sirf union by rank: 

Tree ki height <= log2(n)

Proof: rank r ka tree banane ke liye kam se kam 2^r elements chahiye.
   (Induction: rank r+1 ka tree do rank-r trees se banta hai,
    to size >= 2 * 2^r = 2^(r+1))

   n elements ke saath: 2^r <= n  ->  r <= log2(n)

find:  O(log n)
union: O(log n)

Sirf path compression: 

Amortised O(log n) per operation
(Exact analysis complicated hai)

Dono saath: 

Amortised O(alpha(n)) per operation

alpha = inverse Ackermann function
alpha(n) <= 4 for all practical n

PRACTICALLY O(1)

Tarjan ne 1975 mein prove kiya ki ye bound TIGHT hai — koi bhi pointer-based union-find Omega(alpha(n)) se behtar nahi kar sakta.

Practical numbers:

n Without optimisations Union by rank Both 10^3 ~10^3 ~10 ~2 10^6 ~10^6 ~20 ~3 10^9 ~10^9 ~30 ~3

Space: parent, rank, size — O(n).

Operation Time (amortised) Space __init__(n) O(n) O(n) find(x) O(alpha(n)) ≈ O(1) — union(a, b) O(alpha(n)) ≈ O(1) — connected(a, b) O(alpha(n)) ≈ O(1) — m operations on n elements O(m · alpha(n)) O(n)

docs.title: Stability, in-place, adaptive
docs.text:
Property Value Kyun Supports deletion? Nahi Union-Find sirf merge karta hai, split nahi. Split ke liye "link-cut trees" chahiye Dynamic (incremental) Haan — ye iska main fayda hai Edges add karte jao, connectivity maintained Persistent? Nahi (standard version) Persistent version exist karta hai par complicated Order-independent? Haan Union operations kisi bhi order mein — final grouping same

Deletion ki problem: Union-Find se ek edge hata nahi sakte. Agar aapko dynamic connectivity chahiye deletions ke saath, to "offline dynamic connectivity" (segment tree on time) ya link-cut trees chahiye — dono kaafi complicated.

docs.title: Kab use karna hai / kab nahi
docs.text:
Use karo jab: - Kruskal's MST — cycle detection ke liye. - Connected components jab edges incrementally aa rahe hon. - Cycle detection in undirected graphs. - Equivalence classes — "ye do cheezein same category mein hain?" - Percolation / network reliability simulations. - Image segmentation — pixels ko regions mein group karna. - Account merging — "same person ke kitne accounts hain?"

Mat use karo jab: - Directed graph connectivity — union-find undirected hai. Directed ke liye SCC. - Edges delete hote hain — union-find support nahi karta. - Shortest path chahiye — union-find sirf connectivity batata hai, distance nahi. - Ek hi query hai — DFS/BFS simpler hai.

QA context example:

def cluster_flaky_tests(correlated_pairs, test_names):
    """Tests jo saath mein fail hote hain, unhe clusters mein group karo."""
    idx = {name: i for i, name in enumerate(test_names)}   # 1
    uf = UnionFind(len(test_names))                        # 2
    for a, b in correlated_pairs:                          # 3
        uf.union(idx[a], idx[b])                           # 4
    clusters = defaultdict(list)                           # 5
    for name in test_names:                                # 6
        clusters[uf.find(idx[name])].append(name)          # 7
    return list(clusters.values())                         # 8
  1. Name → index mapping. Union-Find integers par kaam karta hai, to strings ko map karna padta hai.
  2. UF banao. 3-4. Har correlated pair merge karo.
  3. Root → members mapping. 6-7. Har test ko uske root ke under group karo. uf.find() use kiya, uf.parent[] nahi — kyunki parent intermediate node ho sakta hai, root nahi.
  4. Clusters list.

Isse aap dekh sakte ho ki "kaun se tests ek hi root cause se fail ho rahe hain".

docs.title: Kitne tareeke se optimize
docs.text:
# Optimisation Kya deta hai Kya leta hai 1 Path compression find O(n) → amortised O(log n) Kuchh nahi 2 Union by rank/size Height O(n) → O(log n) Ek array 3 Dono saath O(alpha(n)) ≈ O(1) Do arrays 4 Path halving — parent[x] = parent[parent[x]] har step par Same complexity, ek pass, thoda tez Compression thodi kam 5 Path splitting — similar Same — 6 Iterative find Recursion limit ka risk khatam Thoda lamba code 7 components counter Connected components count free Ek integer 8 size array Group size O(1) mein Ek array

Path halving (one-pass alternative):

def find_halving(self, x):
    while self.parent[x] != x:                      # 1
        self.parent[x] = self.parent[self.parent[x]]    # 2
        x = self.parent[x]                          # 3
    return x                                        # 4
  1. Jab tak root na mile.
  2. parent[x] = parent[parent[x]] — x ko uske grandparent se jod do. Path ki length aadhi ho jati hai.
  3. Do steps aage (kyunki line 2 ne parent[x] badal diya, ab x = parent[x] grandparent hai).
  4. Root.

Ye "path halving" hai — full compression nahi karti par: - Ek hi pass (two-pass version do passes karta hai). - Same amortised complexity — O(alpha(n)). - Practically thoda tez kyunki kam memory writes.

Zyadatar competitive programmers path halving use karte hain.

Interview answer: Union-Find maintains a partition of elements into disjoint sets and supports two operations: find, which returns a set's representative, and union, which merges two sets. It's a forest where each element points to a parent and the roots are representatives.

Two optimisations make it fast. Path compression: during find, repoint every node on the path directly to the root, so subsequent finds on that path are O(1). Union by rank or size: always attach the smaller tree under the larger, which keeps heights logarithmic instead of letting a degenerate chain form. With both, the amortised cost per operation is O(alpha(n)), the inverse Ackermann function, which is at most 4 for any n below 2^65536 — practically constant. Tarjan proved that bound is tight.

Its key advantage over DFS-based connectivity is that it's incremental: as edges arrive, the connectivity information stays current with no recomputation. That's why it's the backbone of Kruskal's algorithm — the union returning False tells you exactly that the edge would close a cycle — and of dynamic connected-component tracking.

The limitation is that it only merges, never splits. If edges can be deleted you need something much heavier, like link-cut trees or offline dynamic connectivity.

Cross-question: "Why does rank only increase when the two ranks are equal?"

Because attaching a shorter tree under a taller one doesn't change the taller tree's height — the shorter tree fits entirely within the existing depth. Only when both trees have the same height does merging add a level. That rule is what makes the height logarithmic: you need at least 2^r elements to reach rank r, by induction, so with n elements the rank is at most log2(n).

docs.title: Kya hai
docs.text:
Kruskal's algorithm ek Minimum Spanning Tree (MST) banata hai: saare edges ko weight ke hisaab se sort karo, aur ek-ek karke sabse sasti edge lete jao — par sirf tab jab wo cycle na banaye.

Real-world analogy: Aapko 10 gaanvon ko bijli ki taar se jodna hai, minimum taar mein. Aap saare possible connections ki list banate ho aur unhe sabse saste se mehnge tak sort karte ho. Phir ek-ek karke lete jaate ho: "kya ye connection kisi aise gaanv ko jodta hai jo pehle se juda nahi hai? Haan to lo. Nahi (dono already connected hain) to chhodo, wo taar waste hoga."

docs.title: Kyu hai
docs.text:
MST kya hai: ek connected, undirected, weighted graph mein aisa subset of edges jo: - Saare vertices ko connect kare (spanning) - Koi cycle na ho (tree) - Total weight minimum ho

MST ke real uses: - Network design — minimum cable/pipeline laying. - Clustering — MST ki sabse badi edges hata do, clusters mil jate hain. - Approximation algorithms — TSP ka 2-approximation MST se banta hai. - Image segmentation. - QA: minimum set of integration tests jo saare components ko connect kare.

MST ke do main algorithms:

KRUSKAL:  edges ko sort karo, sasti se mehngi tak lo (agar cycle na bane)
          -> EDGE-centric
          -> O(E log E)
          -> Sparse graphs par behtar

PRIM:     ek vertex se shuru karo, tree ko ek-ek vertex se grow karo
          -> VERTEX-centric
          -> O(E log V) with binary heap, O(V^2) with array
          -> Dense graphs par behtar

docs.title: Kaise kaam karta hai
docs.text:
1. Saare edges ko weight ke ascending order mein sort karo
2. Ek Union-Find banao (har vertex apna component)
3. Har edge (u, v, w) ko order mein dekho:
      agar find(u) != find(v):        <- alag components mein hain
          edge ko MST mein daalo
          union(u, v)
      warna:
          skip (cycle banayegi)
4. Jab MST mein V-1 edges ho jayen -> DONE

Cut property — Kruskal sahi kyun hai:

CUT PROPERTY: Kisi bhi "cut" (vertices ka do groups mein partition) ke liye,
              us cut ko cross karne wali SABSE HALKI edge kisi MST mein hoti hai.

Proof (exchange argument):
   Maan lo e = cut ki sabse halki crossing edge hai, par kisi MST T mein nahi hai.
   T mein e ko add karo -> ek CYCLE ban jayega.
   Us cycle mein koi aur edge f hogi jo same cut ko cross karti hai.
   weight(f) >= weight(e)  (kyunki e sabse halki hai)
   f ko hatao, e ko rakho -> naya spanning tree, weight <= original
   -> e wale MST exist karta hai  QED

Kruskal har step par: current edge cut ki sabse halki crossing edge hai
(kyunki humne sort kiya hai aur pichhli saari edges ya to li hain ya cycle banati thin)
-> har step SAFE hai  -> final answer MST hai

docs.title: Code
docs.text:
def kruskal(n, edges):
    """Minimum Spanning Tree. n = vertices (0 se n-1), edges = [(w, u, v), ...]
    Returns: (total_weight, mst_edges) ya (None, None) agar graph disconnected ho."""
    edges = sorted(edges)                           # 1
    uf = UnionFind(n)                               # 2
    mst = []                                        # 3
    total = 0                                       # 4
    for w, u, v in edges:                           # 5
        if uf.union(u, v):                          # 6
            mst.append((u, v, w))                   # 7
            total += w                              # 8
            if len(mst) == n - 1:                   # 9
                break                               # 10
    if len(mst) != n - 1:                           # 11
        return None, None                           # 12
    return total, mst                               # 13

Line-by-line — kya aur kyun:

  1. sorted(edges) — edges (weight, u, v) format mein hain, to tuple comparison weight par pehle sort karega. Yahi wajah hai ki weight pehle rakha hai. Agar (u, v, w) format hota to sorted(edges, key=lambda e: e[2]) likhna padta — kaam karta par thoda dheema (lambda call per comparison). sorted() naya list banata hai — original input intact rehta. Agar aap edges.sort() likhte to caller ka data modify ho jata (surprising side effect).

  2. Union-Find with n vertices.

3-4. MST edges aur total weight.

  1. for w, u, v in edges — sorted order mein.

  2. if uf.union(u, v) — YE POORA ALGORITHM HAI. union True return karta hai agar merge hua (yaani u aur v alag components mein the), False agar already same (yaani cycle banegi). Ye ek line do kaam kar rahi hai: cycle check aur merge. Alag if uf.find(u) != uf.find(v) likh kar phir uf.union(u,v) karna bhi sahi hai, par wo do extra find calls karta hai.

7-8. MST mein add aur weight jodo.

9-10. len(mst) == n - 1 par EARLY EXIT. Ek spanning tree mein exactly V-1 edges hoti hain. Ye milte hi baaki edges dekhne ka koi matlab nahi. Dense graphs par ye bada fayda deta hai — E = V^2 edges mein se sirf V-1 chahiye.

11-12. len(mst) != n - 1 matlab graph DISCONNECTED hai. Agar saare edges dekh liye aur V-1 nahi mile, to graph connected hi nahi hai — MST exist hi nahi karta. Ye check zaroori hai warna aap ek incomplete forest return kar dete aur caller ko lagta ki wo MST hai. Agar aap Minimum Spanning FOREST chahte ho (har component ka MST), to ye check hata do aur jo mila wo return kar do.

  1. Result.

Different input format ke saath:

def kruskal_from_adjacency(n, adj):
    """adj: {u: [(v, weight), ...]}. Undirected assumed."""
    edges = []                                      # 1
    seen = set()                                    # 2
    for u in adj:                                   # 3
        for v, w in adj[u]:                         # 4
            key = (min(u, v), max(u, v))            # 5
            if key not in seen:                     # 6
                seen.add(key)                       # 7
                edges.append((w, u, v))             # 8
    return kruskal(n, edges)                        # 9

1-2. Edge list aur duplicate tracker. 3-4. Har adjacency entry. 5. (min, max) normalised key — undirected graph mein edge (u,v) aur (v,u) same hai. Adjacency list mein wo dono taraf store hoti hai. 6-8. Duplicate skip. Bina iske har edge do baar aati aur sorting mein 2x kaam hota. 9. Kruskal chalao.

Maximum Spanning Tree (chhota variation):

def maximum_spanning_tree(n, edges):
    """Maximum weight spanning tree. Bas sort order ulta karo."""
    edges = sorted(edges, reverse=True)             # 1
    uf = UnionFind(n)                               # 2
    mst = []                                        # 3
    total = 0                                       # 4
    for w, u, v in edges:                           # 5
        if uf.union(u, v):                          # 6
            mst.append((u, v, w))                   # 7
            total += w                              # 8
            if len(mst) == n - 1:                   # 9
                break                               # 10
    return total, mst                               # 11
  1. reverse=True — bas itna hi farak. Sabse mehngi edges pehle. Cut property ulti direction mein bhi kaam karti hai — kisi bhi cut ki sabse bhaari crossing edge maximum spanning tree mein hoti hai. 2-11. Bilkul same.

Use case: "maximum bandwidth network", "maximum reliability spanning tree".

docs.title: Complexity derive karke
docs.text:
Sorting edges:         O(E log E)
Union-Find operations: E finds + (V-1) unions
                       = O(E * alpha(V))
                       ~ O(E)   (alpha practically constant)

TOTAL: O(E log E + E * alpha(V))
     = O(E log E)              <- sorting dominates

E log E vs E log V:

E <= V^2
log E <= log(V^2) = 2 log V

To  O(E log E) = O(E * 2 log V) = O(E log V)

Dono equivalent hain asymptotically. Log likhne ka convention alag alag hai.

Comparison with Prim:

Graph type Kruskal Prim (binary heap) Prim (array) Winner Sparse (E ~ V) O(V log V) O(V log V) O(V^2) Tie (Kruskal / Prim heap) Medium O(E log V) O(E log V) O(V^2) Tie Dense (E ~ V^2) O(V^2 log V) O(V^2 log V) O(V^2) Prim with array

Kruskal ka fayda: - Simple code (agar Union-Find already hai). - Edge list format natural hai. - Agar edges pehle se sorted hain to O(E·alpha(V)) ~ O(E) — linear! - Disconnected graphs par Minimum Spanning Forest deta hai.

Prim ka fayda: - Dense graphs par (array-based) O(V^2). - Adjacency list format natural hai. - Ek hi tree grow hota hai.

Space: 

Sorted edges:  O(E)
Union-Find:    O(V)
MST result:    O(V)

TOTAL: O(V + E)

Metric Value Time O(E log E) = O(E log V) Time (pre-sorted edges) O(E · alpha(V)) ~ O(E) Space O(V + E) Works on disconnected? Haan (gives forest) Negative weights? Haan

docs.title: Stability, in-place, adaptive
docs.text:
Property Value Kyun Handles negative weights Haan MST mein weight ka sign matter nahi karta, sirf relative order Unique MST? Sirf agar saare weights distinct hon Equal weights par kai MSTs ho sakte hain Deterministic Ties par sort order par depend Stable sort se deterministic Adaptive Haan, agar edges pre-sorted hon O(E log E) becomes O(E)

MST uniqueness ka proof idea: agar saare edge weights distinct hain to MST unique hai. Exchange argument se — agar do alag MSTs hon to unmein ek sabse halki different edge hogi, aur usse contradiction nikalta hai.

docs.title: Kab use karna hai / kab nahi
docs.text:
Use karo jab: - Sparse graph (E bahut kam V^2 se). - Edges pehle se sorted hain — tab ye linear hai. - Edge list format mein data hai. - Disconnected graph — forest chahiye. - Union-Find pehle se available hai codebase mein.

Mat use karo jab: - Dense graph — Prim with array O(V^2) behtar. - Graph implicitly defined hai (edges compute karne padte hain) — Prim behtar, kyunki wo sirf current tree ke neighbours dekhta hai. - Directed graph — MST ka concept undirected ke liye hai. Directed ke liye "minimum spanning arborescence" (Chu-Liu/Edmonds algorithm) chahiye.

docs.title: Kitne tareeke se optimize
docs.text:
# Optimisation Kya deta hai Kya leta hai 1 Early exit at V-1 edges Dense graphs par bahut kam edges process Ek check 2 Union-Find with both optimisations Non-sorting part effectively linear Do arrays 3 Partial sort / heap — sirf zaroorat ke hisaab se Best case mein poora sort nahi Heap overhead 4 Radix sort edges (integer weights) O(E log E) becomes O(E) Weights integer hone chahiye 5 Filter edges pehle — clearly useless edges hatao Kam sorting Filtering logic 6 Boruvka's algorithm Parallelisable, O(E log V) Complicated 7 Karger-Klein-Tarjan Expected O(E) — linear! Randomised, bahut complicated

Heap-based partial sorting:

import heapq


def kruskal_lazy_sort(n, edges):
    """Poora sort nahi karta -- heap se ek-ek edge nikaalta hai."""
    heap = list(edges)                              # 1
    heapq.heapify(heap)                             # 2
    uf = UnionFind(n)                               # 3
    mst = []                                        # 4
    total = 0                                       # 5
    while heap and len(mst) < n - 1:                # 6
        w, u, v = heapq.heappop(heap)               # 7
        if uf.union(u, v):                          # 8
            mst.append((u, v, w))                   # 9
            total += w                              # 10
    return (total, mst) if len(mst) == n - 1 else (None, None)   # 11

1-2. heapify O(E), sorted O(E log E). Ye pehla fayda hai. 3-5. Setup. 6. len(mst) < n - 1 — loop condition mein early exit built-in. 7. heappop O(log E) — sirf jitni edges chahiye utni hi pop hongi. 8-10. Standard. 11. Result.

Kab fayda hai: 

Agar MST ke liye sirf k edges dekhni padin (k bahut kam E se):
   sorted():  O(E log E)  -- POORA sort
   heap:      O(E) heapify + O(k log E) pops

Dense graph mein k ~ V, E ~ V^2:
   sorted():  V^2 log V
   heap:      V^2 + V log V  ~  V^2

   log V factor bach gaya!

Practically ye dense graphs par 10-20x tez ho sakta hai.

Interview answer: Kruskal builds a minimum spanning tree by sorting all edges by weight and greedily taking each one unless it would create a cycle. Union-Find is what makes the cycle test efficient: union returns false exactly when both endpoints are already in the same component, which is precisely when the edge would close a cycle.

Correctness comes from the cut property: for any partition of the vertices, the lightest edge crossing that partition belongs to some MST. Kruskal's current edge is always the lightest edge crossing the cut between the component it would join and everything else, so every choice is safe. That's provable with an exchange argument — if the light edge weren't in some MST, adding it creates a cycle, and swapping out a heavier edge on that cycle gives a tree that's no worse.

Complexity is O(E log E) dominated by the sort; the Union-Find operations total O(E·alpha(V)), which is effectively linear. So if the edges arrive pre-sorted, or you can radix-sort integer weights, Kruskal is effectively O(E).

Versus Prim: Kruskal is edge-centric and better on sparse graphs, and it naturally produces a minimum spanning forest on disconnected graphs. Prim is vertex-centric, and with a simple array priority queue it's O(V^2), which beats both on dense graphs. Two practical details: stop as soon as you have V-1 edges, and if you finish the edge list with fewer than V-1, the graph is disconnected and no spanning tree exists.

Cross-question: "Is the MST unique?"

Only if all edge weights are distinct. With distinct weights, an exchange argument shows any two MSTs must be identical. With ties there can be several MSTs, all with the same total weight — which one you get depends on the tie-breaking order in the sort. If the problem needs a specific one, you have to define the tie-break explicitly.

docs.title: Kya hai
docs.text:
Prim's algorithm ek MST banata hai ek vertex se shuru karke, tree ko ek-ek vertex karke grow karte hue — har baar wo sabse sasti edge lete hue jo tree ko kisi naye vertex se jode.

Real-world analogy: Aap ek naye shehar mein paani ki pipeline bichha rahe ho. Aap main tank se shuru karte ho. Har baar aap poochte ho: "jitne ghar abhi tak jud chuke hain, unse kisi NAYE ghar tak sabse sasti pipe kaunsi hai?" Wo pipe daal do. Dohrao. Kruskal wala thekedaar poore shehar mein bikhri hui pipes daalta rehta hai aur baad mein unhe jodta hai; Prim ek hi jagah se failta hai.

docs.title: Kyu hai
docs.text:
Kruskal edge-centric hai: saare edges sort karo, phir cycle-free wale lo. Uski cost O(E log E) hai — sorting dominate karta hai.

Prim vertex-centric hai: har step par sirf current tree se nikalne wali edges dekho. Ye do faayde deta hai:

1. Dense graphs par tez. Array-based priority queue ke saath Prim O(V²) hai, jo E = V² par Kruskal ke O(V² log V) se behtar hai.

2. Implicit graphs par natural. Agar edges "compute" karne padte hain (jaise points ke beech distance), to Kruskal ko poore V² edges pehle generate karne padte hain. Prim sirf current tree ke neighbours dekhta hai — memory bahut kam.

Example: 10,000 points ke beech Euclidean MST

Kruskal:  saare C(10000, 2) = 5 crore edges generate karo, sort karo
          -> ~2 GB memory, ~1 minute

Prim (array):  har step par V distances scan karo
          -> O(V) memory = 10,000 entries, ~10 seconds

Prim ki kharabi: disconnected graphs par sirf ek component ka MST deta hai (Kruskal poora forest deta hai).

docs.title: Kaise kaam karta hai
docs.text:
1. Koi bhi vertex se shuru karo. Use tree mein daalo.
2. Ek priority queue rakho jisme tree se bahar jaane wali saari edges hon.
3. Jab tak tree mein saare vertices na aa jayein:
      a. PQ se sabse sasti edge nikaalo
      b. Agar uska doosra end already tree mein hai -> skip (cycle)
      c. Warna: us vertex ko tree mein daalo, edge ko MST mein daalo
      d. Us naye vertex ki saari edges PQ mein daalo

Diagram — tree grow hota hua:

Step 0:  tree = {A}
         frontier edges: A-B(7), A-D(5)

Step 1:  sabse sasti A-D(5) lo
         tree = {A, D}
         frontier: A-B(7), D-E(15), D-G(6)

Step 2:  sabse sasti D-G(6) lo
         tree = {A, D, G}
         frontier: A-B(7), D-E(15), G-E(9), G-F(11)

Step 3:  sabse sasti A-B(7) lo
         tree = {A, B, D, G}
         ...

Har step par tree ek vertex badhta hai.

Prim vs Kruskal ka visual farak:

KRUSKAL (edges anywhere):        PRIM (tree grows from one point):

   A--D    C--E                     A
                                    |
   A--D    C--E--F                  A--D

   A--D--G  C--E--F                 A--D--G

   A--B--D--G  C--E--F              A--B--D--G

   sab connect ho gaye              A--B--D--G--E--C--F

Cut property yahan bhi: Prim har step par cut (tree, non-tree) ki sabse halki crossing edge leta hai. Cut property se wo edge kisi MST mein hai → har step safe.

docs.title: Code
docs.text:
Heap-based (sparse graphs ke liye):

import heapq


def prim_heap(graph, start):
    """MST using binary heap. O(E log V). graph: {u: [(v, w), ...]}"""
    in_tree = set()                                 # 1
    mst = []                                        # 2
    total = 0                                       # 3
    heap = [(0, start, None)]                       # 4
    while heap and len(in_tree) < len(graph):       # 5
        w, v, parent = heapq.heappop(heap)          # 6
        if v in in_tree:                            # 7
            continue                                # 8
        in_tree.add(v)                              # 9
        if parent is not None:                      # 10
            mst.append((parent, v, w))              # 11
            total += w                              # 12
        for nb, nw in graph.get(v, []):             # 13
            if nb not in in_tree:                   # 14
                heapq.heappush(heap, (nw, nb, v))   # 15
    if len(in_tree) != len(graph):                  # 16
        return None, None                           # 17
    return total, mst                               # 18

Line-by-line — kya aur kyun:

  1. in_tree — kaun se vertices tree mein hain. 2-3. MST edges aur total weight.
  2. heap = [(0, start, None)] — (weight, vertex, parent) tuple.
  3. Weight pehle — heap isi par order karta hai.
  4. Start ka weight 0 — wo "free" hai (koi edge nahi lagti).

  5. Parent None — start ka koi parent nahi. Tie-breaking note: agar do entries ka weight same ho to Python vertex compare karega. Agar vertices comparable nahi hain (custom objects) to TypeError. Grid coordinates aur strings comparable hain.

  6. while heap and len(in_tree) < len(graph) — do conditions:

  7. heap — kuchh process karne ko bacha hai.

  8. len(in_tree) < len(graph) — early exit jab saare vertices aa jayein. Iske baad heap mein bachi stale entries dekhne ki zaroorat nahi.

  9. Pop — sabse sasti frontier edge.

7-8. if v in in_tree: continue — LAZY DELETION. Ye Dijkstra wali hi baat hai. Heap mein ek vertex ki kai entries ho sakti hain (alag alag parents se, alag weights). Sabse sasti pehle pop hogi, baaki stale hain. Bina is check ke: ek vertex kai baar tree mein add hoga aur MST mein extra edges aa jayengi — wrong answer, sirf slow nahi.

  1. Tree mein add.

10-12. if parent is not None — start vertex ke liye koi edge nahi hai. Bina is check ke mst mein (None, start, 0) aa jata — garbage entry.

13-15. Naye vertex ki saari edges heap mein. if nb not in in_tree — already-tree wale neighbours push karne ka koi matlab nahi (wo line 7 par skip ho jayenge, par push/pop ka cost bach jata hai). Ye ek optimisation hai, correctness ke liye zaroori nahi.

16-17. Disconnected check — agar saare vertices tree mein nahi aaye.

  1. Result.

Array-based (dense graphs ke liye, O(V²)):

def prim_dense(n, weight_matrix):
    """MST for dense graphs. O(V^2), no heap.
    weight_matrix[u][v] = weight, ya float('inf') agar edge nahi."""
    INF = float('inf')                              # 1
    key = [INF] * n                                 # 2
    parent = [-1] * n                               # 3
    in_tree = [False] * n                           # 4
    key[0] = 0                                      # 5
    total = 0                                       # 6
    mst = []                                        # 7

    for _ in range(n):                              # 8
        u = -1                                      # 9
        best = INF                                  # 10
        for v in range(n):                          # 11
            if not in_tree[v] and key[v] < best:    # 12
                best = key[v]                       # 13
                u = v                               # 14
        if u == -1:                                 # 15
            return None, None                       # 16
        in_tree[u] = True                           # 17
        if parent[u] != -1:                         # 18
            mst.append((parent[u], u, key[u]))      # 19
            total += key[u]                         # 20
        for v in range(n):                          # 21
            w = weight_matrix[u][v]                 # 22
            if not in_tree[v] and w < key[v]:       # 23
                key[v] = w                          # 24
                parent[v] = u                       # 25
    return total, mst                               # 26
  1. INF.
  2. key[v] — tree se v tak ki minimum edge weight. Ye "frontier distance" hai.
  3. parent[v] — us minimum edge ka tree-side endpoint. -1 = koi nahi.
  4. Tree membership.

  5. key[0] = 0 — vertex 0 se shuru. 6-7. Total aur MST.

  6. n iterations — har iteration ek vertex add karti hai.

9-14. LINEAR SCAN se minimum key wala non-tree vertex dhoondho. Ye O(V) hai — heap ka O(log V) se dheema. Par ye V baar chalta hai → O(V²). Heap version mein ye O(log V) hota par E baar → O(E log V). Dense graph mein E = V², to heap version V² log V aur array version V² — array jeet gaya.

15-16. Koi reachable vertex nahi mila → disconnected.

  1. Tree mein add.

18-20. MST edge record. parent[u] != -1 — start vertex skip.

21-25. Naye vertex u se saare non-tree vertices ki keys update karo. w < key[v] — agar u se v tak ka raasta ab tak ke best se sasta hai to update. Ye "decrease-key" operation hai, par array par O(1) — heap par O(log V) hoti. Yahi array version ka fayda hai.

  1. Result.

Dono versions ka comparison:

Heap version:
   V pops    x O(log E)  = V log E
   E pushes  x O(log E)  = E log E
   TOTAL: O(E log E) = O(E log V)

Array version:
   V iterations x O(V) scan  = V^2
   V iterations x O(V) update = V^2
   TOTAL: O(V^2)

Sparse (E = V):     heap V log V  vs  array V^2      -> HEAP
Dense (E = V^2):    heap V^2 log V vs array V^2      -> ARRAY
Crossover: E ~ V^2 / log V

Implicit graph Prim (points ke beech Euclidean MST):

import math


def euclidean_mst(points):
    """Points ke beech MST. Edges implicitly compute hoti hain.
    O(V^2) time, O(V) space -- Kruskal O(V^2) memory leta."""
    n = len(points)                                 # 1
    if n <= 1:                                      # 2
        return 0, []                                # 3
    INF = float('inf')                              # 4
    key = [INF] * n                                 # 5
    parent = [-1] * n                               # 6
    in_tree = [False] * n                           # 7
    key[0] = 0                                      # 8
    total = 0                                       # 9
    mst = []                                        # 10

    for _ in range(n):                              # 11
        u, best = -1, INF                           # 12
        for v in range(n):                          # 13
            if not in_tree[v] and key[v] < best:    # 14
                best, u = key[v], v                 # 15
        in_tree[u] = True                           # 16
        if parent[u] != -1:                         # 17
            mst.append((parent[u], u, key[u]))      # 18
            total += key[u]                         # 19
        ux, uy = points[u]                          # 20
        for v in range(n):                          # 21
            if in_tree[v]:                          # 22
                continue                            # 23
            vx, vy = points[v]                      # 24
            d = math.hypot(ux - vx, uy - vy)        # 25
            if d < key[v]:                          # 26
                key[v] = d                          # 27
                parent[v] = u                       # 28
    return total, mst                               # 29

1-3. Guards. 4-10. Setup — koi edge list nahi banai. 11-19. Standard Prim. 20. Current vertex ke coordinates. 21-28. Distance ON THE FLY compute ho rahi hai — koi pre-computed edge list nahi. 25. math.hypot(dx, dy) — overflow-safe Euclidean distance. 29. Result.

Memory comparison for 10,000 points: 

Kruskal:  C(10000,2) = 5 crore edges x 24 bytes = ~1.2 GB
Prim:     3 arrays x 10,000 entries = ~240 KB

5000x kam memory.

docs.title: Kab use karna hai / kab nahi
docs.text:
Use karo jab: - Dense graph — array version O(V²). - Implicit graph — edges compute karne padte hain (geometric MST, complete graphs). - Memory tight — array version O(V) space, Kruskal O(E). - Adjacency list format mein data hai. - Ek hi connected component hai.

Mat use karo jab: - Sparse graph aur edges pehle se sorted hain — Kruskal linear ho jata hai. - Disconnected graph aur forest chahiye — Kruskal use karo (ya har component par Prim alag se). - Edge list format natural hai — Kruskal simpler.

docs.title: Kitne tareeke se optimize
docs.text:
# Optimisation Kya deta hai Kya leta hai 1 Array PQ dense graphs par O(E log V) → O(V²), dense mein tez Sparse par dheema 2 Lazy deletion (heap version) decrease-key ki zaroorat nahi Heap mein duplicates 3 Already-in-tree neighbours skip Kam heap pushes Ek check 4 Early exit at V vertices Bache hue stale entries skip Ek condition 5 Fibonacci heap O(E + V log V) theory Practically dheema 6 d-ary heap Dense graphs par 20-30% Tuning 7 Implicit graph — edges on the fly O(E) memory → O(V) Distance recompute 8 Parallel Boruvka Multi-core Complicated

Prim vs Kruskal — decision table:

Situation Choice Kyun Sparse graph, edge list Kruskal Natural format, O(E log E) Sparse graph, adjacency list Either Same complexity Dense graph Prim (array) O(V²) vs O(V² log V) Complete graph / implicit Prim (array) O(V) memory vs O(V²) Edges pre-sorted Kruskal O(E·alpha) ~ linear Disconnected, forest chahiye Kruskal Automatic Streaming edges Kruskal Edges aate hi process Simplicity Kruskal (if UF available) 13 lines

Interview answer: Prim grows a single tree from a starting vertex. At each step it takes the cheapest edge crossing from the tree to a vertex not yet in the tree, adds that vertex, and repeats until all vertices are covered. Correctness is the same cut property Kruskal uses: the lightest edge crossing the cut between the tree and the rest belongs to some MST.

The implementation choice matters a lot. With a binary heap it's O(E log V), which is best on sparse graphs. With a plain array as the priority queue — scan all V keys for the minimum, then update keys in O(1) — it's O(V²), which beats the heap version on dense graphs where E is around V². That's the opposite of the usual "always use a heap" instinct, and it comes from the fact that a dense graph does O(V²) decrease-key operations, each costing log V with a heap and O(1) with an array.

Prim's other big advantage is implicit graphs. For a Euclidean MST over ten thousand points, Kruskal would need to materialise fifty million edges — over a gigabyte — while Prim computes distances on the fly and needs only O(V) memory. That's a five-thousand-fold difference.

The trade-off versus Kruskal: Prim only spans the component containing the start vertex, so on a disconnected graph it gives you one tree, not the whole minimum spanning forest. Kruskal handles that automatically.

Cross-question: "You said an array priority queue can beat a heap. When exactly?"

When E is large relative to V. Prim does V extract-mins and up to E decrease-keys. With a heap that's V log V + E log V; with an array it's V² + E, since extract-min is a linear scan but decrease-key is a single assignment. The heap wins when E log V is less than V², so the crossover is around E = V²/log V. For a complete graph with a thousand vertices, that's a million versus ten million operations — the array is ten times faster.

docs.title: Kya hai
docs.text:
Topological sort ek directed acyclic graph (DAG) ke vertices ko aisi line mein lagata hai ki har edge u → v ke liye, u line mein v se pehle aaye.

Real-world analogy: Kapde pehnne ka order. Aap underwear se pehle pants nahi pehen sakte, socks se pehle shoes nahi, shirt se pehle tie nahi. Ye "X se pehle Y" wali constraints ek DAG banati hain, aur topological sort aapko ek valid dressing order deta hai. Kai valid orders ho sakte hain (socks pehle ya underwear pehle — dono chalega), par kuchh orders galat hain.

docs.title: Kyu hai
docs.text:
Bahut saare real problems dependency ordering ke baare mein hain:

  • Build systems — make, Bazel: kaunsi file pehle compile karni hai.
  • Package managers — pip, npm: dependencies pehle install karo.
  • Task scheduling — CI/CD pipelines.
  • Course prerequisites — kaunsa course pehle.
  • Spreadsheet formulas — cell recalculation order.
  • Compiler — instruction scheduling, symbol resolution.
  • QA: test execution order jab kuchh tests dusron ka setup banate hain.

Aur ek bonus: topological sort cycle detect kar leta hai. Agar order banana possible hi nahi hai to graph mein cycle hai — jo aksar ek bug hota hai (circular dependency).

Do algorithms:

KAHN's ALGORITHM (BFS-based):
   In-degree count karo, 0-degree wale process karo, degrees ghatate jao
   -> Iterative, cycle detection natural
   -> Lexicographically smallest order de sakta hai (heap se)

DFS-BASED:
   DFS karo, finish times record karo, ULTA order lo
   -> Recursive, simpler code
   -> Cycle detection colours se

docs.title: Kaise kaam karta hai
docs.text:
Kahn's algorithm:

1. Har vertex ka IN-DEGREE count karo (kitni edges usme aa rahi hain)
2. Saare 0-in-degree vertices ko queue mein daalo
   (inki koi dependency nahi hai, ye pehle ho sakte hain)
3. Jab tak queue khali na ho:
      a. Ek vertex u nikaalo, output mein daalo
      b. Uske har neighbour v ka in-degree 1 kam karo
         (kyunki u ho chuka, ab v ki ek dependency kam)
      c. Agar v ka in-degree 0 ho gaya -> queue mein daalo
4. Agar output mein saare V vertices nahi hain -> CYCLE hai

Diagram:

Graph:      A --> B --> D
            |     ^
            v     |
            C ----+

in-degrees:  A:0, B:2, C:1, D:1

Queue: [A]           output: []
Pop A, output: [A]
   B's in-degree: 2->1
   C's in-degree: 1->0  -> queue
Queue: [C]           output: [A]
Pop C, output: [A,C]
   B's in-degree: 1->0  -> queue
Queue: [B]           output: [A,C]
Pop B, output: [A,C,B]
   D's in-degree: 1->0  -> queue
Queue: [D]           output: [A,C,B]
Pop D, output: [A,C,B,D]
Queue: []            DONE

Valid topological order: A, C, B, D

DFS-based:

1. Har unvisited vertex se DFS chalao
2. Jab ek vertex ka DFS KHATAM ho (saare descendants explore ho gaye),
   use ek stack mein push karo
3. Aakhir mein stack ko ULTA karke output karo

Kyun ye kaam karta hai?
   Agar edge u -> v hai, to DFS(u) DFS(v) ko call karega (ya v already visited hoga).
   Dono cases mein, v ka FINISH TIME u se PEHLE hoga.
   To reverse finish order mein u, v se pehle aayega.  QED

CYCLE detection ka example:

Graph with cycle:   A --> B --> C --> A

in-degrees: A:1, B:1, C:1

Queue initially: []   <- KOI ZERO IN-DEGREE VERTEX NAHI!
Loop chalta hi nahi.

0 != 3  ->  CYCLE DETECTED  ✓

docs.title: Code
docs.text:
Kahn's algorithm:

from collections import deque, defaultdict


def topological_sort_kahn(vertices, edges):
    """Kahn's algorithm. Returns order ya None agar cycle ho.
    edges: [(u, v), ...] matlab u must come before v"""
    graph = defaultdict(list)                       # 1
    in_degree = {v: 0 for v in vertices}            # 2
    for u, v in edges:                              # 3
        graph[u].append(v)                          # 4
        in_degree[v] += 1                           # 5

    queue = deque([v for v in vertices if in_degree[v] == 0])   # 6
    order = []                                      # 7

    while queue:                                    # 8
        u = queue.popleft()                         # 9
        order.append(u)                             # 10
        for v in graph[u]:                          # 11
            in_degree[v] -= 1                       # 12
            if in_degree[v] == 0:                   # 13
                queue.append(v)                     # 14

    if len(order) != len(vertices):                 # 15
        return None                                 # 16
    return order                                    # 17

Line-by-line — kya aur kyun:

  1. Adjacency list.
  2. in_degree = {v: 0 for v in vertices} — saare vertices ko initialise karo, sirf jo edges mein hain unhe nahi. Bina iske, isolated vertices (jinki koi edge nahi) dict mein aate hi nahi aur line 6 mein KeyError. 3-5. Graph build aur in-degrees count.
  3. deque([v for v in vertices if in_degree[v] == 0]) — saare zero-in-degree vertices se shuru. deque use kiya, list nahi — popleft() O(1) chahiye. list.pop(0) O(n) hai. Multiple starting points ho sakte hain — ye multi-source BFS jaisa hai.
  4. Output order. 8-9. Standard BFS loop.
  5. Output mein add. 11-12. Har neighbour ka in-degree 1 kam — kyunki u ho chuka hai, v ki ek dependency satisfy ho gayi. 13-14. In-degree 0 ho gaya → saari dependencies satisfy → ab ye process ho sakta hai. 15-16. len(order) != len(vertices) → CYCLE. Kyun? Agar cycle hai to us cycle ke vertices ka in-degree kabhi 0 nahi hoga (har ek ki ek dependency cycle ke andar hai). Wo kabhi queue mein nahi aayenge, to output mein bhi nahi. Ye cycle detection FREE hai — koi extra kaam nahi.
  6. Order return.

Lexicographically smallest topological order:

import heapq
from collections import defaultdict


def topological_sort_lexicographic(vertices, edges):
    """Sabse chhota lexicographic topological order."""
    graph = defaultdict(list)                       # 1
    in_degree = {v: 0 for v in vertices}            # 2
    for u, v in edges:                              # 3
        graph[u].append(v)                          # 4
        in_degree[v] += 1                           # 5

    heap = [v for v in vertices if in_degree[v] == 0]   # 6
    heapq.heapify(heap)                             # 7
    order = []                                      # 8

    while heap:                                     # 9
        u = heapq.heappop(heap)                     # 10
        order.append(u)                             # 11
        for v in graph[u]:                          # 12
            in_degree[v] -= 1                       # 13
            if in_degree[v] == 0:                   # 14
                heapq.heappush(heap, v)             # 15

    return order if len(order) == len(vertices) else None   # 16

1-5. Same. 6-7. deque ki jagah HEAP. heapify O(V). 9-10. heappop — sabse chhota available vertex. Ye ek greedy choice hai — har step par jitne vertices available hain, unme se lexicographically smallest lo. Ye lexicographically smallest overall order deta hai. 15. heappush — O(log V). 16. Same cycle check.

Complexity: O(V log V + E) — heap operations ki wajah se log V extra.

DFS-based topological sort:

from collections import defaultdict

WHITE, GREY, BLACK = 0, 1, 2


def topological_sort_dfs(vertices, edges):
    """DFS-based topological sort. Returns order ya None agar cycle ho."""
    graph = defaultdict(list)                       # 1
    for u, v in edges:                              # 2
        graph[u].append(v)                          # 3

    colour = {v: WHITE for v in vertices}           # 4
    order = []                                      # 5
    has_cycle = [False]                             # 6

    def visit(u):                                   # 7
        if has_cycle[0]:                            # 8
            return                                  # 9
        colour[u] = GREY                            # 10
        for v in graph[u]:                          # 11
            if colour[v] == GREY:                   # 12
                has_cycle[0] = True                 # 13
                return                              # 14
            if colour[v] == WHITE:                  # 15
                visit(v)                            # 16
        colour[u] = BLACK                           # 17
        order.append(u)                             # 18

    for v in vertices:                              # 19
        if colour[v] == WHITE:                      # 20
            visit(v)                                # 21

    if has_cycle[0]:                                # 22
        return None                                 # 23
    order.reverse()                                 # 24
    return order                                    # 25

1-3. Graph. 4. Colours: WHITE (unvisited), GREY (in progress), BLACK (done). 5. Finish order. 6. has_cycle = [False] — list mein wrap kiya taaki nested function modify kar sake. (nonlocal has_cycle bhi likh sakte the.) 7. Nested visit. 8-9. Early termination — cycle mil gaya to aur kaam mat karo. 10. GREY = "abhi explore kar rahe hain" — ye node call stack par hai. 11. Neighbours. 12-14. colour[v] == GREY → BACK EDGE → CYCLE. GREY ka matlab v abhi bhi stack par hai, yaani v u ka ancestor hai. u → v edge us ancestor tak wapas jati hai = cycle. Ye cycle detection ka core hai directed graphs mein. 15-16. WHITE → recurse. BLACK neighbours ko skip karte hain — wo already fully processed hain, unke through koi cycle nahi ho sakti. 17. BLACK — poori tarah done. 18. order.append(u) — FINISH TIME par append. Ye line 17 ke BAAD honi chahiye, aur line 11-16 ke baad — yaani saare descendants process hone ke baad. 19-21. Har vertex se try karo — graph disconnected ho sakta hai. 22-23. Cycle. 24. order.reverse() — FINISH ORDER KA ULTA. Ye critical hai. Finish order mein "sabse gehra" vertex pehle aata hai. Topological order mein wo aakhir mein aana chahiye. Alternative: order.insert(0, u) line 18 mein — par wo O(n) per insert hai, O(n²) total. append + final reverse O(n) hai. 25. Return.

Iterative DFS version (recursion limit se bachne ke liye):

def topological_sort_dfs_iterative(vertices, edges):
    """Iterative DFS topological sort. Koi recursion limit nahi."""
    graph = defaultdict(list)                       # 1
    for u, v in edges:                              # 2
        graph[u].append(v)                          # 3

    colour = {v: WHITE for v in vertices}           # 4
    order = []                                      # 5

    for start in vertices:                          # 6
        if colour[start] != WHITE:                  # 7
            continue                                # 8
        stack = [(start, iter(graph[start]))]       # 9
        colour[start] = GREY                        # 10
        while stack:                                # 11
            u, it = stack[-1]                       # 12
            advanced = False                        # 13
            for v in it:                            # 14
                if colour[v] == GREY:               # 15
                    return None                     # 16
                if colour[v] == WHITE:              # 17
                    colour[v] = GREY                # 18
                    stack.append((v, iter(graph[v])))   # 19
                    advanced = True                 # 20
                    break                           # 21
            if not advanced:                        # 22
                colour[u] = BLACK                   # 23
                order.append(u)                     # 24
                stack.pop()                         # 25

    order.reverse()                                 # 26
    return order                                    # 27

1-5. Setup. 6-8. Har unvisited start se. 9. Stack mein (vertex, iterator) tuple. Iterator store karna key trick hai — recursion mein for v in graph[u] ka "kahan tak pahunche" implicit hota hai (loop variable). Iterative version mein hume wo explicitly store karna padta hai, warna har baar shuru se scan karna padta (O(V·E)). 10. Start ko GREY. 11-12. stack[-1] — peek, pop nahi. Kyunki hum abhi is vertex ke saath kaam kar rahe hain. 13. Flag. 14. Iterator se aage badho — jahan pichhli baar chhoda tha wahin se. 15-16. Cycle. 17-21. Naya vertex mila → stack par push aur BREAK. break zaroori hai — hum "recursive call" simulate kar rahe hain, to current vertex ka loop ruk jana chahiye aur naye vertex par shift hona chahiye. 22-25. Iterator exhaust ho gaya → saare neighbours done → ye vertex FINISH ho gaya. BLACK, order mein add, stack se pop. 26-27. Reverse aur return.

All topological orders (backtracking se):

def all_topological_orders(vertices, edges):
    """SAARE valid topological orders. Exponential -- sirf chhote graphs par."""
    graph = defaultdict(list)                       # 1
    in_degree = {v: 0 for v in vertices}            # 2
    for u, v in edges:                              # 3
        graph[u].append(v)                          # 4
        in_degree[v] += 1                           # 5

    results = []                                    # 6
    current = []                                    # 7
    visited = {v: False for v in vertices}          # 8

    def backtrack():                                # 9
        if len(current) == len(vertices):           # 10
            results.append(current[:])              # 11
            return                                  # 12
        for v in vertices:                          # 13
            if not visited[v] and in_degree[v] == 0:    # 14
                visited[v] = True                   # 15
                current.append(v)                   # 16
                for nb in graph[v]:                 # 17
                    in_degree[nb] -= 1              # 18
                backtrack()                         # 19
                for nb in graph[v]:                 # 20
                    in_degree[nb] += 1              # 21
                current.pop()                       # 22
                visited[v] = False                  # 23

    backtrack()                                     # 24
    return results                                  # 25

1-8. Setup. 9-12. Goal: saare vertices order mein aa gaye → record (copy!). 13-14. Har available vertex try karo — unvisited aur zero in-degree. 15-18. CHOOSE: mark visited, order mein add, neighbours ke in-degrees ghatao. 19. EXPLORE. 20-23. UNCHOOSE — exact reverse: in-degrees wapas badhao, order se pop, unmark. Order matter karta hai — jo pehle kiya wo baad mein undo. 24-25. Run.

Complexity: exponential — worst case V! orders (jab koi edge na ho). Sirf chhote graphs (V ≤ 10) par practical.

docs.title: Kab use karna hai / kab nahi
docs.text:
Kahn's use karo jab: - Cycle detection primary goal hai (count check natural hai). - Lexicographic order chahiye (heap se). - Recursion se bachna hai (bade graphs). - Level-wise processing chahiye — jaise "kaun se tasks parallel chal sakte hain". - Streaming / incremental — vertices aate jate hain.

DFS-based use karo jab: - Code simplicity chahiye (5 lines). - Aap already DFS kar rahe ho kisi aur kaam ke liye. - SCC / other DFS-based algorithms ke saath combine karna hai.

Mat use karo jab: - Graph undirected hai — topological sort ka concept hi directed ke liye hai. - Graph mein cycle hai aur aapko phir bhi ordering chahiye — us case mein SCC condense karo pehle (SCCs ka condensation graph hamesha DAG hota hai).

Parallel task scheduling (level-wise Kahn's):

from collections import deque, defaultdict


def parallel_schedule(vertices, edges):
    """Har 'round' mein kaun se tasks PARALLEL chal sakte hain."""
    graph = defaultdict(list)                       # 1
    in_degree = {v: 0 for v in vertices}            # 2
    for u, v in edges:                              # 3
        graph[u].append(v)                          # 4
        in_degree[v] += 1                           # 5

    queue = deque([v for v in vertices if in_degree[v] == 0])   # 6
    rounds = []                                     # 7
    processed = 0                                   # 8

    while queue:                                    # 9
        level_size = len(queue)                     # 10
        this_round = []                             # 11
        for _ in range(level_size):                 # 12
            u = queue.popleft()                     # 13
            this_round.append(u)                    # 14
            processed += 1                          # 15
            for v in graph[u]:                      # 16
                in_degree[v] -= 1                   # 17
                if in_degree[v] == 0:               # 18
                    queue.append(v)                 # 19
        rounds.append(this_round)                   # 20

    if processed != len(vertices):                  # 21
        return None                                 # 22
    return rounds                                   # 23

1-8. Setup. 9-12. Level-by-level processing — len(queue) snapshot lekar. 10. Is waqt queue mein jo hain, wo SAB PARALLEL chal sakte hain — unki saari dependencies satisfy ho chuki hain aur unke beech koi edge nahi hai (kyunki agar hoti to ek ka in-degree 0 nahi hota). 11-19. Us level ke saare vertices process. 20. Round record. 21-22. Cycle check. 23. Rounds.

QA use case: CI pipeline mein test groups. rounds ka length = minimum number of sequential stages. Har round ke tests parallel chal sakte hain.

Example output:
   Round 1: [unit_tests_a, unit_tests_b, lint]      <- 3 parallel
   Round 2: [integration_tests, build]               <- 2 parallel
   Round 3: [e2e_tests]                              <- 1

Sequential time: 6 tasks
Parallel time:   3 rounds  ->  2x speedup

docs.title: Kitne tareeke se optimize
docs.text:
# Optimisation Kya deta hai Kya leta hai 1 Kahn's (iterative) Recursion limit khatam Thoda zyada code 2 Level-wise processing Parallel scheduling info free Ek variable 3 Heap for lexicographic order Deterministic, smallest order O(log V) per operation 4 Early exit on cycle Cycle mile to turant ruk jao Ek check 5 order.append + reverse (DFS) O(n) instead of O(n²) insert(0,...) — 6 Iterator on stack (iterative DFS) O(V+E) instead of O(V·E) Tuple mein iterator 7 SCC condensation pehle Cyclic graphs par bhi ordering Kosaraju/Tarjan ka cost 8 Incremental topological sort Edge additions par O(1) amortised Complicated

Interview answer: Topological sort orders the vertices of a DAG so that every edge points forward — if there's an edge u to v, u comes before v. It's the algorithm behind build systems, package managers, task schedulers, and spreadsheet recalculation.

There are two standard approaches, both O(V + E). Kahn's algorithm is BFS-based: compute in-degrees, seed a queue with all zero-in-degree vertices, and each time you output a vertex, decrement its neighbours' in-degrees and enqueue any that hit zero. The DFS approach runs a DFS and appends each vertex when it finishes — when all its descendants are done — then reverses the resulting list.

Both detect cycles for free. In Kahn's, if the output has fewer than V vertices, the remaining ones are in a cycle and never reached in-degree zero. In DFS, an edge to a grey vertex — one still on the recursion stack — is a back edge, which means a cycle.

The order isn't unique in general. If Kahn's queue ever holds more than one vertex, multiple valid orders exist. If you need determinism you can use a min-heap instead of a queue to get the lexicographically smallest order, at O(V log V + E).

One extension I find useful in a CI context: process Kahn's queue level by level, taking a snapshot of the queue length each round. Everything in the queue at that moment has all its dependencies satisfied and no edges between them, so those tasks can run in parallel. The number of rounds is the minimum number of sequential stages the pipeline needs.

Cross-question: "What if the graph has cycles but you still need an ordering?"

Condense the strongly connected components first. Contract each SCC into a single super-node — the resulting condensation graph is always a DAG, by construction — and topologically sort that. You get an ordering of the components, which is the best that's possible: within a cycle there genuinely is no valid ordering, so the cycle members have to be treated as one unit. That's what a build system does when it reports a circular dependency: it can order everything else, but the cycle members must be resolved together or the cycle broken.

docs.title: Kya hai
docs.text:
Graph mein cycle dhoondhna — yaani aisa path jo kisi vertex se shuru hokar wapas usi vertex par aa jaye. Directed aur undirected graphs ke liye tareeke ALAG hain.

Real-world analogy: Build system mein "A ko B chahiye, B ko C chahiye, C ko A chahiye" — ye circular dependency hai, aur build kabhi complete nahi hoga. Cycle detection isi ko pakadta hai.

docs.title: Kyu hai
docs.text:
• Circular dependencies — build systems, package managers, import graphs.
  • Deadlock detection — "wait-for graph" mein cycle = deadlock.
  • Topological sort possible hai ya nahi — cycle hai to nahi.
  • Infinite loops in state machines.
  • QA: test fixtures jo ek doosre par depend karte hain.

docs.title: Kaise kaam karta hai — do alag approaches
docs.text:
DIRECTED GRAPH — three-colour DFS:
   WHITE = unvisited, GREY = in progress (stack par), BLACK = done
   Edge to a GREY node = BACK EDGE = CYCLE

   Kyun sirf GREY?  BLACK node already fully processed hai -- uske through
   wapas current node tak koi raasta nahi (warna wo GREY hota).


UNDIRECTED GRAPH — parent tracking:
   DFS karo, har node ka parent yaad rakho.
   Agar koi visited neighbour mile jo PARENT NAHI hai -> CYCLE

   Kyun parent exclude karte hain?  Kyunki undirected mein edge (u,v) ka matlab
   hai v ke adjacency mein u bhi hai. Wo "cycle" nahi, wahi edge hai wapas.

docs.title: Poora dry run
docs.text:
Directed: A → B → C → A

Step Node Colour before Neighbour Neighbour colour Action 1 A WHITE — — A → GREY 2 A GREY B WHITE recurse B 3 B WHITE — — B → GREY 4 B GREY C WHITE recurse C 5 C WHITE — — C → GREY 6 C GREY A GREY CYCLE!

Undirected: A — B — C, plus edge C — A

Step Node Parent Neighbour Visited? Is parent? Action 1 A None B No — visit B 2 B A A Yes Yes skip 3 B A C No — visit C 4 C B B Yes Yes skip 5 C B A Yes No CYCLE!

Step 2 par dhyaan do: B ka neighbour A visited hai, par wo B ka parent hai — ye wahi edge hai jiske through hum aaye, cycle nahi. Step 5 mein A C ka parent nahi hai — to ye ek alag raasta hai wapas A tak = cycle.

docs.title: Code
docs.text:
from collections import defaultdict

WHITE, GREY, BLACK = 0, 1, 2


def has_cycle_directed(vertices, edges):
    """Directed graph mein cycle. Three-colour DFS."""
    graph = defaultdict(list)                       # 1
    for u, v in edges:                              # 2
        graph[u].append(v)                          # 3
    colour = {v: WHITE for v in vertices}           # 4

    def visit(u):                                   # 5
        colour[u] = GREY                            # 6
        for v in graph[u]:                          # 7
            if colour[v] == GREY:                   # 8
                return True                         # 9
            if colour[v] == WHITE and visit(v):     # 10
                return True                         # 11
        colour[u] = BLACK                           # 12
        return False                                # 13

    for v in vertices:                              # 14
        if colour[v] == WHITE and visit(v):         # 15
            return True                             # 16
    return False                                    # 17


def has_cycle_undirected(vertices, adj):
    """Undirected graph mein cycle. Parent tracking."""
    visited = set()                                 # 18

    def visit(u, parent):                           # 19
        visited.add(u)                              # 20
        for v in adj[u]:                            # 21
            if v == parent:                         # 22
                continue                            # 23
            if v in visited:                        # 24
                return True                         # 25
            if visit(v, u):                         # 26
                return True                         # 27
        return False                                # 28

    for v in vertices:                              # 29
        if v not in visited and visit(v, None):     # 30
            return True                             # 31
    return False                                    # 32


def has_cycle_union_find(n, edges):
    """Undirected cycle detection via Union-Find. O(E alpha(V))."""
    uf = UnionFind(n)                               # 33
    for u, v in edges:                              # 34
        if not uf.union(u, v):                      # 35
            return True                             # 36
    return False                                    # 37

Line-by-line:

1-4. Graph aur colours. 5-6. Visit — GREY set karo pehle, recursion se pehle. 7-9. colour[v] == GREY → BACK EDGE → CYCLE. Ye poore algorithm ka core hai. 10-11. WHITE → recurse. and visit(v) short-circuits — sirf WHITE par recurse hoti hai. BLACK neighbours skip — wo already done hain, unke through cycle nahi ho sakti. 12-13. BLACK, no cycle here. 14-16. Har vertex se try karo — disconnected components. 17. No cycle.

  1. Visited set (undirected mein colours ki zaroorat nahi).
  2. parent parameter — ye undirected ka key hai.
  3. Mark. 21-23. v == parent → skip. Ye wahi edge hai jiske through aaye. Caveat: agar graph mein parallel edges (do vertices ke beech do edges) hain to ye check galat hai — wo genuine cycle hai. Us case mein edge IDs track karne padte hain. 24-25. Visited aur parent nahi → CYCLE. 26-27. Recurse.
  4. No cycle. 29-31. Har component.
  5. Clean.

33-37. Union-Find version — bahut simple. Har edge par union. Agar union False return kare (dono already same component mein) to ye edge cycle banayegi. Ye Kruskal ka same logic hai.

docs.title: Complexity
docs.text:
Method Time Space Graph type Three-colour DFS O(V + E) O(V) Directed Parent-tracking DFS O(V + E) O(V) Undirected Union-Find O(E·alpha(V)) O(V) Undirected Kahn's (count check) O(V + E) O(V) Directed

Union-Find version ka fayda: incremental — edges aate jate hain aur aap turant bata sakte ho ki cycle bani ya nahi. DFS ko har baar poora dobara chalana padta.

docs.title: Kab kya use karo
docs.text:
Situation Method Directed, ek baar check Three-colour DFS Directed, topological order bhi chahiye Kahn's algorithm Undirected, ek baar check Parent-tracking DFS Undirected, edges incrementally aa rahi hain Union-Find Undirected, MST bhi chahiye Kruskal (cycle check built-in) Bahut deep graph Iterative DFS ya Union-Find

Interview answer: Cycle detection works differently for directed and undirected graphs.

For directed graphs I use three-colour DFS: white for unvisited, grey for in-progress — still on the recursion stack — and black for fully finished. An edge to a grey vertex is a back edge, and a back edge means a cycle. The subtlety is that an edge to a black vertex is not a cycle: that vertex is fully explored, so there's no path from it back to the current one. Alternatively, Kahn's algorithm detects cycles for free — if the topological order contains fewer than V vertices, the missing ones are in a cycle.

For undirected graphs, colours don't work, because every edge appears in both adjacency lists, so you'd always see a "back edge" to the vertex you came from. Instead I track the parent and skip it: a visited neighbour that isn't the parent means there's a second path back, which is a cycle. One caveat — with parallel edges between the same pair, that parent check wrongly skips a genuine cycle, so you'd track edge identities instead of vertices.

For undirected graphs where edges arrive incrementally, Union-Find is better than either: union returning false means both endpoints were already connected, so the edge closes a cycle. That's O(alpha) per edge and it's incremental — no need to re-run a traversal after each addition.

docs.title: Kya hai
docs.text:
Connected components = graph ke woh alag alag "tukde" jinke andar sab kuchh juda hua hai par tukdon ke beech koi connection nahi.

Real-world analogy: Ek social network mein alag alag friend circles jo aapas mein bilkul nahi jude. Har circle ek component hai.

docs.title: Kyu hai
docs.text:
• "Kya A aur B connected hain?" — same component mein hain ya nahi.
  • Network reliability — kitne alag islands hain.
  • Image segmentation — same-colour regions.
  • Clustering — natural groups.
  • QA: test suites jo aapas mein independent hain (parallel chal sakti hain).

docs.text:
1. Har unvisited vertex ke liye:
      naya component shuru karo
      DFS/BFS se us vertex se reachable SAB kuchh mark karo
      component count badhao

Ya Union-Find se:
   har edge par union karo, aakhir mein distinct roots gino

Step Start Reachable via DFS Component Visited 1 1 1 → 2 → 3 {1,2,3} {1,2,3} 2 4 (unvisited) 4 → 5 {4,5} {1,2,3,4,5} 3 6 (unvisited) 6 → 7 {6,7} all
