docs.title: Code
docs.text:
from collections import deque, defaultdict


def connected_components(vertices, adj):
    """Saare components list of lists mein. O(V + E)."""
    visited = set()                                 # 1
    components = []                                 # 2
    for start in vertices:                          # 3
        if start in visited:                        # 4
            continue                                # 5
        comp = []                                   # 6
        queue = deque([start])                      # 7
        visited.add(start)                          # 8
        while queue:                                # 9
            u = queue.popleft()                     # 10
            comp.append(u)                          # 11
            for v in adj[u]:                        # 12
                if v not in visited:                # 13
                    visited.add(v)                  # 14
                    queue.append(v)                 # 15
        components.append(comp)                     # 16
    return components                               # 17


def count_components_uf(n, edges):
    """Union-Find se component count. Incremental-friendly."""
    uf = UnionFind(n)                               # 18
    for u, v in edges:                              # 19
        uf.union(u, v)                              # 20
    return uf.components                            # 21


def largest_component_size(n, edges):
    uf = UnionFind(n)                               # 22
    for u, v in edges:                              # 23
        uf.union(u, v)                              # 24
    return max(uf.size[uf.find(i)] for i in range(n))   # 25

Line-by-line:

1-2. Visited aur results. 3-5. Har vertex se try karo — already visited to skip. Ye outer loop hi multiple components handle karta hai. Bina iske sirf pehle component milta. 6-8. Naya component, BFS setup. Visited push par mark. 9-15. Standard BFS. 16. Component record. 17. Return.

18-21. Union-Find version — uf.components counter humne UnionFind class mein rakha tha, jo har successful union par ghatta hai. O(E·alpha(V)), aur incremental.

22-25. Largest component. uf.size[uf.find(i)] — root ka size chahiye, uf.size[i] nahi (non-root entries stale hoti hain).

docs.title: Complexity
docs.text: Method Time Space Incremental? BFS/DFS O(V + E) O(V) Nahi Union-Find O(E·alpha(V)) O(V) Haan

docs.title: Kab kya
docs.text:
• Ek baar count chahiye → BFS/DFS (simpler, actual component membership deta hai).
  • Edges incrementally aa rahi hain → Union-Find.
  • Component ke members chahiye → BFS/DFS (Union-Find se members nikalne ke liye extra pass chahiye).
  • Directed graph → ye "weakly connected components" hain (edges ko undirected maan kar). Strongly connected ke liye Kosaraju/Tarjan (agla section).

Interview answer: Connected components are the maximal sets of vertices that are mutually reachable. The straightforward approach is to loop over all vertices and, for each unvisited one, run a BFS or DFS that marks everything reachable — each such traversal discovers exactly one component. That's O(V + E) and gives you the actual membership lists.

The alternative is Union-Find: union the endpoints of every edge, then count distinct roots. Same asymptotic cost, and it's the better choice when edges arrive incrementally, because it maintains the answer continuously instead of requiring a full re-traversal after each addition.

For directed graphs, this gives weakly connected components — you're treating edges as undirected. Strongly connected components, where every vertex can reach every other along directed edges, need Kosaraju's or Tarjan's algorithm.

docs.title: Kya hai
docs.text:
Ek strongly connected component (SCC) directed graph ka aisa maximal set hai jisme har vertex se har doosre vertex tak directed path ho.

Real-world analogy: Ek shehar mein one-way roads. Kuchh mohalle aise hain jahan aap kisi bhi ghar se kisi bhi doosre ghar tak ja sakte ho aur wapas bhi aa sakte ho. Wo ek SCC hai. Kuchh mohalle aise hain jahan aap ja to sakte ho par wapas nahi — wo alag SCCs hain.

docs.title: Kyu hai
docs.text:
• Circular dependency groups — kaun se modules aapas mein circularly depend karte hain.
  • Deadlock cycles — kaun se processes ek doosre ka wait kar rahe hain.
  • 2-SAT solving — implication graph ke SCCs se solution.
  • Web graph analysis — "core" of the web.
  • Condensation — SCCs ko contract karke DAG banao, phir topological sort possible.

docs.title: Kaise kaam karta hai — Kosaraju's algorithm
docs.text:
1. Original graph par DFS chalao, FINISH ORDER record karo (stack mein push)
2. Graph ko REVERSE karo (saari edges ulti kar do)
3. Reverse graph par, FINISH ORDER KE ULTE order mein DFS chalao
   Har DFS tree = ek SCC

Kyun kaam karta hai (intuition):
   Pehli DFS ka reverse finish order SCCs ko "topological order" mein rakhta hai
   (condensation DAG ke hisaab se).
   Reverse graph par us order mein DFS chalane se, ek DFS tree kabhi doosre SCC
   mein "leak" nahi karti -- kyunki reverse graph mein us direction ki edges hi nahi hain.

Diagram:

Graph:   1 --> 2 --> 3 --> 1        (SCC A)
                     |
                     v
                     4 --> 5 --> 4  (SCC B)

SCCs: {1,2,3} aur {4,5}

Condensation:  [A] --> [B]     <- ye DAG hai

docs.title: Poora dry run
docs.text:
Graph: 0→1, 1→2, 2→0, 2→3, 3→4, 4→5, 5→3

Expected SCCs: {0,1,2} aur {3,4,5}

Pass 1 — DFS on original, record finish order:

Step Action Stack Finish order 1 dfs(0) [0] — 2 dfs(1) [0,1] — 3 dfs(2) [0,1,2] — 4 2→0: visited, skip — — 5 dfs(3) [0,1,2,3] — 6 dfs(4) [0,1,2,3,4] — 7 dfs(5) [0,1,2,3,4,5] — 8 5→3: visited, skip — — 9 5 finishes [0,1,2,3,4] [5] 10 4 finishes [0,1,2,3] [5,4] 11 3 finishes [0,1,2] [5,4,3] 12 2 finishes [0,1] [5,4,3,2] 13 1 finishes [0] [5,4,3,2,1] 14 0 finishes [] [5,4,3,2,1,0]

Pass 2 — reverse graph: 1→0, 2→1, 0→2, 3→2, 4→3, 5→4, 3→5

Pass 3 — DFS on reverse, in reverse finish order [0,1,2,3,4,5]:

Step Start Reachable in reverse graph SCC found 1 0 0 → 2 → 1 → (0 visited) {0, 2, 1} ✓ 2 1 already visited skip 3 2 already visited skip 4 3 3 → 2(visited) → 5 → 4 → (3 visited) {3, 5, 4} ✓ 5 4, 5 visited skip

SCCs: {0,1,2} aur {3,4,5} ✓

Dhyaan do step 1 par: reverse graph mein 0 se 2 aur 1 reachable hain, par 3,4,5 nahi — kyunki original mein 2→3 thi, reverse mein 3→2 hai, to 0 se 3 tak koi raasta nahi. Yahi wo containment hai jo Kosaraju ko sahi banata hai.

docs.title: Code
docs.text:
from collections import defaultdict


def kosaraju(vertices, edges):
    """SCCs list of lists mein. O(V + E)."""
    graph = defaultdict(list)                       # 1
    rgraph = defaultdict(list)                      # 2
    for u, v in edges:                              # 3
        graph[u].append(v)                          # 4
        rgraph[v].append(u)                         # 5

    visited = set()                                 # 6
    finish_order = []                               # 7

    def dfs1(start):                                # 8
        stack = [(start, iter(graph[start]))]       # 9
        visited.add(start)                          # 10
        while stack:                                # 11
            u, it = stack[-1]                       # 12
            pushed = False                          # 13
            for v in it:                            # 14
                if v not in visited:                # 15
                    visited.add(v)                  # 16
                    stack.append((v, iter(graph[v])))   # 17
                    pushed = True                   # 18
                    break                           # 19
            if not pushed:                          # 20
                finish_order.append(u)              # 21
                stack.pop()                         # 22

    for v in vertices:                              # 23
        if v not in visited:                        # 24
            dfs1(v)                                 # 25

    visited.clear()                                 # 26
    sccs = []                                       # 27

    def dfs2(start):                                # 28
        comp = []                                   # 29
        stack = [start]                             # 30
        visited.add(start)                          # 31
        while stack:                                # 32
            u = stack.pop()                         # 33
            comp.append(u)                          # 34
            for v in rgraph[u]:                     # 35
                if v not in visited:                # 36
                    visited.add(v)                  # 37
                    stack.append(v)                 # 38
        return comp                                 # 39

    for v in reversed(finish_order):                # 40
        if v not in visited:                        # 41
            sccs.append(dfs2(v))                    # 42

    return sccs                                     # 43

Line-by-line:

1-5. Dono graphs ek saath build karo — original aur reversed. rgraph[v].append(u) — edge ki direction ulti. 6-7. Visited aur finish order. 8-22. Iterative DFS with finish-time recording. Iterator on stack se O(V+E) rehta hai. Line 21: finish_order.append(u) jab iterator exhaust ho jaye — yaani saare descendants done. 23-25. Har unvisited vertex se. 26. visited.clear() — REUSE karne se pehle reset. Bhoolne par pass 2 kuchh nahi karega. 27. Results. 28-39. Pass 2: reverse graph par simple DFS, component collect karke. 40. reversed(finish_order) — ULTA finish order. Ye Kosaraju ka core hai. Finish order mein sabse baad wala vertex "sabse upar" wala SCC hai condensation DAG mein. 41-42. Har unvisited se ek SCC. 43. Return.

Condensation graph banana:

def condensation(vertices, edges):
    """SCCs ko contract karke DAG banao."""
    sccs = kosaraju(vertices, edges)                # 1
    comp_id = {}                                    # 2
    for i, comp in enumerate(sccs):                 # 3
        for v in comp:                              # 4
            comp_id[v] = i                          # 5
    dag_edges = set()                               # 6
    for u, v in edges:                              # 7
        if comp_id[u] != comp_id[v]:                # 8
            dag_edges.add((comp_id[u], comp_id[v])) # 9
    return sccs, sorted(dag_edges)                  # 10
  1. SCCs nikaalo. 2-5. Har vertex ko uske component ID se map karo. 6-9. Sirf inter-component edges rakho. Intra-component edges (comp_id[u] == comp_id[v]) skip — wo cycle ke andar hain aur condensation mein nahi aati. set use kiya — do vertices ke beech kai edges ek hi DAG edge banti hain.
  2. Result hamesha ek DAG hai — ye guaranteed hai (agar cycle hoti to wo SCCs merge ho jaate).

docs.title: Complexity
docs.text:
Pass 1 DFS:       O(V + E)
Graph reversal:   O(V + E)   (build ke waqt hi ho jata hai)
Pass 2 DFS:       O(V + E)

TOTAL: O(V + E)
SPACE: O(V + E)  -- dono graphs
Algorithm Time Space Passes Note Kosaraju O(V + E) O(V + E) 2 DFS Simple, samajhne mein aasan Tarjan O(V + E) O(V) 1 DFS Tez (constant factor), reverse graph nahi chahiye Path-based O(V + E) O(V) 1 DFS Tarjan jaisa

Tarjan practically ~2x tez hai kyunki wo ek hi pass karta hai aur reverse graph nahi banata. Par Kosaraju samajhne aur likhne mein bahut aasan hai — interview mein Kosaraju explain karo aur mention karo ki Tarjan ek-pass alternative hai.

Interview answer: A strongly connected component is a maximal set of vertices where every vertex can reach every other along directed edges. Kosaraju's algorithm finds them in two DFS passes. First, DFS the original graph and record vertices in order of finishing time. Then reverse every edge and DFS again, processing vertices in reverse finishing order — each DFS tree in that second pass is exactly one SCC.

The reason it works: the reverse finishing order is a topological order of the condensation DAG, so when you start a DFS in the reversed graph from the "last-finishing" vertex, all the edges that would lead out of its SCC have been reversed and now point inward, so the traversal is contained within the component.

It's O(V + E), the same as Tarjan's algorithm, but Tarjan does it in a single pass with lowlink values and no reversed graph, so it's roughly twice as fast in practice and uses less memory. I'd mention both — Kosaraju because it's much easier to explain and get right under pressure, Tarjan because it's what you'd ship.

The main application is condensation: contract each SCC into one node and you get a DAG, which can then be topologically sorted. That's how a build system reports circular dependencies — it orders everything it can and flags the cycles as units that must be resolved together.

docs.title: Kya hai
docs.text:
Ek graph bipartite hai agar uske vertices ko do groups mein aise baanta ja sake ki har edge ek group se doosre group mein jaye — kisi group ke andar koi edge na ho.

Real-world analogy: Ek party mein ladke aur ladkiyaan hain, aur sirf ladka-ladki jodiyaan dance kar rahi hain — koi ladka-ladka ya ladki-ladki jodi nahi. Us "dance partner" graph ko aap do groups mein baant sakte ho. Wo bipartite hai.

docs.title: Kyu hai
docs.text:
• Job assignment — workers aur tasks, kaun kya kar sakta hai.
  • Scheduling — do resources ke beech conflicts.
  • 2-colouring — map colouring ka simplest case.
  • Matching problems — maximum bipartite matching (Hopcroft-Karp).
  • QA: tests aur environments — kaun sa test kis environment par chal sakta hai.

Sabse important theorem:

Ek graph BIPARTITE hai  <=>  usme koi ODD-LENGTH CYCLE nahi hai

Proof intuition:
   Bipartite mein colours alternate karte hain: A, B, A, B, ...
   Ek cycle mein wapas start par aana hai.
   Agar cycle ki length EVEN hai: A,B,A,B,...,B -> wapas A par  ✓ OK
   Agar ODD hai: A,B,A,B,...,A -> wapas A par, par edge A-A  ✗ CONTRADICTION

docs.title: Kaise kaam karta hai
docs.text:
2-COLOURING via BFS/DFS:

1. Kisi bhi uncoloured vertex ko colour 0 do
2. BFS/DFS karo:
      har neighbour ko OPPOSITE colour do
      agar neighbour already SAME colour ka hai -> NOT BIPARTITE
3. Saare components ke liye dohrao

docs.title: Poora dry run
docs.text:
Bipartite graph: 1-2, 2-3, 3-4, 4-1 (4-cycle, even)

Step Node Colour Neighbour Neighbour colour Action 1 1 0 — — start 2 1 0 2 uncoloured 2 → 1 3 1 0 4 uncoloured 4 → 1 4 2 1 1 0 (different) OK 5 2 1 3 uncoloured 3 → 0 6 4 1 1 0 (different) OK 7 4 1 3 0 (different) OK 8 3 0 2 1 (different) OK 9 3 0 4 1 (different) OK

BIPARTITE ✓ Groups: {1, 3} aur {2, 4}

Non-bipartite: 1-2, 2-3, 3-1 (triangle, odd cycle)

Step Node Colour Neighbour Neighbour colour Action 1 1 0 — — start 2 1 0 2 uncoloured 2 → 1 3 1 0 3 uncoloured 3 → 1 4 2 1 1 0 OK 5 2 1 3 1 — SAME! NOT BIPARTITE ✗

docs.title: Code
docs.text:
from collections import deque


def is_bipartite(vertices, adj):
    """BFS-based 2-colouring. Returns (bool, colour_dict)."""
    colour = {}                                     # 1
    for start in vertices:                          # 2
        if start in colour:                         # 3
            continue                                # 4
        colour[start] = 0                           # 5
        queue = deque([start])                      # 6
        while queue:                                # 7
            u = queue.popleft()                     # 8
            for v in adj[u]:                        # 9
                if v not in colour:                 # 10
                    colour[v] = 1 - colour[u]       # 11
                    queue.append(v)                 # 12
                elif colour[v] == colour[u]:        # 13
                    return False, None              # 14
    return True, colour                             # 15


def is_bipartite_uf(n, edges):
    """Union-Find version. Har edge ke endpoints ALAG groups mein hone chahiye."""
    uf = UnionFind(2 * n)                           # 16
    for u, v in edges:                              # 17
        if uf.connected(u, v):                      # 18
            return False                            # 19
        uf.union(u, v + n)                          # 20
        uf.union(u + n, v)                          # 21
    return True                                     # 22

Line-by-line:

  1. colour dict — visited tracker bhi hai. v not in colour = unvisited. 2-4. Har component ke liye — graph disconnected ho sakta hai, aur har component independently bipartite ho sakta hai. 5-6. Start colour 0. 7-9. BFS. 10-12. colour[v] = 1 - colour[u] — OPPOSITE colour. 1 - 0 = 1, 1 - 1 = 0. Ye trick 2-colouring ke liye sabse clean hai. colour[u] ^ 1 (XOR) bhi same karta hai. 13-14. Same colour → conflict → NOT bipartite.

  2. Bipartite, colouring return.

  3. Union-Find version — "2n vertices" trick. Har vertex u ke liye do copies: u (group A mein hone ka claim) aur u + n (group B). 17-19. Agar u aur v already same group mein hain to edge illegal hai. 20-21. union(u, v+n) aur union(u+n, v) — "agar u A mein hai to v B mein hai, aur agar u B mein hai to v A mein hai".

  4. Bipartite.

Ye "2n vertices" trick constraint-satisfaction problems mein bahut use hoti hai (jaise "friends and enemies" problems).

docs.title: Complexity
docs.text: Method Time Space BFS/DFS 2-colouring O(V + E) O(V) Union-Find O(E·alpha(V)) O(V)

docs.title: Kab kya
docs.text:
• Ek baar check + colouring chahiye → BFS/DFS.
  • Edges incrementally → Union-Find.
  • Odd cycle actually dhoondhna hai → BFS with parent tracking, phir cycle reconstruct.

Interview answer: A graph is bipartite if its vertices split into two sets with every edge crossing between them. Equivalently — and this is the key theorem — a graph is bipartite exactly when it contains no odd-length cycle. The proof is short: colours must alternate along any path, so returning to the start after an odd number of steps would require an edge between two same-coloured vertices.

The check is a two-colouring via BFS or DFS: give the start colour 0, give every neighbour the opposite colour with 1 - colour[u], and if you ever find a neighbour already coloured the same as the current vertex, it's not bipartite. It's O(V + E), and you have to loop over all vertices as starting points because the graph may be disconnected — each component is checked separately.

There's also a neat Union-Find formulation using two copies of each vertex, u meaning "u is in set A" and u+n meaning "u is in set B". For each edge you union u with v+n and u+n with v; if u and v are ever already connected, you have a contradiction. That version is incremental, which matters when edges arrive over time.

docs.title: Complexity cheat sheet
docs.text:
Algorithm Time Space Weighted? Negative? BFS O(V+E) O(V) No — DFS O(V+E) O(V) No — Dijkstra O(E log V) O(V+E) Yes No Bellman-Ford O(V·E) O(V) Yes Yes Floyd-Warshall O(V³) O(V²) Yes Yes A* O(E log V) O(V) Yes No Kruskal O(E log E) O(V+E) Yes Yes Prim (heap) O(E log V) O(V+E) Yes Yes Prim (array) O(V²) O(V) Yes Yes Topological sort O(V+E) O(V) — — Union-Find (m ops) O(m·alpha(V)) O(V) — — Kosaraju O(V+E) O(V+E) — —

Interview answer: My selection process is: first, is the graph weighted? If not, BFS gives shortest paths in O(V + E) and nothing beats it. If it is weighted, are there negative edges? No negatives means Dijkstra at O(E log V); negatives mean Bellman-Ford at O(V·E), which also detects negative cycles. If the graph happens to be a DAG, neither is needed — relaxing edges in topological order handles negative weights in O(V + E), which beats both.

For all-pairs, Floyd-Warshall's O(V³) is right on dense graphs and its five lines are hard to get wrong; on sparse graphs, running Dijkstra from every vertex or using Johnson's algorithm is much better.

For connectivity questions I ask whether it's a one-shot query or incremental. One shot: BFS or DFS. Edges arriving over time: Union-Find, because it maintains the answer continuously.

And for ordering problems — build systems, task pipelines, prerequisites — it's topological sort, which also gives cycle detection for free. If there are cycles and you still need an order, you condense the strongly connected components first, since the condensation is always a DAG.

docs.title: Part 5: Dynamic Programming
docs.text: DP wo topic hai jahan sabse zyada log atakte hain — kyunki wo ek algorithm nahi, ek technique hai. Is part ka structure ye hai: pehle theory (optimal substructure, overlapping subproblems), phir ek hi problem par poori progression (brute force → memo → tabulation → space-optimised) taaki transformation dikh jaye, phir standard families, aur aakhir mein sabse mushkil hissa — DP recognise kaise karein aur state kaise define karein.

docs.title: Kya hai
docs.text:
DP tabhi lagta hai jab problem mein do properties hon:

  1. Optimal substructure — problem ka optimal solution uske subproblems ke optimal solutions se ban sakta hai.
  2. Overlapping subproblems — same subproblem baar baar aata hai.

Real-world analogy (optimal substructure): Delhi se Chennai ka shortest route agar Nagpur se hokar jata hai, to us route ka Delhi-to-Nagpur hissa bhi Delhi se Nagpur ka shortest route hona chahiye. Agar nahi hota, to aap use behtar se replace kar dete aur poora route chhota ho jata.

Real-world analogy (overlapping): Aap fib(5) nikaal rahe ho — usme fib(3) do baar aata hai. Agar aap use ek baar compute karke yaad rakh len, to aadha kaam bach jata.

docs.title: Kyu hai
docs.text:
Ye do properties hi decide karti hain ki DP lagega ya nahi:

Optimal substructure HAI, overlapping subproblems NAHI
   -> DIVIDE AND CONQUER  (merge sort, binary search)
   -> memoisation ka koi fayda nahi (cache kabhi hit nahi hoga)

Optimal substructure HAI, overlapping subproblems HAI
   -> DYNAMIC PROGRAMMING

Optimal substructure NAHI
   -> DP GALAT ANSWER dega
   -> Backtracking / brute force chahiye

docs.title: Optimal substructure ka test
docs.text:
Test: "Agar main is problem ka optimal solution le loon, to kya uska koi HISSA
      bhi apne subproblem ka optimal solution hoga?"

Shortest path:  HAAN
   Delhi->Chennai ka shortest route Nagpur se guzarta hai
   -> Delhi->Nagpur wala hissa bhi shortest hona chahiye  ✓

LONGEST SIMPLE path:  NAHI
   Delhi->Chennai ka longest simple path Nagpur se guzarta hai
   -> Kya Delhi->Nagpur wala hissa bhi longest hai?
      NAHI! Kyunki longest Delhi->Nagpur path shayad Chennai se hokar jata ho,
      aur phir hum Chennai dobara visit nahi kar sakte (simple path).
   -> Subproblems INDEPENDENT nahi hain  ->  DP LAGTA HI NAHI
   -> Isi wajah se longest path NP-HARD hai

Ye counterexample bahut important hai — ye batata hai ki DP har optimisation problem par nahi lagti.

docs.title: Overlapping subproblems ka test
docs.text:
Recursion tree draw karo aur dekho ki koi node DOBARA dikh raha hai ya nahi.

fib(5):
              5
           /     \
          4       3       <- 3 yahan
        /   \    /  \
       3     2  2    1    <- 3 yahan DOBARA
      ...

   -> OVERLAPPING  ->  memoise karo


merge_sort([1..8]):
              [1..8]
            /        \
       [1..4]        [5..8]     <- alag ranges, kabhi overlap nahi
       /    \        /    \
    [1,2]  [3,4]  [5,6]  [7,8]

   -> NO OVERLAP  ->  memoisation ka koi fayda nahi

Practical test: naive recursion likho, @lru_cache lagao, aur cache_info() dekho. Agar hits misses ke comparable ya zyada hain to overlapping hai.

from functools import lru_cache

@lru_cache(maxsize=None)
def f(n):
    ...

f(30)
print(f.cache_info())
# CacheInfo(hits=28, misses=31, ...)  -> overlapping hai, DP kaam karega
# CacheInfo(hits=0,  misses=31, ...)  -> koi overlap nahi, DP bekaar hai

docs.title: Poora example — dono properties ke saath aur bina
docs.text:
Coin change (DP lagti hai):

Problem: coins = [1, 3, 4], amount = 6. Minimum coins?

Optimal substructure:
   minCoins(6) = 1 + min(minCoins(5), minCoins(3), minCoins(2))
   Agar 6 ka optimal solution mein ek coin 3 hai, to bache hue 3 ka
   solution bhi optimal hona chahiye.  ✓

Overlapping:
   minCoins(6) -> minCoins(5), minCoins(3), minCoins(2)
   minCoins(5) -> minCoins(4), minCoins(2), minCoins(1)
                                  ^^^^^^^^^^^ minCoins(2) DOBARA
   ✓ OVERLAPPING

-> DP LAGEGI

Longest simple path (DP nahi lagti):

Graph:  A --- B
        |     |
        C --- D

A se D ka longest simple path:  A-B-D  ya  A-C-D  (length 2)
                                 ya  A-B-D... nahi, A-C-D-B? wo D par khatam nahi hota

Agar hum kahen: longestPath(A,D) = 1 + max over neighbours n of longestPath(n, D)
   longestPath(B, D) = ?  B se D tak longest = B-A-C-D (length 3)
   Par agar hum A-B se aaye hain to A already visited hai!

-> Subproblem ka answer PATH par depend karta hai, sirf endpoints par nahi
-> OPTIMAL SUBSTRUCTURE NAHI  ->  DP GALAT ANSWER DEGI

docs.title: Kab DP lagti hai — checklist
docs.text:
[ ] Problem "minimum", "maximum", "count ways", "is it possible" poochhta hai?
[ ] Choices ka sequence banana hai?
[ ] Optimal solution ke hisse bhi optimal hain? (optimal substructure)
[ ] Same subproblem baar baar aata hai? (overlapping)
[ ] State ko chhote parameters se describe kar sakte ho?

Sab check -> DP

Interview answer: Dynamic programming applies when a problem has two properties. Optimal substructure means an optimal solution is built from optimal solutions to subproblems — if the shortest path from A to C goes through B, then the A-to-B portion must itself be a shortest path, otherwise you'd swap in a better one. Overlapping subproblems means the same subproblem is reached from multiple branches of the recursion, which is what makes caching worthwhile.

Both matter, and they distinguish DP from its neighbours. Optimal substructure without overlap is divide and conquer — merge sort's subproblems are disjoint ranges, so memoising them would never hit. Overlap without optimal substructure means DP gives wrong answers.

The classic example of missing optimal substructure is longest simple path. If the longest path from A to C goes through B, the A-to-B portion is not necessarily the longest A-to-B path, because that longer path might reuse vertices you still need. The subproblems aren't independent, and that's precisely why longest path is NP-hard while shortest path is polynomial.

In practice my test is empirical: write the naive recursion, wrap it in lru_cache, and check cache_info. If hits are comparable to misses, there's real overlap and DP will pay off.

docs.title: The Full Progression on One Problem
docs.text:
Ye section sabse important hai — ek hi problem par chaar versions, taaki transformation dikh jaye.

Problem: Climbing Stairs. n seedhiyaan hain. Aap ek baar mein 1 ya 2 seedhi chadh sakte ho. Kitne alag tareeke hain n tak pahunchne ke?

docs.title: Version 1 — Brute force recursion
docs.text:
def climb_v1(n):
    """Naive recursion. O(2^n)."""
    if n < 0:                                       # 1
        return 0                                    # 2
    if n == 0:                                      # 3
        return 1                                    # 4
    return climb_v1(n - 1) + climb_v1(n - 2)        # 5

1-2. Negative — invalid, 0 ways. Ye guard zaroori hai warna infinite recursion. 3-4. n == 0 → 1 way (kuchh mat karo — aap already pahunch gaye). return 0 likhna classic bug hai — tab poora answer 0 aa jayega. 5. Do choices: 1 seedhi chadho (n-1 bachi) ya 2 chadho (n-2 bachi). Ways JODTE hain kyunki dono alag tareeke hain.

Recursion tree n = 5: 

                   5
                /     \
              4         3
            /   \      /  \
           3     2    2    1
          / \   / \  / \
         2   1 1   0 1  0
        / \
       1   0

15 calls. climb(3) do baar, climb(2) teen baar.
Time: O(2^n). n=40 → ~30 seconds. n=50 → ~1 ghanta.

docs.title: Version 2 — Memoisation (top-down)
docs.text:
from functools import lru_cache


@lru_cache(maxsize=None)                            # 1
def climb_v2(n):
    """Memoised. O(n) time, O(n) space."""
    if n < 0:                                       # 2
        return 0                                    # 3
    if n == 0:                                      # 4
        return 1                                    # 5
    return climb_v2(n - 1) + climb_v2(n - 2)        # 6
  1. Ek line add ki — bas. Baaki code bilkul same. 2-6. Identical to v1.

Kya badla: 

Recursion tree ab COLLAPSE ho gayi:

                   5
                /     \
              4         [3]     <- CACHE HIT
            /   \
           3     [2]            <- CACHE HIT
          / \
         2   [1]                <- CACHE HIT
        / \
       1   0

Sirf n+1 distinct states compute hoti hain.
Time: O(n). n=50 → microseconds. 10^12 guna tez.

Limitation: climb_v2(3000) → RecursionError (depth 3000 > limit 1000).

docs.title: Version 3 — Tabulation (bottom-up)
docs.text:
def climb_v3(n):
    """Bottom-up DP. O(n) time, O(n) space, koi recursion nahi."""
    if n <= 1:                                      # 1
        return 1                                    # 2
    dp = [0] * (n + 1)                              # 3
    dp[0] = 1                                       # 4
    dp[1] = 1                                       # 5
    for i in range(2, n + 1):                       # 6
        dp[i] = dp[i - 1] + dp[i - 2]               # 7
    return dp[n]                                    # 8

1-2. Base cases handle. n=0 → 1 way, n=1 → 1 way. 3. Table n+1 size ka — indices 0 se n tak. +1 bhoolna sabse common bug hai → IndexError line 8 par. 4-5. Base cases table mein. Ye recursion ke base cases ka exact translation hai. 6. 2 se shuru — 0 aur 1 already bhare hain. n+1 tak (exclusive) taaki dp[n] bhare. 7. Recurrence — recursion ki exact copy, bas dp[] lookups ke saath. Direction ULTI hai: recursion n se neeche jati thi, ye 2 se upar jata hai. Ye order isliye sahi hai ki dp[i] ko dp[i-1] aur dp[i-2] chahiye, jo pehle bhare ja chuke hain. 8. Answer.

Kya mila: - Koi recursion limit nahi — n = 10^6 bhi chalta hai. - Tez — function call overhead nahi, cache locality behtar (contiguous array). - Predictable — har state exactly ek baar.

docs.title: Version 4 — Space optimised
docs.text:
def climb_v4(n):
    """Rolling variables. O(n) time, O(1) space."""
    if n <= 1:                                      # 1
        return 1                                    # 2
    prev2, prev1 = 1, 1                             # 3
    for _ in range(2, n + 1):                       # 4
        prev2, prev1 = prev1, prev1 + prev2         # 5
    return prev1                                    # 6

1-2. Base cases. 3. prev2 = dp[i-2], prev1 = dp[i-1]. Initial: dp[0]=1, dp[1]=1. 4. Loop counter — i ki value use hi nahi ho rahi, isliye _. 5. prev2, prev1 = prev1, prev1 + prev2 — SIMULTANEOUS assignment. Right side poori pehle evaluate hoti hai. Agar aap do lines mein likhte: 

prev2 = prev1          # prev2 ab naya
prev1 = prev1 + prev2  # GALAT -- prev2 already badal chuka
Ye classic bug hai. Tuple assignment isse bacha leti hai. 6. prev1 mein dp[n] hai.

Space: O(n) → O(1). n = 10^9 bhi chalta hai (time O(n) hai to slow, par memory nahi phategi).

docs.title: Progression summary
docs.text:
Version Approach Time Space Max n (Python) Code lines v1 Brute recursion O(2^n) O(n) ~35 5 v2 Memoisation O(n) O(n) ~900 (recursion limit) 6 v3 Tabulation O(n) O(n) ~10^7 (memory) 8 v4 Space-optimised O(n) O(1) 10^9+ 6

Transformation ka recipe (har DP problem par lagta hai):

1. BRUTE FORCE RECURSION likho
      - Base cases identify karo
      - Recurrence likho (choices ka sum/min/max)
      - Bina soche ki wo slow hai

2. MEMOISE karo
      - @lru_cache lagao (ya dict)
      - Ab O(states x work per state)

3. TABULATE karo
      - Table banao (states ke size ka)
      - Base cases fill karo
      - SAHI ORDER mein loop chalao (dependencies pehle)
      - Recursion limit khatam

4. SPACE OPTIMISE karo
      - Dekho recurrence kitne pichhle states use karta hai
      - Sirf utne variables/rows rakho

Order kyun matter karta hai step 3 mein: dp[i] ko dp[i-1] aur dp[i-2] chahiye. To loop i badhte hue chalna chahiye. Agar recurrence dp[i] ko dp[i+1] par depend karati hai to loop ULTA chalega. Ye har problem par sochna padta hai.

Interview answer: I always develop a DP solution in four steps, and I'd walk through all four in an interview because each one shows a different insight.

Start with the brute-force recursion. For climbing stairs it's climb(n) = climb(n-1) + climb(n-2) with climb(0) = 1 — you either took a one-step or a two-step to get here. That's O(2^n), which is unusable past about n = 35, but it's where the recurrence comes from and it's the part that actually requires thinking.

Then memoise — literally one decorator, lru_cache — and it becomes O(n), because there are only n distinct states. That's a twelve-orders-of-magnitude improvement for one line.

Then convert to tabulation: allocate an array, fill the base cases, and loop in an order where every state's dependencies are already computed. That removes Python's recursion limit, which caps the memoised version around n = 900, and it's faster because there are no function calls and the array access is cache-friendly.

Finally, look at what the recurrence actually reads. Here it only reads the previous two values, so the whole array collapses to two rolling variables and space drops from O(n) to O(1). The one thing to be careful about is doing the update as a simultaneous tuple assignment, because updating them one at a time clobbers the value you still need.

Real-world analogy: Khargoshon ki jodiyaan (Fibonacci ka original 1202 ka problem) — har mahine har vayask jodi ek nayi jodi paida karti hai, aur nayi jodi ek mahine mein vayask ho jati hai.

docs.text: Ye DP ka canonical example hai kyunki isme overlapping subproblems ekdum saaf dikhte hain, aur uska naive version spectacularly slow hai — jo memoisation ka motivation dikha deta hai.

docs.title: Code
docs.text:
def fib_naive(n):
    """O(1.618^n) -- exponential."""
    if n <= 1:                                      # 1
        return n                                    # 2
    return fib_naive(n - 1) + fib_naive(n - 2)      # 3


def fib_dp(n):
    """O(n) time, O(1) space."""
    if n <= 1:                                      # 4
        return n                                    # 5
    a, b = 0, 1                                     # 6
    for _ in range(2, n + 1):                       # 7
        a, b = b, a + b                             # 8
    return b                                        # 9


def fib_matrix(n):
    """O(log n) via matrix exponentiation."""
    def mat_mult(A, B):                             # 10
        return [[A[0][0]*B[0][0] + A[0][1]*B[1][0],
                 A[0][0]*B[0][1] + A[0][1]*B[1][1]],
                [A[1][0]*B[0][0] + A[1][1]*B[1][0],
                 A[1][0]*B[0][1] + A[1][1]*B[1][1]]]

    def mat_pow(M, p):                              # 11
        result = [[1, 0], [0, 1]]                   # 12
        while p > 0:                                # 13
            if p & 1:                               # 14
                result = mat_mult(result, M)        # 15
            M = mat_mult(M, M)                      # 16
            p >>= 1                                 # 17
        return result                               # 18

    if n <= 1:                                      # 19
        return n                                    # 20
    return mat_pow([[1, 1], [1, 0]], n)[0][1]       # 21

1-3. Naive. n <= 1 base case dono 0 aur 1 handle karta hai (fib(0)=0, fib(1)=1, dono return n se). 4-5. Base. 6. a = fib(i-2), b = fib(i-1). Initial: fib(0)=0, fib(1)=1. 7-8. Rolling update, tuple assignment se simultaneous. 9. b mein fib(n).

  1. 2×2 matrix multiplication, hand-unrolled (loops se tez chhote matrices par). 11-18. Fast exponentiation on matrices.
  2. Identity matrix — multiplication ka 1. 13-17. Binary exponentiation: p ke har bit ke liye. p & 1 odd check, p >>= 1 halve. M = M*M har step par square. 19-21. [[1,1],[1,0]]^n ka [0][1] entry fib(n) hota hai. Kyun? Kyunki [[1,1],[1,0]] * [F(n), F(n-1)] = [F(n)+F(n-1), F(n)] = [F(n+1), F(n)]. Yaani wo matrix "ek Fibonacci step" hai. n steps = matrix ka n-th power.

docs.title: Complexity
docs.text:
Version Time Space Naive recursion O(1.618^n) O(n) Memoised O(n) O(n) Bottom-up O(n) O(n) Rolling variables O(n) O(1) Matrix exponentiation O(log n) O(1) Binet's formula (float) O(1) O(1) — par precision issues n>70

Ye derivation: naive ka 1.618^n golden ratio se aata hai — T(n) = T(n-1) + T(n-2) + 1 ka solution phi^n hai jahan phi = (1+sqrt(5))/2 = 1.618.

Interview answer: Fibonacci is the standard demonstration of DP. The naive recursion is O(phi^n) where phi is the golden ratio — about 1.618 — because the recurrence for the call count is itself the Fibonacci recurrence. Memoising collapses it to O(n), since there are only n distinct arguments.

The bottom-up version needs only the previous two values, so it's O(1) space with two rolling variables updated as a simultaneous tuple assignment. And there's a genuinely faster method: matrix exponentiation. The matrix [[1,1],[1,0]] raised to the n-th power has F(n) in it, and binary exponentiation computes that in O(log n) multiplications. That's the answer if someone asks for fib of a very large n.

Binet's closed-form formula is O(1) but uses floating point, so it loses precision beyond about n = 70 — worth mentioning as a trap rather than a solution.

docs.title: Climbing Stairs
docs.text: Ye Fibonacci ka hi disguise hai — poori progression pehle wale section mein di gayi hai. Yahan uske variants aur unka state design.

docs.title: Variants
docs.text:
Variant 1 — k steps allowed:

def climb_k_steps(n, k):
    """Ek baar mein 1 se k tak steps. O(n*k) time, O(n) space."""
    dp = [0] * (n + 1)                              # 1
    dp[0] = 1                                       # 2
    for i in range(1, n + 1):                       # 3
        for step in range(1, min(k, i) + 1):        # 4
            dp[i] += dp[i - step]                   # 5
    return dp[n]                                    # 6

1-2. Table, base case. 3. Har position. 4. min(k, i) — clamp. Agar i < k to aap i se zyada steps nahi le sakte (negative index aa jayega). Bina is clamp ke dp[-1] Python mein last element deta hai — silent wrong answer. 5. Sab valid steps se aane ke tareeke jodo. 6. Answer.

Variant 2 — minimum cost climbing:

def min_cost_climbing(cost):
    """Har seedhi ka cost hai. Minimum total cost. O(n) time, O(1) space."""
    prev2, prev1 = 0, 0                             # 1
    for i in range(2, len(cost) + 1):               # 2
        current = min(prev1 + cost[i - 1],          # 3
                      prev2 + cost[i - 2])          # 4
        prev2, prev1 = prev1, current               # 5
    return prev1                                    # 6
  1. Dono base cases 0 — aap seedhi 0 ya 1 se free mein shuru kar sakte ho.
  2. Position 2 se n tak. 3-4. Do choices: ek step pehle se aao (cost[i-1] doge) ya do step pehle se (cost[i-2]). min kyunki hum cost minimise kar rahe hain (ways count karne mein + tha).
  3. Roll.
  4. Answer.

Variant 3 — steps with forbidden positions:

def climb_with_obstacles(n, blocked):
    """blocked = set of positions jahan nahi ja sakte."""
    dp = [0] * (n + 1)                              # 1
    dp[0] = 1                                       # 2
    for i in range(1, n + 1):                       # 3
        if i in blocked:                            # 4
            dp[i] = 0                               # 5
            continue                                # 6
        dp[i] = dp[i - 1] + (dp[i - 2] if i >= 2 else 0)   # 7
    return dp[n]                                    # 8

1-3. Setup. 4-6. Blocked position → 0 ways, aur aage mat badho. continue zaroori hai warna line 7 use overwrite kar degi. 7. Conditional for i >= 2 — negative index se bachne ke liye. 8. Answer.

Interview answer: Climbing stairs is Fibonacci with a different story: the number of ways to reach step n equals ways to reach n-1 plus ways to reach n-2, because your last move was either a one-step or a two-step. Base case is one way to be at step 0 — do nothing — which people often get wrong by writing zero, and then the whole answer collapses to zero.

The variants are where the state design shows. Allowing steps of size one through k turns it into a sum over k previous states, so O(n·k). Adding a per-step cost changes the aggregation from sum to min, because you're now optimising rather than counting — that switch between sum and min or max is the single most common difference between "count the ways" and "find the best way" problems. And blocked positions are just a state that's forced to zero.

docs.text:
Ek line mein ghar hain, har ghar mein kuchh paisa. Aap do adjacent ghar nahi loot sakte (alarm baj jayega). Maximum kitna loot sakte ho?

Real-world analogy: Ek conference mein back-to-back sessions attend nahi kar sakte (breaks chahiye). Har session ki value alag hai. Maximum value kaise nikaalein?

docs.title: Kyu hai
docs.text: Ye "include/exclude" DP pattern ka canonical example hai, jo bahut jagah aata hai — maximum independent set on a path, non-adjacent selection, scheduling with gaps.

docs.title: Kaise kaam karta hai
docs.text:
Har ghar par DO CHOICES:
   1. LOOT karo:  nums[i] + best(i-2)     <- i-1 skip karna padega
   2. SKIP karo:  best(i-1)

dp[i] = max(nums[i] + dp[i-2], dp[i-1])

docs.text:
nums = [2, 7, 9, 3, 1]

i nums[i] Rob: nums[i] + dp[i-2] Skip: dp[i-1] dp[i] = max 0 2 2 + 0 = 2 0 2 1 7 7 + 0 = 7 2 7 2 9 9 + 2 = 11 7 11 3 3 3 + 7 = 10 11 11 4 1 1 + 11 = 12 11 12

Answer: 12 (ghar 0, 2, 4 loote: 2 + 9 + 1 = 12) ✓

Verify alternatives: [7, 3] = 10, [2, 9, 1] = 12, [7, 1] = 8, [2, 3] = 5. 12 maximum hai ✓

docs.title: Code
docs.text:
def rob(nums):
    """Linear houses. O(n) time, O(1) space."""
    rob_prev, skip_prev = 0, 0                      # 1
    for x in nums:                                  # 2
        rob_prev, skip_prev = skip_prev + x, max(rob_prev, skip_prev)   # 3
    return max(rob_prev, skip_prev)                 # 4


def rob_circular(nums):
    """Ghar CIRCLE mein hain -- pehla aur aakhri adjacent hain."""
    if len(nums) == 1:                              # 5
        return nums[0]                              # 6
    return max(rob(nums[:-1]), rob(nums[1:]))       # 7


def rob_tree(root):
    """Binary tree par house robber."""
    def solve(node):                                # 8
        if node is None:                            # 9
            return (0, 0)                           # 10
        lr, ls = solve(node.left)                   # 11
        rr, rs = solve(node.right)                  # 12
        rob_here = node.val + ls + rs               # 13
        skip_here = max(lr, ls) + max(rr, rs)       # 14
        return (rob_here, skip_here)                # 15
    return max(solve(root))                         # 16

Line-by-line:

  1. Do states: rob_prev = "pichhla ghar loota tha to best", skip_prev = "pichhla ghar skip kiya tha to best". Dono 0 se shuru.
  2. Har ghar.
  3. Simultaneous update:
  4. rob_prev (naya) = skip_prev (purana) + x — is ghar ko lootne ke liye pichhla skip hona zaroori tha.
  5. skip_prev (naya) = max(rob_prev, skip_prev) — is ghar ko skip kiya, to pichhla kuchh bhi ho sakta tha. Tuple assignment se right side poori pehle evaluate hoti hai — critical.
  6. Dono states ka max — aakhir mein aap last ghar loot bhi sakte the aur nahi bhi.

5-6. Single house. 7. Circular case ka trick: pehla aur aakhri ghar dono nahi loot sakte. To do cases: - nums[:-1] — aakhri chhod kar (pehla loot sakte ho) - nums[1:] — pehla chhod kar (aakhri loot sakte ho) Jo bada ho wahi answer. Ye ek elegant reduction hai.

8-16. Tree version — har node do values return karta hai. 9-10. Null node → (0, 0). 11-12. Children ke results. lr = left ko rob kiya, ls = left ko skip kiya. 13. rob_here = is node ki value + dono children ko SKIP karna padega. 14. skip_here = har child ke liye best (rob ya skip, jo bhi bada). 15. Tuple return. 16. Root par max.

Ye "har node se tuple return karo" pattern tree DP mein bahut common hai.

docs.title: Complexity
docs.text:
Variant Time Space Linear O(n) O(1) Circular O(n) O(n) (slicing) ya O(1) with indices Tree O(V) O(height) recursion

Interview answer: House robber is the canonical include-exclude DP. At each house you either rob it — adding its value to the best result from two houses back, since the adjacent one must be skipped — or skip it, keeping the best from one house back. So dp[i] = max(nums[i] + dp[i-2], dp[i-1]). Only two previous values are ever read, so it's O(n) time and O(1) space with two rolling variables.

I find it clearer to track two named states — "best if I robbed the previous house" and "best if I skipped it" — because that generalises. The circular variant, where the first and last houses are adjacent, reduces to running the linear version twice: once excluding the last house and once excluding the first, then taking the max. And the tree variant returns a pair from each node — best-if-robbed and best-if-skipped — which is the standard shape for tree DP.

docs.title: Kya hai
docs.text:
Coins ki denominations di hain (unlimited supply). Ek target amount banane ke liye minimum kitne coins chahiye? (Ya: kitne alag tareeke hain?)

Real-world analogy: Dukaandaar ko 87 rupaye ka change dena hai aur uske paas 1, 5, 10, 20, 50 ke note hain. Minimum kitne note dega?

docs.title: Kyu hai
docs.text:
Ye unbounded knapsack ka simplest form hai, aur ye dikhata hai ki greedy kab fail hota hai:

coins = [1, 3, 4],  amount = 6

GREEDY (sabse bada pehle):  4 + 1 + 1  =  3 coins
OPTIMAL (DP):               3 + 3      =  2 coins

GREEDY GALAT HAI.

(Indian/US currency par greedy kaam karta hai kyunki wo "canonical" system hai,
par arbitrary denominations par nahi.)

docs.title: Kaise kaam karta hai
docs.text:
MINIMUM COINS:
   dp[amount] = 1 + min over coins c of dp[amount - c]

COUNT WAYS:
   dp[amount] = sum over coins c of dp[amount - c]     <- PAR ye PERMUTATIONS ginega!

   COMBINATIONS ke liye loop order badalna padta hai (neeche dekho)

docs.title: Poora dry run
docs.text:
Minimum coins. coins = [1, 3, 4], amount = 6. dp[0] = 0, baaki inf.

amount coin 1 coin 3 coin 4 dp[amount] 1 1 + dp[0] = 1 — (1<3) — 1 2 1 + dp[1] = 2 — — 2 3 1 + dp[2] = 3 1 + dp[0] = 1 — 1 4 1 + dp[3] = 2 1 + dp[1] = 2 1 + dp[0] = 1 1 5 1 + dp[4] = 2 1 + dp[2] = 3 1 + dp[1] = 2 2 6 1 + dp[5] = 3 1 + dp[3] = 2 1 + dp[2] = 3 2

Answer: 2 (3 + 3) ✓ Greedy ne 3 diya tha.

Count ways (combinations). Same coins, amount 5. Loop coins bahar:

After coin 1: dp = [1,1,1,1,1,1] (har amount sirf 1s se — ek tareeka) After coin 3: dp = [1,1,1,2,2,2] (3 ko 1+1+1 ya 3 — 2 tareeke) After coin 4: dp = [1,1,1,2,3,3] (4 ko 1111, 1+3, 4 — 3 tareeke)

dp[5] = 3: 1+1+1+1+1, 1+1+3, 1+4 ✓

docs.title: Code
docs.text:
def coin_change_min(coins, amount):
    """Minimum coins. O(amount * len(coins)) time, O(amount) space."""
    INF = float('inf')                              # 1
    dp = [INF] * (amount + 1)                       # 2
    dp[0] = 0                                       # 3
    for a in range(1, amount + 1):                  # 4
        for c in coins:                             # 5
            if c <= a and dp[a - c] + 1 < dp[a]:    # 6
                dp[a] = dp[a - c] + 1               # 7
    return dp[amount] if dp[amount] != INF else -1  # 8


def coin_change_combinations(coins, amount):
    """Kitne alag COMBINATIONS (order matter nahi karta)."""
    dp = [0] * (amount + 1)                         # 9
    dp[0] = 1                                       # 10
    for c in coins:                                 # 11
        for a in range(c, amount + 1):              # 12
            dp[a] += dp[a - c]                      # 13
    return dp[amount]                               # 14


def coin_change_permutations(coins, amount):
    """Kitne alag PERMUTATIONS (order matter karta hai)."""
    dp = [0] * (amount + 1)                         # 15
    dp[0] = 1                                       # 16
    for a in range(1, amount + 1):                  # 17
        for c in coins:                             # 18
            if c <= a:                              # 19
                dp[a] += dp[a - c]                  # 20
    return dp[amount]                               # 21

Line-by-line:

1-2. INF sentinel — "abhi tak reachable nahi". 3. dp[0] = 0 — 0 amount ke liye 0 coins. Ye base case zaroori hai warna kuchh bhi compute nahi hoga. 4-5. Har amount, har coin. 6. c <= a — coin amount se bada nahi hona chahiye (negative index se bachao). dp[a-c] + 1 < dp[a] — improvement check. dp[a-c] INF ho sakta hai — INF + 1 Python mein inf hi rehta hai, jo < INF False deta. Safe. 7. Update. 8. INF matlab impossible → -1 return.

9-13. COMBINATIONS — coins BAHAR ka loop. Ye order hi combinations vs permutations decide karta hai. Coin bahar hone se: hum pehle sirf coin-1 ke saath sab amounts fill karte hain, phir coin-3 add karte hain, etc. Ek combination sirf ek baar count hoti hai kyunki coins ka order fixed hai. 12. range(c, amount+1) — c se shuru (chhote amounts mein wo coin fit hi nahi hoti). 13. dp[a] += dp[a-c] — +=, = nahi. Hum ways jod rahe hain.

15-20. PERMUTATIONS — amount bahar ka loop. Har amount ke liye saare coins try karte hain, to 1+3 aur 3+1 alag count hote hain. 19. Bounds check.

Ye loop-order ka farak sabse zyada poochha jane wala DP detail hai.

COMBINATIONS (coins outer):   {1,1,3} aur {1,3,1} ko EK maana
PERMUTATIONS (amount outer):  dono ALAG maane

Problem statement dhyaan se padho:
   "how many ways to make change"     -> usually COMBINATIONS
   "how many ordered sequences sum"   -> PERMUTATIONS

docs.title: Complexity
docs.text:
Variant Time Space Minimum coins O(amount × coins) O(amount) Count combinations O(amount × coins) O(amount) Count permutations O(amount × coins) O(amount)

Note: O(amount × coins) PSEUDO-POLYNOMIAL hai — amount input ki value hai, uske bits ki sankhya nahi. amount = 10^9 par ye chalega nahi.

Interview answer: Coin change is the standard unbounded knapsack. For minimum coins, dp[a] = 1 + min over coins of dp[a - c], with dp[0] = 0, giving O(amount × coins) time and O(amount) space.

The important thing this problem demonstrates is that greedy fails. With coins 1, 3, 4 and a target of 6, greedy takes 4 then 1 then 1 for three coins, while the optimum is 3 plus 3, two coins. Greedy happens to work on real currency systems because they're designed to be canonical, but not for arbitrary denominations.

For the counting variant, the loop order determines the semantics and this trips a lot of people up. Coins in the outer loop counts combinations — 1+1+3 and 1+3+1 are the same. Amount in the outer loop counts permutations — they're different. Nothing else changes, just which loop is outside.

One caveat on complexity: O(amount × coins) is pseudo-polynomial. The amount is a value, not an input size, so for a target of a billion this is infeasible even though it looks polynomial.

docs.title: Kya hai
docs.text:
n items hain, har ek ka weight aur value hai. Ek bag hai jiski capacity W hai. Har item ko ya to poora lo ya bilkul mat lo (0/1 — aadha nahi). Maximum total value?

Real-world analogy: Aap trekking par ja rahe ho aur backpack mein 10 kg tak le ja sakte ho. Har cheez ka weight aur "usefulness" alag hai. Kya lekar jayein?

docs.title: Kyu hai
docs.text:
Ye DP ka sabse important pattern hai — 2D state (item index, remaining capacity) ka canonical example. Iske variants har jagah aate hain: subset sum, partition equal subset, target sum, budget allocation.

Greedy kyun fail hota hai: "value/weight ratio sabse acchi wali pehle lo" — ye fractional knapsack mein optimal hai, par 0/1 mein nahi:

Capacity 10.  Items: (w=6, v=30), (w=5, v=20), (w=5, v=20)

Greedy by ratio:  item1 (ratio 5.0) lo  ->  4 kg bacha, kuchh fit nahi  ->  value 30
Optimal:          item2 + item3         ->  10 kg exactly              ->  value 40

docs.title: Kaise kaam karta hai
docs.text:
dp[i][w] = pehle i items mein se, capacity w ke saath, maximum value

Har item par DO CHOICES:
   1. SKIP karo:  dp[i-1][w]
   2. LO (agar fit ho):  value[i] + dp[i-1][w - weight[i]]

dp[i][w] = max(dp[i-1][w],  value[i] + dp[i-1][w - weight[i]])

docs.title: Poora dry run
docs.text:
weights = [1, 3, 4, 5], values = [1, 4, 5, 7], W = 7

Table dp[i][w] — rows = items considered, columns = capacity:

i \ w 0 1 2 3 4 5 6 7 0 items 0 0 0 0 0 0 0 0 +item1 (w1,v1) 0 1 1 1 1 1 1 1 +item2 (w3,v4) 0 1 1 4 5 5 5 5 +item3 (w4,v5) 0 1 1 4 5 6 6 9 +item4 (w5,v7) 0 1 1 4 5 7 8 9

Answer: dp[4][7] = 9

Kuchh cells ki calculation:

  • dp[2][4]: skip item2 → dp[1][4] = 1. Take item2 (w=3) → 4 + dp[1][1] = 4 + 1 = 5. max = 5 ✓
  • dp[3][7]: skip item3 → dp[2][7] = 5. Take item3 (w=4) → 5 + dp[2][3] = 5 + 4 = 9. max = 9 ✓
  • dp[4][7]: skip item4 → dp[3][7] = 9. Take item4 (w=5) → 7 + dp[3][2] = 7 + 1 = 8. max = 9 ✓

Optimal selection: item2 (w=3, v=4) + item3 (w=4, v=5) = weight 7, value 9 ✓

docs.title: Code
docs.text:
def knapsack_2d(weights, values, W):
    """0/1 knapsack, 2D table. O(nW) time, O(nW) space."""
    n = len(weights)                                # 1
    dp = [[0] * (W + 1) for _ in range(n + 1)]      # 2
    for i in range(1, n + 1):                       # 3
        wi, vi = weights[i - 1], values[i - 1]      # 4
        for w in range(W + 1):                      # 5
            dp[i][w] = dp[i - 1][w]                 # 6
            if wi <= w:                             # 7
                take = vi + dp[i - 1][w - wi]       # 8
                if take > dp[i][w]:                 # 9
                    dp[i][w] = take                 # 10
    return dp[n][W]                                 # 11


def knapsack_1d(weights, values, W):
    """Space-optimised. O(nW) time, O(W) space."""
    dp = [0] * (W + 1)                              # 12
    for wi, vi in zip(weights, values):             # 13
        for w in range(W, wi - 1, -1):              # 14
            if dp[w - wi] + vi > dp[w]:             # 15
                dp[w] = dp[w - wi] + vi             # 16
    return dp[W]                                    # 17


def knapsack_with_items(weights, values, W):
    """Value + kaun se items liye."""
    n = len(weights)                                # 18
    dp = [[0] * (W + 1) for _ in range(n + 1)]      # 19
    for i in range(1, n + 1):                       # 20
        wi, vi = weights[i - 1], values[i - 1]      # 21
        for w in range(W + 1):                      # 22
            dp[i][w] = dp[i - 1][w]                 # 23
            if wi <= w and vi + dp[i - 1][w - wi] > dp[i][w]:   # 24
                dp[i][w] = vi + dp[i - 1][w - wi]   # 25
    chosen = []                                     # 26
    w = W                                           # 27
    for i in range(n, 0, -1):                       # 28
        if dp[i][w] != dp[i - 1][w]:                # 29
            chosen.append(i - 1)                    # 30
            w -= weights[i - 1]                     # 31
    chosen.reverse()                                # 32
    return dp[n][W], chosen                         # 33

Line-by-line:

1-2. (n+1) × (W+1) table. +1 dono mein — row 0 = "koi item nahi", column 0 = "capacity 0". List comprehension, [[0]*(W+1)]*(n+1) NAHI. 3-4. Har item. i-1 indexing kyunki dp mein row i ka matlab "pehle i items", jo weights[i-1] tak hai. 5. Har capacity. 6. Default: SKIP — pichhli row ka same column. 7. wi <= w — item fit hota hai? 8. TAKE: item ki value + baaki capacity ka best (PICHHLI row se). dp[i-1][...] use kiya, dp[i][...] NAHI — kyunki 0/1 mein har item ek hi baar le sakte hain. dp[i] use karne se wo unbounded knapsack ban jata. 9-10. Max. 11. Answer.

  1. 1D table — sirf ek row.
  2. Har item.
  3. range(W, wi-1, -1) — ULTA (right to left)! Ye sabse critical line hai. Kyun ulta? Kyunki dp[w] ko dp[w - wi] chahiye jo pichhli item iteration ka hona chahiye. Agar hum seedha (left to right) chalte, to dp[w - wi] is item se already update ho chuka hota — yaani hum item ko do baar le lete → unbounded knapsack. Ulta chalne se dp[w - wi] abhi tak purana (pichhli item wala) hai. ✓ Ye ek line ka farak 0/1 aur unbounded knapsack ko separate karta hai. wi - 1 end (exclusive) — taaki w = wi tak jayein (w < wi par item fit nahi hoti). 15-16. Update.
  4. Answer.

18-25. 2D version, items track karne ke liye (1D se items reconstruct nahi ho sakte). 26-31. BACKTRACK karke items nikaalo: 28. Aakhri item se ulta chalo. 29. dp[i][w] != dp[i-1][w] → item i LIYA gaya tha. Agar dono barabar hote to item skip kiya gaya tha (skip wali value hi final thi). 30-31. Item record, capacity kam karo. 32-33. Reverse aur return.

docs.title: Related problems (same pattern)
docs.text:
def can_partition_equal_subset(nums):
    """Kya array ko do EQUAL SUM subsets mein baant sakte hain?"""
    total = sum(nums)                               # 1
    if total % 2 != 0:                              # 2
        return False                                # 3
    target = total // 2                             # 4
    dp = [False] * (target + 1)                     # 5
    dp[0] = True                                    # 6
    for x in nums:                                  # 7
        for s in range(target, x - 1, -1):          # 8
            if dp[s - x]:                           # 9
                dp[s] = True                        # 10
    return dp[target]                               # 11


def count_target_sum(nums, target):
    """+/- signs assign karke target banane ke kitne tareeke."""
    total = sum(nums)                               # 12
    if (total + target) % 2 != 0 or abs(target) > total:   # 13
        return 0                                    # 14
    s = (total + target) // 2                       # 15
    dp = [0] * (s + 1)                              # 16
    dp[0] = 1                                       # 17
    for x in nums:                                  # 18
        for j in range(s, x - 1, -1):               # 19
            dp[j] += dp[j - x]                      # 20
    return dp[s]                                    # 21

1-3. Odd total → impossible (do equal integers ka sum even hota hai). 4. Target = aadha. 5-6. Boolean DP. dp[0] = True — 0 sum hamesha possible (kuchh mat lo). 7-8. Ulta loop — 0/1 knapsack pattern. 9-10. Agar s - x reachable hai to s bhi reachable hai. 11. Answer.

12-15. Ye reduction sundar hai. Agar positive subset ka sum P aur negative ka N hai: P - N = target aur P + N = total. Dono jodo: 2P = total + target, to P = (total + target) / 2. Ab problem ban gaya: "kitne subsets ka sum P hai?" — jo standard knapsack counting hai. 13-14. Parity aur range checks — agar (total+target) odd hai to koi integer solution nahi. 16-20. Standard counting knapsack, ulta loop. 21. Answer.

docs.title: Complexity
docs.text:
Version Time Space 2D O(n·W) O(n·W) 1D O(n·W) O(W) With item reconstruction O(n·W) O(n·W) (2D chahiye)

Pseudo-polynomial: W ek value hai. W = 10^9 par ye chalega nahi, chahe n chhota ho. 0/1 knapsack NP-hard hai — koi truly polynomial algorithm nahi hai.

Interview answer: 0/1 knapsack is the canonical two-dimensional DP. The state is dp[i][w] — the best value using the first i items with capacity w — and the recurrence is the classic take-or-skip: max of dp[i-1][w] and value[i] + dp[i-1][w - weight[i]]. That's O(nW) time and O(nW) space.

The space optimisation to O(W) is the part worth being careful about. You keep one row and iterate capacity from W downward. The reason it must go downward is that dp[w - weight] has to still hold the previous item's value; iterating upward would read a value already updated for the current item, which means taking that item twice — and that's exactly unbounded knapsack. So the direction of that single loop is the whole difference between the two problems.

Greedy by value-to-weight ratio doesn't work here, though it is optimal for the fractional version, where you can take partial items. With capacity 10 and items of weight 6/value 30 and two of weight 5/value 20, greedy takes the best ratio first and gets 30, while the optimum is 40.

A lot of problems reduce to this: subset-sum, partition into equal halves, and target-sum with plus-minus signs, which reduces algebraically to counting subsets that sum to (total + target)/2.

docs.title: Kya hai
docs.text:
Wahi knapsack, par har item ki unlimited copies available hain.

Real-world analogy: Ek vending machine se items khareedne hain budget ke andar, aur har item ka stock unlimited hai. Kya lein, aur kitne?

docs.title: Kyu hai
docs.text:
Ye 0/1 knapsack se structurally alag hai aur uska ek line ka farak DP ka sabse elegant insight hai.

0/1:        dp[i][w] = max(dp[i-1][w], v + dp[i-1][w - wt])
                                              ^^^^^ PICHHLI row -- item dobara nahi

UNBOUNDED:  dp[w]    = max(dp[w],      v + dp[w - wt])
                                              ^^^^ SAME row -- item dobara le sakte hain

1D code mein ye farak sirf LOOP DIRECTION ka hai:

0/1:        for w in range(W, wt-1, -1):    <- ULTA
UNBOUNDED:  for w in range(wt, W+1):        <- SEEDHA

docs.title: Poora dry run
docs.text:
weights = [2, 3, 4], values = [3, 4, 5], W = 7

1D table (seedha loop):

After item dp[0] dp[1] dp[2] dp[3] dp[4] dp[5] dp[6] dp[7] init 0 0 0 0 0 0 0 0 item1 (w2,v3) 0 0 3 3 6 6 9 9 item2 (w3,v4) 0 0 3 4 6 7 9 10 item3 (w4,v5) 0 0 3 4 6 7 9 10

Answer: 10

Item1 wali row ki calculation (w=2 se seedha): - dp[2] = max(0, 3 + dp[0]) = 3 - dp[4] = max(0, 3 + dp[2]) = 3 + 3 = 6 ← dp[2] already is item se update ho chuka! Yahi "item dobara" ka mechanism hai. - dp[6] = max(0, 3 + dp[4]) = 3 + 6 = 9 ← teen copies

Item2 wali row: - dp[3] = max(3, 4 + dp[0]) = 4 - dp[5] = max(6, 4 + dp[2]) = max(6, 4+3) = 7 - dp[7] = max(9, 4 + dp[4]) = max(9, 4+6) = 10 ← item2 ek baar + item1 do baar = 4+3+3 = 10 ✓

docs.title: Code
docs.text:
def unbounded_knapsack(weights, values, W):
    """Unlimited copies. O(nW) time, O(W) space."""
    dp = [0] * (W + 1)                              # 1
    for w in range(1, W + 1):                       # 2
        for wi, vi in zip(weights, values):         # 3
            if wi <= w and dp[w - wi] + vi > dp[w]: # 4
                dp[w] = dp[w - wi] + vi             # 5
    return dp[W]                                    # 6


def unbounded_knapsack_item_outer(weights, values, W):
    """Same answer, items bahar. SEEDHA loop -- yahi 0/1 se farak hai."""
    dp = [0] * (W + 1)                              # 7
    for wi, vi in zip(weights, values):             # 8
        for w in range(wi, W + 1):                  # 9
            if dp[w - wi] + vi > dp[w]:             # 10
                dp[w] = dp[w - wi] + vi             # 11
    return dp[W]                                    # 12


def rod_cutting(prices, n):
    """Rod ko tukdon mein kaato, maximum revenue. Unbounded knapsack ka classic."""
    dp = [0] * (n + 1)                              # 13
    for length in range(1, n + 1):                  # 14
        for cut in range(1, length + 1):            # 15
            if prices[cut - 1] + dp[length - cut] > dp[length]:   # 16
                dp[length] = prices[cut - 1] + dp[length - cut]   # 17
    return dp[n]                                    # 18

Line-by-line:

1-2. Table aur capacity loop. 3-5. Har item. dp[w - wi] SAME array se — jo is item se already update ho chuka ho sakta hai. Yahi unbounded ka mechanism hai. 6. Answer.

7-12. Item-outer version. Line 9 mein range(wi, W+1) — SEEDHA. 0/1 mein ye range(W, wi-1, -1) (ulta) hota. Ek line ka farak, do alag problems.

13-18. Rod cutting — ek rod ko tukdon mein kaat kar bechna hai, prices[i] = length i+1 ke tukde ka daam. 15. cut = pehla tukda kitna lamba. 1 se length tak — har possible pehla cut. 16-17. prices[cut-1] (us tukde ka daam) + dp[length-cut] (bache hue rod ka best). Ye unbounded knapsack hai jahan "weight" = length aur "value" = price.

docs.title: Complexity
docs.text:
Problem Time Space Unbounded knapsack O(n·W) O(W) Rod cutting O(n²) O(n) Coin change (min) O(amount × coins) O(amount)

Note: unbounded knapsack ka 1D version hamesha O(W) space leta hai — 0/1 ki tarah 2D version ki zaroorat hi nahi (kyunki hum same row use kar rahe hain by design).

Interview answer: Unbounded knapsack is 0/1 knapsack with unlimited copies of each item. The recurrence changes from reading the previous row to reading the current one: dp[w] = max(dp[w], value + dp[w - weight]), where dp[w - weight] may already include this item.

In the space-optimised one-dimensional code, that's expressed purely as loop direction. For 0/1 you iterate capacity downward so dp[w - weight] still holds the previous item's value; for unbounded you iterate upward so it holds the current item's value and the item gets reused. One line, two different problems — and it's a favourite interview question precisely because it looks like a typo.

Coin change and rod cutting are both instances: coins are items with unlimited supply, and rod cutting is choosing the first cut length and recursing on the remainder. All three are O(n·W) pseudo-polynomial, so they're only tractable when the capacity or amount is bounded.

docs.title: Kya hai
docs.text: Do strings mein wo sabse lambi sequence dhoondhni hai jo dono mein usi order mein mile — par continuous hone ki zaroorat nahi. Analogy: do logon ki shopping list compare karo aur wo cheezein nikaalo jo dono ne usi order mein likhi hain, beech mein kuchh bhi extra ho to chalega.

docs.title: Kaise kaam karta hai
docs.text: Do pointers i, j — dono strings ke prefixes par. Agar a[i-1] == b[j-1], to wo character answer ka hissa hai: 1 + LCS(i-1, j-1). Agar match nahi, to ya to a ka character chhodo ya b ka — dono try karo aur max lo. State (i, j) baar baar repeat hoti hai, isliye table.

docs.title: Code
docs.text:
def lcs_length(a, b):
    """LCS ki length. dp[i][j] = a ke pehle i aur b ke pehle j chars ka LCS."""
    n, m = len(a), len(b)                           # 1
    dp = [[0] * (m + 1) for _ in range(n + 1)]      # 2
    for i in range(1, n + 1):                       # 3
        for j in range(1, m + 1):                   # 4
            if a[i - 1] == b[j - 1]:                # 5
                dp[i][j] = dp[i - 1][j - 1] + 1     # 6
            else:                                   # 7
                dp[i][j] = max(dp[i - 1][j], dp[i][j - 1])   # 8
    return dp[n][m]                                 # 9


def lcs_string(a, b):
    """Actual subsequence nikaalo — table bana kar peeche chalo (backtrack)."""
    n, m = len(a), len(b)                           # 10
    dp = [[0] * (m + 1) for _ in range(n + 1)]      # 11
    for i in range(1, n + 1):                       # 12
        for j in range(1, m + 1):                   # 13
            dp[i][j] = (dp[i - 1][j - 1] + 1 if a[i - 1] == b[j - 1]
                        else max(dp[i - 1][j], dp[i][j - 1]))    # 14
    out = []                                        # 15
    i, j = n, m                                     # 16
    while i > 0 and j > 0:                          # 17
        if a[i - 1] == b[j - 1]:                    # 18
            out.append(a[i - 1])                    # 19
            i -= 1                                  # 20
            j -= 1                                  # 21
        elif dp[i - 1][j] >= dp[i][j - 1]:          # 22
            i -= 1                                  # 23
        else:                                       # 24
            j -= 1                                  # 25
    return "".join(reversed(out))                   # 26

Line-by-line:

1-2. (n+1) x (m+1) table, row/col 0 = khaali string ka case = 0. Ye padding hi hai jo i-1 ko safe banata hai. 5-6. Match — dono taraf ek character kam karke diagonal se aao, +1. 8. Match nahi — diagonal mat lo, ya upar (a ka char chhoda) ya baayen (b ka char chhoda), jo bada ho. 9. Bottom-right cell = poori strings ka answer.

10-14. Wahi table, ek line mein. 15-26. Backtracking. Bottom-right se shuru. Match mile to character le lo aur diagonal jao (19-21). Warna jis taraf ki value badi hai udhar jao (22-25) — kyunki wahi se ye value aayi thi. Aakhir mein reverse, kyunki hum peeche se aage bana rahe the.

docs.title: Complexity
docs.text:
Value Kyun Time O(n·m) Har cell exactly ek baar bharti hai, constant kaam per cell Space O(n·m), ya O(min(n,m)) Sirf pichhli row chahiye — length ke liye rolling array Backtrack ke saath O(n·m) space compulsory Path reconstruct karne ke liye poora table chahiye

Note: agar sirf length chahiye, do rows kaafi hain. Agar string chahiye, poora table rakhna padega (ya Hirschberg's algorithm — O(n·m) time par O(min(n,m)) space, divide and conquer se; interview mein naam le dena hi kaafi hai).

Interview answer: Longest common subsequence is the classic two-sequence DP. The state is dp[i][j] — the LCS length of the first i characters of A and the first j of B. If the current characters match, the answer is one plus the diagonal; if not, it's the max of dropping a character from either string. That's O(nm) time and O(nm) space, reducible to two rows if I only need the length.

The reason it matters beyond the interview is that diff tools are built on it — git diff finds the LCS of two files and reports everything outside it as an insertion or deletion. In QA I've used the same idea for comparing ordered event streams: the LCS is the part that behaved as expected, and the gaps are exactly the regression.

Two traps: LCS is not longest common substring — substring requires contiguity and has a different recurrence where a mismatch resets to zero rather than taking a max. And if the interviewer wants the actual subsequence rather than its length, I have to keep the whole table and backtrack from the bottom-right corner.

docs.title: Kya hai
docs.text: Ek array mein sabse lambi subsequence jiske elements strictly badhte jaayein (contiguous hona zaroori nahi). Analogy: saal bhar ke test-pass-count ka record hai; sabse lamba stretch dhoondho jisme har agli entry pichhli se behtar thi, beech ke bure mahine ignore karke.

docs.title: Kaise kaam karta hai
docs.text:
O(n²) version: dp[i] = index i par khatam hone wali LIS ki length. Har i ke liye peeche saare j dekho; jahan nums[j] < nums[i], wahan se extend kar sakte ho.

O(n log n) version: ek tails array rakho jahan tails[k] = length k+1 wali kisi bhi increasing subsequence ka sabse chhota possible last element. Har naye number ke liye binary search se uski jagah dhoondho aur replace karo. tails ki length hi answer hai — par tails khud LIS nahi hai.

docs.title: Code
docs.text:
from bisect import bisect_left


def lis_quadratic(nums):
    """O(n^2). dp[i] = i par khatam hone wali LIS ki length."""
    if not nums:                                    # 1
        return 0                                    # 2
    dp = [1] * len(nums)                            # 3
    for i in range(1, len(nums)):                   # 4
        for j in range(i):                          # 5
            if nums[j] < nums[i] and dp[j] + 1 > dp[i]:   # 6
                dp[i] = dp[j] + 1                   # 7
    return max(dp)                                  # 8


def lis_nlogn(nums):
    """O(n log n). tails[k] = length k+1 wali LIS ka sabse chhota last element."""
    tails = []                                      # 9
    for x in nums:                                  # 10
        pos = bisect_left(tails, x)                 # 11
        if pos == len(tails):                       # 12
            tails.append(x)                         # 13
        else:                                       # 14
            tails[pos] = x                          # 15
    return len(tails)                               # 16

Line-by-line:

  1. Har element akela ek LIS hai, isliye base 1. 5-7. Peeche ke har chhote element se extend karne ki koshish; best rakho.
  2. dp[-1] nahi, max(dp) — LIS kahin bhi khatam ho sakti hai. Ye common bug hai.

9-16. Patience sorting. 11. bisect_left — pehli jagah jahan tails[pos] >= x. 12-13. x sabse bada hai — sequence lambi ho gayi. 14-15. Warna us length ka last element chhota kar do — future ke liye zyada room banta hai. Value badalti hai, length nahi. 16. tails ki length = LIS ki length.

Strictly vs non-decreasing: bisect_left = strictly increasing. bisect_right use karo to non-decreasing (duplicates allowed) ho jaata hai. Ek function ka farak.
