x pos tails ke baad length 10 0 [10] 1 9 0 [9] 1 2 0 [2] 1 5 1 [2,5] 2 3 1 [2,3] 2 7 2 [2,3,7] 3 101 3 [2,3,7,101] 4 18 3 [2,3,7,18] 4

Answer 4. Dhyaan do: final tails = [2,3,7,18] — ye ek valid LIS hai yahan, par hamesha nahi hoti. Actual sequence chahiye to har element ke saath uska predecessor index store karna padta hai.

docs.title: Complexity
docs.text:
Version Time Space Kyun Quadratic O(n²) O(n) Har i ke liye i tak peeche dekha — 1+2+…+n = n²/2 Binary search O(n log n) O(n) Har element par ek bisect = log n

Interview answer: Longest increasing subsequence has two standard solutions and knowing both is usually the point of the question. The O(n squared) one defines dp[i] as the length of the LIS ending at index i, and for each i scans everything before it. The answer is the maximum over the whole dp array, not the last element — that's the most common bug.

The O(n log n) one is patience sorting. I keep a tails array where tails[k] is the smallest possible tail value for an increasing subsequence of length k plus one. For each number I binary search for its position: if it's larger than everything I append and the answer grows, otherwise I overwrite that slot with a smaller value, which never shortens anything but leaves more room for future elements. The length of tails is the answer.

The important caveat is that tails is not itself a valid LIS — it's a bookkeeping array that can hold values from incompatible subsequences. If I need the actual sequence I store a predecessor index alongside each element and walk back. Using bisect_left gives a strictly increasing subsequence; bisect_right allows equal values.

docs.title: Kya hai
docs.text: Ek string ko doosri banane ke liye kam se kam kitne single-character operations (insert, delete, replace) lagenge — Levenshtein distance. Analogy: spell-checker "recieve" dekh kar "receive" suggest karta hai kyunki dono ke beech distance sirf 2 hai.

docs.title: Kaise kaam karta hai
docs.text: dp[i][j] = a ke pehle i aur b ke pehle j characters ke beech ki distance. Characters match karein to koi cost nahi, seedha diagonal. Warna teen choices — replace (diagonal), delete (upar), insert (baayen) — sabse sasti + 1.

docs.title: Code
docs.text:
def edit_distance(a, b):
    """Levenshtein distance. O(n*m) time, O(m) space."""
    n, m = len(a), len(b)                           # 1
    prev = list(range(m + 1))                       # 2
    for i in range(1, n + 1):                       # 3
        curr = [i] + [0] * m                        # 4
        for j in range(1, m + 1):                   # 5
            if a[i - 1] == b[j - 1]:                # 6
                curr[j] = prev[j - 1]               # 7
            else:                                   # 8
                curr[j] = 1 + min(prev[j - 1],      # 9  replace
                                  prev[j],          # 10 delete
                                  curr[j - 1])      # 11 insert
        prev = curr                                 # 12
    return prev[m]                                  # 13

Line-by-line:

  1. Base row: khaali a ko b banane ke liye j insertions — isliye 0,1,2,…,m.
  2. Base column: a ke i characters ko khaali string banane ke liye i deletions. 6-7. Match — cost zero. Diagonal se seedha copy. Ye +1 nahi hai, ye sabse zyada galat likhi jaane wali line hai.
  3. Replace — dono ka ek-ek character khatam, diagonal.
  4. Delete from a — a ka character chhoda, upar wali row.
  5. Insert into a — b ka character match kiya, current row ka baayan cell. 12-13. Rolling — sirf do rows chahiye kyunki har cell teen neighbours par depend karta hai jo sab pichhli ya current row mein hain.

docs.title: Compact dry run — a = "cat", b = "cut"
docs.text:
– c u t – 0 1 2 3 c 1 0 1 2 a 2 1 1 2 t 3 2 2 1

Answer 1 — a ko u se replace karo. Cell (a,u) par teenon options ki cost 1+min(0,1,1)=1 thi, aur wahi aage chala.

docs.title: Complexity
docs.text:
Value Kyun Time O(n·m) Har cell ek baar, constant 3-way min Space O(min(n,m)) Rolling rows; alignment chahiye to poora O(n·m)

Variants jo poochhe jaate hain: operations ki alag-alag cost do to 1 + ki jagah cost_replace + likh do — structure same. Damerau-Levenshtein transposition (do adjacent characters swap) ko ek operation maanta hai aur ek chautha case add karta hai. LCS ka rishta: agar sirf insert aur delete allowed hon (replace nahi), to distance = n + m - 2*LCS(a,b).

Interview answer: Edit distance is the minimum number of insertions, deletions and substitutions to turn one string into another. The state dp[i][j] is the distance between the first i characters of A and the first j of B. On a character match it's a free diagonal move; on a mismatch it's one plus the cheapest of three neighbours — diagonal is a replace, the cell above is a delete, the cell to the left is an insert.

The base cases carry real meaning: turning an empty string into a prefix of length j costs j insertions, which is why row zero counts upward. And the match case costs zero, not one — that's the bug interviewers watch for.

It's O(n*m) in both time and space, and space drops to one row because every cell only depends on the previous row and the cell to its left. I keep the full table only when I need the alignment itself. Practically it's behind spell-checkers, fuzzy search and diff-style test assertions — in QA it's useful for asserting that an output is close enough to expected rather than byte-identical.

docs.title: Kya hai
docs.text: Matrices ki ek chain di hai; multiplication ka order aisa chuno ki total scalar multiplications kam se kam ho. Analogy: teen numbers ko multiply karne ka answer order se nahi badalta, par mehnat badalti hai — jaise 100 chhote packets pehle jodo ya bade wale, total same par time alag.

docs.title: Kaise kaam karta hai
docs.text: Matrix i ka dimension dims[i-1] x dims[i] hai. dp[i][j] = i..j chain ka minimum cost. Har possible last multiplication point k try karo: left chain ka cost + right chain ka cost + dono results ko multiply karne ka cost. Ye interval DP hai — chhoti lambaai pehle, badi baad mein.

docs.title: Code
docs.text:
def matrix_chain(dims):
    """dims lambai n+1, n matrices. dp[i][j] = i..j ka min cost."""
    n = len(dims) - 1                               # 1
    dp = [[0] * (n + 1) for _ in range(n + 1)]      # 2
    for length in range(2, n + 1):                  # 3
        for i in range(1, n - length + 2):          # 4
            j = i + length - 1                      # 5
            dp[i][j] = float("inf")                 # 6
            for k in range(i, j):                   # 7
                cost = (dp[i][k] + dp[k + 1][j]
                        + dims[i - 1] * dims[k] * dims[j])   # 8
                if cost < dp[i][j]:                 # 9
                    dp[i][j] = cost                 # 10
    return dp[1][n]                                 # 11

Line-by-line:

  1. n matrices ke liye n+1 dimensions chahiye — chain valid tabhi hai jab adjacent dims match karein.
  2. Diagonal dp[i][i] = 0 — ek akeli matrix ko multiply karne ka cost zero.
  3. Length ke order mein bharo, index ke order mein nahi. dp[i][j] ko chhote intervals chahiye, isliye wo pehle ready hone chahiye. Yahi interval DP ki asli seekh hai. 4-5. Har starting point, aur usse length wala end.
  4. k = jahan chain toot rahi hai — A(i..k) * A(k+1..j).
  5. Left ka cost + right ka cost + final multiply: result matrices dims[i-1] x dims[k] aur dims[k] x dims[j] hain, to unhe multiply karne mein dims[i-1]*dims[k]*dims[j] lagte hain.
  6. Poori chain 1..n.

docs.title: Complexity
docs.text:
Value Kyun Time O(n³) O(n²) intervals × har interval ke liye O(n) split points Space O(n²) Table

Brute force Catalan number hota hai (~4ⁿ/n^1.5) — n=20 par arbon possibilities. DP usko 8000 operations mein le aata hai.

Interview answer: Matrix chain multiplication asks for the cheapest parenthesisation of a chain of matrix products. Matrix multiplication is associative so the result never changes, but the cost does — dramatically. For three matrices of dimensions 10x30, 30x5 and 5x60, one grouping costs 4,500 scalar multiplications and the other 27,000.

It's the canonical interval DP. The state is dp[i][j], the minimum cost of multiplying matrices i through j, and I try every split point k, adding the cost of the two halves plus the cost of the final multiply. The crucial implementation detail is loop order: I iterate by interval length rather than by index, because a longer interval depends on shorter ones that must already be solved.

That's O(n cubed) time and O(n squared) space, against a Catalan-number brute force. The same pattern covers burst balloons, optimal binary search trees and polygon triangulation — once you recognise "choose a split point in a range", they're the same problem wearing different clothes.

docs.title: Kya hai
docs.text: Ek string ko aise tukdon mein kaato ki har tukda palindrome ho, aur kam se kam cuts lagein. Analogy: ek lambi ribbon ko aise kaatna hai ki har piece dono taraf se ek jaisa dikhe, aur kainchi kam se kam baar chale.

docs.title: Kaise kaam karta hai
docs.text: Do layers. Pehle ek is_pal[i][j] table banao — s[i..j] palindrome hai ya nahi, jo is_pal[i+1][j-1] par depend karta hai. Phir cuts[i] = s[0..i] ke liye minimum cuts — har j <= i par dekho ki agar s[j..i] palindrome hai to cuts[j-1] + 1.

docs.title: Code
docs.text:
def min_cut(s):
    """Minimum cuts taaki har piece palindrome ho. O(n^2)."""
    n = len(s)                                      # 1
    is_pal = [[False] * n for _ in range(n)]        # 2
    for i in range(n - 1, -1, -1):                  # 3
        for j in range(i, n):                       # 4
            if s[i] == s[j] and (j - i < 2 or is_pal[i + 1][j - 1]):   # 5
                is_pal[i][j] = True                 # 6
    cuts = [0] * n                                  # 7
    for i in range(n):                              # 8
        if is_pal[0][i]:                            # 9
            cuts[i] = 0                             # 10
            continue                                # 11
        cuts[i] = i                                 # 12
        for j in range(1, i + 1):                   # 13
            if is_pal[j][i] and cuts[j - 1] + 1 < cuts[i]:   # 14
                cuts[i] = cuts[j - 1] + 1           # 15
    return cuts[n - 1]                              # 16


def all_partitions(s):
    """Saare palindromic partitions — backtracking, DP nahi."""
    res, path = [], []                              # 17

    def back(start):                                # 18
        if start == len(s):                         # 19
            res.append(path[:])                     # 20
            return                                  # 21
        for end in range(start + 1, len(s) + 1):    # 22
            piece = s[start:end]                    # 23
            if piece == piece[::-1]:                # 24
                path.append(piece)                  # 25
                back(end)                           # 26
                path.pop()                          # 27

    back(0)                                         # 28
    return res                                      # 29

Line-by-line:

  1. i ulta chalta hai — is_pal[i][j] ko is_pal[i+1][...] chahiye, jo badi i hai. Direction galat ho to table khaali padhega.
  2. s[i] == s[j] aur ya to lambaai 1-2 hai (j-i < 2) ya andar wala hissa palindrome hai.
  3. cuts[i] = prefix s[0..i] ka answer. 9-11. Poora prefix hi palindrome hai to zero cuts. Ye check zaroori hai warna cuts[-1] chahiye hota jo exist nahi karta.
  4. Worst case i cuts (har character alag). 13-15. Aakhri palindromic piece s[j..i] maano; usse pehle ka best cuts[j-1], plus ek cut.

17-29. Saare partitions chahiye to DP nahi, backtracking — answers ki sankhya exponential hai (2^(n-1) tak), to koi polynomial algorithm ho hi nahi sakta.

docs.title: Compact dry run — s = "aab"
docs.text:
i prefix is_pal[0][i]? cuts[i] 0 a haan 0 1 aa haan 0 2 aab nahi j=2: s[2..2]="b" pal, cuts[1]+1 = 1 → 1

Answer 1 — "aa" | "b".

docs.title: Complexity
docs.text:
Task Time Space Min cuts O(n²) O(n²) palindrome table Min cuts, O(n) space O(n²) O(n) — har center se expand karo, table ke bina Saare partitions O(n · 2ⁿ) O(n) recursion depth

Interview answer: Palindrome partitioning with minimum cuts is a two-stage DP, and saying so up front is half the answer. First I precompute an is-palindrome table for every substring, which is itself a DP: s[i..j] is a palindrome if the outer characters match and the inner substring already is. That table has to be filled with the start index moving backwards, because each entry depends on a larger start index.

Then the cut DP: cuts[i] is the minimum cuts for the prefix ending at i. If the whole prefix is a palindrome the answer is zero; otherwise I try every position j where s[j..i] is a palindrome and take cuts[j-1] plus one. Both stages are O(n squared).

If the question instead asks for all palindromic partitions rather than the minimum, DP is the wrong tool — the number of answers is exponential, so it's backtracking with a palindrome check at each extension. Recognising which of the two is being asked is the actual test: "count" or "minimum" means DP, "list them all" means backtracking.

docs.title: Kya hai
docs.text: Grid par ek corner se doosre corner tak jaana hai — kitne raaste hain, ya sabse sasta raasta kaunsa hai. Analogy: sheher ka block-wise map; sirf right aur down ja sakte ho, aur har block par toll lagta hai.

docs.title: Kaise kaam karta hai
docs.text: Har cell tak pahunchne ke sirf do tareeke hain — upar se ya baayen se. Isliye dp[i][j] = f(dp[i-1][j], dp[i][j-1]), jahan f counting ke liye sum hai aur cost ke liye min. Obstacles ka matlab sirf dp = 0 set karna hai.

docs.title: Code
docs.text:
def unique_paths(m, n):
    """m x n grid mein top-left se bottom-right tak raaste. O(n) space."""
    row = [1] * n                                   # 1
    for _ in range(1, m):                           # 2
        for j in range(1, n):                       # 3
            row[j] += row[j - 1]                    # 4
    return row[n - 1]                               # 5


def unique_paths_obstacles(grid):
    """1 = obstacle. Blocked cell ke raaste zero."""
    m, n = len(grid), len(grid[0])                  # 6
    row = [0] * n                                   # 7
    row[0] = 1 if grid[0][0] == 0 else 0            # 8
    for i in range(m):                              # 9
        for j in range(n):                          # 10
            if grid[i][j] == 1:                     # 11
                row[j] = 0                          # 12
            elif j > 0:                             # 13
                row[j] += row[j - 1]                # 14
    return row[n - 1]                               # 15


def min_path_sum(grid):
    """Har cell par cost; top-left se bottom-right tak minimum total."""
    m, n = len(grid), len(grid[0])                  # 16
    dp = list(grid[0])                              # 17
    for j in range(1, n):                           # 18
        dp[j] += dp[j - 1]                          # 19
    for i in range(1, m):                           # 20
        dp[0] += grid[i][0]                         # 21
        for j in range(1, n):                       # 22
            dp[j] = grid[i][j] + min(dp[j], dp[j - 1])   # 23
    return dp[n - 1]                                # 24

Line-by-line:

  1. Pehli row ke har cell tak sirf ek raasta (seedha right).
  2. row[j] += row[j-1] — row[j] abhi bhi pichhli row ki value hai (= upar se), aur row[j-1] already update ho chuka hai (= baayen se). Ek line mein 2D recurrence.
  3. Agar start hi blocked hai to zero raaste — ye edge case chhoot jaata hai. 11-12. Obstacle par count zero; aage ke cells apne aap sahi ho jaate hain.
  4. j > 0 guard — pehla column sirf upar se aata hai, jo row[j] mein pehle se hai.

17-19. Pehli row ka prefix sum — sirf ek hi raasta hai, isliye saare costs jodo. 21. Har nayi row ka pehla cell: sirf upar se aa sakte ho. 23. min(dp[j], dp[j-1]) — dp[j] = upar wala (abhi tak update nahi hua), dp[j-1] = baayen wala (ho gaya). Plus current cell ka cost.

docs.title: Compact dry run — min_path_sum([[1,3,1],[1,5,1],[4,2,1]])
docs.text:
Row dp ke baad init (row 0) [1, 4, 5] row 1 [2, min(4,2)+5=7, min(5,7)+1=6] row 2 [6, min(7,6)+2=8, min(6,8)+1=7]

Answer 7 — raasta 1→3→1→1→1.

docs.title: Complexity
docs.text:
Problem Time Space Unique paths O(m·n) O(n) rolling row Unique paths (formula) O(min(m,n)) O(1) — C(m+n-2, m-1) With obstacles O(m·n) O(n) Min path sum O(m·n) O(n)

Note: bina obstacles wala unique paths asal mein combinatorics hai — total m+n-2 moves mein se m-1 down chunne hain. DP tab zaroori hota hai jab obstacles ya costs aa jaayein.

Ek warning: agar movement chaaron directions mein allowed ho jaaye, to ye DP nahi rehta — cycles ban sakti hain, aur ye Dijkstra ban jaata hai. DP ko acyclic dependency chahiye.

Interview answer: Grid path problems are the gentlest introduction to two-dimensional DP. Because you can only move right or down, every cell is reachable from exactly two predecessors, so dp[i][j] is a function of the cell above and the cell to the left — a sum when counting paths, a min when finding the cheapest one.

All of them compress to a single row of size n, because I only ever need the previous row and the current row's left neighbour. In the one-dimensional form dp[j] still holds the value from above when I read it, and dp[j-1] has already been overwritten with the current row — so one line encodes the whole recurrence.

Two things worth flagging. Without obstacles, unique paths is really a binomial coefficient — choose which m-1 of the m+n-2 moves go down — so the DP is unnecessary. And if the movement rules allow going up or left, it stops being a DP at all, because the dependency graph gains cycles; at that point it's a shortest-path problem and I'd reach for Dijkstra or BFS instead.

docs.title: How to Recognise a DP Problem
docs.text: Ye section aur agla — is poore Part ke sabse kaam ke do sections hain. Algorithm yaad rakhna aasan hai; pehchaanna ki problem DP hai, mushkil hai.

docs.title: Teen signals jo saath aane chahiye
docs.text:
1. Optimisation ya counting ka shabd. "Minimum", "maximum", "longest", "how many ways", "is it possible". Agar problem saare answers maang rahi hai ("list all partitions"), to DP nahi — backtracking. DP ek number ya ek best answer deta hai.

2. Choices ka sequence. Aap answer ko ek-ek decision karke bana sakte ho: ye item lo ya chhodo, yahan cut lagao ya nahi, ye character match karo ya skip. Agar ek hi formula se answer aa raha hai (jaise C(n, k)), DP ki zaroorat nahi.

3. Overlapping subproblems. Recursion likho aur dekho ki wahi arguments dobara aa rahe hain ya nahi. Ye sabse zaroori signal hai — iske bina DP nahi hai, sirf divide and conquer hai.

Merge sort mein sort(0,4) kabhi dobara call nahi hoti — isliye merge sort DP nahi hai, chahe wo optimal substructure rakhta ho. Fibonacci mein fib(3) teen baar aati hai — wahi DP banata hai.

docs.title: Practical test — 60 second mein
docs.text:
1. Brute force recursion likho, bhale hi exponential ho. Sirf signature aur recurrence.
  2. Arguments ginno. Kitne alag (i, j, ...) combinations possible hain? Agar wo polynomial hain aur recursion tree exponential hai, to repeat ho rahe hain → DP.
  3. @lru_cache laga do. Agar kaam kar gaya, DP mil gaya. Bottom-up baad mein.

Ye teesra step interview mein bilkul valid hai — top-down memo likh do, phir bolo "I can convert this to bottom-up and drop the recursion stack if you want."

docs.title: Kab DP nahi hai — worked counterexample
docs.text:
Problem: "N cities, har pair ke beech distance, sabse chhota tour jo har city ek baar visit kare." (TSP)

Ye optimisation hai, choices ka sequence hai, aur subproblems overlap bhi karte hain. Phir bhi standard DP fail ho jaata hai — kyunki state sirf "abhi kis city par hoon" nahi ho sakti; "kaunsi cities visit ho chuki hain" bhi state ka hissa hai. Aur wo ek subset hai, to states 2ⁿ · n ho jaate hain. Bitmask DP kaam karta hai par sirf n ≤ 20 tak. Seekh: DP tab tak useful hai jab tak state space polynomial hai — warna wo sirf brute force ka organised version hai.

Doosra counterexample: "Array ko sort karo." Optimisation lagta hai, par yahan koi overlapping subproblem nahi — har subarray alag hai. Ye divide and conquer hai, DP nahi.

docs.title: Greedy vs DP — pehla filter
docs.text:
Agar har step par ek local rule se optimal answer nikal aata hai (aur aap wo prove kar sakte ho), greedy kaafi hai — DP overkill hai. Agar local best baad mein galat sabit ho sakta hai (coin change [1,3,4], amount 6), to DP chahiye. Jab shaq ho, DP likho — wo hamesha sahi hoga, bas dhima hoga. Greedy tabhi likho jab exchange argument dimaag mein taiyaar ho.

Interview answer: I look for three things together. First, the question asks for a minimum, a maximum, a count of ways, or a yes-no feasibility — not for the full list of solutions, which would mean backtracking instead. Second, the answer is built through a sequence of choices, so I can write a recurrence over "what do I do with the current element". Third, and most importantly, that recursion revisits the same arguments — without overlapping subproblems it's divide and conquer, not DP. Merge sort has optimal substructure but never repeats a subproblem, which is exactly why memoising it buys nothing.

My practical method is to write the brute-force recursion first, count the distinct argument combinations, and if that count is polynomial while the recursion tree is exponential, memoise it. In an interview I'll write the top-down version with an lru_cache, confirm it's correct, and then offer to convert it to bottom-up to remove the recursion stack.

The limit worth naming is when the state has to include a set rather than an index — travelling salesman, for example. The DP is correct but the state space is two to the n, so it's only a practical answer for small inputs.

docs.title: How to Define the State
docs.text: State galat define kar di to baaki sab bekaar hai. Ye sabse zyada slip yahin hoti hai.

docs.title: State kya hoti hai
docs.text: State = minimum information jo aapko chahiye taaki aage ke decisions le sako, bina ye jaane ki aap yahan tak pahunche kaise. Isi ko "Markov property" kehte hain. Agar aage ka answer past ke kisi detail par depend karta hai jo state mein nahi hai, to state incomplete hai.

docs.title: Teen sawaal poochho
docs.text: 1. Main abhi kahan hoon? — index, position, remaining capacity. Ye lagbhag hamesha state ka hissa hota hai. 2. Aage ka faisla kis cheez par depend karta hai? — bacha hua budget, pichhla element, kitne transactions ho chuke. Har aisi cheez ek dimension hai. 3. Kya main state ko chhota kar sakta hoon? — agar ek dimension ki value sirf 2-3 ho sakti hai (bought/not bought), to wo boolean flag hai, poora array nahi.

docs.title: Do standard shapes
docs.text:
Shape Matlab Kahan dp[i] = i tak ka answer (prefix) i ke baad ki cheezein irrelevant Coin change, climbing stairs dp[i] = i par khatam hone wala answer i mandatory hai answer mein LIS, max subarray, house robber ke variants

Ye do alag cheezein hain aur inko mila dena classic bug hai. Prefix wale mein answer dp[n] hota hai; "ending at i" wale mein max(dp) hota hai. LIS mein dp[-1] return karna isi confusion se aata hai.

docs.title: Worked example — state galat se sahi tak
docs.text:
Problem: stock prices ka array, do transactions tak allowed, maximum profit.

Attempt 1: dp[i] = day i tak ka max profit. Fail — kyunki aage ka faisla is baat par depend karta hai ki kitni transactions bachi hain aur abhi stock haath mein hai ya nahi. Ye dono information dp[i] mein nahi hai.

Attempt 2: dp[i][k] = day i tak, k transactions use karke max profit. Abhi bhi fail — "stock haath mein hai ya nahi" missing hai. Agar haath mein hai, to aaj bech sakta hoon; nahi hai to sirf khareed sakta hoon. Do bilkul alag situations, ek hi state.

Attempt 3: dp[i][k][holding] jahan holding ∈ {0, 1}. Ab complete hai. Transitions: dp[i][k][0] = max(dp[i-1][k][0], dp[i-1][k][1] + price[i]) (hold karo ya becho), dp[i][k][1] = max(dp[i-1][k][1], dp[i-1][k-1][0] - price[i]) (hold karo ya khareedo).

Seekh: state tab tak badhao jab tak transition deterministic na ban jaaye. Agar transition likhte waqt aapko "par ye to depend karta hai ki…" bolna pad raha hai, wahi missing dimension hai.

docs.title: State chhoti rakhne ke tareeke
docs.text:
• Symmetry — dp[i][j] mein agar sirf j - i matter karta hai, to ek dimension kaafi hai.
  • Rolling — agar sirf pichhli row chahiye, dp[i] ki jagah do arrays.
  • Bitmask — subset chahiye aur n chhota hai (≤ 20) to integer mein pack karo.
  • Normalise — dp[remaining] aksar dp[used] se chhota hota hai agar capacity bandhi hai.

Interview answer: The state is the smallest amount of information that makes the rest of the decisions independent of how I got there. I build it by asking two questions: where am I, and what else does the next decision depend on. Each thing in that second answer becomes a dimension.

The test I apply is whether I can write the transition without saying "but that depends on". The stock-trading problem is the clearest example — dp[day] is not enough, dp[day][transactions used] is still not enough, and only dp[day][transactions][holding] makes the transition deterministic, because whether I currently own the stock decides which moves are even legal.

The other distinction I'm careful about is prefix states versus ending-at states. dp[i] meaning "best answer using the first i elements" gives the answer at dp[n]; dp[i] meaning "best answer that ends at i" gives the answer as the max over the whole array. Longest increasing subsequence is the ending-at kind, and returning dp of the last index instead of the maximum is the single most common bug in that problem.

docs.title: Part 6: Greedy Algorithms
docs.text: Greedy sabse aasan likhne wali cheez hai aur sabse mushkil prove karne wali. Code aksar paanch line ka hota hai. Interview mein sawaal ye nahi hota ki "greedy likh sakte ho" — sawaal ye hota hai ki "ye greedy sahi kyun hai?" Isliye is Part mein do sections code se pehle aate hain: correctness kaise sabit karte hain, aur exchange argument kya hai.

docs.title: Do conditions — dono chahiye
docs.text:
1. Greedy choice property. Ek globally optimal solution aisa maujood hai jo pehli greedy choice ko include karta hai. Dhyaan do: ye nahi kaha ki "greedy choice hamesha optimal solution mein hoti hai" — kaha ye hai ki koi ek optimal solution use include karta hai. Ye farak chhota lagta hai par proof ka poora dhaancha isi par khada hai.

2. Optimal substructure. Pehli choice lene ke baad jo bachta hai, wo usi problem ka chhota version hai, aur uska optimal solution poore ka optimal solution banata hai.

DP mein optimal substructure hota hai par greedy choice property nahi hoti — isliye DP saare options try karta hai. Greedy mein dono hote hain, isliye wo ek option try karke aage badh jaata hai. Yahi poora farak hai.

docs.title: Proof ka standard structure
docs.text:
Greedy correctness ke do standard proofs hote hain:

Exchange argument (agla section) — optimal solution lo, usse greedy jaisa banao bina kharaab kiye. Sabse zyada use hota hai.

Greedy stays ahead — induction se dikhao ki har step k par greedy ka partial solution kisi bhi doosre solution ke partial solution se kam se kam utna hi accha hai. Activity selection ke liye: greedy ke pehle k activities ka finish time har doosre valid choice ke k-th finish time se <= hota hai. Agar greedy har jagah aage hai, to wo peeche kaise reh sakta hai.

docs.title: Matroid — jab greedy hamesha kaam karta hai
docs.text: Formally, greedy hamesha optimal hota hai agar problem ek matroid hai — do properties: subsets of a valid set are valid (hereditary), aur agar ek valid set doosre se bada hai to bade wale se ek element utha kar chhote wale mein daala ja sakta hai (exchange property). Kruskal's MST isi wajah se kaam karta hai — forests ek matroid banate hain. Interview mein ye naam le dena bohot achha signal hai, par baaki sab problems ke liye exchange argument hi likhna padega.

docs.title: Ek chhota worked proof — fractional knapsack
docs.text: Claim: highest value/weight ratio wala item pehle poora bharna optimal hai. Proof: maano optimal solution O mein us item (ratio r_max) ka x weight hai jabki hum y > x bhar sakte the. To O mein kisi doosre item ka y - x weight hai jiska ratio r < r_max. Us y - x weight ko hata kar highest-ratio item se badal do. Weight same rahega, value badhegi ya barabar rahegi ((y-x)·r_max >= (y-x)·r). Matlab O se buri nahi, aur ab wo greedy choice include karti hai. Isliye greedy choice safe hai. ∎

docs.title: Red flags — greedy shayad galat hai
docs.text:
• Choices ek doosre ko constrain karti hain (0/1 knapsack — ek item lene se capacity kam hoti hai jo baad ke better combos rok deti hai).
  • Answer mein combination matter karti hai, individual elements nahi (coin change).
  • Aapko "yahan lena behtar hai ya wahan" ka trade-off dikh raha hai jiska jawaab aage ke data par depend karta hai.

Interview answer: A greedy algorithm is correct when two properties hold. The greedy choice property says there exists an optimal solution that contains the first greedy choice — note that it's "there exists", not "every optimal solution contains it", and that phrasing is what makes the proof work. Optimal substructure says that after making that choice, what remains is a smaller instance of the same problem.

Dynamic programming needs only the second property, which is why it explores all the choices. Greedy has both, so it can commit to one and never look back — that's the entire difference between the two paradigms.

To prove it I use one of two arguments. The exchange argument takes an arbitrary optimal solution and transforms it step by step into the greedy one without ever making it worse. "Greedy stays ahead" uses induction to show the greedy partial solution is at least as good as any other after every step. If I can't sketch one of those in a couple of sentences, I don't trust the greedy and I write the DP instead — a correct slow answer beats a fast wrong one.

docs.title: Kya hai
docs.text: Greedy ko prove karne ka sabse standard tareeka: koi bhi optimal solution lo, aur usme ek-ek badlaav karke usse greedy solution bana do — har badlaav se answer kharaab nahi hona chahiye. Analogy: aap keh rahe ho "tumhara jo bhi best plan hai, main usme ek cheez badal doonga jisse wo mera plan jaisa ho jaayega aur utna hi accha rahega — matlab mera plan bhi best hai."

docs.title: Template — chaar steps
docs.text:
1. Maano O ek optimal solution hai jo greedy G se alag hai.
  2. Pehli jagah dhoondho jahan dono alag hain (ye zaroori hai — "pehli" se induction chalta hai).
  3. O mein us jagah swap karo taaki wo G se match kar jaaye.
  4. Dikhao ki swap ke baad O abhi bhi valid hai aur utna hi accha ya behtar hai.

Nateeja: G jitne bhi points par O se alag tha, sab badle ja sakte hain bina kharaab kiye — matlab G bhi optimal hai. ∎

Step 4 ke do hisse dono zaroori hain. Sirf "value kharaab nahi hui" kaafi nahi — swap ke baad solution feasible bhi rehna chahiye (constraints toote nahi).

docs.title: Worked example — activity selection
docs.text:
Greedy: sabse pehle khatam hone wali activity chuno.

Proof: maano O optimal hai aur usme pehli activity a1 hai, jabki greedy g1 chunta hai jiska finish time sabse kam hai. To finish(g1) <= finish(a1).

Ab O mein a1 ko hata kar g1 daal do. Valid hai kya? O ki doosri activity a2 ka start time >= finish(a1) >= finish(g1) hai — to g1 uske saath clash nahi karti. Count badla? Nahi, ek hataayi ek daali — count same. Matlab naya solution bhi optimal hai aur greedy choice include karta hai. Yahi induction har step par lagao. ∎

docs.title: Worked example 2 — job sequencing (deadline wala)
docs.text:
Greedy: profit ke ghatte order mein jobs dekho, har job ko uske deadline ke sabse late khaali slot mein daalo.

Exchange: maano O mein job x (profit 100) reject hai par job y (profit 40) accept hai, aur x ka koi valid slot y ke slot se compatible tha. y hata kar x daal do — deadline abhi bhi satisfy hoti hai (kyunki hum y ka slot use kar rahe hain jo x ke deadline ke andar tha), aur profit 60 badh gaya. Matlab O optimal tha hi nahi — contradiction. Isliye greedy ka "zyada profit pehle" sahi hai.

"Sabse late slot" wala hissa alag se justify hota hai: late slot bharne se pehle wale slots khaali rehte hain, jo tight deadline wali jobs ke liye bache rehte hain. Early slot bharna kabhi behtar nahi ho sakta.

docs.title: Jab exchange argument fail hota hai — counterexample
docs.text:
0/1 knapsack, ratio ke hisaab se greedy. Items: (w=10, v=60), (w=20, v=100), (w=30, v=120). Capacity 50. Ratios: 6, 5, 4.

Greedy: item1 (10, 60) + item2 (20, 100) = 30 weight, 160 value. Bacha 20 weight, item3 (30) fit nahi hota. Total 160. Optimal: item2 + item3 = 50 weight, 220 value.

Exchange kyun fail hua? Kyunki O mein se item3 hata kar item1 daalne se weight badalta hai — hum "ek ke badle ek" swap nahi kar sakte, kyunki items indivisible hain aur weights alag hain. Exchange argument tabhi chalta hai jab swap feasibility todhe bina ho sake. Fractional knapsack mein ye chalta hai kyunki wahan hum exactly y-x weight exchange kar sakte hain.

Yahi ek line yaad rakhne layak hai: greedy tab tootta hai jab swap karne par feasibility ya to tootti hai ya usse compensate karne mein value girti hai.

Interview answer: The exchange argument is how I prove a greedy is optimal. I take an arbitrary optimal solution, find the first place where it differs from the greedy choice, and swap that element for the greedy one. Then I show two things: the modified solution is still feasible, and it's no worse than before. Repeating that transforms any optimal solution into the greedy one without loss, so the greedy must itself be optimal.

For activity selection, the greedy picks the earliest finishing activity. If an optimal solution starts with a different activity, that one finishes no earlier, so replacing it with the greedy choice can't create a conflict with whatever came next, and the count is unchanged. Induction does the rest.

Where it fails is just as instructive. In 0/1 knapsack the swap isn't weight-neutral — exchanging one item for another changes how much capacity is left, so feasibility breaks and the argument collapses. That's precisely why fractional knapsack is greedy and 0/1 is DP: divisibility is what makes the exchange legal.

docs.title: Kya hai
docs.text: Start-end times wali activities di hain; maximum kitni activities kar sakte ho bina overlap ke. Analogy: ek conference room hai aur bees meeting requests — sabse zyada meetings kaise fit karein.

docs.title: Kaise kaam karta hai
docs.text: Finish time se sort karo, aur har wo activity utha lo jiska start pichhli chuni hui activity ke finish ke baad ho. Intuition: jaldi khatam hone wali activity sabse zyada baaki time chhodti hai, aur count maximise karna hai — duration se koi matlab nahi.

docs.title: Code
docs.text:
def activity_selection(intervals):
    """(start, end) list se maximum non-overlapping activities."""
    if not intervals:                               # 1
        return []                                   # 2
    order = sorted(intervals, key=lambda x: x[1])   # 3
    chosen = [order[0]]                             # 4
    last_end = order[0][1]                          # 5
    for s, e in order[1:]:                          # 6
        if s >= last_end:                           # 7
            chosen.append((s, e))                   # 8
            last_end = e                            # 9
    return chosen                                   # 10


def erase_overlap_intervals(intervals):
    """Kam se kam kitne intervals hataane padenge taaki koi overlap na bache."""
    if not intervals:                               # 11
        return 0                                    # 12
    order = sorted(intervals, key=lambda x: x[1])   # 13
    kept, last_end = 1, order[0][1]                 # 14
    for s, e in order[1:]:                          # 15
        if s >= last_end:                           # 16
            kept += 1                               # 17
            last_end = e                            # 18
    return len(intervals) - kept                    # 19

Line-by-line:

  1. key=x[1] — end time se sort. Start se sort karna galat hai (neeche counterexample), duration se sort karna bhi galat hai.
  2. last_end hi poori state hai — pichhli chuni gayi activity ka end. Isse zyada kuchh yaad rakhne ki zaroorat nahi, aur yahi greedy ko O(n) banata hai.
  3. s >= last_end — agar meetings back-to-back allowed hain ([1,3] aur [3,5] clash nahi). Agar strict gap chahiye to s > last_end. 11-19. Same algorithm, ulta sawaal. "Kitne hataao" = total minus "kitne rakh sakte ho". Interview mein ye do problems alag lagti hain, hain ek hi.

docs.title: Compact dry run — [(1,4), (3,5), (0,6), (5,7), (3,9), (5,9), (6,10), (8,11)]
docs.text:
Sort by end: (1,4), (3,5), (0,6), (5,7), (3,9), (5,9), (6,10), (8,11)

Activity s >= last_end? Chuna? last_end (1,4) — (pehla) haan 4 (3,5) 3 >= 4? nahi nahi 4 (0,6) 0 >= 4? nahi nahi 4 (5,7) 5 >= 4? haan haan 7 (3,9) nahi nahi 7 (5,9) nahi nahi 7 (6,10) nahi nahi 7 (8,11) 8 >= 7? haan haan 11

Answer 3: (1,4), (5,7), (8,11).

docs.title: Galat greedy — counterexample
docs.text:
Start time se sort: (0, 100), (1, 2), (3, 4). Start se chalne par (0,100) pehle aayegi aur baaki dono block ho jaayengi → answer 1. Sahi answer 2.

Shortest duration pehle: (0, 5), (4, 6), (5, 10). Sabse chhoti (4,6) hai, wo chunne par baaki dono block → answer 1. End-time greedy (0,5) aur (5,10) deti hai → 2.

docs.title: Complexity
docs.text:
Value Kyun Time O(n log n) Sorting hi dominate karti hai; scan sirf O(n) Space O(1) extra (ya O(n) output ke liye) Sirf last_end yaad hai

Agar input pehle se end-time sorted aa raha ho (jaise database ORDER BY end_time se), to O(n).

Interview answer: Activity selection asks for the maximum number of non-overlapping intervals. Sort by end time and greedily take any interval that starts at or after the last chosen one's end. Sorting dominates, so it's O(n log n) with O(1) extra state — just the last end time.

Sorting by end time is the whole trick, and I can justify it two ways. Intuitively, finishing earliest leaves the most room for everything after. Formally, by an exchange argument: if some optimal solution starts with a different activity, that one finishes no earlier, so swapping in the earliest-finishing activity can't conflict with what follows and keeps the count identical.

Sorting by start time or by duration both fail on small examples, and I'd expect to be asked for one. A single long interval starting at zero defeats start-time ordering; a short interval in the middle that straddles two others defeats duration ordering.

The same algorithm answers "minimum intervals to remove so none overlap" — that's just the total minus the maximum you can keep, which catches people who treat them as separate problems.

docs.title: Kya hai
docs.text: 0/1 knapsack ka wo version jahan items ko kaata ja sakta hai — aadha item bhi le sakte ho, aur value bhi aadhi milegi. Analogy: chor bori mein sona, chandi aur gehun bhar raha hai — powder aur dhaatu ko tol kar aadha bhi le sakta hai.

docs.title: Kaise kaam karta hai
docs.text: Har item ka value per unit weight nikalo, us ratio ke ghatte order mein sort karo, aur bag bharte jao. Jo aakhri item poora fit na ho, usko fraction mein le lo. Divisibility hi wo cheez hai jo greedy ko yahan sahi banati hai — 0/1 mein ye nahi hai isliye wahan DP chahiye.

docs.title: Code
docs.text:
def fractional_knapsack(items, capacity):
    """items = [(weight, value), ...]. Maximum value, fractions allowed."""
    order = sorted(items, key=lambda it: it[1] / it[0], reverse=True)   # 1
    total = 0.0                                     # 2
    remaining = capacity                            # 3
    for w, v in order:                              # 4
        if remaining <= 0:                          # 5
            break                                   # 6
        take = min(w, remaining)                    # 7
        total += v * (take / w)                     # 8
        remaining -= take                           # 9
    return total                                    # 10

Line-by-line:

  1. Ratio v/w ke ghatte order mein sort — yahi poora algorithm hai. reverse=True bhoolna sabse common bug hai (tab aap sabse bekaar items pehle bharoge). 5-6. Bag bhar gaya, ruk jao.
  2. min(w, remaining) — ya to poora item, ya jitna bacha hai. Yahi ek line "fraction" handle karti hai; alag if ki zaroorat nahi.
  3. take/w = kitna fraction liya, usi hisaab se value. Poora item ho to take/w == 1.

docs.title: Compact dry run — items [(10, 60), (20, 100), (30, 120)], capacity 50
docs.text:
Ratios: 6.0, 5.0, 4.0 — already sorted.

Item ratio remaining (pehle) take value add remaining (baad) (10, 60) 6.0 50 10 60 40 (20, 100) 5.0 40 20 100 20 (30, 120) 4.0 20 20 (2/3) 80 0

Total 240. Wahi input 0/1 knapsack mein sirf 220 deta hai ((20,100) + (30,120)) — kyunki wahan aakhri item ko kaata nahi ja sakta. Yahi do problems ka farak hai.

docs.title: Complexity
docs.text:
Value Kyun Time O(n log n) Sorting; scan O(n) Time (theoretical best) O(n) Quickselect se ratio ka median nikaal kar partition — median-of-medians wala approach Space O(1) extra Sirf running total

Floating point ka dhyaan: v/w compare karte waqt precision issues aa sakte hain. Safe compare: v1 * w2 > v2 * w1 (cross-multiplication, integers mein).

Interview answer: Fractional knapsack is the greedy sibling of 0/1 knapsack. Because items can be split, I sort by value-to-weight ratio descending and fill the bag, taking a fraction of whichever item doesn't fit whole. That's O(n log n), dominated by the sort.

The exchange argument is clean here: if an optimal solution takes less of the highest-ratio item than it could, it must be taking some weight of a lower-ratio item instead. Swapping that exact weight over keeps the bag equally full and never decreases the value. Because the weights match exactly, feasibility is preserved — and that is exactly what fails in 0/1 knapsack, where items are indivisible and swapping changes the remaining capacity.

On the same input — weights 10, 20, 30 with values 60, 100, 120 and a capacity of 50 — greedy gives 240 fractionally but only 160 if you apply it to the 0/1 version, where the true optimum is 220. That example is worth memorising because it demonstrates both algorithms in one breath.

A detail I'd mention: comparing ratios as floats can misbehave, so I cross-multiply integers instead.

docs.title: Kya hai
docs.text: Characters ko variable-length binary codes do — jo character zyada baar aata hai use chhota code, kam aane wale ko lamba — taaki total encoded size minimum ho. Analogy: Morse code mein E (sabse common letter) ek dot hai aur Q chaar symbols ka — wahi idea, par data se automatically nikaala gaya.

docs.title: Kaise kaam karta hai
docs.text: Har character ko ek leaf node banao jiska weight = uski frequency. Baar baar do sabse halke nodes utha kar unhe ek naye parent ke neeche jodo (parent ka weight = dono ka sum). Jab ek node bache, wo root hai — left edge 0, right edge 1, aur har leaf tak ka path uska code hai. Sabse zyada frequency wala character sabse upar rehta hai, isliye uska code sabse chhota.

docs.title: Code
docs.text:
import heapq
from collections import Counter


def huffman_codes(text):
    """Har character ka prefix-free binary code."""
    freq = Counter(text)                            # 1
    if len(freq) == 1:                              # 2
        return {next(iter(freq)): "0"}              # 3
    heap = [[w, i, {ch: ""}] for i, (ch, w) in enumerate(freq.items())]   # 4
    heapq.heapify(heap)                             # 5
    counter = len(heap)                             # 6
    while len(heap) > 1:                            # 7
        w1, _, left = heapq.heappop(heap)           # 8
        w2, _, right = heapq.heappop(heap)          # 9
        merged = {}                                 # 10
        for ch, code in left.items():               # 11
            merged[ch] = "0" + code                 # 12
        for ch, code in right.items():              # 13
            merged[ch] = "1" + code                 # 14
        heapq.heappush(heap, [w1 + w2, counter, merged])   # 15
        counter += 1                                # 16
    return heap[0][2]                               # 17


def encoded_length(text):
    """Huffman ke baad total bits."""
    codes = huffman_codes(text)                     # 18
    return sum(len(codes[ch]) for ch in text)       # 19

Line-by-line:

2-3. Edge case: sirf ek unique character ho to loop kabhi nahi chalega aur code khaali reh jaayega. Manually "0" do. 4. Har entry [weight, tiebreak, {char: code}]. counter isliye chahiye kyunki weights tie hone par Python dict compare karne ki koshish karega aur TypeError dega. 8-9. Do sabse halke — heap ka poora point yahi hai. 11-14. Left subtree ke saare codes ke aage 0, right ke aage 1. Prefix aage lagta hai, peeche nahi — kyunki hum neeche se upar bana rahe hain. 17. Ek hi node bacha = root, uska dict hi saare codes hai.

docs.title: Compact dry run — "aaabbc" → freq a:3, b:2, c:1
docs.text:
Step Heap (weights) Action init 1(c), 2(b), 3(a) — 1 pop 1, 2 → push 3 c="0", b="1" under node(3) 2 3(a), 3(bc) pop dono → push 6 final 6 a="0", c="10", b="11"

Bits: a×3 = 3, b×2 = 4, c×1 = 2 → 9 bits. Fixed 2-bit code se 12 bits lagte — 25% bachat.

docs.title: Complexity
docs.text:
Value Kyun Time O(n log n) n unique characters, har merge par do pops + ek push, sab log n Space O(n) Heap + code table Optimality Provable Exchange argument: do sabse kam frequency wale characters hamesha sabse gehre level par bhaai-behen ban sakte hain

Prefix-free property: koi bhi code kisi doosre ka prefix nahi hota, kyunki saare characters leaves par hain — leaf tak pahunchne ke baad path khatam. Isi wajah se decoding bina separator ke ho jaati hai.

Interview answer: Huffman coding builds an optimal prefix-free code from character frequencies. I put every character in a min-heap keyed by frequency, repeatedly pop the two lightest nodes, merge them under a new parent whose weight is their sum, and push it back. When one node remains it's the root; labelling left edges zero and right edges one gives each leaf its code. That's O(n log n) for n distinct symbols.

The greedy choice is that the two least frequent characters can always be placed as siblings at the deepest level of some optimal tree — if they weren't, swapping them with whatever is down there would reduce the total cost, because you'd be moving smaller weights to longer paths.

The property that makes it usable is prefix-freeness: every character sits at a leaf, so no code is a prefix of another and the decoder never needs delimiters. It's the entropy-coding stage inside DEFLATE, so it's running every time you gzip a response body.

Two implementation details I watch for: a single distinct character produces an empty code unless special-cased, and heap entries need a tiebreaker so equal frequencies don't force Python to compare the payloads.

docs.title: Kya hai
docs.text: Har job ka ek deadline aur ek profit hai; har job ko ek unit time lagta hai aur ek time par ek hi job chal sakti hai. Maximum profit kaise? Analogy: aaj shaam tak paanch clients ke kaam nipatane hain, har ek ka alag deadline aur alag paisa — kaunse kaam lo.

docs.title: Kaise kaam karta hai
docs.text: Profit ke ghatte order mein jobs dekho. Har job ke liye uske deadline se peeche ki taraf pehla khaali slot dhoondho aur wahan daal do. Late slot bharne se early slots un jobs ke liye bache rehte hain jinki deadline tight hai.

docs.title: Code
docs.text:
def job_sequencing(jobs):
    """jobs = [(job_id, deadline, profit)]. Simple O(n^2) version."""
    order = sorted(jobs, key=lambda j: j[2], reverse=True)   # 1
    max_dl = max(j[1] for j in jobs)                # 2
    slots = [None] * (max_dl + 1)                   # 3
    profit = 0                                      # 4
    for jid, dl, p in order:                        # 5
        t = min(dl, max_dl)                         # 6
        while t > 0 and slots[t] is not None:       # 7
            t -= 1                                  # 8
        if t > 0:                                   # 9
            slots[t] = jid                          # 10
            profit += p                             # 11
    return profit, [s for s in slots if s]          # 12


def job_sequencing_dsu(jobs):
    """O(n log n) — union find se agla khaali slot O(alpha) mein."""
    order = sorted(jobs, key=lambda j: j[2], reverse=True)   # 13
    max_dl = max(j[1] for j in jobs)                # 14
    parent = list(range(max_dl + 1))                # 15

    def find(x):                                    # 16
        while parent[x] != x:                       # 17
            parent[x] = parent[parent[x]]           # 18
            x = parent[x]                           # 19
        return x                                    # 20

    profit, picked = 0, []                          # 21
    for jid, dl, p in order:                        # 22
        slot = find(min(dl, max_dl))                # 23
        if slot > 0:                                # 24
            parent[slot] = slot - 1                 # 25
            profit += p                             # 26
            picked.append(jid)                      # 27
    return profit, picked                           # 28

Line-by-line:

  1. Profit ghatte order — exchange argument isi ko justify karta hai (pichhla section).
  2. Slots 1..max_dl; index 0 jaanbujh kar unused rakha hai taaki "koi slot nahi mila" ka matlab t == 0 ho jaaye. 6-8. Deadline se peeche chalo, pehla khaali slot lo. Aage nahi — deadline cross nahi kar sakte. 9-11. Slot mila to job accept.

13-28. Optimised. parent[t] = "t ya usse pehle ka pehla khaali slot". 23. find seedha khaali slot deta hai, while loop ke bina. 25. Slot bhar gaya to usko slot-1 par point kara do — agli baar find khud aage skip kar dega. Yahi trick O(n²) ko O(n log n) banati hai.

docs.title: Compact dry run — [(a,2,100), (b,1,19), (c,2,27), (d,1,25), (e,3,15)]
docs.text:
Profit se sort: a(2,100), c(2,27), d(1,25), b(1,19), e(3,15)

Job dl Slot dhoondha Result Profit a 2 2 khaali slot 2 100 c 2 2 bhara → 1 khaali slot 1 127 d 1 1 bhara → 0 reject 127 b 1 1 bhara → 0 reject 127 e 3 3 khaali slot 3 142

Answer 142, jobs c, a, e (slots 1, 2, 3).

docs.title: Complexity
docs.text:
Version Time Space Simple O(n log n + n·D) O(D) slots Union-find O(n log n) O(D)

D = maximum deadline. Agar D bada ho aur jobs kam, to union-find wala clearly behtar hai.

Interview answer: Job sequencing with deadlines gives each unit-length job a deadline and a profit, one machine, and asks for maximum profit. The greedy is: sort by profit descending, and schedule each job in the latest free slot at or before its deadline.

Both halves need justification. Taking higher profit first follows from an exchange argument — if an optimal schedule rejects a job it could have run in place of a less profitable one, swapping them keeps every deadline satisfied and raises the profit, so it wasn't optimal. Filling the latest slot is the second half: it leaves earlier slots free for jobs with tighter deadlines, and can never be worse than filling an earlier one.

The naive slot search is O(n times D). I can get it to near O(n log n) with a disjoint set union where each slot points to the first free slot at or before it — when I fill a slot I union it into slot minus one, so the next lookup skips the filled run in nearly constant time. That DSU trick shows up in several scheduling problems and is usually what the interviewer is fishing for once the basic greedy is on the board.

docs.title: Kya hai
docs.text: Intervals ka ek family of problems — merge karna, insert karna, overlap ginna, minimum rooms nikaalna. Sab ek hi do ideas par khade hain: sort karo, aur sirf ek boundary yaad rakho. Analogy: calendar par blocks; kabhi unhe jodna hai, kabhi ginna hai ki ek waqt par kitne overlap ho rahe hain.

docs.title: Kaise kaam karta hai
docs.text: Merging ke liye start se sort karo — tabhi overlapping intervals adjacent aate hain. Counting/rooms ke liye events banao (+1 on start, -1 on end) aur time ke order mein chalo — running sum ka maximum hi answer hai. Selection ke liye end se sort karo (pichhla section).

docs.title: Code
docs.text:
def merge_intervals(intervals):
    """Overlapping intervals ko jodo. Start se sort."""
    if not intervals:                               # 1
        return []                                   # 2
    order = sorted(intervals, key=lambda x: x[0])   # 3
    out = [list(order[0])]                          # 4
    for s, e in order[1:]:                          # 5
        if s <= out[-1][1]:                         # 6
            out[-1][1] = max(out[-1][1], e)         # 7
        else:                                       # 8
            out.append([s, e])                      # 9
    return out                                      # 10


def min_meeting_rooms(intervals):
    """Ek waqt par maximum kitne overlap — sweep line."""
    events = []                                     # 11
    for s, e in intervals:                          # 12
        events.append((s, 1))                       # 13
        events.append((e, -1))                      # 14
    events.sort()                                   # 15
    active = best = 0                               # 16
    for _, delta in events:                         # 17
        active += delta                             # 18
        if active > best:                           # 19
            best = active                           # 20
    return best                                     # 21


def insert_interval(intervals, new):
    """Sorted non-overlapping list mein ek naya interval daalo. O(n)."""
    out, i, n = [], 0, len(intervals)               # 22
    s, e = new                                      # 23
    while i < n and intervals[i][1] < s:            # 24
        out.append(intervals[i])                    # 25
        i += 1                                      # 26
    while i < n and intervals[i][0] <= e:           # 27
        s = min(s, intervals[i][0])                 # 28
        e = max(e, intervals[i][1])                 # 29
        i += 1                                      # 30
    out.append((s, e))                              # 31
    out.extend(intervals[i:])                       # 32
    return out                                      # 33

Line-by-line:

  1. Start se sort — merging ke liye. End se sort karoge to [1,10] aur [2,3] alag alag jagah pahunch jaayenge.
  2. s <= out[-1][1] — touch karte intervals ([1,3], [3,5]) merge honge. Sirf strict overlap chahiye to < kar do.
  3. max zaroori hai — [1,10] ke baad [2,3] aane par end ko 3 mat kar dena. Ye sabse common bug hai.

13-15. (time, +1) aur (time, -1). Sort mein -1 pehle aata hai jab time barabar ho (kyunki -1 < 1) — matlab ek meeting jis waqt khatam hoti hai usi waqt doosri shuru ho sakti hai, same room mein. Agar cleanup time chahiye to end event ko (e, 1) se pehle force karna padega. 18-20. Running count ka maximum = minimum rooms.

24-26. Naye interval se poori tarah pehle wale, jaise ke taise. 27-30. Overlap karne wale sab absorb karo, boundaries ko stretch karte hue. 31-32. Merged interval daalo, phir baaki.

docs.title: Complexity
docs.text: Problem Time Space Merge O(n log n) O(n) output Min rooms (sweep) O(n log n) O(n) events Insert into sorted list O(n) O(n) — sorting ki zaroorat nahi

docs.title: Kaunsa sort — ek line ka rule
docs.text:
Sawaal Sort by Maximum non-overlapping count end Intervals merge karo start Minimum rooms / max overlap events, ya start-heap Sorted list mein insert koi nahi — linear scan

Interview answer: Interval problems are one family with one decision at the front: what do I sort by. If I need the maximum number of non-overlapping intervals, I sort by end time. If I need to merge them, I sort by start time, because only then are overlapping intervals adjacent. If I need the maximum concurrency — minimum meeting rooms — I don't sort intervals at all, I turn each into a plus-one event at its start and a minus-one at its end, sort the events, and track the running maximum.

Merging is O(n log n) and the classic bug is extending the current interval's end to the new interval's end rather than to the max of the two, which silently truncates when a short interval sits inside a long one.

Tie handling is worth stating explicitly: when one meeting ends exactly as another begins, whether they share a room depends on whether the end event sorts before the start event. I'd confirm that convention with the interviewer rather than assume it.

Inserting into an already-sorted, non-overlapping list is a special case that needs no sort at all — a single linear pass in three phases: before, overlapping, after.

docs.title: When Greedy Looks Right and Is Wrong
docs.text: Ye section deliberately code ke bina hai. Greedy ka asli khatra ye hai ki wo chhote test cases par pass ho jaata hai — aap confident ho jaate ho, aur production mein ya interview ke doosre example par toot jaata hai.

docs.title: Counterexample 1 — Coin change
docs.text:
Greedy: hamesha sabse bada coin lo jo fit ho. Coins [1, 3, 4], amount 6.

Approach Choices Coins Greedy 4, phir 1, phir 1 3 Optimal 3, 3 2

Kyun toota: 4 lene se 2 bacha, jo sirf 1+1 se banta hai. 4 ne ek badi jagah to bhari par remainder ko kharaab kar diya. Local best ne future ko constrain kar diya — yahi greedy ke fail hone ki asli definition hai.

Dhyaan dene layak: Indian currency (1, 2, 5, 10, 20, 50, 100) aur US currency par greedy kaam karta hai, kyunki ye "canonical coin systems" hain. Isliye aap zindagi bhar greedy se change dete aaye ho aur kabhi galat nahi hua — aur isliye interview mein greedy pehla instinct banta hai. Arbitrary denominations par wo instinct galat hai.

docs.title: Counterexample 2 — 0/1 Knapsack
docs.text:
Greedy: highest value/weight ratio pehle. Items (w=10,v=60), (w=20,v=100), (w=30,v=120), capacity 50.

Approach Items Value Greedy (ratio) 10 + 20 = 30 wt 160 (20 wt barbaad) Optimal 20 + 30 = 50 wt 220

Kyun toota: indivisibility. Greedy ne 20 units capacity khaali chhod di kyunki bacha hua item fit nahi hua. Fractional version mein yahi greedy perfect hai — ek shabd (fractional) poora paradigm badal deta hai.

docs.title: Counterexample 3 — Longest path in a graph
docs.text:
Greedy: har node par sabse bhaari edge lo.

A --10--> B --1--> D
A --2---> C --50-> D

Greedy A→B→D = 11. Optimal A→C→D = 52. Shortest path ke liye Dijkstra greedy hai aur correct hai; longest path ke liye greedy correct nahi hai aur asal mein longest path NP-hard hai. Same graph, ulta objective, bilkul alag difficulty.

docs.title: Counterexample 4 — Task assignment ("sabse jaldi wale ko pehle")
docs.text: Do workers, tasks [8, 4, 4, 4] hours. Greedy "sabse bada task pehle, sabse khaali worker ko": W1 gets 8, W2 gets 4+4+4=12 → makespan 12. Optimal: W1 = 8+4 = 12, W2 = 4+4 = 8 → 12. Yahan greedy sahi nikla. Ab tasks [7, 6, 5, 4, 3]: greedy 7+4+3=14 / 6+5=11 → 14; optimal 7+6=13 / 5+4+3=12 → 13. Ek input par pass, doosre par fail — aur yahi sabse khatarnaak pattern hai, kyunki aapka pehla test case aksar aasan hota hai.

docs.title: Ek chhoti checklist — greedy likhne se pehle
docs.text: Sawaal Agar haan Kya ek choice baad ki choices ki feasibility badalti hai? Greedy shaq ke ghere mein Kya items indivisible hain aur capacity bandhi hai? Zyaadatar DP Kya main exchange argument do line mein bol sakta hoon? Greedy likho Kya maine sirf do test cases par check kiya? Teesra banao, jaanbujh kar adversarial Kya problem "maximum/minimum count" maang rahi hai, values nahi? Greedy ka chance zyada

docs.title: Adversarial test case kaise banayein
docs.text:
Ye QA wali skill hai aur interview mein bohot achhi lagti hai:

  1. Ek bada element daalo jo pehle aata hai — greedy usse utha lega aur baaki block ho jaayenge (activity selection ka (0, 100)).
  2. Do medium elements banao jinka sum ek bade se behtar ho — coin change [1,3,4] par 6.
  3. Capacity aisi rakho ki greedy ke baad thoda sa space bache jo waste ho — knapsack wala 20.
  4. Ties daalo — barabar values par greedy ka tie-break aksar undefined hota hai aur wahi bug ban jaata hai.

docs.title: Interview mein sahi behaviour
docs.text:
Greedy dikhe to bolo: "My first instinct is greedy — sort by X and take the best each time. Let me test that against a case designed to break it before I commit." Phir jaanbujh kar ek counterexample banane ki koshish karo. Do nateeje hain aur dono achhe hain: ya to greedy tootega (aur aapne DP par time bacha liya), ya nahi tootega (aur ab aapke paas confidence + ek proof sketch hai). Interviewer ko yahi process dekhna hai, sirf answer nahi.

Interview answer: Greedy is the paradigm I trust least without a proof, because it passes small tests and fails on the interesting ones. The canonical failure is coin change: with denominations 1, 3 and 4 and a target of 6, greedy takes a 4 and needs three coins, while the optimum is two 3s. It fails because taking the locally largest coin leaves a remainder that's expensive to fill — the local choice constrained the future.

The reason the instinct is so strong is that real currency systems are canonical, so greedy does work on rupees and dollars. That's a habit, not a proof.

The same shape appears elsewhere: 0/1 knapsack by value-to-weight ratio wastes capacity because items are indivisible, and greedy on longest path fails outright while the identical greedy on shortest path is Dijkstra and is correct. Before committing I ask whether one choice changes what remains feasible; if it does, I go to DP. And I deliberately construct an adversarial case — one big early element, or two medium elements that beat one large one — rather than trusting the examples I was given.

docs.title: Part 7: String Algorithms
docs.text:
String matching un chand jagahon mein se hai jahan ek algorithm ka farak naap kar dikh jaata hai. Naive matching 10 MB log file mein ek pattern dhoondhne mein minutes le sakta hai; KMP seconds mein kar dega. Aur QA mein ye roz kaam aata hai — logs, HTML, API responses, diffs.

Yahan ek cheez shuru mein saaf kar dena zaroori hai: Python ka in operator pehle se optimised hai (CPython mein a mixed Boyer-Moore-Horspool / two-way algorithm). To in algorithms ko aap production mein rarely likhoge — inko seekhne ki wajah ye hai ki interview mein poochhe jaate hain aur inke andar ke ideas (prefix function, rolling hash) doosri jagah reuse hote hain.

docs.title: Kya hai
docs.text: Text ke har position par pattern ko rakh kar character-by-character compare karo. Analogy: ek chaabi ke gucchhe se har chaabi taala mein daal kar dekhna — koi chaturai nahi, sirf mehnat.

docs.title: Kaise kaam karta hai
docs.text: i ko 0 se n - m tak ghumao. Har i par pattern ke saare characters match karo; ek bhi mismatch mile to turant break karo aur i + 1 par phir se shuru se compare karo. Yahi "shuru se" wali baat hi iski kamzori hai — pichhle comparisons se jo information mili thi, wo phenk di jaati hai.

docs.title: Code
docs.text:
def naive_search(text, pattern):
    """Saare occurrences ke starting indices."""
    n, m = len(text), len(pattern)                  # 1
    if m == 0 or m > n:                             # 2
        return []                                   # 3
    result = []                                     # 4
    for i in range(n - m + 1):                      # 5
        j = 0                                       # 6
        while j < m and text[i + j] == pattern[j]:  # 7
            j += 1                                  # 8
        if j == m:                                  # 9
            result.append(i)                        # 10
    return result                                   # 11


def naive_search_slice(text, pattern):
    """Wahi cheez, Python slicing se — chhota par same complexity."""
    m = len(text) - len(pattern) + 1                # 12
    return [i for i in range(m)
            if text[i:i + len(pattern)] == pattern]  # 13

Line-by-line:

2-3. Khaali pattern ya text se lamba pattern — edge cases jo interview mein poochhe jaate hain. 5. n - m + 1 positions — isse aage pattern text se bahar nikal jaayega. n likh dena classic off-by-one hai. 7-8. Jab tak match ho rahi hai aage badho. 9-10. j poore m tak pahuncha = poora pattern mil gaya.

12-13. Slicing wala version padhne mein saaf hai par har slice ek naya string banata hai (O(m) copy), to constant factor kharaab hai — chhote inputs par phir bhi tez chalta hai kyunki comparison C level par hota hai.

docs.title: Worst case — kab sach mein O(n·m) hota hai
docs.text: text = "AAAAAAAAAB", pattern = "AAAB". Har position par pehle teen A match honge aur chautha character fail karega — matlab har shift par poora m kaam. Ye pattern real logs mein bhi banta hai: repeated whitespace, ==== separators, base64 padding.

docs.title: Complexity
docs.text:
Case Time Kyun Best O(n) Har position par pehla hi character mismatch Average (random text) O(n) Expected comparisons per position constant hoti hain Worst O(n·m) n-m+1 positions × m comparisons Space O(1) Koi extra structure nahi

Yahi wajah hai ki naive bura nahi hai — random-ish text par wo practically linear hai aur zero preprocessing leta hai. KMP ka faayda tabhi milta hai jab pattern mein khud ke andar repetition ho.

Interview answer: Naive pattern matching slides the pattern across every starting position and compares characters until a mismatch. It's O(n times m) in the worst case, O(1) space, and needs no preprocessing.

The worst case needs a highly repetitive text and pattern — something like a long run of As with a B at the end of the pattern — because only then does every alignment do near-m work before failing. On typical English or log text the expected work per position is a small constant, so it behaves close to linear, which is why it's a perfectly reasonable answer for short patterns.

Its real weakness is that it throws away information. After matching three characters and failing on the fourth, it restarts from scratch one position over, even though those three characters already told it something about the text. That discarded information is exactly what KMP captures in its prefix table, and framing it that way is how I'd motivate KMP as the next step.

docs.title: Kya hai
docs.text: Knuth-Morris-Pratt — mismatch hone par text pointer ko kabhi peeche nahi le jaata; pattern ko kitna aage khiskana hai ye ek precomputed table se aata hai. Analogy: aapko pata hai ki "AABA" ke aakhir mein bhi "A" hai aur shuru mein bhi "A" — to fail hone par poora shuru se nahi, us "A" ke baad se continue karo.

docs.title: Kaise kaam karta hai
docs.text: Pehle pattern ka LPS array banao: lps[i] = pattern[0..i] ka sabse lamba proper prefix jo suffix bhi ho. Phir matching ke waqt jab pattern[j] mismatch kare, j = lps[j-1] kar do — matlab utne characters hum already match kar chuke hain, unhe dobara compare mat karo. i kabhi decrement nahi hota, isliye text ek hi baar padha jaata hai.

docs.title: Code
docs.text:
def build_lps(pattern):
    """lps[i] = pattern[0..i] ka longest proper prefix jo suffix bhi ho."""
    m = len(pattern)                                # 1
    lps = [0] * m                                   # 2
    length = 0                                      # 3
    i = 1                                           # 4
    while i < m:                                    # 5
        if pattern[i] == pattern[length]:           # 6
            length += 1                             # 7
            lps[i] = length                         # 8
            i += 1                                  # 9
        elif length > 0:                            # 10
            length = lps[length - 1]                # 11
        else:                                       # 12
            lps[i] = 0                              # 13
            i += 1                                  # 14
    return lps                                      # 15


def kmp_search(text, pattern):
    """Saare occurrences. O(n + m)."""
    n, m = len(text), len(pattern)                  # 16
    if m == 0 or m > n:                             # 17
        return []                                   # 18
    lps = build_lps(pattern)                        # 19
    result = []                                     # 20
    i = j = 0                                       # 21
    while i < n:                                    # 22
        if text[i] == pattern[j]:                   # 23
            i += 1                                  # 24
            j += 1                                  # 25
            if j == m:                              # 26
                result.append(i - m)                # 27
                j = lps[j - 1]                      # 28
        elif j > 0:                                 # 29
            j = lps[j - 1]                          # 30
        else:                                       # 31
            i += 1                                  # 32
    return result                                   # 33

Line-by-line:

3-4. lps[0] hamesha 0 hai (proper prefix khud poori string nahi ho sakti), isliye i 1 se. 6-9. Match — current prefix-suffix length badhao aur record karo. 10-11. Ye poore algorithm ki sabse gehri line hai. Mismatch hua par length > 0 — matlab hum chhote prefix-suffix par fall back kar sakte hain. length = lps[length-1] recursively agla candidate deta hai, bina i ko hilaye. 12-14. length == 0 — koi fallback nahi bacha, lps[i] = 0.

23-25. Match, dono aage. 26-28. Poora pattern mil gaya. j = lps[j-1] karke overlapping matches bhi milte hain ("AAA" mein "AA" do baar). j = 0 karoge to overlapping chhoot jaayenge. 29-30. Mismatch par sirf j peeche jaata hai, i nahi. Yahi O(n) guarantee hai. 31-32. j already 0 hai — text mein ek kadam aage badho.

docs.title: Complexity
docs.text:
Value Kyun Preprocessing O(m) i kabhi peeche nahi jaata; length har step par max 1 badhta hai aur total ghatna badhne se zyada nahi ho sakta Search O(n) i monotonically badhta hai; j bhi total mein n se zyada nahi ghat sakta Total O(n + m) Space O(m) LPS array

Amortised argument: j har match par +1 hota hai (max n baar), aur har fallback par ghatta hai. Ghatne ka total badhne ke total se zyada nahi ho sakta — isliye fallbacks bhi kul milakar O(n) hain, chahe ek iteration mein kai baar chalein.

Interview answer: KMP finds all occurrences in O(n plus m) with O(m) extra space, and the key property is that the text pointer never moves backwards.

It preprocesses the pattern into an LPS array, where lps[i] is the length of the longest proper prefix of the pattern's first i-plus-one characters that is also a suffix. When a mismatch happens at pattern position j, instead of restarting, I set j to lps[j-1] — those characters are already known to match, so re-comparing them is wasted work.

The linearity argument is amortised, and it's worth stating properly: the text index only ever increases, and j increases by at most one per step, so the total amount j can decrease across all fallbacks is bounded by the total it increased. That's why the inner while loop doesn't make it quadratic.

One detail: after a full match I reset j to lps[m-1] rather than zero, which is what lets it find overlapping occurrences. The LPS array is also independently useful — the shortest repeating unit of a string is n minus lps of the last index, when that divides n.

docs.title: Kya hai
docs.text: Pattern aur har window ka hash compare karo; hash match hone par hi asli characters check karo. Analogy: do badi files ko compare karne se pehle unka checksum compare karna — checksum alag hai to file dekhne ki zaroorat hi nahi.

docs.title: Kaise kaam karta hai
docs.text: Ek rolling hash use hota hai: window ek kadam aage khiskane par poora dobara hash karne ki zaroorat nahi — bas pehla character ka contribution ghatao, naya character jodo. Isse har shift O(1) ho jaata hai. Hash barabar hone par bhi string compare karna zaroori hai (collision ho sakti hai).

docs.title: Code
docs.text:
def rabin_karp(text, pattern, base=256, mod=1_000_000_007):
    """Saare occurrences. Average O(n + m), worst O(n*m)."""
    n, m = len(text), len(pattern)                  # 1
    if m == 0 or m > n:                             # 2
        return []                                   # 3
    high = pow(base, m - 1, mod)                    # 4
    ph = th = 0                                     # 5
    for k in range(m):                              # 6
        ph = (ph * base + ord(pattern[k])) % mod    # 7
        th = (th * base + ord(text[k])) % mod       # 8
    result = []                                     # 9
    for i in range(n - m + 1):                      # 10
        if ph == th and text[i:i + m] == pattern:   # 11
            result.append(i)                        # 12
        if i < n - m:                               # 13
            th = (th - ord(text[i]) * high) % mod   # 14
            th = (th * base + ord(text[i + m])) % mod   # 15
    return result                                   # 16

Line-by-line:

  1. base^(m-1) mod p — nikalte waqt sabse aage wale character ka place value. pow ke teen arguments modular exponentiation karte hain, O(log m) mein. 6-8. Dono initial hashes ek saath — polynomial hash: c0·b^(m-1) + c1·b^(m-2) + … + cm-1.
  2. ph == th ke baad bhi actual compare — ye line hatana sabse badi galti hai. Hash match hona sirf candidate deta hai, proof nahi.
  3. Sabse aage wala character hatao (ord(text[i]) * high).
  4. Baaki ko ek place shift karo (* base) aur naya character jodo. Ye do lines mil kar rolling hash hain. Python ka % negative numbers ko bhi sahi handle karta hai, isliye line 14 ke baad extra + mod ki zaroorat nahi (C++ mein hoti hai).

docs.title: Compact dry run — text = "ABCDE", pattern = "CD", chhota base=10, mod=997
Complexity
docs.text:
Case Time Kyun Preprocessing O(m) Dono hashes Average O(n + m) Har shift O(1); collisions bohot kam Worst O(n·m) Har window par hash match par string alag — adversarial input, ya bekaar hash Space O(1) Sirf do integers

Worst case kab: agar attacker ko base aur mod pata ho to wo jaanbujh kar colliding strings bana sakta hai. Isliye security-sensitive jagah par random base chunna chahiye.

docs.title: Kab Rabin-Karp KMP se behtar hai
docs.text:
Multiple patterns ek saath dhoondhne mein. Agar 1000 patterns hain jinki length same hai, to unke hashes ek set mein daal do aur text par ek hi pass mein saare check ho jaayenge — O(n + total pattern length). KMP ke liye 1000 alag automata banane padte. 2D pattern matching aur plagiarism detection (document ke saare k-length substrings ke hashes) bhi isi par khade hain.

Interview answer: Rabin-Karp compares hashes instead of characters. I compute a polynomial rolling hash of the pattern and of the first window, then slide: subtract the leading character's contribution, multiply by the base, add the new character. Each shift is O(1), so the average case is O(n plus m) with constant extra space.

Two things I always state. First, a hash match is only a candidate — I still compare the actual substring, because collisions exist. Skipping that verification is the classic bug and it makes the algorithm silently wrong. Second, the worst case is O(n times m) when every window collides, which an adversary can construct if the base and modulus are known, so I'd randomise them if the input is untrusted.

Where it genuinely beats KMP is multiple patterns of the same length: put all their hashes in a set and one pass over the text checks all of them. That's how plagiarism detection and content deduplication work — hash every k-length window and look for repeats. It also extends naturally to two-dimensional matching, which KMP doesn't.

docs.title: Kya hai
docs.text: Ek string ke liye Z array banata hai jahan Z[i] = us position se shuru hone wala sabse lamba substring jo poori string ka prefix bhi ho. Analogy: har position par poochhna — "yahan se aage kitne characters bilkul shuruaat jaise hain?"

docs.title: Kaise kaam karta hai
docs.text: Ek [l, r] window maintain hoti hai — abhi tak mila hua sabse door tak jaane wala prefix match. Agar i us window ke andar hai, to Z[i] ka answer pehle se compute ho chuki mirror position Z[i-l] se shuru mein hi mil jaata hai; sirf window ke bahar wala hissa manually extend karna padta hai. Isliye total kaam linear rehta hai.

docs.title: Code
docs.text:
def z_array(s):
    """Z[i] = s[i:] aur s ka longest common prefix. Z[0] convention se len(s)."""
    n = len(s)                                      # 1
    z = [0] * n                                     # 2
    if n == 0:                                      # 3
        return z                                    # 4
    z[0] = n                                        # 5
    l = r = 0                                       # 6
    for i in range(1, n):                           # 7
        if i < r:                                   # 8
            z[i] = min(r - i, z[i - l])             # 9
        while i + z[i] < n and s[z[i]] == s[i + z[i]]:   # 10
            z[i] += 1                               # 11
        if i + z[i] > r:                            # 12
            l, r = i, i + z[i]                      # 13
    return z                                        # 14


def z_search(text, pattern, sep="\x00"):
    """Pattern matching: pattern + separator + text ka Z array."""
    combined = pattern + sep + text                 # 15
    z = z_array(combined)                           # 16
    m = len(pattern)                                # 17
    return [i - m - 1 for i in range(m + 1, len(combined))
            if z[i] == m]                           # 18

Line-by-line:

  1. Z[0] ko poori length maan lena convention hai (khud se match to poora hi hoga).
  2. [l, r) = sabse right tak pahunchne wala known prefix-match ka interval. 8-9. Ye line hi Z algorithm hai. i window ke andar hai, to s[i..r) = s[i-l..r-l) already pata hai. min isliye kyunki mirror ka answer window se bahar nikal sakta hai — uske aage ka data hume abhi confirm nahi. 10-11. Bache hue characters manually match karo. Ye loop kul milakar O(n) baar hi chalta hai kyunki har successful comparison r ko aage badhata hai, aur r kabhi ghatta nahi. 12-13. Nayi window agar zyada door tak jaati hai to update.

15-18. Concatenation trick. Separator aisa chuno jo dono strings mein na ho, warna Z[i] m se bada ho sakta hai aur galat matches milenge. z[i] == m matlab poora pattern wahan se match hua; original index = i - m - 1.
