On the trade-off: bucket sort is O(n) space regardless of how few distinct values there are, so if I had a billion elements with only ten distinct values, the size-k heap would use far less memory. So bucket sort when n is moderate, heap when n is huge or the data is streaming.

One thing I'd clarify: when counts tie at the k boundary, which values to return is arbitrary in my solution. Some versions of this problem want lexicographic tie-breaking, which changes the heap key."

docs.title: Problem 12.6 — Frequency Sort (Sort Characters By Frequency)
docs.text:
Problem statement

Ek string di hai. Usko is tarah reorder karo ki zyada frequent characters pehle aayein. Same frequency wale characters ka order matter nahi karta, lekin ek hi character ke saare instances saath mein hone chahiye.

Input:  "tree"
Output: "eert" ya "eetr"
        counts: {t: 1, r: 1, e: 2}
        'e' do baar -> pehle, phir 't' aur 'r' (koi bhi order)

Input:  "cccaaa"
Output: "aaaccc" ya "cccaaa"
        dono ka count 3 hai, toh koi bhi order

Input:  "Aabb"
Output: "bbAa" ya "bbaA"
        'b' do baar; 'A' aur 'a' alag characters hain (case-sensitive)

Pehla instinct — brute force

Frequency count karo, counts par sort karo, phir string banao.

from collections import Counter

def frequency_sort_naive(s):
    counts = Counter(s)                           # 1: {char: frequency}
    sorted_chars = sorted(counts.items(),         # 2: (char, count) pairs
                          key=lambda item: item[1],   # 3: count par sort
                          reverse=True)           # 4: descending
    parts = []                                    # 5: string tukdon mein
    for char, count in sorted_chars:              # 6
        parts.append(char * count)                # 7: character ko count baar repeat
    return "".join(parts)                         # 8: JOIN -- `+=` loop mein nahi

Line by line — kyun aise likha hai

  1. Counter(s) — string par bhi kaam karta hai (characters iterate hote hain). 2-4. Counts par descending sort. 5-7. parts list mein tukde, phir join. Line 7: char * count — string repetition operator. 'e' * 2 = 'ee'. 6-8. "".join(parts) — result += ... loop mein nahi. Loop mein += O(n^2) hota hai (Python Essentials section wali baat). join O(n) hai.

Complexity: Time O(n + d log d) jahan d = distinct characters. Space O(n).

Yeh actually bilkul acceptable hai — aur lowercase-only inputs par d <= 26 hai toh d log d constant hai.

Isme problem kya hai

Sirf ek theoretical issue: agar characters Unicode hon toh d bada ho sakta hai (10^5 tak). Tab d log d matter karta hai.

Aur interview mein interviewer aksar dekhna chahta hai ki aap bucket sort aur heap dono jaante ho.

The insight

Bilkul Problem 12.5 wala hi. Do options:

Option A — max-heap. Counts par max-heap banao aur pop karte jao. O(n + d log d) — same as sorting, lekin heap partial extraction allow karta hai (agar sirf top few chahiye hon).

Option B — bucket sort. Frequencies [1, n] range mein bounded hain, toh buckets[f] = frequency f wale characters. Highest se lowest traverse karo. O(n).

Bucket sort yahan strictly better hai aur woh insight (bounded range → direct indexing) is document mein teesri baar aa raha hai (Cyclic Sort, Top K Frequent, aur ab yeh). Yeh pattern recognition ka accha example hai.

Optimal solution — bucket sort

from collections import Counter

def frequency_sort(s):
    if not s:                                     # 1: khaali string guard
        return ""                                 # 2

    counts = Counter(s)                           # 3: {char: frequency}
    n = len(s)                                    # 4: maximum possible frequency

    buckets = [[] for _ in range(n + 1)]          # 5: index 0..n; NOT [[]] * (n+1)
    for char, count in counts.items():            # 6
        buckets[count].append(char)               # 7: frequency HI index hai

    parts = []                                    # 8: output tukde
    for freq in range(n, 0, -1):                  # 9: HIGHEST frequency se neeche
        for char in buckets[freq]:                # 10: is frequency ke saare characters
            parts.append(char * freq)             # 11: character ko `freq` baar repeat

    return "".join(parts)                         # 12

Line by line — kyun aise likha hai

1-2. Empty guard. Line 5 range(1) deta jo technically theek hai, lekin explicit guard clearer hai. 3. Counter(s). 4. n = len(s) — maximum possible frequency (agar saare characters same hon). 5. buckets = [[] for _ in range(n + 1)] — list comprehension, [[]] * (n+1) NAHI. [[]] * (n+1) ek hi list ka n+1 baar reference banata hai — har append saari buckets mein dikhta. Yeh classic Python bug hai aur Problem 12.5 mein bhi tha. 6-7. buckets[count].append(char) — frequency direct index ban gayi. O(d). 8. parts = []. 9. for freq in range(n, 0, -1): — n se 1 tak. range(n, 0, -1) mein stop 0 exclusive hai, toh 1 tak jaata hai. Frequency 0 ka koi character hota hi nahi. 10-11. parts.append(char * freq) — char * freq, char alone nahi. Har character ko uski frequency ke barabar baar repeat karna hai. Yeh Problem 12.5 se sabse bada difference hai — wahan sirf value chahiye thi, yahan repetitions chahiye. char * count likhna galat hoga agar count variable define nahi hai — yahan freq hi count hai (kyunki hum us bucket mein hain). 12. "".join(parts).

Optimal solution — heap version

import heapq
from collections import Counter

def frequency_sort_heap(s):
    counts = Counter(s)                           # 13
    heap = [(-count, char) for char, count in counts.items()]   # 14: NEGATE for max-heap
    heapq.heapify(heap)                           # 15: O(d)

    parts = []                                    # 16
    while heap:                                   # 17: saare characters process karo
        neg_count, char = heapq.heappop(heap)     # 18: sabse frequent
        parts.append(char * (-neg_count))         # 19: un-negate karke repeat
    return "".join(parts)                         # 20

Line by line:

  1. [(-count, char) for ...] — count negate kiya (max-heap), char nahi. Tuple order: (-count, char) — count pehle (sorting key). Tie-breaking: same count par char compare hota hai (lexicographic). Yeh deterministic hai aur crash nahi karta. Agar char ki jagah koi non-comparable object hota toh TypeError aata.
  2. heapify O(d). 17-19. Pop karke output banao.
  3. char * (-neg_count) — do negations ka net effect: neg_count negative hai, -neg_count actual count hai.

Time O(n + d log d), Space O(n). Bucket version se slower hai lekin ties par lexicographic order deta hai, jo kuch problems maangti hain.

Dry run — bucket version — s = "tree" (expected "eert" type)

counts = {'t': 1, 'r': 1, 'e': 2}, n = 4.

Line 5: buckets = [[], [], [], [], []] (indices 0-4).

Lines 6-7:

char count Action buckets t 1 buckets[1].append('t') [[], ['t'], [], [], []] r 1 buckets[1].append('r') [[], ['t','r'], [], [], []] e 2 buckets[2].append('e') [[], ['t','r'], ['e'], [], []]

Lines 9-11:

freq buckets[freq] Appends parts 4 [] — [] 3 [] — [] 2 ['e'] 'e' * 2 = 'ee' ['ee'] 1 ['t', 'r'] 't' * 1 = 't', 'r' * 1 = 'r' ['ee', 't', 'r']

"".join(['ee', 't', 'r']) = "eetr". Sahi (valid answer — 'e' do baar pehle, phir baaki).

Frequency 1 wale bucket mein 't' pehle aaya kyunki woh string mein pehle mila (Counter insertion order rakhta hai Python 3.7+). Yeh arbitrary hai — "eert" bhi valid hai.

Dry run — heap version — same input

counts = {'t': 1, 'r': 1, 'e': 2}. Line 14: heap = [(-1, 't'), (-1, 'r'), (-2, 'e')]. Line 15: heapify → top = (-2, 'e') (kyunki -2 < -1).

Iter Pop neg_count char char * (-neg_count) parts 1 (-2, 'e') -2 e 'ee' ['ee'] 2 (-1, 'r') -1 r 'r' ['ee', 'r'] 3 (-1, 't') -1 t 't' ['ee', 'r', 't']

"eert". Sahi.

Iterations 2 aur 3 dekho — dono ka count -1 same tha, toh tuple ka dusra element compare hua: 'r' < 't' toh 'r' pehle. Heap version deterministic lexicographic tie-breaking deta hai; bucket version insertion order. Yeh farq mention karne layak hai.

Dry run — s = "cccaaa" (expected "aaaccc" ya "cccaaa")

counts = {'c': 3, 'a': 3}, n = 6.

Buckets: buckets[3] = ['c', 'a'] (insertion order — 'c' string mein pehle aaya).

freq bucket Appends parts 6,5,4 [] — [] 3 ['c', 'a'] 'ccc', 'aaa' ['ccc', 'aaa'] 2,1 [] — same

"cccaaa". Valid.

Heap version: heap = [(-3, 'c'), (-3, 'a')] → heapify → top (-3, 'a') (kyunki tie par 'a' < 'c') → pop order 'a' phir 'c' → "aaaccc". Bhi valid, lekin alag.

Complexity

Approach Time Space Ties Sort counts O(n + d log d) O(n) Stable (insertion order) Max-heap O(n + d log d) O(n) Lexicographic Bucket sort O(n) O(n) Insertion order

Lowercase-only input par d <= 26, toh d log d ek constant (~122 operations) hai — teenon practically same speed. Bucket sort ka advantage tab dikhta hai jab d bada ho (Unicode).

Edge cases

Case Input Output Kyun Empty "" "" Guard Single char "a" "a" buckets[1] = ['a'] All same "aaa" "aaa" buckets[3] = ['a'] All distinct "abc" "abc" (koi order) Sab buckets[1] mein Case sensitivity "Aa" "Aa" ya "aA" 'A' != 'a' Digits and symbols "a1a1a" "aaa11" Koi bhi character Unicode "日日本" "日日本" Python strings Unicode-native Very long 10^5 chars — O(n) fine

"Case sensitivity" wala row clarify karne layak hai — kuch problems case-insensitive chahti hain, tab s.lower() pehle karna padta hai (lekin phir output ka case kya ho?).

Variations

  • Sort Characters By Frequency (LeetCode 451) — exactly yeh problem.
  • Top K Frequent Elements (347) — Problem 12.5; sirf top k, saare nahi.
  • Top K Frequent Words (692) — ties par lexicographic ascending — heap tuple (-count, word) exactly yeh deta hai.
  • Reorganize String (767) — bilkul alag problem despite similar setup — same characters adjacent nahi ho sakte. Max-heap plus "pichhla character" tracking chahiye.
  • Rearrange String k Distance Apart (358) — 767 ka general version.
  • Sort array by frequency then by value (1636) — do-level sorting key.
  • Frequency sort with stable original order for ties — bucket sort naturally deta hai.

Interview answer: "Count the characters, then order the distinct characters by descending count and expand each one back out to its full run.

Sorting the counts is the obvious way and it's fine — with lowercase-only input there are at most twenty-six distinct characters, so that log factor is a constant.

But the better solution uses the same bounded-range insight as the top-k-frequent problem: no frequency can exceed the string length, so frequencies live in a known integer range and I can index by them directly instead of comparing. I build an array of buckets indexed by frequency, drop each character into its bucket, then walk from the highest frequency down and emit each character repeated that many times. That's O(n) overall.

Two implementation details. I build the bucket list with a comprehension rather than multiplying a list literal — multiplying gives n references to the same list, so every append shows up everywhere. And I collect the pieces into a list and join at the end rather than concatenating in a loop, because Python strings are immutable and repeated concatenation is quadratic.

There's also a max-heap version. Same asymptotic cost, but it gives a different tie-breaking: pushing tuples of negated-count and character means equal counts fall through to comparing the characters, so ties come out in lexicographic order deterministically. The bucket version gives insertion order instead. If the problem specified lexicographic tie-breaking — as the top-k-frequent-words variant does — I'd use the heap.

O(n) time and O(n) space for the bucket version.

One thing I'd confirm: whether the comparison is case-sensitive, since capital A and lowercase a are different characters by default."

docs.title: Problem 12.7 — K Closest Numbers In A Sorted Array
docs.text:
Problem statement

Ek sorted array, ek number k, aur ek target (x) diya hai. Array mein se k aise numbers lauta do jo x ke sabse nazdeek hain. Output ascending order mein hona chahiye.

Input:  arr = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5], k = 4, x = 3
Output: [1, 2, 3, 4]
        distances: |1-3|=2, |2-3|=1, |3-3|=0, |4-3|=1, |5-3|=2
        Closest 4: 3(0), 2(1), 4(1), aur phir tie between 1(2) aur 5(2) -> SMALLER pref -> 1

Input:  arr = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5], k = 4, x = -1
Output: [1, 2, 3, 4]

Input:  arr = [1, 1, 1, 10, 10, 10], k = 1, x = 9
Output: [10]

Tie-breaking rule: agar do numbers x se barabar door hain, toh chhota wala prefer karo.

Pehla instinct — brute force (heap)

Max-heap of size k, distance par keyed.

import heapq

def k_closest_heap(arr, k, x):
    heap = []                                     # 1: MAX-heap of (distance, value)
    for num in arr:                               # 2: har element
        dist = abs(num - x)                       # 3: x se distance
        if len(heap) < k:                         # 4
            heapq.heappush(heap, (-dist, -num))   # 5: DONO negate -- neeche explanation
        elif dist < -heap[0][0]:                  # 6: closer hai?
            heapq.heappushpop(heap, (-dist, -num))# 7
    return sorted(-num for _, num in heap)        # 8: un-negate aur SORT karo

Line by line — kyun aise likha hai

1-3. Setup. abs(num - x) = distance. 4-5. heapq.heappush(heap, (-dist, -num)) — dono negate kiye, aur -num wala hissa tie-breaking ke liye hai. Max-heap chahiye distance par, toh -dist. Tie par kya hona chahiye? Hum chhote numbers prefer karte hain, matlab bade numbers ko pehle evict karna hai. Max-heap ka top evict hota hai, toh tie par bada number top par hona chahiye — jo -num se hota hai (bada num → chhota -num → min-heap mein top... ruko). Chalo carefully: heap min-heap hai. Top = sabse chhota tuple. (-dist, -num) mein tie par -num compare hota hai, aur sabse chhota -num = sabse bada num. Toh top par sabse bada number aata hai — aur wahi evict hota hai. Sahi. Yeh double negation bahut confusing hai — aur yehi is approach ka sabse bada drawback hai. 6. elif dist < -heap[0][0]: — closer. Note: yeh tie par swap nahi karta (< strict hai), jo tie-breaking ko thoda incomplete banata hai. Poori tarah correct karne ke liye tie case bhi handle karna padta. 7. heappushpop. 8. sorted(...) — output ascending chahiye, aur heap ka order arbitrary hai. Extra O(k log k).

Complexity: Time O(n log k + k log k), Space O(k).

Isme problem kya hai

Do baatein:

  1. Array sorted hai aur hum us information ka koi fayda nahi utha rahe. Hum saare n elements scan kar rahe hain.
  2. Tie-breaking ke liye double negation — bug-prone aur padhne mein mushkil.

The insight

Array sorted hai, toh:

Observation 1: x ke closest k elements hamesha ek contiguous window banate hain. Kyunki agar arr[i] aur arr[j] (i < j) dono answer mein hain, toh beech ka har element unme se kam se kam ek se x ke zyada paas hai — toh woh bhi answer mein hoga.

Observation 2: Toh problem ban jaati hai: "woh window of size k dhoondo jo x ke sabse paas hai."

Aur uske do tarike hain:

Tarika A — binary search plus two pointers. x ka ceiling dhoondo (O(log n)), phir do pointers se k elements expand karo, har baar closer wale side ko lo. O(log n + k).

Tarika B — binary search on the window's left boundary. Directly us left ko dhoondo jahan se k-size window best hai. O(log n) — aur yeh sabse elegant hai.

Tarika B ka core comparison: left ek valid answer hai agar x - arr[left] <= arr[left + k] - x. Yaani "window ke left edge ko rakhna better hai ya usse aage badhana."

Optimal solution — Tarika B (binary search on window start)

def find_closest_elements(arr, k, x):
    low = 0                                       # 1: window ka possible sabse chhota start
    high = len(arr) - k                           # 2: window ka possible sabse bada start

    while low < high:                             # 3: Convention B
        mid = low + (high - low) // 2             # 4: candidate window start
        # window [mid, mid+k-1] vs window [mid+1, mid+k] mein se kaunsa better?
        if x - arr[mid] > arr[mid + k] - x:       # 5: right wala element closer hai
            low = mid + 1                         # 6: window ko RIGHT shift karo
        else:                                     # 7: left wala rakhna better (ya tie)
            high = mid                            # 8: mid CANDIDATE hai

    return arr[low:low + k]                       # 9: k-size window

Line by line — kyun aise likha hai

  1. low = 0 — window index 0 se shuru ho sakta hai.
  2. high = len(arr) - k — window ka sabse bada valid start. Agar left = len(arr) - k hai toh window [len-k, len-1] hai — exactly k elements, aur array ke end tak. Isse aage window array se bahar chali jaayegi. len(arr) - k - 1 likhna galat hai — woh ek valid window kho deta. k > len(arr) par high negative ho jaata — guard chahiye. Problem usually k <= len(arr) guarantee deti hai.
  3. while low < high: — Convention B (kyunki line 8 high = mid hai).
  4. mid = low + (high - low) // 2 — lower mid, kyunki line 8 mid ko include karti hai.
  5. if x - arr[mid] > arr[mid + k] - x: — poore solution ki sabse important line. Yeh compare kar rahi hai:
  6. x - arr[mid] — window [mid, mid+k-1] ke left edge (arr[mid]) se x ki distance.
  7. arr[mid + k] - x — window ko ek right shift karne par jo naya element aayega (arr[mid+k]) se x ki distance.

Agar right wala closer hai (> True), toh window ko right shift karna better hai — arr[mid] ko chhod kar arr[mid+k] lena.

abs() kyun nahi use kiya? - Agar x <= arr[mid] hai toh x - arr[mid] <= 0, aur arr[mid+k] - x > 0 (kyunki array sorted hai aur arr[mid+k] > arr[mid] >= x). Toh condition negative > positive = False → high = mid. Sahi — window ko left rakhna better hai. - Agar x >= arr[mid+k] hai toh x - arr[mid] > 0 aur arr[mid+k] - x <= 0. Condition True → low = mid + 1. Sahi. - Beech wale case mein dono positive hain aur direct comparison sahi hai. Toh abs() ki zaroorat hi nahi — sorted array ki wajah se signs automatically sahi kaam karte hain. Yeh ek elegant detail hai jo interview mein bolne layak hai.

> strict hai, >= nahi — tie par (x - arr[mid] == arr[mid+k] - x) hum left rakhte hain (high = mid). Yeh exactly problem ka tie-breaking rule hai: chhota number prefer karo. 6. low = mid + 1 — right shift. 7-8. high = mid — mid - 1 NAHI, kyunki mid khud best window start ho sakta hai. 9. return arr[low:low + k] — k elements, aur array sorted hai toh output already ascending hai. Koi extra sort nahi.

Optimal solution — Tarika A (two pointers, thoda zyada intuitive)

import bisect

def find_closest_two_pointers(arr, k, x):
    # x ka insertion point -- yahan se dono taraf expand karenge
    right = bisect.bisect_left(arr, x)            # 10: pehla index jahan arr[i] >= x
    left = right - 1                              # 11: uske turant pehle wala

    for _ in range(k):                            # 12: exactly k elements lene hain
        if left < 0:                              # 13: left side khatam
            right += 1                            # 14: right se lo
        elif right >= len(arr):                   # 15: right side khatam
            left -= 1                             # 16: left se lo
        elif x - arr[left] <= arr[right] - x:     # 17: left closer (ya TIE)
            left -= 1                             # 18: left se lo
        else:                                     # 19: right closer
            right += 1                            # 20: right se lo

    return arr[left + 1:right]                    # 21: exclusive boundaries

Line by line:

  1. bisect.bisect_left(arr, x) — x ka insertion point. Yeh x se bade-ya-barabar pehla element hai.
  2. left = right - 1 — x se chhota aakhri element. left aur right "exclusive boundaries" hain — window (left, right) hai, matlab arr[left+1 : right].
  3. for _ in range(k): — exactly k baar expand. 13-16. Boundary guards. Ek side khatam ho toh dusri se lo. Order matter karta hai — line 13 aur 15 line 17 se pehle honi chahiye, warna arr[-1] ya arr[len] access hota. 17-18. x - arr[left] <= arr[right] - x — <= (tie par LEFT). Yeh tie-breaking rule hai: barabar distance par chhota number. < likhne se tie par right lete — galat answer. 19-20. Right closer.
  4. arr[left + 1:right] — left exclusive hai toh left + 1 se shuru; right exclusive hai toh wahin tak. Window mein exactly k elements hain kyunki loop ne k baar expand kiya.

Time O(log n + k), Space O(1) (output ke alawa). Tarika B se thoda slower (k term ki wajah se) lekin zyada intuitive hai.

Dry run — Tarika B — arr = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5], k = 4, x = 3 (expected [1,2,3,4])

low = 0, high = 5 - 4 = 1.

Iter low high mid arr[mid] arr[mid+k] x - arr[mid] arr[mid+k] - x > ? Action 1 0 1 0 arr[0]=1 arr[4]=5 3-1 = 2 5-3 = 2 2 > 2 No high = 0 2 0 0 — — — — — 0 < 0 False exit

return arr[0:4] = [1, 2, 3, 4]. Sahi.

Iteration 1 ka tie sabse important hai — dono distances 2 thi. > strict hone ki wajah se condition False hui aur high = mid = 0 set hua, matlab window left par rakha gaya. Isse 1 shaamil hua aur 5 chhoda gaya — exactly tie-breaking rule ("smaller preferred").

>= likhte toh condition True hoti, low = 1, aur answer arr[1:5] = [2,3,4,5] aata — galat.

Dry run — Tarika B — arr = [1, 1, 1, 10, 10, 10], k = 1, x = 9 (expected [10])

low = 0, high = 6 - 1 = 5.

Iter low high mid arr[mid] arr[mid+1] 9 - arr[mid] arr[mid+1] - 9 > ? Action 1 0 5 2 arr[2]=1 arr[3]=10 9-1 = 8 10-9 = 1 8 > 1 Yes low = 3 2 3 5 4 arr[4]=10 arr[5]=10 9-10 = -1 10-9 = 1 -1 > 1 No high = 4 3 3 4 3 arr[3]=10 arr[4]=10 -1 1 No high = 3 4 3 3 — — — — — exit —

return arr[3:4] = [10]. Sahi.

Iterations 2 aur 3 mein x - arr[mid] negative tha (-1), aur comparison bilkul sahi kaam kiya bina abs() ke. Yeh line 5 ke design ka proof hai.

Dry run — Tarika A — arr = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5], k = 4, x = 3

Line 10: bisect_left([1,2,3,4,5], 3) = 2 (index of 3). right = 2, left = 1.

Iter left right Guards x - arr[left] arr[right] - x <= ? Action 1 1 2 ok 3 - arr[1] = 3-2 = 1 arr[2] - 3 = 0 1 <= 0 No right = 3 2 1 3 ok 1 arr[3]-3 = 1 1 <= 1 Yes left = 0 3 0 3 ok 3 - arr[0] = 2 1 2 <= 1 No right = 4 4 0 4 ok 2 arr[4]-3 = 2 2 <= 2 Yes left = -1

return arr[-1+1 : 4] = arr[0:4] = [1,2,3,4]. Sahi.

Iterations 2 aur 4 mein ties the, aur <= ki wajah se dono baar left liya gaya — jo chhote numbers ko prefer karta hai. Iteration 4 ne 1 liya 5 ke bajaye — exactly expected.

Complexity

Approach Time Space Notes Heap of size k O(n log k + k log k) O(k) Sorted-ness ignore karta hai Two pointers O(log n + k) O(1) Intuitive Binary search on window O(log n) O(1) Sabse fast, output slicing O(k)

Note: teenon mein output banane ki O(k) cost hai. Toh "binary search on window" ki asli cost O(log n + k) hai — lekin comparison ka kaam O(log n) hai, jo two-pointers ke O(k) se better hai jab k bada ho.

Edge cases

Case arr k x Output Kyun k == len(arr) [1,2,3] 3 2 [1,2,3] high = 0, loop nahi chalta x array se chhota [1,2,3] 2 -5 [1,2] Left edge par x array se bada [1,2,3] 2 100 [2,3] Right edge par x exactly present [1,2,3] 1 2 [2] All same [5,5,5] 2 5 [5,5] k = 1 [1,5,10] 1 6 [5] |6-5|=1 < |10-6|=4 Tie at boundary [1,3] 1 2 [1] Tie → smaller Duplicates [1,1,2,2] 2 2 [2,2] k > len(arr) [1,2] 5 1 high negative Guard chahiye

Aakhri row important hai — high = len(arr) - k negative ho jaata aur while low < high turant False hoti, phir arr[0:5] = [1,2] return hota. Sanyog se reasonable answer hai, lekin explicitly guard karna better hai.

Variations

  • Find K Closest Elements (LeetCode 658) — exactly yeh problem.
  • Unsorted array — heap version (Problem 12.3 jaisa), O(n log k).
  • K closest to a target in a BST (272) — inorder traversal plus sliding window, ya do stacks.
  • Ties par bada prefer karo — comparisons flip karo (>= ki jagah > etc.).
  • K closest strings by edit distance — heap, kyunki koi sorted structure nahi.
  • K closest in a stream — heap, kyunki binary search ke liye random access chahiye.

Interview answer: "The array is sorted, and that gives me a key structural fact: the k closest elements are always a contiguous window. If two elements are in the answer, everything between them is at least as close to x as one of them, so it must be in the answer too.

So the problem reduces to finding the best starting index for a window of size k, and I can binary search on that index. The candidate range for the start is zero through length minus k.

The comparison at each step is: for a candidate start mid, is it better to keep the window where it is or shift it one step right? Shifting drops arr at mid and picks up arr at mid plus k. So I compare x minus arr-at-mid against arr-at-mid-plus-k minus x, and shift right if the incoming element is closer.

Two nice details there. I don't need absolute values — because the array is sorted, if x is below the window then the first expression is negative and the second positive, and if x is above the window it's the reverse, so the signed comparison already gives the right answer in every case. And the comparison is strictly greater-than, so on a tie I keep the window where it is, which prefers the smaller element — exactly the tie-breaking rule the problem specifies. Flipping that to greater-or-equal produces the wrong answer on the tied example.

That's O(log n) for the search plus O(k) to slice the result, and O(1) extra space. And because the array is sorted, the output is already in ascending order — no extra sort.

I'd also mention two alternatives. Two pointers expanding outward from x's insertion point is more intuitive, at O(log n plus k). And a max-heap of size k works on an unsorted array at O(n log k) — but here it would ignore the sortedness entirely and also needs awkward double-negation to get the tie-breaking right, so it's the wrong tool for this input."

Ek line mein poore pattern ka summary:

Heap ka size hamesha k rakho, n nahi — isse time O(n log k) aur space O(k) ho jaata hai. Heap ki direction ulti hoti hai: K largest ke liye min-heap, K smallest ke liye max-heap — kyunki aap hamesha sabse kamzor candidate ko evict karna chahte ho aur woh top par hona chahiye. Aur agar values ka range bounded hai (jaise frequencies, jo n se zyada nahi ho sakti), toh bucket sort heap se bhi better hai — O(n), koi comparison nahi.

Aur ek decision table jo har top-K problem par lagti hai:

Situation Best approach k chhota, n bada, streaming Heap of size k — O(n log k), O(k) space Static array, sirf kth value chahiye Quickselect — O(n) average Values ka range bounded (frequencies) Bucket sort — O(n) Input already sorted Binary search plus window — O(log n) k n ke barabar Sort — kuch bhi fancy karna waste hai

docs.title: 13. K Way Merge
docs.text: Note: yahan se aage ke pattern sections condensed hain — recognition signals, template, do fully-solved problems (poore line-by-line explanation aur dry run ke saath), aur practice list. Structure wahi hai jo Sections 1-12 mein tha, bas har section mein 5-7 ki jagah 2 problems solved hain. Baaki problems practice list mein hain.

docs.title: Recognition signals
docs.text:
• "K sorted lists/arrays" merge karni hon.
  • "Kth smallest in M sorted lists", "smallest range covering all lists".
  • "merge K sorted linked lists".
  • Sorted matrix ho aur uske rows/columns sorted hon.
  • Input already sorted tukdon mein ho — poora sort karna waste hoga.

docs.title: Core idea
docs.text:
k sorted lists hain. Kisi bhi waqt, global minimum hamesha kisi list ke head par hota hai — kyunki har list andar se sorted hai.

Toh: ek min-heap mein har list ka current head rakho (size at most k). Minimum pop karo, aur usi list se agla element push karo. Repeat.

Yeh Problem 4.6 (Employee Free Time) mein already dikh chuka hai — wahan bhi yehi refill trick tha.

Kyun better hai: saare n elements ko ek saath heap mein daalna O(n log n) hota. Sirf k heads rakhne se O(n log k) — aur k << n par yeh bada farq hai.

docs.title: Template
docs.text:
import heapq

def merge_k_sorted(lists):
    heap = []                                  # (value, list_index, element_index)
    for i, lst in enumerate(lists):            # har list ka PEHLA element
        if lst:                                # khaali list guard
            heapq.heappush(heap, (lst[0], i, 0))
    result = []
    while heap:
        value, list_idx, elem_idx = heapq.heappop(heap)   # global minimum
        result.append(value)
        next_idx = elem_idx + 1                # USI list ka agla element
        if next_idx < len(lists[list_idx]):    # bacha hai?
            heapq.heappush(heap, (lists[list_idx][next_idx], list_idx, next_idx))
    return result

Tuple mein list_index zaroori hai — do kaam karta hai: (a) pata chalta hai ki refill kahan se karna hai, aur (b) tie-breaking deta hai jab values barabar hon, taaki Python kabhi non-comparable objects compare na kare.

docs.title: Problem 13.1 — Merge K Sorted Lists
docs.text:
Problem statement

k sorted linked lists di hain. Unhe ek sorted list mein merge karo.

Input:  [1->4->5, 1->3->4, 2->6]
Output: 1->1->2->3->4->4->5->6

Pehla instinct — brute force

Saari values ek array mein nikaalo, sort karo, nayi list banao.

def merge_brute(lists):
    values = []                                   # 1: saari values
    for head in lists:                            # 2: har list
        node = head                               # 3
        while node:                               # 4: poori list traverse
            values.append(node.val)               # 5
            node = node.next                      # 6
    values.sort()                                 # 7: O(n log n) -- SORTEDNESS waste
    dummy = ListNode(0)                           # 8: naya list banane ke liye
    tail = dummy                                  # 9
    for v in values:                              # 10
        tail.next = ListNode(v)                   # 11: naya node
        tail = tail.next                          # 12
    return dummy.next                             # 13

Line by line

1-6. Saari values collect. O(n). 7. values.sort() — O(n log n). Yahin waste hai — input already sorted tukdon mein tha aur humne woh information phenk di. 8-9. Dummy node (Section 6 wali technique) — head ka special case hataata hai. 10-12. Nayi list banao. Note: naye nodes bana rahe hain, purane reuse nahi kar rahe — O(n) extra memory. 13. Return.

Complexity: Time O(n log n), Space O(n).

Isme problem kya hai

O(n log n) jab O(n log k) possible hai. Aur k = 2 par yeh O(n log n) vs O(n) ka farq hai — bahut bada.

The insight

Har list ka head hi uska minimum hai. Toh global minimum in k heads mein se ek hai. Ek min-heap of size k rakho, minimum pop karo, aur usi list ka agla node push karo.

Optimal solution

import heapq

def merge_k_lists(lists):
    heap = []                                     # 1: min-heap of (value, list_index, node)
    for i, head in enumerate(lists):              # 2: har list ka pehla node
        if head is not None:                      # 3: khaali list skip
            heapq.heappush(heap, (head.val, i, head))   # 4: `i` TIE-BREAKER hai

    dummy = ListNode(0)                           # 5: output list ka fake head
    tail = dummy                                  # 6

    while heap:                                   # 7: jab tak koi node bacha hai
        value, i, node = heapq.heappop(heap)      # 8: GLOBAL minimum
        tail.next = node                          # 9: node ko REUSE karo, naya mat banao
        tail = node                               # 10
        if node.next is not None:                 # 11: usi list mein aur nodes hain?
            heapq.heappush(heap, (node.next.val, i, node.next))   # 12: REFILL

    tail.next = None                              # 13: aakhri node terminate karo
    return dummy.next                             # 14

Line by line — kyun aise likha hai

  1. heap = []. 2-4. Sirf k heads daale, saare n nodes nahi. Yehi O(n log k) ka source hai. Line 3: if head is not None — khaali lists ([None, 1->2]) crash se bachati hai. Line 4: tuple mein i (list index) hai aur woh zaroori hai. Agar do nodes ki val same ho toh Python dusre element par compare karega — i ek integer hai toh safe. Bina i ke Python ListNode objects compare karta aur TypeError deta, kyunki ListNode mein __lt__ nahi hai. Yeh sabse common crash hai is problem mein. 5-6. Dummy node. 9-10. tail.next = node — purane nodes reuse kar rahe hain. Brute force naye banata tha (O(n) extra memory). Yeh in-place relinking hai. 11-12. Refill — usi list ka agla node. Heap ka size at most k rehta hai.
  2. tail.next = None — zaroori hai. Aakhri node ka next abhi bhi apni original list ke agle node ko point kar raha ho sakta hai (jo already output mein aa chuka hai) — cycle ban jaata.
  3. return dummy.next.

Dry run — [1->4->5, 1->3->4, 2->6] (lists ko A, B, C kehte hain)

Initial heap: [(1, 0, A1), (1, 1, B1), (2, 2, C1)]. Top = (1, 0, A1) (tie par i=0 < i=1).

Iter Pop Output so far Refill push Heap (values) 1 (1,0,A1) 1 (4,0,A4) {(1,1),(2,2),(4,0)} 2 (1,1,B1) 1,1 (3,1,B3) {(2,2),(3,1),(4,0)} 3 (2,2,C1) 1,1,2 (6,2,C6) {(3,1),(4,0),(6,2)} 4 (3,1,B3) 1,1,2,3 (4,1,B4) {(4,0),(4,1),(6,2)} 5 (4,0,A4) ...,4 (5,0,A5) {(4,1),(5,0),(6,2)} 6 (4,1,B4) ...,4,4 none (B khatam) {(5,0),(6,2)} 7 (5,0,A5) ...,5 none {(6,2)} 8 (6,2,C6) ...,6 none {}

Output: 1->1->2->3->4->4->5->6. Sahi.

Iterations 1-2 mein tie tha (val = 1 dono). Tuple ke i par compare hua (0 < 1), toh list A wala pehle aaya. Deterministic aur crash-free — yeh line 4 ka poora justification hai.

Iteration 5-6 mein bhi tie (val = 4), phir i par resolve hua.

Complexity

  • Time: O(n log k). n total nodes, har ek ek baar push aur ek baar pop hota hai, aur heap ka size at most k hai.
  • Space: O(k) heap ke liye. Output nodes reuse hote hain toh koi extra node memory nahi.

Edge cases

Case Input Output Kyun Empty input [] None Heap khaali All lists empty [None, None] None Line 3 guard One list [1->2] 1->2 Trivial Some empty [None, 1->2] 1->2 Line 3 Single node each [1, 2, 3] 1->2->3 All duplicates [1, 1, 1] 1->1->1 i tie-breaker Very large k k = 10^4 — O(n log k) fine

Variations

  • Divide and conquer merge — lists ko pairs mein merge karte jao (merge sort ka merge step). Same O(n log k), O(1) space (recursion O(log k)). Yeh alternative bolna acha hai.
  • Merge K sorted arrays — same heap, indices track karo.
  • Kth smallest in K sorted lists — Problem 13.2.
  • Smallest range covering elements from K lists (LeetCode 632) — heap plus running max tracking.

Interview answer: "Flattening everything and sorting is O(n log n), which throws away the fact that each list is already sorted. The heap version keeps that: at any moment, the global minimum has to be at the head of one of the k lists, so I only need k candidates in the heap at a time, not n. Pop the minimum, append it, then refill from that same list. That's O(n log k).

One Python detail that causes a real crash: the heap entries are tuples, and when two values tie, Python falls through to comparing the next element. If that's a ListNode it raises a TypeError, because ListNode has no ordering. So I put the list index in between as a tiebreaker — it's an integer, always comparable, and it also tells me which list to refill from.

I relink the existing nodes rather than allocating new ones, and I null the final tail — otherwise the last node still points into its original list and I get a cycle.

O(n log k) time, O(k) space. An alternative with the same complexity is divide and conquer: merge lists pairwise, halving the count each round. That uses O(log k) stack instead of a heap, and is often slightly faster in practice."

docs.title: Problem 13.2 — Kth Smallest Element In A Sorted Matrix
docs.text:
Problem statement

Ek n x n matrix di hai jiski har row aur har column sorted hai. Kth smallest element lauta do.

Input:  matrix = [[1,  5,  9],
                  [10, 11, 13],
                  [12, 13, 15]], k = 8
Output: 13
        Sorted order: 1, 5, 9, 10, 11, 12, 13, 13, 15 -> 8th = 13

Pehla instinct — brute force

Sab flatten karo, sort karo, index k-1.

def kth_smallest_brute(matrix, k):
    flat = [x for row in matrix for x in row]     # 1: nested comprehension
    flat.sort()                                   # 2: O(n^2 log n)
    return flat[k - 1]                            # 3: 1-indexed -> 0-indexed

Line by line

  1. [x for row in matrix for x in row] — nested comprehension; outer loop pehle likhte hain.
  2. O(n^2 log n^2) = O(n^2 log n) — sortedness waste.
  3. k - 1.

Complexity: Time O(n^2 log n), Space O(n^2).

The insight — do bilkul alag approaches

Approach A — k-way merge. Har row ek sorted list hai. Heap mein har row ka pehla element daalo, k baar pop karo. O(k log n).

Approach B — binary search on the value. Matrix ke min (matrix[0][0]) aur max (matrix[n-1][n-1]) ke beech binary search karo. Har candidate mid ke liye count karo ki kitne elements <= mid hain. Agar count >= k hai toh answer mid ya usse chhota. O(n log(max - min)).

Approach B ka counting step staircase walk se O(n) mein hota hai — bottom-left corner se shuru karo aur monotonically chalo.

Kaunsa better: agar k chhota hai toh A. Agar k bada hai (~n^2) toh B, kyunki B k par depend nahi karta.

Optimal solution — k-way merge

import heapq

def kth_smallest_heap(matrix, k):
    n = len(matrix)                               # 1
    heap = [(matrix[r][0], r, 0) for r in range(min(k, n))]   # 2: har row ka pehla; min(k,n) rows kaafi
    heapq.heapify(heap)                           # 3: O(min(k,n))

    for _ in range(k - 1):                        # 4: k-1 baar pop, kth baar peek
        value, r, c = heapq.heappop(heap)         # 5
        if c + 1 < n:                             # 6: usi ROW mein aur elements hain?
            heapq.heappush(heap, (matrix[r][c + 1], r, c + 1))   # 7: REFILL

    return heap[0][0]                             # 8: kth smallest = ab ka top

Line by line — kyun aise likha hai

  1. n = len(matrix).
  2. min(k, n) rows — optimisation. Agar k = 3 aur n = 1000 hai toh sirf pehli 3 rows relevant hain (kyunki row i ka pehla element i elements se bada hai jo uske upar ki rows mein hain... approximately). Chhota optimisation, correctness ke liye zaroori nahi. Tuple (value, row, col) — row aur col refill ke liye aur tie-breaking ke liye.
  3. heapify O(min(k,n)).
  4. for _ in range(k - 1): — k - 1 pops. Uske baad heap ka top hi kth smallest hai (line 8 peek karta hai). range(k) likhne se k+1th milta — off-by-one. 5-7. Pop aur usi row se refill. Line 6: c + 1 < n — row ke andar bounds.
  5. return heap[0][0] — peek, pop nahi.

Optimal solution — binary search on value

def kth_smallest_binary(matrix, k):
    n = len(matrix)                               # 9

    def count_less_equal(target):                 # 10: kitne elements <= target
        count = 0                                 # 11
        r, c = n - 1, 0                           # 12: BOTTOM-LEFT corner se shuru
        while r >= 0 and c < n:                   # 13: staircase walk
            if matrix[r][c] <= target:            # 14: yeh aur uske UPAR ki poori column
                count += r + 1                    # 15: r+1 elements is column mein <= target
                c += 1                            # 16: agli column
            else:                                 # 17: yeh bada hai
                r -= 1                            # 18: upar jao (chhote elements)
        return count                              # 19

    low, high = matrix[0][0], matrix[n - 1][n - 1]   # 20: value range
    while low < high:                             # 21: Convention B
        mid = low + (high - low) // 2             # 22
        if count_less_equal(mid) >= k:            # 23: kth element mid ya usse chhota
            high = mid                            # 24
        else:                                     # 25
            low = mid + 1                         # 26
    return low                                    # 27

Line by line — kyun aise likha hai

10-19. Counting via staircase walk — yeh sabse clever hissa hai. Line 12: bottom-left corner se shuru. Kyun? Kyunki wahan se do directions monotonic hain — upar jaane par values ghatti hain, daaye jaane par badhti hain. Toh har step par ek clear decision hai. Line 14-16: agar matrix[r][c] <= target toh is column ke r+1 elements (index 0 se r tak) sab <= target hain (column sorted hai). Count mein add karo aur agli column par jao. Line 17-18: agar bada hai toh upar jao. Har step mein ya c badhta hai ya r ghatta hai, toh at most 2n steps — O(n). 20. low, high = matrix ka min aur max. matrix[0][0] hi minimum hai kyunki rows aur columns dono sorted hain. 21-26. Binary search on the answer (Section 11 wala pattern). Line 23: count_less_equal(mid) >= k — agar mid tak k ya zyada elements hain toh kth element mid ya usse chhota hai. 27. return low — aur yeh guaranteed matrix mein exist karta hai. Kyun? Kyunki loop low ko sirf tab badhata hai jab count(low) < k, aur high ko tab set karta hai jab count(high) >= k. Convergence par low woh sabse chhoti value hai jiske liye count >= k — aur woh matrix ka ek actual element hona chahiye (warna count waha jump nahi karta).

Dry run — binary search — matrix = [[1,5,9],[10,11,13],[12,13,15]], k = 8 (expected 13)

low = 1, high = 15.

Iter low high mid count_less_equal(mid) >= 8? Action 1 1 15 8 1, 5 → 2 No low = 9 2 9 15 12 1,5,9,10,11,12 → 6 No low = 13 3 13 15 14 1,5,9,10,11,12,13,13 → 8 Yes high = 14 4 13 14 13 8 Yes high = 13 5 13 13 — — exit —

return 13. Sahi.

count_less_equal(13) ka staircase trace: r=2, c=0. - matrix[2][0] = 12 <= 13 → count += 3 (column 0 ke teenon), c = 1. count = 3. - matrix[2][1] = 13 <= 13 → count += 3, c = 2. count = 6. - matrix[2][2] = 15 > 13 → r = 1. - matrix[1][2] = 13 <= 13 → count += 2, c = 3. count = 8. - c = 3 >= n → exit. count = 8. Sahi.

Complexity

Approach Time Space Sort all O(n^2 log n) O(n^2) Heap (k-way merge) O(k log n) O(n) Binary search on value O(n log(max-min)) O(1)

Binary search version k par bilkul depend nahi karta — yeh uska sabse bada fayda hai. k = n^2 par heap version O(n^2 log n) ho jaata hai; binary search O(n log(range)) hi rehta hai.

Edge cases

Case Input k Output Kyun k = 1 any 1 matrix[0][0] Minimum k = n^2 any n*n matrix[n-1][n-1] Maximum 1x1 matrix [[5]] 1 5 All same [[3,3],[3,3]] 3 3 low == high turant Duplicates upar wala example 7 ya 8 13 dono baar Duplicates alag ginte hain Negative values [[-5,-1],[0,3]] 2 -1

Variations

  • Kth Smallest Element in a Sorted Matrix (LeetCode 378) — exactly yeh.
  • Find K Pairs with Smallest Sums (373) — same heap structure, pairs par.
  • Kth Smallest in M Sorted Lists — same heap, rows ki jagah lists.
  • Search a 2D Matrix II (240) — same staircase walk, counting ki jagah searching.
  • Kth smallest in a multiplication table (668) — binary search on value plus counting formula.

Interview answer: "Two solutions, and which one wins depends on k.

The k-way merge treats each row as a sorted list: put every row's first element into a min-heap, then pop k minus one times, refilling from the same row each pop. The kth smallest is then the heap's top. That's O(k log n).

The binary search solution searches on the value rather than the position. The candidate range is matrix zero-zero to the bottom-right corner, and for each candidate I count how many elements are at most that value. If the count reaches k, the answer is at or below the candidate.

The counting is the elegant part: I start at the bottom-left corner and walk a staircase. From there, moving up decreases values and moving right increases them, so at each step there's an unambiguous decision. If the current cell is at most the target, then the entire column above it is too, so I add row-index plus one and move right; otherwise I move up. Each step either moves right or up, so it's O(n), not O(n squared).

The binary search version doesn't depend on k at all — O(n log of the value range) with O(1) space. So for k near n squared it's much better, while the heap wins when k is small.

Flattening and sorting is O(n squared log n) and discards the fact that every row and column is already sorted."

docs.title: Recognition signals
docs.text:
• "all combinations / permutations / arrangements" jinme constraints hon.
  • "place N queens", "solve the sudoku", "word search in a grid", "partition into palindromes".
  • "is there a valid X" — aur validity check karne ke liye poora construct karna pade.
  • Constraints mein n chhota ho (n <= 20 type) aur output exponential ho.
  • Problem "generate karo" bole aur beech mein hi galat raaste pata chal sakte hon — tab pruning se bachat hoti hai.

docs.title: Core idea — choose, explore, un-choose
docs.text:
Section 10 mein yeh skeleton aa chuka hai. Backtracking = DFS on the space of partial solutions, plus pruning.

def backtrack(state):
    if is_solution(state):          # poora answer ban gaya
        record(copy_of(state))      # COPY -- reference nahi
        return
    for choice in candidates(state):
        if not is_valid(choice, state):   # PRUNING -- yahin asli bachat hai
            continue
        make(choice, state)         # CHOOSE
        backtrack(state)            # EXPLORE
        undo(choice, state)         # UN-CHOOSE

Backtracking aur brute force ka farq sirf ek line hai — is_valid wala check. Brute force poora candidate banata hai phir check karta hai; backtracking banate waqt check karta hai aur galat subtree ko poora kaat deta hai.

Pruning ka asli asar: N-Queens n = 8 par brute force 64 choose 8 ≈ 4 billion placements try karta hai; backtracking ~2000 nodes visit karta hai. Ek million guna farq.

docs.title: Problem 14.1 — N-Queens
docs.text:
Problem statement

n x n chessboard par n queens rakho taaki koi do ek dusre ko attack na karein (same row, column, ya diagonal mein na hon). Saare valid arrangements lauta do.

Input:  n = 4
Output: [[".Q..", "...Q", "Q...", "..Q."],
         ["..Q.", "Q...", "...Q", ".Q.."]]
        (2 solutions)

Input:  n = 1  ->  [["Q"]]
Input:  n = 2 ya 3  ->  []  (koi solution nahi)

Pehla instinct — brute force

Saari C(n^2, n) placements try karo aur har ek validate karo.

from itertools import combinations

def n_queens_brute(n):
    cells = [(r, c) for r in range(n) for c in range(n)]   # 1: saare n^2 cells
    results = []                                  # 2
    for placement in combinations(cells, n):      # 3: n cells choose karo
        if is_valid_placement(placement):         # 4: validate
            results.append(placement)             # 5
    return results                                # 6


def is_valid_placement(queens):
    for i in range(len(queens)):                  # 7: har PAIR check
        for j in range(i + 1, len(queens)):
            r1, c1 = queens[i]                    # 8
            r2, c2 = queens[j]
            if r1 == r2 or c1 == c2:              # 9: same row ya column
                return False
            if abs(r1 - r2) == abs(c1 - c2):      # 10: same DIAGONAL
                return False
    return True                                   # 11

Line by line

  1. combinations(cells, n) — C(n^2, n) placements. n = 8 par C(64, 8) ≈ 4.4 * 10^9. Impossible.
  2. Same row ya column.
  3. abs(r1 - r2) == abs(c1 - c2) — diagonal test. Do cells ek diagonal par hain agar row-difference aur column-difference ki magnitude same ho. Yeh formula yaad rakhna hai.

Complexity: Time O(C(n^2, n) * n^2) — astronomically bad.

The insight

Do observations jo search space ko cut karti hain:

Observation 1 — har row mein exactly ek queen. n queens aur n rows, aur ek row mein do queens nahi ho sakti. Toh "kaunse n cells" ki jagah sawaal ban jaata hai "har row mein queen kaunse column par?" — search space C(n^2, n) se n^n ho gaya.

Observation 2 — pruning. Row-by-row jao, aur jaise hi ek queen conflict kare, us branch ko turant chhod do. Isse n^n practically bahut chhota ho jaata hai.

Aur conflict check O(1) mein kaise? Teen sets rakho: - used_cols — kaunse columns occupied hain. - used_diag1 — row - col constant hota hai ek \ diagonal par. - used_diag2 — row + col constant hota hai ek / diagonal par.

Yeh do formulas hi is problem ka core hain, aur inhe derive karke bolna interview mein bahut strong hai.

Optimal solution

def solve_n_queens(n):
    results = []                                  # 1: saare valid boards
    queen_col = [-1] * n                          # 2: queen_col[row] = us row ka column
    used_cols = set()                             # 3: occupied columns
    used_diag1 = set()                            # 4: occupied `\` diagonals (row - col)
    used_diag2 = set()                            # 5: occupied `/` diagonals (row + col)

    def backtrack(row):                           # 6: `row` = kaunsi row fill karni hai
        if row == n:                              # 7: saari rows fill ho gayi -> SOLUTION
            results.append(build_board(queen_col, n))   # 8: snapshot save karo
            return                                # 9

        for col in range(n):                      # 10: is row mein har column try karo
            d1 = row - col                        # 11: `\` diagonal ka id
            d2 = row + col                        # 12: `/` diagonal ka id
            if col in used_cols or d1 in used_diag1 or d2 in used_diag2:   # 13: PRUNE
                continue                          # 14: yeh column conflict karta hai

            queen_col[row] = col                  # 15: CHOOSE
            used_cols.add(col)                    # 16
            used_diag1.add(d1)                    # 17
            used_diag2.add(d2)                    # 18

            backtrack(row + 1)                    # 19: EXPLORE agli row

            used_cols.remove(col)                 # 20: UN-CHOOSE (ulte order mein)
            used_diag1.remove(d1)                 # 21
            used_diag2.remove(d2)                 # 22
            queen_col[row] = -1                   # 23: optional, clarity ke liye

    backtrack(0)                                  # 24
    return results                                # 25


def build_board(queen_col, n):
    board = []                                    # 26
    for col in queen_col:                         # 27: har row ka queen column
        row_str = "." * col + "Q" + "." * (n - col - 1)   # 28: string banao
        board.append(row_str)                     # 29
    return board                                  # 30

Line by line — kyun aise likha hai

  1. queen_col = [-1] * n — row-indexed. queen_col[3] = 1 matlab row 3 mein queen column 1 par hai. Yeh representation hi Observation 1 ko encode karti hai — har row mein exactly ek entry hai, toh "do queens ek row mein" wala case structurally impossible ho gaya. 3-5. Teen sets. Har ek O(1) lookup deta hai.
  2. def backtrack(row): — row hi state ka poora index hai. Baaki state sets aur queen_col mein hai. 7-9. Base case: row == n matlab saari rows mein queens rakh di. Line 8: build_board(...) — naya list banata hai, toh yeh already ek copy hai. queen_col[:] alag se copy karne ki zaroorat nahi.
  3. for col in range(n): — is row ke saare columns try karo.
  4. d1 = row - col — \ diagonal (top-left se bottom-right). Proof: agar (r1, c1) aur (r2, c2) ek \ diagonal par hain toh r1 - c1 == r2 - c2. Check: (0,0) aur (1,1) → 0 - 0 = 0 aur 1 - 1 = 0. Same. Sahi. d1 negative ho sakta hai (row=0, col=3 → -3) — sets negative keys handle karte hain, koi problem nahi. Agar array use karte toh offset add karna padta.
  5. d2 = row + col — / diagonal (top-right se bottom-left). Check: (0,3) aur (1,2) → 0+3 = 3 aur 1+2 = 3. Same. Sahi. 13-14. PRUNING — yeh line hi poori efficiency hai. Teen O(1) set lookups. Agar koi bhi conflict kare toh poora subtree skip ho jaata hai — us column se aage ki n-row-1 rows kabhi explore nahi hoti. 15-18. CHOOSE — chaar cheezein update hoti hain.
  6. EXPLORE. 20-23. UN-CHOOSE — chaaron ko undo karo. Order ulta rakha (used_cols last added tha... actually order yahan matter nahi karta kyunki teenon independent sets hain). Lekin symmetric likhna habit banani chahiye. remove use kiya, discard nahi — remove missing key par KeyError deta, jo ek bug detector hai. Agar kabhi remove fail ho toh matlab add/remove ka pairing toot gaya. Line 23: queen_col[row] = -1 — strictly zaroori nahi (kyunki line 15 use overwrite kar degi), lekin backtracking invariant maintain karta hai. 24-25. 26-30. build_board — queen_col ko strings mein badalta hai. Line 28: "." * col + "Q" + "." * (n - col - 1) — total length col + 1 + n - col - 1 = n. Sahi.

Dry run — n = 4

Notation: har row par kaunsa column try hua.

Step row col tried d1 = r-c d2 = r+c Conflict? Action 1 0 0 0 0 No (sets khaali) place → row 1 2 1 0 1 1 col 0 used skip 3 1 1 0 2 d1=0 used skip 4 1 2 -1 3 No place → row 2 5 2 0 2 2 col 0 used skip 6 2 1 1 3 d2=3 used skip 7 2 2 0 4 col 2 used skip 8 2 3 -1 5 d1=-1 used skip 9 2 — — — saare columns fail backtrack to row 1 10 1 3 -2 4 No place → row 2 11 2 1 1 3 No place → row 3 12 3 0..3 — — sab conflict backtrack ... (search continues)

Eventually do solutions milte hain: [1, 3, 0, 2] aur [2, 0, 3, 1] (row-wise columns).

Step 9 sabse important hai — row 2 par saare 4 columns conflict kar gaye, toh algorithm turant row 1 par wapas gaya aur agla column try kiya. Brute force yahan poora board bhar kar phir check karta.

Solution [1, 3, 0, 2] ko verify karte hain: - Queens: (0,1), (1,3), (2,0), (3,2). - Columns: 1, 3, 0, 2 — sab distinct. ✓ - d1 = r - c: -1, -2, 2, 1 — sab distinct. ✓ - d2 = r + c: 1, 4, 2, 5 — sab distinct. ✓

Board: 

.Q..
...Q
Q...
..Q.
Match.

Complexity

  • Time: O(n!) upper bound, practically bahut kam pruning ki wajah se. Row 0 mein n choices, row 1 mein at most n-1 (ek column already used), row 2 mein at most n-2, ... → n!. Pruning se actual node count bahut kam hai: n = 8 par ~2057 nodes visit hote hain, 8! = 40320 ke bajaye.
  • Space: O(n) — teen sets (at most n entries each), queen_col, aur recursion depth n. Plus output.

Edge cases

Case n Output Kyun n = 1 1 [["Q"]] Trivial n = 2 2 [] Koi arrangement possible nahi n = 3 3 [] Bhi impossible n = 4 4 2 solutions Upar n = 8 8 92 solutions Classic n = 0 0 [[]] Base case turant — clarify karo n = 12 12 14,200 solutions Slow lekin doable

Variations

  • N-Queens II (LeetCode 52) — sirf count chahiye, boards nahi. build_board hata do, counter rakho. Bahut faster kyunki string building nahi hoti.
  • Bitmask optimisation — teen sets ki jagah teen integers, aur bit operations. Bahut faster, lekin padhna mushkil. Interview mein mention karna acha hai.
  • Sudoku Solver (37) — same structure, 3x3 box constraint bhi.
  • Rat in a maze / word search — grid par backtracking.
  • Only one solution chahiye — pehla milte hi True return karke propagate karo.

Interview answer: "Brute force would try every way to choose n cells from n squared, which for an eight-by-eight board is over four billion placements. Two observations collapse that.

First, with n queens and n rows, every row holds exactly one queen. So instead of choosing cells, I choose a column for each row — and the 'two queens in a row' conflict becomes structurally impossible rather than something I check.

Second, I check conflicts as I place, not at the end. Three sets give O(1) checks: used columns, and used diagonals. The diagonal encoding is the piece worth deriving out loud: two cells share a top-left-to-bottom-right diagonal exactly when row minus column is equal, and a top-right-to-bottom-left diagonal exactly when row plus column is equal. So I key the two diagonal sets on those two expressions.

Then it's the standard choose-explore-unchoose: pick a column, add to all three sets, recurse to the next row, then remove all three. I use set.remove rather than discard, because if the add and remove ever get out of sync it raises instead of silently corrupting state.

The pruning is where the win is. As soon as a partial placement conflicts, the entire subtree below it — all the remaining rows — is skipped. For n equals eight that takes the search from forty thousand permutations down to roughly two thousand visited nodes.

Upper bound O(n factorial) time and O(n) extra space beyond the output. If only the count were needed I'd drop the board construction entirely, which is a big constant-factor saving, and I'd mention that the three sets can be replaced with three integers and bit operations for a further speedup at the cost of readability."

docs.title: Problem 14.2 — Word Search In A Grid
docs.text:
Problem statement

Ek m x n grid of characters aur ek word diya hai. Bataao ki word grid mein exist karta hai ya nahi. Word adjacent cells (horizontally ya vertically) se banta hai, aur ek cell do baar use nahi ho sakta.

Input:  board = [["A","B","C","E"],
                 ["S","F","C","S"],
                 ["A","D","E","E"]], word = "ABCCED"
Output: True    (A(0,0) -> B(0,1) -> C(0,2) -> C(1,2) -> E(2,2) -> D(2,1))

Input:  same board, word = "SEE"
Output: True

Input:  same board, word = "ABCB"
Output: False   ('B' dobara use nahi ho sakta)

Pehla instinct — brute force

Har cell se shuru karke saare possible paths generate karo aur compare karo. Yeh actually backtracking hi hai — bina pruning ke.

The insight

Har cell se ek DFS shuru karo jo word ko character by character match karta jaaye. Do pruning:

  1. Mismatch par turant return — agar current cell word[index] se match nahi karta toh us raaste par aage jaane ka koi matlab nahi. Yeh Problem 8.4 (Path With Given Sequence) wali hi baat hai.
  2. Visited tracking — cell dobara use na ho.

Aur visited tracking ka ek elegant trick hai: alag visited set banane ki jagah, cell ko temporarily ek sentinel character (#) se replace kar do, aur wapas aate waqt restore kar do. O(1) extra space (grid ke alawa).

Optimal solution

def word_exists(board, word):
    if not board or not board[0] or not word:     # 1: guards
        return False                              # 2
    rows, cols = len(board), len(board[0])        # 3

    def dfs(r, c, index):                         # 4: (r,c) se word[index:] match karna hai
        if index == len(word):                    # 5: poora word match ho gaya
            return True                           # 6

        if r < 0 or r >= rows or c < 0 or c >= cols:   # 7: BOUNDS check
            return False                          # 8
        if board[r][c] != word[index]:            # 9: MISMATCH -- prune
            return False                          # 10

        original = board[r][c]                    # 11: bacha lo (restore ke liye)
        board[r][c] = "#"                         # 12: CHOOSE -- visited mark
                                                  #     "#" word mein kabhi nahi hoga
        found = (dfs(r + 1, c, index + 1)         # 13: EXPLORE -- chaaron directions
                 or dfs(r - 1, c, index + 1)      # 14: `or` SHORT-CIRCUITS
                 or dfs(r, c + 1, index + 1)      # 15
                 or dfs(r, c - 1, index + 1))     # 16

        board[r][c] = original                    # 17: UN-CHOOSE -- restore
        return found                              # 18

    for r in range(rows):                         # 19: HAR cell se try karo
        for c in range(cols):                     # 20
            if dfs(r, c, 0):                      # 21: index 0 se shuru
                return True                       # 22: mil gaya
    return False                                  # 23

Line by line — kyun aise likha hai

1-2. Guards. not board[0] khaali rows handle karta hai. 3. rows, cols. 4. def dfs(r, c, index): — teen state variables. index word mein position hai. 5-6. Base case: index == len(word) matlab poora word match ho gaya. Yeh check bounds check se PEHLE hai — deliberate. Agar word "AB" hai aur hum (0,1) par B match karke dfs(0, 2, 2) call karein, toh index == 2 == len(word) pehle check hoti hai aur True milta hai — chahe (0,2) grid se bahar ho. Order badalne se sahi answers reject ho jaate. 7-8. Bounds check. Chaar comparisons. 9-10. Mismatch — turant return. Yehi poora pruning hai. Aur yeh visited check bhi hai: agar cell "#" hai (already visited) toh woh kabhi word[index] se match nahi karega (word mein # nahi hai), toh automatically reject ho jaata hai. Ek check, do kaam. 11-12. Visited marking via in-place mutation. Line 11: original bachao. Line 12: "#" sentinel. Assumption: word mein # nahi hai. Agar ho sakta hai toh alag visited set chahiye. Clarify karo. 13-16. Chaaron directions. or short-circuits — pehla True milte hi baaki teen calls hoti hi nahi. 17. Restore — yeh line hataane par sab toot jaata hai. Grid permanently corrupt ho jaata aur baad ki starting cells se search galat answer deta. Aur yeh line 18 se pehle honi chahiye — agar return found pehle likh dete toh restore skip ho jaata. 18. Return. 19-23. Har cell se try karo. Worst case m*n starting points.

Dry run — board = [["A","B","C","E"],["S","F","C","S"],["A","D","E","E"]], word = "SEE" (expected True)

Starting cells scan karte hain. (1,0) = 'S' par pehla match milta hai.

Step Call (r,c) index board[r][c] word[index] Match? Action 1 dfs(1,0,0) (1,0) 0 S S Yes mark #, explore 2 dfs(2,0,1) (2,0) 1 A E No return False 3 dfs(0,0,1) (0,0) 1 A E No return False 4 dfs(1,1,1) (1,1) 1 F E No return False 5 dfs(1,-1,1) — — out of bounds — — return False 6 back in (1,0) — — — — — restore S, return False

(1,0) fail. Scan continue... (1,3) = 'S' par next match.

Step Call (r,c) index board[r][c] word[index] Match? Action 7 dfs(1,3,0) (1,3) 0 S S Yes mark #, explore 8 dfs(2,3,1) (2,3) 1 E E Yes mark #, explore 9 dfs(3,3,2) — — out of bounds — — False 10 dfs(1,3,2) (1,3) 2 # E No False (visited) 11 dfs(2,4,2) — — out of bounds — — False 12 dfs(2,2,2) (2,2) 2 E E Yes mark #, explore 13 dfs(*, *, 3) — 3 — — index == 3 == len return True

True propagate hota hai upar tak. Sahi.

Step 10 sabse important hai — (1,3) already visited tha ("#" set kiya step 7 mein), aur woh mismatch ke roop mein reject ho gaya. Bina alag visited set ke. Yeh line 12 ka poora fayda hai.

Step 13 dekho — index 3 ho gaya jo len("SEE") = 3 ke barabar hai, toh line 5 ne turant True diya bina bounds check kiye. Yeh line 5 ka placement justify karta hai.

Complexity

  • Time: O(m * n * 4^L) jahan L = word ki length. m*n starting cells, aur har path se chaar directions L deep. Practically pruning se bahut kam.
  • Space: O(L) recursion stack. Grid mutation ki wajah se koi extra visited structure nahi. Trade-off: grid temporarily mutate hota hai. Concurrent access ho toh yeh unsafe hai — alag visited set chahiye.

Edge cases

Case Input Output Kyun Empty word word = "" False (guard) Clarify — True bhi defensible Empty board [] False Guard Single cell match [["A"]], "A" True Line 5 base case Word longer than cells [["A"]], "AA" False Cell reuse nahi Word not present — False Saare starts fail Repeated letters "ABCB" False Visited marking Whole board is the word — True Word contains # — Bug Sentinel collision — clarify

Variations

  • Word Search II (LeetCode 212) — bahut se words ek saath; Trie plus backtracking (Section 23).
  • Number of Islands (200) — same grid DFS, backtracking nahi (visited permanent hota hai).
  • Rat in a Maze / path count — same structure, count karo.
  • 8-directional movement — diagonals bhi add karo (8 recursive calls).
  • Alag visited set — grid mutate na karna ho toh.

Interview answer: "This is grid DFS with backtracking. From each cell I try to match the word character by character, and the moment the current cell doesn't match the expected character I return — that pruning is what keeps it tractable, since a wrong first letter kills the whole subtree immediately.

For the 'no cell reused' constraint I use a trick instead of a separate visited set: I temporarily overwrite the cell with a sentinel character that can't appear in the word, then restore it on the way out. That means the mismatch check doubles as the visited check — a visited cell never matches, so one comparison handles both. It's also O(1) extra space beyond the recursion stack.

The restore is not optional; without it the grid stays corrupted and subsequent starting cells give wrong answers. And it has to happen before the return, not after.

One ordering detail: the 'word fully matched' check comes before the bounds check. Otherwise, matching the last character of the word at the edge of the grid would recurse off the board and be rejected before the success check runs.

O(m times n times four-to-the-word-length) worst case, O(word length) space.

Two things I'd confirm: whether the word could contain my sentinel character — if so I'd need a real visited set — and whether the board can be mutated at all, which it can't if anything else reads it concurrently."

docs.title: Recognition signals
docs.text:
• "minimum / maximum / longest / shortest / count the ways" — optimisation ya counting.
  • Problem ko chhote same-shape sub-problems mein toda ja sakta ho.
  • Recursive solution likhne par same sub-problems baar baar aayein (overlapping subproblems).
  • "can you do better than exponential?" — backtracking solution 2^n ho aur n bada ho.
  • Choices ka sequence ho jahan har choice future ko affect kare.
  • Constraints n <= 1000 ya n <= 5000 type hon — yeh O(n^2) DP ka signal hai.

docs.title: DP kab lagta hai — do conditions
docs.text:
1. Optimal substructure — bade problem ka optimal answer chhote problems ke optimal answers se banta hai.
  2. Overlapping subproblems — same sub-problem baar baar compute hota hai.

Agar sirf (1) hai aur (2) nahi, toh woh divide-and-conquer hai (merge sort), DP nahi. Agar (1) nahi hai toh greedy ya backtracking chahiye.

docs.title: DP likhne ka reliable process — yeh order follow karo
docs.text:
Zyadatar log seedha table banane ki koshish karte hain aur phas jaate hain. Yeh order kabhi fail nahi hota:

Step 1 — brute force recursion likho. Bina soche ki efficient hai ya nahi. Sirf yeh decide karo: "har step par kya choices hain, aur base case kya hai?"

Step 2 — memoise karo. Ek dict ya array add karo jo already-computed results cache kare. Yeh top-down DP hai, aur yahin 90 percent kaam ho jaata hai.

Step 3 — bottom-up mein convert karo (optional). Recursion hataakar loops likho. Faster hai (koi call overhead nahi) aur stack overflow se bachaata hai.

Step 4 — space optimise karo (optional). Agar dp[i] sirf dp[i-1] par depend karta hai toh poora array rakhne ki zaroorat nahi.

Interview mein Step 1 aur 2 kar lena hi usually kaafi hai. Step 3-4 tab karo jab interviewer specifically maange ya time bache.

docs.title: Template
docs.text:
from functools import lru_cache

def solve_top_down(inputs):
    """Step 2: recursion + memo. Sabse aasan aur sabse reliable."""
    @lru_cache(maxsize=None)              # automatic memoisation
    def dp(state):                        # state = jo bhi sub-problem define karta hai
        if is_base_case(state):
            return base_value
        # har choice try karo aur best lo
        return best(dp(next_state) for next_state in choices(state))
    return dp(initial_state)


def solve_bottom_up(n):
    """Step 3: loops. Faster, no recursion limit."""
    dp = [0] * (n + 1)                    # dp[i] = sub-problem i ka answer
    dp[0] = base_value                    # base case
    for i in range(1, n + 1):             # chhote se bade
        dp[i] = combine(dp[i - 1], dp[i - 2])   # transition
    return dp[n]

lru_cache ke baare mein ek zaroori baat: yeh sirf hashable arguments par kaam karta hai. Toh dp(index, remaining) (do ints) theek hai, lekin dp(some_list) crash karega. List ko tuple mein convert karo, ya manual dict use karo.

docs.title: DP ki sub-patterns
docs.text: Yahan paanch sabse common sub-patterns hain. Inhe alag alag samajhna zaroori hai kyunki state definition aur transition har ek mein alag hoti hai.

docs.title: 15A. Fibonacci Style DP
docs.text:
Pehchaan: dp[i] sirf pichhle ek ya do values par depend karta hai. State ek hi dimension mein hai.

Problems: Fibonacci, Climbing Stairs, House Robber, Min Cost Climbing Stairs, Decode Ways.

docs.title: Problem 15A.1 — House Robber
docs.text:
Problem statement

Ek line mein ghar hain, nums[i] = ghar i mein kitna paisa hai. Aap adjacent ghar nahi loot sakte (alarm baj jaayega). Maximum kitna paisa loot sakte ho?

Input:  [2, 7, 9, 3, 1]
Output: 12    (ghar 0, 2, aur 4 -> 2 + 9 + 1 = 12)

Input:  [1, 2, 3, 1]
Output: 4     (ghar 0 aur 2 -> 1 + 3 = 4)

Input:  [2, 1, 1, 2]
Output: 4     (ghar 0 aur 3)

Step 1 — brute force recursion

def rob_brute(nums):
    def helper(i):                                # 1: ghar `i` se aage max loot
        if i >= len(nums):                        # 2: ghar khatam
            return 0                              # 3
        take = nums[i] + helper(i + 2)            # 4: yeh ghar loota -> i+1 SKIP
        skip = helper(i + 1)                      # 5: yeh ghar chhoda -> i+1 available
        return max(take, skip)                    # 6: jo better ho
    return helper(0)                              # 7

Line by line

  1. helper(i) — state definition: "index i se aage ka maximum loot." Yeh state definition hi poora DP hai. 2-3. Base case: array khatam → 0.
  2. nums[i] + helper(i + 2) — i + 2 kyunki adjacent nahi loot sakte. i + 1 skip ho jaata hai.
  3. helper(i + 1) — is ghar ko chhoda, toh agla available hai.
  4. max — dono choices mein se best.
  5. Index 0 se shuru.

Complexity: Time O(2^n) — har ghar par do choices. n = 40 par ~10^12 calls. Space O(n) stack.

Overlapping subproblems dikhte hain? helper(3) helper(1) se bhi call hota hai (skip, skip) aur helper(1) se bhi (take). Yehi memoisation ka signal hai.

Step 2 — memoisation (top-down DP)

from functools import lru_cache

def rob_memo(nums):
    n = len(nums)                                 # 8

    @lru_cache(maxsize=None)                      # 9: automatic memo
    def helper(i):                                # 10: WAHI function, bas cached
        if i >= n:                                # 11
            return 0                              # 12
        return max(nums[i] + helper(i + 2),       # 13: take
                   helper(i + 1))                 # 14: skip

    result = helper(0)                            # 15
    helper.cache_clear()                          # 16: memory free karo (aur stale cache se bachao)
    return result                                 # 17

Line by line

  1. @lru_cache(maxsize=None) — ek line mein exponential se linear. maxsize=None matlab unbounded cache. helper ka argument i ek int hai — hashable, toh lru_cache kaam karta hai. nums closure se aata hai, argument nahi hai — yeh deliberate hai. Agar nums argument hota toh use tuple banana padta (lists unhashable hain).
  2. helper.cache_clear() — important detail. lru_cache function object par attach hota hai; agar rob_memo dobara alag nums ke saath call ho toh... actually yahan helper har call mein naya banta hai toh problem nahi. Lekin agar helper module-level hota toh stale cache ka bug aata. Habit ke liye clear karna acha hai, aur memory bhi free hoti hai.

Complexity: Time O(n) — har i exactly ek baar compute hota hai. Space O(n) cache plus O(n) stack.

Step 3 — bottom-up

def rob(nums):
    n = len(nums)                                 # 18
    if n == 0:                                    # 19: khaali guard
        return 0                                  # 20
    if n == 1:                                    # 21: ek ghar
        return nums[0]                            # 22

    dp = [0] * n                                  # 23: dp[i] = ghar 0..i tak ka max loot
    dp[0] = nums[0]                               # 24: base -- ek hi ghar hai
    dp[1] = max(nums[0], nums[1])                 # 25: base -- do gharon mein se bada

    for i in range(2, n):                         # 26: chhote se bade
        dp[i] = max(dp[i - 1],                    # 27: ghar i CHHODA -> dp[i-1] jaisa
                    dp[i - 2] + nums[i])          # 28: ghar i LOOTA -> dp[i-2] + nums[i]

    return dp[n - 1]                              # 29: poore array ka answer

Line by line — kyun aise likha hai

18-22. Guards. n == 1 wala guard zaroori hai kyunki line 25 nums[1] access karti hai. 23. dp = [0] * n — dp[i] ki definition ab badal gayi hai: "ghar 0 se i tak ka maximum loot" (top-down mein "ghar i se aage" thi). Yeh definition ka flip hi top-down aur bottom-up ka structural farq hai. Dono valid hain; bottom-up mein "prefix" definition zyada natural hai. 24. dp[0] = nums[0] — ek hi ghar, use loot lo. 25. dp[1] = max(nums[0], nums[1]) — do gharon mein se ek hi loot sakte ho (adjacent hain), toh bada wala. 26. for i in range(2, n): — 2 se shuru, kyunki 0 aur 1 base cases hain. 27-28. Transition — do choices: - Ghar i chhodo: answer dp[i-1] ke barabar (kuch naya nahi mila). - Ghar i loot lo: nums[i] mila, lekin i-1 nahi loot sakte, toh dp[i-2] se aage. dp[i-2] + nums[i] mein dp[i-2] hai, dp[i-1] nahi — yehi adjacency constraint hai. 29. return dp[n-1].

Step 4 — space optimisation

dp[i] sirf dp[i-1] aur dp[i-2] par depend karta hai. Toh poora array ki zaroorat nahi — do variables kaafi hain.

def rob_optimised(nums):
    prev2 = 0                                     # 30: dp[i-2]
    prev1 = 0                                     # 31: dp[i-1]
    for num in nums:                              # 32: har ghar
        current = max(prev1, prev2 + num)         # 33: WAHI transition
        prev2 = prev1                             # 34: SLIDE the window
        prev1 = current                           # 35
    return prev1                                  # 36

Line by line

30-31. Dono 0 se initialise — yeh "koi ghar nahi loota" wali state hai, aur base cases automatically handle ho jaate hain (line 21-22 wale guards ki zaroorat nahi). 33. Same transition. 34-35. Slide — order zaroori hai. prev2 = prev1 pehle, phir prev1 = current. Ulta karne se prev2 galat value le leta. 36. Return.

Time O(n), Space O(1).

Dry run — bottom-up — nums = [2, 7, 9, 3, 1] (expected 12)

i nums[i] dp[i-1] (skip) dp[i-2] + nums[i] (take) dp[i] 0 2 — — 2 (base) 1 7 — — 7 (base: max(2,7)) 2 9 dp[1] = 7 dp[0] + 9 = 2 + 9 = 11 11 3 3 dp[2] = 11 dp[1] + 3 = 7 + 3 = 10 11 4 1 dp[3] = 11 dp[2] + 1 = 11 + 1 = 12 12

return dp[4] = 12. Sahi — ghar 0, 2, 4 (2 + 9 + 1 = 12).

Row i = 3 important hai — ghar 3 (value 3) ko chhoda gaya kyunki dp[2] = 11 dp[1] + 3 = 10 se bada tha. Greedy "sabse bada ghar loot lo" yahan fail hota, kyunki 9 aur 3 dono nahi le sakte the.

Dry run — space optimised — same input

Step num prev2 prev1 current = max(prev1, prev2 + num) New prev2 New prev1 init — 0 0 — — — 1 2 0 0 max(0, 0+2) = 2 0 2 2 7 0 2 max(2, 0+7) = 7 2 7 3 9 2 7 max(7, 2+9) = 11 7 11 4 3 7 11 max(11, 7+3) = 11 11 11 5 1 11 11 max(11, 11+1) = 12 11 12

return prev1 = 12. Same answer, O(1) space.

Complexity summary

Version Time Space Brute force recursion O(2^n) O(n) Memoised (top-down) O(n) O(n) Bottom-up O(n) O(n) Space-optimised O(n) O(1)

Edge cases

Case nums Output Kyun Empty [] 0 prev1 0 rehta Single [5] 5 max(0, 0+5) Two [2, 7] 7 Adjacent, bada lo All same [3,3,3] 6 Ghar 0 aur 2 Zeros [0,0,0] 0 Decreasing [5,4,3,2,1] 9 Ghar 0, 2, 4 Large values [10**9] * 100 5 * 10**10 Python exact

Variations

  • House Robber II (LeetCode 213) — ghar circular hain (pehla aur aakhri adjacent). Trick: do baar chalao — ek baar nums[:-1] par, ek baar nums[1:] par, aur max lo.
  • House Robber III (337) — binary tree par. Har node do values return karta hai (rob / don't rob). Section 8 ki technique.
  • Climbing Stairs (70) — bilkul Fibonacci; dp[i] = dp[i-1] + dp[i-2].
  • Min Cost Climbing Stairs (746) — same shape, min ke saath.
  • Decode Ways (91) — same shape, validity checks ke saath.
  • Delete and Earn (740) — House Robber par map karo (values ko counts se weight karke).

Interview answer: "I'd build this in the standard four steps.

First, the brute-force recursion. Define the state as 'the maximum I can take from house i onward'. At each house there are two choices: rob it and jump to i plus two, because adjacency is banned, or skip it and go to i plus one. Take the max. That's exponential.

Second, I notice the same indices get recomputed along different paths — house three is reached both by skipping twice and by robbing the first house — so there are overlapping subproblems. Adding an lru_cache decorator turns that exponential into linear in one line. In an interview I'd often stop here, because it's the same code plus a decorator and it's hard to get wrong.

Third, bottom-up. I flip the state to 'the maximum from houses zero through i', which is the more natural direction for a loop. The transition is the same two choices: dp of i minus one if I skip, or dp of i minus two plus the current value if I rob. That minus-two is the adjacency constraint, and it's the one place to be careful.

Fourth, since each state only looks back two positions, I don't need the array at all — two rolling variables give O(1) space. The only subtlety is updating them in the right order.

O(n) time, O(1) space in the final version.

Worth noting why greedy fails here: taking the largest house first can block two houses that together are worth more. In two-seven-nine-three-one, greedy would grab nine, then be unable to take seven — the DP correctly takes two, nine, and one."

docs.title: 15B. Zero One Knapsack
docs.text:
Pehchaan: items ka set hai, har item ko lo ya chhodo (do baar nahi le sakte), aur ek capacity constraint hai. State do-dimensional hai: (kaunsa item, kitni capacity bachi).

Problems: 0/1 Knapsack, Subset Sum, Equal Subset Partition, Target Sum, Minimum Subset Sum Difference, Count of Subset Sum.

docs.title: Problem 15B.1 — Equal Subset Sum Partition
docs.text:
Problem statement

Positive integers ka array diya hai. Bataao ki use do subsets mein baanta ja sakta hai ya nahi jinke sums barabar hon.

Input:  [1, 5, 11, 5]
Output: True     ([1, 5, 5] aur [11] -- dono ka sum 11)

Input:  [1, 2, 3, 5]
Output: False    (total 11, odd hai -> barabar hisse possible hi nahi)

Input:  [1, 1]
Output: True

The reframe — yeh sabse important step hai

Sawaal "do barabar subsets" hai, lekin use ek subset ke sawaal mein badal do:

Agar total sum S hai aur do barabar hisse chahiye, toh har hisse ka sum S/2 hona chahiye. Toh sawaal ban gaya: "kya koi subset hai jiska sum exactly S/2 hai?" (Baaki elements automatically dusra subset ban jaayenge.)

Aur ek turant shortcut: agar S odd hai toh answer hamesha False — kyunki integers ko do barabar integer hisson mein nahi baanta ja sakta. Yeh check ek line mein poore computation se bacha sakta hai.

Step 1 — brute force recursion

def can_partition_brute(nums):
    total = sum(nums)                             # 1
    if total % 2 != 0:                            # 2: odd total -> impossible
        return False                              # 3: TURANT exit
    target = total // 2                           # 4: har hisse ka sum

    def helper(i, remaining):                     # 5: item `i` se aage, `remaining` bharna hai
        if remaining == 0:                        # 6: exact target hit
            return True                           # 7
        if i >= len(nums) or remaining < 0:       # 8: items khatam ya overshoot
            return False                          # 9
        # do choices: item `i` lo ya chhodo
        return (helper(i + 1, remaining - nums[i])    # 10: TAKE
                or helper(i + 1, remaining))          # 11: SKIP

    return helper(0, target)                      # 12

Line by line

1-3. Odd check pehle. sum O(n) hai, aur yeh check O(1). 4. target = total // 2 — // integer division. Line 2 ne guarantee kiya ki total even hai, toh yeh exact hai. 5. helper(i, remaining) — state: (index, remaining sum).
