  3. headers = dict(default_headers) — dict(...) constructor ek naya dict banata hai aur original ke saare key-value pairs usmein daal deta hai. Ye shallow copy hai: keys aur values wahi objects hain, par top-level container naya hai. Agar aap dict(...) hata kar sirf default_headers likh doge, upar wala bug wapas aa jaayega. Alternatives: default_headers.copy() (same cheez) ya {**default_headers} (same cheez, dict-unpacking syntax se).
  4. headers["Authorization"] = token — ye mutation hai, rebinding nahi. headers naam nahi badla; jis object par wo laga hai wo object andar se badla. Isliye mutation ka asar har us naam par dikhta hai jo usi object par laga ho.
  5. return headers — object ka reference return hota hai (copy nahi). Caller ko wahi object milta hai jo function ke andar banaya tha. Function khatm hone par local naam headers gayab ho jaata hai, par object zinda rehta hai kyunki caller ke paas uska reference hai.

docs.title: Kaise kaam karta hai — id() se proof
docs.text:
id(obj) CPython mein us object ka memory address deta hai. Do naam same object par hain ya nahi, ye check karne ka sabse seedha tareeka.

a = [1, 2, 3]              # heap par ek list object; naam 'a' usse bind
b = a                      # koi naya object nahi bana; 'b' bhi usi object par
print(id(a) == id(b))      # True  -- ek hi object
print(a is b)              # True  -- 'is' internally yahi id comparison hai

b.append(4)                # MUTATION: object andar se badla
print(a)                   # [1, 2, 3, 4]  -- 'a' se bhi wahi badla hua object dikh raha hai

b = [9, 9]                 # REBINDING: 'b' ab ek naye object par chala gaya
print(a)                   # [1, 2, 3, 4]  -- 'a' bilkul nahi badla
print(a is b)              # False

Line-by-line walkthrough:

  1. a = [1, 2, 3] — list display (literal) evaluate hoke ek naya list object banata hai, phir naam a bind hota hai. List har baar naya object banati hai — do baar [1,2,3] likhoge toh do alag objects milenge (ye int/str se alag hai, wo aage).
  2. b = a — right side a evaluate hua → wahi list object. Us object ko naam b bhi mil gaya. Kuch copy nahi hua. Sirf object ka refcount 1 se 2 ho gaya.
  3. print(id(a) == id(b)) — id() object ki identity deta hai. True ka matlab literally "same memory address". Agar aap id ki jagah len lagao toh dono ka length same aayega par wo identity prove nahi karta — length toh do alag lists ka bhi same ho sakta hai. Isliye identity check ke liye id/is hi sahi hai.
  4. print(a is b) — is operator identity compare karta hai, value nahi. Line 3 aur 4 equivalent hain; is idiomatic hai, id(x) == id(y) sirf demo ke liye.
  5. b.append(4) — append list ko jagah par badalta hai aur None return karta hai. b = b.append(4) likhna classic beginner bug hai — b None ban jaayega. Mutating methods None isliye lautate hain taaki aap galti se "ye naya object deta hai" na maan lo.
  6. print(a) — [1, 2, 3, 4]. Yahi wo line hai jo box model believer ko chaukaati hai: "maine toh b badla tha, a kaise badal gaya?" Kyunki a aur b do naam the, ek object.
  7. b = [9, 9] — ab rebinding hui: naya list object bana, b ka tag purane object se hat kar naye par chala gaya. Purane object ka refcount 2 se 1 ho gaya (a abhi bhi laga hai).
  8. print(a) — unchanged. Rebinding sirf naam ko chhoti hai, object ko nahi. Mutation vs rebinding ka farak yahi ek line samjha deti hai.

docs.title: Function arguments: "pass by value" nahi, "pass by object reference"
docs.text:
def add_test_tag(tags, new_tag):        # tags -> caller ke object par ek naya local naam
    tags.append(new_tag)                # MUTATION -> caller ko dikhega

def replace_test_tags(tags, new_tags):
    tags = new_tags                     # REBINDING -> sirf local naam badla, caller ko nahi dikhega

suite_tags = ["smoke"]
add_test_tag(suite_tags, "regression")
print(suite_tags)                       # ['smoke', 'regression']   <- badal gaya

replace_test_tags(suite_tags, ["e2e"])
print(suite_tags)                       # ['smoke', 'regression']   <- nahi badla

Line-by-line walkthrough:

  1. def add_test_tag(tags, new_tag): — call ke waqt Python parameter naam ko caller ke object se bind karta hai. Na object copy hota hai (pass-by-value nahi), na caller ke naam ka reference milta hai (pass-by-reference bhi nahi). Isko "pass by assignment" ya "pass by object reference" kehte hain.
  2. tags.append(new_tag) — object ko mutate kiya, isliye caller ko dikhega. Agar list ki jagah tuple hoti toh yahan AttributeError: 'tuple' object has no attribute 'append' milta — kyunki tuple immutable hai.
  3. def replace_test_tags(tags, new_tags): ... tags = new_tags — ye assignment hai, method call nahi. Assignment hamesha local naam ko rebind karta hai. Caller ka naam suite_tags abhi bhi purane object par laga hai.
  4. print(suite_tags) doosri baar — isliye unchanged. Agar aapko caller ka list replace hi karna hai toh do options hain: tags[:] = new_tags (slice assignment — object ko in-place overwrite karta hai) ya function se naya value return karke caller mein assign karna. Second option better hai — mutation ko chhupana testing mein dukh deta hai.

docs.title: Kab kaunsa pattern use karein
docs.text: Situation Karo Kyun Shared config se per-test copy chahiye dict(base) / base.copy() / {**base} shared state corrupt na ho Nested config (dict ke andar dict/list) copy.deepcopy(base) shallow copy inner objects share karti hai Function ko sirf padhna hai direct pass, no copy copy costly hai, aur mutate karna hi nahi Function result dena chahta hai return new_value mutation-based API hidden coupling banata hai Immutable chahiye taaki koi mutate na kare tuple, frozenset, types.MappingProxyType enforcement, discipline se better

docs.title: Gotchas
docs.text:
Gotcha 1 — += list par mutation hai, string par rebinding.

lst = [1, 2]
lst2 = lst
lst += [3]                    # list.__iadd__ -> IN-PLACE extend
print(lst2)                   # [1, 2, 3]   <- lst2 bhi badal gaya!

s = "ab"
s2 = s
s += "c"                      # str immutable -> naya object bana, 's' rebind hua
print(s2)                     # 'ab'        <- s2 bilkul nahi badla
  1. lst += [3] — list par += __iadd__ call karta hai, jo list ko jagah par extend karke wahi object return karta hai. Isliye lst2 ko bhi change dikha.
  2. s += "c" — str mein __iadd__ hai hi nahi, toh Python fallback karta hai s = s + "c" par, jo naya string object banata hai. Purana "ab" object waise ka waisa hai, aur s2 usi par laga hai. Ek hi operator, do alag semantics — kyunki mutability alag hai. Yahi is section ka asli sabak hai.

Gotcha 2 — augmented assignment tuple ke andar list par.

t = ([1], [2])
try:
    t[0] += [99]                 # ye line error bhi degi AUR kaam bhi kar degi
except TypeError as e:
    print("error:", e)           # error: 'tuple' object does not support item assignment
print(t)                         # ([1, 99], [2])   <- list to badal hi gayi!
  1. t[0] += [99] do kaam karta hai: pehle t[0].__iadd__([99]) — list in-place extend ho gayi (ye safal ho gaya), phir t[0] = <result> — tuple par item assignment, jo TypeError deta hai. Isliye exception ke baad bhi list mutate ho chuki hai.
  2. Sabak: tuple "immutable" hai ka matlab hai tuple ke slots nahi badal sakte, andar ke objects nahi badal sakte — ye galat hai. Isi wajah se ([1],[2]) hashable nahi hai.

Interview answer: "In Python a variable is not a box holding a value — it's a name bound to an object that lives on the heap. Assignment evaluates the right-hand side to an object and then binds the name to it, so b = a creates a second name for the same object rather than a copy. That distinction shows up as the difference between mutation and rebinding: b.append(4) changes the object, so every name pointing at it sees the change, whereas b = [9, 9] only moves the name b to a new object and leaves a untouched. Argument passing follows the same rule — parameters are bound to the caller's objects, which is why mutating a list argument is visible to the caller but reassigning the parameter is not. I care about this in automation because shared configuration dictionaries get corrupted exactly this way: a helper does headers = DEFAULT_HEADERS, adds an auth token, and now every later test sends the wrong token. The fix is an explicit copy, shallow or deep depending on nesting."

Cross-question — "So is Python pass by value or pass by reference?" "Neither, strictly. It's pass by object reference, sometimes called pass by assignment. The function parameter is bound to the same object the caller passed — no copy of the object is made, so it isn't pass by value; but the function receives no handle on the caller's name, so rebinding the parameter can't affect the caller, which means it isn't pass by reference in the C++ sense either. The practical rule I use is: if the object is mutable and I mutate it, the caller sees it; if I rebind the parameter, the caller never sees it."

docs.title: Kya hai
docs.text:
Python mein sab kuch object hai — number, string, function, class, module, even None. Har object ke teen guna hote hain:

  • identity — id(), banne ke baad kabhi nahi badalti,
  • type — type(), banne ke baad kabhi nahi badalti (normal cases mein),
  • value — badal sakti hai agar type mutable ho.

Analogy: aadhaar number (identity, kabhi nahi badalta), aap insaan ho (type), aapka address (value, badal sakta hai).

docs.title: Poori type table
docs.text:
Category Type Literal example Mutable? Hashable? QA use Numeric int 42, 0xFF, 1_000_000 No Yes retry counts, status codes Numeric float 3.14, 1e-3 No Yes timeouts, durations Numeric complex 2+3j No Yes practically never in QA Numeric bool True, False No Yes assertions, flags Numeric (stdlib) Decimal Decimal("0.1") No Yes money assertions Numeric (stdlib) Fraction Fraction(1, 3) No Yes exact ratios Sequence str "passed", 'a', """x""" No Yes everything Sequence list [1, 2] Yes No collected results Sequence tuple (1, 2), 1, No Yes* fixed records, dict keys Sequence range range(5) No Yes loop counters Binary bytes b"abc" No Yes file/network payloads Binary bytearray bytearray(b"abc") Yes No buffer building Binary memoryview memoryview(b"abc") view No zero-copy slicing Set set {1, 2} Yes No dedup, membership Set frozenset frozenset({1, 2}) No Yes set as dict key Mapping dict {"k": 1} Yes No config, JSON, kwargs Null NoneType None No Yes "no value" sentinel Callable function, method, type def, lambda, class attrs mutable Yes fixtures, decorators Special Ellipsis ... No Yes stubs, typing Special NotImplemented NotImplemented No Yes __eq__ fallback signalling

* tuple hashable tabhi hai jab uske saare elements hashable hon. (1, [2]) hashable nahi.

docs.title: Code — types ko chhoo kar dekho
docs.text:
values = [                             # ek list jismein alag-alag types ke objects hain
    42,                                # int
    3.14,                              # float
    True,                              # bool -- dhyaan do, ye int ka SUBCLASS hai
    "passed",                          # str
    b"raw",                            # bytes
    [1, 2],                            # list
    (1, 2),                            # tuple
    {1, 2},                            # set
    {"status": "passed"},              # dict
    None,                              # NoneType
    range(3),                          # range object (lazy)
]

for v in values:                                     # har object par ghoomo
    print(f"{str(v):<22} {type(v).__name__:<10} hashable={isinstance(v, __import__('collections.abc', fromlist=['Hashable']).Hashable)}")

Simple aur readable version (upar wali line jaan-boojh kar ugly hai — neeche wali aisi likhni chahiye):

from collections.abc import Hashable     # abstract base class: "kya ye hash ho sakta hai?"

def describe(value):                     # ek object ka poora parichay
    return {
        "repr": repr(value),             # repr = developer-facing text, str = user-facing
        "type": type(value).__name__,    # class ka naam, e.g. 'int'
        "mutable": not isinstance(value, Hashable),   # rough proxy, exceptions neeche
        "id": id(value),                 # identity
    }

print(describe(42))
print(describe([1, 2]))

Line-by-line walkthrough:

  1. from collections.abc import Hashable — collections.abc mein abstract base classes hain jo "capability" describe karti hain, concrete type nahi. isinstance(x, Hashable) puchhta hai "kya is type ne __hash__ implement kiya hai (aur None set nahi kiya)". Ye type(x) in (int, str, tuple) se behtar hai kyunki wo list kabhi complete nahi hogi — custom classes bhi hashable ho sakti hain.
  2. def describe(value): — ek plain function, koi class nahi, kyunki yahan state nahi hai. "Function se kaam ho jaaye toh class mat banao" — Part 5 ka theme.
  3. "repr": repr(value) — repr() wo string deta hai jo (ideally) eval() karke wapas object bana de: repr("a") → "'a'" (quotes ke saath). str("a") → "a" (bina quotes). Debug logs mein hamesha repr use karo — str mein "1" aur 1 ek jaise dikhte hain, repr mein farak dikh jaata hai. Ye QA ke liye seedha kaam ka hai: assertion failure message mein repr na ho toh aap 10 minute barbaad karte ho.
  4. "type": type(value).__name__ — type(value) class object deta hai (<class 'int'>); .__name__ usse sirf naam nikaalta hai ('int'). __name__ isliye kyunki poora <class 'int'> log mein noise hai.
  5. "mutable": not isinstance(value, Hashable) — ye ek approximation hai, aur maine jaan-boojh kar rakha hai taaki aap iska hole dekho: tuple hashable hai aur immutable bhi, theek. Par (1, [2]) hashable nahi hai fir bhi tuple hai. Aur ek custom mutable class default se hashable hoti hai (identity-based hash). Toh "hashable == immutable" galat hai; sirf built-in scalars ke liye kaam chalta hai. Interview mein ye distinction pooch liya jaata hai.
  6. "id": id(value) — identity. Note: describe(42) do baar call karoge toh same id aayega (small int caching, 1.5 mein), par describe([1,2]) do baar mein alag id — nayi list.

docs.title: bool actually int hai — aur ye bug banta hai
docs.text:
print(isinstance(True, int))      # True   -- bool, int ka subclass hai
print(True + True)                # 2      -- kyunki True == 1
print(sum([True, False, True]))   # 2      -- ye actually useful hai: count of passes

results = ["passed", "failed", "passed", "passed"]
pass_count = sum(r == "passed" for r in results)   # generator of bools -> sum
print(pass_count)                                   # 3

Line-by-line walkthrough:

  1. isinstance(True, int) — bool int se inherit karta hai (historical reason: Python 2.2 se pehle bool tha hi nahi, 1/0 use hota tha; backward compatibility ke liye subclass banaya gaya).
  2. True + True → 2 — kyunki bool ke paas apna __add__ nahi hai, int ka use hota hai.
  3. sum([True, False, True]) → 2 — ye idiomatic counting hai.
  4. sum(r == "passed" for r in results) — andar ek generator expression hai (Part 6) jo har result ke liye True/False deta hai; sum unhe 1/0 ki tarah jodta hai. Ye len([r for r in results if r == "passed"]) se behtar hai kyunki beech mein poori list nahi banti — 50,000 test results par ye farak dikhta hai. Agar aap square brackets laga do (sum([r == "passed" for r in results])) toh kaam chalega par ek pooori list allocate hogi.

Gotcha: kyunki True == 1, dict mein ye hota hai:

d = {1: "one", True: "bool-true", 1.0: "float-one"}
print(d)          # {1: 'float-one'}  -- ek hi key!
print(len(d))     # 1
  1. 1, True aur 1.0 ka hash same hai aur wo == bhi hain, isliye dict inhe ek hi key maanta hai. Pehli key (1) reh jaati hai, value baar-baar overwrite hoti hai.
  2. Iska real impact: agar aapke test-data mein IDs kabhi 1 aur kabhi True (ya 1.0 JSON se) aate hain, dedup silently galat ho sakta hai.

Interview answer: "Everything in Python is an object with three properties: identity, type, and value. Only the value can change, and only for mutable types. The built-ins split into numerics — int, float, bool, complex — sequences — str, list, tuple, range, bytes — sets, mappings, and None. The one that surprises people is that bool is a subclass of int, so True + True is 2 and {1: 'a', True: 'b'} collapses to a single key because 1 and True hash the same and compare equal. I actually use that on purpose: sum(r.passed for r in results) counts passing tests without building an intermediate list."

Cross-question — "Is hashable the same as immutable?" "No, and the two directions fail differently. Immutable built-ins are hashable, but a tuple containing a list is immutable at the tuple level and still unhashable, because hashing recurses into the elements. In the other direction, an ordinary mutable custom class is hashable by default — Python gives it an identity-based __hash__ — which is fine until you define __eq__, at which point Python sets __hash__ to None and the class becomes unhashable unless you define __hash__ yourself. The real rule is: hashable means the hash stays constant for the object's lifetime and equal objects hash equal."

docs.title: 1.4 Mutability vs immutability — aur wo classic default-argument bug
Kya hai
docs.text:
Mutable = banne ke baad andar se badla ja sakta hai (list, dict, set, bytearray, most custom classes). Immutable = banne ke baad kabhi nahi badalta (int, float, str, tuple, frozenset, bytes, None).

Analogy: mutable ek whiteboard hai — wahi board, content badal do. Immutable ek printed receipt hai — badalna ho toh nayi receipt print karni padegi, purani jaisi ki taisi.

docs.title: Kyu hai — immutability ka faayda kya
docs.text:
1. Safety: aap kisi ko str de do, wo usse corrupt nahi kar sakta. Isliye dict keys immutable honi chahiye — key badal jaaye toh dict apna hi entry dhoondh nahi paayega.
  2. Hashing: hash value constant rehni chahiye. Immutable objects ka hash ek baar compute karke cache kiya ja sakta hai (str yahi karta hai).
  3. Sharing/caching: kyunki koi badal hi nahi sakta, Python chhote ints aur kuch strings ko reuse kar leta hai (1.5).
  4. Concurrency: immutable object share karne mein lock nahi chahiye.

docs.title: Kaise kaam karta hai
docs.text:
Mutable object ka "badalna" matlab uski memory mein bytes badalna, id wahi rehti hai. Immutable object ka "badalna" matlab naya object banana, id badal jaati hai.

lst = [1, 2]
print(id(lst))          # e.g. 140234...
lst.append(3)
print(id(lst))          # WAHI id -- object badla, identity nahi

s = "ab"
print(id(s))            # e.g. 140111...
s = s + "c"
print(id(s))            # ALAG id -- naya object bana
  1. lst.append(3) — list.append C level par internal array mein element daal deta hai (zarurat pade toh array grow karta hai, Part 3). Object header wahi hai, isliye id same.
  2. s = s + "c" — str.__add__ naya str object allocate karta hai jismein dono ke bytes copy hote hain, phir naam s us naye object par rebind hota hai. Purana "ab" refcount 0 hone par free ho jaata hai (agar koi aur naam us par nahi laga).

docs.title: THE classic bug — mutable default argument
docs.text:
Ye interview mein sabse zyada poochha jaane wala Python gotcha hai, aur QA frameworks mein sach mein aata hai.

# --- BUG ---
def record_failure(test_name, failures=[]):     # default ek LIST hai -- khatra
    failures.append(test_name)                  # us list ko mutate kar rahe hain
    return failures

print(record_failure("test_login"))     # ['test_login']
print(record_failure("test_logout"))    # ['test_login', 'test_logout']   <- BUG!
print(record_failure("test_cart"))      # ['test_login', 'test_logout', 'test_cart']

Line-by-line walkthrough — exactly kya ho raha hai:

  1. def record_failure(test_name, failures=[]): — def line sirf EK BAAR chalti hai, jab module import hota hai. Us waqt [] evaluate hoke ek list object banata hai, aur wo object function ke __defaults__ tuple mein store ho jaata hai. Har call par naya [] nahi banta. Isko khud dekho: 
    print(record_failure.__defaults__)     # ([...],)  -- wahi ek list, har call ke baad badi
  2. failures.append(test_name) — jab caller ne failures pass nahi kiya, failures usi shared default list par bind hota hai. Mutation us shared object par ho rahi hai.
  3. return failures — har call wahi object lauta rahi hai, isliye teeno prints ek hi list dikha rahe hain jo badhti ja rahi hai.
  4. Ye record_failure(...) calls independent lag rahi thi par nahi hain — QA mein iska matlab hai "test A ka failure test B ki report mein aa gaya".

Fix:

def record_failure(test_name, failures=None):   # sentinel: None (immutable, safe)
    if failures is None:                        # 'is' use karo, '==' nahi (neeche kyun)
        failures = []                           # har call par NAYI list -- yahi asli fix hai
    failures.append(test_name)
    return failures

print(record_failure("test_login"))     # ['test_login']
print(record_failure("test_logout"))    # ['test_logout']   <- ab independent

Line-by-line walkthrough:

  1. failures=None — None immutable aur singleton hai, toh usse share karne mein koi khatra nahi. Ye Python ka standard "sentinel" idiom hai: "caller ne kuch diya hi nahi" ko represent karna.
  2. if failures is None: — is isliye, == nahi. Agar caller ne aisi cheez pass ki jiska __eq__ overridden hai (numpy array, pandas Series, ya aapki custom class), toh failures == None ya toh array return karega ya ValueError: truth value of an array is ambiguous. is identity check hai, koi user code call nahi hota — isliye hamesha safe.
  3. failures = [] — ab ye har call par chalta hai, kyunki ye function body mein hai, def line mein nahi. Yahi poora fix hai.
  4. failures.append(test_name) — ab ya toh caller ki di hui list hai (jo unhone jaan-boojh kar di), ya fresh list.

Aur behtar (mutation hi mat karo):

def record_failure(test_name, failures=()):     # tuple default -- immutable, safe by design
    return (*failures, test_name)               # naya tuple, purana chhua tak nahi
  1. failures=() — empty tuple immutable hai, toh shared hone se koi farak nahi padta. Ye "default ko mutable mat banao" ka doosra tareeka hai.
  2. return (*failures, test_name) — unpacking se naya tuple banta hai. Function ab pure hai: same input → same output, koi side effect nahi. Test karna trivially aasan. Trade-off: har call par O(n) copy. 10 items ke liye theek, 100k ke liye nahi.

docs.title: Ye bug default arguments se aage bhi hai — class attributes
docs.text:
# --- BUG: har instance ne class-level list share kar li ---
class TestSuite:
    tests = []                          # CLASS attribute, sab instances ke beech shared

    def add(self, name):
        self.tests.append(name)         # self.tests lookup class tak jaata hai -> shared list

s1 = TestSuite()
s2 = TestSuite()
s1.add("test_a")
print(s2.tests)                         # ['test_a']   <- s2 ne kabhi add nahi kiya!
  1. tests = [] class body mein hai — ye class object ka attribute hai, instance ka nahi. Class body bhi ek baar chalti hai.
  2. self.tests.append(name) — attribute lookup pehle instance __dict__ mein dekhta hai, nahi mila toh class mein. Instance mein tests hai hi nahi, toh class wali list mil gayi aur wahi mutate ho gayi. Note: agar aap self.tests = self.tests + [name] likhte, toh assignment instance attribute banata aur behaviour alag hota — ye phir wahi "mutation vs rebinding" hai.

Fix:

class TestSuite:
    def __init__(self):
        self.tests = []                 # har instance ke liye NAYI list

    def add(self, name):
        self.tests.append(name)

s1, s2 = TestSuite(), TestSuite()
s1.add("test_a")
print(s2.tests)                         # []   <- ab independent
  1. def __init__(self): — __init__ har instance banne par chalti hai, isliye [] har baar naya banta hai.
  2. s1, s2 = TestSuite(), TestSuite() — right side ek tuple banata hai (obj1, obj2), phir tuple unpacking se do naam bind hote hain. Do alag calls, do alag instances.

docs.title: Kab mutable default use karna chahiye
docs.text:
Kabhi nahi — sivay ek jaan-boojh kar kiye gaye cache ke:

def parse_report(path, _cache={}):       # underscore = "private, mat chhedo"
    if path in _cache:                   # shared mutable default = memo table
        return _cache[path]
    result = {"path": path, "parsed": True}
    _cache[path] = result
    return result
  1. Ye jaan-boojh kar shared state use kar raha hai — memoization. Par isko aise mat likho; functools.lru_cache (Part 4) yahi kaam thread-safety aur cache_clear() ke saath karta hai. Ye example sirf ye dikhane ke liye hai ki mechanism samajh mein aa gaya.

Interview answer: "Default argument values are evaluated once, when the def statement executes, and stored on the function object in __defaults__. So a mutable default like def f(items=[]) gives every call that omits the argument the same list, and mutations accumulate across calls. In a test framework that shows up as one test's failures leaking into another test's report. The fix is to default to None and create the real object inside the body, comparing with is None rather than == None so that objects with a custom __eq__ don't misbehave. The same bug appears one level up with class attributes: a list defined in the class body is shared by every instance, so it belongs in __init__."

Cross-question — "Why did Python choose late binding for the body but early binding for defaults? Isn't that inconsistent?" "It's a deliberate trade-off. Evaluating defaults once means the function object is fully built at definition time — the default is just a stored object, so calls stay cheap and you can introspect the signature. Late-binding defaults would mean re-evaluating an arbitrary expression on every call, which costs time and makes the value depend on whatever the surrounding scope happens to hold at call time. Languages that do late-bind defaults, like Ruby, pay that cost. Python's answer is the None sentinel idiom, and the standard library uses it consistently — that's why you see def f(x=None) everywhere in CPython's own code."

docs.title: Kya hai
docs.text:
• == puchhta hai: "kya inki value barabar hai?" → object ka __eq__ chalta hai.
  • is puchhta hai: "kya ye literally ek hi object hai?" → id() compare hota hai, koi user code nahi chalta.

Analogy: do bilkul ek jaise Aadhaar cards ki photocopies — == (same content), par is nahi (do alag kaagaz). Aur agar aap ek hi card do haathon se pakdo — is bhi True.

docs.title: Kyu hai — do operators kyun chahiye
docs.text:
Kyunki dono sawaal alag hain aur dono ki zarurat padti hai:

a = [1, 2, 3]
b = [1, 2, 3]
print(a == b)     # True   -- content same
print(a is b)     # False  -- do alag list objects

c = a
print(a is c)     # True   -- ek hi object

Aap == ke bina "kya do API responses same hain?" nahi puchh sakte. Aur is ke bina "kya ye wahi cached page object hai?" nahi puchh sakte.

docs.title: Kaise kaam karta hai — mechanism
docs.text:
x == y → CPython pehle type(x).__eq__(x, y) try karta hai. Agar wo NotImplemented de, toh reflected type(y).__eq__(y, x) try karta hai. Dono NotImplemented de toh fallback identity comparison (x is y) hai.

x is y → seedha pointer comparison, overridable nahi. Isliye is hamesha tez hai aur hamesha safe hai (koi property/__eq__ side-effect nahi).

docs.title: Integer caching (small int cache)
docs.text:
CPython startup par -5 se 256 tak ke int objects pehle se bana kar rakhta hai, kyunki ye sabse zyada use hote hain. Har baar naya allocate karna waste hoga.

a = 256
b = 256
print(a is b)          # True   -- dono cached object 256 par point kar rahe hain

x = 257
y = 257
print(x is y)          # False (usually) -- 257 cache mein nahi, do alag objects
print(x == y)          # True   -- value toh same hai hi

Line-by-line walkthrough:

  1. a = 256 / b = 256 — compiler ne dono ke liye LOAD_CONST kiya; 256 chhota int hai toh interpreter ke pre-allocated pool se wahi object aaya. Isliye is True.
  2. x = 257 / y = 257 — 257 pool ke bahar hai. Har literal ke liye naya object banta hai... lekin ek twist hai: agar dono literal ek hi code object mein ho (jaise ek function ke andar, ya ek hi REPL line par), toh compiler constant-folding/dedup kar deta hai aur is True aa sakta hai. Isliye maine "usually" likha.
  3. Ye demonstrate karta hai ki is ko value comparison ke liye kabhi mat use karo — uska result implementation detail par depend karta hai, aur wo Python version ke saath badal sakta hai.

Khud dekho ki version-dependence real hai:

def f():
    x = 257          # ek hi code object ke andar
    y = 257
    return x is y

print(f())           # True  -- constant dedup within one code object

x = 257              # module level, alag statements
y = 257
print(x is y)        # 3.8+ mein bhi aksar True (module bhi ek code object hai),
                     # par REPL mein alag lines par False
  1. Function ke andar dono 257 ek hi co_consts tuple mein jaate hain, aur compiler equal constants ko dedup karta hai — isliye ek hi object.
  2. REPL mein har line alag code object hai, toh dedup nahi hota → False.
  3. Sabak: ye behaviour "Python ka rule" nahi hai, "CPython ka optimization" hai. Interview mein yahi kehna hai.

docs.title: String interning
docs.text:
Chhoti, identifier-jaisi strings ko CPython ek global table mein intern karta hai, taaki same text ki ek hi copy rahe. Ye dict key lookups tez karta hai — kyunki pointer equality se hi match ho jaata hai, character-by-character compare nahi karna padta.

a = "passed"
b = "passed"
print(a is b)                # True  -- identifier-like literal, interned

c = "test passed!"           # space aur '!' hai -> identifier-like nahi
d = "test passed!"
print(c is d)                # True (same code object mein constant dedup ki wajah se)

e = "test" + " passed!"      # constant folding: compile time par hi jud gaya
f = "test passed!"
print(e is f)                # True

g = " ".join(["test", "passed!"])   # RUNTIME par bana -> naya object
print(g is f)                # False
print(g == f)                # True

Line-by-line walkthrough:

  1. a = "passed" — passed letters-only hai, toh compile time par intern ho gaya. Dono naam ek hi object par.
  2. c = "test passed!" — ye interning ke identifier rule mein fit nahi hota, par same code object mein do baar likha hai toh compiler constants dedup kar deta hai — True.
  3. e = "test" + " passed!" — dono operands literals hain, toh CPython ka peephole optimizer compile time par hi jod deta hai (constant folding). Result wahi constant hai.
  4. g = " ".join([...]) — ye runtime call hai, compiler kuch pre-compute nahi kar sakta. Naya str object bana. Isliye g is f False, par g == f True.
  5. Yahi wo exact jaal hai jo naye log phasate hain: aapne test mein if response_status is "passed": likha, local testing mein literal se compare ho raha tha toh True aaya, aur production mein status API se runtime par bana toh False — flaky test, koi error nahi.

Manual interning (rarely needed):

import sys
a = sys.intern("some dynamic " + "string")   # explicitly intern table mein daalo
b = sys.intern("some dynamic string")
print(a is b)                                 # True
  1. sys.intern(s) — string ko global intern table mein daalta hai aur canonical object lautata hai. Use case: aap lakhs baar wahi keys parse kar rahe ho (bade JSON/CSV reports), toh interning memory bachaata hai aur dict lookup tez karta hai.
  2. Rozana code mein iski zarurat nahi hai. Interview mein iska naam pata hona kaafi hai.

docs.title: is kab use karna hai — sirf teen jagah
docs.text:
Use is Kyun x is None / x is not None None singleton hai; == custom __eq__ chala sakta hai x is True / x is False (rare) jab exactly bool chahiye, truthy nahi Sentinel objects (_MISSING = object()) identity hi poora point hai Cache/identity check (page is self._cached_page) "wahi object hai?" hi sawaal hai

Baaki har jagah ==.

docs.title: Gotchas
docs.text:
Gotcha 1 — == custom class mein silent-True ban sakta hai.

class AlwaysEqual:
    def __eq__(self, other):
        return True                    # jaan-boojh kar bura implementation

a = AlwaysEqual()
print(a == None)                       # True   <- yahi khatra hai
print(a is None)                       # False  <- 'is' bewakoof nahi banta
  1. def __eq__(self, other): return True — == user code call karta hai, isliye wo jhooth bol sakta hai. Mock objects (unittest.mock.MagicMock) exactly aisa behave karte hain — MagicMock() == anything aksar truthy-ish surprise deta hai.
  2. Isliye if x is None likhna sirf style nahi, correctness hai.

Gotcha 2 — linter warning SyntaxWarning: "is" with a literal.

>>> x = 1000
>>> x is 1000
<stdin>:1: SyntaxWarning: "is" with a literal. Did you mean "=="?
False

Python 3.8+ khud warn karta hai kyunki ye itni common galti hai. Warning ko ignore mat karo.

Gotcha 3 — != aur is not do alag operators hain, not ... is mat likho.

x = None
print(x is not None)          # sahi, ek operator: 'is not'
print(not x is None)          # kaam karta hai par padhne mein bura -- 'not (x is None)'

Interview answer: "== compares values by calling the objects' __eq__, is compares identity by comparing memory addresses, and is can't be overridden. You get confusing results because CPython caches some immutable objects: small integers from -5 to 256 are pre-allocated, and identifier-like string literals are interned, so a = 256; b = 256; a is b is True while the same with 257 is usually False. Those are CPython optimisations, not language guarantees, which is exactly why you should never use is for value comparison. I reserve is for three things: None checks, sentinel objects created with object(), and genuine identity questions like 'is this the same cached page object'. The None case matters in practice because x == None runs user code, and with a mock or a numpy array that either lies or raises."

Cross-question — "You said x == y calls __eq__. What happens if the left operand's __eq__ returns NotImplemented?" "Python then tries the reflected operation, type(y).__eq__(y, x). If that also returns NotImplemented, Python falls back to identity comparison, so x == y becomes x is y. There's an extra rule worth knowing: if the right operand's type is a proper subclass of the left operand's type and it overrides __eq__, Python tries the right side first. That's how subclasses get to define equality against their parents. NotImplemented is also why you should return it — not False — from __eq__ when you don't know how to compare against the other type; returning False short-circuits the reflected call and silently gives the wrong answer."

docs.title: Kya hai
docs.text:
Har object ko if, while, and, or, not ke context mein bool banaya ja sakta hai. Ye conversion bool(obj) hai.

Analogy: ek dabbe mein saamaan hai ya nahi — Python ke liye "khaali = False, bhara = True".

docs.title: Kyu hai
docs.text:
Iske bina har check verbose ho jaata:

# --- WITHOUT truthiness ---
failures = []
if len(failures) == 0:                     # length nikaalo, 0 se compare karo
    print("all green")

config = None
if config is None or len(config) == 0:     # do checks, ordering matters
    print("no config")

# --- WITH truthiness ---
failures = []
if not failures:                           # khaali list falsy hai
    print("all green")

config = None
if not config:                             # None falsy, {} bhi falsy -- ek hi check
    print("no config")

docs.title: Kaise kaam karta hai — exact rules
docs.text:
bool(x) ka algorithm:

  1. Agar type par __bool__ hai → usko call karo, result bool hona hi chahiye warna TypeError.
  2. Warna agar __len__ hai → len(x) == 0 ho toh False, warna True.
  3. Warna → True (default: har object truthy hai).

Falsy values ki poori list:

Falsy Type False bool None NoneType 0, 0.0, 0j, Decimal(0), Fraction(0) numerics "" str (), [], {}, set(), frozenset(), range(0) empty containers b"", bytearray(b"") empty binary datetime.time(0, 0) only in Python < 3.5, ab truthy hai custom object jiska __bool__ False de ya __len__ 0 de anything

Baaki sab truthy — including "False", "0", [0], {0: 0}, -1, 0.0001.

docs.title: Code — QA context mein truthiness
docs.text:
class TestReport:
    def __init__(self, failures):
        self.failures = failures                    # list of failed test names

    def __bool__(self):                             # "kya ye report 'good' hai?"
        return len(self.failures) == 0              # no failures -> truthy

    def __len__(self):                              # fallback + len() support
        return len(self.failures)

report = TestReport([])
if report:                                          # __bool__ chala -> True
    print("suite passed")                           # ye print hoga

report2 = TestReport(["test_login"])
if report2:
    print("never")
else:
    print("suite failed with", len(report2), "failures")   # __len__ chala -> 1

Line-by-line walkthrough:

  1. class TestReport: — plain class. Ye __bool__ demo ke liye hai, real design ke liye nahi — neeche gotcha mein bataunga ki ye design kyun kharab hai.
  2. def __init__(self, failures): self.failures = failures — note: yahan maine caller ki list store kar li, copy nahi ki. Matlab caller baad mein us list ko badal de toh report bhi badal jaayegi. Production mein self.failures = list(failures) likhna chahiye (1.2 ka sabak).
  3. def __bool__(self): — jab bhi ye object boolean context mein aayega, ye method chalega. Return value bool honi chahiye; agar aap return len(self.failures) likh do (int), toh TypeError: __bool__ should return bool, returned int milega.
  4. return len(self.failures) == 0 — comparison bool deta hai. Yahan not self.failures bhi likh sakte the — same cheez, chhota.
  5. def __len__(self): — len(report2) ke liye. Agar __bool__ na hota, toh Python __len__ se truthiness nikaalta — aur semantics ulti ho jaati: khaali failures → len()==0 → falsy → "suite passed" wala branch nahi chalta. Isliye jab dono define karo toh unke meanings ko align karna zaruri hai, warna if report aur if len(report) ulte jawab denge.
  6. if report: — __bool__ call hua, True mila.
  7. len(report2) — __len__ call hua. Note len() ka return non-negative int hona chahiye, warna ValueError.

docs.title: Kab truthiness use karo, kab explicit check
docs.text: Situation Likho Kyun "list khaali hai kya" if not items: idiomatic, fast "value di gayi hai ya nahi" jahan 0/"" valid hain if value is not None: 0 falsy hai par valid value ho sakti hai "flag on hai kya" if flag: fine "exactly True chahiye, truthy nahi" if flag is True: rare, par API validation mein useful Numpy array / pandas if arr.size: / if df.empty: plain truthiness ValueError deta hai

docs.title: Gotchas
docs.text:
Gotcha 1 — sabse mehnga wala: 0 aur "" valid values ho sakti hain.

def get_timeout(config):
    # BUG: agar user ne jaan-boojh kar timeout=0 diya (no wait), hum usko overwrite kar denge
    timeout = config.get("timeout") or 30
    return timeout

print(get_timeout({"timeout": 0}))       # 30   <- user ne 0 maanga tha!
print(get_timeout({"timeout": 5}))       # 5

Fix:

def get_timeout(config):
    timeout = config.get("timeout")           # missing ho toh None
    if timeout is None:                       # sirf 'missing' ko default karo
        timeout = 30
    return timeout

print(get_timeout({"timeout": 0}))       # 0    <- ab sahi
  1. config.get("timeout") — dict.get missing key par None deta hai (KeyError nahi). Ye config["timeout"] se alag hai jo raise karta.
  2. if timeout is None: — sirf "key thi hi nahi" case handle kar rahe hain. or wala version 0, "", False, [] sab ko "missing" maan leta tha — yahi bug tha.
  3. Ek line mein: timeout = config.get("timeout", 30) — ye bhi sahi hai aur behtar hai, kyunki dict.get ka doosra argument sirf key absent hone par use hota hai, value falsy hone par nahi. Par agar key exist karti ho aur value None ho (JSON null), toh get None hi dega — tab explicit check chahiye.

Gotcha 2 — if x == True mat likho.

x = 1
print(x == True)          # True  -- kyunki 1 == True
print(x is True)          # False -- alag objects
print(bool(x))            # True

y = [1]
print(y == True)          # False!  -- non-empty list truthy hai par True ke barabar nahi
if y:
    print("but y is truthy")     # ye print hoga
  1. x == True — value comparison hai, aur 1 == True sach hai, toh accidentally kaam kar gaya. Confusing.
  2. y == True — list kabhi bool ke barabar nahi hoti, toh False. Par if y: truthy hai. == True aur truthiness alag cheezein hain — isliye if y == True: kabhi mat likho, if y: likho.

Gotcha 3 — and/or bool nahi, operand lautate hain.

print(0 or "default")            # 'default'   -- pehla truthy operand
print("a" or "b")                # 'a'
print("a" and "b")               # 'b'         -- last operand agar sab truthy
print(0 and "b")                 # 0           -- pehla falsy operand
  1. or left-to-right chalta hai aur pehla truthy operand lautata hai; sab falsy hon toh aakhri operand. and ulta: pehla falsy, warna aakhri.
  2. Ye short-circuit hai — 0 and expensive() mein expensive() chalta hi nahi. Isliye if response is not None and response.status == 200: safe hai; ordering ulti kar do toh AttributeError milega.
  3. Yahi wajah hai ki x = a or b value-defaulting ke liye kaam karta hai — par Gotcha 1 wali trap ke saath.

Interview answer: "Every object has a truth value. Python asks __bool__ first; if that's missing it falls back to __len__ being non-zero; if neither exists the object is truthy. The falsy set is small and worth memorising: False, None, zero of any numeric type, and every empty container or string. That gives you if not failures: instead of if len(failures) == 0:. The trap is using truthiness where you actually mean 'was a value supplied', because 0, empty string and False are all legitimate values that are falsy — I've seen timeout = cfg.get('timeout') or 30 silently override a deliberate timeout=0. For that case I check is None explicitly. Also worth knowing that and and or return one of their operands, not a bool, and they short-circuit — which is what makes if resp is not None and resp.ok: safe."

Cross-question — "What happens if __bool__ returns a non-bool, say an int?" "Python raises TypeError: __bool__ should return bool. That's stricter than __len__, which must return a non-negative int and Python converts it for you. It's deliberate — the boolean protocol is meant to give an unambiguous yes/no, so CPython refuses to guess. The practical consequence is that return len(self.items) in __bool__ is a bug and return bool(self.items) or return len(self.items) > 0 is the fix."

docs.title: 1.7 Operators — sab, aur unke peechhe ke dunder methods
Kya hai
docs.text: Operator ek syntactic shortcut hai method call ka. a + b ka matlab CPython ke liye type(a).__add__(a, b) hai. Isliye Python mein operators "built-in magic" nahi hain — wo protocol hain jinhe aap apni class mein implement kar sakte ho (Part 5).

docs.title: Poori operator table with dunder mapping
docs.text:
Arithmetic

Operator Meaning Dunder Note a + b add / concat __add__ / __radd__ str, list, tuple par concat a - b subtract __sub__ set par difference a * b multiply / repeat __mul__ [0] * 3 → [0,0,0] a / b true division __truediv__ hamesha float: 4/2 → 2.0 a // b floor division __floordiv__ neeche ki taraf: -7//2 → -4 a % b modulo / old-style format __mod__ Python mein sign divisor ka: -7 % 3 → 2 a ** b power __pow__ 2**10 → 1024 -a, +a unary __neg__, __pos__ abs(a) absolute __abs__

Comparison

Operator Dunder a == b __eq__ a != b __ne__ (default: __eq__ ka ulta) a < b __lt__ a <= b __le__ a > b __gt__ a >= b __ge__

Logical / identity / membership

Operator Meaning Dunder and, or, not short-circuit logic __bool__ (via truthiness) is, is not identity none (not overridable) in, not in membership __contains__, warna __iter__, warna __getitem__

Bitwise

Operator Meaning Dunder QA use a & b AND __and__ set intersection a \| b OR __or__ set union; 3.9+ dict merge; 3.10+ type union a ^ b XOR __xor__ set symmetric difference ~a NOT __invert__ ~0 → -1 a << n left shift __lshift__ rare a >> n right shift __rshift__ rare

Augmented — +=, -=, *=, /=, //=, %=, **=, &=, |=, ^=, <<=, >>= → __iadd__, __isub__, ... Agar in-place dunder na ho toh Python a = a + b par fallback karta hai (1.2 wala gotcha yahi tha).

Walrus — := (Part 2 mein detail).

docs.title: Precedence — upar sabse strong
docs.text:
1.  (), [], {}                       grouping / display
2.  x[i], x.attr, f()                subscription, attribute, call
3.  await x
4.  **                               power (RIGHT associative!)
5.  +x, -x, ~x                       unary
6.  *, @, /, //, %
7.  +, -
8.  <<, >>
9.  &
10. ^
11. |
12. in, not in, is, is not, <, <=, >, >=, !=, ==   (chained!)
13. not x
14. and
15. or
16. if-else (conditional expression)
17. lambda
18. :=                               walrus (lowest)

docs.title: Code — precedence bugs jo sach mein hote hain
docs.text:
# Bug 1: '**' right-associative hai
print(2 ** 3 ** 2)                 # 512, kyunki 2 ** (3 ** 2) = 2 ** 9
print((2 ** 3) ** 2)               # 64 -- jo shayad aap chahte the

# Bug 2: 'not' 'and'/'or' se strong hai par comparison se kamzor
print(not 1 == 2)                  # True   -> not (1 == 2)
print((not 1) == 2)                # False  -> (False) == 2

# Bug 3: '%' ka precedence '+' se zyada hai
print(1 + 2 % 3)                   # 3, kyunki 1 + (2 % 3) = 1 + 2

# Bug 4: bitwise '&' comparison se KAMZOR nahi hai -- ye classic pandas trap
# print(x == 1 & y == 2)           # actually (x == (1 & y)) == 2  -> nonsense

Line-by-line walkthrough:

  1. 2 ** 3 ** 2 — ** right associative hai (maths ki tarah), toh 3 ** 2 = 9 pehle, phir 2 ** 9 = 512. Baaki saare binary operators left-associative hain. Agar aapko left chahiye toh brackets lagane hi padenge.
  2. not 1 == 2 — comparison (==) not se zyada strong hai, toh pehle 1 == 2 → False, phir not False → True. Ye intuitive hai aur isliye ise brackets nahi chahiye.
  3. (not 1) == 2 — brackets se force kiya. not 1 → False, False == 2 → False. Ye dikhaata hai ki brackets se meaning kitni badal sakti hai.
  4. 1 + 2 % 3 — % + se strong hai → 1 + (2 % 3) = 1 + 2 = 3. Log aksar (1+2) % 3 = 0 expect karte hain.
  5. x == 1 & y == 2 — & == se strong hai, toh ye x == (1 & y) == 2 ban jaata hai, jo chained comparison hai. Pandas/numpy mein & hi logical AND hota hai, isliye (df.a == 1) & (df.b == 2) mein brackets mandatory hain. Ye QA mein data validation scripts likhte waqt bar-bar milta hai.

docs.title: Chained comparison — Python ki khaas cheez
docs.text:
status_code = 204
if 200 <= status_code < 300:                   # ek hi expression, do comparisons
    print("2xx success")

# Ye equivalent hai:
if 200 <= status_code and status_code < 300:   # par 'status_code' do baar evaluate hota
    print("same result")

Line-by-line walkthrough:

  1. if 200 <= status_code < 300: — Python isko (200 <= status_code) and (status_code < 300) mein expand karta hai, lekin beech wala operand sirf ek baar evaluate hota hai. Ye tab matter karta hai jab wo function call ho: 200 <= get_status() < 300 mein get_status() ek hi baar chalega. Manual and version mein do baar chalta — do network calls!
  2. Ye short-circuit bhi karta hai: agar pehla comparison False ho, doosra evaluate hi nahi hota.

Gotcha: chaining is aur in ke saath bhi chalti hai, aur wahan surprise deti hai:

print(1 in [1, 2] == True)      # False!
# expand: (1 in [1,2]) and ([1,2] == True)  ->  True and False  ->  False
  1. Yahan in aur == dono same precedence level par hain, toh chain ban gayi. Aapne socha tha (1 in [1,2]) == True → True. Actual: [1,2] == True bhi check ho gaya → False.
  2. Sabak: comparison chain sirf tab likho jab wo genuinely range check ho.

docs.title: / vs // vs % — negative numbers ke saath
docs.text:
print(7 / 2)          # 3.5    -- true division, hamesha float
print(7 // 2)         # 3      -- floor
print(-7 // 2)        # -4     -- floor matlab NEECHE, -3.5 ka floor -4 hai (not -3)
print(7 % 2)          # 1
print(-7 % 2)         # 1      -- Python mein result ka sign DIVISOR ka hota hai
print(7 % -2)         # -1
print(divmod(-7, 2))  # (-4, 1)  -- quotient aur remainder ek saath

Line-by-line walkthrough:

  1. 7 / 2 → 3.5. Python 3 mein / hamesha float deta hai, chahe dono int hon. Python 2 mein 7/2 3 deta tha — ye sabse bada Py2→Py3 breaking change tha aur legacy test scripts port karte waqt silent wrong numbers deta hai.
  2. -7 // 2 → -4. // "floor division" hai, "truncate toward zero" nahi. C/Java -3 dete hain. Agar aapko truncation chahiye toh int(-7 / 2) → -3 ya math.trunc(-7/2).
  3. -7 % 2 → 1. Python guarantee karta hai a == (a // b) * b + (a % b), aur % ka sign divisor jaisa hota hai. Isliye -7 % 2 = -7 - (-4 * 2) = -7 + 8 = 1. QA use: round-robin par test distribute karte waqt index % worker_count hamesha valid index deta hai, chahe index negative ho.
  4. divmod(-7, 2) — ek call mein dono. Jab dono chahiye toh ye tez hai (ek hi division).

docs.title: in operator ka mechanism
docs.text:
class TestSuite:
    def __init__(self, tests):
        self._tests = tests

    def __contains__(self, name):                # 'in' ka fast path
        return name in self._tests               # yahan list ka __contains__ chal raha hai

suite = TestSuite(["test_login", "test_cart"])
print("test_login" in suite)                     # True  -- __contains__ chala
print("test_xyz" in suite)                       # False
  1. def __contains__(self, name): — jab bhi x in obj likha jaaye, Python pehle ye method dhoondhta hai. Ye hone se aap O(1) lookup de sakte ho (agar andar set ho), warna Python poore object par iterate karega.
  2. Agar __contains__ na ho, Python __iter__ se iterate karke == compare karega — O(n). Aur agar __iter__ bhi na ho par __getitem__ ho, toh purana sequence protocol use hoga (obj[0], obj[1], ... IndexError tak).
  3. Isliye 100k test names ke liye name in list_of_names slow hai (O(n)) par name in set_of_names fast (O(1)). Suite filtering mein ye seedha dikhta hai.

docs.title: Gotchas
docs.text:
Gotcha 1 — float equality.

print(0.1 + 0.2)                    # 0.30000000000000004
print(0.1 + 0.2 == 0.3)             # False !!

import math
print(math.isclose(0.1 + 0.2, 0.3))                   # True
print(round(0.1 + 0.2, 10) == round(0.3, 10))         # True (kaam chalau)

from decimal import Decimal
print(Decimal("0.1") + Decimal("0.2") == Decimal("0.3"))   # True (exact)
  1. 0.1 + 0.2 — IEEE-754 double mein 0.1 exactly represent nahi hota (binary fraction nahi hai), toh chhoti si error jamaa ho jaati hai. Ye Python ka bug nahi, har language mein hai.
  2. math.isclose(a, b) — default relative tolerance 1e-09. Ye default choice hai float assertions ke liye. pytest.approx internally isi type ki logic use karta hai: assert total == pytest.approx(0.3).
  3. Decimal("0.1") — string se banao, float se nahi. Decimal(0.1) toh already-broken float ko exact represent karega → 0.1000000000000000055511151231257827. Money assertions ke liye hamesha Decimal + string.

Gotcha 2 — * list par shallow repeat karta hai.

grid = [[0] * 3] * 2                # do rows... ya nahi?
grid[0][0] = 9
print(grid)                         # [[9, 0, 0], [9, 0, 0]]   <- dono rows badal gayi!
  1. [0] * 3 → [0, 0, 0]. Ye theek hai kyunki 0 immutable hai.
  2. [...] * 2 → us ek hi inner list ka reference do baar. Do rows nahi, ek row do baar.
  3. Fix: grid = [[0] * 3 for _ in range(2)] — comprehension har iteration mein naya inner list banata hai. Ye 1.2 ka name-tag model dobara hai, list repetition ke roop mein.

Interview answer: "Operators in Python are syntax for dunder method calls — a + b is type(a).__add__(a, b) with a reflected __radd__ fallback — which is why the same operator means concatenation on strings, union on sets, and dict merge since 3.9. The precedence rules I actively watch are: ** is right-associative, so 2**3**2 is 512; bitwise & binds tighter than ==, which is why pandas conditions need parentheses; and comparisons chain, so 200 <= code < 300 works and evaluates code only once. Two arithmetic details bite people coming from Java: / is always true division returning a float, and // floors rather than truncates, so -7 // 2 is -4. And floats are never compared with == — I use math.isclose or pytest.approx, and Decimal constructed from strings when money is involved."

Cross-question — "How does Python decide between __add__ and __radd__?" "For a + b Python calls type(a).__add__(a, b) first. If that returns NotImplemented, it calls type(b).__radd__(b, a). There's one reordering rule: if type(b) is a proper subclass of type(a) and overrides __radd__, the reflected call goes first, so the more specific class gets the chance to decide. This is exactly how 2 * my_vector can work even though int.__mul__ has no idea what a vector is — int.__mul__ returns NotImplemented and MyVector.__rmul__ handles it."

docs.title: 1.8 Strings and formatting — f-strings ka poora dum
Kya hai
docs.text: String immutable sequence of Unicode code points hai. Formatting matlab values ko text mein embed karna. Python mein iske 4 tareeke hain, aur teen mein se ek hi aaj likhna chahiye.

docs.title: Chaaron tareeke, evolution ke order mein
docs.text:
name, count, duration = "checkout_flow", 12, 3.14159

# 1. %-formatting (Python 1.x se, C ka printf) -- legacy
print("Suite %s ran %d tests in %.2fs" % (name, count, duration))

# 2. str.format (Python 2.6+) -- verbose par flexible
print("Suite {} ran {} tests in {:.2f}s".format(name, count, duration))

# 3. Template strings (string module) -- user-supplied templates ke liye safe
from string import Template
print(Template("Suite $n ran $c tests").substitute(n=name, c=count))

# 4. f-strings (Python 3.6+) -- YE likho
print(f"Suite {name} ran {count} tests in {duration:.2f}s")

Line-by-line walkthrough:

  1. name, count, duration = "checkout_flow", 12, 3.14159 — right side pehle ek tuple banata hai, phir unpacking se teen naam bind hote hain. Agar left par 4 naam hote toh ValueError: not enough values to unpack (expected 4, got 3).
  2. "..." % (name, count, duration) — % operator str.__mod__ call karta hai. %s = str, %d = int, %.2f = 2-decimal float. Khatra: ek single argument tuple ho toh "%s" % (1, 2) TypeError dega, aur "%s" % some_tuple galat expand ho jaayega. Isliye modern code mein iska ek hi bacha hua use case hai: logging (neeche).
  3. "...".format(...) — positional {} ya named {name} dono support karta hai. f-string se pehle ye best tha. Aaj bhi ek jagah useful hai: jab template string runtime par aaye (config file se), kyunki f-string compile time par hi bind hoti hai.
  4. Template(...).substitute(...) — sabse restricted, isliye sabse safe jab template user se aaye. $name ke alawa kuch nahi kar sakta — koi attribute access, koi method call nahi. f-string user input se banana code injection hai.
  5. f"...{duration:.2f}..." — compile time par ye duration.__format__(".2f") calls mein badal jaati hai; koi dict lookup, koi parsing runtime par nahi. Isliye ye sabse tez bhi hai.

docs.title: f-string ki poori capability
docs.text:
test = "test_login_with_invalid_password"
duration = 3.14159
passed = True
data = {"env": "staging", "retries": 2}

# 1. Simple substitution
print(f"{test}")

# 2. Expressions -- koi bhi expression chal sakti hai
print(f"{duration * 1000:.0f}ms")                      # 3142ms

# 3. Format spec: alignment, width, fill
print(f"{test:<40}|")                                  # left align, width 40
print(f"{test:>40}|")                                  # right align
print(f"{test:^40}|")                                  # center
print(f"{test:.<40}|")                                 # fill char '.'
print(f"{duration:>10.2f}")                            # right-aligned float

# 4. Number formatting
print(f"{1234567:,}")                                  # 1,234,567   thousands separator
print(f"{1234567:_}")                                  # 1_234_567
print(f"{0.8523:.1%}")                                 # 85.2%       percentage
print(f"{255:#x}  {255:#o}  {255:#b}")                 # 0xff  0o377  0b11111111
print(f"{3.14159:e}")                                  # 3.141590e+00
print(f"{42:05d}")                                     # 00042       zero-padded

# 5. Nested/dynamic format spec
width = 30
print(f"{test:<{width}}|")                             # width variable se aaya

# 6. Conversions: !r (repr), !s (str), !a (ascii)
print(f"{test!r}")                                     # 'test_login_...'  quotes ke saath

# 7. Self-documenting '=' (Python 3.8+) -- DEBUGGING ka best friend
print(f"{duration=}")                                  # duration=3.14159
print(f"{duration * 2=:.2f}")                          # duration * 2=6.28
print(f"{data['env']=}")                               # data['env']='staging'

# 8. Multi-line f-strings
msg = (
    f"Test: {test}\n"
    f"Env:  {data['env']}\n"
    f"Time: {duration:.2f}s"
)
print(msg)

# 9. Dict access, method calls, ternary -- sab allowed
print(f"{data['retries']} retries, status={'PASS' if passed else 'FAIL'}")
print(f"{test.upper()}")

# 10. Literal braces -- double karo
print(f"{{not a placeholder}} but {duration:.1f} is")

Line-by-line walkthrough (numbers upar ke comments se match karte hain):

  1. f"{test}" — test ka __format__("") call hota hai, jo str(test) jaisa hai. Bina f prefix ke ye literally {test} print karta — f hi placeholder parsing on karta hai.
  2. f"{duration * 1000:.0f}ms" — braces ke andar poori expression allowed hai. : ke baad format spec hai. .0f matlab 0 decimals ke saath float → rounding hoti hai, truncation nahi (3141.59 → 3142).
  3. Alignment: < left, > right, ^ center; </> se pehle jo char likho wo fill hai (. yahan). str ka default alignment left hai, numbers ka default right hai — isliye table banate waqt explicit likhna behtar hai. Ye test report tables banane ke liye seedha kaam ka hai.
  4. {1234567:,} — comma grouping. {0.8523:.1%} — pehle 100 se multiply, phir 1 decimal, phir % lagta hai. {255:#x} — # prefix (0x) add karta hai. {42:05d} — 0 fill + width 5. Ye sab format() mini-language hai jo str.format mein bhi kaam karti hai.
  5. f"{test:<{width}}|" — format spec ke andar dobara braces! Ye runtime par resolve hota hai, isliye aap column width config se le sakte ho.
  6. {test!r} — repr() lagta hai format() se pehle. Logs mein !r use karo: Got status '' vs Got status — pehle wala turant batata hai ki value empty string thi.
  7. f"{duration=}" — Python 3.8+ ka self-documenting expression. Ye expression ka source text + = + uski value print karta hai, aur default repr use karta hai (jab tak aap format spec na do). Debug prints mein ye print("duration:", duration) se strictly better hai kyunki rename karne par label apne aap update ho jaata hai.
  8. Adjacent string literals automatically concatenate hote hain — isliye brackets ke andar teen f-strings likhne se ek hi string banti hai, compile time par. Backslash \n normal escape hai. Note: Python 3.12 se pehle f-string ke expression part mein backslash allowed nahi tha; 3.12+ mein allowed hai.
  9. {'PASS' if passed else 'FAIL'} — conditional expression braces ke andar. Quotes ka dhyaan rakho: 3.12 se pehle andar wahi quote type nahi use kar sakte the jo bahar hai; 3.12+ mein allowed hai. Safe rehna ho toh bahar " aur andar ' rakho.
  10. {{ aur }} — literal brace. JSON template banate waqt ye zaruri hota hai.

docs.title: Kab f-string mat use karo
docs.text:
Logging mein %s style hi likho:

import logging
log = logging.getLogger(__name__)

# GALAT: string hamesha banega, chahe DEBUG level off ho
log.debug(f"Payload: {build_huge_payload()}")     # build_huge_payload() ALWAYS chalega

# SAHI: lazy -- arguments tabhi format hote hain jab record actually emit ho
log.debug("Payload: %s", build_huge_payload)      # (callable pass karna ek trick hai)
log.debug("Status: %s, retries: %d", status, retries)   # normal lazy form
  1. f-string argument evaluate hone se pehle hi poori string bana deta hai. Agar log level INFO hai toh wo string banane ka kaam bekaar gaya — aur ek bade payload par ye seconds kha sakta hai.
  2. log.debug("... %s", value) — logging module string ko tabhi format karta hai jab record handler tak pahunchta hai. Ye standard hai, aur ruff/pylint iske liye warning (G004 / logging-fstring-interpolation) deta hai.
  3. Note: %s mein bhi build_huge_payload() call ho jaayega agar aap brackets lagao — lazy hone ke liye argument ko un-called rakhna padta hai ya lazy wrapper use karna padta hai.

User-supplied templates mein f-string ya eval bilkul nahi:

# KHATRA: agar template user/config se aaya
user_template = "{obj.__class__.__init__.__globals__}"   # attribute walk se secrets
print(user_template.format(obj=object()))                # information disclosure

# SAFE
from string import Template
print(Template("Hello $name").safe_substitute(name="Ritik"))
  1. str.format templates attribute access aur indexing allow karte hain, jisse aap object graph traverse karke __globals__ tak pahunch sakte ho — ye ek known Python security issue hai jab template untrusted ho.
  2. Template.safe_substitute sirf $name replace karta hai aur missing keys par crash bhi nahi karta. Config-driven test data templates ke liye yahi sahi hai.

docs.title: String methods jo QA mein roz kaam aate hain
docs.text:
s = "  Test Suite: Checkout_Flow  "

print(s.strip())                       # 'Test Suite: Checkout_Flow'  -- dono taraf whitespace
print(s.lstrip(), s.rstrip())          # ek taraf
print(s.strip().lower())               # normalise for comparison
print(s.strip().replace(" ", "_"))     # 'Test_Suite:_Checkout_Flow'
print("a,b,c".split(","))              # ['a', 'b', 'c']
print("a,b,c".split(",", 1))           # ['a', 'b,c']   -- maxsplit
print("a,b,c".rsplit(",", 1))          # ['a,b', 'c']   -- right se
print("|".join(["a", "b"]))            # 'a|b'
print("test_login".startswith("test_"))# True   -- pytest collection ka rule
print("report.html".endswith((".html", ".htm")))   # True -- tuple of suffixes
print("Checkout".find("out"))          # 5   -- not found par -1
print("Checkout".index("out"))         # 5   -- not found par ValueError
print("abc".center(11, "-"))           # '----abc----'
print("Test".ljust(10, ".") + "PASS")  # 'Test......PASS'
print("test_login_v2".rpartition("_")) # ('test_login', '_', 'v2')
print("Hello".casefold())              # 'hello' -- lower() se stronger, i18n-safe
print("abc123".isalnum(), "abc".isalpha(), "123".isdigit())   # True True True
print("Line1\nLine2".splitlines())     # ['Line1', 'Line2']
print("%.2f" % 3.14159)                # '3.14'
print("test".removeprefix("te"))       # 'st'   -- Python 3.9+
print("report.html".removesuffix(".html"))  # 'report'  -- 3.9+

Kuch important walkthrough points:

  1. s.strip() — koi argument na do toh whitespace hatata hai. Argument do toh wo ek character set hai, substring nahi: "xxabcxx".strip("xa") → "bc", kyunki wo x aur a dono ko dono taraf se kaatta hai. Ye sabse common misunderstanding hai. Substring hatane ke liye removeprefix/removesuffix (3.9+) use karo.
  2. s.split(",", 1) — maxsplit. "key=value=extra".split("=", 1) → ['key', 'value=extra'] — config parsing ke liye exactly yahi chahiye hota hai.
  3. "|".join(list) — separator par method hai, list par nahi. Kyunki join kisi bhi iterable par kaam karta hai. Agar list mein non-str item ho toh TypeError — isliye ",".join(str(x) for x in ids).
  4. find vs index — find -1 deta hai, index raise karta hai. -1 valid index bhi hai, isliye if s.find(x): bug hai (-1 truthy hai). Sahi: if s.find(x) != -1: ya seedha if x in s:.
  5. endswith(tuple) — multiple suffixes ek call mein. startswith bhi tuple leta hai.
  6. casefold() vs lower() — "STRASSE".lower() aur "straße".lower() alag rehte hain, par casefold() dono ko "strasse" bana deta hai. Case-insensitive comparison ke liye casefold technically sahi hai.
  7. removeprefix/removesuffix — 3.9 se pehle log s[len(p):] if s.startswith(p) else s likhte the, ya galti se s.strip(p) likh dete the jo bug tha.

docs.title: Gotchas
docs.text:
Gotcha 1 — += loop mein quadratic. (Part 3 mein poora treatment)

# BURA: O(n^2) -- har += naya string banata hai
lines = ""
for i in range(10000):
    lines += f"line {i}\n"

# ACHHA: O(n)
lines = "\n".join(f"line {i}" for i in range(10000))

Gotcha 2 — strip() ka character-set behaviour.

print("test_login_test".strip("test"))    # '_login_'   <- 't','e','s','t' chars kaate
print("test_login_test".removeprefix("test").removesuffix("test"))  # '_login_'  -- yahan same,
# par:
print("stest".strip("test"))              # ''   <- poora khatam!
print("stest".removeprefix("test"))       # 'stest'  <- sahi, prefix match nahi hua

Gotcha 3 — mutable-looking string operations naya object dete hain.

s = "hello"
s.upper()               # return value discard ho gaya
print(s)                # 'hello'  -- kuch nahi badla
s = s.upper()           # assign karna padega
print(s)                # 'HELLO'

Interview answer: "I use f-strings everywhere except two places. They're compiled into direct __format__ calls at compile time, so they're the fastest option, and the format mini-language handles alignment, thousands separators, percentages, and precision — which is how I build readable report tables. The self-documenting form, f'{value=}', is my default debug print because the label can't drift from the variable name. The two exceptions: logging, where I pass %s style arguments so the string is only built if the record is actually emitted, and user-supplied templates, where str.format can walk attributes like __class__.__init__.__globals__ and leak state — there I use string.Template, which only substitutes $name."

Cross-question — "Why is str.format still in the standard library if f-strings are better?" "Because f-strings bind their expressions at compile time, so they can't express a template that arrives at runtime. If a test's message template comes from a YAML config or a database row, you need template.format(**values) — an f-string literally cannot do that without eval. str.format is also what logging's {}-style formatter and many templating layers use under the hood. And %-formatting survives because that's the interface logging itself takes."

docs.title: Kya hai
docs.text: if ek statement hai: condition truthy ho toh block chalao. elif "warna agar", else "warna". Python mein switch nahi tha (3.10 tak) — elif chain hi tha.

docs.title: Kaise kaam karta hai
docs.text: Compile hone par ye jump instructions banta hai. Condition ki truthiness 1.6 wale rules se nikalti hai. Sirf pehla matching branch chalta hai — baaki conditions evaluate hi nahi hoti. Isliye ordering matters aur costly checks baad mein rakhne chahiye.

docs.title: Code
docs.text:
def classify_status(code):                      # HTTP status ko category mein daalo
    if code is None:                            # sabse pehle 'no value' -- guard clause
        return "no-response"
    if not isinstance(code, int):               # type guard: str "200" bhi aa sakta hai
        raise TypeError(f"code must be int, got {type(code).__name__}: {code!r}")
    if 200 <= code < 300:                       # chained comparison, code ek baar evaluate
        return "success"
    elif 300 <= code < 400:                     # yahan pahunche matlab 2xx nahi tha
        return "redirect"
    elif 400 <= code < 500:
        return "client-error"
    elif 500 <= code < 600:
        return "server-error"
    else:                                       # 100-199 ya 600+ jaise weird codes
        return "unknown"

print(classify_status(204))      # success
print(classify_status(404))      # client-error
print(classify_status(None))     # no-response

Line-by-line walkthrough:

  1. def classify_status(code): — function ka contract: ek input, ek string output, ya exception. Ek hi cheez karta hai — testable.
  2. if code is None: return "no-response" — guard clause. Ye pattern important hai: special cases pehle handle karke jaldi return kar do, taaki main logic nesting-free rahe. is None isliye (1.5 ka sabak). Agar ye guard na hota toh agli line isinstance(None, int) → False → TypeError uthata, jo shayad aap nahi chahte.
  3. if not isinstance(code, int): — type(code) != int nahi likha, kyunki isinstance subclass ko bhi accept karta hai (jaise bool, ya enum.IntEnum ka member). QA mein status codes aksar http.HTTPStatus enum se aate hain jo IntEnum hai — type() != int usko reject kar deta, isinstance accept karta hai. Ye choice deliberate honi chahiye.
  4. raise TypeError(f"...{type(code).__name__}...{code!r}") — error message mein type aur value dono daale. !r isliye ki "200" aur 200 mein farak dikhe. Ek achha error message aapke debugging ke 10 minute bachaata hai.
  5. if 200 <= code < 300: — chained comparison (1.7). code sirf ek baar evaluate hota hai.
  6. elif 300 <= code < 400: — elif isliye, do alag if nahi. Do alag if likhne se dono conditions evaluate hoti (yahan harmless, par jab conditions mein side effects ya costly calls hon toh nahi). Aur return ke saath toh elif optional hai — par wo intent clearly dikhata hai ki ye branches mutually exclusive hain.
  7. else: return "unknown" — hamesha ek else rakho jo exhaustive ho. Agar else na ho toh function chupchaap None return karega — aur None ko downstream .upper() karne par AttributeError milega bahut door kahin, actual bug se 5 files door.

docs.title: Conditional expression (ternary)
docs.text:
status = "PASS" if exit_code == 0 else "FAIL"          # ek expression, ek value
  1. Syntax A if cond else B hai — condition beech mein (C-style cond ? A : B nahi). Ye readable hai jab aap ise angrezi ki tarah padho: "PASS, agar exit_code 0 hai, warna FAIL".
  2. Ye expression hai, statement nahi — matlab isko return, function argument, ya comprehension ke andar rakh sakte ho. if statement ye nahi kar sakta.
  3. else mandatory hai. x = 1 if cond SyntaxError hai — kyunki expression ko hamesha ek value deni hi hai.
  4. Nesting mat karo: a if c1 else (b if c2 else c) do level tak theek, uske baad if/elif likho ya dict lookup.

docs.title: Dict dispatch — elif chain ka alternative
docs.text:
# --- 8 branches ka elif chain ---
def get_locator_bad(element_type):
    if element_type == "button":
        return "//button"
    elif element_type == "input":
        return "//input"
    elif element_type == "link":
        return "//a"
    else:
        return "//*"

# --- dict dispatch ---
LOCATORS = {                                   # module-level constant, ek baar banta hai
    "button": "//button",
    "input": "//input",
    "link": "//a",
}

def get_locator(element_type):
    return LOCATORS.get(element_type, "//*")   # missing key par default
  1. LOCATORS = {...} — module level par hai, toh import time par ek baar banta hai. Function ke andar likhne se har call par naya dict banta — 1000 calls mein 1000 allocations.
  2. LOCATORS.get(element_type, "//*") — O(1) hash lookup vs O(n) comparisons. Aur naya type add karna ek line hai, naya elif nahi.
  3. Kab nahi: jab branches sirf value nahi, alag logic chalate hon aur unke arguments alag hon. Tab functions ka dict rakho (HANDLERS = {"button": handle_button}), ya match.

Interview answer: "Beyond the syntax, the things I actually apply are: guard clauses first so the happy path isn't buried in nesting; elif rather than repeated if so mutually exclusive branches don't all get evaluated; always an explicit else, because a missing one makes the function silently return None and the failure surfaces far from the cause; and once a chain grows past a handful of branches, replace it with a dict lookup, which turns O(n) comparisons into one hash lookup and makes adding a case a data change instead of a code change."

Cross-question — "When would you deliberately use type(x) is int instead of isinstance(x, int)?" "When subclasses genuinely must be rejected. The classic example is bool, which is a subclass of int, so isinstance(True, int) is True. If I'm validating that a JSON field is a real integer and true should be rejected, type(x) is int is the correct check. Another case is a __eq__ implementation where I want exact-type semantics rather than letting a subclass compare equal. Everywhere else isinstance is right, because rejecting subclasses breaks the Liskov substitution principle — an IntEnum HTTP status should be usable anywhere an int is."

docs.title: Kya hai
docs.text:
match ek structural pattern matching construct hai. Ye C/Java ka switch nahi hai — wo sirf value compare karta hai. match shape compare karta hai aur saath mein destructure bhi karta hai.

Analogy: courier package sorting. Switch = "label par likha city naam dekho". Match = "dabba khol kar dekho: agar andar ek envelope hai jisme ek cheque hai jiska amount X hai, toh ye rule; agar andar do items hain toh wo rule" — aur saath hi X ko nikaal bhi lo.

docs.title: Kyu hai
docs.text:
Bina match ke, nested JSON responses ko handle karna aisa dikhta hai:

# --- PAINFUL: nested dict ko handle karna without match ---
def handle_response_bad(resp):
    if isinstance(resp, dict):
        if "error" in resp:
            err = resp["error"]
            if isinstance(err, dict) and "code" in err and "message" in err:
                return f"Error {err['code']}: {err['message']}"
            return f"Error: {err}"
        if "data" in resp:
            data = resp["data"]
            if isinstance(data, list) and len(data) == 0:
                return "empty result"
            if isinstance(data, list):
                return f"{len(data)} rows"
            return "single object"
    if isinstance(resp, list):
        return f"bare list of {len(resp)}"
    return "unknown shape"

Ye 15 lines mein 8 nested checks hain, aur har check isinstance + in + indexing ka combination hai. Ek key ka naam badla toh 3 jagah badalna padega.

# --- WITH match ---
def handle_response(resp):
    match resp:
        case {"error": {"code": int(code), "message": str(msg)}}:
            return f"Error {code}: {msg}"
        case {"error": err}:
            return f"Error: {err}"
        case {"data": []}:
            return "empty result"
        case {"data": [*rows]}:
            return f"{len(rows)} rows"
        case {"data": dict()}:
            return "single object"
        case [*items]:
            return f"bare list of {len(items)}"
        case _:
            return "unknown shape"

Shape hi code hai. Ye padhne mein bhi seedha hai aur galti karne ki jagah kam hai.

docs.title: Kaise kaam karta hai
docs.text: match subject: subject ko ek baar evaluate karta hai, phir har case pattern ko top-to-bottom try karta hai. Pehla matching case chalta hai, baaki skip. Har pattern compile hoke isinstance checks + __getitem__/__match_args__ lookups mein badalta hai — matlab ye syntactic sugar hai, magic nahi, par safe sugar.

docs.title: Saare pattern types
docs.text:
from dataclasses import dataclass

@dataclass
class TestResult:                          # __match_args__ auto-generate hota hai dataclass se
    name: str
    status: str
    duration: float

def describe(subject):
    match subject:

        # 1. LITERAL pattern -- value se match
        case 200:
            return "ok literal"

        # 2. CAPTURE pattern -- kuch bhi match karo aur naam bind karo
        #    (yahan nahi likh sakte pehle, kyunki ye sab kuch kha jaata hai)

        # 3. VALUE pattern -- dotted name se compare (plain name capture ban jaata hai!)
        case http_ok if subject == 200:
            return f"guarded {http_ok}"

        # 4. OR pattern
        case 301 | 302 | 307 | 308:
            return "redirect"

        # 5. SEQUENCE pattern with capture and star
        case [first, second, *rest]:
            return f"list: first={first}, second={second}, rest={len(rest)}"

        # 6. MAPPING pattern -- SUBSET match, extra keys allowed
        case {"status": "failed", "error": err}:
            return f"failed: {err}"

        # 7. MAPPING with rest capture
        case {"status": status, **extra}:
            return f"status={status}, extra_keys={sorted(extra)}"

        # 8. CLASS pattern with positional args (uses __match_args__)
        case TestResult(name, "passed", duration):
            return f"{name} passed in {duration}s"

        # 9. CLASS pattern with keyword args
        case TestResult(status="failed", name=name):
            return f"{name} FAILED"

        # 10. CLASS pattern as a type check
        case str() as s:
            return f"a string of length {len(s)}"

        # 11. GUARD -- pattern match ke BAAD extra condition
        case int(n) if n > 500:
            return f"big int {n}"

        # 12. WILDCARD -- hamesha match, kuch bind nahi karta
        case _:
            return "no match"

Line-by-line walkthrough:

  1. @dataclass class TestResult: — dataclass automatically __match_args__ = ("name", "status", "duration") set karta hai, jo positional class patterns ko enable karta hai. Plain class mein aapko __match_args__ khud likhna padega, warna TypeError: TestResult() accepts 0 positional sub-patterns.
  2. match subject: — subject ek baar evaluate. Agar aap match get_response(): likho toh network call ek hi baar hoga, chahe 10 cases hon.
  3. case 200: — literal pattern. Comparison == se hoti hai (is se nahi), sivay None, True, False ke — un teeno ke liye is use hota hai. Ye deliberate hai: case True: 1 ko match nahi karega, jabki 1 == True.
  4. case http_ok if subject == 200: — yahan trap hai. http_ok ek plain naam hai, toh ye capture pattern hai — ye har cheez match karega aur usko http_ok naam de dega. Guard (if ...) usko restrict kar raha hai. Agar aap chahte the ki kisi constant HTTP_OK se compare ho, toh dotted likhna padega: case status.HTTP_OK:. Ye Python ka sabse counterintuitive match rule hai: bare name = capture, dotted name = compare.
  5. case 301 | 302 | 307 | 308: — | "or" hai patterns ke beech. Agar alternatives naam bind karte hain toh sab alternatives ko same naam bind karne honge, warna SyntaxError.
  6. case [first, second, *rest]: — sequence pattern. Ye list, tuple, aur zyadatar sequences par kaam karta hai — par str, bytes, bytearray par NAHI, jaan-boojh kar, warna har string char-by-char match hone lagti. *rest baaki sab leta hai (empty bhi ho sakta hai).
  7. case {"status": "failed", "error": err}: — mapping pattern subset match hai: dict mein aur bhi keys ho sakti hain, koi problem nahi. Sequence pattern exact length match karta hai (star ke bina). Ye asymmetry yaad rakhna interview material hai.
  8. case {"status": status, **extra}: — **extra baaki keys ko ek dict mein capture karta hai. **_ bhi likh sakte ho (ignore), par ** akela nahi.
  9. case TestResult(name, "passed", duration): — positional sub-patterns __match_args__ ke order se map hote hain. Doosra sub-pattern "passed" ek literal hai, toh wo constrain kar raha hai; pehla aur teesra capture kar rahe hain.
  10. case TestResult(status="failed", name=name): — keyword form, order-independent aur refactor-safe. Production code mein yahi prefer karo.
  11. case str() as s: — str() ek class pattern hai jiska matlab isinstance(subject, str) hai (constructor call nahi!). as s matched value ko bind karta hai. Ye pattern "type check + bind" ka idiom hai.
  12. case int(n) if n > 500: — int(n) matlab "int hai, aur usko n bind karo" (ye built-in types ka special-case behaviour hai: single positional sub-pattern poore object ko capture karta hai). if n > 500 guard hai — guard match hone ke baad chalta hai, aur fail ho toh agla case try hota hai.
  13. case _: — wildcard. _ special hai: match karta hai par bind nahi karta. Isko hamesha aakhir mein rakho; iske baad koi case likhoge toh wo dead code hai (aur Python SyntaxError: wildcard makes remaining patterns unreachable deta hai).

docs.title: Real QA example — Playwright ka action dispatcher
docs.text:
def perform(step):
