    """step ek dict hai jo YAML test-case file se aaya hai."""
    match step:
        case {"action": "click", "selector": str(sel)}:
            return f"page.click({sel!r})"
        case {"action": "fill", "selector": str(sel), "value": str(val)}:
            return f"page.fill({sel!r}, {val!r})"
        case {"action": "wait", "seconds": int() | float() as secs} if secs <= 30:
            return f"page.wait_for_timeout({secs * 1000})"
        case {"action": "wait", "seconds": _}:
            raise ValueError("wait must be a number <= 30 seconds")
        case {"action": "goto", "url": str(url)} if url.startswith("https://"):
            return f"page.goto({url!r})"
        case {"action": "goto", "url": str(url)}:
            raise ValueError(f"refusing non-https url: {url!r}")
        case {"action": str(unknown)}:
            raise ValueError(f"unknown action: {unknown!r}")
        case _:
            raise ValueError(f"malformed step: {step!r}")

print(perform({"action": "click", "selector": "#submit"}))
print(perform({"action": "wait", "seconds": 2}))

Line-by-line walkthrough:

  1. case {"action": "click", "selector": str(sel)}: — teen cheezein ek saath: action key "click" honi chahiye, selector key honi chahiye, aur wo string honi chahiye. Agar YAML mein galti se selector: 123 likha ho toh ye case match nahi karega aur neeche case _ par pahunch kar clear error milega — silently page.click(123) nahi hoga. Ye pattern matching ka asli faayda hai: validation aur dispatch ek hi jagah.
  2. case {"action": "wait", "seconds": int() | float() as secs} if secs <= 30: — int() | float() matlab "int ya float"; as secs matched value bind karta hai. Guard bound value par condition lagata hai. Note: as poore or-pattern par lagta hai, isliye dono types se bind hota hai.
  3. case {"action": "wait", "seconds": _}: — ye jaan-boojh kar upar wale ke turant baad hai. Agar upar wala guard fail ho (secs > 30), toh execution yahan aati hai aur clear error milta hai. Ye "fallback for a nearly-matching case" pattern hai — bina iske aap case _ par pahunchte aur error message useless hota.
  4. case {"action": "goto", "url": str(url)} if url.startswith("https://"): — security guard pattern ke andar. Isse http URLs silently pass nahi hote.
  5. case {"action": str(unknown)}: — yahan pahunche matlab action key toh hai par kisi specific case se match nahi hui. Error message actionable hai.
  6. case _: raise ValueError(...) — exhaustive. match exhaustiveness enforce nahi karta (Rust ke ulat), toh agar aap case _ na likho aur kuch match na ho toh match block chupchaap kuch nahi karta — poora block skip. Ye silent-failure ka source hai, isliye case _ hamesha likho.

docs.title: Kab use karein / kab nahi
docs.text:
Use match Use if/elif ya dict Nested structures destructure karni hain Simple value equality Multiple shapes handle karne hain (API responses, AST, events) Do-teen branches Type + shape + guard ek saath Ek hi condition Config/YAML-driven step interpreters Hot loop mein — match dict dispatch se dheema hai

Kab NAHI: ek simple if x == "a": ... elif x == "b": ko match mein badalna showing-off hai. Aur agar aapki team 3.9 par hai toh match compile hi nahi hoga — SyntaxError, poori file fail. CI mein Python version pin karo.

docs.title: Gotchas
docs.text:
Gotcha 1 — bare name hamesha capture hai.

OK = 200
def check(code):
    match code:
        case OK:                       # ye "OK naam se bind karo" hai, "200 se compare" nahi
            return "matched anything!"
        case _:
            return "unreachable"

print(check(404))                      # 'matched anything!'   <- BUG

Fix:

import http

def check(code):
    match code:
        case http.HTTPStatus.OK:       # DOTTED name -> value pattern, compare hota hai
            return "ok"
        case _:
            return "other"

print(check(404))                      # 'other'
print(check(200))                      # 'ok'
  1. case OK: — Python parser ke liye ye ek irrefutable capture pattern hai. Isliye wo hamesha match karta hai aur baaki cases dead ho jaate hain (Python 3.11+ isko SyntaxError: name capture 'OK' makes remaining patterns unreachable bhi bol deta hai jab wo aakhri case na ho).
  2. case http.HTTPStatus.OK: — dot hone se ye value pattern ban jaata hai, aur == se compare hota hai. Isliye constants ko hamesha ek class/module/Enum ke andar rakho.

Gotcha 2 — strings sequence pattern se match nahi hoti.

def f(x):
    match x:
        case [a, b]:
            return f"two elements: {a}, {b}"
        case _:
            return "not a 2-sequence"

print(f([1, 2]))     # 'two elements: 1, 2'
print(f("ab"))       # 'not a 2-sequence'   <- deliberate! str sequence pattern se exempt hai

Gotcha 3 — mapping subset, sequence exact.

def f(x):
    match x:
        case {"a": 1}:
            return "dict matched (extra keys ok)"
        case [1]:
            return "list matched (exact length)"
        case _:
            return "no"

print(f({"a": 1, "b": 2}))    # 'dict matched (extra keys ok)'
print(f([1, 2]))              # 'no'   <- length exact hona chahiye

Interview answer: "match is structural pattern matching, not a switch. It matches the shape of a value and destructures it in the same expression, so a nested API response check that would be four levels of isinstance plus key lookups becomes one readable case. The rules that catch people out: a bare name in a pattern is a capture, so case OK: binds everything rather than comparing to the constant — you need a dotted name like case HTTPStatus.OK: for a value comparison. Mapping patterns match a subset of keys, sequence patterns match exact length unless you use a star. Strings are deliberately exempt from sequence patterns so case [a, b] doesn't match a two-character string. And match doesn't enforce exhaustiveness, so I always end with case _ that raises — otherwise an unmatched value silently falls through the whole block."

Cross-question — "Is match faster than an if/elif chain?" "Not automatically. It compiles to roughly the same sequence of checks, plus the destructuring work, so for plain equality on a few values an if/elif chain or a dict dispatch is faster — a dict is one hash lookup versus N sequential pattern attempts. match wins on clarity and correctness for structured data, not on speed. In a hot loop I'd still reach for a dict of handlers."

docs.title: Kya hai
docs.text: for iteration protocol par chalta hai: kisi bhi iterable ke items par ghoomta hai. while ek condition par chalta hai. Python mein C-style for (i=0; i<n; i++) hai hi nahi — uski jagah for i in range(n) hai.

docs.title: Kyu — for i in range(len(x)) ka nuksaan
docs.text:
tests = ["test_login", "test_cart", "test_pay"]

# --- C-programmer style: index se ghoomna ---
for i in range(len(tests)):              # index banao, phir index se element nikalo
    print(i, tests[i])                   # do lookups: range se i, list se tests[i]

# --- Pythonic: seedha element par ghoomo ---
for test in tests:                       # iterator seedha element deta hai
    print(test)

# --- Index bhi chahiye? enumerate ---
for i, test in enumerate(tests, start=1):   # index aur element dono, ek pass mein
    print(f"{i}. {test}")

Line-by-line walkthrough:

  1. for i in range(len(tests)): — len() ek baar chalta hai, range object banta hai, phir har iteration mein tests[i] ek __getitem__ call hai. Ye kaam karta hai par: (a) sirf sequences par chalta hai, generators/sets/dicts par nahi; (b) do operations per item; (c) i ke off-by-one bugs ka darwaza khula hai.
  2. for test in tests: — for pehle iter(tests) call karta hai (jo list_iterator deta hai), phir baar-baar next(). Ye har iterable par same tareeke se chalta hai — list, set, dict, file, generator, database cursor. Yahi Python ka polymorphism hai.
  3. for i, test in enumerate(tests, start=1): — enumerate ek lazy iterator hai jo (index, item) tuples deta hai. start=1 se human-readable numbering milti hai (report mein "Test 1" likhna hai, "Test 0" nahi). Left side par tuple unpacking ho rahi hai. Agar aap for pair in enumerate(tests): likho toh pair ek tuple hoga aur pair[0], pair[1] karna padega — unpacking readable hai.

docs.title: while — kab
docs.text:
import time

def wait_for_element(page, selector, timeout=10.0, poll=0.5):
    """Element dikhne tak wait karo, warna timeout par raise karo."""
    deadline = time.monotonic() + timeout        # absolute deadline, ek baar compute
    while time.monotonic() < deadline:           # condition har iteration par check
        if page.is_visible(selector):            # sasti check pehle
            return True                          # mil gaya -> turant nikal jao
        time.sleep(poll)                         # CPU ko saans do
    raise TimeoutError(f"{selector!r} not visible after {timeout}s")

Line-by-line walkthrough:

  1. def wait_for_element(page, selector, timeout=10.0, poll=0.5): — defaults immutable hain (float), toh 1.4 wala bug nahi. timeout aur poll alag isliye hain ki caller tez polling maang sake bina timeout badle.
  2. deadline = time.monotonic() + timeout — time.monotonic(), time.time() nahi. time.time() wall clock hai — NTP sync ya DST change se peechhe ja sakta hai, jisse aapka loop kabhi khatam nahi hoga ya turant khatam ho jaayega. monotonic sirf aage badhta hai. Ye ek real production bug ka source hai aur interview mein achha point hai.
  3. while time.monotonic() < deadline: — condition har iteration ke shuru mein check hoti hai. Isliye agar timeout=0 ho toh body ek baar bhi nahi chalegi.
  4. if page.is_visible(selector): return True — early return. Loop ke andar se return karna theek hai aur break + flag se saaf hai.
  5. time.sleep(poll) — bina iske ye ek busy-wait hai jo ek CPU core 100% kha jaayega, aur CI runner par doosre tests ko starve karega.
  6. raise TimeoutError(...) — loop ke baad. Yahan pahunchna matlab condition false ho gayi bina success ke. Ye while-else ka natural replacement hai — neeche dekho ki else kab better hai.

Ek classic while bug:

retries = 3
while retries > 0:
    print("attempt")
    # retries -= 1   <- ye bhool gaye toh INFINITE LOOP

Isliye jab bhi while likho, turant socho: "wo kaunsi line hai jo condition ko false ki taraf le jaayegi?" — agar jawab nahi hai toh loop infinite hai.

docs.title: break, continue, pass
docs.text:
results = [
    {"name": "test_a", "status": "passed"},
    {"name": "test_b", "status": "skipped"},
    {"name": "test_c", "status": "failed"},
    {"name": "test_d", "status": "failed"},
]

for r in results:
    if r["status"] == "skipped":
        continue                             # is item ko chhodo, agle par jao
    if r["status"] == "failed":
        print("first failure:", r["name"])
        break                                # poora loop khatam, aage nahi jaana
    print("ok:", r["name"])
  1. continue — current iteration ka bacha hua body skip karke agli iteration par jaata hai. for mein iterator se agla item aata hai; while mein condition dobara check hoti hai. while mein continue khatarnak hai agar increment continue ke neeche ho — infinite loop.
  2. break — poora loop khatam. Nested loops mein sirf sabse andar wala loop tootta hai. Bahar wala todne ke liye flag, exception, ya function + return chahiye.
  3. pass — koi operation nahi, sirf syntactic placeholder jahan Python ko statement chahiye. if x: pass legal hai. pass aur continue alag hain: pass ke baad body ki agli lines chalti hain, continue ke baad nahi.
for r in results:
    if r["status"] == "skipped":
        pass                                 # kuch nahi kiya
    print(r["name"])                         # ye HAR item ke liye chalega -- skipped ke liye bhi

docs.title: for-else aur while-else — jo lagbhag koi nahi jaanta
Kya hai
docs.text:
Loop ke saath else block laga sakte ho. Wo tab chalta hai jab loop break ke bina poora ho jaaye. Naam bhramit karta hai — ise else ki jagah nobreak samajho.

for ... :
    ...
    break        <-- agar ye chal gaya
else:
    ...          <-- toh YE nahi chalega

docs.title: Kyu hai — flag variable se chhutkara
docs.text:
# --- WITHOUT for-else: flag variable ---
target = "test_payment"
found = False                           # extra state, extra chance of bug
for t in tests:
    if t == target:
        found = True                    # flag set
        break
if not found:                           # loop ke bahar flag check
    raise LookupError(f"{target} not in suite")

# --- WITH for-else ---
for t in tests:
    if t == target:
        break                           # mil gaya
else:
    raise LookupError(f"{target} not in suite")   # loop bina break ke khatam hua

Line-by-line walkthrough:

  1. found = False — ye ek extra mutable variable hai. Uske teen failure modes hain: initialise karna bhool jao, break se pehle set karna bhool jao, ya loop ke andar kahin aur galti se reset kar do. for-else ye variable hi hata deta hai.
  2. break — loop se nikalo. for-else mein break hi wo signal hai jo else ko cancel karta hai.
  3. else: raise LookupError(...) — else loop ka hissa hai, if ka nahi. Wo tab chalta hai jab iterator exhaust ho gaya ho bina break ke. Zero-iteration case bhi else chalata hai (khaali list par else chalega) — jo yahan bilkul sahi hai: khaali suite mein target nahi mila.
  4. Indentation dhyaan se: else for ke saath same level par hai, andar nahi.

while-else:

import time

attempts = 0
max_attempts = 3
while attempts < max_attempts:
    attempts += 1
    if try_api_call():                       # maan lo ye bool deta hai
        print(f"succeeded on attempt {attempts}")
        break
    time.sleep(2 ** attempts)                # exponential backoff
else:
    raise RuntimeError(f"API failed after {max_attempts} attempts")
  1. while attempts < max_attempts: — condition false hone par else chalega.
  2. attempts += 1 — body ke shuru mein increment kiya, taaki koi bhi continue/break path isko skip na kar sake. Ye ek defensive habit hai.
  3. time.sleep(2 ** attempts) — 2, 4, 8 seconds. Exponential backoff isliye ki agar service down hai toh hum usko hammer na karein. Real code mein isme jitter bhi add karna chahiye (+ random.uniform(0, 1)) taaki 50 parallel workers ek saath retry na karein — ye "thundering herd" problem hai.
  4. else: raise RuntimeError(...) — ye tab chalta hai jab loop condition false hui, matlab saare attempts khatam. Agar break hua (success) toh else skip.

docs.title: Kab for-else use karo
docs.text:
Use it Don't "search loop" — kuch dhoondho, na mile toh error/default Jab loop ka har item process karna ho Retry loop — sab attempts fail toh raise Jab break hai hi nahi (else bekaar hai) Validation — koi violation na mile toh pass Jab team ko else semantics nahi pata (comment likho)

Real talk: kuch teams for-else ban karti hain kyunki naam confusing hai. Interview mein ise jaanna plus point hai; production PR mein ek short comment (# else runs if we never broke out) lagana samajhdaari hai.

docs.title: Nested loops se bahar nikalna
docs.text:
# --- Problem: inner break sirf inner loop todta hai ---
def find_flaky_pair_bad(runs):
    for i, run_a in enumerate(runs):
        for run_b in runs[i + 1:]:
            if run_a["result"] != run_b["result"]:
                found = (run_a, run_b)
                break                  # sirf inner loop toota
        # yahan aakar outer loop chalta rehta hai -- bug
    return None

# --- Solution 1: function + return (sabse saaf) ---
def find_flaky_pair(runs):
    for i, run_a in enumerate(runs):
        for run_b in runs[i + 1:]:
            if run_a["result"] != run_b["result"]:
                return run_a, run_b        # dono loops se ek saath bahar
    return None

# --- Solution 2: for-else + break chain ---
def find_flaky_pair_v2(runs):
    for i, run_a in enumerate(runs):
        for run_b in runs[i + 1:]:
            if run_a["result"] != run_b["result"]:
                break                       # inner break
        else:
            continue                        # inner poora hua bina break ke -> outer continue
        break                               # yahan sirf tab pahunchte hain jab inner ne break kiya
    else:
        return None
    return run_a, run_b

Line-by-line walkthrough:

  1. Solution 1 mein return dono loops se ek saath bahar nikal jaata hai kyunki return function se return karta hai, loop se nahi. Ye sabse readable hai — isliye "nested loop se bahar nikalna hai" ka sabse achha jawab hai "loop ko function mein daalo".
  2. Solution 2 ka for-else + continue/break chain kaam karta hai par padhne mein bura hai. Maine ise jaan-boojh kar dikhaya taaki aap interview mein bol sako ki "ye possible hai par main ise nahi likhunga" — yahi senior wala jawab hai.
  3. runs[i + 1:] — slice har outer iteration mein naya list object banata hai (O(n) copy). Bade data par itertools.combinations(runs, 2) behtar hai — wo lazy hai aur copy nahi karta.

docs.title: Gotchas
docs.text:
Gotcha 1 — iterate karte waqt list modify mat karo.

tests = ["a", "b_skip", "c", "d_skip", "e"]
for t in tests:
    if t.endswith("_skip"):
        tests.remove(t)                    # iterator ka index aur list shift ho gaya
print(tests)                               # ['a', 'c', 'd_skip', 'e']   <- 'd_skip' bach gaya!
  1. list_iterator internally ek index rakhta hai. remove ke baad saare elements ek position left shift ho gaye, par iterator ka index badha hi tha — toh ek element skip ho gaya.
  2. Fix (do sahi tareeke): 
    tests = [t for t in tests if not t.endswith("_skip")]   # naya list -- sabse saaf
# ya, agar aapko wahi object rakhna hai (kisi aur ne reference pakda hai):
tests[:] = [t for t in tests if not t.endswith("_skip")]   # in-place, slice assignment
    Pehla naya object banata hai; doosra usi object ko overwrite karta hai — jo tab zaruri hai jab kisi aur ne us list ka reference pakad rakha ho.
  3. Dict par iterate karte hue key add/remove karo toh Python turant RuntimeError: dictionary changed size during iteration deta hai — list se behtar behaviour, kyunki silent nahi hai.

Gotcha 2 — loop variable loop ke baad zinda rehta hai.

for i in range(3):
    pass
print(i)                    # 2   <- 'i' abhi bhi exist karta hai (Python mein loop ka apna scope nahi)

for j in []:
    pass
# print(j)                  # NameError -- kyunki loop kabhi chala hi nahi
  1. Python mein for loop apna scope nahi banata (comprehensions banati hain — 2.4). Isliye loop variable function scope mein leak karta hai.
  2. Khaali iterable par loop variable bind hi nahi hota, toh baad mein use karna NameError deta hai — aur ye conditional bug hai jo sirf khaali input par dikhta hai.

Gotcha 3 — for ke andar bahut kaam repeat.

# BURA: har iteration mein attribute lookup + method lookup
for t in tests:
    self.report.results.append(t.upper())

# BEHTAR: lookups loop se bahar hoist karo
append = self.report.results.append       # ek baar lookup
for t in tests:
    append(t.upper())
  1. self.report.results.append har iteration mein teen attribute lookups hai (dict lookups). 10 lakh iterations par ye measurable hai.
  2. Ye micro-optimisation hai — pehle profile karo, phir karo. Par interview mein ye dikhata hai ki aap jaante ho ki attribute access sasta nahi hai.

Interview answer: "Python's for is a foreach over the iterator protocol, not a counter loop, so I never write for i in range(len(x)) — I iterate the object directly and use enumerate when I need the index. while is for condition-driven loops, and my rule there is: the moment I write while, I identify the line that will eventually make the condition false. For polling loops I use time.monotonic rather than time.time, because the wall clock can jump backwards on an NTP sync and hang the loop. The feature most people don't know is loop else: it runs when the loop finishes without hitting break, so a search loop or a retry loop doesn't need a found flag. I read it as nobreak, not else. And the two loop gotchas I check for in review are mutating a list while iterating it — which silently skips elements because the iterator's index and the list shift out of sync — and assuming the loop variable exists afterwards, which fails on an empty iterable."

Cross-question — "Why does for not create a new scope, when comprehensions do?" "Historically neither did — in Python 2 a list comprehension leaked its variable too, and [x for x in ...] would clobber an outer x. Python 3 gave comprehensions their own implicit function scope specifically to stop that leak, and that also made generator expressions and comprehensions behave consistently. The plain for statement wasn't changed because too much existing code deliberately uses the loop variable after the loop — the classic for line in f: ... then print(line) pattern. So it's a backwards-compatibility decision, not a design principle. The practical consequence is that the loop variable is a normal local, and if the iterable is empty it was never bound at all."

docs.title: Kya hai
docs.text:
Comprehension ek expression hai jo iterable se naya container banati hai. Chaar kism:

Form Syntax Result List [expr for x in it] list Set {expr for x in it} set Dict {k: v for x in it} dict Generator (expr for x in it) lazy generator

Tuple comprehension nahi hoti — (x for x in it) generator hai. Tuple chahiye toh tuple(x for x in it).

docs.title: Kyu hai
docs.text:
results = [
    {"name": "test_login", "status": "passed", "duration": 1.2},
    {"name": "test_cart", "status": "failed", "duration": 4.5},
    {"name": "test_pay", "status": "failed", "duration": 0.8},
]

# --- WITHOUT comprehension ---
failed_names = []                              # khaali container banao
for r in results:                              # loop
    if r["status"] == "failed":                # filter
        failed_names.append(r["name"])         # transform + append
# 4 lines, 1 mutable variable, 1 method call per item

# --- WITH comprehension ---
failed_names = [r["name"] for r in results if r["status"] == "failed"]
# 1 line, koi mutable intermediate nahi, aur tez bhi

Comprehension tez kyun hai: CPython comprehension ko ek special bytecode sequence mein compile karta hai jo LIST_APPEND opcode use karta hai — koi append method lookup nahi hota har iteration mein. Manual loop mein results.append har baar dict lookup karta hai. Farak 20-40% ka hota hai.

docs.title: Kaise kaam karta hai
docs.text:
[expr for x in it if cond] internally lagbhag isme compile hota hai:

def _implicit():                    # comprehension ka APNA scope hota hai (Python 3+)
    _result = []
    for x in it:                    # 'it' bahar se evaluate hoke aata hai
        if cond:
            _result.append(expr)
    return _result

Do important consequences:

  1. Comprehension ka loop variable bahar leak nahi karta.
  2. Comprehension ke andar se bahar ke variables read ho sakte hain (closure), par nonlocal/global ke bina write nahi.
x = "outer"
squares = [x for x in range(3)]     # andar ka x alag scope mein hai
print(x)                            # 'outer'  <- bilkul nahi badla (Python 2 mein badal jaata tha)

docs.title: Saare forms — ek-ek karke
docs.text:
results = [
    {"name": "test_login", "status": "passed", "duration": 1.2, "tags": ["smoke", "auth"]},
    {"name": "test_cart", "status": "failed", "duration": 4.5, "tags": ["regression"]},
    {"name": "test_pay", "status": "failed", "duration": 0.8, "tags": ["smoke", "payment"]},
]

# 1. Basic map
names = [r["name"] for r in results]
print(names)                    # ['test_login', 'test_cart', 'test_pay']

# 2. Map + filter
slow = [r["name"] for r in results if r["duration"] > 1.0]
print(slow)                     # ['test_login', 'test_cart']

# 3. Transform with expression
upper_names = [r["name"].upper().replace("_", " ") for r in results]
print(upper_names)              # ['TEST LOGIN', 'TEST CART', 'TEST PAY']

# 4. Conditional EXPRESSION (ternary) -- 'if' expr ke andar, filter nahi
labels = ["SLOW" if r["duration"] > 1.0 else "fast" for r in results]
print(labels)                   # ['SLOW', 'SLOW', 'fast']

# 5. Ternary + filter ek saath
labels2 = ["SLOW" if r["duration"] > 1.0 else "fast"
           for r in results
           if r["status"] == "failed"]
print(labels2)                  # ['SLOW', 'fast']

# 6. Nested loops (flatten)
all_tags = [tag for r in results for tag in r["tags"]]
print(all_tags)                 # ['smoke', 'auth', 'regression', 'smoke', 'payment']

# 7. Nested loops + filter
smoke_names = [r["name"] for r in results for tag in r["tags"] if tag == "smoke"]
print(smoke_names)              # ['test_login', 'test_pay']

# 8. Nested COMPREHENSION (list of lists)
matrix = [[r["name"], r["status"]] for r in results]
print(matrix)                   # [['test_login', 'passed'], ...]

# 9. Set comprehension -- duplicates hat jaate hain
unique_tags = {tag for r in results for tag in r["tags"]}
print(unique_tags)              # {'smoke', 'auth', 'regression', 'payment'}  (order random)

# 10. Dict comprehension
durations = {r["name"]: r["duration"] for r in results}
print(durations)                # {'test_login': 1.2, 'test_cart': 4.5, 'test_pay': 0.8}

# 11. Dict comprehension: invert a dict
inverted = {v: k for k, v in durations.items()}
print(inverted)                 # {1.2: 'test_login', 4.5: 'test_cart', 0.8: 'test_pay'}

# 12. Generator expression -- LAZY, memory nahi khaata
total_duration = sum(r["duration"] for r in results)
print(round(total_duration, 1)) # 6.5

Line-by-line walkthrough:

  1. [r["name"] for r in results] — for r in results iterate karta hai, r["name"] har item par expression evaluate karta hai. Order guaranteed hai (list order preserve hoti hai).
  2. if r["duration"] > 1.0 — ye filter hai, for ke baad aata hai. Filter pehle chalta hai, phir expression — matlab filtered-out items par expression evaluate hi nahi hota. Ye tab matter karta hai jab expression costly ho.
  3. .upper().replace("_", " ") — method chaining. Har call naya string banati hai (str immutable), toh yahan 2 temporary strings banti hain per item. 3 items ke liye theek, 10 lakh ke liye socho.
  4. "SLOW" if r["duration"] > 1.0 else "fast" — ye conditional expression hai jo for se pehle aata hai. Yahi comprehension ka sabse confusing part hai:
  5. for ke baad wala if = filter (item ko chhodo ya rakho),
  6. for ke pehle wala if...else = transform (har item ke liye value chuno). Filter mein else nahi ho sakta; ternary mein else mandatory hai. Yahi mnemonic hai.
  7. Line 5 mein dono hain — pehle filter (status == "failed"), phir bache hue items par ternary. Multi-line likha kyunki ek line mein padhna mushkil hota.
  8. [tag for r in results for tag in r["tags"]] — nested loops ka order wahi hai jo nested for statements ka hota: bahar wala pehle, andar wala baad mein. Isko aise padho: 
    out = []
for r in results:            # pehla 'for'
    for tag in r["tags"]:    # doosra 'for'
        out.append(tag)      # expression
    Log aksar order ulta likh dete hain (for tag in r["tags"] for r in results) — wo NameError: name 'r' is not defined dega, kyunki r abhi bind hi nahi hua.
  9. Line 7 mein filter sabse andar wale loop par lag raha hai. Note: smoke_names mein duplicates aa sakte hain agar ek test ke do smoke tags hon.
  10. [[r["name"], r["status"]] for r in results] — expression khud ek list literal hai, toh list of lists banti hai. Ye "nested comprehension" nahi hai, sirf nested data hai.
  11. {tag for ...} — curly braces + koi colon nahi = set. Duplicates automatically hat jaate hain. Order guaranteed nahi hai (hash order). Agar deterministic output chahiye (test assertions!) toh sorted(unique_tags) karo.
  12. {r["name"]: r["duration"] for r in results} — colon hone se dict banti hai. Duplicate keys par last wins silently — agar do tests ka naam same ho toh ek gayab ho jaayega bina kisi warning ke. Ye report-parsing mein real bug hai.
  13. {v: k for k, v in durations.items()} — .items() (key, value) tuples deta hai, jinhe k, v mein unpack kiya. Inversion tabhi safe hai jab values unique aur hashable hon.
  14. sum(r["duration"] for r in results) — generator expression, koi square brackets nahi. Jab genexp function ka akela argument ho toh extra brackets ki zarurat nahi. Ye list nahi banata, toh 10 lakh results par memory constant rehti hai.

docs.title: Walrus operator comprehension ke andar
docs.text:
import re

log_lines = [
    "2026-08-23 10:00:01 PASS test_login 1.2s",
    "garbage line",
    "2026-08-23 10:00:05 FAIL test_cart 4.5s",
]

PATTERN = re.compile(r"(?P<status>PASS|FAIL) (?P<name>\w+) (?P<dur>[\d.]+)s")

# --- WITHOUT walrus: regex do baar chalta hai ---
parsed_bad = [PATTERN.search(line).groupdict()
              for line in log_lines
              if PATTERN.search(line)]              # search() DO baar per line

# --- WITH walrus: ek baar ---
parsed = [m.groupdict()
          for line in log_lines
          if (m := PATTERN.search(line))]           # match ko bind kiya aur test bhi kiya

print(parsed)
# [{'status': 'PASS', 'name': 'test_login', 'dur': '1.2'},
#  {'status': 'FAIL', 'name': 'test_cart', 'dur': '4.5'}]

Line-by-line walkthrough:

  1. PATTERN = re.compile(...) — module level par compile kiya, taaki ye ek baar ho. Har call mein re.search(pattern_string, line) likhna bhi kaam karta hai (internal cache hai) par explicit compile clearer aur thoda tez hai.
  2. (?P<status>PASS|FAIL) — named group. groupdict() se {"status": ...} milta hai — m.group(1) se behtar hai kyunki pattern badalne par index nahi tootta.
  3. parsed_bad version: filter PATTERN.search(line) chalata hai, phir expression dobara chalata hai. Do regex passes per line. 50 MB log par ye seedha 2x time hai.
  4. if (m := PATTERN.search(line)) — walrus := assign karta hai aur value bhi deta hai. Toh m bind ho gaya aur uski truthiness filter ban gayi (match object truthy, None falsy). Phir expression mein m use kar liya.
  5. Brackets (m := ...) zaruri hain comprehension ke if mein — bina brackets ke SyntaxError. Ye jaan-boojh kar hai, taaki = aur := ki galti kam ho.

docs.title: Kab comprehension use karo, kab nahi
docs.text:
Use Don't Ek transform + ek filter 3+ nested for, ya 2+ conditions Result poora chahiye aur chhota hai Bade data — genexp use karo Expression side-effect free hai Side effects ([print(x) for x in y] — ye paap hai) Ek line mein padh sakte ho Padhne ke liye do baar dekhna pade toh loop likho 
# ANTI-PATTERN: side effect ke liye comprehension
[print(r["name"]) for r in results]      # ek bekaar list banti hai [None, None, None]

# SAHI
for r in results:
    print(r["name"])
  1. Comprehension ka maqsad ek container banana hai. Agar aap result discard kar rahe ho toh aap galat tool use kar rahe ho — aur aap chupchaap memory allocate kar rahe ho.
  2. ruff isko C417/B018 type rules se pakadta hai.

docs.title: Gotchas
docs.text:
Gotcha 1 — nested comprehension mein late binding.

matrix = [[1, 2], [3, 4]]
# Transpose
transposed = [[row[i] for row in matrix] for i in range(2)]
print(transposed)                # [[1, 3], [2, 4]]   -- sahi
  1. Andar wali comprehension apna scope banati hai par i bahar wali comprehension ke scope se closure ke through padh leti hai. Ye kaam karta hai kyunki andar wali comprehension turant evaluate ho jaati hai. Agar andar generator expression hota ((row[i] for ...)) toh wo lazy hota aur i ki final value pakad leta — classic late-binding bug (Part 4).

Gotcha 2 — dict comprehension mein duplicate keys silently drop.

results = [{"name": "test_a", "d": 1}, {"name": "test_a", "d": 9}]
d = {r["name"]: r["d"] for r in results}
print(d)                          # {'test_a': 9}   <- pehla record gayab, koi warning nahi
print(len(results), len(d))       # 2 1

Fix — grouping karo, overwrite nahi:

from collections import defaultdict
grouped = defaultdict(list)
for r in results:
    grouped[r["name"]].append(r["d"])
print(dict(grouped))              # {'test_a': [1, 9]}

Gotcha 3 — comprehension mein exception poore comprehension ko kill karti hai.

raw = ["1.2", "bad", "4.5"]
# durations = [float(x) for x in raw]     # ValueError, poora comprehension fail

durations = []
for x in raw:
    try:
        durations.append(float(x))
    except ValueError:
        continue                          # sirf ye item chhoda
print(durations)                          # [1.2, 4.5]
  1. Comprehension ke andar try/except nahi likh sakte — wo statement hai, expression nahi.
  2. Do options: (a) upar wala explicit loop, (b) ek helper function jo None deta hai aur phir filter: [v for x in raw if (v := safe_float(x)) is not None].

Gotcha 4 — bade data par list comprehension memory kha jaati hai.

# 5 GB log file
# lines = [line for line in open("huge.log")]     # poori file RAM mein -- MemoryError

with open("huge.log") as f:
    error_count = sum(1 for line in f if "ERROR" in line)   # constant memory

Interview answer: "A comprehension is an expression that builds a container from an iterable. There are four forms — list, set, dict, and generator — and the generator one is the lazy version, so sum(x.duration for x in results) never materialises a list. They're faster than the equivalent loop because CPython compiles them to a dedicated LIST_APPEND opcode instead of looking up the append method every iteration, and since Python 3 they get their own scope so the loop variable doesn't leak. The syntax detail people mix up is the two positions for if: after the for it's a filter with no else allowed; before the for it's a conditional expression where else is mandatory. My rule for when to stop using them: one transform and one filter is fine; two nested loops is borderline; anything with three, or anything that needs a try/except, becomes a plain loop. And I never write a comprehension purely for side effects, because it allocates a list of Nones nobody reads."

Cross-question — "Why is a comprehension faster than the equivalent for loop that appends?" "Two reasons, and the second is the bigger one. First, the comprehension body runs inside an implicit function, so the list being built and the loop variable are function locals accessed by array index via LOAD_FAST, rather than globals accessed through a dictionary. Second, the append is a single LIST_APPEND opcode operating on a list held on the value stack — no LOAD_ATTR for .append and no function call frame per item. In a microbenchmark that's typically 20 to 40 percent. It isn't a reason to rewrite loops as comprehensions though; it's a reason not to feel bad about using them."

docs.title: Kya hai
docs.text:
:= ek assignment expression hai: assign bhi karta hai aur value bhi deta hai. Normal = ek statement hai — wo value nahi deta, isliye if x = f(): Python mein SyntaxError hai (C mein ye legal hai aur wahan == vs = ke bugs famous hain).

Analogy: ATM se paise nikalte waqt receipt bhi mil jaati hai. Ek hi kaam, do outputs — paise (side effect) aur receipt (value).

docs.title: Kyu hai
docs.text:
# --- WITHOUT walrus: function do baar call karna padta hai ---
if get_element_count() > 0:                       # call 1
    print(f"found {get_element_count()} elements")  # call 2 -- dobara DOM query!

# --- ya, ek extra line lagti hai jo scope gandaa karti hai ---
count = get_element_count()
if count > 0:
    print(f"found {count} elements")

# --- WITH walrus ---
if (count := get_element_count()) > 0:
    print(f"found {count} elements")

Bara faayda while loops mein hai:

# --- WITHOUT walrus: "loop and a half" problem ---
line = log_file.readline()                # pehle read (duplicate code)
while line:
    process(line)
    line = log_file.readline()            # phir read (duplicate code)

# --- WITH walrus ---
while (line := log_file.readline()):
    process(line)                         # ek hi jagah read

Duplicate readline() line hi asli problem thi: usme se ek badal do, doosra bhool jao, aur infinite loop mil jaata hai. Walrus wo duplication khatm karta hai.

docs.title: Kaise kaam karta hai
docs.text:
:= ek expression hai jo target ko enclosing scope mein bind karta hai — comprehension ke andar likho toh bhi wo comprehension ke bahar wale function scope mein bind hota hai. Ye deliberately alag hai comprehension ke loop variable se.

data = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]
filtered = [y for x in data if (y := x * 2) > 4]
print(filtered)       # [6, 8, 10]
print(y)              # 10  <- 'y' bahar bhi visible hai! (loop var 'x' nahi hai)
# print(x)            # NameError
  1. x comprehension ka loop variable hai → comprehension ke implicit scope mein → leak nahi karta.
  2. y walrus se bind hua → enclosing scope mein → leak karta hai, aur uski value aakhri iteration wali hai.
  3. Ye jaan-boojh kar design kiya gaya (PEP 572) taaki aap comprehension ke andar compute ki hui cheez baad mein use kar sako. Par surprise dene wala hai, isliye is par bharosa mat karo.

docs.title: Real QA examples
docs.text:
import re
import json

# 1. Regex match ko test bhi karo aur use bhi
TIMING = re.compile(r"took (\d+)ms")
line = "request took 342ms"
if (m := TIMING.search(line)):
    print(int(m.group(1)))                    # 342

# 2. Chunked file reading
def read_in_chunks(path, size=8192):
    with open(path, "rb") as f:
        while chunk := f.read(size):          # b"" falsy -> loop khatam
            yield chunk

# 3. Expensive call ka result reuse
def find_slow_tests(results, threshold=3.0):
    return [
        {"name": name, "over_by": round(d - threshold, 2)}
        for r in results
        if (d := r["duration"]) > threshold
        for name in [r["name"]]                # (thoda hack; simple version neeche)
    ]

# Simpler, better:
def find_slow_tests_v2(results, threshold=3.0):
    return [
        {"name": r["name"], "over_by": round(d - threshold, 2)}
        for r in results
        if (d := r["duration"]) > threshold
    ]

# 4. API pagination
def fetch_all(client):
    page = 1
    results = []
    while (batch := client.get_page(page)):    # khaali list falsy -> ruk jao
        results.extend(batch)
        page += 1
    return results

Line-by-line walkthrough:

  1. if (m := TIMING.search(line)): — search Match object ya None deta hai. Match object hamesha truthy hota hai (empty match bhi!) — isliye ye check safe hai. Brackets if mein technically optional hain (if m := TIMING.search(line): legal hai), par comparison ke saath mandatory hain: if (n := f()) > 5:. Consistency ke liye hamesha brackets lagao.
  2. while chunk := f.read(size): — read file end par b"" deta hai, jo falsy hai → loop khatam. Khatra: agar file mein genuinely ek chunk aisa ho jo falsy ho... binary mein nahi ho sakta (read sirf EOF par khaali deta hai), toh yahan safe hai. Par while x := next_value(): mein agar 0 valid value ho toh loop galat time par ruk jaayega — tab while (x := next_value()) is not None: likho.
  3. yield chunk — generator (Part 6). Poori file memory mein nahi aati.
  4. if (d := r["duration"]) > threshold — dict lookup ek baar, use do jagah (filter aur expression). Bina walrus ke r["duration"] do baar likhna padta.
  5. while (batch := client.get_page(page)): — pagination ka classic. Khaali list falsy hai → loop khatam. Note: agar API khaali page ke baad bhi data de sakta hai (sparse pages), toh ye galat hai — tab explicit has_more flag chahiye. Truthiness par bharosa tabhi karo jab semantics genuinely "khaali matlab khatam" ho.

docs.title: Kab NAHI use karna
docs.text:
# 1. Simple assignment ki jagah -- ye sirf confusing hai
# (y := 5)          # bas 'y = 5' likho

# 2. Nested walrus -- padhne layak nahi
# if (a := (b := f()) + 1) > 10:

# 3. Jahan side effect chhup jaaye
# results = [process(x) for x in data if (logged := log(x))]   # log() side effect chhupa hai

# 4. Lambda ke andar
# f = lambda x: (y := x * 2)      # legal par bekaar

Rule: walrus duplication hataane ke liye hai. Agar wo duplication nahi hata raha, use mat karo.

docs.title: Gotchas
docs.text:
Gotcha 1 — attribute ya subscript par walrus nahi chalta.

# self.count := 5        # SyntaxError
# d["k"] := 5            # SyntaxError

Walrus ka target simple name hona chahiye. Ye deliberate restriction hai.

Gotcha 2 — top-level expression statement mein brackets chahiye.

# y := 5          # SyntaxError
(y := 5)          # legal (par bekaar)
print(y)          # 5

Gotcha 3 — while (line := f.readline()): vs for line in f:

# Walrus version -- kaam karta hai par zaruri nahi
with open("test.log") as f:
    while line := f.readline():
        print(line.rstrip())

# Iterator version -- BEHTAR, kyunki file khud iterable hai
with open("test.log") as f:
    for line in f:
        print(line.rstrip())
  1. File object khud ek iterator hai jo line-by-line deta hai, aur internally buffered read karta hai — readline() loop se tez bhi hai.
  2. Sabak: walrus ek tool hai, default nahi. Pehle poocho "kya iske bina saaf tareeka hai?"

Interview answer: "The walrus operator is an assignment expression: it binds a name and evaluates to the value, so you can assign inside a condition. It exists to remove duplication, not to save a line. The two cases where it genuinely helps are the loop-and-a-half pattern — while chunk := f.read(8192) instead of reading once before the loop and again at the bottom — and reusing a match object, if (m := pattern.search(line)): so the regex runs once instead of twice. Inside a comprehension it binds in the enclosing scope rather than the comprehension's own scope, which is deliberate but surprising. I don't use it for plain assignment, and I don't nest it — if it isn't eliminating a duplicated call, it's just making the line harder to read."

Cross-question — "Why did PEP 572 restrict the target to a plain name?" "To keep the feature small and unambiguous. Allowing self.count := 5 or d['k'] := 5 would mean assignment expressions could trigger __setattr__ and __setitem__ inside conditions and comprehensions, where side effects are hardest to see. The restriction also avoids parsing ambiguity with annotations and slices. The PEP was famously contentious — it's the proposal after which Guido stepped down as BDFL — so the final design is deliberately conservative: one form, plain names only, and parentheses required almost everywhere."

docs.title: Kya hai
docs.text:
Teeno lazy hain: wo apna poora result pehle se nahi banate, ek-ek item on demand dete hain.

  • range(start, stop, step) — arithmetic sequence, sequence hai (indexable, len hai).
  • enumerate(iterable, start=0) — (index, item) tuples ka iterator.
  • zip(*iterables) — parallel iterables ko (a, b, ...) tuples mein jodne wala iterator.

docs.title: Kyu lazy hain
docs.text:
# Agar range eager hota:
# r = range(10_000_000)      # 10 million ints ki list -> ~400 MB RAM
import sys
print(sys.getsizeof(range(10_000_000)))    # 48 bytes -- CONSTANT, size se independent
print(sys.getsizeof(list(range(10))))      # 136 bytes -- 10 items ke liye
print(sys.getsizeof(list(range(1000))))    # ~8056 bytes -- 1000 items ke liye

Line-by-line walkthrough:

  1. sys.getsizeof(range(10_000_000)) — 48 bytes. range sirf teen ints store karta hai: start, stop, step. Wo values compute karta hai jab maanga jaaye: r[i] == start + i*step. Isliye range(10**18) bhi banaya ja sakta hai bina memory ke.
  2. 10_000_000 — underscore digit separator (3.6+). Ye sirf padhne ke liye hai, parser ignore karta hai. Bade numbers likhte waqt hamesha use karo — 10000000 mein zeros ginne padte hain.
  3. sys.getsizeof(list(range(1000))) — list ko har element ka pointer store karna padta hai (8 bytes per pointer on 64-bit), plus over-allocation. Isliye size linear badhta hai.
  4. Note: getsizeof sirf container ka size deta hai, uske andar ke objects ka nahi. sys.getsizeof([big_string]) chhota aayega. Deep size ke liye pympler chahiye (Part 14).

docs.title: range ki poori API
docs.text:
print(list(range(5)))                # [0, 1, 2, 3, 4]        stop only
print(list(range(2, 5)))             # [2, 3, 4]              start, stop
print(list(range(0, 10, 3)))         # [0, 3, 6, 9]           step
print(list(range(10, 0, -1)))        # [10, 9, ..., 1]        reverse
print(list(range(5, 5)))             # []                     empty (start == stop)
print(list(range(5, 0)))             # []                     empty (galat direction)

r = range(0, 100, 5)
print(len(r))                        # 20      -- O(1), compute hota hai
print(r[3])                          # 15      -- O(1), start + 3*step
print(r[-1])                         # 95      -- negative index bhi chalta hai
print(50 in r)                       # True    -- O(1) for int! arithmetic check hai
print(51 in r)                       # False
print(r[2:5])                        # range(10, 25, 5)  -- slice bhi range deta hai
print(list(reversed(r))[:3])         # [95, 90, 85]

Line-by-line walkthrough:

  1. range(5) — ek argument ho toh wo stop hai, start=0, step=1. stop exclusive hai — ye deliberate hai taaki range(len(x)) exactly valid indices de, aur range(a,b) ka length b-a ho.
  2. range(10, 0, -1) — negative step. Note ye 1 par rukta hai, 0 par nahi (stop exclusive). 0 chahiye toh range(10, -1, -1).
  3. range(5, 0) — khaali. Ye silent hai — koi error nahi. Agar aapka loop kabhi nahi chal raha toh sabse pehle range ki direction check karo.
  4. len(r) — (stop - start + step - 1) // step se compute hota hai, iterate nahi karta.
  5. 50 in r — range.__contains__ int ke liye O(1) hai: wo check karta hai ki (50 - start) % step == 0 aur range ke andar hai. Ye special-case optimization hai. Non-int (jaise 50.0 ya string) ke liye wo fallback karta hai linear scan par.
  6. r[2:5] — slicing ek naya range deti hai, list nahi. Lazy hi rehta hai.
  7. reversed(r) — range __reversed__ implement karta hai, toh ye bhi O(1) hai.

docs.title: enumerate
docs.text:
tests = ["test_login", "test_cart", "test_pay"]

for i, name in enumerate(tests):                # default start=0
    print(i, name)

for i, name in enumerate(tests, start=1):       # report ke liye 1-based
    print(f"{i}/{len(tests)} {name}")

# enumerate ek iterator hai -- ek baar consume ho gaya toh khatam
e = enumerate(tests)
print(list(e))          # [(0, 'test_login'), (1, 'test_cart'), (2, 'test_pay')]
print(list(e))          # []   <- KHATAM! dobara nahi mila

Line-by-line walkthrough:

  1. enumerate(tests) — ek enumerate object banta hai jo tests ke iterator ko wrap karta hai aur ek counter rakhta hai. Har next() par (counter, next_item) tuple banta hai.
  2. for i, name in ... — tuple unpacking. Agar aap for x in enumerate(tests): likho toh x tuple hoga.
  3. start=1 — keyword se do, positional se nahi (enumerate(tests, 1) bhi chalta hai par 1 ka matlab code padhne wale ko nahi pata chalta).
  4. list(e) doosri baar [] — kyunki enumerate ek iterator hai, iterable nahi. Iterator ek baar hi chalte hain. Ye Part 6 ka core concept hai, aur real bug banta hai jab aap ek generator ko do baar loop karne ki koshish karte ho.

docs.title: zip
docs.text:
names = ["test_login", "test_cart", "test_pay"]
durations = [1.2, 4.5, 0.8]
statuses = ["passed", "failed", "failed"]

for name, dur, status in zip(names, durations, statuses):
    print(f"{name:<15} {dur:>5.1f}s  {status}")

# zip SHORTEST par rukta hai -- silent data loss!
short = [1, 2]
print(list(zip(names, short)))        # [('test_login', 1), ('test_cart', 2)]  -- test_pay gayab

# Python 3.10+: strict=True se galti pakdo
try:
    print(list(zip(names, short, strict=True)))
except ValueError as e:
    print("caught:", e)               # zip() argument 2 is shorter than argument 1

# zip ka ulta -- unzip
pairs = [("a", 1), ("b", 2), ("c", 3)]
letters, numbers = zip(*pairs)        # * se unpack, phir zip transpose kar deta hai
print(letters)                        # ('a', 'b', 'c')
print(numbers)                        # (1, 2, 3)

# dict banane ka idiom
lookup = dict(zip(names, durations))
print(lookup)                         # {'test_login': 1.2, 'test_cart': 4.5, 'test_pay': 0.8}

Line-by-line walkthrough:

  1. zip(names, durations, statuses) — teeno ke iterators se ek-ek item leke tuple banata hai. Kitne bhi iterables de sakte ho.
  2. f"{name:<15} {dur:>5.1f}s {status}" — aligned table output. <15 left-align width 15, >5.1f right-align width 5 with 1 decimal.
  3. list(zip(names, short)) — short mein 2 items hain toh zip 2 tuples deke ruk jaata hai. Ye silently hota hai. Report generation mein agar ek column chhota reh jaaye toh aapke test results chup-chaap kat jaayenge. Ye real hai — CSV parsing mein sabse zyada.
  4. strict=True (3.10+) — length mismatch par ValueError. Jab bhi aap expect karte ho ki lengths equal hain, strict=True likho. Ye ek free assertion hai.
  5. zip(*pairs) — * list ko alag arguments mein todta hai: zip(("a",1), ("b",2), ("c",3)). Phir zip pehle-pehle elements ko jodta hai aur doosre-doosre ko. Effectively transpose. Note: result tuples hain, lists nahi.
  6. dict(zip(names, durations)) — do parallel lists se dict. Ye idiom bahut common hai (CSV header + row).

Purana Python (<3.10) mein strict ka substitute:

if len(names) != len(durations):                 # explicit length check
    raise ValueError(f"length mismatch: {len(names)} vs {len(durations)}")
pairs = list(zip(names, durations))

itertools.zip_longest — jab short hona expected ho:

from itertools import zip_longest
print(list(zip_longest(names, short, fillvalue=None)))
# [('test_login', 1), ('test_cart', 2), ('test_pay', None)]
  1. fillvalue missing values ke liye. Default None.
  2. Use case: do test runs compare karna jahan ek run mein extra tests hain.

docs.title: Lazy hone ka asli faayda — chaining
docs.text:
# 10 lakh log lines, sirf ERROR wali chahiye, sirf pehli 5
def first_n_errors(path, n=5):
    with open(path) as f:                                  # file ek lazy iterator hai
        numbered = enumerate(f, start=1)                    # lazy: (lineno, line)
        errors = ((i, ln) for i, ln in numbered if "ERROR" in ln)   # lazy filter
        return [next(errors) for _ in range(n)]             # sirf 5 items pull kiye

Line-by-line walkthrough:

  1. with open(path) as f: — file object khud iterator hai, buffered read karta hai. Poori file memory mein nahi aati.
  2. enumerate(f, start=1) — abhi tak ek bhi line nahi padhi. Sirf ek wrapper object bana.
  3. ((i, ln) for ... if ...) — generator expression, abhi bhi kuch nahi chala.
  4. [next(errors) for _ in range(n)] — ab actual reading shuru hoti hai, aur sirf tab tak jab tak 5 errors na mil jaayein. Agar file ke pehle 100 lines mein 5 errors hain toh baaki 99.99 lakh lines padhi hi nahi jaayengi.
  5. Yahi hai laziness ka asli faayda: aap pipeline banate ho, aur sirf jitna chahiye utna kaam hota hai. Eager version (list comprehensions) mein poori file padh kar poori filter list banti, phir aap 5 leke baaki phenk dete.
  6. Bug alert: agar file mein 5 se kam errors hain toh next(errors) StopIteration uthayega, jo comprehension ke andar 3.7+ se RuntimeError mein badal jaata hai. Safe version: list(itertools.islice(errors, n)) — wo kam items par bhi shanti se ruk jaata hai.

docs.title: Gotchas
docs.text:
Gotcha 1 — iterator ek baar chalta hai.

z = zip([1, 2], ["a", "b"])
print(list(z))       # [(1, 'a'), (2, 'b')]
print(list(z))       # []
print(sum(1 for _ in z))   # 0

Fix: pairs = list(zip(...)) ek baar materialise kar lo agar do baar chahiye.

Gotcha 2 — range float nahi leta.

# range(0, 1, 0.1)     # TypeError: 'float' object cannot be interpreted as an integer
# Fix:
steps = [i / 10 for i in range(0, 10)]     # [0.0, 0.1, ..., 0.9]
print(steps)
  1. range sirf ints leta hai. Float steps ke liye int range banake divide karo (accumulation error se bachne ke liye), ya numpy.arange / numpy.linspace use karo.
  2. 0.1 ko baar-baar add karna (x += 0.1) float error jamaa karta hai — 10 additions ke baad 0.9999999999999999 milta hai.

Gotcha 3 — zip ke arguments consume ho jaate hain, chahe zip complete na ho.

a = iter([1, 2, 3])
b = iter([10, 20])
print(list(zip(a, b)))     # [(1, 10), (2, 20)]
print(list(a))             # [] ya [3] -- CPython 3.x mein zip ne 'a' se 3 nikal liya
                           # aur discard kar diya jab 'b' khatam hua
  1. zip pehle a se leta hai, phir b se. b khatam hone par a ka nikala hua item phenk diya jaata hai. Isliye shared iterators ke saath zip data kha sakta hai.
  2. Ye documented behaviour hai aur zip_longest/strict isliye exist karte hain.

Interview answer: "range, enumerate, and zip are all lazy, which is the reason range(10**9) is 48 bytes rather than gigabytes — a range stores only start, stop, and step and computes start + i*step on demand, so len, indexing, slicing, and even in for integers are O(1). enumerate and zip are one-shot iterators wrapping other iterators, so they compose into a pipeline where nothing is materialised until something consumes it — that's how I scan a multi-gigabyte log for the first five errors without loading the file. The one that has actually bitten me is zip stopping at the shortest input silently; since 3.10 I pass strict=True whenever the lengths are supposed to match, which turns a silent truncation into a ValueError. And because they're iterators, consuming them twice gives you an empty result the second time — if I need the data twice I wrap it in list once."

Cross-question — "Is range an iterator?" "No, it's a lazy sequence. That's an important distinction: it implements __getitem__, __len__, __contains__, and __reversed__, so you can index it, slice it, take its length, and iterate it as many times as you like. iter(range(3)) gives you a separate range_iterator object each time. enumerate and zip, by contrast, are iterators — they return themselves from __iter__ and are exhausted after one pass. You can see it: r = range(3); list(r); list(r) gives the full list twice, whereas the same with zip gives an empty list the second time."

docs.title: 3.1 Lists — dynamic array kaise grow karta hai
Kya hai
docs.text:
Python ki list ek dynamic array hai: contiguous memory mein pointers ka array, jo zarurat padne par apne aap bada ho jaata hai. Ye linked list nahi hai.

list object                 pointer array (ob_item)         heap objects
+----------------+          +-----+-----+-----+-----+       +-----+
| ob_size   = 3  |  ----->  | ptr | ptr | ptr |  -  |  -->  | 'a' |
| allocated = 4  |          +-----+-----+-----+-----+       +-----+
| ob_item   = *  |             |     |     |               +-----+
+----------------+             |     |     +-------------> | 'c' |
                               |     +-------------------> ...
                               +-------------------------> ...

Do alag numbers hain: ob_size (kitne items hain) aur allocated (kitni jagah reserve hai). len() ob_size deta hai. Beech ka farak hi "spare capacity" hai.

docs.title: Kyu — append amortised O(1) kaise hai
docs.text:
Agar list har append par exactly ek slot bada hoti, toh har baar poora array naye bade memory block mein copy karna padta → har append O(n) → n appends O(n²).

Isliye CPython extra jagah reserve karta hai. listobject.c ka actual growth formula:

new_allocated = ((newsize + (newsize >> 3) + 6) & ~3)   # roughly newsize * 1.125 + 6, 4 ka multiple

Matlab har resize par capacity ~12.5% badhti hai (plus a small constant). Growth pattern lagbhag aisa hai:

0, 4, 8, 16, 25, 35, 46, 58, 72, 88, ...

Kyunki resize har baar nahi hota, aur jab hota hai toh proportionally, n appends ka total cost O(n) hai → per append amortised O(1).

docs.title: Kaise kaam karta hai — khud dekho
docs.text:
import sys

lst = []                                        # khaali list
prev = sys.getsizeof(lst)                       # base size (64 bytes typically)
print(f"len=0  size={prev}")

for i in range(20):                             # 20 baar append karo
    lst.append(i)                               # ek item add
    size = sys.getsizeof(lst)                   # ab kitna memory le raha hai
    if size != prev:                            # sirf tab print karo jab REALLOC hua ho
        print(f"len={len(lst):<3} size={size:<4} (grew by {size - prev} bytes)")
        prev = size

Output kuch aisa:

len=0  size=56
len=1  size=88  (grew by 32)
len=5  size=120 (grew by 32)
len=9  size=184 (grew by 64)
len=17 size=248 (grew by 64)

Line-by-line walkthrough:

  1. import sys — sys.getsizeof object ka memory footprint deta hai (bytes mein), bina uske andar wale objects ke.
  2. lst = [] — khaali list. CPython khaali list ke liye pointer array allocate nahi karta (allocated = 0), sirf header.
  3. prev = sys.getsizeof(lst) — baseline. Ye 56 ya 64 hota hai depending on build.
  4. for i in range(20): — 20 appends.
  5. lst.append(i) — pehle check hota hai ob_size < allocated. Agar haan, toh sirf pointer likh do aur ob_size += 1 — O(1), koi copy nahi. Agar nahi, toh list_resize chalta hai jo naya bada block allocate karke saare pointers copy karta hai — O(n).
  6. if size != prev: — sirf resize wale moments dikhaane ke liye. Aap dekh sakte ho ki resize kabhi-kabhi hota hai, har append par nahi — yahi amortisation ka proof hai.
  7. size - prev — jump ka size. Har jump 8 bytes ka multiple hai (64-bit pointer), aur jumps badhte jaate hain — kyunki growth proportional hai.

docs.title: insert(0, x) O(n) kyun hai
docs.text:
lst = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]
lst.insert(0, 0)         # index 0 par daalo

Memory level par:

Pehle:  [1][2][3][4][5][ ]
                          ^ spare slot

Step 1: saare elements ek position RIGHT shift karo (memmove)
        [ ][1][2][3][4][5]

Step 2: index 0 par naya pointer likho
        [0][1][2][3][4][5]

Step 1 n pointers copy karta hai → O(n). Ye C level memmove hai toh constant kam hai, par asymptotically O(n) hi hai.

import timeit

# 100k appends at the end
t_append = timeit.timeit(
    "lst.append(1)",                            # jo measure karna hai
    setup="lst = []",                           # setup, timing mein count nahi hota
    number=100_000,                             # kitni baar
)

# 100k inserts at the front
t_insert = timeit.timeit(
    "lst.insert(0, 1)",
    setup="lst = []",
    number=100_000,
)

print(f"append: {t_append:.4f}s")               # ~0.005s
print(f"insert: {t_insert:.4f}s")               # ~1.5s  -- 300x dheema
print(f"ratio:  {t_insert / t_append:.0f}x")

Line-by-line walkthrough:

  1. timeit.timeit(stmt, setup, number) — setup ek baar chalta hai, stmt number baar. Timing mein sirf stmt count hota hai. Ye manual time.time() se behtar hai kyunki ye garbage collection disable karta hai aur best-of measurement karta hai.
  2. setup="lst = []" — string hai kyunki timeit alag namespace mein execute karta hai. Function version bhi hai: timeit.timeit(lambda: lst.append(1), number=...).
  3. number=100_000 — kam number par noise zyada hota hai. Rule of thumb: total time 0.1s se zyada hona chahiye.
  4. Result: insert(0) sirf 300x dheema nahi hai — wo quadratic hai. 200k par ratio 600x ho jaayega. Ye difference asymptotic hai, constant nahi.
  5. Fix: front insertion chahiye toh collections.deque use karo — wo dono taraf O(1) hai (3.6 mein).

docs.title: List ke saare methods, complexity ke saath
docs.text:
results = ["test_a", "test_b"]

# --- ADD ---
results.append("test_c")                  # O(1) amortised -- end mein ek item
results.extend(["test_d", "test_e"])      # O(k) -- k items end mein
results.insert(1, "test_x")               # O(n) -- shift chahiye
results += ["test_f"]                     # O(k) -- extend ke barabar (IN-PLACE!)
new = results + ["test_g"]                # O(n+k) -- NAYA list banata hai

# --- REMOVE ---
last = results.pop()                      # O(1) -- end se nikalo aur return karo
first = results.pop(0)                    # O(n) -- shift chahiye
results.remove("test_x")                  # O(n) -- pehle dhoondho (linear), phir shift
del results[0]                            # O(n)
del results[1:3]                          # O(n)
results.clear()                           # O(n) -- har item ka refcount kam karna padta hai

# --- QUERY ---
results = ["test_a", "test_b", "test_c", "test_b"]
print(results.index("test_b"))            # O(n) -- 1 (pehla match)
print(results.index("test_b", 2))         # O(n) -- 3 (index 2 se dhoondho)
print(results.count("test_b"))            # O(n) -- 2
print("test_a" in results)                # O(n) -- linear scan
print(len(results))                       # O(1) -- ob_size field

# --- ORDER ---
results.sort()                            # O(n log n) IN-PLACE, None return karta hai
results.sort(key=len, reverse=True)       # key function + reverse
s = sorted(results)                       # O(n log n) NAYA list, original safe
results.reverse()                         # O(n) in-place
r = list(reversed(results))               # O(n) naya list (reversed() lazy iterator hai)

# --- COPY ---
c1 = results.copy()                       # O(n) shallow
c2 = results[:]                           # O(n) shallow, same cheez
c3 = list(results)                        # O(n) shallow, same cheez

Important walkthrough points:

  1. results.append(x) vs results += [x] vs results = results + [x]:
  2. append — ek item, in-place, fastest.
  3. += — __iadd__, in-place extend, shared references ko dikhta hai (1.2 gotcha).
  4. + — naya list, O(n+k). Loop mein lst = lst + [x] likhna quadratic hai — ye ek real performance bug hai jo review mein pakadna chahiye.
  5. results.pop() O(1) hai (end se) par results.pop(0) O(n). Queue banane ke liye list use karna isliye galat hai — deque sahi hai.
  6. results.remove(x) — pehla match hatata hai. Na mile toh ValueError. Sab hatane ke liye comprehension: [r for r in results if r != x].
  7. results.sort() None return karta hai — x = results.sort() classic bug hai. sorted() naya list deta hai. Rule: in-place methods None dete hain (sort, reverse, append, extend, insert, clear, remove).
  8. results.sort(key=len, reverse=True) — key har element par ek baar call hota hai (Decorate-Sort-Undecorate, n calls not n log n). cmp parameter Python 3 mein hata diya gaya; comparison chahiye toh functools.cmp_to_key.
  9. Python ka sort Timsort hai — hybrid merge/insertion sort, stable (equal elements ka relative order preserve hota hai), aur already-sorted ya partially-sorted data par O(n). Stability important hai: pehle name se sort karo, phir status se — result status ke andar name-sorted hoga.

docs.title: Sorting — QA examples
docs.text:
results = [
    {"name": "test_pay", "status": "failed", "duration": 4.5},
    {"name": "test_login", "status": "passed", "duration": 1.2},
    {"name": "test_cart", "status": "failed", "duration": 0.8},
]

# 1. Ek field se
by_duration = sorted(results, key=lambda r: r["duration"])
print([r["name"] for r in by_duration])         # ['test_cart', 'test_login', 'test_pay']

# 2. Descending
slowest_first = sorted(results, key=lambda r: r["duration"], reverse=True)
print([r["name"] for r in slowest_first])       # ['test_pay', 'test_login', 'test_cart']

# 3. Multi-key: pehle status, phir duration descending
#    Trick: tuple key. Numeric field ko negate karke descending kar sakte ho.
multi = sorted(results, key=lambda r: (r["status"], -r["duration"]))
print([(r["status"], r["duration"]) for r in multi])
# [('failed', 4.5), ('failed', 0.8), ('passed', 1.2)]

# 4. Multi-key jahan ek field string hai (negate nahi kar sakte) -- stable sort ka use
tmp = sorted(results, key=lambda r: r["name"])            # secondary key pehle
final = sorted(tmp, key=lambda r: r["status"])            # primary key baad mein
print([(r["status"], r["name"]) for r in final])
# [('failed', 'test_cart'), ('failed', 'test_pay'), ('passed', 'test_login')]

# 5. operator.itemgetter -- lambda se tez (C mein implemented)
from operator import itemgetter
fast = sorted(results, key=itemgetter("duration"))
print([r["name"] for r in fast])

# 6. Objects par attrgetter
from operator import attrgetter
# sorted(test_objects, key=attrgetter("duration"))

Line-by-line walkthrough:

  1. key=lambda r: r["duration"] — key har element par ek baar call hota hai aur uska result compare hota hai. Original elements ka __lt__ use nahi hota. Isliye dicts sort ho paye (dicts orderable nahi hain!).
  2. reverse=True — sorting ke baad reverse nahi hota, comparison ulta hota hai. Isliye stability preserve rehti hai (sorted(x, reverse=True) aur list(reversed(sorted(x))) ties ke liye alag order dete hain).
  3. key=lambda r: (r["status"], -r["duration"]) — tuple comparison element-wise hoti hai: pehle [0] compare, tie ho toh [1]. -duration se us field ka order ulta ho gaya. Ye trick sirf numbers par kaam karti hai.
  4. Do-pass sort — Timsort stable hai, isliye pehle secondary key se sort karo, phir primary se. Primary sort equal elements ka order nahi bigaadega. Ye technique tab chahiye jab mixed ascending/descending par string fields hon.
  5. itemgetter("duration") — C level callable, lambda se ~20-30% tez. Multiple keys bhi le sakta hai: itemgetter("status", "duration") ek tuple deta hai.
  6. attrgetter("duration") — objects ke liye, lambda o: o.duration ka fast version. Nested bhi chalta hai: attrgetter("result.duration").

docs.title: Gotchas
docs.text:
Gotcha 1 — sort() None deta hai.

names = ["c", "a", "b"]
# names = names.sort()          # names ab None hai!
names.sort()                    # sahi
print(names)                    # ['a', 'b', 'c']

Gotcha 2 — mixed types sort nahi hote.

# sorted([1, "a"])              # TypeError: '<' not supported between 'str' and 'int'
print(sorted([1, "a"], key=str))  # [1, 'a']  -- key se sab ko comparable banao

Python 2 mein ye chalta tha (arbitrary but consistent order) — Python 3 ne ise error banaya kyunki wo order meaningless tha.

Gotcha 3 — list.remove iterate karte waqt. (2.3 mein dekha, dobara yaad rakho)

Gotcha 4 — list of lists mein shared inner lists.

row = [0, 0, 0]
grid = [row, row, row]              # teen naam, ek hi list!
grid[0][0] = 9
print(grid)                         # [[9,0,0],[9,0,0],[9,0,0]]

grid = [[0, 0, 0] for _ in range(3)]   # har baar naya inner list
grid[0][0] = 9
print(grid)                         # [[9,0,0],[0,0,0],[0,0,0]]

Gotcha 5 — bade list ka in slow hai.

import timeit
setup = "data = [f'test_{i}' for i in range(100000)]; target = 'test_99999'"
print(timeit.timeit("target in data", setup=setup, number=1000))          # ~1.0s

setup_set = "data = {f'test_{i}' for i in range(100000)}; target = 'test_99999'"
print(timeit.timeit("target in data", setup=setup_set, number=1000))      # ~0.00005s
  1. List membership O(n) hai — worst case poora scan. Set O(1) average.
  2. Agar aap ek list mein baar-baar in check kar rahe ho, set bana lo: known = set(items). Ek baar O(n) cost, phir har lookup O(1).
  3. Ye QA mein tab dikhta hai jab aap 5000 test IDs ki list mein 5000 baar membership check karte ho — O(n²) = 25 million comparisons.

Interview answer: "A Python list is a dynamic array of pointers, not a linked list. It keeps two numbers: the number of items and the allocated capacity. append writes into spare capacity in constant time; when capacity runs out CPython reallocates to roughly 1.125 times the new size plus a small constant and copies the pointers, so the occasional O(n) resize is spread over many appends — that's why append is amortised O(1). insert(0, x) and pop(0) are O(n) because every remaining pointer has to be shifted; for a queue I use collections.deque, which is a doubly-linked list of blocks and gives O(1) at both ends. The other complexity facts I keep in mind are that membership on a list is O(n) — so if I'm checking repeatedly I build a set once — and that sorting is Timsort: O(n log n), stable, and linear on already-sorted data. Stability is what lets me sort by name and then by status to get a two-level ordering."

Cross-question — "Why does CPython over-allocate by only ~12.5% rather than doubling, like C++ vector?" "It's a memory-versus-copies trade-off, and CPython chose memory. Doubling gives fewer reallocations but wastes up to 50 percent of the allocation; growing by an eighth wastes far less, which matters because a typical Python process holds a very large number of small lists. The amortised cost is still O(1) either way — any geometric growth factor greater than 1 gives amortised constant time; the factor only changes the constant. CPython also adds a fixed term so tiny lists don't reallocate on every single append, and rounds the capacity to a multiple of 4 for allocator friendliness. And if you know the final size, list(range(n)) or a comprehension is faster than repeated appends because CPython can pre-size the array from the iterable's __length_hint__."

docs.title: 3.2 Tuples — immutable sequences aur unka asli maqsad
Kya hai
docs.text:
Tuple ek immutable sequence hai. Ek baar bana, uske slots nahi badal sakte.

Analogy: list ek shopping bag hai (cheezein daalo-nikalo). Tuple ek sealed courier packet hai — andar kya hai wo fix hai. Packet ke andar agar ek khula dabba (list) ho toh us dabbe ka saamaan badal sakta hai, par packet mein kaunsa dabba hai wo nahi.

docs.title: Kyu hai — sirf "immutable list" nahi
docs.text:
Log kehte hain "tuple = immutable list". Ye galat framing hai. Asli farak semantic hai:

List Tuple Semantics homogeneous — same kism ki cheezein, variable count heterogeneous — ek record ke alag-alag fields Mental model "test names ki list" "(name, status, duration) ek test ka record" Position ka matlab koi nahi (order bas order hai) har position ka alag matlab hai Hashable Nahi Haan (agar elements hashable) Memory zyada (spare capacity) kam (exact)

Isliye ("test_login", "passed", 1.2) tuple hai, aur ["test_a", "test_b", "test_c"] list.

docs.title: Practical reasons — chaar concrete faayde
docs.text:
1. Dict key ban sakta hai

# Test result cache: (test_name, browser, env) -> result
cache = {}
cache[("test_login", "chromium", "staging")] = "passed"
cache[("test_login", "firefox", "staging")] = "failed"

print(cache[("test_login", "chromium", "staging")])     # passed

# List key se error:
# cache[["test_login", "chromium"]] = "x"     # TypeError: unhashable type: 'list'
  1. cache[("test_login", "chromium", "staging")] — composite key. Ye ek nested dict (cache["test_login"]["chromium"]["staging"]) se saaf hai jab teeno dimensions hamesha saath aate hain.
  2. Tuple hashable hai kyunki wo immutable hai → uska hash lifetime bhar constant rahega → dict apna entry dobara dhoondh sakta hai. List mutable hai, toh agar wo key hoti aur badal jaati toh dict ka bucket galat ho jaata aur entry "kho" jaati. Isliye Python list ko hashable hi nahi banata.

2. Multiple return values

def run_test(name):
    # ... test chalao ...
    return name, "passed", 1.23                # ye ek TUPLE hai (brackets optional)

name, status, duration = run_test("test_login")   # unpacking
print(status)                                      # passed

result = run_test("test_cart")                     # tuple as a whole
print(result[1])                                   # passed  (par ye readable nahi hai)
  1. return name, "passed", 1.23 — comma se tuple banti hai, brackets se nahi. (1) ek int hai, (1,) ek tuple. Ye Python ki sabse common syntax galti hai.
  2. name, status, duration = ... — tuple unpacking. Count exactly match hona chahiye warna ValueError: too many values to unpack.
  3. result[1] — magic index. 3+ fields ho toh NamedTuple ya dataclass use karo (3.6, 5.11).

3. Unpacking / swapping

a, b = 1, 2
a, b = b, a                       # swap -- temp variable ki zarurat nahi
print(a, b)                       # 2 1

first, *middle, last = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]      # starred unpacking
print(first, middle, last)                  # 1 [2, 3, 4] 5

(name, (status, duration)) = ("test_a", ("passed", 1.2))   # nested unpacking
print(name, status, duration)               # test_a passed 1.2

first, _, third = (1, 2, 3)                 # '_' = "mujhe ye nahi chahiye"
print(first, third)                         # 1 3
  1. a, b = b, a — right side pehle poora evaluate hoke ek tuple (2, 1) banta hai, phir unpack hota hai. Isliye temp variable nahi chahiye. C mein ye nahi ho sakta.
  2. first, *middle, last = [...] — *middle list deta hai (tuple nahi), aur exactly ek star allowed hai. Ye "pehla aur aakhri chahiye, beech ka chahe jitna ho" ke liye perfect hai.
  3. Nested unpacking structure ko match karta hai.
  4. _ ek normal naam hai (convention se "ignored"), aur linters isko unused nahi maante. Multiple ignores ke liye _ reuse kar sakte ho ya __, ___ use kar sakte ho.

4. Memory aur speed

import sys, timeit

print(sys.getsizeof([1, 2, 3]))       # 88   -- list mein spare capacity ka overhead
print(sys.getsizeof((1, 2, 3)))       # 64   -- tuple exact size

print(timeit.timeit("(1, 2, 3)", number=1_000_000))       # ~0.01s -- constant, folded
print(timeit.timeit("[1, 2, 3]", number=1_000_000))       # ~0.05s -- har baar naya object
  1. Tuple chhota hai kyunki usme allocated field ki zarurat nahi — size fix hai.
  2. (1, 2, 3) constant folding se compile time par hi ban jaata hai aur co_consts mein store hota hai — runtime par sirf LOAD_CONST. [1, 2, 3] har baar BUILD_LIST karta hai kyunki list mutable hai aur usko share nahi kiya ja sakta.
  3. CPython chhote tuples ka free list bhi rakhta hai (reuse), toh allocation bhi sasta hai.

docs.title: Tuple ke methods — sirf do
docs.text:
t = ("passed", "failed", "passed")
print(t.count("passed"))          # 2   -- O(n)
print(t.index("failed"))          # 1   -- O(n), not found par ValueError
print(len(t))                     # 3   -- O(1)
print("passed" in t)              # True -- O(n)
print(t + ("skipped",))           # naya tuple -- O(n+k)
print(t * 2)                      # naya tuple, repeat
print(t[::-1])                    # ('passed', 'failed', 'passed') reversed slice

Sirf count aur index hain kyunki baaki sab methods mutate karte — tuple pe unka matlab hi nahi.

docs.title: Gotchas
docs.text:
Gotcha 1 — single-element tuple ke liye comma zaruri hai.

not_a_tuple = ("test_login")           # ye bas ek STRING hai, brackets grouping ke liye
print(type(not_a_tuple))               # <class 'str'>
print(len(not_a_tuple))                # 10  -- string ki length!

a_tuple = ("test_login",)              # comma se tuple
print(type(a_tuple), len(a_tuple))     # <class 'tuple'> 1

also_tuple = "test_login",             # brackets ki zarurat hi nahi
print(type(also_tuple))                # <class 'tuple'>
  1. Comma tuple banata hai, brackets nahi. Brackets sirf precedence/grouping ke liye hain.
  2. Ye bug real hai: @pytest.mark.parametrize("x", ("a")) chalega par har character alag test ban jaayega ("a" iterate hoke 'a'), aur ("a",) ek test dega. Aur function call mein f(x) vs f((x,)) ka farak.
  3. Empty tuple ke liye () kaafi hai — koi ambiguity nahi.

Gotcha 2 — immutable ka matlab "andar ka bhi immutable" nahi.

config = ("staging", ["chromium", "firefox"])
config[1].append("webkit")                 # list mutate ho gayi -- LEGAL
print(config)                              # ('staging', ['chromium', 'firefox', 'webkit'])

# config[0] = "prod"                       # TypeError: 'tuple' object does not support item assignment

# print(hash(config))                      # TypeError: unhashable type: 'list'
  1. Tuple ke slots fix hain — config[0] = ... fail hoga.
  2. Par slot mein jo object hai wo agar mutable hai toh wo badal sakta hai.
  3. Aur isi wajah se ye tuple hashable nahi hai — kyunki hash(tuple) apne elements ke hashes ko combine karta hai, aur list ka hash hai hi nahi. Ye ek achha proof hai ki "hashable = deep immutability" hai, "shallow immutability" nahi.
  4. Poori immutability chahiye toh ("staging", ("chromium", "firefox")).

Gotcha 3 — trailing comma se accidental tuple.

timeout = 30,                              # <- galti se comma
print(timeout)                             # (30,)
# print(timeout * 2)                       # (30, 30)  -- 60 nahi!

Ye copy-paste karte waqt hota hai aur error message door milta hai.

Gotcha 4 — += tuple par naya object banata hai.

t = (1, 2)
t2 = t
t += (3,)
print(t, t2)                               # (1, 2, 3) (1, 2)   -- t2 nahi badla

Kyunki tuple mein __iadd__ nahi hai, fallback t = t + (3,) par hota hai. Loop mein ye quadratic hai — list mein collect karo phir tuple() kar lo.

Interview answer: "The textbook answer is that a tuple is an immutable list, but that's the wrong framing. The real distinction is semantic: a list is a homogeneous collection of variable length where the position carries no meaning, while a tuple is a heterogeneous record where each position means something specific — (name, status, duration). That's why tuples are what functions return for multiple values and what unpacking works on. Practically, immutability buys three things: tuples are hashable so they work as dict keys and set members — I use (test_name, browser, env) as a cache key rather than a triple-nested dict — they're smaller and constant-folded by the compiler, and they're safe to share. The two traps are that a single-element tuple needs the trailing comma, since it's the comma and not the parentheses that makes a tuple, and that immutability is shallow: ('env', ['a']) lets you append to the inner list, and that same tuple is unhashable because hashing recurses into the elements."

Cross-question — "If tuples are immutable, why does hash(('a', [])) fail rather than just hashing the identity of the list?" "Because hashing has a contract: objects that compare equal must hash equal, and an object's hash must not change while it's in a hash table. tuple.__hash__ combines the hashes of its elements, so equal tuples hash equal. If it fell back to the list's identity, two tuples that compare equal — ('a', [1]) and ('a', [1]) with different list objects — would hash differently, which silently breaks dict and set lookups. Python's answer is to refuse: list.__hash__ is None, so the recursive hash raises TypeError immediately rather than letting you build a container that misbehaves later."

docs.title: Kya hai
docs.text:
set ek unordered collection of unique hashable objects hai. Internally wo ek hash table hai jismein sirf keys hain, values nahi.

Analogy: ek guest list jahan har naam sirf ek baar likha ja sakta hai, aur order matter nahi karta — sirf "ye naam hai ya nahi" matter karta hai.

docs.title: Kyu hai
docs.text:
# --- WITHOUT set: dedup karna O(n^2) ---
all_tags = ["smoke", "auth", "smoke", "regression", "auth"]
unique = []
for tag in all_tags:
    if tag not in unique:              # O(n) scan har item ke liye -> O(n^2) total
        unique.append(tag)
print(unique)                          # ['smoke', 'auth', 'regression']

# --- WITH set: O(n) ---
unique = list(set(all_tags))           # O(n), par ORDER kho gaya
print(unique)                          # ['auth', 'smoke', 'regression'] -- random order

# --- Order preserve karke dedup: dict.fromkeys (3.7+) ---
unique = list(dict.fromkeys(all_tags))  # O(n) AUR order preserved
print(unique)                           # ['smoke', 'auth', 'regression']

Line-by-line walkthrough:

  1. if tag not in unique: — list par in O(n) hai, aur ye har item ke liye chalta hai → O(n²). 10,000 tags par 50 million comparisons.
  2. set(all_tags) — har element ka hash compute hota hai aur hash table mein daala jaata hai. Duplicate ka hash same hoga aur == bhi, toh wo skip ho jaayega. Total O(n).
  3. list(set(...)) — set ka iteration order hash order hai, insertion order nahi. Aur strings ka hash PYTHONHASHSEED se randomise hota hai (security feature), toh har run mein order alag ho sakta hai. Isliye test assertions mein kabhi list(set(...)) ka order assume mat karo — sorted(set(...)) likho.
  4. dict.fromkeys(all_tags) — dict banata hai jismein keys wahi hain aur values None. Python 3.7+ mein dict insertion-ordered hai, toh order preserve rehta hai. Ye "ordered dedup" ka standard idiom hai.
