  4. Practical rule: reverse karna hai toh [::-1] likho ya reversed() use karo. Manual negative-step slices sirf tab likho jab genuinely partial reverse chahiye, aur tab test likho.

docs.title: Copy semantics
docs.text:
original = [[1, 2], [3, 4]]
sliced = original[:]                  # SHALLOW copy
sliced[0].append(99)                  # inner list SHARED hai
print(original)                       # [[1, 2, 99], [3, 4]]   <- original bhi badla!

import copy
deep = copy.deepcopy(original)        # 3.8 mein detail
deep[0].append(100)
print(original)                       # unchanged

Slicing hamesha shallow hai. Ye agla section hai.

Interview answer: "Slicing uses a half-open interval — start inclusive, stop exclusive — with indices sitting between elements rather than on them. That's what makes len(s[a:b]) equal b - a and s[:k] + s[k:] always equal s. Negative indices count from the end, and a negative step reverses direction, which also swaps the meaning of the omitted defaults: lst[::-1] starts at the last element and runs past the front. Slicing clamps out-of-range bounds instead of raising, so lst[100:200] is an empty list while lst[100] is an IndexError — that asymmetry hides bugs, because an empty slice from an unexpectedly short list fails somewhere far away. On the assignment side, a[1:3] = [...] can change the length, but an extended slice with a step requires exactly matching lengths. And a[:] = new replaces the contents while keeping the same object, which matters when something else holds a reference. I also use named slice objects for fixed-width log formats — line[TIMESTAMP] documents itself where line[0:19] doesn't."

Cross-question — "Is a list slice a view or a copy? What about NumPy?" "For built-in sequences it's always a copy — a new list object with new pointers, though the pointed-to objects are shared, so it's a shallow copy. That's O(k) in the slice length, which is why slicing inside a loop can quietly turn an algorithm quadratic. NumPy goes the other way: basic slicing returns a view sharing the same buffer, so writing through the slice mutates the original array, and you need .copy() to detach. Both designs are defensible — Python's copy semantics are safer for general code, NumPy's view semantics are essential when the arrays are gigabytes. The practical consequence is that you can't assume slice behaviour transfers between the two."

docs.title: Kya hai
docs.text:
• Assignment (b = a) — koi copy nahi, doosra naam.
  • Shallow copy (a.copy(), a[:], list(a), copy.copy(a)) — naya top-level container, andar ke objects shared.
  • Deep copy (copy.deepcopy(a)) — poora tree recursively naya.

docs.title: Kyu — real bug
docs.text:
import copy

BASE_CONFIG = {
    "env": "staging",
    "browser": {"name": "chromium", "args": ["--headless"]},
    "retries": 2,
}

# --- BUG: shallow copy ---
def make_test_config_buggy(**overrides):
    cfg = BASE_CONFIG.copy()               # SHALLOW -- inner dict/list shared
    cfg.update(overrides)
    return cfg

c1 = make_test_config_buggy()
c1["browser"]["args"].append("--slow-mo=500")     # SHARED list mutate ho gayi

c2 = make_test_config_buggy()
print(c2["browser"]["args"])                       # ['--headless', '--slow-mo=500']  <- LEAK!
print(BASE_CONFIG["browser"]["args"])              # ['--headless', '--slow-mo=500']  <- BASE bhi corrupt!

# --- FIX: deep copy ---
BASE_CONFIG["browser"]["args"] = ["--headless"]    # reset

def make_test_config(**overrides):
    cfg = copy.deepcopy(BASE_CONFIG)               # poora naya tree
    cfg.update(overrides)
    return cfg

c1 = make_test_config()
c1["browser"]["args"].append("--slow-mo=500")

c2 = make_test_config()
print(c2["browser"]["args"])                       # ['--headless']   <- clean
print(BASE_CONFIG["browser"]["args"])              # ['--headless']   <- safe

Line-by-line walkthrough:

  1. BASE_CONFIG.copy() — naya dict banata hai, par values wahi objects hain. Toh cfg["browser"] aur BASE_CONFIG["browser"] ek hi dict hai.
  2. c1["browser"]["args"].append(...) — ye us shared inner list ko mutate kar raha hai. Naya config banane ka poora point khatam.
  3. Ye exactly wo bug hai jo test suites mein "test order matters" banata hai: test 1 config mutate karta hai, test 5 fail hota hai, aur akele chalane par test 5 pass hota hai. Parallel run mein ye non-deterministic ho jaata hai.
  4. copy.deepcopy(BASE_CONFIG) — recursively har mutable object ka naya version banata hai. Ab koi sharing nahi.

docs.title: copy.deepcopy kaise kaam karta hai
docs.text:
import copy

# 1. Recursion + memo dict (cycles handle karne ke liye)
a = [1, 2]
a.append(a)                       # SELF-REFERENCE -- infinite structure
b = copy.deepcopy(a)              # koi infinite loop nahi -- memo se handle hua
print(b[2] is b)                  # True   -- structure preserve hui
print(b is a)                     # False

# 2. Immutable objects deep copy mein bhi share hote hain (optimization)
s = "hello"
t = copy.deepcopy(s)
print(t is s)                     # True   -- string immutable hai, copy ka kya faayda

# 3. Custom classes __deepcopy__ / __reduce__ se control kar sakti hain
class Page:
    def __init__(self, url, browser):
        self.url = url
        self.browser = browser              # ek non-copyable resource

    def __deepcopy__(self, memo):
        # browser connection copy nahi karni chahiye -- share karo
        new = Page(copy.deepcopy(self.url, memo), self.browser)
        memo[id(self)] = new
        return new

Line-by-line walkthrough:

  1. a.append(a) — list apne aap ko contain karti hai. Naive recursion infinite hoti. deepcopy ek memo dict rakhta hai (id(original) -> copy), toh dobara wahi object milne par pehle se bani copy return karta hai. Isliye cycles safe hain.
  2. copy.deepcopy("hello") is "hello" → True — immutable atomic types (int, str, bytes, None, functions, classes) deep copy mein bhi share hote hain, kyunki unhe copy karne ka koi matlab nahi.
  3. __deepcopy__(self, memo) — custom control. Ye tab zaruri hota hai jab object mein ek resource ho (file handle, socket, browser instance) jo copy nahi honi chahiye. Playwright ke Page/Browser objects deep-copyable nahi hain — unhe copy karne ki koshish TypeError: cannot pickle de sakti hai. QA framework mein ye real issue hai.

docs.title: Kaunsa copy kab
docs.text: Situation Use Kyun Flat list/dict of immutables x.copy() / x[:] / dict(x) shallow kaafi hai, tez hai Nested config, test data factory copy.deepcopy(x) inner sharing se bachna hai Bade objects, performance critical naya object banao (factory function) deepcopy slow hai (pickle-jaisi machinery) Object mein resource hai (file, socket, browser) __deepcopy__ custom, ya factory resource copy nahi ho sakti Immutable structure chahiye tuple/frozenset use karo copy ki zarurat hi nahi JSON-able data json.loads(json.dumps(x)) deepcopy se tez, par sirf JSON types

docs.title: Deepcopy alternatives — performance
docs.text:
import copy, json, timeit

data = {"a": [1, 2, 3], "b": {"c": [4, 5]}, "d": "text"}

t_deep = timeit.timeit(lambda: copy.deepcopy(data), number=100_000)
t_json = timeit.timeit(lambda: json.loads(json.dumps(data)), number=100_000)
print(f"deepcopy: {t_deep:.3f}s")     # ~1.2s
print(f"json:     {t_json:.3f}s")     # ~0.6s
  1. json.loads(json.dumps(x)) deepcopy se ~2x tez hai chhote JSON-able structures par, kyunki wo C mein hai aur usko arbitrary object graphs handle nahi karne padte.
  2. Limitations: sirf JSON types (dict, list, str, int, float, bool, None). Tuples list ban jaate hain. Dict keys strings ban jaati hain. datetime, set, custom objects fail karte hain. Cycles par ValueError: Circular reference detected.
  3. Test data factories ke liye ye theek hai (data usually JSON-shaped hota hai). General purpose ke liye deepcopy.

Sabse achha option — factory function:

def make_base_config():
    """Har call par ek fresh, independent config banao."""
    return {
        "env": "staging",
        "browser": {"name": "chromium", "args": ["--headless"]},
        "retries": 2,
    }

c1 = make_base_config()
c2 = make_base_config()
c1["browser"]["args"].append("--x")
print(c2["browser"]["args"])       # ['--headless']  -- kabhi shared tha hi nahi
  1. Koi copy hi nahi — har baar naya banta hai. Ye deepcopy se tez hai aur samajhne mein saaf.
  2. Ye default approach honi chahiye test data factories ke liye. deepcopy tab use karo jab base object bahar se aaya ho aur aap uska construction control nahi karte.
  3. pytest fixtures exactly yahi karte hain — har test ke liye factory chalti hai (Part 15).

docs.title: Gotchas
docs.text:
Gotcha 1 — copy.copy vs list() vs [:] — teeno same hain.

import copy
a = [[1], [2]]
print(copy.copy(a) == a[:] == list(a))       # True -- teeno shallow

Gotcha 2 — deepcopy custom __eq__/__hash__ wale objects par slow.

deepcopy memo dict id() se keyed hai toh __hash__ use nahi hota, par har object ke liye __reduce_ex__ ya __deepcopy__ dhoondhna padta hai — bade graphs par ye seconds le sakta hai.

Gotcha 3 — deepcopy modules aur classes ko copy nahi karta.

import copy, os
print(copy.deepcopy(os) is os)               # True  -- modules share hote hain
print(copy.deepcopy(int) is int)             # True  -- classes bhi

Ye deliberate hai — module/class ki do copies ka koi matlab nahi hota aur wo isinstance checks tod deti.

Gotcha 4 — deepcopy locks/threads/files par fail karti hai.

import copy, threading
lock = threading.Lock()
# copy.deepcopy(lock)          # TypeError: cannot pickle '_thread.lock' object

Isliye agar aapke config object mein logger ya lock ho toh deepcopy fail hogi — us case mein __deepcopy__ define karo jo unhe share kare.

Interview answer: "There are three levels. Assignment just binds another name to the same object. A shallow copy — list(x), x[:], x.copy(), or copy.copy(x) — makes a new top-level container whose slots still point at the original inner objects. A deep copy walks the whole graph and rebuilds every mutable object, using a memo dict keyed on id so shared subobjects stay shared in the copy and reference cycles don't cause infinite recursion. The bug this prevents is the one that makes a suite order-dependent: a base config gets shallow-copied per test, one test appends to a nested list, and every later test sees it — which then only reproduces in a full run, never when you run the failing test alone. My default isn't actually deepcopy though; it's a factory function that constructs a fresh object each time, because that's faster and there's nothing to share by accident. I reach for deepcopy when the base object comes from somewhere I don't control, and I watch out for objects holding resources — a lock, a file handle, a Playwright browser — because deepcopy will either fail or duplicate something that shouldn't be duplicated."
