docs.title: Ek concrete before/after
docs.text:
# --- BEFORE: O(n*m) -- 5000 tests, 3000 known-flaky ---
def filter_flaky_slow(all_tests, flaky_list):
    return [t for t in all_tests if t not in flaky_list]     # list mein 'in' -> O(m) har baar
# Total: 5000 * 3000 = 15,000,000 comparisons

# --- AFTER: O(n + m) ---
def filter_flaky_fast(all_tests, flaky_list):
    flaky = set(flaky_list)                                   # O(m) ek baar
    return [t for t in all_tests if t not in flaky]           # O(1) har baar
# Total: 3000 + 5000 = 8,000 operations

Line-by-line walkthrough:

  1. t not in flaky_list — list membership O(m). Comprehension n baar chalti hai → O(n*m).
  2. flaky = set(flaky_list) — ek baar O(m) hash table banayi.
  3. t not in flaky — O(1) average.
  4. Ye ek line ka change 15 million operations ko 8 thousand mein badalta hai — ~1800x. Aur ye exactly wo tarah ka change hai jo interviewer sunna chahta hai: "maine set banaya" nahi, balki "maine O(n*m) ko O(n+m) banaya".

Interview answer: "The core facts are: list is a dynamic array, so indexing and append are O(1) but anything at the front is O(n); dict and set are hash tables, so lookup, insert, and delete are O(1) average and O(n) worst case if everything collides; deque is a linked list of blocks, so both ends are O(1) but the middle is O(n) and slicing isn't supported; and strings are immutable, so every concatenation is O(n) in the combined length, which makes += in a loop quadratic. The one I apply most in review is converting a repeatedly-searched list into a set once — that turns an O(n times m) filter into O(n plus m), and on a few thousand test IDs that's the difference between fifteen million comparisons and eight thousand. And I check sort versus heapq.nlargest: if I only need the ten slowest tests out of fifty thousand, nlargest is O(n log k) rather than O(n log n)."

Cross-question — "Dict lookup is O(1) average and O(n) worst case. When does the worst case actually happen in practice?" "Two ways. Deliberately, if an attacker controls the keys — they can craft strings that all hash to the same slot and turn every lookup linear, which is a denial-of-service attack on anything that puts request parameters into a dict. That's why CPython randomises string hashes per process using PYTHONHASHSEED. Accidentally, if you write a custom __hash__ that returns a constant, or one based on a field with very low cardinality — I've seen def __hash__(self): return hash(self.status) on a class with three possible statuses, which makes a set of ten thousand of them behave like three linked lists. The rule I follow is that __hash__ should combine all the fields that __eq__ compares, and the easiest correct way is hash((self.a, self.b)) — let the tuple do the mixing."

docs.title: Kya hai
docs.text:
def ek statement hai jo chalne par ek function object banata hai aur usko naam se bind kar deta hai. Function ek normal object hai — usko variable mein rakho, list mein daalo, argument banao, return karo, attributes lagao.

Analogy: recipe ek kaagaz hai. Aap us kaagaz ko kisi ko de sakte ho, uski copy bana sakte ho, uspar sticky note laga sakte ho, ya use ek recipe-book mein rakh sakte ho — bina khana banaye. Function ko call karna hi khana banana hai; baaki sab kaagaz ke saath khela ja raha hai.

docs.title: Code — function object ke saare attributes
docs.text:
def click(selector, timeout=5000, force=False):
    """Click an element, waiting up to `timeout` ms."""
    return f"clicked {selector}"

# --- Function ek object hai ---
print(type(click))                  # <class 'function'>
print(click)                        # <function click at 0x10a...>
print(click.__name__)               # 'click'
print(click.__qualname__)           # 'click'  (nested ho toh 'Outer.click')
print(click.__doc__)                # 'Click an element, waiting up to `timeout` ms.'
print(click.__module__)             # '__main__'
print(click.__defaults__)           # (5000, False)   -- positional defaults ka tuple
print(click.__kwdefaults__)         # None            -- keyword-only defaults ka dict
print(click.__annotations__)        # {}              -- type hints ka dict
print(click.__code__.co_varnames)   # ('selector', 'timeout', 'force')
print(click.__code__.co_argcount)   # 3

# --- Naam bind karna ---
tap = click                         # ek aur naam, koi copy nahi
print(tap("#submit"))               # 'clicked #submit'
print(tap is click)                 # True

# --- Container mein rakhna ---
ACTIONS = {"click": click, "tap": click}
print(ACTIONS["click"]("#login"))   # dict se nikaal kar call kiya

# --- Attribute lagana (functions ka __dict__ hota hai) ---
click.call_count = 0                # runtime par attribute add
click.call_count += 1
print(click.call_count)             # 1

Line-by-line walkthrough:

  1. def click(...) — jab ye line chalti hai toh: compile-time par bana hua code object (click.__code__) ek function object mein wrap hota hai, defaults evaluate hote hain aur __defaults__ mein store hote hain, aur naam click bind hota hai. Defaults yahin ek baar evaluate hote hain — 1.4 wala bug isi line se aata hai.
  2. click.__name__ — original naam. Ye important hai kyunki decorators (Part 7) isko chhupa dete hain, aur functools.wraps isko wapas laata hai.
  3. click.__qualname__ — "qualified name", nesting ke saath: Page.click ya outer.<locals>.inner. Debugging aur logging mein ye __name__ se zyada useful hai.
  4. click.__defaults__ → (5000, False) — ye ek tuple hai jo function object par live rehta hai. Aap ise dekh sakte ho aur (dangerously) badal bhi sakte ho.
  5. click.__code__.co_varnames — code object ke andar locals ke naam. co_argcount positional parameters ki count. Ye introspection pytest fixtures ke liye zaruri hai — pytest aapke test function ke parameter names padh kar decide karta hai ki kaunsi fixtures inject karni hain.
  6. tap = click — 1.2 ka name-tag model. Function object ek hi hai, do naam.
  7. ACTIONS = {"click": click} — functions ko data structure mein rakhna hi dispatch table pattern hai (2.1 mein dekha).
  8. click.call_count = 0 — functions ka __dict__ hota hai, toh unpar arbitrary attributes lag sakte hain. pytest markers isi mechanism par bane hain: @pytest.mark.smoke function par ek attribute set karta hai jo collection ke waqt padha jaata hai.

docs.title: def vs lambda
docs.text:
# def -- statement, naam deta hai, multiple lines, docstring
def is_failed(result):
    """Return True if the test failed."""
    return result["status"] == "failed"

# lambda -- expression, anonymous, ek hi expression
is_failed_l = lambda result: result["status"] == "failed"

print(is_failed.__name__)      # 'is_failed'
print(is_failed_l.__name__)    # '<lambda>'   <- tracebacks mein bekaar
  1. lambda ek expression hai, toh use wahan likh sakte ho jahan statement nahi likh sakte (dict value, function argument, default value).
  2. Lambda mein sirf ek expression ho sakti hai — koi return, if statement, try, assignment (walrus chhod ke), ya multiple lines nahi.
  3. lambda ko variable mein assign mat karo — f = lambda x: x ka koi faayda nahi def f(x): return x se, aur __name__ <lambda> reh jaata hai jo traceback mein useless hai. PEP 8 aur ruff (E731) dono isko flag karte hain.
  4. Lambda ka sahi use: inline callable jo turant kisi function ko pass ho rahi ho — sorted(x, key=lambda r: r["duration"]).

Interview answer: "Functions are first-class objects. def is a statement that, when it runs, wraps a compiled code object into a function object, evaluates the defaults once, and binds the name — which is exactly why a mutable default is shared across calls. Because they're objects you can put them in dicts for dispatch tables, pass them as callbacks, return them from other functions, and set attributes on them; pytest's marker system is literally attributes set on the test function, and pytest's fixture injection works by reading the parameter names off __code__. lambda is the expression form, limited to a single expression and with __name__ set to <lambda>, so I only use it inline as a key or a small callback — never assigned to a name, because then def is strictly better for the traceback."

docs.title: Kya hai
docs.text:
Jab Python ek naam dekhta hai (x), wo use chaar jagah, isi order mein dhoondhta hai:

L  Local        -- current function ka scope
E  Enclosing    -- bahar wale function ka scope (nested functions)
G  Global       -- module ka top-level scope
B  Built-in     -- Python ke built-ins (print, len, ...)

Pehla match jeetta hai. Kahin na mile → NameError.

Analogy: aap office mein kuch dhoondh rahe ho. Pehle apni desk (Local), phir apni team ke common cupboard (Enclosing), phir poore office ka store (Global), phir building ka common supply room (Built-in). Jahan pehle mil gaya, wahin ruk gaye.

docs.title: Code — chaaron levels ek saath
docs.text:
timeout = "GLOBAL timeout"                    # G -- module level

def outer():
    timeout = "ENCLOSING timeout"             # E -- outer ka local, inner ke liye enclosing

    def inner():
        timeout = "LOCAL timeout"             # L -- inner ka apna
        print("1:", timeout)                  # L jeeta

    inner()
    print("2:", timeout)                      # outer ke liye 'timeout' local hai

outer()
print("3:", timeout)                          # G

print("4:", len)                              # B -- builtins se

Output:

1: LOCAL timeout
2: ENCLOSING timeout
3: GLOBAL timeout
4: <built-in function len>

Line-by-line walkthrough:

  1. timeout = "GLOBAL timeout" — module ke __dict__ mein entry banti hai. Ye "global" hai par actually module-level hai — poore program mein nahi, sirf is module mein.
  2. def outer(): ... timeout = "ENCLOSING timeout" — outer ke andar assignment hai, toh compiler ne timeout ko outer ka local maan liya. Global wala shadow ho gaya.
  3. def inner(): ... timeout = "LOCAL timeout" — inner ka apna local.
  4. print("1:", timeout) — inner ke andar. L mein mil gaya, ruk gaye.
  5. print("2:", timeout) — inner() call ke baad. inner ka local khatam ho chuka. outer ka apna timeout mila.
  6. print("4:", len) — len kahin define nahi hai, toh builtins mein mila.

docs.title: Kaise kaam karta hai — compile time par decide hota hai
docs.text:
Ye sabse important mechanism hai: Python compile time par hi decide kar leta hai ki har naam local hai ya nahi. Rule: agar function body mein us naam ko kahin bhi assign kiya gaya hai (=, for x in, import x, def x, class x, with ... as x, except ... as x), toh wo naam us poore function mein local hai.

counter = 0

def broken():
    print(counter)         # UnboundLocalError!
    counter = 1            # ye line UPAR wali line ko bhi affect karti hai

# broken()
# UnboundLocalError: cannot access local variable 'counter' where it is not associated with a value

Line-by-line walkthrough:

  1. counter = 0 — module-level global.
  2. def broken(): — compile time par CPython poori body scan karta hai. Usne dekha counter = 1 — assignment hai — toh counter ko broken ka local mark kar diya, aur uske liye locals array mein ek slot allocate kar diya.
  3. print(counter) — ye LOAD_FAST counter mein compile hua (local access). Par us slot mein abhi kuch bhi assign nahi hua → UnboundLocalError.
  4. Note: ye NameError nahi hai, UnboundLocalError hai — jo NameError ka subclass hai. Alag naam isliye ki wo aapko exactly ye batata hai: "naam local hai par abhi bind nahi hua", "naam exist hi nahi karta" nahi.
  5. Iska proof: 
    import dis
dis.dis(broken)
# LOAD_FAST  0 (counter)   <- FAST = local slot, GLOBAL nahi

docs.title: global aur nonlocal
docs.text:
retry_count = 0                             # module-level

def increment_global():
    global retry_count                      # "mujhe module-level wala chahiye"
    retry_count += 1                        # ab ye global ko modify karta hai

increment_global()
increment_global()
print(retry_count)                          # 2


def make_counter():
    count = 0                               # enclosing scope ka variable

    def increment():
        nonlocal count                      # "mujhe enclosing wala chahiye, global nahi"
        count += 1
        return count

    return increment

c = make_counter()
print(c(), c(), c())                        # 1 2 3

Line-by-line walkthrough:

  1. global retry_count — ye ek declaration hai, statement nahi. Ye compiler ko batata hai "is function mein retry_count ko local mat samajhna, module-level use karo". Iske bina retry_count += 1 UnboundLocalError deta (kyunki += assignment hai).
  2. retry_count += 1 — ye retry_count = retry_count + 1 hai: pehle read (global se), phir write (global par).
  3. nonlocal count — enclosing function scope ka variable. Ye global se alag hai: global seedha module-level dhoondhta hai, nonlocal sabse nazdeeki enclosing function scope dhoondhta hai (module-level ko nahi).
  4. Agar enclosing scope mein wo naam na ho toh nonlocal compile time par SyntaxError: no binding for nonlocal 'count' found deta hai. global naya naam bana bhi sakta hai. Ye asymmetry deliberate hai — nonlocal sirf existing closure variables ke liye hai.
  5. return increment — ye ek closure hai (4.5). count make_counter ke return hone ke baad bhi zinda rehta hai.

docs.title: Read vs write ka asymmetry
docs.text:
config = {"timeout": 30}
names = ["a"]

def mutate_ok():
    config["timeout"] = 60        # MUTATION -- global keyword ki zarurat NAHI
    names.append("b")             # MUTATION -- theek

def rebind_broken():
    # config = {}                 # REBINDING -- 'config' local ban jaata, global untouched
    pass

mutate_ok()
print(config, names)              # {'timeout': 60} ['a', 'b']
  1. Mutation ke liye global nahi chahiye — kyunki aap naam ko rebind nahi kar rahe, sirf object ko badal rahe ho. Naam lookup normal LEGB se ho jaata hai.
  2. Rebinding ke liye global chahiye — kyunki assignment se naam local ban jaata hai.
  3. Isliye ye rule hai: global/nonlocal sirf tab likho jab aap = kar rahe ho.

docs.title: globals(), locals(), vars()
docs.text:
x = 1

def demo():
    y = 2
    print(locals())              # {'y': 2}       -- is function ke locals
    print(globals()["x"])        # 1              -- module ke globals
    print(len(globals()))        # kaafi (module ke saare naam + dunder)

demo()

# locals() function mein READ-ONLY-ish hai
def cant_write():
    locals()["z"] = 99           # CPython mein ye kuch nahi karta
    # print(z)                   # NameError
  1. locals() — CPython mein function ke andar ye locals array ka snapshot dict deta hai. Usme likhne se actual locals nahi badalte (kyunki wo array hai, dict nahi). Module level par locals() is globals() hai.
  2. globals() — module ka actual __dict__ hai, aur usme likhne se sach mein global banta hai. globals()["new"] = 1 ke baad new use kar sakte ho.
  3. vars(obj) — obj.__dict__ deta hai. Argument ke bina locals() ke barabar.
  4. Ye debugging aur framework code (jaise pytest fixtures) ke liye hain, normal code ke liye nahi.

docs.title: Class body ka scope — ek exception
docs.text:
class TestSuite:
    default_timeout = 30                         # class body ka naam
    doubled = default_timeout * 2                # yahan visible hai

    def get_timeout(self):
        # return default_timeout                 # NameError! class body scope enclosing NAHI hai
        return self.default_timeout              # sahi -- attribute lookup se

print(TestSuite.doubled)                          # 60
print(TestSuite().get_timeout())                  # 30
  1. Class body ek alag scope hai jo methods ke liye enclosing scope nahi banta. Ye LEGB ka ek deliberate exception hai.
  2. Kyun: class body ek baar chalti hai aur uske naam class ke attributes ban jaate hain. Agar wo enclosing scope hoti toh self.x aur x ka farak dhundhla ho jaata.
  3. Isliye method ke andar class attributes ko self.x ya ClassName.x se access karo.
  4. Ek aur gotcha: class body ke andar comprehension apna scope banati hai, aur wo class scope ko nahi dekh sakti: 
    class Bad:
    values = [1, 2, 3]
    # doubled = [v * multiplier for v in values]   # 'values' iterable hai toh chalega...
    multiplier = 2
    # doubled = [v * multiplier for v in values]   # NameError: 'multiplier' not defined
    Sirf pehla iterable comprehension ke bahar evaluate hota hai, isliye values chalta hai; body ke andar wale naam class scope se resolve nahi ho paate.

docs.title: Gotchas
docs.text:
Gotcha 1 — loop variable overwriting a builtin.

list = [1, 2, 3]                  # builtin 'list' ko shadow kar diya
# new = list(range(5))            # TypeError: 'list' object is not callable
del list                          # shadow hata do

Common shadows jo bug banate hain: list, dict, set, str, id, type, input, next, filter, max, min, sum, bytes, hash, object, format. ruff ka A001/A002 rule inhe pakadta hai.

Gotcha 2 — import bhi assignment hai.

import os

def broken():
    # print(os.getcwd())          # UnboundLocalError -- neeche 'import os' hai
    import os                     # ye 'os' ko LOCAL bana deta hai poore function mein
    return os.getcwd()

Gotcha 3 — del ke baad naam gayab.

def demo():
    x = 1
    del x
    # print(x)                    # UnboundLocalError -- slot exist karta hai par unbound hai

Gotcha 4 — exception variable automatically delete hoti hai.

try:
    raise ValueError("boom")
except ValueError as e:
    print(e)                      # 'boom'
# print(e)                        # NameError: name 'e' is not defined
  1. Python 3 mein except ... as e: block ke end par del e implicitly hota hai. Ye deliberate hai: exception object apne traceback ko reference karta hai, jo frame ko reference karta hai, jo e ko reference karta hai — ek reference cycle. Isko todne ke liye Python e ko delete kar deta hai.
  2. Agar aapko exception baad mein chahiye toh doosre naam mein copy karo: 
    error = None
try:
    raise ValueError("boom")
except ValueError as e:
    error = e                  # alag naam mein rakha
print(error)                   # 'boom'

Interview answer: "Name resolution follows LEGB: local, then enclosing function scopes, then module globals, then builtins, and the first match wins. The key mechanism is that whether a name is local is decided at compile time, not at runtime — if a name is assigned anywhere in the function body, it's local for the whole body, including lines before the assignment. That's why reading a global and then assigning to it in the same function raises UnboundLocalError rather than reading the global. global and nonlocal are declarations that override that: global targets module level, nonlocal targets the nearest enclosing function scope and is a SyntaxError if no such binding exists. Crucially, you only need them for rebinding — mutating a global list or dict works fine without any declaration, because you're not rebinding the name. One exception to LEGB worth knowing: a class body is a scope, but it isn't an enclosing scope for its methods, so a method has to say self.x or ClassName.x."

Cross-question — "Why is local variable access faster than global access?" "Because they use different storage. Function locals are known at compile time, so CPython allocates them slots in an array on the frame and compiles access to LOAD_FAST, which is an array index. Globals live in the module's dictionary, so access compiles to LOAD_GLOBAL, which is a dict lookup in globals and then possibly a second lookup in builtins if it misses. That's roughly a two-to-three times difference per access, and it's why the classic micro-optimisation is to bind a hot global or method to a local before a tight loop — append = results.append before the loop. Python 3.11 added inline caching for LOAD_GLOBAL, which narrowed the gap considerably, so I'd measure before doing it."

docs.title: 4.3 Arguments — har kism, aur unka order
Kya hai — poora signature grammar
docs.text:
def f(pos_only, /, standard, *args, kw_only, **kwargs):
    ...
Part Naam Kaise pass karo pos_only positional-only sirf position se: f(1, ...) / marker iske pehle sab positional-only standard positional-or-keyword dono tareeke se *args var-positional extra positional arguments ka tuple kw_only keyword-only sirf naam se: f(..., kw_only=x) **kwargs var-keyword extra keyword arguments ka dict

* akela bhi likh sakte ho *args ki jagah — matlab "yahan se aage sab keyword-only".

docs.title: Ek-ek karke
docs.text:
1. Positional aur keyword

def click(selector, timeout):
    return f"click {selector} in {timeout}ms"

print(click("#submit", 5000))                 # dono positional
print(click("#submit", timeout=5000))         # doosra keyword
print(click(selector="#submit", timeout=5000))# dono keyword
print(click(timeout=5000, selector="#submit"))# keyword hone se ORDER matter nahi
# click(timeout=5000, "#submit")              # SyntaxError: positional after keyword
  1. Keyword arguments ka order matter nahi karta — kyunki naam se match hote hain.
  2. Positional argument keyword ke baad nahi aa sakta — parser ko ambiguity ho jaati.

2. Defaults

def click(selector, timeout=5000, force=False):     # defaults RIGHT side par
    return f"{selector} {timeout} {force}"

print(click("#a"))                    # #a 5000 False
print(click("#a", 1000))              # #a 1000 False
print(click("#a", force=True))        # #a 5000 True   -- middle skip kiya
# def bad(a=1, b): ...                # SyntaxError: non-default argument follows default
  1. Defaults hamesha non-default parameters ke baad aane chahiye, warna call ambiguous hoti.
  2. click("#a", force=True) — beech wala timeout skip karke naam se aage wala diya. Yahi keyword arguments ka asli faayda hai.
  3. Defaults ek baar evaluate hote hain (1.4).

3. *args

def run_tests(suite_name, *test_names):
    print(f"suite={suite_name}, tests={test_names}, type={type(test_names).__name__}")

run_tests("smoke")                              # tests=() type=tuple
run_tests("smoke", "test_a")                    # tests=('test_a',)
run_tests("smoke", "test_a", "test_b")          # tests=('test_a', 'test_b')

names = ["test_x", "test_y"]
run_tests("regression", *names)                 # UNPACKING -- list ko args mein todo
  1. *test_names extra positional arguments ko ek tuple mein collect karta hai. Tuple isliye (list nahi) taaki accidentally mutate na ho.
  2. Koi extra na ho toh khaali tuple milta hai, None nahi — toh for t in test_names: hamesha safe hai.
  3. run_tests("regression", *names) — call site par * ka matlab ulta hai: "is iterable ko alag-alag arguments mein todo". Definition mein collect, call mein spread.
  4. Naam args convention hai, requirement nahi. Meaningful naam behtar hai (*test_names).

4. **kwargs

def configure(browser, **options):
    print(f"browser={browser}, options={options}, type={type(options).__name__}")

configure("chromium")                                  # options={}
configure("chromium", headless=True, slow_mo=100)      # options={'headless': True, 'slow_mo': 100}

opts = {"headless": False, "timeout": 30000}
configure("firefox", **opts)                           # dict ko kwargs mein todo
  1. **options extra keyword arguments ko dict mein collect karta hai. Keys hamesha strings hoti hain.
  2. configure("firefox", **opts) — call site par ** dict ko keyword arguments mein spread karta hai. Agar opts mein browser key hoti toh TypeError: got multiple values for argument 'browser'.
  3. **kwargs insertion order preserve karta hai (3.7+).

5. Keyword-only (via *) — ye aapke ix.click() wala hai

# --- BINA keyword-only: call site padhne mein bekaar ---
def click_bad(selector, timeout=5000, force=False, no_wait_after=False, trial=False):
    ...

click_bad("#submit", 1000, True, False, True)      # ye kya kar raha hai?? paanch magic values

# --- KEYWORD-ONLY ke saath ---
def click(selector, *, timeout=5000, force=False, no_wait_after=False, trial=False):
    """`*` ke BAAD sab arguments sirf naam se pass ho sakte hain."""
    return f"click({selector!r}, timeout={timeout}, force={force})"

print(click("#submit", timeout=1000, force=True))   # self-documenting
# click("#submit", 1000, True)                      # TypeError: takes 1 positional argument but 3 were given

Line-by-line walkthrough:

  1. def click(selector, *, timeout=5000, ...) — bare * ek separator hai. Uske baad ke saare parameters keyword-only ho jaate hain. Wo *args nahi hai — wo koi value collect nahi karta, sirf boundary banata hai.
  2. click("#submit", timeout=1000, force=True) — har argument ka matlab call site par likha hai. Code review mein, git diff mein, aur 6 mahine baad khud padhte waqt — sab jagah saaf.
  3. click("#submit", 1000, True) — ab ye error hai. Ye achhi baat hai: aapne API contract enforce kar diya.

Aap ye kyun karte ho — chaar concrete faayde:

Faayda Kaise Readability click("#a", force=True) vs click("#a", 5000, True, False) Refactor safety Parameters ka order badal do — koi caller nahi tootega, kyunki koi position par depend nahi karta Boolean trap se bachna click("#a", True, False, True) — kaunsa True kya hai? Keyword-only ye bug hi khatam kar deta hai API evolve karne ki azaadi Naya optional parameter beech mein add kar sakte ho; positional hota toh sirf end mein add kar paate

Standard library bhi yahi karti hai: sorted(iterable, *, key=None, reverse=False), json.dumps(obj, *, indent=None, ...), dataclasses.field(*, default=..., ...). Ye ek established, senior-level API design pattern hai.

6. Positional-only (via /, Python 3.8+)

def get_locator(page, selector, /, timeout=5000):
    """`page` aur `selector` sirf positional -- unke naam API ka hissa nahi hain."""
    return f"{selector} on {page}"

print(get_locator("home", "#submit"))                    # theek
print(get_locator("home", "#submit", timeout=1000))      # theek
# get_locator(page="home", selector="#submit")           # TypeError: got some positional-only
#                                                        # arguments passed as keyword arguments

Kyun positional-only chahiye:

  1. Parameter naam ko implementation detail rakhna. Agar page keyword se pass ho sakta hai toh aap use kabhi rename nahi kar sakte — wo public API ban gaya. / ke baad wo private rehta hai.
  2. **kwargs ke saath clash se bachna: 
    def set_headers(headers, /, **extra):
    result = dict(headers)
    result.update(extra)
    return result

print(set_headers({"a": 1}, headers="b"))    # {'a': 1, 'headers': 'b'}  -- kaam kiya!
# '/' ke bina ye TypeError deta: multiple values for 'headers'
    Ye asli reason hai jiske liye / add kiya gaya — dict.update(**kwargs) jaise functions ko fix karne ke liye.
  3. Built-ins hamesha se positional-only the (C mein likhe hain): len(obj), abs(x) — len(obj=[1,2]) TypeError deta hai. / ne ye capability Python-level functions ko di.

docs.title: Poora example — sab ek saath
docs.text:
def run_suite(suite_path, /, browser="chromium", *tags, headless=True, **playwright_opts):
    """
    suite_path       : positional-only
    browser          : positional-or-keyword (default hai)
    *tags            : baaki positional
    headless         : keyword-only (kyunki *tags ke baad hai)
    **playwright_opts: baaki keyword
    """
    return {
        "suite": suite_path,
        "browser": browser,
        "tags": tags,
        "headless": headless,
        "opts": playwright_opts,
    }

print(run_suite("tests/smoke", "firefox", "auth", "cart", headless=False, slow_mo=100))
# {'suite': 'tests/smoke', 'browser': 'firefox', 'tags': ('auth', 'cart'),
#  'headless': False, 'opts': {'slow_mo': 100}}

Line-by-line walkthrough:

  1. suite_path, / — sirf position se. run_suite(suite_path="x") error dega.
  2. browser="chromium" — position ya naam dono se. Yahan "firefox" positional gaya.
  3. *tags — "auth" aur "cart" yahan collect hue.
  4. headless=True — *tags ke baad hai, isliye automatically keyword-only. Ye important rule hai: *args ke baad sab keyword-only ho jaata hai, alag * ki zarurat nahi.
  5. **playwright_opts — slow_mo=100 yahan aaya.
  6. Ye signature real code ke liye zyada complex hai — maine sirf grammar dikhane ke liye likha. Production mein 2-3 kism se zyada mat mix karo.

docs.title: Argument passing ke gotchas
docs.text:
Gotcha 1 — mutable default. (1.4 mein detail)

Gotcha 2 — *args ke baad sab keyword-only ho jaata hai.

def f(a, *args, b):
    return a, args, b

print(f(1, 2, 3, b=4))          # (1, (2, 3), 4)
# f(1, 2, 3, 4)                 # TypeError: missing 1 required keyword-only argument: 'b'

Gotcha 3 — dict unpacking mein duplicate key.

def f(a, b):
    return a + b

d = {"a": 1, "b": 2}
print(f(**d))                   # 3
# print(f(1, **{"a": 5}))       # TypeError: got multiple values for argument 'a'

# Merge karke bhejo
defaults = {"a": 1, "b": 2}
overrides = {"b": 99}
print(f(**{**defaults, **overrides}))    # 100

Gotcha 4 — arguments hamesha eagerly evaluate hote hain.

def get_default():
    print("expensive call!")
    return 30

def f(timeout=None):
    return timeout if timeout is not None else get_default()

f(10)                            # "expensive call!" print NAHI hoga -- lazy
# vs
def g(timeout=get_default()):    # ye 'def' line par EK BAAR chalta hai (import time!)
    return timeout
  1. f(10) — get_default() sirf tab chalta hai jab zarurat ho. Ye pattern (None sentinel + body mein compute) lazy defaults ka standard tareeka hai.
  2. def g(timeout=get_default()) — ye function define hote waqt chalta hai, matlab import time par. Agar wo network call ho toh aapka import hang ho jaayega. Real bug.

Gotcha 5 — * ko unpacking mein bhool jaana.

def f(a, b, c):
    return a + b + c

args = [1, 2, 3]
# print(f(args))                # TypeError: missing 2 required positional arguments
print(f(*args))                 # 6

docs.title: inspect.signature — introspection
docs.text:
import inspect

def click(selector, /, *, timeout=5000, force=False):
    ...

sig = inspect.signature(click)
print(sig)                                    # (selector, /, *, timeout=5000, force=False)
for name, param in sig.parameters.items():
    print(f"{name:<10} kind={param.kind.name:<20} default={param.default!r}")

Output:

selector   kind=POSITIONAL_ONLY      default=<class 'inspect._empty'>
timeout    kind=KEYWORD_ONLY         default=5000
force      kind=KEYWORD_ONLY         default=False
  1. inspect.signature(f) — poora signature object deta hai. Ye f.__defaults__ etc. padhne se behtar hai kyunki wo decorators ke through bhi kaam karta hai (agar functools.wraps laga ho).
  2. param.kind — paanch kinds: POSITIONAL_ONLY, POSITIONAL_OR_KEYWORD, VAR_POSITIONAL, KEYWORD_ONLY, VAR_KEYWORD.
  3. inspect._empty — "koi default nahi" ka sentinel. None use nahi kiya kyunki None khud ek valid default ho sakta hai. Ye sentinel pattern ka textbook example hai.
  4. pytest isi machinery se aapke test function ke parameters padh kar fixtures resolve karta hai.

Interview answer: "Python has five parameter kinds: positional-only before a /, normal positional-or-keyword, *args for extra positionals, keyword-only after a bare * or after *args, and **kwargs for extra keywords. The design decision I actually make is keyword-only. Any function with more than one or two optional flags gets a bare *, because click('#submit', 1000, True, False) is unreadable at the call site and impossible to review — that's the boolean-trap anti-pattern. Making them keyword-only buys three things beyond readability: I can reorder or insert parameters without breaking any caller, callers can skip middle arguments, and a boolean can never be silently passed into the wrong slot. The standard library does exactly this — sorted(iterable, *, key=None, reverse=False). Positional-only with / is the mirror image: it keeps a parameter's name out of the public API so I can rename it, and it lets a function take **kwargs containing a key that collides with a parameter name."

Cross-question — "You made timeout keyword-only. Doesn't that break existing callers?" "Yes, and that's the trade-off — adding a * to an existing signature is a breaking change for anyone passing those arguments positionally. So it's a decision you make when you design the function, not a refactor you do casually. If I have to do it to an existing API, the migration is to accept both for a release: keep the parameters positional but emit a DeprecationWarning when they arrive positionally, then flip to keyword-only in the next major version. For internal test-framework code where I own every caller, I just make the change and let the TypeError at import time point me at the call sites — a loud failure at collection time is much better than a boolean silently landing in the wrong slot."

docs.title: Kya hai
docs.text: First-class = function ek value hai (variable, argument, return value, container item). Higher-order function = wo function jo ya toh function leta hai, ya function deta hai (ya dono).

docs.title: Kyu — dispatch aur configuration
docs.text:
# --- WITHOUT higher-order functions: har variation ke liye naya function ---
def sort_by_duration(results):
    return sorted(results, key=lambda r: r["duration"])

def sort_by_name(results):
    return sorted(results, key=lambda r: r["name"])

def sort_by_status(results):
    return sorted(results, key=lambda r: r["status"])
# ... 10 fields = 10 functions

# --- WITH: ek function jo behaviour ko parameter banata hai ---
def sort_results(results, key_fn):
    return sorted(results, key=key_fn)

from operator import itemgetter
sort_results(results, itemgetter("duration"))

sorted khud ek higher-order function hai — wo key naam ka function leta hai.

docs.title: Built-in higher-order functions
docs.text:
results = [
    {"name": "test_login", "status": "passed", "duration": 1.2},
    {"name": "test_cart", "status": "failed", "duration": 4.5},
    {"name": "test_pay", "status": "failed", "duration": 0.8},
]

# --- map: har item par function lagao (LAZY iterator deta hai) ---
names = map(lambda r: r["name"], results)
print(list(names))                              # ['test_login', 'test_cart', 'test_pay']

# --- filter: predicate True wale rakho (LAZY) ---
failed = filter(lambda r: r["status"] == "failed", results)
print([r["name"] for r in failed])              # ['test_cart', 'test_pay']

# --- sorted: key function se ---
print([r["name"] for r in sorted(results, key=lambda r: r["duration"])])

# --- max / min: key function se ---
slowest = max(results, key=lambda r: r["duration"])
print(slowest["name"])                          # test_cart

# --- any / all: predicate ke saath ---
print(any(r["status"] == "failed" for r in results))      # True
print(all(r["duration"] < 10 for r in results))           # True

# --- sum with generator ---
print(round(sum(r["duration"] for r in results), 1))      # 6.5

Line-by-line walkthrough:

  1. map(fn, iterable) — lazy iterator deta hai. list() kiye bina kuch compute nahi hota. Ye Python 2 se badla hai (wahan list deta tha).
  2. filter(pred, iterable) — lazy. pred=None do toh truthy items filter karta hai: filter(None, [0, 1, "", "a"]) → [1, "a"].
  3. Pythonic choice: map/filter ki jagah aksar comprehension likhna behtar hai: 
    names = [r["name"] for r in results]                     # map se saaf
failed = [r for r in results if r["status"] == "failed"]  # filter se saaf
    map tab jeetta hai jab function already exist karta ho: map(str.strip, lines) [s.strip() for s in lines] se tez aur saaf hai, kyunki koi lambda call frame nahi banta.
  4. max(results, key=...) — key ke bina max dicts ko compare karne ki koshish karta aur TypeError deta.
  5. any/all — short-circuit karte hain. any pehla True milte hi ruk jaata hai. Ye important hai jab predicate costly ho: 
    if any(is_element_visible(sel) for sel in selectors):   # pehla visible milte hi ruk gaya
    ...
    Khaali iterable par: any([]) → False, all([]) → True (vacuous truth). Ye surprise deta hai: all(r.passed for r in []) True hai — khaali suite "sab pass" ban jaati hai. Isliye pehle if not results: raise likhna chahiye.

docs.title: QA example — pluggable retry policies
docs.text:
import time
import random

# --- Retry policies as functions ---
def fixed_delay(attempt, base=1.0):
    """Har attempt par same delay."""
    return base

def exponential_backoff(attempt, base=1.0, cap=30.0):
    """1, 2, 4, 8, ... capped."""
    return min(base * (2 ** (attempt - 1)), cap)

def exponential_jitter(attempt, base=1.0, cap=30.0):
    """Exponential + randomness -- thundering herd se bachne ke liye."""
    delay = min(base * (2 ** (attempt - 1)), cap)
    return random.uniform(0, delay)                  # full jitter

# --- Ek retry function jo policy ko parameter maanta hai ---
def retry(fn, *, attempts=3, delay_policy=exponential_backoff, exceptions=(Exception,)):
    """`fn` ko `attempts` baar try karo, beech mein policy ke hisaab se ruko."""
    last_error = None
    for attempt in range(1, attempts + 1):
        try:
            return fn()
        except exceptions as exc:
            last_error = exc
            if attempt == attempts:
                break
            wait = delay_policy(attempt)
            print(f"attempt {attempt} failed ({exc}); retrying in {wait:.2f}s")
            time.sleep(wait)
    raise RuntimeError(f"all {attempts} attempts failed") from last_error

Line-by-line walkthrough:

  1. def fixed_delay(attempt, base=1.0): — teeno policies ka same signature hai (attempt leti hain, seconds deti hain). Yahi contract unhe interchangeable banata hai. Ye "strategy pattern" hai, bina kisi class ke.
  2. def retry(fn, *, attempts=3, delay_policy=exponential_backoff, exceptions=(Exception,)): — fn ek callable hai. * ke baad sab keyword-only (4.3 ka sabak). delay_policy ka default ek function object hai — brackets nahi lagaye, kyunki hum call nahi kar rahe, pass kar rahe hain. exceptions ka default ek tuple hai (immutable, toh 1.4 wala bug nahi) — aur tuple isliye ki except multiple types leta hai.
  3. last_error = None — loop ke bahar declare kiya taaki loop ke baad accessible ho.
  4. for attempt in range(1, attempts + 1): — 1-based, kyunki backoff formula 2**(attempt-1) 1 se shuru hota hai aur logs mein "attempt 1" padhna natural hai.
  5. return fn() — success par turant return. try block mein sirf ek call hai — jitna chhota try block, utna kam chance ki aap galti se koi aur exception pakad lo (Part 9).
  6. except exceptions as exc: — exceptions ek tuple hai. Default (Exception,) sab kuch pakadta hai sivay KeyboardInterrupt/SystemExit ke (wo BaseException se aate hain) — ye deliberate hai, warna Ctrl+C bhi retry ho jaata.
  7. if attempt == attempts: break — aakhri attempt ke baad sleep karne ka koi matlab nahi. Ye chhoti si detail 3 retries par 30 second bacha deti hai.
  8. wait = delay_policy(attempt) — yahan policy inject ho rahi hai. Caller ne jo function diya, wahi chala.
  9. raise RuntimeError(...) from last_error — exception chaining (Part 9). from original error ko __cause__ mein rakhta hai, toh traceback mein dono dikhte hain. Ye raise RuntimeError(...) se bahut behtar hai — warna asli exception (jaise TimeoutError: waiting for #submit) gayab ho jaati hai.

Use:

flaky_counter = {"n": 0}

def flaky_api_call():
    flaky_counter["n"] += 1
    if flaky_counter["n"] < 3:
        raise ConnectionError("service unavailable")
    return {"status": "ok"}

result = retry(flaky_api_call, attempts=5, delay_policy=lambda a: 0.01)
print(result)                     # {'status': 'ok'}
  1. delay_policy=lambda a: 0.01 — test mein hum real sleep nahi chahte, toh policy ko override kar diya. Yahi higher-order design ka faayda hai — testability. Agar retry ke andar time.sleep(2 ** attempt) hardcoded hota toh test 7 second lagta.
  2. flaky_counter = {"n": 0} — dict use kiya kyunki nested function se int rebind karne ke liye nonlocal chahiye hota; mutable container se bina nonlocal ke kaam ho jaata hai. (Cleaner tareeka: nonlocal ya ek class.)

docs.title: Callables — sirf functions nahi
docs.text:
# 1. Function
def f(): pass

# 2. Lambda
g = lambda: None

# 3. Class (call karne se instance banta hai)
class Page: pass

# 4. Instance jiski class mein __call__ ho
class RetryPolicy:
    def __init__(self, base, cap):
        self.base = base
        self.cap = cap

    def __call__(self, attempt):                  # instance ko callable banata hai
        return min(self.base * (2 ** (attempt - 1)), self.cap)

policy = RetryPolicy(base=0.5, cap=10)
print(policy(3))                                   # 2.0   -- instance ko call kiya!
print(callable(policy))                            # True

# 5. Bound method
class Suite:
    def run(self): return "running"
s = Suite()
runner = s.run                                     # bound method, ek object
print(runner())                                    # 'running'

# 6. functools.partial
from functools import partial
slow_policy = partial(exponential_backoff, base=5.0)
print(slow_policy(2))                              # 10.0
  1. __call__ — instance ko function ki tarah call karne deta hai. Faayda: state rakh sakte ho (yahan base, cap) aur configuration __init__ mein alag rakh sakte ho. Ye closure ka class-based alternative hai, aur tab better hai jab state complex ho ya introspect karni ho.
  2. callable(x) — check karta hai ki type(x) par __call__ hai ya nahi.
  3. s.run — bound method: ek object jo function aur instance dono ko pakde hue hai. s.run is s.run False hai — har attribute access naya bound method object banata hai (descriptor protocol, Part 5).
  4. partial(fn, base=5.0) — kuch arguments pre-fill karke naya callable. 4.7 mein detail.

Interview answer: "Functions being first class means I can pass behaviour as a parameter instead of duplicating code. The pattern I use most in test infrastructure is injecting a policy: a retry helper takes the callable to run and a delay_policy function, so fixed delay, exponential backoff, and jittered backoff are three small functions with the same signature rather than three copies of the retry loop. The testability payoff is the real one — in a unit test I pass lambda attempt: 0.01 and the test runs in milliseconds instead of thirty seconds, which would be impossible if the sleep were hardcoded. Beyond plain functions, anything with __call__ is callable: classes, bound methods, functools.partial objects, and instances that carry configuration in __init__ — I use the last one when the strategy needs state that would make a closure awkward."

Cross-question — "When would you use map/filter instead of a comprehension?" "When the function already exists as a name. map(str.strip, lines) is both clearer and faster than [s.strip() for s in lines], because the comprehension builds a Python-level frame per item while map calls the C-level method directly. The moment I'd need a lambda, the comprehension wins — map(lambda r: r['name'], results) is strictly worse than the comprehension in both readability and speed. There's also a laziness difference: map and filter return iterators, so they compose into a pipeline without materialising intermediates, which matters on large inputs; a list comprehension is eager, and the lazy equivalent is a generator expression."

docs.title: 4.5 Closures — aur wo loop-variable capture bug
Kya hai
docs.text:
Closure = ek nested function jo apne enclosing scope ke variables ko yaad rakhti hai, chahe outer function return ho chuka ho.

Analogy: aap ek shop se ek gift card lete ho jo ek specific branch se juda hai. Aap shop se nikal gaye (outer function returned), par card us branch ko yaad rakhta hai. Card use karoge toh wo usi branch se paise kaatega.

docs.title: Kyu hai
docs.text:
# --- WITHOUT closure: har baar sab kuch pass karna padta hai ---
def build_url_bad(base_url, path):
    return f"{base_url.rstrip('/')}/{path.lstrip('/')}"

print(build_url_bad("https://staging.example.com", "/api/tests"))
print(build_url_bad("https://staging.example.com", "/api/results"))
print(build_url_bad("https://staging.example.com", "/api/runs"))
# base_url har baar repeat -- copy-paste, aur ek jagah badalna bhool jao toh bug

# --- WITH closure: base_url ek baar capture karo ---
def make_url_builder(base_url):
    clean_base = base_url.rstrip("/")                    # ek baar compute hua

    def build(path):                                     # closure: clean_base yaad rakhta hai
        return f"{clean_base}/{path.lstrip('/')}"

    return build

url = make_url_builder("https://staging.example.com/")
print(url("/api/tests"))          # https://staging.example.com/api/tests
print(url("api/results"))         # https://staging.example.com/api/results

Line-by-line walkthrough:

  1. def make_url_builder(base_url): — ye ek factory hai: ek function jo function banata hai.
  2. clean_base = base_url.rstrip("/") — ye kaam ek baar hota hai, har call par nahi. Agar ye expensive hota (config load, regex compile, DB connection) toh ye bachat bahut badi hoti.
  3. def build(path): — nested function. clean_base iske liye free variable hai (na local, na global — enclosing).
  4. return build — function object return kiya, call nahi kiya (build() nahi likha). Ye difference critical hai.
  5. url = make_url_builder(...) — ab url ek function hai jiske andar clean_base "band" (closed over) hai. make_url_builder ka frame khatam ho gaya, par clean_base zinda hai.

docs.title: Kaise kaam karta hai — cell objects
docs.text:
Python closures ko cell objects se implement karta hai. Cell ek chhota container hai jo value ko hold karta hai; outer aur inner dono usi cell ko point karte hain.

def make_counter(start=0):
    count = start                      # ye ek CELL variable ban jaata hai

    def increment():
        nonlocal count                 # cell ko write karne ki permission
        count += 1
        return count

    return increment

c = make_counter(10)
print(c(), c(), c())                   # 11 12 13

# --- Closure ko andar se dekho ---
print(c.__closure__)                   # (<cell at 0x...: int object at 0x...>,)
print(c.__closure__[0].cell_contents)  # 13   -- live value!
print(c.__code__.co_freevars)          # ('count',)  -- kaunse naam closed over hain

Line-by-line walkthrough:

  1. count = start — compiler ne dekha ki increment count ko use karta hai aur nonlocal declare karta hai, toh usne count ko normal local slot ki jagah ek cell mein rakha.
  2. nonlocal count — bina iske count += 1 UnboundLocalError deta (4.2 ka rule: assignment se naam local ban jaata hai).
  3. c.__closure__ — cells ka tuple. Har free variable ke liye ek cell.
  4. cell_contents — cell ki current value. Ye live hai — c() call karne ke baad dobara padho toh badla hua milega. Ye proof hai ki closure ne value copy nahi ki, reference pakda hai.
  5. co_freevars — free variables ke naam. Debugging mein useful.

Do independent counters:

a = make_counter(0)
b = make_counter(100)
print(a(), a(), b(), a(), b())         # 1 2 101 3 102

Har make_counter() call ek naya cell banati hai, toh counters independent hain. Ye closure aur global variable ka core farak hai.

docs.title: THE loop-variable capture bug
docs.text:
Ye interview mein bahut poochha jaata hai aur real code mein bhi aata hai.

# --- BUG ---
def make_click_handlers_bad(selectors):
    handlers = []
    for sel in selectors:
        handlers.append(lambda: f"clicking {sel}")     # 'sel' ko CAPTURE kiya... ya nahi?
    return handlers

hs = make_click_handlers_bad(["#login", "#cart", "#pay"])
for h in hs:
    print(h())

Output:

clicking #pay
clicking #pay
clicking #pay

Kyun — mechanism:

  1. Closure variable ki value capture nahi karta, cell capture karta hai.
  2. Loop mein sel ek hi variable hai jo baar-baar rebind hota hai — ek hi cell.
  3. Teeno lambdas usi ek cell ko point kar rahe hain.
  4. Jab aap unhe call karte ho (loop ke baad), cell mein aakhri value "#pay" padi hai.
  5. Isko late binding kehte hain: naam lookup call time par hota hai, definition time par nahi.

Fix 1 — default argument (value ko definition time par bind karo):

def make_click_handlers(selectors):
    handlers = []
    for sel in selectors:
        handlers.append(lambda s=sel: f"clicking {s}")   # 's' ka default ABHI evaluate hua
    return handlers

for h in make_click_handlers(["#login", "#cart", "#pay"]):
    print(h())
# clicking #login
# clicking #cart
# clicking #pay
  1. lambda s=sel: ... — default arguments def/lambda chalte waqt evaluate hote hain (1.4 wala mechanism, yahan faayde ke liye use ho raha hai). Toh har lambda ke __defaults__ mein us iteration ki value store ho gayi.
  2. Downside: ab lambda ka signature (s=...) hai — koi caller galti se h("#other") pass kar sakta hai. Ye leaky abstraction hai.

Fix 2 — factory function (sabse saaf):

def make_handler(sel):                     # har call ka apna scope, apna cell
    def handler():
        return f"clicking {sel}"
    return handler

def make_click_handlers_v2(selectors):
    return [make_handler(sel) for sel in selectors]

for h in make_click_handlers_v2(["#login", "#cart", "#pay"]):
    print(h())
# clicking #login / #cart / #pay
  1. Har make_handler(sel) call ka apna frame aur apna cell hai. Toh har handler alag cell dekh raha hai.
  2. Signature saaf rehta hai (handler() koi argument nahi leta).
  3. Ye production code ke liye recommended fix hai.

Fix 3 — functools.partial:

from functools import partial

def click_message(sel):
    return f"clicking {sel}"

handlers = [partial(click_message, sel) for sel in ["#login", "#cart", "#pay"]]
for h in handlers:
    print(h())
  1. partial argument ko turant bind kar leta hai (object mein store karta hai), toh late binding ka sawaal hi nahi.
  2. Sabse saaf jab function pehle se exist karta ho.

docs.title: Ye bug pytest mein kaise dikhta hai
docs.text:
import pytest

# --- BUG: saare parametrized tests same URL check karenge ---
URLS = ["/home", "/cart", "/checkout"]

def make_tests_bad():
    tests = {}
    for url in URLS:
        def test(page):
            page.goto(url)                          # LATE BINDING -- hamesha '/checkout'
        tests[f"test_{url.strip('/')}"] = test
    return tests

# --- FIX ---
def make_tests(url):
    def test(page):
        page.goto(url)
    return test

TESTS = {f"test_{u.strip('/')}": make_tests(u) for u in URLS}

Practically pytest mein iska sahi hal @pytest.mark.parametrize hai — wo aapke liye ye scoping handle kar deta hai. Par dynamically-generated tests likhte waqt ye bug real hai.

docs.title: Closure kab use karein / kab nahi
docs.text:
Use closure Use class Ek hi behaviour, thoda sa state Multiple related methods Configuration ko pre-bind karna State ko introspect/serialise karna hai Decorators (Part 7) Inheritance chahiye Callbacks jinhe context chahiye Testing mein state check karni hai

Closure ka downside: state chhupa hua hai. Aap c.__closure__[0].cell_contents se hi dekh sakte ho — jo debugging mein bura hai. Class mein counter.count seedha dikhta hai.

docs.title: Gotchas
docs.text:
Gotcha 1 — closure late binding. (upar detail mein)

Gotcha 2 — nonlocal ke bina rebind nahi kar sakte.

def outer():
    total = 0
    def add(x):
        # total += x        # UnboundLocalError
        pass
    return add

Gotcha 3 — mutable state ke liye nonlocal ki zarurat nahi.

def make_collector():
    items = []                        # mutable
    def add(x):
        items.append(x)               # MUTATION -- nonlocal ki zarurat nahi
        return items
    return add

c = make_collector()
print(c("a"), c("b"))                 # ['a', 'b'] ['a', 'b']  -- same list!

Note ki dono prints same list object dikha rahe hain — kyunki add har baar usi list ka reference lauta raha hai. Agar copy chahiye toh return list(items).

Gotcha 4 — closure memory pakde rakhta hai.

def make_handler():
    huge_data = [0] * 10_000_000       # 80 MB
    def handler(x):
        return x * 2                   # huge_data use HI nahi kar raha
    return handler

h = make_handler()
print(h.__closure__)                   # None  -- CPython smart hai, unused var capture nahi kiya
  1. CPython sirf actually used free variables ko cell banata hai. huge_data use nahi hua toh capture bhi nahi hua, aur wo frame ke saath free ho gaya.
  2. Par agar aap usko use karte (return x * len(huge_data)) toh 80 MB closure ke saath zinda rehta — ye long-running test suites mein memory leak ka source hai (Part 14).

Interview answer: "A closure is a nested function that keeps access to variables from its enclosing scope after that scope has returned. CPython implements it with cell objects: the compiler notices the inner function references an outer local, promotes that local to a cell, and both functions point at the same cell — which you can inspect through func.__closure__[0].cell_contents. The consequence people get caught by is that closures capture the variable, not its value, and lookup happens at call time. So creating lambdas in a loop gives you N functions all sharing one cell, and after the loop that cell holds the last value — every handler does the same thing. There are three fixes: bind the value as a default argument, which is evaluated at definition time; use functools.partial, which stores the argument immediately; or, the one I'd write in production, use a factory function so each call gets its own frame and its own cell. That last one keeps the signature clean, whereas the default-argument trick leaves a parameter a caller can accidentally override."

Cross-question — "Why did Python choose late binding for closures? Wouldn't early binding be less surprising?" "Because late binding is what makes closures useful for the case they were designed for — mutual recursion and forward references. If a nested function captured values at definition time, two nested functions couldn't call each other, and a closure couldn't observe changes the outer function makes after defining it, which is exactly what decorators and the nonlocal counter pattern depend on. It also keeps one consistent rule: names are always resolved when the code runs, whether they're local, enclosing, global, or builtin — early binding would make closures the one special case. The cost is the loop gotcha, and the language's answer to that is 'don't create closures over a loop variable; create them in a function call'. JavaScript hit exactly the same problem with var and solved it by giving let per-iteration bindings; Python never added that because the factory-function fix was considered good enough."

docs.title: Kya hai
docs.text:
Recursion = function apne aap ko call kare. Har call ek naya frame stack par push karta hai, jismein us call ke locals rehte hain.

Analogy: aap ek almari mein dabbe dhoondh rahe ho. Har dabbe ke andar aur chhote dabbe ho sakte hain. Aap ek dabba kholte ho, uske andar dekhte ho, agar dabba mila toh use bhi kholte ho — aur har khula hua dabba aapke haath mein "pending" pada hai. Haath mein kitne dabbe pakad sakte ho — wahi stack limit hai.

docs.title: Kaise kaam karta hai
docs.text:
def factorial(n):
    if n <= 1:                    # BASE CASE -- yahan recursion rukti hai
        return 1
    return n * factorial(n - 1)   # RECURSIVE CASE -- chhoti problem par khud ko call

print(factorial(5))               # 120

Call stack:

factorial(5)  -> 5 * factorial(4)      frame 1  [n=5]
                     4 * factorial(3)  frame 2  [n=4]
                         3 * factorial(2)  frame 3  [n=3]
                             2 * factorial(1)  frame 4  [n=2]
                                 return 1      frame 5  [n=1]  <- base case
                             return 2*1 = 2
                         return 3*2 = 6
                     return 4*6 = 24
                 return 5*24 = 120

Line-by-line walkthrough:

  1. if n <= 1: return 1 — base case pehle likho, hamesha. Ye recursion ka "stop" condition hai. Iske bina infinite recursion → RecursionError.
  2. <= 1 likha, == 1 nahi — kyunki factorial(0) bhi 1 hona chahiye, aur negative input par == 1 infinite recursion deta (n ghatta rehta, kabhi 1 nahi hota). Ye defensive detail hai. Aur behtar: if n < 0: raise ValueError(...).
  3. return n * factorial(n - 1) — problem chhoti honi chahiye har call mein, warna base case tak kabhi nahi pahunchoge. factorial(n) likh dena (bina -1) infinite recursion hai.
  4. Har pending call ka frame stack par hai — factorial(5) ke liye 5 frames ek saath. Yahi recursion ki memory cost hai.

docs.title: Recursion limit
docs.text:
import sys

print(sys.getrecursionlimit())          # 1000 (default)

def countdown(n):
    if n == 0:
        return 0
    return countdown(n - 1)

# print(countdown(2000))                # RecursionError: maximum recursion depth exceeded

sys.setrecursionlimit(3000)             # badhaya
print(countdown(2000))                  # 0   -- ab chalega
sys.setrecursionlimit(1000)             # wapas

Line-by-line walkthrough:

  1. sys.getrecursionlimit() — default 1000. Ye Python-level guard hai, C stack ka actual size nahi.
  2. sys.setrecursionlimit(3000) — badha sakte ho, par khatarnak hai: agar aap actual C stack se aage nikal gaye toh Python RecursionError nahi, segfault dega — process crash, koi traceback nahi. Limit isliye exist karti hai ki wo crash se pehle ek clean error de.
  3. Practical safe upper bound thread stack size par depend karta hai (typically 8 MB main thread par, ~10,000-30,000 frames simple functions ke liye). Zyada chahiye toh: 
    import threading
threading.stack_size(64 * 1024 * 1024)      # 64 MB stack
t = threading.Thread(target=deep_function)
t.start()
  4. Behtar hal: recursion ko iteration mein badlo.

docs.title: Recursion → iteration
docs.text:
# Recursive
def factorial_rec(n):
    return 1 if n <= 1 else n * factorial_rec(n - 1)

# Iterative -- koi stack limit nahi, tez bhi
def factorial_iter(n):
    result = 1
    for i in range(2, n + 1):
        result *= i
    return result

print(factorial_rec(10), factorial_iter(10))       # 3628800 3628800

# Tree traversal: recursive
def walk_recursive(node, depth=0):
    yield node["name"], depth
    for child in node.get("children", []):
        yield from walk_recursive(child, depth + 1)

# Tree traversal: iterative with explicit stack
def walk_iterative(root):
    stack = [(root, 0)]                              # apna stack, heap par -- unlimited
    while stack:
        node, depth = stack.pop()
        yield node["name"], depth
        for child in reversed(node.get("children", [])):   # reversed -> DFS order preserve
            stack.append((child, depth + 1))

tree = {
    "name": "suite",
    "children": [
        {"name": "auth", "children": [{"name": "test_login"}, {"name": "test_logout"}]},
        {"name": "cart", "children": [{"name": "test_add"}]},
    ],
}

print(list(walk_recursive(tree)))
print(list(walk_iterative(tree)))

Line-by-line walkthrough (iterative version):

  1. stack = [(root, 0)] — apna stack banaya, list par. Ye heap par hai, C stack par nahi — toh koi recursion limit nahi, sirf RAM ki limit.
  2. while stack: — khaali hone tak. Ye recursion ke "abhi kaam bacha hai" ka equivalent hai.
  3. node, depth = stack.pop() — pop() end se O(1). Ye LIFO hai, matlab depth-first. popleft() (deque se) karo toh breadth-first ho jaata hai — ek line ka farak.
  4. for child in reversed(...) — reversed isliye ki stack LIFO hai: agar hum children ko normal order mein push karein toh aakhri child pehle pop hoga. reversed se recursive version ka same output milta hai.
  5. yield — generator (Part 6). Ye poori list nahi banata, jo bade trees par memory bachaata hai.

docs.title: Tail recursion — Python mein nahi hai
docs.text:
def sum_list_tail(items, acc=0):
    """Tail-recursive: recursive call HI aakhri operation hai."""
    if not items:
        return acc
    return sum_list_tail(items[1:], acc + items[0])    # tail call

# print(sum_list_tail(list(range(2000))))    # RecursionError -- Python optimize nahi karta
  1. Ye tail call hai: recursive call ke baad kuch nahi karna. Scheme/Haskell isko loop mein badal dete hain (TCO — tail call optimisation) aur stack nahi badhta.
  2. Python jaan-boojh kar TCO nahi karta. Guido ka reason: TCO se stack traces kharab ho jaate hain — aapko wo frames dikhte hi nahi jinse aap yahan pahunche. Python debugging ko priority deta hai.
  3. Aur items[1:] yahan ek aur problem hai: har call ek naya list slice banata hai → O(n²) memory aur time. Iterative version O(n) hai.

docs.title: Memoisation — recursion ko tez karna
docs.text:
from functools import lru_cache
import timeit

def fib_slow(n):
    if n < 2:
        return n
    return fib_slow(n - 1) + fib_slow(n - 2)        # exponential: O(2^n) calls

@lru_cache(maxsize=None)
def fib_fast(n):
    if n < 2:
        return n
    return fib_fast(n - 1) + fib_fast(n - 2)        # O(n) -- har n ek baar compute hota hai

print(timeit.timeit(lambda: fib_slow(28), number=1))     # ~0.15s
print(timeit.timeit(lambda: fib_fast(28), number=1))     # ~0.00002s
print(fib_fast.cache_info())     # CacheInfo(hits=26, misses=29, maxsize=None, currsize=29)
  1. fib_slow(28) ke liye fib_slow(26) do baar compute hota hai, fib_slow(25) teen baar, etc. — total calls exponential.
  2. @lru_cache(maxsize=None) — result cache karta hai n ke hisaab se. Har n ek baar compute hota hai → O(n).
  3. cache_info() — hits/misses. misses=29 matlab 0-28 ke liye ek-ek baar compute hua.
  4. Caveat: arguments hashable hone chahiye. lru_cache list argument par TypeError: unhashable type dega.
  5. Python 3.9+ mein functools.cache = lru_cache(maxsize=None) ka short form.

docs.title: Recursion kab use karein — QA context
Gotchas
docs.text:
Gotcha 1 — circular references par infinite recursion.

a = {"name": "a"}
a["self"] = a                       # cycle
# find_nulls(a)                     # RecursionError

# Fix: seen set
def walk_safe(data, seen=None):
    seen = set() if seen is None else seen
    if id(data) in seen:            # id() se identity check
        return ["<cycle>"]
    if isinstance(data, (dict, list)):
        seen = seen | {id(data)}    # naya set (branch-local)
    ...

id() use kiya kyunki dicts hashable nahi hain.

Gotcha 2 — default mutable accumulator.

def collect_bad(node, result=[]):    # 1.4 ka bug, recursion mein aur bhi bura
    result.append(node)
    return result

Gotcha 3 — RecursionError ko except Exception pakad leta hai.

try:
    deep_function()
except Exception as e:               # RecursionError, RuntimeError ka subclass hai
    print("caught")                  # par ab stack lagbhag full hai...
    # yahan aur kuch karna khatarnak hai -- handler bhi RecursionError de sakta hai

RecursionError handle karne ke baad stack lagbhag bhara hua hai, toh handler mein complex kaam (logging with formatting, ek aur function call) khud fail ho sakta hai.

Interview answer: "Each recursive call pushes a frame, so recursion trades stack space for expressiveness. CPython's default limit is 1000 frames, which is a guard rather than a hard limit — it exists so you get a RecursionError with a traceback instead of blowing the C stack and segfaulting. You can raise it with sys.setrecursionlimit, but I treat that as a smell; the right fix is usually to convert to iteration with an explicit stack, which moves the state to the heap and removes the limit entirely — and swapping stack.pop() for popleft() on a deque turns depth-first into breadth-first for free. Python deliberately has no tail-call optimisation; Guido's reasoning was that eliminating frames destroys tracebacks, and Python prioritises debuggability. Where recursion genuinely wins for me is tree-shaped data: validating a nested API response, walking a DOM, or merging nested configs — I have a find_nulls helper that recurses through a JSON response and returns JSONPath-style paths to every null, which goes straight into a bug report. For production versions of those I add a max_depth guard and an identity-based seen set, so malformed or circular data gives a meaningful error rather than a RecursionError."

docs.title: Kya hai
docs.text:
Type hints annotations hain jo batati hain ki ek naam mein kis kism ka object aana chahiye. Runtime par Python inhe enforce nahi karta — wo sirf __annotations__ dict mein store hoti hain. Enforcement mypy, pyright, ya pydantic jaise tools karte hain.

Analogy: medicine ke box par "adults only, 2 tablets" likha hai. Box aapko rok nahi sakta, par pharmacist (mypy) aapko batayega ki aap galat kar rahe ho.

docs.title: Kyu hai
docs.text:
# --- WITHOUT hints: signature se kuch pata nahi chalta ---
def process(data, config, retries):
    ...
# data kya hai? list? dict? kis shape ka? config object hai ya dict? retries int hai ya str?
# Jawab dhoondhne ke liye poora function padhna padega, ya callers dekhne padenge.

# --- WITH hints ---
def process(
    data: list[dict[str, str | float]],
    config: "TestConfig",
    retries: int = 3,
) -> tuple[int, int]:
    """Returns (passed_count, failed_count)."""
    ...

Teen concrete faayde:

  1. IDE autocomplete — data[0]. par IDE keys suggest kar sakta hai.
  2. mypy refactor ke waqt saare callers check kar deta hai — QA ke liye ye ek free regression suite hai.
  3. Documentation jo purani nahi hoti — docstring galat ho sakti hai, type hint ko mypy check karta hai.

docs.title: Basic syntax
docs.text:
# --- Variables ---
name: str = "test_login"
timeout: int = 5000
duration: float = 1.23
passed: bool = True
tags: list[str] = ["smoke", "auth"]
config: dict[str, int] = {"timeout": 5000}
coords: tuple[int, int] = (0, 0)
statuses: set[str] = {"passed", "failed"}
anything: object = 42                     # koi bhi object (par methods nahi call kar sakte)

# --- Functions ---
def click(selector: str, timeout: int = 5000) -> None:
    """-> None matlab kuch return nahi karta."""
    pass

def get_duration(name: str) -> float:
    return 1.23

def run_all(tests: list[str]) -> dict[str, bool]:
    return {t: True for t in tests}

# --- Annotations dekh sakte ho ---
print(click.__annotations__)     # {'selector': <class 'str'>, 'timeout': <class 'int'>, 'return': None}

Line-by-line walkthrough:

  1. tags: list[str] — Python 3.9+ built-in generics. 3.9 se pehle from typing import List karke List[str] likhna padta tha. Aaj typing.List deprecated hai.
  2. dict[str, int] — key type, value type.
  3. tuple[int, int] — exactly do ints. Variable length ke liye tuple[int, ...] (literal ellipsis).
  4. -> None — function kuch return nahi karta (implicitly None). Ye likhna zaruri hai warna mypy --disallow-untyped-defs mein complain karega.
  5. click.__annotations__ — annotations ek dict hai. Runtime par ye sirf metadata hai; click(123) bilkul chalega.

docs.title: Optional aur Union
docs.text:
from typing import Optional, Union

# Optional[X] == Union[X, None] == X | None
def find_test(name: str) -> Optional[dict]:
    """Test mile toh dict, warna None."""
    return None

def find_test_modern(name: str) -> dict | None:      # Python 3.10+ syntax
    return None

# Union: in mein se koi ek
def parse_timeout(value: Union[int, str]) -> int:
    if isinstance(value, str):
        return int(value.rstrip("ms"))
    return value

def parse_timeout_modern(value: int | str) -> int:   # 3.10+
    if isinstance(value, str):
        return int(value.rstrip("ms"))
    return value

Line-by-line walkthrough:

  1. Optional[dict] — ye "optional parameter" nahi hai; ye "value None ho sakti hai" hai. Naam confusing hai — dict | None clearer hai aur ab preferred hai.
  2. dict | None — 3.10+ ka X | Y syntax. Ye types.UnionType object banata hai. 3.7-3.9 mein from __future__ import annotations likh ke aap ye syntax use kar sakte ho (annotations strings ban jaati hain, evaluate nahi hoti).
  3. if isinstance(value, str): — type narrowing. Is if ke andar mypy jaanta hai ki value str hai, toh .rstrip() allowed hai. if ke baad wo int hai. Ye narrowing hi Union ko usable banati hai.
  4. Important design rule: Optional return karne se caller ko None check karna padta hai. Agar wo check bhool gaya toh AttributeError: 'NoneType' object has no attribute ... — aur ye bug production mein hi milega. Isliye jahan possible ho, None ki jagah exception raise karo ya empty container do: 
    def get_tags(name: str) -> list[str]:
    return []                     # khaali list, None nahi -- caller ko check nahi karna padta

docs.title: Any, NoReturn, Never
docs.text:
from typing import Any, NoReturn

def load_json(path: str) -> Any:
    """JSON ka shape pata nahi -- Any."""
    import json
    with open(path) as f:
        return json.load(f)

def fail_test(message: str) -> NoReturn:
    """Ye function kabhi normally return nahi karta."""
    raise AssertionError(message)
  1. Any — type checking off kar deta hai us value ke liye. Any par kuch bhi kar sakte ho. Ye escape hatch hai; zyada use karoge toh type hints ka faayda khatam. object behtar hai jab aap sach mein "koi bhi object" chahte ho par usko safely use karna hai.
  2. NoReturn — function hamesha raise karta hai ya infinite loop mein jaata hai. mypy isse jaanta hai ki fail_test() ke baad ka code unreachable hai — jo useful narrowing deta hai. Python 3.11+ mein Never bhi hai (same cheez, better naam).

docs.title: Generics aur TypeVar
docs.text:
from typing import TypeVar, Generic

T = TypeVar("T")                              # ek "type variable" -- koi bhi type

def first(items: list[T]) -> T:
    """Jo type andar hai, wahi bahar aayega."""
    return items[0]

x: int = first([1, 2, 3])                     # mypy jaanta hai: T = int
y: str = first(["a", "b"])                    # T = str
# z: int = first(["a"])                       # mypy error: incompatible types

# --- Bounded TypeVar ---
from typing import SupportsFloat
N = TypeVar("N", bound=float)                 # sirf float ya uske subtypes

def average(values: list[N]) -> float:
    return sum(values) / len(values)

# --- Constrained TypeVar ---
S = TypeVar("S", str, bytes)                  # sirf str YA bytes, kuch aur nahi

def double(x: S) -> S:
    return x + x

# --- Generic class ---
class Result(Generic[T]):
    """Ek test result jismein koi bhi payload ho sakta hai."""

    def __init__(self, value: T, passed: bool) -> None:
        self.value = value
        self.passed = passed

    def unwrap(self) -> T:
        if not self.passed:
            raise ValueError("cannot unwrap a failed result")
        return self.value

r: Result[dict] = Result({"id": 1}, passed=True)
data = r.unwrap()                              # mypy jaanta hai: data ek dict hai

Line-by-line walkthrough:

  1. T = TypeVar("T") — ek placeholder. String argument variable ke naam se match hona chahiye (T = TypeVar("T")), warna confusing errors milte hain.
  2. def first(items: list[T]) -> T: — ye kehta hai "input list ka element type, wahi output type". Bina TypeVar ke aapko -> Any likhna padta aur saara type info kho jaata.
  3. N = TypeVar("N", bound=float) — bounded: N float ya uska subtype ho sakta hai. Note int mypy ke liye float ke saath compatible hai (numeric tower special case).
  4. S = TypeVar("S", str, bytes) — constrained: exactly in do mein se ek. Bounded se alag — bounded mein koi bhi subtype chalega, constrained mein sirf listed types.
  5. class Result(Generic[T]): — generic class. Result[dict] se instantiate karne par mypy unwrap() ka return dict maan leta hai.
  6. Python 3.12+ mein naya syntax hai jo TypeVar declaration ki zarurat khatam kar deta hai: 
    def first[T](items: list[T]) -> T:
    return items[0]

class Result[T]:
    ...

docs.title: Protocol — structural typing (duck typing ko type-safe banao)
docs.text:
Kya hai: Protocol kehti hai "mujhe koi bhi object chahiye jiske paas ye methods hon" — inheritance ki zarurat nahi. Ye Python ke duck typing ka type-checked version hai.

from typing import Protocol

class Clickable(Protocol):
    """Koi bhi cheez jisme click() aur is_visible() ho."""

    def click(self, timeout: int = ...) -> None: ...
    def is_visible(self) -> bool: ...


def safe_click(element: Clickable, retries: int = 3) -> bool:
    """Ye function kisi bhi Clickable ke saath kaam karega."""
    for _ in range(retries):
        if element.is_visible():
            element.click()
            return True
    return False


# --- Ye class Clickable se INHERIT nahi karti, par fit ho jaati hai ---
class PlaywrightLocator:
    def click(self, timeout: int = 5000) -> None:
        print("playwright click")

    def is_visible(self) -> bool:
        return True


class MockElement:                       # test double, koi inheritance nahi
    def __init__(self, visible: bool = True):
        self._visible = visible
        self.clicks = 0

    def click(self, timeout: int = 5000) -> None:
        self.clicks += 1

    def is_visible(self) -> bool:
        return self._visible


print(safe_click(PlaywrightLocator()))   # True  -- mypy khush
print(safe_click(MockElement()))         # True  -- mypy khush

Line-by-line walkthrough:

  1. class Clickable(Protocol): — ye ek structural type hai. Koi class isse inherit nahi karti; mypy sirf check karta hai ki methods match karte hain ya nahi.
  2. def click(self, timeout: int = ...) -> None: ... — body mein ... (Ellipsis) hai, matlab "implementation nahi hai". Default value bhi ... hai — protocol mein default ki actual value matter nahi karti, sirf "default hai" matter karta hai.
  3. def safe_click(element: Clickable, ...) — ye kisi bhi object ko accept karega jismein ye do methods hon.
  4. class MockElement: — yahi Protocol ka killer use case QA mein hai. Aapka test double real class se inherit nahi karta (Playwright ke internals se coupling nahi chahiye), par type checker use accept kar leta hai. Nominal typing (ABC inheritance) mein aapko class MockElement(Clickable) likhna padta.
  5. Runtime checking chahiye toh: 
    from typing import runtime_checkable

@runtime_checkable
class Clickable(Protocol):
    def click(self, timeout: int = ...) -> None: ...

print(isinstance(PlaywrightLocator(), Clickable))     # True
    runtime_checkable sirf method ke naam check karta hai, signature nahi — toh ye incomplete check hai. Use carefully.

docs.title: Callable, Iterable, Sequence, Mapping
docs.text:
from collections.abc import Callable, Iterable, Sequence, Mapping, Iterator

# Callable[[arg_types], return_type]
def retry(fn: Callable[[], bool], attempts: int = 3) -> bool:
    for _ in range(attempts):
        if fn():
            return True
    return False

def with_key(items: list, key: Callable[[dict], float]) -> list:
    return sorted(items, key=key)

# --- Input types: sabse GENERAL type maango ---
def count_failures(results: Iterable[dict]) -> int:      # list, tuple, generator -- sab chalega
    return sum(1 for r in results if r["status"] == "failed")

def get_first(results: Sequence[dict]) -> dict:          # indexing chahiye -> Sequence
    return results[0]

def read_config(cfg: Mapping[str, str]) -> str:          # sirf padhna hai -> Mapping (read-only)
    return cfg.get("env", "staging")

# --- Output types: sabse SPECIFIC type do ---
def get_names(results: Iterable[dict]) -> list[str]:     # list do, Iterable nahi
    return [r["name"] for r in results]

Line-by-line walkthrough:

  1. Callable[[], bool] — koi argument nahi, bool return. Callable[[str, int], None] do arguments. Callable[..., bool] — arguments kuch bhi.
  2. Iterable[dict] — sirf iterate karna hai. Ye list[dict] se behtar hai kyunki caller generator, tuple, set — kuch bhi de sakta hai.
  3. Sequence[dict] — indexing aur len chahiye. list aur tuple dono fit hain, generator nahi.
  4. Mapping[str, str] — read-only dict interface. MutableMapping tab jab aap likhne wale ho. Mapping maangna caller ko batata hai "main aapka dict modify nahi karunga".
  5. "Be liberal in what you accept, conservative in what you return" — inputs mein Iterable/Mapping (general), outputs mein list/dict (specific). Agar aap -> Iterable return karo toh caller len() nahi kar paayega.
  6. Note: collections.abc se import karo, typing se nahi — typing.Callable ab deprecated alias hai.

docs.title: TypedDict — JSON responses ke liye
docs.text:
from typing import TypedDict, NotRequired

class TestResult(TypedDict):
    name: str
    status: str
    duration: float
    error: NotRequired[str]              # optional key (Python 3.11+)

def summarise(result: TestResult) -> str:
    base = f"{result['name']}: {result['status']}"
    if "error" in result:
        base += f" ({result['error']})"
    return base

r: TestResult = {"name": "test_a", "status": "failed", "duration": 1.2, "error": "timeout"}
print(summarise(r))
# r2: TestResult = {"name": "test_b"}    # mypy error: missing keys
  1. TypedDict — ek dict hai (runtime par bilkul normal dict), par mypy uski keys aur value types check karta hai. JSON API responses ke liye ye perfect hai kyunki aapko dict hi chahiye, class nahi.
  2. NotRequired[str] — 3.11+. Purane versions mein total=False wali second class banani padti thi.
  3. Runtime validation nahi hoti — uske liye pydantic chahiye.

docs.title: Type hints kaise chalao
docs.text:
pip install mypy

# Basic
mypy tests/

# Strict -- naya code hamesha isi mein likho
mypy --strict tests/

# Legacy code mein gradually adopt karo
mypy --ignore-missing-imports --check-untyped-defs tests/

pyproject.toml mein:

[tool.mypy]
python_version = "3.11"
warn_return_any = true
warn_unused_configs = true
disallow_untyped_defs = true
no_implicit_optional = true

[[tool.mypy.overrides]]
