docs.title: Gotchas
docs.text:
Gotcha 1 — hints runtime par enforce nahi hote.

def add(a: int, b: int) -> int:
    return a + b

print(add("hello", " world"))       # 'hello world'  -- koi error nahi!

Ye jaan-boojh kar hai: runtime checking har call ko slow kar deti. Enforcement chahiye toh pydantic, beartype, ya typeguard use karo.

Gotcha 2 — mutable default ke saath Optional.

def f(items: list[str] | None = None) -> list[str]:      # SAHI
    return items if items is not None else []

# def f(items: list[str] = []) -> list[str]:             # 1.4 wala bug + type hint isko chhupa raha hai

Gotcha 3 — forward references.

from __future__ import annotations       # saari annotations STRING ban jaati hain (lazy)

class Suite:
    def add_child(self, other: Suite) -> Suite:      # 'Suite' abhi define nahi hui thi
        return self

# Bina __future__ import ke, quotes lagao:
class Suite2:
    def add_child(self, other: "Suite2") -> "Suite2":
        return self
  1. Class body ke andar class ka apna naam abhi bind nahi hua hota. String annotation ("forward reference") se ye kaam chalta hai.
  2. from __future__ import annotations (PEP 563) saari annotations ko automatically strings bana deta hai — ye startup bhi tez karta hai (annotations evaluate nahi hoti) aur naya syntax purane Python par bhi chalne deta hai.
  3. Caveat: agar koi library runtime par annotations padhti hai (pydantic, dataclasses with get_type_hints), toh use typing.get_type_hints() call karna padta hai jo strings ko resolve karta hai.

Gotcha 4 — list[str] 3.9 se pehle nahi chalta.

# Python 3.8 par:
# def f(x: list[str]): ...            # TypeError: 'type' object is not subscriptable
from typing import List
def f(x: List[str]): ...              # 3.8 par chalega

Interview answer: "Type hints are annotations stored in __annotations__; the interpreter doesn't enforce them at runtime — that's deliberate, because per-call checking would cost real performance. Enforcement comes from mypy or pyright in CI, and that's where the value is: when I rename a field or change a return type, mypy finds every caller in seconds instead of me discovering it in a failing test three days later. The distinctions I actually use: X | None rather than Optional[X], because 'optional' misleadingly sounds like an optional parameter; general types on inputs and specific types on outputs — Iterable[dict] in, list[str] out, so callers can pass generators but still get something they can index; and Protocol for anything I need to fake in tests. Protocol is structural, so my MockElement just needs click and is_visible with the right signatures — it doesn't have to inherit from anything Playwright-specific, which keeps the test double decoupled from the library. For JSON responses I use TypedDict, since at runtime it's a plain dict but the checker knows the keys."

Cross-question — "If type hints aren't enforced, what stops them from drifting out of sync with the code?" "Only CI. A hint that isn't checked is just a comment, and it rots the same way. So the rule I'd set on a team is that mypy runs in the pipeline and fails the build — that's what turns hints from documentation into a contract. I'd add it in strict mode for new modules and a permissive mode for legacy ones, using per-module overrides in pyproject.toml, so the untyped code doesn't block the pipeline while new code can't regress. And for data crossing a real boundary — an HTTP response, a YAML config — static checking isn't enough anyway, because the checker can only verify what your code claims about it. There I use pydantic, which validates at runtime against the same annotations, so a schema change in the API surfaces as a clear validation error rather than a KeyError somewhere deep in the test."

docs.title: 4.8.1 functools.wraps
docs.text:
Kya hai: decorator likhte waqt wrapper function original ki identity (__name__, __doc__, __module__, __qualname__, __wrapped__, __dict__) chura leta hai. wraps usko wapas de deta hai. (Part 7 mein poora detail — yahan sirf functools ka parichay.)

import functools

def timer(fn):
    @functools.wraps(fn)                 # <- ye ek line poora farak daalti hai
    def wrapper(*args, **kwargs):
        import time
        start = time.perf_counter()
        result = fn(*args, **kwargs)
        print(f"{fn.__name__} took {time.perf_counter() - start:.3f}s")
        return result
    return wrapper

@timer
def slow_test():
    """A deliberately slow test."""
    return "done"

print(slow_test.__name__)     # 'slow_test'   (wraps ke bina: 'wrapper')
print(slow_test.__doc__)      # 'A deliberately slow test.'   (wraps ke bina: None)
print(slow_test.__wrapped__)  # <function slow_test at ...>   -- original tak pahunch

Bina wraps ke kya tootta:

  1. pytest test collection — pytest __name__ se test dhoondhta hai; saare tests wrapper ban jaayenge aur naam clash hoga.
  2. functools.singledispatch, inspect.signature — introspection tootta hai.
  3. Tracebacks aur logs mein wrapper dikhta hai, actual function ka naam nahi.
  4. help() bekaar ho jaata hai.
  5. unittest.mock.patch.object ka autospec galat signature pakadta hai.

docs.title: 4.8.2 functools.lru_cache / functools.cache
docs.text:
Kya hai: memoisation decorator. Function ke results ko arguments ke hisaab se cache karta hai. "LRU" = Least Recently Used — cache full ho toh sabse purana access hataao.

import functools
import time

@functools.lru_cache(maxsize=128)
def load_test_data(fixture_name: str) -> dict:
    """Disk se test data padho -- expensive, aur data badalta nahi."""
    print(f"  [loading {fixture_name} from disk]")
    time.sleep(0.1)                                # I/O simulate
    return {"fixture": fixture_name, "records": 100}

print(load_test_data("users"))       # disk se
print(load_test_data("users"))       # CACHE se -- print nahi hoga
print(load_test_data("orders"))      # disk se

print(load_test_data.cache_info())
# CacheInfo(hits=1, misses=2, maxsize=128, currsize=2)

load_test_data.cache_clear()         # cache khaali karo
print(load_test_data.cache_info())   # CacheInfo(hits=0, misses=0, maxsize=128, currsize=0)

Line-by-line walkthrough:

  1. @functools.lru_cache(maxsize=128) — maxsize cache mein kitne results rakhne hain. None do toh unbounded (memory leak ka khatra long-running processes mein). maxsize ko power of 2 rakhna faayda nahi deta — ye ek dict + linked list hai.
  2. def load_test_data(fixture_name: str) -> dict: — arguments hashable hone chahiye. load_test_data(["users"]) TypeError: unhashable type: 'list' dega.
  3. Cache key arguments se banti hai — positional aur keyword alag treat hote hain: f(1) aur f(x=1) do alag cache entries hain, chahe result same ho.
  4. cache_info() — hits, misses, maxsize, currsize. Ye monitoring ke liye zaruri hai — agar hits 0 hai toh cache bekaar hai (shayad arguments har baar alag hain).
  5. cache_clear() — test isolation ke liye critical. conftest.py mein: 
    @pytest.fixture(autouse=True)
def clear_caches():
    yield
    load_test_data.cache_clear()      # har test ke baad cache saaf
    Bina iske ek test ka cached data doosre test mein leak karega.

functools.cache (3.9+):

@functools.cache                        # == lru_cache(maxsize=None)
def compute_selector(page: str, element: str) -> str:
    return f"[data-page='{page}'] [data-testid='{element}']"

Chhota aur thoda tez (LRU eviction ki bookkeeping nahi). Par unbounded hai — sirf tab use karo jab possible arguments limited hon.

functools.cached_property (3.8+):

import functools

class TestSuite:
    def __init__(self, path: str):
        self.path = path

    @functools.cached_property
    def test_files(self) -> list[str]:
        """Pehli baar par compute, phir instance par store."""
        print("  [scanning disk]")
        return ["test_a.py", "test_b.py"]

s = TestSuite("tests/")
print(s.test_files)        # [scanning disk] -> ['test_a.py', 'test_b.py']
print(s.test_files)        # cached -- print nahi hua
print(s.__dict__)          # {'path': 'tests/', 'test_files': [...]}   <- instance par store
  1. cached_property result ko instance ke __dict__ mein usi naam se store karta hai. Agli baar normal attribute lookup instance dict mein mil jaata hai aur descriptor chalta hi nahi (Part 5 mein descriptors).
  2. lru_cache se alag: ye per-instance hai, global nahi — toh do suites ka data mix nahi hoga.
  3. Cache clear karne ke liye del s.test_files.
  4. Requirement: class mein __slots__ nahi hona chahiye (kyunki __dict__ chahiye).

Kab lru_cache use NAHI karna:

Situation Kyun nahi Function ke side effects hain Second call side effect nahi karega — silent bug Result time ke saath badalta hai (API status) Stale data Arguments unhashable hain (list, dict) TypeError Arguments mein self hai aur instances bahut hain Cache saare instances ko zinda rakhega — memory leak Bahut alag-alag arguments Sirf misses, cache bekaar

Methods par lru_cache ka khatra:

class Page:
    @functools.lru_cache(maxsize=None)              # KHATRA
    def get_locator(self, name):
        return f"#{name}"
  1. Cache key mein self bhi hai, toh cache har Page instance ka reference pakde rahega — wo objects kabhi garbage collect nahi honge. Long-running suite mein ye memory leak hai.
  2. Fix: cached_property (per-instance), ya method ko @staticmethod banao, ya module-level function bana kar cache lagao.

docs.title: 4.8.3 functools.partial
docs.text:
Kya hai: ek naya callable jismein kuch arguments pehle se bhare hue hain.

import functools

def click(page, selector, *, timeout=5000, force=False):
    return f"click({page}, {selector}, timeout={timeout}, force={force})"

# --- Ek specific page ke liye click ---
home_click = functools.partial(click, "home_page")
print(home_click("#login"))                        # click(home_page, #login, timeout=5000, ...)

# --- Slow environment ke liye longer timeout ---
slow_click = functools.partial(click, timeout=30000)
print(slow_click("checkout", "#pay"))              # timeout=30000

# --- Dono ---
slow_home_click = functools.partial(home_click, timeout=30000)
print(slow_home_click("#login"))

# --- partial object ko inspect karo ---
print(slow_click.func)         # <function click at ...>
print(slow_click.args)         # ()
print(slow_click.keywords)     # {'timeout': 30000}

Line-by-line walkthrough:

  1. functools.partial(click, "home_page") — pehla positional argument bind ho gaya. Baaki arguments call ke waqt aayenge, bind kiye hue ke baad.
  2. functools.partial(click, timeout=30000) — keyword bind kiya. Keywords override ho sakte hain: slow_click("a", "b", timeout=1000) mein 1000 jeetega.
  3. functools.partial(home_click, timeout=30000) — partials nest ho sakte hain (aur CPython unhe flatten kar deta hai).
  4. .func, .args, .keywords — introspectable. Ye lambda se bada faayda hai: lambda ke andar kya bind hua ye dekhna mushkil hai, partial mein saaf dikhta hai.

partial vs lambda:

# lambda
slow_click_l = lambda page, sel: click(page, sel, timeout=30000)

# partial
slow_click_p = functools.partial(click, timeout=30000)
lambda partial Introspectable Nahi Haan (.func, .args, .keywords) Picklable (multiprocessing!) Nahi Haan Late binding bug Haan (4.5) Nahi — abhi bind hota hai Speed thoda dheema (extra frame) thoda tez (C mein) Flexible logic likh sakte ho Haan Nahi, sirf argument binding

Picklability QA mein matter karti hai: pytest-xdist aur multiprocessing ko functions pickle karne padte hain workers ko bhejne ke liye. Lambda pickle nahi hota → PicklingError.

QA use case — parametrised fixtures:

import functools

def api_request(method: str, endpoint: str, *, base_url: str, timeout: int = 10):
    return f"{method} {base_url}{endpoint} (timeout={timeout})"

# Environment-specific clients
staging = functools.partial(api_request, base_url="https://staging.example.com")
prod_readonly = functools.partial(api_request, "GET", base_url="https://api.example.com")

print(staging("POST", "/tests"))              # POST https://staging.example.com/tests
print(prod_readonly("/health"))               # GET https://api.example.com/health

functools.partialmethod — class methods ke liye same cheez:

import functools

class Page:
    def _wait(self, selector, *, state):
        return f"wait for {selector} to be {state}"

    wait_visible = functools.partialmethod(_wait, state="visible")
    wait_hidden = functools.partialmethod(_wait, state="hidden")

p = Page()
print(p.wait_visible("#submit"))      # wait for #submit to be visible
print(p.wait_hidden("#spinner"))      # wait for #spinner to be hidden

docs.title: 4.8.4 functools.reduce
docs.text:
Kya hai: ek iterable ko ek single value mein "fold" karna, ek binary function se.

import functools
import operator

nums = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]

# reduce(fn, iterable, initial)
print(functools.reduce(operator.add, nums))          # 15
print(functools.reduce(operator.mul, nums))          # 120
print(functools.reduce(operator.add, nums, 100))     # 115  (initial=100)

# Manually kya ho raha hai:
# step 1: fn(1, 2)  -> 3
# step 2: fn(3, 3)  -> 6
# step 3: fn(6, 4)  -> 10
# step 4: fn(10, 5) -> 15

Kab reduce use karo — sirf tab jab built-in na ho:

import functools
import operator

# BURA: built-in already hai
total = functools.reduce(operator.add, nums)         # sum(nums) likho
maximum = functools.reduce(max, nums)                # max(nums) likho

# ACHHA: nested config merge
configs = [
    {"timeout": 30, "retries": 1},
    {"timeout": 60},
    {"headless": False},
]
merged = functools.reduce(lambda a, b: {**a, **b}, configs, {})
print(merged)                    # {'timeout': 60, 'retries': 1, 'headless': False}

# ACHHA: multiple sets ka intersection
suites = [{"test_a", "test_b", "test_c"}, {"test_b", "test_c"}, {"test_c", "test_d"}]
common = functools.reduce(operator.and_, suites)
print(common)                    # {'test_c'}

# ACHHA: nested attribute access
def get_nested(data, path):
    """get_nested(resp, 'user.address.city') -> resp['user']['address']['city']"""
    return functools.reduce(lambda d, key: d[key], path.split("."), data)

resp = {"user": {"address": {"city": "Bengaluru"}}}
print(get_nested(resp, "user.address.city"))         # Bengaluru

Line-by-line walkthrough (get_nested):

  1. path.split(".") — "user.address.city" → ["user", "address", "city"].
  2. functools.reduce(lambda d, key: d[key], keys, data) — data initial value hai. Har step par current dict se ek level neeche jaate hain.
  3. Ye API response validation mein bahut useful hai: config se path aata hai, aur aap deeply nested value nikal lete ho.
  4. Safe version: 
    def get_nested_safe(data, path, default=None):
    try:
        return functools.reduce(lambda d, key: d[key], path.split("."), data)
    except (KeyError, TypeError, IndexError):
        return default
  5. Guido ka opinion: unhone reduce ko builtins se hata kar functools mein daala kyunki "99% cases mein explicit loop zyada readable hai". Interview mein ye jaanna achha hai.

docs.title: 4.8.5 functools.singledispatch
docs.text:
Kya hai: function overloading by first argument ka type. Ek generic function, aur type-specific implementations.

import functools
from pathlib import Path

@functools.singledispatch
def load_test_data(source):
    """Default implementation -- unsupported types ke liye."""
    raise TypeError(f"cannot load test data from {type(source).__name__}")

@load_test_data.register
def _(source: str) -> dict:
    """String = JSON content."""
    import json
    return json.loads(source)

@load_test_data.register
def _(source: Path) -> dict:
    """Path = file se padho."""
    import json
    return json.loads(source.read_text())

@load_test_data.register
def _(source: dict) -> dict:
    """Already a dict -- bas copy do."""
    return dict(source)

@load_test_data.register(list)
def _(source) -> dict:
    """List of pairs -> dict.  (purana syntax: type explicitly diya)"""
    return dict(source)

print(load_test_data('{"a": 1}'))              # {'a': 1}
print(load_test_data({"b": 2}))                # {'b': 2}
print(load_test_data([("c", 3)]))              # {'c': 3}
# print(load_test_data(42))                    # TypeError: cannot load test data from int

Line-by-line walkthrough:

  1. @functools.singledispatch — base function ko generic banata hai. Ye default/fallback implementation hai — jab koi registered type match na kare.
  2. @load_test_data.register — registration. Type annotation se type nikalta hai (3.7+). Function ka naam _ rakha kyunki wo kabhi directly call nahi hoga.
  3. @load_test_data.register(list) — purana syntax jahan type explicitly diya jaata hai. Ye tab chahiye jab annotation na ho ya generic type ho.
  4. Dispatch pehle argument ke type par hota hai, aur MRO follow karta hai — agar bool register nahi hai par int hai, toh bool ke liye int wali chalegi.
  5. load_test_data.registry — saare registrations ka mapping. load_test_data.dispatch(str) batata hai ki str ke liye kaunsi function chalegi.

Kyu isinstance chain se behtar:

# --- WITHOUT singledispatch ---
def load_test_data_bad(source):
    if isinstance(source, str):
        return json.loads(source)
    elif isinstance(source, Path):
        return json.loads(source.read_text())
    elif isinstance(source, dict):
        return dict(source)
    elif isinstance(source, list):
        return dict(source)
    raise TypeError(...)
  1. isinstance chain open/closed principle todta hai: naya type add karne ke liye is function ko edit karna padta hai.
  2. singledispatch mein naya type kahin bhi register ho sakta hai — doosri file se bhi. Ye library design ke liye important hai.
  3. Trade-off: chhote cases mein isinstance chain readable hai. singledispatch tab jeetta hai jab implementations bade hain ya extensibility chahiye.

singledispatchmethod — methods ke liye (3.8+):

import functools

class ReportWriter:
    @functools.singledispatchmethod
    def write(self, item):
        raise TypeError(f"cannot write {type(item).__name__}")

    @write.register
    def _(self, item: str) -> str:
        return f"TEXT: {item}"

    @write.register
    def _(self, item: dict) -> str:
        return f"JSON: {item}"

w = ReportWriter()
print(w.write("hello"))          # TEXT: hello
print(w.write({"a": 1}))         # JSON: {'a': 1}

Note: dispatch doosre argument par hota hai (self ko skip karta hai).

docs.title: functools ka baaki hissa
docs.text:
import functools

# --- total_ordering: sirf __eq__ aur __lt__ do, baaki auto ---
@functools.total_ordering
class TestDuration:
    def __init__(self, seconds: float):
        self.seconds = seconds

    def __eq__(self, other):
        if not isinstance(other, TestDuration):
            return NotImplemented
        return self.seconds == other.seconds

    def __lt__(self, other):
        if not isinstance(other, TestDuration):
            return NotImplemented
        return self.seconds < other.seconds

a, b = TestDuration(1.5), TestDuration(2.5)
print(a < b, a <= b, a > b, a >= b, a == b, a != b)    # sab kaam karte hain

# --- cmp_to_key: purane comparison functions ko key mein badlo ---
def compare_versions(v1: str, v2: str) -> int:
    p1 = [int(x) for x in v1.split(".")]
    p2 = [int(x) for x in v2.split(".")]
    return (p1 > p2) - (p1 < p2)                        # -1, 0, ya 1

versions = ["1.10.0", "1.2.0", "1.9.5"]
print(sorted(versions, key=functools.cmp_to_key(compare_versions)))
# ['1.2.0', '1.9.5', '1.10.0']    -- string sort se alag!

# --- reduce ke saath initial value ---
print(functools.reduce(lambda a, b: a + b, [], 0))      # 0  -- khaali par initial mila
# functools.reduce(lambda a, b: a + b, [])              # TypeError: empty sequence with no initial

Walkthrough:

  1. @functools.total_ordering — aap __eq__ aur ek ordering method (__lt__) do, ye baaki teen (__le__, __gt__, __ge__) derive kar deta hai. Boilerplate bachaata hai. Trade-off: derived methods thode dheeme hain (do calls). Performance critical ho toh sab khud likho.
  2. return NotImplemented — False nahi. NotImplemented Python ko batata hai "main is type se compare nahi kar sakta, doosre ka reflected method try karo". False return karne se TestDuration(1) == "x" chupchaap False ho jaata bina doosre ko mauka diye.
  3. functools.cmp_to_key(f) — purana 3-way comparison function (-1/0/1) ko key function mein badalta hai. Python 3 mein sort(cmp=...) hata diya gaya tha kyunki key faster hai (n calls vs n log n calls).
  4. (p1 > p2) - (p1 < p2) — ye classic idiom hai -1/0/1 banane ka: True - False = 1, False - True = -1, False - False = 0.
  5. Version sorting: ["1.10.0", "1.2.0"] string sort mein "1.10.0" < "1.2.0" hai (kyunki '1' < '2'), jo galat hai. Ye release testing mein real bug hai. (Behtar: packaging.version.)

Interview answer: "The five I use regularly: wraps is mandatory in any decorator, because without it the wrapper's name and docstring replace the original's and pytest collection, inspect.signature, and tracebacks all break. lru_cache memoises by hashable arguments and gives you cache_info and cache_clear — I always wire cache_clear into a fixture, because otherwise one test's cached data leaks into another. I avoid putting it on methods, since self becomes part of the cache key and the cache then keeps every instance alive; cached_property is the per-instance alternative. partial pre-binds arguments and is better than a lambda for it, because it's introspectable and, importantly, picklable — which matters when pytest-xdist or multiprocessing has to ship the callable to a worker. reduce I use rarely and only where no builtin exists, like folding a list of config dicts into one or walking a dotted path into a nested API response. And singledispatch gives type-based overloading without an isinstance chain, so new types can register themselves from another module instead of editing the original function."

Cross-question — "You said lru_cache on a method causes a memory leak. Walk me through exactly why." "The cache is stored on the function object, which lives on the class, so there's one cache shared by all instances. The cache key is the full argument tuple, and for a method that includes self. So every instance you ever call the method on becomes a key in a dictionary that lives as long as the class does — which is the whole process. Its refcount never drops to zero, so it's never collected, and the leak is proportional to the number of instances, not the number of distinct results. In a long-running suite that creates a page object per test, that's every page object plus everything it references still resident at the end. The fixes are cached_property if the value depends only on the instance, a module-level cached function taking the values it actually needs instead of self, or a per-instance dict populated in __init__."

docs.title: 5.1 Classes and instances — aur self ka asli matlab
Kya hai
docs.text:
Class = ek blueprint jo batata hai ki is kism ke objects ke paas kaunse data (attributes) aur kaunse behaviours (methods) honge. Instance = us blueprint se bana ek actual object.

Analogy: class ek form ka template hai (khaali form). Instance ek bhara hua form hai. Ek template se hazaron bhare hue form ban sakte hain, har ek mein alag data.

docs.title: Kyu hai — page object ka before/after
docs.text:
# --- WITHOUT class: functions + parameters har jagah ---
def login_page_fill_username(page, value):
    page.fill("#username", value)

def login_page_fill_password(page, value):
    page.fill("#password", value)

def login_page_submit(page):
    page.click("#submit")

def login_page_error_text(page):
    return page.text_content(".error")

# Har call par 'page' pass karo. Selectors 4 functions mein bikhre hue.
# Selector badla -> dhoondho kahan-kahan use hua.
login_page_fill_username(page, "ritik")
login_page_fill_password(page, "secret")
login_page_submit(page)

# --- WITH class: state ek jagah, behaviour uske saath ---
class LoginPage:
    USERNAME = "#username"                     # selectors ek jagah, class ke saath
    PASSWORD = "#password"
    SUBMIT = "#submit"
    ERROR = ".error"

    def __init__(self, page):
        self.page = page                       # state instance mein rakha

    def fill_username(self, value):
        self.page.fill(self.USERNAME, value)
        return self                            # method chaining ke liye

    def fill_password(self, value):
        self.page.fill(self.PASSWORD, value)
        return self

    def submit(self):
        self.page.click(self.SUBMIT)
        return self

    @property
    def error_text(self):
        return self.page.text_content(self.ERROR)

# Use:
# LoginPage(page).fill_username("ritik").fill_password("secret").submit()

Class kya deta hai:

  1. Cohesion — selectors aur unse related actions ek hi jagah. Selector badla toh ek line.
  2. State ko implicit banana — page har call mein pass nahi karna.
  3. Namespace — do pages par submit() naam clash nahi karta.
  4. Discoverability — IDE mein login_page. type karo, saare actions dikh jaate hain.

docs.title: self — kya hai actually
docs.text:
self koi keyword nahi hai. Wo bas method ka pehla parameter hai, aur convention se uska naam self rakha jaata hai.

class Page:
    def __init__(this_object, url):        # 'self' ki jagah kuch bhi likh sakte ho
        this_object.url = url

    def describe(whatever):                # ye bhi chalega
        return f"Page at {whatever.url}"

p = Page("https://example.com")
print(p.describe())                        # Page at https://example.com

Ye chalega — par kabhi mat likhna. self universal convention hai aur har linter usko expect karta hai.

docs.title: Kaise kaam karta hai — p.describe() ka poora mechanism
docs.text:
class Page:
    def __init__(self, url):
        self.url = url

    def describe(self):
        return f"Page at {self.url}"

p = Page("https://example.com")

# Ye do lines EXACTLY same hain:
print(p.describe())              # bound method call
print(Page.describe(p))          # unbound: class se function, instance explicitly diya

Poora flow jab aap p.describe() likhte ho:

  1. p.describe — attribute lookup shuru. Pehle p.__dict__ mein describe dhoondha — nahi mila (methods instance par nahi hote).
  2. Phir type(p).__mro__ mein dhoondha → Page.__dict__["describe"] mila. Ye ek function object hai.
  3. Functions descriptors hain (unke paas __get__ hai). Toh Python describe.__get__(p, Page) call karta hai.
  4. Wo ek bound method object deta hai, jismein __self__ = p aur __func__ = describe store hai.
  5. () lagane par bound method describe(p) call karta hai — p pehle argument ke roop mein automatically inject ho jaata hai.
bound = p.describe
print(type(bound))               # <class 'method'>
print(bound.__self__ is p)       # True   -- instance yaad rakha hua hai
print(bound.__func__)            # <function Page.describe at ...>
print(p.describe is p.describe)  # False  -- har baar NAYA bound method object banta hai
  1. p.describe is p.describe False hai — kyunki har attribute access par naya bound method banta hai. Isliye methods ko is se compare mat karo, aur unhe callback registry mein store karte waqt dhyaan rakho (weak reference wale patterns mein ye bug banta hai).
  2. bound.__self__ — yahi wo mechanism hai jo self ko implicit banata hai.

Yahi wajah hai ki self explicit likhna padta hai: Python mein "namespaces are one honking great idea". self.url saaf batata hai ki ye instance ka attribute hai, url local variable se alag. Java mein this implicit hai aur url vs this.url ambiguous ho sakta hai.

docs.title: Attribute lookup ka poora order
docs.text:
Jab aap obj.x likhte ho:

1. type(obj).__mro__ mein DATA DESCRIPTOR dhoondho (jiske paas __get__ AUR __set__ dono ho)
   -> mila? use call karo. RUKO.
2. obj.__dict__ mein 'x' dhoondho
   -> mila? wahi return karo. RUKO.
3. type(obj).__mro__ mein 'x' dhoondho (class attributes, methods, non-data descriptors)
   -> mila? agar non-data descriptor (sirf __get__) hai toh call karo, warna value do. RUKO.
4. type(obj).__getattr__ hai? use call karo.
5. AttributeError

class Demo:
    class_attr = "from class"

    def __init__(self):
        self.instance_attr = "from instance"

d = Demo()
print(d.class_attr)              # 'from class'      -- step 3
print(d.instance_attr)           # 'from instance'   -- step 2

d.class_attr = "shadowed"        # INSTANCE par naya attribute bana
print(d.class_attr)              # 'shadowed'        -- step 2 jeeta
print(Demo.class_attr)           # 'from class'      -- class untouched
print(d.__dict__)                # {'instance_attr': ..., 'class_attr': 'shadowed'}

del d.class_attr                 # instance wala hataao
print(d.class_attr)              # 'from class'      -- class wala wapas dikhne laga
  1. d.class_attr = "shadowed" — assignment hamesha instance par hoti hai (jab tak data descriptor na ho). Class ka attribute nahi badla.
  2. Ye "shadowing" hai — bilkul waisa jaisa local variable global ko shadow karta hai (4.2).
  3. Ye bug banta hai: aap sochte ho aapne class-level config badla, par sirf ek instance ka badla.

docs.title: Class attributes vs instance attributes
docs.text:
class TestSuite:
    # CLASS attributes -- sab instances mein shared
    DEFAULT_TIMEOUT = 30_000                    # constant (immutable -- safe)
    BROWSERS = ("chromium", "firefox")          # tuple (immutable -- safe)
    all_results = []                            # LIST (mutable -- KHATRA!)

    instance_count = 0                          # counter -- deliberately shared

    def __init__(self, name):
        # INSTANCE attributes -- har object ka apna
        self.name = name
        self.results = []                       # har suite ka apna list -- SAHI
        TestSuite.instance_count += 1           # class attribute explicitly update

s1 = TestSuite("smoke")
s2 = TestSuite("regression")

s1.results.append("test_a")                     # sirf s1
print(s2.results)                               # []       -- independent

s1.all_results.append("test_a")                 # CLASS ka list -- shared!
print(s2.all_results)                           # ['test_a']  -- s2 mein bhi dikha

print(TestSuite.instance_count)                 # 2

Line-by-line walkthrough:

  1. DEFAULT_TIMEOUT = 30_000 — immutable constant. Class attribute ke liye ye sahi use hai. Naming convention: UPPER_CASE.
  2. all_results = [] — mutable class attribute. Ye 1.4 wala bug hai. s1.all_results lookup class tak jaata hai (instance par nahi hai), toh .append shared list par lagta hai.
  3. self.results = [] — __init__ mein, toh har instance ka naya list. Ye sahi hai.
  4. TestSuite.instance_count += 1 — self.instance_count += 1 nahi likha, kyunki wo self.instance_count = self.instance_count + 1 hota, jo instance par naya attribute banata aur class wala kabhi nahi badhta. Class attribute ko update karne ke liye class ka naam (ya type(self)) use karna padta hai. 
    # Galat:
# self.instance_count += 1        # instance par shadow ban jaata hai
  5. Subclass ke saath: type(self).instance_count += 1 likhoge toh har subclass ka apna counter ban jaayega (kyunki assignment subclass par hogi). TestSuite.instance_count likhne se sabka ek hi counter rehta hai. Choice deliberate karo.

docs.title: Naming conventions
docs.text:
class Page:
    def __init__(self, url):
        self.url = url                  # public -- API ka hissa
        self._session = None            # protected by convention -- "andar ka hai, mat chhedo"
        self.__secret = "hidden"        # name mangling -- _Page__secret ban jaata hai

    def click(self):                    # public method
        pass

    def _wait_for_load(self):           # internal helper
        pass

    def __private_helper(self):         # mangled -- _Page__private_helper
        pass

p = Page("x")
print(p._session)                       # kaam karta hai -- Python mein sach mein private nahi hai
# print(p.__secret)                     # AttributeError
print(p._Page__secret)                  # 'hidden'   -- mangled naam se access
print([a for a in dir(p) if "secret" in a])   # ['_Page__secret']

Line-by-line walkthrough:

  1. self._session — single underscore sirf convention hai. Python kuch enforce nahi karta. Ye "ye internal hai, backward compatibility ka waada nahi hai" kehta hai. from module import * isko skip karta hai.
  2. self.__secret — double underscore se name mangling hoti hai: compiler naam ko _ClassName__secret bana deta hai.
  3. Mangling ka asli maqsad "private" nahi hai — subclass collision se bachna hai: 
    class Base:
    def __init__(self):
        self.__data = "base data"        # _Base__data

    def get(self):
        return self.__data               # _Base__data

class Child(Base):
    def __init__(self):
        super().__init__()
        self.__data = "child data"       # _Child__data -- ALAG attribute!

c = Child()
print(c.get())                            # 'base data'  -- Base ka apna data safe hai
print(c.__dict__)                          # {'_Base__data': 'base data', '_Child__data': 'child data'}
    Agar mangling na hoti toh Child ka __data Base ka overwrite kar deta aur Base.get() tootta. Ye framework/library code ke liye zaruri hai.
  4. Practical rule: _single use karo (99% cases). __double sirf tab jab aap ek base class likh rahe ho jise log inherit karenge aur aap collision se bachna chahte ho.

docs.title: Gotchas
docs.text:
Gotcha 1 — self bhoolna.

class Page:
    def click():                        # 'self' nahi hai
        return "clicked"

p = Page()
# p.click()                             # TypeError: click() takes 0 positional arguments but 1 was given
print(Page.click())                     # 'clicked'  -- class se direct call chalega

Error message confusing hai ("0 arguments but 1 was given") jab tak aap na jaano ki self automatically inject hota hai.

Gotcha 2 — __init__ return nahi kar sakta.

class Page:
    def __init__(self):
        # return "something"            # TypeError: __init__() should return None
        return None                     # ye chalega (implicit bhi ho jaata hai)

Gotcha 3 — instance attribute ko class body mein type-hint karna attribute nahi banata.

class Page:
    url: str                            # sirf ANNOTATION hai, koi attribute nahi bana
    timeout: int = 5000                 # ye CLASS attribute hai (value di hai)

print(Page.__annotations__)             # {'url': <class 'str'>, 'timeout': <class 'int'>}
print(Page.timeout)                     # 5000
# print(Page.url)                       # AttributeError -- value hi nahi thi

Ye dataclass samajhne ke liye zaruri hai — dataclass exactly in annotations ko padh kar __init__ generate karta hai (5.10).

Interview answer: "A class is a blueprint; an instance is an object built from it. self isn't a keyword — it's just the first parameter, and Python passes the instance into it automatically. The mechanism is the descriptor protocol: functions defined in a class body are descriptors, so instance.method triggers function.__get__(instance, cls), which returns a bound method object carrying __self__ and __func__. That's why p.describe() and Page.describe(p) are exactly equivalent, and why every attribute access creates a fresh bound method object. The distinction that causes real bugs is class versus instance attributes: a mutable class attribute is shared by every instance, so a list defined in the class body accumulates across the whole suite. Anything mutable belongs in __init__. And incrementing a class counter has to go through the class name — self.count += 1 silently creates a shadowing instance attribute instead of updating the class one."

Cross-question — "Why does Python require explicit self when Java and C++ have implicit this?" "Guido's stated reasons are consistency and explicitness. Because methods are just functions stored on the class, Page.describe(p) has to work, and that only makes sense if self is a real parameter. It also removes ambiguity inside the body — self.url is unmistakably an attribute while url is unmistakably a local, whereas in C++ you need a naming convention or this-> to tell them apart. It makes decorators and metaclass tricks straightforward, since a method is an ordinary function you can wrap. And it's what allows staticmethod and classmethod to exist as plain decorators rather than language keywords: they just change what gets bound as the first argument."

docs.title: Kya hai
docs.text:
• __new__ — object banata hai (allocation). Static method hai, pehla argument cls. Naya object return karta hai.
  • __init__ — banaye hue object ko initialise karta hai. Pehla argument self. None return karta hai.

Analogy: __new__ gaadi ki body factory se nikalna hai. __init__ us gaadi mein seats lagana, colour karna, number plate lagana hai.

docs.title: Kaise kaam karta hai — Page("url") ka poora flow
docs.text:
class Page:
    def __new__(cls, *args, **kwargs):
        print(f"1. __new__ called with cls={cls.__name__}, args={args}")
        instance = super().__new__(cls)              # object.__new__ actual allocation karta hai
        print(f"2. instance created: {id(instance)}")
        return instance                              # ISKO RETURN KARNA ZARURI HAI

    def __init__(self, url):
        print(f"3. __init__ called on {id(self)} with url={url}")
        self.url = url

p = Page("https://example.com")
print(f"4. done: {p.url}")

Output:

1. __new__ called with cls=Page, args=('https://example.com',)
2. instance created: 4382920976
3. __init__ called on 4382920976 with url=https://example.com
4. done: https://example.com

Line-by-line walkthrough:

  1. Page("https://example.com") — ye actually type.__call__(Page, "https://...") hai.
  2. type.__call__ pehle Page.__new__(Page, "https://...") call karta hai.
  3. def __new__(cls, *args, **kwargs): — cls class object hai (Page), instance nahi — kyunki instance abhi bana hi nahi. __new__ implicitly staticmethod hai (Python khud banata hai), isliye self nahi cls milta hai.
  4. super().__new__(cls) — object.__new__ actual memory allocate karta hai. cls pass karna zaruri hai taaki sahi class ka object bane (subclass ke liye important). object.__new__(cls) extra arguments accept nahi karta — isliye *args usko forward mat karo (jab tak __init__ override na ho).
  5. return instance — agar aap return nahi karte (ya None return karte) toh __init__ chalta hi nahi aur Page(...) None deta hai. Ye sabse common __new__ bug hai.
  6. type.__call__ phir check karta hai: agar __new__ ka result cls ka instance hai, tabhi __init__ call karta hai. Warna nahi.

docs.title: Kyu — __new__ kab chahiye
docs.text:
99% cases mein aapko __new__ ki zarurat nahi hai. Chaar legitimate use cases:

1. Immutable types ko subclass karna

class TestId(str):
    """Ek test ID jo hamesha lowercase aur trimmed ho."""

    def __new__(cls, value):
        # str immutable hai -- value __new__ mein hi set karni padegi
        normalised = str(value).strip().lower()
        return super().__new__(cls, normalised)          # str.__new__ ko normalised do

    @property
    def module(self) -> str:
        return self.split("::")[0]

tid = TestId("  Tests/Test_Login.py::TEST_ok  ")
print(repr(tid))                # 'tests/test_login.py::test_ok'
print(tid.module)               # tests/test_login.py
print(isinstance(tid, str))     # True

Line-by-line walkthrough:

  1. class TestId(str): — str immutable hai. __init__ mein self.value = ... nahi kar sakte kyunki string ka content banne ke baad fix hai.
  2. def __new__(cls, value): — yahan hum wo value decide kar rahe hain jisse object banega.
  3. super().__new__(cls, normalised) — str.__new__(TestId, "tests/...") — ye ek TestId object banata hai jiska string content normalised hai.
  4. Ye pattern int, float, tuple, frozenset, bytes — sab immutable types ke saath same hai.
  5. NamedTuple bhi internally yahi karta hai.

2. Singleton pattern

class ConfigManager:
    """Poore test run mein ek hi config object rahe."""
    _instance = None

    def __new__(cls, *args, **kwargs):
        if cls._instance is None:                        # pehli baar?
            cls._instance = super().__new__(cls)
            cls._instance._initialised = False           # marker
        return cls._instance                             # hamesha WAHI object

    def __init__(self, config_path="config.yaml"):
        if self._initialised:                            # dobara init mat karo
            return
        print(f"loading config from {config_path}")
        self.config_path = config_path
        self.data = {"env": "staging"}
        self._initialised = True

a = ConfigManager("prod.yaml")     # loading config from prod.yaml
b = ConfigManager("other.yaml")    # kuch print nahi hua
print(a is b)                      # True
print(b.config_path)               # 'prod.yaml'   -- doosri call ignore hui

Line-by-line walkthrough:

  1. _instance = None — class attribute, shared across all "instances".
  2. if cls._instance is None: — sirf pehli baar object banao.
  3. cls._instance._initialised = False — ek flag, kyunki __init__ HAR call par chalta hai chahe __new__ ne purana object hi lautaya ho. Bina flag ke a ka config b ki call se overwrite ho jaata.
  4. if self._initialised: return — guard.
  5. Ye pattern QA mein aksar galat use hota hai. Singleton testing ko mushkil banata hai: ek test ne config badla, doosre test ko wahi mila. Behtar alternatives:
  6. module-level object — Python modules already singletons hain: 
    # config.py
_config = load_config()
def get_config(): return _config
  7. pytest fixture with scope="session" — framework hi lifecycle manage karta hai, aur test isolation ke liye override kar sakte ho.
  8. Interview mein: "I know how to write a singleton with __new__, but in Python a module is already a singleton, and in a test framework I'd use a session-scoped fixture instead because it's overridable per test."

3. Object caching / interning

class Browser:
    """Ek browser type ka ek hi object -- flyweight pattern."""
    _cache = {}

    def __new__(cls, name):
        key = name.lower()
        if key not in cls._cache:
            instance = super().__new__(cls)
            instance.name = key                    # __init__ mein karna better hai, demo ke liye yahan
            cls._cache[key] = instance
        return cls._cache[key]

a = Browser("Chromium")
b = Browser("chromium")
print(a is b)                                      # True
print(len(Browser._cache))                         # 1

4. Factory / subclass dispatch

class Locator:
    def __new__(cls, selector: str):
        # Selector ke type ke hisaab se sahi subclass return karo
        if cls is not Locator:                     # subclass se aaya? normal banao
            return super().__new__(cls)
        if selector.startswith("//"):
            return super().__new__(XPathLocator)
        if selector.startswith("text="):
            return super().__new__(TextLocator)
        return super().__new__(CssLocator)

    def __init__(self, selector):
        self.selector = selector

class CssLocator(Locator): pass
class XPathLocator(Locator): pass
class TextLocator(Locator): pass

print(type(Locator("#submit")).__name__)           # CssLocator
print(type(Locator("//button")).__name__)          # XPathLocator
print(type(Locator("text=Login")).__name__)        # TextLocator
  1. if cls is not Locator: — subclass ko directly instantiate karne par infinite recursion se bachne ke liye.
  2. Note: __init__ tabhi chalega jab returned object cls ka instance ho — yahan subclasses Locator ke instances hain, toh chalta hai.
  3. Simpler alternative: ek classmethod factory (Locator.create(selector)) — kam magic, zyada explicit. Ye usually better hai.

docs.title: Gotchas
docs.text:
Gotcha 1 — __new__ se return nahi kiya.

class Broken:
    def __new__(cls):
        super().__new__(cls)               # return bhool gaye!

    def __init__(self):
        print("never printed")

b = Broken()
print(b)                                   # None

Gotcha 2 — __new__ mein arguments forward karna.

class Page:
    def __new__(cls, url):
        # return super().__new__(cls, url)     # TypeError: object.__new__() takes exactly one argument
        return super().__new__(cls)            # sahi
    def __init__(self, url):
        self.url = url

object.__new__ sirf cls leta hai (jab __init__ override kiya gaya ho). Extra arguments __init__ ke liye hain.

Gotcha 3 — __init__ sirf tab chalta hai jab type match kare.

class A:
    def __new__(cls):
        return "not an A"                  # string return kiya

    def __init__(self):
        print("never runs")

x = A()
print(x, type(x))                          # not an A <class 'str'>

Interview answer: "__new__ allocates and returns the object; __init__ configures the object it was handed. SomeClass(args) is really type.__call__, which calls __new__ first and then only calls __init__ if what __new__ returned is actually an instance of that class. __new__ is implicitly a static method taking cls, and it must return the instance — forgetting the return is the classic bug and gives you None back with __init__ never running. In practice I almost never override it. The cases where you genuinely need it are subclassing an immutable type — a TestId(str) that normalises the value has to do that in __new__ because a string's content is fixed at creation — plus instance caching, flyweight patterns, and singletons. For singletons specifically I'd push back in a review: a module is already a singleton in Python, and in a test framework a session-scoped fixture is better because it can be overridden per test, whereas a __new__-based singleton leaks state between tests and makes them order-dependent."

Cross-question — "In a singleton implemented with __new__, __init__ still runs on every call. Why, and how do you handle it?" "Because type.__call__ doesn't know or care that __new__ returned a cached object — its only check is whether the returned value is an instance of the class, and it is, so it calls __init__ on it. That means the second ConfigManager('other.yaml') would re-run initialisation and overwrite the first caller's configuration. The usual fix is an _initialised flag set in __new__ and checked at the top of __init__. A cleaner fix is to move initialisation out of __init__ entirely — do the work inside __new__ when the instance is first created — or to use a metaclass whose __call__ skips both. Honestly, the fact that you need any of these workarounds is a good argument that the singleton is the wrong tool in Python."
