docs.text: Kind Decorator Pehla arg Kya access hai Kab Instance method (koi nahi) self instance + class zyadatar cheezein Class method @classmethod cls class only alternative constructors, class-level state Static method @staticmethod (kuch nahi) kuch nahi related utility, namespace ke liye class mein

docs.title: Code — teeno ek saath
docs.text:
from datetime import datetime

class TestRun:
    _total_runs = 0                                  # class-level counter

    def __init__(self, suite: str, browser: str, started_at: datetime):
        self.suite = suite
        self.browser = browser
        self.started_at = started_at
        self.results: list[dict] = []
        TestRun._total_runs += 1

    # ---------- INSTANCE METHOD ----------
    def add_result(self, name: str, status: str) -> None:
        """Instance ka data change karta hai -> instance method."""
        self.results.append({"name": name, "status": status})

    def pass_rate(self) -> float:
        """Instance ka data padhta hai -> instance method."""
        if not self.results:
            return 0.0
        passed = sum(1 for r in self.results if r["status"] == "passed")
        return passed / len(self.results)

    # ---------- CLASS METHOD ----------
    @classmethod
    def from_config(cls, config: dict) -> "TestRun":
        """Alternative constructor -- ye sabse common classmethod use hai."""
        return cls(
            suite=config["suite"],
            browser=config.get("browser", "chromium"),
            started_at=datetime.now(),
        )

    @classmethod
    def from_json_file(cls, path: str) -> "TestRun":
        """Ek aur constructor -- alag input, wahi object."""
        import json
        with open(path) as f:
            return cls.from_config(json.load(f))

    @classmethod
    def total_runs(cls) -> int:
        """Class-level state padhna."""
        return cls._total_runs

    # ---------- STATIC METHOD ----------
    @staticmethod
    def normalise_status(raw: str) -> str:
        """Na instance chahiye, na class -- par ye logically TestRun se juda hai."""
        mapping = {"ok": "passed", "pass": "passed", "fail": "failed", "error": "failed"}
        return mapping.get(raw.strip().lower(), raw.strip().lower())


# --- Use ---
run = TestRun.from_config({"suite": "smoke", "browser": "firefox"})
run.add_result("test_login", TestRun.normalise_status("OK"))
run.add_result("test_cart", TestRun.normalise_status("Fail"))
print(run.results)                    # [{'name': 'test_login', 'status': 'passed'}, ...]
print(run.pass_rate())                # 0.5
print(TestRun.total_runs())           # 1
print(TestRun.normalise_status("ok")) # 'passed'  -- instance ke bina call kiya

Line-by-line walkthrough:

  1. def add_result(self, ...) — instance method. self chahiye kyunki self.results modify kar rahe hain. Rule: agar self use ho raha hai toh instance method.
  2. @classmethod def from_config(cls, config) — cls class object hai. Ye "alternative constructor" pattern hai — Python mein overloaded constructors nahi hote, isliye alag input formats ke liye classmethods banate hain. Standard library mein bhi: dict.fromkeys, datetime.fromtimestamp, Path.cwd.
  3. return cls(...) — TestRun(...) nahi, cls(...). Ye critical hai for inheritance: 
    class ParallelTestRun(TestRun):
    pass

r = ParallelTestRun.from_config({"suite": "smoke"})
print(type(r).__name__)             # ParallelTestRun   -- cls() ne sahi class banayi
# Agar 'TestRun(...)' hardcode karte toh yahan TestRun milta -- bug
  4. from_json_file cls.from_config(...) call kar raha hai — classmethods aapas mein compose ho sakti hain, aur cls chain ke through pass hota rehta hai.
  5. @classmethod def total_runs(cls) — class-level state. cls._total_runs padha. Note: subclass se call karne par cls subclass hoga, aur agar subclass ne apna _total_runs set nahi kiya toh parent ka milega (MRO lookup).
  6. @staticmethod def normalise_status(raw) — na self, na cls. Ye ek pure function hai. Toh isko class mein rakha hi kyun? Kyunki wo logically TestRun se juda hai — namespace ke liye. TestRun.normalise_status("ok") padhne mein utils.normalise_status("ok") se behtar hai jab wo sirf test runs ke liye ho.
  7. TestRun.normalise_status("OK") — class se directly call kiya, instance ki zarurat nahi.

docs.title: Kaise kaam karta hai — descriptors
docs.text:
class Demo:
    def instance_m(self): return "instance"
    @classmethod
    def class_m(cls): return "class"
    @staticmethod
    def static_m(): return "static"

d = Demo()

# Class se access
print(type(Demo.instance_m))     # <class 'function'>        -- plain function
print(type(Demo.class_m))        # <class 'method'>          -- Demo par bound
print(type(Demo.static_m))       # <class 'function'>        -- plain function

# Instance se access
print(type(d.instance_m))        # <class 'method'>          -- d par bound
print(type(d.class_m))           # <class 'method'>          -- Demo par bound (d par nahi!)
print(type(d.static_m))          # <class 'function'>        -- kuch bind nahi hua

print(d.class_m())               # 'class'   -- instance se bhi call ho sakta hai
print(d.static_m())              # 'static'
  1. classmethod aur staticmethod descriptors hain jo __get__ ko override karte hain:
  2. classmethod.__get__ class ko bind karta hai (chahe instance se access karo).
  3. staticmethod.__get__ kuch bind nahi karta — plain function deta hai.
  4. Isliye d.class_m() mein cls Demo hai, d nahi.
  5. Python 3.10 mein classmethod property ke saath chain ho sakta tha; wo 3.11 mein deprecate ho gaya — ab uske liye alag pattern chahiye.

docs.title: Kab kaunsa — decision rule
docs.text:
Method ko 'self' chahiye?          -> instance method
    |
    Nahi
    |
Method ko 'cls' chahiye?
    (naya instance banana hai, ya class-level state)
    |
    Haan -> @classmethod
    Nahi -> @staticmethod
                |
                aur agar ye class se logically juda bhi nahi hai
                -> class se BAHAR nikaalo, module-level function banao

docs.title: QA-specific patterns
docs.text:
Pattern 1 — Page object ka alternative constructor

class LoginPage:
    URL = "/login"

    def __init__(self, page, base_url: str):
        self.page = page
        self.base_url = base_url

    @classmethod
    def open(cls, page, base_url: str) -> "LoginPage":
        """Page banao AUR navigate bhi kar do."""
        instance = cls(page, base_url)
        page.goto(f"{base_url}{cls.URL}")
        return instance

# Use: LoginPage.open(page, "https://staging.example.com")
  1. cls.URL — class attribute ko cls se access kiya, taaki subclass apna URL de sake.
  2. Ye "constructor + side effect" pattern hai. __init__ mein navigation nahi daala kyunki tab aap page object bana hi nahi sakte bina navigate kiye — jo testing mein flexibility khatam kar deta hai.

Pattern 2 — test data factory

from dataclasses import dataclass, field
import random
import string

@dataclass
class User:
    email: str
    password: str
    role: str = "user"
    verified: bool = True

    @staticmethod
    def _random_string(n: int = 8) -> str:
        return "".join(random.choices(string.ascii_lowercase, k=n))

    @classmethod
    def random(cls, **overrides) -> "User":
        """Random valid user -- test data factory."""
        defaults = {
            "email": f"{cls._random_string()}@test.example.com",
            "password": cls._random_string(12),
        }
        return cls(**{**defaults, **overrides})

    @classmethod
    def admin(cls, **overrides) -> "User":
        return cls.random(role="admin", **overrides)

    @classmethod
    def unverified(cls, **overrides) -> "User":
        return cls.random(verified=False, **overrides)

print(User.random())
print(User.admin(email="fixed@test.com"))
print(User.unverified())

Line-by-line walkthrough:

  1. @staticmethod _random_string — helper jo na instance ka data use karta hai na class ka. Class ke andar isliye ki wo sirf User ke liye hai.
  2. @classmethod random(cls, **overrides) — factory. **overrides se caller koi bhi field fix kar sakta hai.
  3. cls._random_string() — staticmethod ko cls se call kiya. User._random_string() bhi chalta par cls se subclass ka override bhi kaam karega.
  4. cls(**{**defaults, **overrides}) — defaults pehle, overrides baad mein → overrides jeette hain (3.4).
  5. cls.random(role="admin", **overrides) — factories compose ho rahi hain. Agar caller ne role bhi diya toh TypeError: got multiple values — isse bachne ke liye: return cls.random(**{"role": "admin", **overrides}).
  6. Ye pattern test data ke liye best practice hai: har test apna specific data maangta hai (User.admin()), baaki fields random aur valid rehti hain — jo hidden coupling pakadta hai.

docs.title: Gotchas
docs.text:
Gotcha 1 — classmethod mein hardcoded class naam.

class Base:
    @classmethod
    def create(cls):
        return Base()                   # BUG -- hamesha Base

    @classmethod
    def create_ok(cls):
        return cls()                    # sahi

class Child(Base): pass

print(type(Child.create()).__name__)     # Base    <- galat
print(type(Child.create_ok()).__name__)  # Child   <- sahi

Gotcha 2 — staticmethod ko self ki tarah use karna.

class Page:
    @staticmethod
    def helper():
        # return self.url               # NameError -- 'self' hai hi nahi
        return "no state"

Gotcha 3 — class attribute mutate karna cls se.

class Base:
    registry = []

    @classmethod
    def register(cls, item):
        cls.registry.append(item)       # MUTATION -- shared list!

class ChildA(Base): pass
class ChildB(Base): pass

ChildA.register("a")
print(ChildB.registry)                   # ['a']   <- shared, kyunki lookup Base tak gaya

# Fix: har subclass ka apna
class Base2:
    def __init_subclass__(cls, **kwargs):
        super().__init_subclass__(**kwargs)
        cls.registry = []                # har subclass ke liye NAYA list

    @classmethod
    def register(cls, item):
        cls.registry.append(item)

class ChildC(Base2): pass
class ChildD(Base2): pass
ChildC.register("c")
print(ChildD.registry)                   # []   <- independent
  1. cls.registry.append(...) — cls.registry lookup MRO se Base tak jaata hai, toh shared list mutate hoti hai.
  2. __init_subclass__ — ek hook jo har subclass define hone par chalta hai (Python 3.6+). Ye metaclass ka simple, modern replacement hai. Yahan har subclass ko apna registry mila.

Interview answer: "Instance methods take self and work on one object. Class methods take cls and are mostly alternative constructors — Python has no constructor overloading, so TestRun.from_config and TestRun.from_json_file are how you offer multiple ways to build the same type, exactly like dict.fromkeys and datetime.fromtimestamp in the standard library. The critical detail is returning cls(...) rather than the hardcoded class name, so a subclass building through the same factory gets an instance of itself. Static methods take neither and are just functions living in the class's namespace for cohesion — if it isn't logically tied to the class, it should be a module-level function instead. Mechanically all three are descriptors: classmethod.__get__ binds the class even when accessed through an instance, and staticmethod.__get__ binds nothing. In test code my most-used pattern is a classmethod factory on a dataclass — User.random(**overrides) and User.admin() — so each test states only the field it actually cares about."

docs.title: 5.4.1 @property
docs.text:
Kya hai: ek method jo attribute ki tarah access hota hai — brackets ke bina.

Kyu hai:

# --- Java-style: getters/setters har jagah (Python mein ANTI-PATTERN) ---
class PageBad:
    def __init__(self, url):
        self._url = url

    def get_url(self):
        return self._url

    def set_url(self, value):
        self._url = value

p = PageBad("x")
p.set_url("y")
print(p.get_url())               # verbose, aur har attribute ke liye do methods

# --- Python: seedha public attribute rakho ---
class Page:
    def __init__(self, url):
        self.url = url           # bas. Getter/setter ki zarurat NAHI.

p = Page("x")
p.url = "y"                      # seedha
print(p.url)

Toh property kab chahiye? Jab aapko baad mein us attribute par logic add karni ho — bina caller ka code tode.

class Page:
    def __init__(self, url: str):
        self.url = url                     # ye setter ko call karega

    @property
    def url(self) -> str:
        """Getter -- 'page.url' padhne par chalta hai."""
        return self._url

    @url.setter
    def url(self, value: str) -> None:
        """Setter -- 'page.url = x' par chalta hai. Validation yahan."""
        if not isinstance(value, str):
            raise TypeError(f"url must be str, got {type(value).__name__}")
        if not value.startswith(("http://", "https://")):
            raise ValueError(f"url must be absolute, got {value!r}")
        self._url = value.rstrip("/")      # normalisation

    @url.deleter
    def url(self) -> None:
        """'del page.url' par chalta hai."""
        raise AttributeError("url cannot be deleted")


p = Page("https://staging.example.com/")
print(p.url)                        # https://staging.example.com   -- trailing slash gaya

p.url = "https://prod.example.com"  # setter chala, validate hua
# p.url = "not-a-url"               # ValueError: url must be absolute
# p.url = 123                       # TypeError: url must be str
# del p.url                         # AttributeError: url cannot be deleted

Line-by-line walkthrough:

  1. self.url = url __init__ mein — ye seedha self._url set nahi karta; ye setter ko trigger karta hai. Ye deliberate hai — validation constructor par bhi lagni chahiye. Agar aap self._url = url likhte toh constructor validation bypass kar deta.
  2. @property def url(self) — getter. Method ka naam wahi hona chahiye jo attribute ka naam hai.
  3. return self._url — actual data underscore-prefixed attribute mein hai. Agar aap return self.url likh doge toh infinite recursion hogi (getter khud ko call karega) → RecursionError.
  4. @url.setter — url (property object) ka .setter method ek naya property object banata hai jismein setter bhi hai. Decorator ka naam property ke naam se aana chahiye, @setter nahi.
  5. def url(self, value) — setter ka naam bhi wahi hai. Isse url naam property object par rebind hota hai (getter + setter dono ke saath).
  6. if not value.startswith(("http://", "https://")) — tuple deke ek call mein do prefixes check kiye (1.8).
  7. self._url = value.rstrip("/") — normalisation setter mein. Ab har jagah se aayi URL consistent hai.
  8. @url.deleter — del ko block kar diya. Ye tab useful hai jab attribute ka delete hona bug ka source ho.

docs.title: Computed properties — sabse common use
docs.text:
class TestRun:
    def __init__(self, results: list[dict]):
        self.results = results

    @property
    def total(self) -> int:
        return len(self.results)

    @property
    def passed(self) -> int:
        return sum(1 for r in self.results if r["status"] == "passed")

    @property
    def failed(self) -> int:
        return sum(1 for r in self.results if r["status"] == "failed")

    @property
    def pass_rate(self) -> float:
        """Derived value -- store karne ki zarurat nahi, compute kar lo."""
        return self.passed / self.total if self.total else 0.0

    @property
    def is_green(self) -> bool:
        return self.failed == 0 and self.total > 0

run = TestRun([
    {"name": "a", "status": "passed"},
    {"name": "b", "status": "failed"},
    {"name": "c", "status": "passed"},
])
print(run.total, run.passed, run.failed)        # 3 2 1
print(f"{run.pass_rate:.1%}")                    # 66.7%
print(run.is_green)                              # False

Kyun property, method nahi:

  1. run.pass_rate padhne mein run.get_pass_rate() se natural hai — ye ek value hai, ek action nahi.
  2. Agar aap self.pass_rate = ... __init__ mein store karte toh wo stale ho jaata jab results mein naya item add hota. Property hamesha fresh compute karti hai.
  3. Rule: property tab jab: (a) sasti compute ho, (b) side effect na ho, (c) semantically attribute lage. Agar koi bhi condition tootti hai toh method banao.

Kab property NAHI:

class Page:
    @property
    def screenshot(self):
        """BURA -- ye slow hai aur side effect hai (file likhta hai)."""
        return self.page.screenshot(path="shot.png")

    # SAHI:
    def take_screenshot(self, path="shot.png"):
        return self.page.screenshot(path=path)
  1. page.screenshot padhne wale ko lagta hai ye sasta hai. Actually wo 500ms leta hai aur disk par likhta hai.
  2. Debugger property ko automatically evaluate kar deta hai jab wo variables panel dikhata hai — toh aapka debugger screenshots leta rahega!
  3. Rule: property mein I/O, network, ya kuch bhi jo fail kar sakta hai — mat rakho.

docs.title: Read-only property (setter na do)
docs.text:
class TestResult:
    def __init__(self, name: str, status: str):
        self._name = name
        self._status = status

    @property
    def name(self) -> str:
        return self._name                    # sirf getter -> read-only

r = TestResult("test_a", "passed")
print(r.name)
# r.name = "other"                           # AttributeError: property 'name' of 'TestResult' object has no setter

Note: r._name = "other" abhi bhi chalega — Python mein sach mein private kuch nahi hai. Ye "accidental change" rokta hai, "deliberate hack" nahi.

docs.title: 5.4.2 Descriptors — property ke peeche ka mechanism
docs.text:
Kya hai: ek object jo __get__, __set__, ya __delete__ define karta hai, aur jab wo kisi class ka attribute ho toh attribute access ko intercept karta hai.

Types:

Type Methods Priority Data descriptor __get__ aur (__set__ ya __delete__) instance __dict__ se zyada Non-data descriptor sirf __get__ instance __dict__ se kam

Yahi wo priority hai jo 5.1 ke attribute lookup order mein dikhi thi.

Kyu — same validation baar-baar likhne se bachne ke liye:

# --- WITHOUT descriptor: har field ke liye poora property block ---
class Config:
    @property
    def timeout(self): return self._timeout
    @timeout.setter
    def timeout(self, v):
        if not isinstance(v, int) or v <= 0:
            raise ValueError("timeout must be positive int")
        self._timeout = v

    @property
    def retries(self): return self._retries
    @retries.setter
    def retries(self, v):
        if not isinstance(v, int) or v <= 0:
            raise ValueError("retries must be positive int")
        self._retries = v
    # ... 10 fields = 60 lines of near-identical code

# --- WITH descriptor: validation logic ek baar ---
class PositiveInt:
    """Ek reusable descriptor jo positive integer enforce karta hai."""

    def __set_name__(self, owner, name):
        """Class banate waqt Python ye call karta hai -- attribute ka naam batata hai."""
        self.public_name = name
        self.private_name = f"_{name}"

    def __get__(self, obj, objtype=None):
        if obj is None:                             # class se access (Config.timeout)
            return self
        return getattr(obj, self.private_name)

    def __set__(self, obj, value):
        if not isinstance(value, int) or isinstance(value, bool):
            raise TypeError(f"{self.public_name} must be an int, got {type(value).__name__}")
        if value <= 0:
            raise ValueError(f"{self.public_name} must be positive, got {value}")
        setattr(obj, self.private_name, value)


class Config:
    timeout = PositiveInt()                          # ek line
    retries = PositiveInt()                          # ek line
    workers = PositiveInt()                          # ek line

    def __init__(self, timeout: int, retries: int, workers: int):
        self.timeout = timeout                       # descriptor ka __set__ chalega
        self.retries = retries
        self.workers = workers


c = Config(timeout=30, retries=3, workers=4)
print(c.timeout)                    # 30
# c.timeout = -5                    # ValueError: timeout must be positive, got -5
# c.retries = "3"                   # TypeError: retries must be an int, got str
# c.workers = True                  # TypeError -- bool ko bhi reject kiya

Line-by-line walkthrough:

  1. class PositiveInt: — ye descriptor class hai. Iska koi instance Config ke class body mein rakha jaayega.
  2. def __set_name__(self, owner, name): — Python 3.6+. Class creation ke waqt Python har descriptor par ye call karta hai aur batata hai ki wo kis naam se class mein rakha gaya hai. Iske bina aapko PositiveInt("timeout") likhna padta — naam do baar, aur typo ka khatra.
  3. self.private_name = f"_{name}" — actual value kahan store hogi. Descriptor object khud value store nahi kar sakta, kyunki wo class par ek hi hai aur saare instances share karenge. Isliye value instance ke __dict__ mein alag naam se rakhi jaati hai.
  4. def __get__(self, obj, objtype=None): — obj wo instance hai jispar access hua, objtype uski class.
  5. if obj is None: return self — jab Config.timeout (class se, instance ke bina) access ho toh obj None hota hai. Descriptor object khud return karna convention hai — isse introspection kaam karta hai (help(), inspect). Ye line bhoolne par AttributeError ya confusing errors milte hain.
  6. return getattr(obj, self.private_name) — instance se actual value nikali.
  7. def __set__(self, obj, value): — __set__ hone se ye data descriptor hai, matlab ye instance __dict__ par priority leta hai. Isliye c.timeout = -5 ko intercept kar paata hai.
  8. isinstance(value, bool) check — kyunki bool int ka subclass hai (1.3), aur Config(timeout=True) shayad bug hai. Ye deliberate strictness hai.
  9. setattr(obj, self.private_name, value) — obj._timeout = value. obj.timeout = value likhna infinite recursion hai (__set__ khud ko call karega).
  10. timeout = PositiveInt() — class body mein descriptor instance. Ye class attribute hai, ek hi object saare instances ke liye — isliye state instance par store karna zaruri tha.

docs.title: Descriptors kahan pehle se use ho rahe hain
docs.text:
class Demo:
    def method(self): pass                # function -- NON-data descriptor
    prop = property(lambda self: 1)       # property -- DATA descriptor
    cm = classmethod(lambda cls: 1)       # classmethod -- non-data descriptor
    sm = staticmethod(lambda: 1)          # staticmethod -- non-data descriptor
    __slots__ = ()                        # slots -- DATA descriptors banate hain
  1. Functions non-data descriptors hain — isliye aap instance par same naam ka attribute set karke method ko shadow kar sakte ho: 
    class P:
    def click(self): return "real"
p = P()
p.click = lambda: "mocked"            # instance dict jeeta (non-data descriptor)
print(p.click())                       # 'mocked'
    Ye monkeypatching ka mechanism hai — unittest.mock isi par bana hai.
  2. property data descriptor hai — isliye use instance dict se shadow nahi kar sakte: 
    class P:
    @property
    def url(self): return "real"
p = P()
# p.url = "mocked"                     # AttributeError: no setter
# p.__dict__["url"] = "mocked"         # set to ho jaayega...
# print(p.url)                         # ...par 'real' hi milega -- data descriptor jeeta
    Isliye properties ko mock karne ke liye class par patch karna padta hai: mock.patch.object(P, "url", new_callable=mock.PropertyMock).
  3. functools.cached_property non-data descriptor hai (sirf __get__) — isliye wo pehli baar compute karke instance __dict__ mein daal deta hai, aur agli baar step 2 (instance dict) jeet jaata hai aur descriptor chalta hi nahi. Yahi uska poora trick hai.

docs.title: QA use case — lazy page object components
docs.text:
class LazyComponent:
    """Ek page component jo pehli baar access par banta hai, phir cache ho jaata hai."""

    def __init__(self, factory):
        self.factory = factory

    def __set_name__(self, owner, name):
        self.name = name

    def __get__(self, obj, objtype=None):
        if obj is None:
            return self
        if self.name not in obj.__dict__:                 # pehli baar?
            obj.__dict__[self.name] = self.factory(obj)   # bana kar instance dict mein daalo
        return obj.__dict__[self.name]


class NavBar:
    def __init__(self, page):
        self.page = page
        print("  [NavBar created]")

class Footer:
    def __init__(self, page):
        self.page = page
        print("  [Footer created]")


class HomePage:
    nav = LazyComponent(lambda self: NavBar(self.page))
    footer = LazyComponent(lambda self: Footer(self.page))

    def __init__(self, page):
        self.page = page


home = HomePage(page="fake_page")           # kuch nahi bana
print("accessing nav...")
print(home.nav)                              # [NavBar created] -> object
print(home.nav)                              # cached -- dobara nahi bana
print("footer never accessed")               # Footer kabhi nahi bana

Line-by-line walkthrough:

  1. LazyComponent(lambda self: NavBar(self.page)) — factory ek callable hai jo instance leta hai. Ye closure page tak pahunch deta hai.
  2. if self.name not in obj.__dict__: — cache check. Note: sirf __get__ hai, koi __set__ nahi → non-data descriptor.
  3. obj.__dict__[self.name] = ... — value ko instance dict mein usi naam se rakh diya. Kyunki ye non-data descriptor hai, agli baar attribute lookup step 2 par ruk jaayega aur descriptor chalega hi nahi. Zero overhead after first access.
  4. Ye exactly functools.cached_property ka mechanism hai.
  5. QA faayda: ek bade page object mein 15 components ho sakte hain. Sab __init__ mein banana matlab har test mein 15 objects, chahe test sirf ek use kare. Lazy hone se sirf jo chahiye wahi banta hai.

docs.title: Gotchas
docs.text:
Gotcha 1 — property mein self.x ki jagah self._x.

class Bad:
    @property
    def url(self):
        return self.url          # INFINITE RECURSION -> RecursionError

Gotcha 2 — descriptor instance-level nahi ho sakta.

class Demo:
    def __init__(self):
        self.field = PositiveInt()     # ye descriptor ki tarah kaam NAHI karega

d = Demo()
d.field = -5                            # koi validation nahi -- bas object replace ho gaya

Descriptor protocol sirf class attributes par kaam karta hai. Ye deliberate hai (performance — har instance attribute par descriptor check karna mehnga hoga).

Gotcha 3 — __set_name__ ke bina naam pata nahi chalta.

3.6 se pehle log PositiveInt("timeout") likhte the — naam do baar likhna padta tha aur mismatch se weird bugs aate the. __set_name__ ne ye solve kiya.

Gotcha 4 — property inheritance mein setter override.

class Base:
    @property
    def url(self):
        return self._url

class Child(Base):
    @Base.url.setter                    # parent ki property se setter add karo
    def url(self, value):
        self._url = value.lower()

c = Child()
c.url = "HTTPS://X.COM"
print(c.url)                             # https://x.com

Agar aap Child mein sirf @property def url likhoge toh parent ka getter/setter dono replace ho jaayenge — partial override ke liye @Base.url.setter chahiye.

Interview answer: "A property lets a method be accessed like an attribute, which matters because Python has no tradition of writing getters and setters upfront — you expose a plain attribute and convert it to a property later if you need validation or a computed value, without any caller changing. I use it for derived values like run.pass_rate, which stays correct as results are added, whereas storing it in __init__ would go stale. The rule I apply is that a property must be cheap, side-effect free, and semantically a value; anything doing I/O should be a method, partly because debuggers evaluate properties automatically when they render the variables pane — a screenshot property means your debugger takes screenshots.

Underneath, a property is just a descriptor — an object with __get__ and __set__ living on the class. Writing my own descriptor pays off when the same validation repeats across many fields: one PositiveInt descriptor replaces ten near-identical property pairs, and __set_name__ tells it what attribute name it was assigned to. The distinction that explains a lot of Python behaviour is data versus non-data descriptors: a data descriptor has __set__ and beats the instance dictionary, while a non-data descriptor loses to it. Functions are non-data descriptors, which is exactly why you can monkeypatch a method by assigning to the instance — and why you can't do that to a property, so mocking one requires patching the class with PropertyMock."

Cross-question — "How does functools.cached_property avoid recomputing, and why can't property do the same trick?" "cached_property is a non-data descriptor: it defines __get__ but not __set__. On first access it computes the value and writes it into the instance's __dict__ under the same attribute name. Because non-data descriptors rank below the instance dictionary in the lookup order, every subsequent access finds the cached value in __dict__ and the descriptor is never consulted again — so after the first call there's zero overhead. A regular property is a data descriptor, since it defines __set__, and data descriptors always win over the instance dictionary, so the getter runs on every single access no matter what you put in __dict__. That's also the practical constraint: cached_property needs the class to have a __dict__, so it doesn't work with __slots__, and you invalidate the cache with del obj.attr."

docs.title: Kya hai
docs.text: Inheritance = ek class doosri class ka behaviour "le leti" hai, aur usme add/override kar sakti hai. "Is-a" relationship: LoginPage is a BasePage.

docs.title: Kyu hai
docs.text:
# --- WITHOUT inheritance: har page mein wahi code repeat ---
class LoginPage:
    def __init__(self, page, base_url):
        self.page = page
        self.base_url = base_url

    def wait_for_load(self):
        self.page.wait_for_load_state("networkidle")

    def screenshot(self, name):
        self.page.screenshot(path=f"screenshots/{name}.png")

class CartPage:
    def __init__(self, page, base_url):     # exactly same
        self.page = page
        self.base_url = base_url

    def wait_for_load(self):                # exactly same
        self.page.wait_for_load_state("networkidle")

    def screenshot(self, name):             # exactly same
        self.page.screenshot(path=f"screenshots/{name}.png")
# ... 20 pages = 20 copies. Ek fix karo toh 20 jagah karo.

# --- WITH inheritance ---
class BasePage:
    URL_PATH = ""                                        # subclass override karegi

    def __init__(self, page, base_url: str):
        self.page = page
        self.base_url = base_url.rstrip("/")

    @property
    def url(self) -> str:
        return f"{self.base_url}{self.URL_PATH}"

    def open(self):
        self.page.goto(self.url)
        self.wait_for_load()
        return self

    def wait_for_load(self):
        self.page.wait_for_load_state("networkidle")

    def screenshot(self, name: str):
        self.page.screenshot(path=f"screenshots/{name}.png")


class LoginPage(BasePage):
    URL_PATH = "/login"                                  # sirf ye badla
    USERNAME = "#username"

    def login(self, user, pwd):                          # sirf naya behaviour
        self.page.fill(self.USERNAME, user)
        return self


class CartPage(BasePage):
    URL_PATH = "/cart"

    def wait_for_load(self):                             # OVERRIDE -- cart ko extra wait chahiye
        super().wait_for_load()                          # parent ka kaam pehle
        self.page.wait_for_selector(".cart-total")       # phir apna extra

Line-by-line walkthrough:

  1. class LoginPage(BasePage): — BasePage base class (parent) hai. LoginPage ke paas BasePage ke saare methods aa gaye.
  2. URL_PATH = "/login" — class attribute override. BasePage.open() mein self.URL_PATH likha hai, toh wo subclass wala milega — ye "template method pattern" hai.
  3. def wait_for_load(self): CartPage mein — method override. Same naam se method define karne se parent ka version chhup jaata hai.
  4. super().wait_for_load() — parent ka version explicitly call kiya. Ye "extend, don't replace" pattern hai: parent ka kaam bhi ho, aur apna extra bhi.
  5. Agar aap super() na likho toh parent ka wait bilkul nahi chalega — jo shayad aap nahi chahte the.

docs.title: super() — kya karta hai actually
docs.text:
Galat mental model: "super() parent class ko call karta hai." Sahi mental model: "super() MRO mein agle class ko call karta hai."

Single inheritance mein dono same hai. Multiple inheritance mein bilkul alag hai — aur wahin super() ka asli design dikhta hai.

class BasePage:
    def __init__(self, page):
        print("BasePage.__init__")
        self.page = page

class LoginPage(BasePage):
    def __init__(self, page, username):
        print("LoginPage.__init__")
        super().__init__(page)                    # BasePage.__init__ chalega
        self.username = username

p = LoginPage("fake_page", "ritik")
# LoginPage.__init__
# BasePage.__init__
  1. super().__init__(page) — super() bina arguments ke Python 3 mein kaam karta hai; compiler chupke se __class__ aur self inject kar deta hai. Python 2 mein super(LoginPage, self).__init__(page) likhna padta tha.
  2. super().__init__(page) pehle ya baad — depends. Agar parent ka setup chahiye toh pehle; agar aapko parent se pehle kuch set karna hai toh baad mein. Common convention: pehle.
  3. super().__init__() bhoolna sabse common inheritance bug hai — parent ka state initialise hi nahi hota aur AttributeError baad mein kahin milta hai.

docs.title: MRO — Method Resolution Order
docs.text:
Kya hai: wo linear order jisme Python attribute dhoondhta hai. ClassName.__mro__ ya ClassName.mro() se dekh sakte ho.

class BasePage:
    def describe(self): return "BasePage"

class LoggingMixin:
    def describe(self): return "LoggingMixin"

class RetryMixin:
    def describe(self): return "RetryMixin"

class LoginPage(LoggingMixin, RetryMixin, BasePage):
    pass

print(LoginPage.__mro__)
# (<class 'LoginPage'>, <class 'LoggingMixin'>, <class 'RetryMixin'>,
#  <class 'BasePage'>, <class 'object'>)

print(LoginPage().describe())     # 'LoggingMixin'  -- MRO mein pehla jo mila

MRO kaise compute hota hai — C3 linearisation

C3 algorithm teen cheezein guarantee karta hai:

  1. Child hamesha parent se pehle aata hai.
  2. Parents ka order preserve rehta hai (jaise class definition mein likha).
  3. Monotonic hai — subclass ka MRO parent ke MRO ko contradict nahi karta.
# Diamond problem
class A:
    def who(self): return "A"

class B(A):
    def who(self): return "B -> " + super().who()

class C(A):
    def who(self): return "C -> " + super().who()

class D(B, C):
    def who(self): return "D -> " + super().who()

print([c.__name__ for c in D.__mro__])    # ['D', 'B', 'C', 'A', 'object']
print(D().who())                           # 'D -> B -> C -> A'

Line-by-line walkthrough — ye output sabse important cheez hai:

  1. Diamond: D B aur C dono se inherit karta hai, aur dono A se.
  2. MRO: D, B, C, A, object. Note A ek hi baar hai, chahe wo do raaston se aata hai.
  3. D().who() — D.who chala, usne super().who() kiya.
  4. super() D ke context mein hai, toh MRO mein D ke baad wala = B. B.who chala.
  5. B.who ne super().who() kiya. Yahan magic hai: super() B ke context mein hai, toh MRO mein B ke baad wala = C, A nahi! Chahe B ka parent A hai.
  6. C.who chala, usne super().who() kiya → A.who → "A".
  7. Result: A sirf EK BAAR chala, chahe wo do baar reachable tha. Ye C3 ka poora point hai — diamond mein duplicate calls se bachna.
  8. Agar super() ki jagah A.who(self) hardcode karte toh C bilkul skip ho jaata aur A do baar chalta. Ye cooperative multiple inheritance ka core hai.

Jab MRO possible hi nahi:

class A: pass
class B(A): pass
# class Bad(A, B): pass
# TypeError: Cannot create a consistent method resolution order (MRO) for bases A, B

A, B order kehta hai A pehle. Par B A ka subclass hai, toh child-before-parent rule kehta hai B pehle. Contradiction → TypeError at class creation. Ye compile-time safety hai.

docs.title: Cooperative multiple inheritance — mixins
docs.text:
import time
import functools

class TimingMixin:
    """Har action ka time measure karo."""

    def perform(self, action: str, *args, **kwargs):
        start = time.perf_counter()
        try:
            return super().perform(action, *args, **kwargs)     # chain aage badhao
        finally:
            elapsed = time.perf_counter() - start
            print(f"  [timing] {action} took {elapsed * 1000:.1f}ms")


class RetryMixin:
    """Failure par retry karo."""
    MAX_ATTEMPTS = 3

    def perform(self, action: str, *args, **kwargs):
        last_error = None
        for attempt in range(1, self.MAX_ATTEMPTS + 1):
            try:
                return super().perform(action, *args, **kwargs)
            except Exception as exc:
                last_error = exc
                print(f"  [retry] attempt {attempt} failed: {exc}")
        raise RuntimeError(f"{action} failed after {self.MAX_ATTEMPTS} attempts") from last_error


class ScreenshotOnFailureMixin:
    """Failure par screenshot lo."""

    def perform(self, action: str, *args, **kwargs):
        try:
            return super().perform(action, *args, **kwargs)
        except Exception:
            print(f"  [screenshot] capturing failure_{action}.png")
            raise                                     # exception ko aage badhne do


class BasePage:
    """Chain ka aakhri hissa -- actual kaam yahan hota hai."""
    _fail_count = 0

    def perform(self, action: str, *args, **kwargs):
        BasePage._fail_count += 1
        if BasePage._fail_count < 3:                  # pehle do attempts fail karo (demo)
            raise TimeoutError(f"{action} timed out")
        return f"{action} succeeded"


class ResilientPage(TimingMixin, ScreenshotOnFailureMixin, RetryMixin, BasePage):
    pass


print([c.__name__ for c in ResilientPage.__mro__])
# ['ResilientPage', 'TimingMixin', 'ScreenshotOnFailureMixin', 'RetryMixin', 'BasePage', 'object']

print(ResilientPage().perform("click"))

Output:

  [retry] attempt 1 failed: click timed out
  [retry] attempt 2 failed: click timed out
  [timing] click took 0.3ms
click succeeded

Line-by-line walkthrough:

  1. Har mixin ka method super().perform(...) call karta hai — isliye wo compose hote hain. Agar koi mixin super() na kare toh chain wahin toot jaayegi aur neeche wale mixins/base kabhi nahi chalenge.
  2. class ResilientPage(TimingMixin, ScreenshotOnFailureMixin, RetryMixin, BasePage) — order matters aur wo semantically meaningful hai:
  3. TimingMixin sabse bahar → total time measure karega (retries samet).
  4. ScreenshotOnFailureMixin → agar sab retries fail ho jaayein tab screenshot.
  5. RetryMixin → retry loop.
  6. BasePage → actual kaam. Agar aap RetryMixin ko ScreenshotOnFailureMixin se pehle rakhte toh har failed attempt par screenshot milta — 3 screenshots. Dono designs valid hain, par aapko pata hona chahiye ki aap kya chun rahe ho.
  7. try/finally TimingMixin mein — finally hamesha chalta hai, chahe exception aaye. Toh timing failure par bhi print hoti hai.
  8. raise bina argument ScreenshotOnFailureMixin mein — current exception ko re-raise karta hai, apne original traceback ke saath. raise exc likhne se traceback ka ek hissa kho jaata (Part 9).
  9. raise RuntimeError(...) from last_error — chaining.
  10. Mixin naming convention: naam Mixin se khatam ho, aur mixin akela instantiate na ho — wo hamesha kisi base ke saath mix hota hai.

docs.title: Composition vs inheritance
docs.text:
# --- INHERITANCE: "is-a" ---
class ChromePage(BasePage):                # ChromePage IS A BasePage
    pass

# --- COMPOSITION: "has-a" ---
class LoginPage:
    def __init__(self, page):
        self.page = page                   # LoginPage HAS A page
        self.nav = NavBar(page)            # LoginPage HAS A navbar
        self.api = ApiClient()             # LoginPage HAS AN api client

    def login(self, user, pwd):
        self.api.reset_user(user)          # composed object ka method
        self.page.fill("#user", user)

Kab kaunsa:

Inheritance Composition Genuine "is-a" (LoginPage is a BasePage) "has-a" ya "uses-a" Subclass parent ke har method ke liye valid hai (Liskov) Sirf kuch behaviour chahiye Framework contract (unittest.TestCase) Runtime par behaviour badalna hai Shallow hierarchy (2-3 levels max) Deep hierarchy ban rahi ho

"Favour composition over inheritance" kyun:

  1. Inheritance compile-time hai, composition runtime hai. Aap self.retry_policy ko test mein badal sakte ho; base class nahi badal sakte.
  2. Inheritance poora interface le leta hai. Agar BasePage mein 30 methods hain toh LoginPage ke paas bhi 30 hain, chahe 25 uske liye meaningless hon.
  3. Fragile base class problem: BasePage mein ek method badla → 20 subclasses mein se koi toot sakta hai, aur pata nahi chalega.
  4. Deep hierarchies debug karna narak hai — self.foo() ka source dhoondhne ke liye 5 classes padhni padti hain.

QA mein practical rule:

# Inheritance: BasePage se page objects -- ye theek hai (genuine is-a, shallow)
class LoginPage(BasePage): ...

# Composition: page object mein API client, test data factory, config -- ye behtar hai
class LoginPage(BasePage):
    def __init__(self, page, api_client, config):
        super().__init__(page)
        self.api = api_client            # inject kiya, inherit nahi
        self.config = config

Injection se test mein aap fake API client de sakte ho — inheritance mein wo mushkil hota.

docs.title: Gotchas
docs.text:
Gotcha 1 — super().__init__() bhoolna.

class Base:
    def __init__(self):
        self.page = None

class Child(Base):
    def __init__(self, url):
        self.url = url                    # super().__init__() nahi kiya

c = Child("x")
# print(c.page)                           # AttributeError: 'Child' object has no attribute 'page'

Gotcha 2 — super() sirf class ke andar chalta hai.

class A:
    def f(self): return "A"

# super().f()                              # RuntimeError: super(): no arguments (bahar se)

Bahar se: super(B, b_instance).f().

Gotcha 3 — MRO order galat samajhna.

class Loud:
    def speak(self): return "LOUD"
class Quiet:
    def speak(self): return "quiet"

class Both(Loud, Quiet): pass
print(Both().speak())                     # 'LOUD'  -- BAAYAN wala jeetta hai

Python left-to-right hai. Java mein multiple inheritance hai hi nahi (interfaces hain), C++ mein aapko explicitly qualify karna padta hai.

Gotcha 4 — mixin mein __init__ aur **kwargs.

class LoggingMixin:
    def __init__(self, *args, log_level="INFO", **kwargs):
        self.log_level = log_level
        super().__init__(*args, **kwargs)      # baaki arguments aage bhejo

class BasePage:
    def __init__(self, page):
        self.page = page

class LoggedPage(LoggingMixin, BasePage):
    pass

p = LoggedPage("fake_page", log_level="DEBUG")
print(p.log_level, p.page)                     # DEBUG fake_page
  1. Mixin apna keyword nikaal leta hai (log_level) aur baaki *args, **kwargs aage bhej deta hai. Ye cooperative __init__ ka standard pattern hai.
  2. Bina **kwargs forwarding ke, chain toot jaati hai aur base class ko arguments nahi milte.

Gotcha 5 — isinstance vs type.

class Base: pass
class Child(Base): pass
c = Child()
print(isinstance(c, Base))      # True   -- subclass bhi count hota hai
print(type(c) is Base)          # False  -- exact type check
print(issubclass(Child, Base))  # True   -- classes ke liye

Interview answer: "Inheritance expresses an is-a relationship and lets a subclass extend or override behaviour. super() is the part people get wrong: it doesn't call 'the parent class', it calls the next class in the MRO — the method resolution order computed by C3 linearisation. In single inheritance those are the same thing, but with a diamond they aren't: in D(B, C) where both derive from A, B's super() resolves to C, not A, so A runs exactly once no matter how many paths reach it. That's the whole point of cooperative multiple inheritance, and it's why hardcoding A.method(self) instead of super().method() breaks the chain and can run code twice. C3 guarantees children precede parents, declaration order is preserved, and the ordering is monotonic; if no such order exists Python refuses to create the class at all.

In a page-object framework I use shallow inheritance — one BasePage — and mixins for cross-cutting behaviour like retry, timing, and screenshot-on-failure, each calling super().perform(...) so they compose. The class declaration order then actually means something: putting retry inside the screenshot mixin gives you one screenshot after all retries, putting it outside gives you one per attempt. For everything that isn't a genuine is-a — an API client, a config, a test-data factory — I use composition and inject it, because that's what lets me substitute a fake in a test."

Cross-question — "What's the diamond problem, and how do languages other than Python solve it?" "The diamond problem is that when D inherits from B and C, which both inherit from A, it's ambiguous which A you get and how many times A's initialiser should run. C++ solves it with virtual inheritance, which you have to opt into explicitly, and otherwise you get two copies of the base subobject. Java sidesteps it by banning multiple inheritance of classes entirely — you get single inheritance plus interfaces, and since Java 8 default methods, where a conflict is a compile error you must resolve by hand. Python solves it at the language level with C3 linearisation plus cooperative super(): there's exactly one MRO, A appears once, and each class calls the next one along. The cost is that super() becomes non-local — you can't tell what it resolves to by reading one class, only by reading the MRO of whatever concrete class was instantiated. That's the main reason I keep hierarchies shallow and mixins small and single-purpose."

docs.title: Kya hai
docs.text:
"Dunder" = double underscore. Ye methods Python ke protocols implement karte hain: aap __len__ likhte ho, Python len() ko usse jodta hai. Ye "operator overloading" se zyada hai — ye poora object model hai.

Analogy: electrical socket ka standard. Aapka koi bhi appliance us shape ka plug lagata hai aur bijli mil jaati hai. __len__ ek plug shape hai; jo bhi wo shape banata hai, len() usmein "plug in" ho jaata hai.

docs.title: Object lifecycle
docs.text:
class TestRun:
    def __new__(cls, *args, **kwargs):
        """Object banata hai."""
        return super().__new__(cls)

    def __init__(self, name: str, results: list):
        """Object ko initialise karta hai."""
        self.name = name
        self.results = results

    def __del__(self):
        """Object destroy hone par -- BHAROSA MAT KARO"""
        pass

__del__ par kyun bharosa nahi:

  1. Kab chalega ye guarantee nahi (reference cycles, interpreter shutdown).
  2. Usme exception aaye toh wo ignore ho jaati hai (sirf stderr par warning).
  3. Interpreter shutdown par globals already None ho sakte hain → weird AttributeError.
  4. Cleanup ke liye context manager (__enter__/__exit__) use karo — Part 8.

docs.title: Representation — __repr__ vs __str__ vs __format__
docs.text:
class TestResult:
    def __init__(self, name: str, status: str, duration: float):
        self.name = name
        self.status = status
        self.duration = duration

    def __repr__(self) -> str:
        """DEVELOPER ke liye -- unambiguous, ideally eval() ho sake."""
        return f"TestResult(name={self.name!r}, status={self.status!r}, duration={self.duration!r})"

    def __str__(self) -> str:
        """USER ke liye -- readable."""
        return f"{self.name}: {self.status.upper()} ({self.duration:.2f}s)"

    def __format__(self, spec: str) -> str:
        """f-string format spec handle karo."""
        if spec == "short":
            return f"{self.name[:20]}: {self.status[0].upper()}"
        if spec == "csv":
            return f"{self.name},{self.status},{self.duration}"
        return str(self)                       # default: __str__ par gir jao


r = TestResult("test_login_with_valid_credentials", "failed", 4.523)

print(repr(r))          # TestResult(name='test_login_with_valid_credentials', status='failed', duration=4.523)
print(str(r))           # test_login_with_valid_credentials: FAILED (4.52s)
print(r)                # str() -- print() str use karta hai
print(f"{r}")           # str() -- f-string default __format__ -> __str__
print(f"{r!r}")         # repr()
print(f"{r:short}")     # test_login_with_val: F
print(f"{r:csv}")       # test_login_with_valid_credentials,failed,4.523
print([r])              # [TestResult(...)]   <- containers REPR use karte hain!

Line-by-line walkthrough:

  1. __repr__ — unambiguous. Convention: aisa likho ki eval(repr(obj)) object wapas bana de. Ye hamesha possible nahi, tab <TestResult test_login failed> jaisa likho.
  2. !r in f-string — repr() lagta hai. Isliye name='test_login' quotes ke saath dikha — jo batata hai ki wo string hai.
  3. __str__ — readable. Agar __str__ na ho toh Python __repr__ par gir jaata hai. Ulta nahi — __repr__ na ho toh <__main__.TestResult object at 0x...> milta hai.
  4. print([r]) — list ka __str__ apne elements ka __repr__ use karta hai. Isliye __repr__ sabse important hai: debugging mein aap aksar list/dict print karte ho.
  5. __format__(self, spec) — f-string ka :spec yahan aata hai. Custom specs se aap ek hi object ko report, CSV, aur log ke liye alag-alag format kar sakte ho.

QA ke liye critical: achha __repr__ assertion failures ko readable banata hai.

class BadRepr:
    def __init__(self, name): self.name = name

class GoodRepr:
    def __init__(self, name): self.name = name
    def __repr__(self): return f"GoodRepr(name={self.name!r})"

# assert BadRepr("a") == BadRepr("b")
# AssertionError: assert <__main__.BadRepr object at 0x10> == <__main__.BadRepr object at 0x20>
#                        ^^^ poori tarah bekaar

# assert GoodRepr("a") == GoodRepr("b")
# AssertionError: assert GoodRepr(name='a') == GoodRepr(name='b')
#                        ^^^ turant pata chal gaya

Rule: har class jo test data represent karti hai, usme __repr__ hona chahiye. (@dataclass ye free mein deta hai — 5.10.)

docs.title: Comparison — __eq__, __lt__, __hash__
docs.text:
import functools

@functools.total_ordering
class Version:
    def __init__(self, major: int, minor: int, patch: int):
        self.major, self.minor, self.patch = major, minor, patch

    def _key(self) -> tuple[int, int, int]:
        """Comparison ka aadhaar -- ek hi jagah define kiya."""
        return (self.major, self.minor, self.patch)

    def __eq__(self, other) -> bool:
        if not isinstance(other, Version):
            return NotImplemented                   # 'False' NAHI
        return self._key() == other._key()

    def __lt__(self, other) -> bool:
        if not isinstance(other, Version):
            return NotImplemented
        return self._key() < other._key()

    def __hash__(self) -> int:
        return hash(self._key())                    # tuple hash use karo

    def __repr__(self) -> str:
        return f"Version({self.major}, {self.minor}, {self.patch})"


v1, v2, v3 = Version(1, 2, 0), Version(1, 10, 0), Version(1, 2, 0)
print(v1 < v2)                       # True   -- 2 < 10 numerically
print(v1 == v3)                      # True
print(v1 is v3)                      # False
print(sorted([v2, v1]))              # [Version(1, 2, 0), Version(1, 10, 0)]
print({v1, v3})                      # {Version(1, 2, 0)}   -- dedup hua, hash + eq se
print(v1 <= v2, v1 >= v2)            # True False   -- total_ordering se aaye

Line-by-line walkthrough:

  1. def _key(self) — comparison logic ek jagah. Isse __eq__, __lt__, aur __hash__ sab consistent rehte hain. Ye ek design discipline hai jo bugs rokti hai.
  2. return NotImplemented — False nahi. Ye Python ko batata hai "main is type ko handle nahi kar sakta, doosre operand ka reflected method try karo". False return karne se Version(1,0,0) == SomeOtherVersionClass(1,0,0) chupchaap False ho jaata bina doosre ko mauka diye.
  3. __hash__ — hash(tuple) use kiya, jo elements ko properly mix karta hai. Manual mixing (self.major * 1000 + self.minor) mat likho — collisions zyada honge.
  4. Contract: a == b ho toh hash(a) == hash(b) hona hi chahiye. _key() dono mein same hone se ye guarantee ho gaya.
  5. Critical Python rule: agar aap __eq__ define karte ho aur __hash__ nahi, toh Python __hash__ ko None set kar deta hai aur class unhashable ban jaati hai: 
    class NoHash:
    def __eq__(self, other): return True
# {NoHash()}                    # TypeError: unhashable type: 'NoHash'
print(NoHash.__hash__)          # None
    Kyun: default __hash__ identity-based hai, par aapka __eq__ value-based hai — do equal objects ke alag hash honge, jo dict/set tod dega. Python isse silently galat hone ki jagah loud error deta hai.
  6. @functools.total_ordering — __le__, __gt__, __ge__ derive kar deta hai.

docs.title: Container protocol
docs.text:
class TestSuite:
    def __init__(self, name: str):
        self.name = name
        self._tests: list[dict] = []

    # ---------- SIZE ----------
    def __len__(self) -> int:
        """len(suite)"""
        return len(self._tests)

    # ---------- ITEM ACCESS ----------
    def __getitem__(self, index):
        """suite[0], suite[1:3], suite['name']"""
        if isinstance(index, slice):                    # slice object aaya
            new = TestSuite(f"{self.name}[slice]")
            new._tests = self._tests[index]
            return new
        if isinstance(index, str):                      # naam se lookup
            for t in self._tests:
                if t["name"] == index:
                    return t
            raise KeyError(index)
        return self._tests[index]                       # int index

    def __setitem__(self, index, value):
        """suite[0] = x"""
        self._tests[index] = value

    def __delitem__(self, index):
        """del suite[0]"""
        del self._tests[index]

    # ---------- ITERATION ----------
    def __iter__(self):
        """for t in suite"""
        return iter(self._tests)

    def __reversed__(self):
        """reversed(suite)"""
        return reversed(self._tests)

    # ---------- MEMBERSHIP ----------
    def __contains__(self, name: str) -> bool:
        """'test_a' in suite"""
        return any(t["name"] == name for t in self._tests)

    # ---------- TRUTHINESS ----------
    def __bool__(self) -> bool:
        """if suite:"""
        return len(self._tests) > 0

    # ---------- OPERATORS ----------
    def __add__(self, other: "TestSuite") -> "TestSuite":
        """suite1 + suite2"""
        if not isinstance(other, TestSuite):
            return NotImplemented
        combined = TestSuite(f"{self.name}+{other.name}")
        combined._tests = self._tests + other._tests
        return combined

    def __iadd__(self, other: "TestSuite") -> "TestSuite":
        """suite1 += suite2 -- IN-PLACE"""
        if not isinstance(other, TestSuite):
            return NotImplemented
        self._tests.extend(other._tests)
        return self                                     # WAHI object return karo

    def add(self, name: str, status: str = "pending"):
        self._tests.append({"name": name, "status": status})
        return self

    def __repr__(self):
        return f"TestSuite({self.name!r}, {len(self._tests)} tests)"


suite = TestSuite("smoke").add("test_login").add("test_cart").add("test_pay")

print(len(suite))                    # 3
print(suite[0])                      # {'name': 'test_login', 'status': 'pending'}
print(suite["test_cart"])            # {'name': 'test_cart', 'status': 'pending'}
print(suite[:2])                     # TestSuite('smoke[slice]', 2 tests)
print("test_login" in suite)         # True
print([t["name"] for t in suite])    # ['test_login', 'test_cart', 'test_pay']
print(bool(suite), bool(TestSuite("empty")))   # True False

other = TestSuite("regression").add("test_refund")
print(suite + other)                 # TestSuite('smoke+regression', 4 tests)

Line-by-line walkthrough:

  1. __len__ — len() ke liye. Non-negative int return karna zaruri hai. Ye __bool__ ke na hone par truthiness bhi decide karta hai.
  2. __getitem__(self, index) — yahan teen kism ke index handle kiye. isinstance(index, slice) check zaruri hai kyunki suite[:2] par Python slice(None, 2, None) object bhejta hai, int nahi.
  3. __getitem__ hone se class automatically iterable ban jaati hai (purana sequence protocol: Python obj[0], obj[1], ... IndexError tak call karta hai). Par __iter__ define karna behtar hai — clearer aur tez.
  4. __iter__ — iter(self._tests) return kiya, khud generator nahi banaya. Ye simplest aur correct hai — delegation.
  5. __contains__ — in operator. Iske bina Python __iter__ se linear scan karta. Yahan hum bhi linear kar rahe hain, par agar hum ek set maintain karte toh O(1) de sakte the.
  6. __bool__ — bina iske __len__ se truthiness aati (jo yahan same hai). Maine explicitly likha taaki intent saaf ho.
  7. __add__ — naya object banata hai. NotImplemented return kiya galat type par.
  8. __iadd__ — self return karna zaruri hai, warna suite += other mein suite None ban jaayega. Aur ye in-place mutate karta hai — yahi + se farak hai.

docs.title: Callable, attribute access, aur context manager
docs.text:
class ActionRecorder:
    """Har call record karta hai -- ye ek mock/spy jaisa hai."""

    def __init__(self):
        self.calls = []

    def __call__(self, *args, **kwargs):
        """recorder(...) -- instance ko function bana deta hai."""
        self.calls.append((args, kwargs))
        return f"recorded call #{len(self.calls)}"

    def __getattr__(self, name: str):
        """Sirf tab chalta hai jab normal lookup FAIL ho."""
        if name.startswith("_"):
            raise AttributeError(name)                # dunder/private ko fake mat karo
        child = ActionRecorder()
        setattr(self, name, child)                    # cache kar lo
        return child

    def __setattr__(self, name: str, value):
        """HAR attribute assignment par chalta hai."""
        object.__setattr__(self, name, value)         # infinite recursion se bachne ke liye

    def __enter__(self):
        """with recorder:"""
        return self

    def __exit__(self, exc_type, exc_val, exc_tb):
        print(f"recorded {len(self.calls)} calls")
        return False                                  # exception ko suppress mat karo


rec = ActionRecorder()
print(rec("click", selector="#submit"))               # recorded call #1
print(rec.page.click("#login"))                        # nested attributes auto-create hue
print(rec.calls)                                       # [(('click',), {'selector': '#submit'})]

Line-by-line walkthrough:

  1. __call__ — instance ko callable banata hai. unittest.mock.Mock isi par bana hai.
  2. __getattr__ — sirf tab chalta hai jab normal attribute lookup fail ho (instance dict, class, MRO — sab mein na mile). Ye __getattribute__ se alag hai jo har access par chalta hai.
  3. if name.startswith("_"): raise AttributeError(name) — ye line critical hai. Bina iske copy.copy(rec) __deepcopy__, __reduce__ jaise dunders maangega aur aapka __getattr__ unke liye fake objects bana dega — jisse pickling, copying, aur debugging sab tootenge. Ye ek real, hard-to-debug bug hai.
  4. setattr(self, name, child) — cache kar liya, taaki rec.page do baar alag objects na de.
  5. __setattr__ — har assignment intercept karta hai. self.name = value likhna infinite recursion hai (__setattr__ khud ko call karega). object.__setattr__(self, name, value) ya self.__dict__[name] = value likhna padta hai.
  6. __enter__/__exit__ — context manager protocol (Part 8).

docs.title: Numeric aur conversion dunders
docs.text:
class Duration:
    """Seconds ka wrapper jo arithmetic support karta hai."""

    def __init__(self, seconds: float):
        self.seconds = float(seconds)

    def __add__(self, other):
        if isinstance(other, Duration):
            return Duration(self.seconds + other.seconds)
        if isinstance(other, (int, float)):
            return Duration(self.seconds + other)
        return NotImplemented

    def __radd__(self, other):
        """other + self -- jab left operand nahi jaanta"""
        return self.__add__(other)                    # addition commutative hai

    def __sub__(self, other):
        if isinstance(other, Duration):
            return Duration(self.seconds - other.seconds)
        return NotImplemented

    def __mul__(self, factor: float):
        if isinstance(factor, (int, float)):
            return Duration(self.seconds * factor)
        return NotImplemented

    __rmul__ = __mul__                                 # 2 * duration bhi chale

    def __truediv__(self, other):
        if isinstance(other, Duration):
            return self.seconds / other.seconds        # ratio -- plain float
        if isinstance(other, (int, float)):
            return Duration(self.seconds / other)
        return NotImplemented

    def __neg__(self):
        return Duration(-self.seconds)

    def __abs__(self):
        return Duration(abs(self.seconds))

    def __float__(self):
        """float(duration)"""
        return self.seconds

    def __int__(self):
        """int(duration)"""
        return int(self.seconds)

    def __round__(self, ndigits=None):
        """round(duration, 2)"""
        return Duration(round(self.seconds, ndigits))

    def __repr__(self):
        return f"Duration({self.seconds!r})"


d1, d2 = Duration(1.5), Duration(2.25)
print(d1 + d2)                     # Duration(3.75)
print(d1 + 0.5)                    # Duration(2.0)
print(0.5 + d1)                    # Duration(2.0)   -- __radd__ se
print(d2 - d1)                     # Duration(0.75)
print(d1 * 3)                      # Duration(4.5)
print(3 * d1)                      # Duration(4.5)   -- __rmul__ se
print(d2 / d1)                     # 1.5             -- ratio, float
print(sum([d1, d2], Duration(0)))  # Duration(3.75)  -- sum ko start value chahiye
print(float(d1), int(d2))          # 1.5 2
print(round(Duration(1.23456), 2)) # Duration(1.23)

Line-by-line walkthrough:

  1. __radd__ — 0.5 + d1 mein Python pehle float.__add__(0.5, d1) try karta hai, jo NotImplemented deta hai, phir Duration.__radd__(d1, 0.5) call karta hai.
  2. __rmul__ = __mul__ — ek line mein reflected version. Ye tabhi safe hai jab operation commutative ho. Subtraction ke liye __rsub__ alag likhna padega: def __rsub__(self, other): return Duration(other - self.seconds).
  3. sum([d1, d2], Duration(0)) — sum default start=0 (int) use karta hai, aur 0 + Duration(...) __radd__ se chalega, toh actually sum([d1, d2]) bhi chalta. Par explicit start clearer hai aur type-consistent.
  4. __truediv__ — do Durations ka ratio ek plain float hai (unit cancel ho gaya), par Duration/number ek Duration hai. Ye dimensional analysis hai aur ye achhe API design ka example hai.

docs.title: Gotchas
docs.text:
Gotcha 1 — __eq__ define karne se class unhashable ban jaati hai. (upar detail mein)

Gotcha 2 — __getattr__ infinite recursion.

class Bad:
    def __getattr__(self, name):
        return self.data[name]        # 'data' bhi nahi hai -> __getattr__ -> infinite

# Fix:
class Good:
    def __init__(self):
        self.data = {}
    def __getattr__(self, name):
        try:
            return self.__dict__["data"][name]     # __dict__ se seedha, __getattr__ bypass
        except KeyError:
            raise AttributeError(name) from None

Gotcha 3 — dunder lookup type par hota hai, instance par nahi.

class Demo:
    pass

d = Demo()
d.__len__ = lambda: 42            # instance par set kiya
# print(len(d))                   # TypeError: object of type 'Demo' has no len()
Demo.__len__ = lambda self: 42    # CLASS par set karo
print(len(d))                     # 42

Ye implicit special method lookup hai — performance ke liye Python dunders ko instance dict mein nahi dhoondhta. Isliye instance-level mocking of dunders kaam nahi karta; unittest.mock.MagicMock isi liye special handling karta hai.

Gotcha 4 — __iadd__ se self return nahi kiya.

class Bad:
    def __iadd__(self, other):
        self.items.extend(other)      # return bhool gaye -> None
b = Bad()
# b += [1]                            # b ab None hai

Interview answer: "Dunder methods are how a class plugs into Python's protocols — you implement __len__ and len() works, __iter__ and for works, __enter__/__exit__ and with works. The one I'd never skip is __repr__, because containers use repr for their elements and pytest puts it directly into assertion failure messages; <TestResult object at 0x7f...> in a failed assertion costs real debugging time. __str__ is the human-readable form and falls back to __repr__ if absent. On comparison, the contract matters: __eq__ should return NotImplemented rather than False for unknown types, so Python can try the reflected operation; and defining __eq__ sets __hash__ to None, making the class unhashable — deliberately, because value equality with identity hashing would silently break dicts and sets. I define both from a single _key() tuple so they can't drift apart. One mechanism worth knowing: dunder lookup happens on the type, not the instance, so assigning obj.__len__ does nothing — that's why mocking magic methods needs MagicMock rather than plain attribute assignment."

docs.title: Kya hai
docs.text:
ABC ek class hai jise directly instantiate nahi kiya ja sakta, aur jo subclasses par "ye methods implement karne hi honge" ka contract lagati hai.

Analogy: driving licence ka form. Form khud koi gaadi nahi chalata; wo kehta hai "jo bhi driver banega usko ye teen cheezein aani chahiye". Form bharoge nahi toh licence nahi milega.

docs.title: Kyu hai
docs.text:
# --- WITHOUT ABC: contract sirf documentation mein hai ---
class BaseReporter:
    def report(self, results):
        raise NotImplementedError("subclasses must implement report()")

class BrokenReporter(BaseReporter):
    def repot(self, results):                       # TYPO -- 'repot'
        print(results)

r = BrokenReporter()                                 # ye chal gaya! koi error nahi
# r.report([])                                       # NotImplementedError -- RUNTIME par, test ke beech

Problem: galti runtime par pata chali, wo bhi tab jab wo specific line chali. Aapka test 30 minute chal kar us line par fail hua.

# --- WITH ABC: contract INSTANTIATION par enforce hota hai ---
from abc import ABC, abstractmethod

class BaseReporter(ABC):
    @abstractmethod
    def report(self, results: list[dict]) -> str:
        """Generate a report string from results."""

    @abstractmethod
    def save(self, content: str, path: str) -> None:
        """Persist the report."""

    def run(self, results: list[dict], path: str) -> None:
        """Concrete method -- ABC mein normal methods bhi ho sakte hain."""
        content = self.report(results)
        self.save(content, path)


class BrokenReporter(BaseReporter):
    def repot(self, results):                        # TYPO
        return ""

# r = BrokenReporter()
# TypeError: Can't instantiate abstract class BrokenReporter with abstract methods report, save
#            ^^^ IMPORT/COLLECTION time par pakda gaya, test chalne se pehle

Line-by-line walkthrough:

  1. from abc import ABC, abstractmethod — ABC ek convenience class hai jo ABCMeta metaclass use karti hai. Aap class X(metaclass=ABCMeta) bhi likh sakte ho, par ABC readable hai.
  2. @abstractmethod — method ko abstract mark karta hai. Ye ek flag set karta hai (__isabstractmethod__ = True) jo ABCMeta padhta hai.
  3. def report(self, results) -> str: — body mein sirf docstring hai. pass ya ... bhi likh sakte ho. Ye body kabhi nahi chalti (jab tak super().report() na karo).
  4. def run(self, ...) — concrete method. ABC mein sirf abstract methods nahi hote — ye "template method" pattern hai: run ka flow fix hai, uske steps subclass define karti hai.
  5. BrokenReporter() par TypeError — ABCMeta.__call__ check karta hai ki cls.__abstractmethods__ khaali hai ya nahi. Naya subclass define karte waqt ABCMeta calculate karta hai ki kaunse abstract methods abhi bhi unimplemented hain.
  6. Error message mein exactly kaunse methods missing hain, wo likha hai — ye debugging time bachaata hai.

docs.title: Poora working example
docs.text:
from abc import ABC, abstractmethod
import json
from pathlib import Path


class BaseReporter(ABC):
    """Har reporter ko ye contract follow karna hai."""

    FILE_EXTENSION: str = ".txt"                     # subclass override karegi

    @abstractmethod
    def format_results(self, results: list[dict]) -> str:
        """Results ko is format ki string mein badlo."""

    @property
    @abstractmethod
    def name(self) -> str:
        """Reporter ka naam -- abstract PROPERTY."""

    def save(self, results: list[dict], output_dir: str) -> Path:
        """Concrete -- saare reporters ke liye same."""
        path = Path(output_dir) / f"report{self.FILE_EXTENSION}"
        path.parent.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
        path.write_text(self.format_results(results), encoding="utf-8")
        return path

    def __repr__(self) -> str:
        return f"{type(self).__name__}(name={self.name!r})"


class JsonReporter(BaseReporter):
    FILE_EXTENSION = ".json"

    @property
    def name(self) -> str:
        return "json"

    def format_results(self, results: list[dict]) -> str:
        return json.dumps(results, indent=2)


class MarkdownReporter(BaseReporter):
    FILE_EXTENSION = ".md"

    @property
    def name(self) -> str:
        return "markdown"

    def format_results(self, results: list[dict]) -> str:
        lines = ["| Test | Status | Duration |", "|---|---|---|"]
        for r in results:
            lines.append(f"| {r['name']} | {r['status']} | {r['duration']:.2f}s |")
        return "\n".join(lines)


REPORTERS: dict[str, type[BaseReporter]] = {
    "json": JsonReporter,
    "markdown": MarkdownReporter,
}


def get_reporter(fmt: str) -> BaseReporter:
    try:
        return REPORTERS[fmt]()
    except KeyError:
        raise ValueError(f"unknown format {fmt!r}; available: {sorted(REPORTERS)}") from None


results = [{"name": "test_login", "status": "passed", "duration": 1.234}]
print(get_reporter("markdown").format_results(results))
print(get_reporter("json").format_results(results))

Line-by-line walkthrough:

  1. FILE_EXTENSION: str = ".txt" — annotated class attribute with default. Subclass override karti hai. Ye "hook" pattern hai — subclass ko poora method override karne ki zarurat nahi.
  2. @property @abstractmethod ke UPAR — order matter karta hai. @abstractmethod sabse andar (function ke sabse paas) hona chahiye, warna property object par flag lagega aur ABCMeta usko detect nahi karega. Yahi classmethod/staticmethod ke saath bhi hai: 
    @classmethod
@abstractmethod
def create(cls): ...            # sahi order
  3. def save(self, ...) — concrete method jo abstract method ko call karta hai. Template method pattern — flow parent mein, details child mein.
  4. path.parent.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True) — directory bana do agar nahi hai. exist_ok=True se race condition (parallel tests) mein FileExistsError nahi aata.
  5. encoding="utf-8" — hamesha explicitly likho (Part 11).
  6. dict[str, type[BaseReporter]] — type[X] matlab "X ki class, X ka instance nahi".
  7. raise ValueError(...) from None — from None original KeyError ko chhupata hai, kyunki wo user ke liye noise hai. from None deliberately use karo, raise ke saath default chaining behaviour se ye alag hai (Part 9).

docs.title: abstractmethod ke saath dusre decorators
docs.text:
from abc import ABC, abstractmethod

class Base(ABC):
    @classmethod
    @abstractmethod
    def from_config(cls, config: dict) -> "Base":
        """Abstract classmethod."""

    @staticmethod
    @abstractmethod
    def validate(data: dict) -> bool:
        """Abstract staticmethod."""

    @property
    @abstractmethod
    def name(self) -> str:
        """Abstract property (read-only)."""

    @name.setter
    @abstractmethod
    def name(self, value: str) -> None:
        """Abstract property setter."""

Rule: @abstractmethod hamesha sabse andar (function ke sabse paas).

docs.title: Virtual subclasses — register
docs.text:
from abc import ABC, abstractmethod

class Clickable(ABC):
    @abstractmethod
    def click(self) -> None: ...


class ThirdPartyWidget:                          # kisi library se aayi class, hum badal nahi sakte
    def click(self) -> None:
        print("third party click")


Clickable.register(ThirdPartyWidget)             # "ye bhi Clickable maana jaaye"

w = ThirdPartyWidget()
print(isinstance(w, Clickable))                  # True
print(issubclass(ThirdPartyWidget, Clickable))   # True
  1. register — ek class ko ABC ka "virtual subclass" banata hai bina inheritance ke.
  2. Caveat: ye sirf isinstance/issubclass ko affect karta hai. Koi method inherit nahi hota, aur koi enforcement nahi — agar ThirdPartyWidget mein click na hota toh bhi register kaam kar jaata aur isinstance True deta.
  3. Ye tab useful hai jab aap third-party classes ko apne type system mein fit karna chahte ho.
  4. Protocol (4.7) aksar better hai — wo structural hai aur static checker verify karta hai.

docs.title: ABC vs Protocol — kaunsa kab
docs.text:
ABC Protocol Typing Nominal (inherit karna padega) Structural (bas shape match ho) Enforcement Runtime (instantiation par) Static (mypy) — runtime_checkable se partial runtime Concrete methods de sakta hai Haan (template method) Haan (3.8+, par unusual) Third-party classes register se Automatic (agar shape match kare) Coupling Zyada (inheritance) Kam Kab use Aapke apne class hierarchy mein shared behaviour + contract Test doubles, third-party integration, loose coupling

QA mein practical: BasePage ABC banao (aapke saare pages usse inherit karte hain, aur usme shared concrete methods hain). Par Clickable Protocol banao (kyunki aap mocks aur third-party locators dono accept karna chahte ho).

docs.title: Standard library ke ABCs
docs.text:
from collections.abc import Sequence, Mapping, Iterable, Iterator, Callable, Sized

print(isinstance([1, 2], Sequence))        # True
print(isinstance({"a": 1}, Mapping))       # True
print(isinstance("abc", Iterable))         # True
print(isinstance(iter([1]), Iterator))     # True
print(isinstance(len, Callable))           # True
print(isinstance({1, 2}, Sized))           # True

# Apna sequence banao -- ABC se mixin methods free milte hain
from collections.abc import Sequence

class TestSuite(Sequence):
    def __init__(self, tests):
        self._tests = list(tests)

    def __getitem__(self, i):              # ABSTRACT -- implement karna hi hai
        return self._tests[i]

    def __len__(self):                     # ABSTRACT
        return len(self._tests)

suite = TestSuite(["test_a", "test_b", "test_c"])
# Ye sab MUFT mein mile, sirf do methods likhne se:
print(len(suite))                          # 3
print(suite[1])                            # test_b
print("test_a" in suite)                   # True   <- __contains__ mixin
print(list(reversed(suite)))               # <- __reversed__ mixin
print(suite.index("test_b"))               # 1      <- index mixin
print(suite.count("test_a"))               # 1      <- count mixin
for t in suite: pass                       # <- __iter__ mixin
  1. collections.abc.Sequence ke abstract methods sirf __getitem__ aur __len__ hain.
  2. Baaki (__contains__, __iter__, __reversed__, index, count) mixin methods hain jo ABC free mein deta hai.
  3. Ye ABC ka sabse practical faayda hai: thoda likho, bahut milo, aur wo sab standard semantics ke saath.
  4. MutableSequence ke liye __setitem__, __delitem__, insert bhi chahiye, aur badle mein append, extend, pop, remove, __iadd__ free milte hain.

docs.title: Gotchas
docs.text:
Gotcha 1 — ABC subclass ho par ek method miss ho.

from abc import ABC, abstractmethod

class Base(ABC):
    @abstractmethod
    def a(self): ...
    @abstractmethod
    def b(self): ...

class Partial(Base):
    def a(self): return 1
    # b missing

# Partial()                       # TypeError: ... abstract method b

class Complete(Partial):          # ek aur level
    def b(self): return 2
print(Complete().a(), Complete().b())    # 1 2   -- ab chalega

Abstract methods inherit hoti hain jab tak implement na ho jaayein.

Gotcha 2 — @abstractmethod bina ABCMeta ke kuch nahi karta.

from abc import abstractmethod

class NotABC:                     # ABC se inherit NAHI kiya
    @abstractmethod
    def f(self): ...

n = NotABC()                      # chal gaya! koi error nahi

@abstractmethod sirf ek flag set karta hai. Enforcement ABCMeta karta hai. Ye common mistake hai.

Gotcha 3 — abstract method ki body chal sakti hai.

from abc import ABC, abstractmethod

class Base(ABC):
    @abstractmethod
    def setup(self):
        print("base setup")           # ye chal SAKTA hai

class Child(Base):
    def setup(self):
        super().setup()               # deliberately parent ka bhi chalao
        print("child setup")

Child().setup()
# base setup
# child setup

Ye actually useful pattern hai: abstract method mein common setup rakho aur subclass ko super() call karne ko bolo.

Interview answer: "An ABC defines a contract and refuses instantiation until every abstract method is implemented. The value is when the failure happens: without it, a typo in a subclass method name surfaces as a NotImplementedError thirty minutes into a run, on whichever line happened to call it. With @abstractmethod, ABCMeta checks __abstractmethods__ at instantiation and raises a TypeError naming exactly which methods are missing — at import or collection time, before any test runs. ABCs also hold concrete methods, which gives you the template method pattern: save in the base defines the flow and calls the abstract format_results that each reporter implements. When stacking decorators, @abstractmethod must be innermost, or the flag lands on the property object and ABCMeta never sees it.

The choice against Protocol comes down to nominal versus structural typing. I use an ABC for my own hierarchy where I want shared concrete behaviour and a hard runtime guarantee — a BasePage, or a reporter interface. I use a Protocol at boundaries: test doubles and third-party objects, where I don't want to force anything to inherit from my types. The standard library's collections.abc also gives a big practical win — inherit from Sequence, implement __getitem__ and __len__, and you get __contains__, __iter__, __reversed__, index and count for free with standard semantics."

Cross-question — "If ABCs check at instantiation, can a bug still slip through?" "Yes, in three ways. First, the check is only on names, not signatures — a subclass can implement report(self) when the base declares report(self, results), and that's a TypeError at call time, not instantiation time. mypy catches it, ABCMeta doesn't. Second, register creates a virtual subclass with no checking at all: isinstance returns True even if the registered class implements nothing. Third, @abstractmethod on a class that doesn't use ABCMeta is a no-op — it just sets a flag nobody reads, and the class instantiates happily. So I treat ABCs as one layer: they catch missing methods early, mypy catches wrong signatures, and a contract test that runs the same suite against every implementation catches behavioural divergence."

docs.title: Kya hai
