docs.text: @dataclass ek decorator hai jo class ke annotations padh kar __init__, __repr__, __eq__, aur (option se) __lt__, __hash__ etc. generate kar deta hai.

docs.title: Kyu hai
docs.text:
# --- WITHOUT dataclass: 30 lines boilerplate ---
class TestResult:
    def __init__(self, name, status, duration, browser="chromium", tags=None):
        self.name = name
        self.status = status
        self.duration = duration
        self.browser = browser
        self.tags = tags if tags is not None else []

    def __repr__(self):
        return (f"TestResult(name={self.name!r}, status={self.status!r}, "
                f"duration={self.duration!r}, browser={self.browser!r}, tags={self.tags!r})")

    def __eq__(self, other):
        if not isinstance(other, TestResult):
            return NotImplemented
        return (self.name, self.status, self.duration, self.browser, self.tags) == \
               (other.name, other.status, other.duration, other.browser, other.tags)
# Naya field add karo -> teen jagah edit karo -> ek bhool jao -> silent bug

# --- WITH dataclass ---
from dataclasses import dataclass, field

@dataclass
class TestResult:
    name: str
    status: str
    duration: float
    browser: str = "chromium"
    tags: list[str] = field(default_factory=list)

r = TestResult("test_login", "passed", 1.23)
print(r)                       # TestResult(name='test_login', status='passed', duration=1.23, browser='chromium', tags=[])
print(r == TestResult("test_login", "passed", 1.23))    # True

Line-by-line walkthrough:

  1. @dataclass — decorator class body ke __annotations__ padhta hai aur code generate karke class par set karta hai. Ye runtime code generation hai (source string banake exec).
  2. name: str — annotation zaruri hai, warna dataclass us field ko dekhega hi nahi: 
    @dataclass
class Bad:
    name = "x"              # koi annotation nahi -> ye field NAHI hai, sirf class attribute
print(Bad())                # Bad()   -- __init__ mein koi parameter nahi
  3. browser: str = "chromium" — default. Defaults ke baad non-default field nahi aa sakti (function parameters ka same rule) — TypeError: non-default argument follows default argument class definition ke waqt.
  4. tags: list[str] = field(default_factory=list) — mutable default ke liye ye zaruri hai. 
    # @dataclass
# class Bad:
#     tags: list = []      # ValueError: mutable default <class 'list'> for field tags
    Dataclass aapko rok deta hai — ye 1.4 wale bug se bachne ka built-in guard hai. default_factory har instance ke liye list() call karta hai.

docs.title: Poora feature set
docs.text:
from dataclasses import dataclass, field, asdict, astuple, replace, fields
from datetime import datetime

@dataclass(
    order=True,          # __lt__, __le__, __gt__, __ge__ generate karo
    frozen=False,        # True -> immutable (attributes set nahi kar sakte)
    slots=False,         # True -> __slots__ use karo (3.10+)
    kw_only=False,       # True -> saare fields keyword-only (3.10+)
    eq=True,             # __eq__ generate karo (default True)
    repr=True,           # __repr__ generate karo (default True)
    init=True,           # __init__ generate karo (default True)
    unsafe_hash=False,   # __hash__ force karo
)
class TestResult:
    # order=True ke liye SORT ORDER field order se aata hai
    duration: float                                   # primary sort key
    name: str                                          # secondary
    status: str = "pending"
    browser: str = "chromium"

    tags: list[str] = field(default_factory=list)

    # Field-level options
    started_at: datetime = field(default_factory=datetime.now, compare=False)
    #                                                          ^^^ __eq__ aur ordering mein ignore

    screenshot_path: str | None = field(default=None, repr=False)
    #                                                 ^^^ __repr__ mein mat dikhao

    _internal_id: int = field(default=0, init=False, repr=False)
    #                                    ^^^ __init__ ka parameter mat banao

    retry_count: int = field(default=0, metadata={"unit": "attempts", "reset_on": "rerun"})
    #                                   ^^^ arbitrary metadata, tools ke liye

    def __post_init__(self):
        """__init__ ke BAAD chalta hai -- validation aur derived fields yahan."""
        if self.duration < 0:
            raise ValueError(f"duration cannot be negative: {self.duration}")
        self.status = self.status.lower()
        self._internal_id = hash((self.name, self.browser)) % 10_000


r1 = TestResult(duration=1.2, name="test_login", status="PASSED")
r2 = TestResult(duration=4.5, name="test_cart", status="failed")

print(r1)                          # started_at dikhega, screenshot_path aur _internal_id nahi
print(r1.status)                   # 'passed'   -- __post_init__ ne lowercase kiya
print(sorted([r2, r1])[0].name)    # test_login -- duration se sort hua
print(asdict(r1))                  # nested dict (recursive!)
print(astuple(r1))                 # tuple
print(replace(r1, status="failed"))# naya object, ek field badla
print([f.name for f in fields(r1)])# saare field names

Line-by-line walkthrough:

  1. order=True — comparison methods generate karta hai jo fields ko field-definition order mein tuple ki tarah compare karte hain. Isliye field ka order sort order banta hai — ye surprise deta hai, isliye documented rakho.
  2. field(..., compare=False) — is field ko __eq__ aur ordering se hata do. started_at ke liye ye zaruri hai: do same tests jo alag time par chale, wo equal hone chahiye.
  3. field(..., repr=False) — long ya sensitive fields ko repr se hataao (passwords, tokens, base64 screenshots).
  4. field(..., init=False) — __init__ ka parameter nahi banega; __post_init__ mein ya default se set hoga.
  5. field(..., metadata={...}) — arbitrary dict jo fields() se padha ja sakta hai. Ye serialisation libraries, validation, ya documentation generators ke liye hai.
  6. def __post_init__(self): — generated __init__ ke aakhir mein call hota hai. Validation aur derived values ke liye ye sahi jagah hai.
  7. asdict(r1) — recursive hai: nested dataclasses, lists, dicts sab convert hote hain. JSON serialisation ke liye seedha. astuple bhi recursive.
  8. replace(r1, status="failed") — naya object banata hai jismein ek field badla ho. Ye namedtuple._replace ka equivalent hai aur immutable-style updates ke liye hai.
  9. fields(r1) — Field objects ka tuple. Introspection ke liye — generic serialisers, CSV headers, validation.

docs.title: frozen=True — immutable dataclass
docs.text:
from dataclasses import dataclass, field, replace

@dataclass(frozen=True)
class TestConfig:
    env: str
    base_url: str
    timeout: int = 30_000
    browsers: tuple[str, ...] = ("chromium",)          # tuple, list nahi!

cfg = TestConfig(env="staging", base_url="https://staging.example.com")
print(cfg)
# cfg.timeout = 60_000            # FrozenInstanceError: cannot assign to field 'timeout'

new_cfg = replace(cfg, timeout=60_000)                 # naya object
print(new_cfg.timeout, cfg.timeout)                    # 60000 30000

# frozen=True se __hash__ bhi milta hai
print(hash(cfg) is not None)                           # True
configs = {cfg, new_cfg}                                # set mein daal sakte ho
print(len(configs))                                     # 2

Line-by-line walkthrough:

  1. @dataclass(frozen=True) — __setattr__ aur __delattr__ override karke FrozenInstanceError raise karta hai. Ye shallow immutability hai (3.2 ka sabak): 
    @dataclass(frozen=True)
class Bad:
    tags: list = field(default_factory=list)
b = Bad()
b.tags.append("x")             # ye chalega! list mutable hai
print(b)                       # Bad(tags=['x'])
# hash(b)                      # TypeError: unhashable type: 'list'
    Isliye frozen dataclass mein tuple aur frozenset use karo, list/set nahi.
  2. browsers: tuple[str, ...] = ("chromium",) — variable-length tuple. Immutable default hai toh field(default_factory=...) ki zarurat nahi.
  3. frozen=True + eq=True (default) → __hash__ automatically generate hota hai. Isliye frozen dataclasses dict keys aur set members ban sakti hain.
  4. replace(cfg, timeout=60_000) — functional update. Ye test config ke liye perfect pattern hai: base config immutable, har test apna variant replace se banaye. Koi test doosre ka config corrupt nahi kar sakta.

docs.title: slots=True — memory optimisation (3.10+)
docs.text:
from dataclasses import dataclass
import sys

@dataclass
class Normal:
    a: int
    b: str

@dataclass(slots=True)
class Slotted:
    a: int
    b: str

n, s = Normal(1, "x"), Slotted(1, "x")
print(sys.getsizeof(n) + sys.getsizeof(n.__dict__))   # ~152 bytes (object + dict)
print(sys.getsizeof(s))                                # ~48 bytes  (no dict)
# print(s.__dict__)                                    # AttributeError -- __dict__ hai hi nahi
# s.c = 1                                              # AttributeError: 'Slotted' object has no attribute 'c'

Detail 5.9 mein.

docs.title: kw_only=True (3.10+)
docs.text:
from dataclasses import dataclass, field, KW_ONLY

@dataclass(kw_only=True)
class TestResult:
    name: str
    status: str
    duration: float = 0.0

# TestResult("test_a", "passed")        # TypeError: takes 1 positional argument but 3 were given
r = TestResult(name="test_a", status="passed")         # sirf keyword se

# Partial kw_only -- KW_ONLY sentinel se
@dataclass
class Mixed:
    name: str                      # positional ho sakta hai
    _: KW_ONLY                     # iske BAAD sab keyword-only
    status: str = "pending"
    duration: float = 0.0

m = Mixed("test_a", status="passed")
  1. kw_only=True — 4.3 ka keyword-only argument, dataclass level par. Fayda: field order badal sakte ho bina callers tode, aur non-default field defaults ke baad bhi aa sakti hai (kyunki ordering constraint sirf positional ke liye hai).
  2. _: KW_ONLY — ek pseudo-field jo boundary marker hai (* ka equivalent). Uska naam kuch bhi ho sakta hai; _ convention hai.

docs.title: Inheritance ke saath
docs.text:
from dataclasses import dataclass, field

@dataclass
class BaseResult:
    name: str
    status: str = "pending"

@dataclass
class UITestResult(BaseResult):
    screenshot: str | None = None                # default HONA hi chahiye
    # browser: str                               # ERROR: non-default after default

    def __post_init__(self):
        if hasattr(super(), "__post_init__"):
            super().__post_init__()              # parent ka post_init bhi chalao
        self.status = self.status.lower()

r = UITestResult(name="test_a", status="PASSED", screenshot="s.png")
print(r)                # UITestResult(name='test_a', status='passed', screenshot='s.png')
  1. Parent ke fields pehle aate hain generated __init__ mein. Toh agar parent mein default hai toh child ke saare fields mein bhi default hona padega.
  2. Ye ek real limitation hai — kw_only=True isko solve karta hai.
  3. super().__post_init__() — parent ke __post_init__ ko manually call karna padta hai; dataclass automatically nahi karta.

docs.title: Dataclass vs NamedTuple vs TypedDict vs plain class vs pydantic
docs.text:
@dataclass NamedTuple TypedDict plain class pydantic.BaseModel Mutable Haan (frozen se nahi) Nahi Haan Haan Haan (config se nahi) Runtime validation Sirf __post_init__ mein manual Nahi Nahi Manual Haan, automatic Tuple-like (unpacking) Nahi Haan Nahi Nahi Nahi Hashable frozen=True se Haan Nahi Default haan Config se Methods/properties Haan Haan Nahi Haan Haan Memory Normal (slots se kam) Sabse kam dict jitna Normal Zyada Inheritance Haan Limited Haan Haan Haan JSON se banana manual manual seedha (wo dict hi hai) manual automatic + validated Kab use default choice immutable record, tuple compat JSON response ka shape complex behaviour API boundary

QA mein decision:

  • Test data objects, config, results → @dataclass
  • API response ka type describe karna → TypedDict
  • API response ko validate karna → pydantic
  • Coordinates, small immutable pairs → NamedTuple

docs.title: QA use case — poora test data factory
docs.text:
from dataclasses import dataclass, field, replace, asdict
import random
import string
import json


@dataclass(frozen=True, kw_only=True)
class Address:
    line1: str
    city: str
    pincode: str
    country: str = "IN"


@dataclass(frozen=True, kw_only=True)
class User:
    email: str
    password: str
    first_name: str = "Test"
    last_name: str = "User"
    role: str = "customer"
    verified: bool = True
    address: Address | None = None
    tags: tuple[str, ...] = ()

    @staticmethod
    def _rand(n: int = 8) -> str:
        return "".join(random.choices(string.ascii_lowercase, k=n))

    @classmethod
    def random(cls, **overrides) -> "User":
        defaults = {
            "email": f"{cls._rand()}@test.example.com",
            "password": f"Pw!{cls._rand(10)}",
        }
        return cls(**{**defaults, **overrides})

    @classmethod
    def admin(cls, **overrides) -> "User":
        return cls.random(**{"role": "admin", **overrides})

    @classmethod
    def with_address(cls, **overrides) -> "User":
        addr = Address(line1="1 Test Street", city="Bengaluru", pincode="560001")
        return cls.random(**{"address": addr, **overrides})

    def to_api_payload(self) -> dict:
        """API ke liye JSON-ready dict."""
        payload = asdict(self)                             # recursive
        payload["tags"] = list(payload["tags"])            # tuple -> list for JSON
        return payload


u = User.with_address(role="admin", tags=("beta", "internal"))
print(u.email, u.role, u.address.city)
print(json.dumps(u.to_api_payload(), indent=2)[:200])

# Ek field badal kar variant banao -- original safe
u2 = replace(u, verified=False)
print(u.verified, u2.verified)                             # True False

Line-by-line walkthrough:

  1. @dataclass(frozen=True, kw_only=True) — frozen se koi test doosre ka data corrupt nahi kar sakta; kw_only se call sites self-documenting hain aur field order refactor-safe hai.
  2. tags: tuple[str, ...] = () — tuple kyunki frozen dataclass hashable rahni chahiye.
  3. cls(**{**defaults, **overrides}) — overrides jeette hain.
  4. cls.random(**{"role": "admin", **overrides}) — agar caller ne role diya toh wo jeetega (dict mein baad wala). Bina is trick ke cls.random(role="admin", **overrides) mein duplicate role par TypeError aata.
  5. asdict(self) — nested Address bhi dict ban gaya, recursively.
  6. list(payload["tags"]) — JSON tuple nahi jaanta; json.dumps tuple ko list bana deta hai, par explicit rehna behtar hai.
  7. replace(u, verified=False) — variant banaya. Original u bilkul safe hai — frozen hai.

docs.title: Gotchas
docs.text:
Gotcha 1 — annotation ke bina field nahi banta.

from dataclasses import dataclass

@dataclass
class Config:
    timeout = 30                 # NO annotation -> class attribute, field nahi
    retries: int = 3             # field

c = Config()
print(c.timeout, c.retries)      # 30 3
print(Config(retries=5))         # Config(retries=5)  -- timeout repr mein nahi

Gotcha 2 — mutable default.

# @dataclass
# class Bad:
#     tags: list = []            # ValueError at class definition

Dataclass detect karta hai (list/dict/set ke liye) — par custom mutable class detect nahi hota:

from dataclasses import dataclass

class Counter:
    def __init__(self): self.n = 0

@dataclass
class Sneaky:
    counter: Counter = Counter()      # koi error nahi -- par SHARED hai!

a, b = Sneaky(), Sneaky()
a.counter.n = 5
print(b.counter.n)                     # 5   <- shared!

Fix: field(default_factory=Counter).

Gotcha 3 — frozen=True __post_init__ mein assignment nahi karne deta.

from dataclasses import dataclass, field

@dataclass(frozen=True)
class Result:
    name: str
    normalised: str = field(init=False, default="")

    def __post_init__(self):
        # self.normalised = self.name.lower()      # FrozenInstanceError
        object.__setattr__(self, "normalised", self.name.lower())    # escape hatch

r = Result("TEST_A")
print(r.normalised)                    # test_a

object.__setattr__ frozen check bypass karta hai. Ye deliberately ugly hai — taaki aap soch samajh kar karo.

Gotcha 4 — eq=True ke saath __hash__ gayab ho jaata hai.

from dataclasses import dataclass

@dataclass                       # eq=True default, frozen=False
class R:
    a: int

# {R(1)}                         # TypeError: unhashable type: 'R'

Kyunki __eq__ define hone se Python __hash__ None set kar deta hai (5.6). Fix: frozen=True (recommended) ya unsafe_hash=True (naam se hi pata chalta hai ki khatarnak hai — mutable object ka hash badal sakta hai).

Interview answer: "@dataclass reads the class's annotations and generates __init__, __repr__, and __eq__ — and optionally ordering and hashing. That removes the boilerplate where adding a field means editing three methods and forgetting one. The options I actually use: frozen=True for test data and config, because immutability plus dataclasses.replace means one test can't corrupt another's data and the object is hashable; kw_only=True so field order isn't part of the API and I'm not forced to give every field a default just because the parent did; and field(default_factory=list) for mutable defaults — dataclasses actually refuse a bare tags: list = [], which is a nice built-in guard against the shared-mutable-default bug. __post_init__ is where validation and derived fields go. On a frozen class you have to use object.__setattr__ there, which is deliberately awkward.

Compared to alternatives: NamedTuple when I want tuple compatibility and unpacking, TypedDict when the thing genuinely is a dict — a JSON response — and I only want the checker to know its shape, and pydantic when data crosses a real boundary and I need runtime validation, because a dataclass annotation is not enforced at all. For everything internal, a dataclass is my default."

docs.title: Kya hai
docs.text:
Normally har Python object ke paas ek __dict__ hota hai jismein uske attributes rehte hain. __slots__ us dict ko hata kar attributes ko fixed array slots mein rakh deta hai.

BINA __slots__:
   instance --> [ header | pointer to __dict__ ] --> {'name': ..., 'status': ...}
                                                     ^ ek poora dict, ~104+ bytes

__slots__ ke SAATH:
   instance --> [ header | slot0 | slot1 ]
                          ^ seedha pointers, koi dict nahi

docs.title: Kyu hai
docs.text:
import sys

class Normal:
    def __init__(self, name, status, duration):
        self.name = name
        self.status = status
        self.duration = duration

class Slotted:
    __slots__ = ("name", "status", "duration")

    def __init__(self, name, status, duration):
        self.name = name
        self.status = status
        self.duration = duration

n = Normal("test_a", "passed", 1.2)
s = Slotted("test_a", "passed", 1.2)

print(sys.getsizeof(n), sys.getsizeof(n.__dict__))    # 48 104   -> total ~152
print(sys.getsizeof(s))                                # 64      -> total 64
# print(sys.getsizeof(s.__dict__))                     # AttributeError -- __dict__ nahi hai

Line-by-line walkthrough:

  1. __slots__ = ("name", "status", "duration") — ye ek class attribute hai jo attribute names ka sequence rakhta hai. Class creation ke waqt Python har naam ke liye ek descriptor banata hai (5.4) aur __dict__ allocate nahi karta.
  2. sys.getsizeof(n.__dict__) — dict ka apna overhead. 3 items ke liye ~104 bytes. Ye fixed-ish overhead hai — 3 attributes hon ya 5, dict ki minimum size hoti hai.
  3. Total: ~152 vs 64 bytes → ~58% bachat.
  4. Kab matter karta hai: 1 lakh objects par 152 MB vs 64 MB. QA mein ye tab dikhta hai jab aap bade log files parse karke har line ka object banate ho, ya 50,000 test results memory mein rakhte ho.

docs.title: Speed ka faayda bhi hai
docs.text:
import timeit

setup = """
class Normal:
    def __init__(self): self.x = 1

class Slotted:
    __slots__ = ('x',)
    def __init__(self): self.x = 1

n, s = Normal(), Slotted()
"""

print(timeit.timeit("n.x", setup=setup, number=10_000_000))        # ~0.30s
print(timeit.timeit("s.x", setup=setup, number=10_000_000))        # ~0.25s
print(timeit.timeit("n.x = 2", setup=setup, number=10_000_000))    # ~0.35s
print(timeit.timeit("s.x = 2", setup=setup, number=10_000_000))    # ~0.28s
  1. Slots access array index hai (descriptor ke through), dict lookup nahi. ~15-20% tez.
  2. Ye chhota faayda hai — __slots__ ka main reason memory hai, speed nahi. Agar aap sirf speed ke liye add kar rahe ho toh profile pehle karo.

docs.title: Restrictions
docs.text:
class Slotted:
    __slots__ = ("name",)

s = Slotted()
s.name = "test_a"                 # theek
# s.status = "passed"             # AttributeError: 'Slotted' object has no attribute 'status'
# s.__dict__                      # AttributeError

# 1. Naye attributes add nahi kar sakte  -- ye actually FAYDA hai (typo pakadta hai)
class Config:
    __slots__ = ("timeout", "retries")
    def __init__(self, timeout, retries):
        self.timeout = timeout
        self.retries = retries

c = Config(30, 3)
# c.timout = 60                   # AttributeError -- TYPO turant pakda gaya!
# Bina slots ke ye chupchaap ek naya attribute bana deta aur bug chhup jaata

Ye typo-catching __slots__ ka underrated faayda hai. Config aur page objects mein ye real bugs pakadta hai.

# 2. Class attribute aur slot ka naam same nahi ho sakta
# class Bad:
#     __slots__ = ("x",)
#     x = 1                       # ValueError: 'x' in __slots__ conflicts with class variable

# 3. Multiple inheritance mein dono parents ke slots ho toh error
class A:
    __slots__ = ("a",)
class B:
    __slots__ = ("b",)
# class C(A, B): pass             # TypeError: multiple bases have instance lay-out conflict

# 4. Ek parent mein slots ho toh chalega
class D(A):
    __slots__ = ("d",)            # A ke slots inherit + apne
d = D()
d.a, d.d = 1, 2
# d.x = 3                         # AttributeError

# 5. Parent mein slots na ho toh child ka __slots__ bekaar hai
class NoSlots: pass
class Child(NoSlots):
    __slots__ = ("x",)
c = Child()
c.anything = 1                    # chal gaya! kyunki NoSlots ne __dict__ diya
print(c.__dict__)                 # {'anything': 1}

Ye point 5 sabse common galti hai: __slots__ tabhi kaam karta hai jab poori inheritance chain mein slots hon.

# 6. weakref chahiye toh explicitly add karo
import weakref
class NoWeakref:
    __slots__ = ("x",)
n = NoWeakref()
# weakref.ref(n)                  # TypeError: cannot create weak reference

class WithWeakref:
    __slots__ = ("x", "__weakref__")
w = WithWeakref()
print(weakref.ref(w))             # <weakref at ...>

# 7. Dict bhi chahiye (dynamic attributes) toh
class Hybrid:
    __slots__ = ("x", "__dict__")
h = Hybrid()
h.x = 1                           # slot
h.anything = 2                    # dict
print(h.__dict__)                 # {'anything': 2}   -- 'x' isme nahi hai

Point 7 ka koi practical faayda nahi hai (aapne dict wapas add kar diya) — sirf tab jab kuch attributes hot path mein hon.

docs.title: Dataclass ke saath (3.10+)
docs.text:
from dataclasses import dataclass

@dataclass(slots=True)
class TestResult:
    name: str
    status: str
    duration: float

r = TestResult("test_a", "passed", 1.2)
print(r)                          # normal dataclass repr
# r.other = 1                     # AttributeError
  1. slots=True ek naya class object banata hai (kyunki __slots__ class creation ke waqt process hota hai, baad mein add nahi ho sakta). Ye tab matter karta hai jab aapne class ka reference kahin pehle pakad liya ho ya decorators stack kiye hon.
  2. cached_property slots=True ke saath kaam nahi karta — usko __dict__ chahiye.

docs.title: Kab use karein / kab nahi
docs.text: Use __slots__ Don't Lakhs instances (log lines, test results, graph nodes) Do-chaar instances Memory profiling ne bataya ki ye hotspot hai Speculative optimisation Typo-catching chahiye (config, page objects) Class ko dynamically extend karna ho Class ka shape fix hai Mixins ya multiple inheritance heavy design cached_property use kar rahe ho Library ki public class jise log subclass karenge

docs.title: QA-specific example
docs.text:
class LogEntry:
    """5 lakh log lines parse karni hain -- memory matters."""
    __slots__ = ("timestamp", "level", "logger", "message", "trace_id")

    def __init__(self, timestamp, level, logger, message, trace_id=None):
        self.timestamp = timestamp
        self.level = level
        self.logger = logger
        self.message = message
        self.trace_id = trace_id

    def __repr__(self):
        return f"LogEntry({self.timestamp} {self.level} {self.message[:30]!r})"

    @property
    def is_error(self) -> bool:
        return self.level in ("ERROR", "CRITICAL")


# Memory comparison for 500k entries:
# Without slots: 500_000 * ~250 bytes = ~125 MB
# With slots:    500_000 * ~90 bytes  = ~45 MB
  1. @property __slots__ ke saath chalta hai — property class attribute hai, instance attribute nahi.
  2. __repr__ mein message[:30] — bade messages ko truncate kiya, warna debug output unusable ho jaata.
  3. Sabse important: yahan pehle profile karo. Agar aap log ko stream karke process kar rahe ho (Part 6, generators) toh saare entries memory mein hi nahi aate aur __slots__ ki zarurat hi nahi. Streaming > slots.

docs.title: Gotchas
docs.text:
Gotcha 1 — inheritance chain mein ek link toota toh sab bekaar. (point 5 upar)

Gotcha 2 — __slots__ string diya toh har character alag slot ban jaata hai.

class Oops:
    __slots__ = "name"            # string, tuple nahi -- ye actually kaam karta hai
o = Oops()
o.name = "x"                      # theek

class Worse:
    __slots__ = "name, status"    # ek slot jiska naam 'name, status' hai -- unusable
# w = Worse(); w.name = 1         # AttributeError

Hamesha tuple likho: __slots__ = ("name",) — trailing comma zaruri hai single element ke liye (3.2)!

Gotcha 3 — pickling.

import pickle

class Slotted:
    __slots__ = ("x",)
    def __init__(self, x): self.x = x

s = Slotted(1)
data = pickle.dumps(s)            # protocol 2+ mein chalta hai (default 5)
print(pickle.loads(data).x)       # 1

Modern pickle protocols slots handle karte hain. Purane protocol 0/1 mein nahi karte the.

Interview answer: "By default every instance carries a __dict__ to hold its attributes, which costs around a hundred bytes of overhead per object. __slots__ replaces that with a fixed array of descriptors, so instances get about 50 to 60 percent smaller and attribute access is slightly faster because it's an array index instead of a dict lookup. It only matters at scale — I'd use it for a class I create hundreds of thousands of, like a parsed log line, and only after profiling showed it mattered. There's a second benefit people undersell: it turns a typo into an immediate AttributeError instead of silently creating a new attribute, which is genuinely useful for config and page-object classes.

The constraints are what catch people. __slots__ only helps if every class in the MRO defines it — one parent without it reintroduces __dict__ and the whole thing is a no-op. Multiple inheritance from two slotted classes is a layout conflict and raises TypeError. weakref needs __weakref__ added explicitly. And cached_property doesn't work at all because it needs a __dict__ to write into. In test code, though, my first move for memory pressure isn't slots — it's streaming with generators, so the objects never all exist at once."

docs.title: Kya hai
docs.text:
Class bhi ek object hai. Aur har object ki ek class hoti hai. Toh class ki class kya hai? Uska naam metaclass hai, aur default type hai.

class Page:
    pass

p = Page()
print(type(p))          # <class '__main__.Page'>     -- p ki class Page hai
print(type(Page))       # <class 'type'>              -- Page ki class 'type' hai
print(type(type))       # <class 'type'>              -- type khud ka type type hai

Analogy: class ek cookie cutter hai jo cookies (instances) banata hai. Metaclass ek machine hai jo cookie cutters banati hai.

docs.title: Class actually kaise banti hai
docs.text:
# Ye do bilkul equivalent hain:

class Page:
    url = "/home"
    def open(self): return f"opening {self.url}"

# ...aur ye:
def open_fn(self):
    return f"opening {self.url}"

Page2 = type(
    "Page2",                                    # 1. class ka naam
    (),                                         # 2. base classes ka tuple
    {"url": "/home", "open": open_fn},          # 3. class body ka namespace (dict)
)

print(Page().open())        # opening /home
print(Page2().open())       # opening /home
print(type(Page) is type(Page2) is type)        # True

class statement chalne par kya hota hai:

  1. Class body ek naye namespace dict mein execute hoti hai.
  2. Metaclass determine hota hai (metaclass= keyword se, warna base classes ke type se, warna type).
  3. metaclass(name, bases, namespace, **kwargs) call hota hai.
  4. type.__call__ → type.__new__ (class object banata hai) → type.__init__.
  5. Result naam se bind hota hai.

docs.title: Custom metaclass
docs.text:
class ValidatedPageMeta(type):
    """Har page class mein URL_PATH aur ek locator hona chahiye."""

    def __new__(mcls, name, bases, namespace, **kwargs):
        # 1. Pehle normal class banao
        cls = super().__new__(mcls, name, bases, namespace, **kwargs)

        # 2. Base class ko exempt karo
        if not bases:                                   # koi base nahi = ye base class hai
            return cls

        # 3. Validation
        if "URL_PATH" not in namespace:
            raise TypeError(f"{name} must define URL_PATH")

        locators = [k for k in namespace if k.isupper() and k != "URL_PATH"]
        if not locators:
            raise TypeError(f"{name} must define at least one locator constant")

        # 4. Auto-register
        PAGE_REGISTRY[namespace["URL_PATH"]] = cls
        return cls


PAGE_REGISTRY: dict[str, type] = {}


class BasePage(metaclass=ValidatedPageMeta):
    """Base -- exempt from validation."""


class LoginPage(BasePage):
    URL_PATH = "/login"
    USERNAME = "#username"
    PASSWORD = "#password"


# class BrokenPage(BasePage):
#     USERNAME = "#u"
# TypeError: BrokenPage must define URL_PATH

print(PAGE_REGISTRY)          # {'/login': <class 'LoginPage'>}

Line-by-line walkthrough:

  1. class ValidatedPageMeta(type): — metaclass type se inherit karti hai.
  2. def __new__(mcls, name, bases, namespace, **kwargs): — mcls metaclass hai (jaise cls normal class mein). Chaar arguments class creation ke hain.
  3. super().__new__(mcls, name, bases, namespace, **kwargs) — actual class object banaya.
  4. if not bases: return cls — base class ko skip kiya. Ye pattern har metaclass mein chahiye, warna aapki apni base class hi validation fail kar deti.
  5. namespace — class body ka dict. Yahan aap dekh sakte ho ki class mein kya-kya define hua. Note: ye sirf is class mein define hue naam hain, inherited nahi.
  6. PAGE_REGISTRY[...] = cls — auto-registration. Ye metaclass ka classic use hai (Django ORM, SQLAlchemy, pytest plugins isi tarah kaam karte hain).

docs.title: Aap ise kabhi likhoge nahi — kyun
docs.text:
Python 3.6 se do simpler hooks aa gaye hain jo 99% metaclass use cases cover karte hain:

1. __init_subclass__ — subclass creation par hook

class BasePage:
    registry: dict[str, type] = {}

    def __init_subclass__(cls, **kwargs):
        """Har subclass define hone par ye chalta hai."""
        super().__init_subclass__(**kwargs)

        if not hasattr(cls, "URL_PATH"):
            raise TypeError(f"{cls.__name__} must define URL_PATH")

        BasePage.registry[cls.URL_PATH] = cls


class LoginPage(BasePage):
    URL_PATH = "/login"

class CartPage(BasePage):
    URL_PATH = "/cart"

# class Broken(BasePage): pass       # TypeError: Broken must define URL_PATH

print(BasePage.registry)             # {'/login': <class 'LoginPage'>, '/cart': <class 'CartPage'>}
  1. __init_subclass__ implicitly classmethod hai — @classmethod likhne ki zarurat nahi (Python khud lagata hai).
  2. cls subclass hai, base nahi. Base class par ye chalta hi nahi.
  3. super().__init_subclass__(**kwargs) — cooperative chain, bilkul super().__init__() ki tarah.
  4. Ye metaclass se kitna simple hai — koi type inheritance nahi, koi mcls/bases/ namespace nahi. Aur ye normal class ke andar hai, alag file mein nahi.
  5. Keyword arguments bhi accept karta hai: 
    class Base:
    def __init_subclass__(cls, *, plugin_name=None, **kwargs):
        super().__init_subclass__(**kwargs)
        cls.plugin_name = plugin_name

class MyPlugin(Base, plugin_name="html-reporter"):
    pass
print(MyPlugin.plugin_name)       # html-reporter

2. __set_name__ — descriptor ko apna naam batana (5.4 mein dekha)

3. Class decorator — class ko modify karna

def auto_repr(cls):
    """Class par ek __repr__ laga do jo saare instance attributes dikhaye."""
    def __repr__(self):
        attrs = ", ".join(f"{k}={v!r}" for k, v in vars(self).items())
        return f"{type(self).__name__}({attrs})"
    cls.__repr__ = __repr__
    return cls


@auto_repr
class TestResult:
    def __init__(self, name, status):
        self.name = name
        self.status = status

print(TestResult("test_a", "passed"))     # TestResult(name='test_a', status='passed')
  1. Class decorator ek function hai jo class leta hai aur class deta hai.
  2. vars(self) — self.__dict__.
  3. Ye @dataclass ka mechanism hai — dataclass ek class decorator hai, metaclass nahi.

docs.title: Metaclass kab genuinely chahiye
docs.text:
Chahiye Kyun __init_subclass__ kaafi nahi Class banne se pehle namespace modify karna __init_subclass__ class banne ke baad chalta hai __prepare__ se custom namespace (ordered, ya duplicate-detecting) Sirf metaclass ye de sakta hai Class-level __call__ override (instantiation control) Metaclass ka __call__ hi ye kar sakta hai isinstance/issubclass ko override (ABCMeta) __instancecheck__ metaclass par hai Base class khud modify karni ho __init_subclass__ base par nahi chalta

Real examples jinme metaclass use hota hai:

  • abc.ABCMeta — abstract method enforcement aur register.
  • Django ORM ModelBase — field declarations ko database columns mein badalta hai.
  • SQLAlchemy declarative base.
  • enum.EnumMeta — members ko unique banata hai aur Color.RED lookup deta hai.
  • typing.Protocol ka _ProtocolMeta.

docs.title: Gotchas
docs.text:
Gotcha 1 — metaclass conflict.

from abc import ABCMeta

class MyMeta(type): pass

# class Bad(metaclass=MyMeta):
#     pass
# class Worse(Bad, SomeABC): ...
# TypeError: metaclass conflict: the metaclass of a derived class must be a
#            (non-strict) subclass of the metaclasses of all its bases

Fix: class MyMeta(ABCMeta): pass — dono ko combine karo. Ye real problem hai jab aap ABC aur custom metaclass dono chahte ho.

Gotcha 2 — metaclass inherit hoti hai.

class Meta(type):
    def __new__(mcls, name, bases, ns):
        print(f"creating {name}")
        return super().__new__(mcls, name, bases, ns)

class A(metaclass=Meta): pass       # creating A
class B(A): pass                    # creating B   <- metaclass inherit hui
class C(B): pass                    # creating C

Gotcha 3 — "Metaclasses are deeper magic than 99% of users should ever worry about. If you wonder whether you need them, you don't." — Tim Peters. Ye quote interview mein bolna theek hai.

Interview answer: "A metaclass is the class of a class. Everything in Python is an object, including classes, so classes have a type too — and by default that's type. When a class statement runs, the body is executed in a fresh namespace dict and then the metaclass is called with the name, bases, and that namespace, which is exactly what type('Page', (), {...}) does manually. A custom metaclass lets you hook into class creation: validate that subclasses declare required attributes, auto-register them in a plugin registry, or rewrite the namespace before the class exists. That's how abc.ABCMeta enforces abstract methods, how Django turns field declarations into columns, and how Enum makes members unique.

In practice I've never needed to write one, and I'd push back in review if someone did. Since 3.6, __init_subclass__ covers almost every case — it's a plain classmethod on the base that runs whenever a subclass is created, so registration and validation are a few lines inside a normal class instead of a separate metaclass hierarchy. __set_name__ covers descriptors learning their own attribute name, and a class decorator covers modifying a class after creation — that's what @dataclass actually is. The genuine remaining cases are controlling instantiation through the metaclass's __call__, overriding isinstance via __instancecheck__, or using __prepare__ to supply a custom namespace. The other practical reason to avoid them is metaclass conflicts: mixing a custom metaclass with an ABC is a TypeError until you make yours a subclass of ABCMeta."

docs.title: Kya hai
docs.text:
• Inheritance — "is-a". LoginPage is a BasePage.
  • Composition — "has-a". LoginPage has a ApiClient.

docs.title: Kyu — inheritance ke chaar concrete problems
docs.text:
Problem 1 — Fragile base class

class BasePage:
    def click(self, selector):
        self.page.click(selector)

    def click_all(self, selectors):
        for s in selectors:
            self.click(selector=s)              # apne hi click ko call kiya

class LoggingPage(BasePage):
    def click(self, selector):
        print(f"clicking {selector}")
        super().click(selector)

# Ab BasePage ke author ne "optimise" kiya:
class BasePageV2:
    def click(self, selector):
        self.page.click(selector)

    def click_all(self, selectors):
        self.page.click_many(selectors)         # ab click() call NAHI karta -- tez hai

# LoggingPage ka logging ab click_all par KAAM NAHI KARTA
# Aur ye kahin document nahi tha, koi test nahi toota

Base class ka internal refactor subclass ka behaviour tod deta hai. Ye fragile base class problem hai, aur ye inheritance ki fundamental limitation hai.

Problem 2 — Interface leak

class BasePage:
    # 30 methods
    def click(self): ...
    def fill(self): ...
    def upload_file(self): ...
    def download_file(self): ...
    def handle_dialog(self): ...
    # ...

class ApiOnlyPage(BasePage):
    """Ye page sirf API se verify hota hai, koi UI interaction nahi."""
    pass

p = ApiOnlyPage()
p.upload_file()          # ye method exist karta hai par yahan meaningless hai

Subclass ko 25 methods mil gaye jo uske liye meaningless hain — ye Interface Segregation Principle todta hai aur autocomplete ko noise se bhar deta hai.

Problem 3 — Combinatorial explosion

Aapko chahiye: retry, logging, screenshots, timing -- kisi bhi combination mein

Inheritance se:
    BasePage
    RetryPage
    LoggingPage
    RetryLoggingPage
    ScreenshotPage
    RetryScreenshotPage
    LoggingScreenshotPage
    RetryLoggingScreenshotPage
    ... 2^4 = 16 classes

Composition se: 4 objects, jo bhi chahiye wo inject karo.

Problem 4 — Testing

# Inheritance: behaviour class mein baked hai
class LoginPage(BasePage):
    def login(self, user, pwd):
        self.api_reset(user)                    # BasePage ka method
        self.page.fill("#u", user)

# Test mein 'api_reset' ko fake karne ke liye subclass banani padegi ya patch karna padega

# Composition: behaviour inject hui hai
class LoginPage:
    def __init__(self, page, api_client):
        self.page = page
        self.api = api_client                   # INJECTED

    def login(self, user, pwd):
        self.api.reset_user(user)
        self.page.fill("#u", user)

# Test mein:
# LoginPage(page=fake_page, api_client=FakeApiClient())

docs.title: Poora before/after — QA framework
docs.text:
# ============ INHERITANCE-HEAVY (problematic) ============
class BasePage:
    def __init__(self, page):
        self.page = page

class RetryablePage(BasePage):
    MAX_RETRIES = 3
    def click_with_retry(self, sel):
        for i in range(self.MAX_RETRIES):
            try:
                return self.page.click(sel)
            except Exception:
                if i == self.MAX_RETRIES - 1:
                    raise

class LoggingRetryablePage(RetryablePage):
    def click_with_retry(self, sel):
        print(f"clicking {sel}")
        return super().click_with_retry(sel)

class LoginPage(LoggingRetryablePage):
    def login(self, u, p): ...
# Deep chain. LoginPage ka behaviour samajhne ke liye 4 classes padhni padengi.

# ============ COMPOSITION (better) ============
from dataclasses import dataclass
from typing import Protocol
import time


class Logger(Protocol):
    def info(self, msg: str) -> None: ...


class NullLogger:
    def info(self, msg: str) -> None:
        pass


class PrintLogger:
    def info(self, msg: str) -> None:
        print(f"[INFO] {msg}")


@dataclass
class RetryPolicy:
    max_attempts: int = 3
    base_delay: float = 0.5

    def run(self, fn, description: str, logger: Logger):
        last_error = None
        for attempt in range(1, self.max_attempts + 1):
            try:
                return fn()
            except Exception as exc:
                last_error = exc
                logger.info(f"{description} attempt {attempt} failed: {exc}")
                if attempt < self.max_attempts:
                    time.sleep(self.base_delay * attempt)
        raise RuntimeError(f"{description} failed after {self.max_attempts} attempts") from last_error


class Interactor:
    """Page interactions -- retry aur logging ke saath, par inheritance ke bina."""

    def __init__(self, page, retry: RetryPolicy | None = None, logger: Logger | None = None):
        self.page = page
        self.retry = retry or RetryPolicy()
        self.logger = logger or NullLogger()

    def click(self, selector: str):
        self.logger.info(f"click {selector}")
        return self.retry.run(lambda: self.page.click(selector), f"click({selector})", self.logger)

    def fill(self, selector: str, value: str):
        self.logger.info(f"fill {selector}")
        return self.retry.run(lambda: self.page.fill(selector, value), f"fill({selector})", self.logger)


class LoginPage:
    URL_PATH = "/login"
    USERNAME = "#username"
    PASSWORD = "#password"
    SUBMIT = "#submit"

    def __init__(self, interactor: Interactor):
        self.ix = interactor                      # HAS-A interactor

    def login(self, username: str, password: str):
        self.ix.fill(self.USERNAME, username)
        self.ix.fill(self.PASSWORD, password)
        self.ix.click(self.SUBMIT)
        return self

Line-by-line walkthrough:

  1. class Logger(Protocol): — structural type (4.7). Koi bhi cheez jisme info ho, wo Logger hai. Test mein NullLogger ya ek recording fake pass kar sakte ho.
  2. class NullLogger: — Null Object pattern. if self.logger: checks ki zarurat nahi rehti — hamesha ek object hai, bas wo kuch nahi karta.
  3. @dataclass class RetryPolicy: — policy ek object hai, ek base class nahi. Ye test mein RetryPolicy(max_attempts=1, base_delay=0) se replace ho sakti hai — test 0 second mein chalega.
  4. def run(self, fn, description, logger): — policy ko koi bhi callable diya ja sakta hai. Ye page se completely decoupled hai — aap isko API calls par bhi use kar sakte ho.
  5. self.retry = retry or RetryPolicy() — sensible default, par override possible. or yahan safe hai kyunki RetryPolicy object kabhi falsy nahi hota (koi __bool__ ya __len__ nahi hai).
  6. class LoginPage: — BasePage se inherit nahi karti. Uske paas ek Interactor hai.
  7. self.ix — short naam kyunki wo har method mein use hota hai.
  8. Test mein: 
    page = LoginPage(Interactor(
    page=fake_playwright_page,
    retry=RetryPolicy(max_attempts=1, base_delay=0),      # tez test
    logger=PrintLogger(),                                  # debug ke liye
))
    Har cheez inject ki ja sakti hai. Koi monkeypatching nahi, koi subclass nahi.

docs.title: Decision framework
docs.text:
Kya subclass HAR JAGAH parent ki tarah use ho sakta hai? (Liskov Substitution)
  |
  NAHI -> COMPOSITION
  |
  HAAN
  |
Kya relationship "is-a" hai, "has-a"/"uses-a" nahi?
  |
  NAHI -> COMPOSITION
  |
  HAAN
  |
Kya hierarchy 2-3 levels se zyada gehri ho rahi hai?
  |
  HAAN -> COMPOSITION
  |
  NAHI
  |
Kya behaviour RUNTIME par badalni hai?
  |
  HAAN -> COMPOSITION (strategy pattern)
  |
  NAHI
  |
Kya framework contract chahta hai? (unittest.TestCase, ABC, Django Model)
  |
  HAAN -> INHERITANCE (koi choice nahi)
  |
  NAHI -> INHERITANCE theek hai, par COMPOSITION bhi consider karo

docs.title: QA framework mein practical mix
docs.text:
Inheritance yahan sahi hai:

  • BasePage → LoginPage, CartPage — genuine is-a, shallow (ek level), aur shared concrete behaviour hai (open(), wait_for_load()).
  • unittest.TestCase subclassing — framework requirement.
  • Custom exception hierarchy — TestError → ElementNotFoundError.
  • ABC se interface define karna.

Composition yahan sahi hai:

  • API client, DB client, config, logger, retry policy — sab inject karo.
  • Page components (nav bar, footer, modal) — page has them.
  • Test data factories.
  • Reporters aur formatters.

Ek line ka rule: "Inheritance for what something IS, composition for what something HAS or USES."

Interview answer: "Inheritance expresses is-a and gives you code reuse for free, but it couples the subclass to the base class's internals — the fragile base class problem, where refactoring the parent silently changes the child's behaviour because the parent stopped calling the method the child overrode. It also forces the subclass to inherit the entire interface, and it composes badly: four orthogonal behaviours give you sixteen classes.

Composition avoids all of that by making behaviour an injected object. In my page-object framework I keep one shallow inheritance level — a BasePage with genuinely shared concrete methods — and everything else is composed: the retry policy, the logger, the API client, and the page components are all constructor parameters. The payoff is directly in testing: to make a test fast I pass RetryPolicy(max_attempts=1, base_delay=0) rather than monkeypatching time.sleep, and to fake an API I pass a different client rather than patching an import path. I still use inheritance where the framework demands it or where the relationship really is is-a and the hierarchy stays two or three levels deep. The heuristic I apply is Liskov: if I can't use the subclass everywhere the base is expected without surprises, it isn't inheritance."

Cross-question — "Mixins are inheritance. Doesn't your argument rule them out too?" "Mixins are the case where inheritance composes well, provided you follow two rules: each mixin does exactly one thing, and every mixin cooperates via super() rather than calling a specific parent. Then the MRO gives you a pipeline you assemble by declaration order, which is genuinely composition-like. What breaks them is state — a mixin that adds instance attributes has to participate in __init__ correctly, forwarding *args, **kwargs, and it becomes order-dependent in ways that aren't visible from any one file. So my rule is: mixins for stateless cross-cutting behaviour like timing, logging, or retry around a single named method; injected objects the moment state or configuration is involved. And in either case I'd keep the total number small, because reading a class's behaviour shouldn't require mentally executing an MRO."

docs.title: Part 6 — Iterators, Generators, and Lazy Evaluation
6.1 The iterator protocol — haath se banao
Kya hai
docs.text:
Do alag cheezein hain, aur inhe mila dena sabse badi confusion hai:

  • Iterable — jispar for chal sakta hai. __iter__ deta hai jo ek naya iterator lautata hai. Baar-baar iterate ho sakta hai.
  • Iterator — wo cheez jo actually values deti hai. __next__ deta hai. Ek baar chalta hai, phir khatam.

Analogy: ek kitaab iterable hai. Us kitaab mein rakha bookmark iterator hai. Ek kitaab ko do log padh sakte hain — do bookmarks. Ek bookmark aakhri page par pahunch gaya toh wo khatam, par kitaab abhi bhi wahi hai.

iterable                     iterator
+-----------+   iter()      +------------------+
| [1, 2, 3] | -----------> | position = 0      |
+-----------+               | __next__() -> 1   |
      |                     | __next__() -> 2   |
      |  iter()             | __next__() -> 3   |
      +------------------>  | __next__() -> StopIteration
                            +------------------+
                            (doosra iterator, apni position ke saath)

docs.title: for loop actually kya karta hai
docs.text:
tests = ["test_a", "test_b", "test_c"]

# --- Ye 'for' loop ---
for t in tests:
    print(t)

# --- ...internally EXACTLY ye hai ---
iterator = iter(tests)                # 1. iterable se iterator maanga
while True:
    try:
        t = next(iterator)            # 2. agla item maanga
    except StopIteration:             # 3. khatam hone ka signal
        break
    print(t)                          # 4. body chalayi

Line-by-line walkthrough:

  1. iter(tests) — tests.__iter__() call hota hai, jo ek list_iterator object deta hai. Agar __iter__ na ho toh Python __getitem__ se purana sequence protocol try karta hai; wo bhi na ho toh TypeError: 'X' object is not iterable.
  2. next(iterator) — iterator.__next__() call. Agla item milta hai.
  3. except StopIteration: break — StopIteration ek normal exception hai, error nahi. for loop use pakad kar chupchaap ruk jaata hai. Ye important hai: agar aapke iterator ke andar galti se StopIteration uthh jaaye toh loop chupchaap khatam ho jaayega — bug chhup jaayega. (Isi liye generators mein PEP 479 aaya, 6.2 mein.)
  4. Ye poora loop C level par hota hai, isliye Python-level while se tez hai.

docs.title: Apna iterator banao — haath se
docs.text:
class TestSuiteIterator:
    """Ek explicit iterator -- sirf mechanism dikhane ke liye."""

    def __init__(self, tests: list[str]):
        self._tests = tests
        self._index = 0                              # STATE -- yahi iterator ka poora kaam hai

    def __iter__(self):
        """Iterator khud ko return karta hai -- ye protocol ka hissa hai."""
        return self

    def __next__(self):
        """Agla item, ya StopIteration."""
        if self._index >= len(self._tests):
            raise StopIteration                      # khatam
        value = self._tests[self._index]
        self._index += 1                             # state aage badhi
        return value


class TestSuite:
    """Ek ITERABLE -- har baar naya iterator deta hai."""

    def __init__(self, tests: list[str]):
        self._tests = tests

    def __iter__(self):
        return TestSuiteIterator(self._tests)        # HAR BAAR NAYA


suite = TestSuite(["test_a", "test_b", "test_c"])

print(list(suite))          # ['test_a', 'test_b', 'test_c']
print(list(suite))          # ['test_a', 'test_b', 'test_c']   <- DOBARA chala!

it = iter(suite)
print(next(it))             # test_a
print(next(it))             # test_b
print(list(it))             # ['test_c']   -- baaki bacha hua
print(list(it))             # []           -- ab khatam

Line-by-line walkthrough:

  1. self._index = 0 — iterator ka poora kaam yahi state rakhna hai. Iterable ke paas position nahi hoti; iterator ke paas hoti hai.
  2. def __iter__(self): return self — iterator mein __iter__ hona zaruri hai jo khud ko return kare. Kyun? Taaki iterator bhi iterable ho — for x in some_iterator: kaam kare, aur itertools functions use accept karein. Ye protocol requirement hai.
  3. raise StopIteration — signal. return mat karo — plain return None dega aur loop infinite ho jaayega... actually nahi, __next__ mein return None None value degi, aur loop chalta rahega None ke saath. Ye ek real bug hai.
  4. self._index += 1 — return se pehle ya baad mein? Pehle value nikaali (value = ...), phir index badhaya, phir return. Agar aap return self._tests[self._index] likh kar phir self._index += 1 likhte toh wo line kabhi chalti hi nahi (return ke baad).
  5. TestSuite.__iter__ naya iterator banata hai — isliye list(suite) do baar kaam karta hai. Ye "iterable" ka defining feature hai.
  6. list(it) doosri baar [] — iterator exhaust ho gaya. Exhausted iterator reset nahi hota.

docs.title: Iterable vs iterator — practical test
docs.text:
from collections.abc import Iterable, Iterator

data = [1, 2, 3]
it = iter(data)

print(isinstance(data, Iterable), isinstance(data, Iterator))    # True  False
print(isinstance(it, Iterable), isinstance(it, Iterator))        # True  True

print(iter(data) is iter(data))     # False -- har baar naya iterator
print(iter(it) is it)               # True  -- iterator khud ko return karta hai

iter(x) is x — yahi ek line iterator aur iterable ka farak batati hai.

Iterable Iterator __iter__ Haan (naya iterator deta hai) Haan (self deta hai) __next__ Nahi Haan Multiple passes Haan Nahi Examples list, dict, set, str, range, file path zip, map, filter, enumerate, generator, open file

docs.title: Kyu ye farak matter karta hai — real bug
docs.text:
# --- BUG: generator ko do baar use karne ki koshish ---
def analyse(results):
    total = sum(1 for _ in results)                       # results CONSUME ho gaya
    failed = sum(1 for r in results if r["status"] == "failed")    # ab khaali hai
    return total, failed

gen = (r for r in [{"status": "failed"}, {"status": "passed"}])
print(analyse(gen))               # (2, 0)   <- failed count galat!

# --- FIX 1: materialise kar lo ---
def analyse_v1(results):
    results = list(results)                               # ek baar list bana lo
    total = len(results)
    failed = sum(1 for r in results if r["status"] == "failed")
    return total, failed

gen = (r for r in [{"status": "failed"}, {"status": "passed"}])
print(analyse_v1(gen))            # (2, 1)   <- sahi

# --- FIX 2: ek hi pass mein sab compute karo (memory-efficient) ---
def analyse_v2(results):
    total = failed = 0
    for r in results:                                     # SIRF EK pass
        total += 1
        if r["status"] == "failed":
            failed += 1
    return total, failed

gen = (r for r in [{"status": "failed"}, {"status": "passed"}])
print(analyse_v2(gen))            # (2, 1)

Line-by-line walkthrough:

  1. sum(1 for _ in results) — poora generator consume kar gaya.
  2. Doosri line par results khaali hai → sum 0 deta hai. Koi error nahi, koi warning nahi — bas galat answer.
  3. results = list(results) — memory kharch karke multiple passes possible banaye.
  4. analyse_v2 — ek pass mein sab. Ye best hai jab data bada ho: constant memory, ek pass.
  5. Interview mein ye "single-pass algorithm" wala point achha hai — bade log files ya test result streams par yahi likhna padta hai.

Defensive check:

from collections.abc import Iterator

def analyse_safe(results):
    if isinstance(results, Iterator):
        raise TypeError("analyse() needs a re-iterable collection, got a one-shot iterator; "
                        "wrap it in list() if that's intentional")
    ...

Ye API design ka achha pattern hai — galat use ko loud banao.

docs.title: iter() ka doosra form — sentinel
docs.text:
# iter(callable, sentinel) -- callable ko baar-baar call karo jab tak sentinel na mile

# 1. File se fixed-size chunks
def read_chunks(path, size=4096):
    with open(path, "rb") as f:
        yield from iter(lambda: f.read(size), b"")       # b"" milne par ruk jao

# 2. Queue drain karna
import queue
q = queue.Queue()
for item in ("a", "b", "c", None):
    q.put(item)

for item in iter(q.get, None):                            # None sentinel
    print(item)                                            # a b c

# 3. Input tab tak lo jab tak 'quit' na aaye
# for line in iter(input, "quit"):
#     process(line)
  1. iter(callable, sentinel) — do-argument form. Har next() par callable() call hota hai; agar result == sentinel ho toh StopIteration.
  2. Comparison == se hoti hai, is se nahi — toh sentinel choose karte waqt dhyaan rakho.
  3. Ye "loop and a half" ka ek aur solution hai (walrus, 2.5, ka alternative).

docs.title: Gotchas
docs.text:
Gotcha 1 — iterator mein __iter__ bhoolna.

class Broken:
    def __init__(self):
        self.i = 0
    def __next__(self):
        self.i += 1
        if self.i > 3:
            raise StopIteration
        return self.i

b = Broken()
# for x in b: print(x)         # TypeError: 'Broken' object is not iterable
print(next(b), next(b))        # 1 2   -- next() to chalta hai

Gotcha 2 — __next__ mein StopIteration ki jagah return.

class Broken2:
    def __init__(self): self.i = 0
    def __iter__(self): return self
    def __next__(self):
        if self.i >= 3:
            return None                 # BUG -- StopIteration nahi uthaya
        self.i += 1
        return self.i

# for x in Broken2(): print(x)          # INFINITE LOOP: 1 2 3 None None None ...

Gotcha 3 — dict iterate karte waqt modify.

d = {"a": 1, "b": 2}
# for k in d:
#     d["c"] = 3               # RuntimeError: dictionary changed size during iteration

Dict ka iterator ek version counter check karta hai.

Gotcha 4 — file object iterator hai, iterable nahi (practically).

with open("test.log", "w") as f:
    f.write("line1\nline2\n")

with open("test.log") as f:
    print(len(list(f)))        # 2
    print(len(list(f)))        # 0   <- file iterator exhaust ho gaya
    f.seek(0)                  # wapas shuru par
    print(len(list(f)))        # 2   <- ab chala

f.seek(0) file-specific reset hai; generators mein aisa kuch nahi hota.

Interview answer: "The protocol has two distinct roles that people collapse into one. An iterable has __iter__ and returns a fresh iterator each time, so it supports multiple passes — a list, a dict, a range. An iterator has __next__ and holds the position, and its __iter__ returns self, which is what makes it usable in a for loop; it's single-use and doesn't reset. The for statement is sugar for calling iter, then next in a loop, catching StopIteration to stop. The single quickest test is iter(x) is x — true for an iterator, false for an iterable.

This matters because zip, map, filter, enumerate, generators, and open files are all iterators. Passing one into a function that loops over it twice gives you a wrong answer with no error at all — the second pass just sees nothing. I've hit exactly that computing a total and a failure count from the same generator. The fixes are either to materialise once with list() if the data fits, or to restructure into a single pass that accumulates both counters — which is what I'd do for a large log stream, since it keeps memory constant."

docs.title: Kya hai
docs.text:
Generator function = koi bhi function jismein yield hai. Call karne par wo body chalati nahi — ek generator object (jo ek iterator hai) return karti hai.

Analogy: normal function ek Netflix download hai — poori movie pehle aati hai, phir dekhte ho. Generator streaming hai — jitna dekha utna aaya, aur aap pause kar sakte ho, aur baaki tabhi aayega jab aap play daboge.

docs.title: Kyu hai
docs.text:
# --- WITHOUT generator: poora result memory mein ---
def parse_log_eager(path: str) -> list[dict]:
    entries = []
    with open(path) as f:
        for line in f:
            parts = line.split(" ", 3)
            if len(parts) == 4:
                entries.append({
                    "date": parts[0], "time": parts[1],
                    "level": parts[2], "message": parts[3].rstrip(),
                })
    return entries                            # 5 GB log -> 5+ GB RAM -> MemoryError

# --- WITH generator: ek waqt mein ek entry ---
def parse_log(path: str):
    with open(path) as f:
        for line in f:
            parts = line.split(" ", 3)
            if len(parts) == 4:
                yield {                        # ek entry di, aur RUK gaye
                    "date": parts[0], "time": parts[1],
                    "level": parts[2], "message": parts[3].rstrip(),
                }

# Memory constant rehti hai chahe file 5 GB ho
errors = (e for e in parse_log("huge.log") if e["level"] == "ERROR")
first_10 = [next(errors) for _ in range(10)]     # sirf pehle 10 errors tak file padhi

Line-by-line walkthrough:

  1. def parse_log(path): — yield hone se ye generator function hai. Call karne par body ka ek bhi statement nahi chalta.
  2. with open(path) as f: — ye tab chalta hai jab pehli baar next() call hoti hai. Important: file tab tak khuli rehti hai jab tak generator zinda hai. Agar aap generator ko half-consume karke chhod do toh file khuli reh sakti hai (GC par depend).
  3. yield {...} — value caller ko di, aur function ka poora state freeze ho gaya: locals (f, line, parts), instruction pointer, sab. Agli next() par execution isi line ke baad se resume hoti hai.
  4. line.split(" ", 3) — maxsplit=3 se message mein spaces safe rehte hain (1.8).
  5. (e for e in parse_log(...) if ...) — generator expression, jo doosre generator ko wrap kar raha hai. Poori chain lazy hai — abhi tak file khuli bhi nahi.
  6. [next(errors) for _ in range(10)] — ab actual reading shuru hoti hai, aur sirf 10 errors milne tak.

docs.title: Kaise kaam karta hai — paused frame ka mechanism
docs.text:
Normal function call:

call        -> naya FRAME banta hai (locals, instruction pointer) stack par
return      -> frame DESTROY ho jaata hai, locals gayab
next call   -> bilkul naya frame, zero se shuru

Generator:

call        -> generator OBJECT banta hai. Frame bhi banta hai par SUSPENDED state mein.
               Ye frame HEAP par rehta hai, stack par nahi.
next()      -> frame ko stack par "resume" kiya jaata hai, code chalta hai
yield       -> value return hoti hai, frame SUSPEND ho jaata hai (heap par wapas),
               instruction pointer yaad rehta hai, locals zinda rehte hain
next()      -> wahi frame dobara resume, agle statement se
return/end  -> StopIteration raise hoti hai, frame destroy

import inspect

def counter():
    print("  [start]")
    x = 0
    while x < 3:
        print(f"  [before yield {x}]")
        yield x
        print(f"  [after yield {x}]")
        x += 1
    print("  [done]")

gen = counter()
print("1. generator created, nothing ran yet")
print("   state:", inspect.getgeneratorstate(gen))     # GEN_CREATED

print("2. first next():")
print("   got", next(gen))
print("   state:", inspect.getgeneratorstate(gen))     # GEN_SUSPENDED
print("   locals:", gen.gi_frame.f_locals)             # {'x': 0}   <- frame ZINDA hai

print("3. second next():")
print("   got", next(gen))
print("   locals:", gen.gi_frame.f_locals)             # {'x': 1}

print("4. rest:")
print("   got", next(gen))
try:
    next(gen)
except StopIteration:
    print("   StopIteration")
print("   state:", inspect.getgeneratorstate(gen))     # GEN_CLOSED
print("   frame:", gen.gi_frame)                        # None -- frame free ho gaya

Output:

1. generator created, nothing ran yet
   state: GEN_CREATED
2. first next():
  [start]
  [before yield 0]
   got 0
   state: GEN_SUSPENDED
   locals: {'x': 0}
3. second next():
  [after yield 0]
  [before yield 1]
   got 1
   locals: {'x': 1}
4. rest:
  [after yield 1]
  [before yield 2]
   got 2
  [after yield 2]
  [done]
   StopIteration
   state: GEN_CLOSED
   frame: None

Line-by-line walkthrough — yahan sabse important observations:

  1. gen = counter() — [start] print nahi hua. Body bilkul nahi chali.
  2. Pehli next() par [start] aur [before yield 0] chale, phir yield 0 par ruk gaye.
  3. gen.gi_frame.f_locals — frame abhi bhi exist karta hai aur locals mein x zinda hai. Ye normal function se sabse bada farak hai — normal function ka frame return par destroy ho jaata hai.
  4. Doosri next() par [after yield 0] chala — matlab execution yield ke baad se resume hui, function ke shuru se nahi.
  5. inspect.getgeneratorstate — chaar states: GEN_CREATED, GEN_RUNNING, GEN_SUSPENDED, GEN_CLOSED.
  6. Aakhir mein gi_frame None ho gaya — frame free ho gaya, memory wapas mil gayi.

docs.title: Generator expression vs list comprehension
docs.text:
import sys

results = [{"name": f"test_{i}", "duration": i * 0.1} for i in range(100_000)]

# List comprehension -- EAGER
durations_list = [r["duration"] for r in results]
print(sys.getsizeof(durations_list))          # ~800,000 bytes

# Generator expression -- LAZY
durations_gen = (r["duration"] for r in results)
print(sys.getsizeof(durations_gen))           # 208 bytes   <- CONSTANT

print(sum(durations_gen))                      # kaam karta hai, memory nahi khaata
print(sum(durations_gen))                      # 0   <- EXHAUSTED

Kab kaunsa:

Use genexp ( ) Use list comp [ ] Sirf ek baar iterate karna hai Multiple passes chahiye Bada data (memory matters) Chhota data sum, any, all, max, min, join ko feed karna len(), indexing, slicing chahiye Pipeline bana rahe ho Result store karna hai Early exit possible hai (any, next) Poora result chahiye hi 
# Genexp shine karta hai jahan early exit hai
results = ({"name": f"test_{i}", "status": "failed" if i == 5 else "passed"} for i in range(1_000_000))
has_failure = any(r["status"] == "failed" for r in results)     # 6 items ke baad ruk gaya
print(has_failure)                                               # True

Genexp ka syntax shortcut:

# Jab genexp function ka AKELA argument ho, extra brackets ki zarurat nahi
print(sum(x * 2 for x in range(5)))          # theek
print(max((x for x in range(5)), default=0)) # ek se zyada arg -> brackets chahiye
# print(max(x for x in range(5), default=0)) # SyntaxError

docs.title: Generator methods — send, throw, close
docs.text:
def retry_coordinator(max_attempts: int = 3):
    """Coroutine: caller batata hai attempt safal hui ya nahi."""
    attempt = 0
    failures = []
    while attempt < max_attempts:
        attempt += 1
        outcome = yield attempt                       # value BHEJI, aur value LI
        if outcome == "success":
            print(f"  succeeded on attempt {attempt}")
            return                                     # generator khatam
        failures.append(outcome)
        print(f"  attempt {attempt} failed: {outcome}")
    print(f"  giving up after {max_attempts}: {failures}")


coord = retry_coordinator(max_attempts=3)
print(next(coord))                    # 1    <- PRIME the generator (pehla yield tak chalao)
print(coord.send("timeout"))          # attempt 1 failed: timeout  -> 2
print(coord.send("timeout"))          # attempt 2 failed: timeout  -> 3
try:
    coord.send("success")             # succeeded on attempt 3 -> return -> StopIteration
except StopIteration:
    print("coordinator finished")

Line-by-line walkthrough:

  1. outcome = yield attempt — yield ek expression hai, statement nahi. Wo do kaam karta hai: attempt caller ko bhejta hai, aur send() se aayi value outcome mein rakhta hai.
  2. next(coord) — priming. Pehli baar send(value) nahi kar sakte kyunki generator abhi pehle yield tak pahuncha hi nahi — TypeError: can't send non-None value to a just-started generator. next(coord) send(None) ke barabar hai.
  3. coord.send("timeout") — generator resume hua, outcome "timeout" bana, loop aage badha, agle yield par ruka aur 2 return kiya.
  4. return generator ke andar — StopIteration raise karta hai. Agar return value likho toh wo value StopIteration.value mein aati hai (yield from mein ye kaam ka hai).
# throw() -- generator ke andar exception bhejo
def resilient_processor():
    while True:
        try:
            item = yield
            print(f"  processed {item}")
        except ValueError as e:
            print(f"  recovered from: {e}")

p = resilient_processor()
next(p)                                  # prime
p.send("item1")                          # processed item1
p.throw(ValueError("bad data"))          # recovered from: bad data
p.send("item2")                          # processed item2   <- generator zinda hai
p.close()                                # cleanup

# close() -- generator ke andar GeneratorExit raise karta hai
def with_cleanup():
    try:
        while True:
            yield "data"
    finally:
        print("  cleanup ran!")           # close() par ya GC par chalega

g = with_cleanup()
print(next(g))                            # data
g.close()                                 # cleanup ran!
  1. throw(exc) — generator ke current yield point par exception raise karta hai. Generator use pakad sakta hai aur chalta reh sakta hai.
  2. close() — GeneratorExit raise karta hai. finally block chalta hai. Ye important hai resource cleanup ke liye — file/browser band karna.
  3. GeneratorExit ko pakad kar yield mat karo — RuntimeError: generator ignored GeneratorExit.

docs.title: yield from — delegation
docs.text:
def collect_from_file(path: str):
    """Ek file se test names."""
    for name in ["test_a", "test_b"]:                # simulated
        yield f"{path}::{name}"

def collect_all_v1(paths: list[str]):
    """Manual delegation -- verbose."""
    for path in paths:
        for name in collect_from_file(path):
            yield name

def collect_all_v2(paths: list[str]):
    """yield from -- same cheez, ek line."""
    for path in paths:
        yield from collect_from_file(path)

print(list(collect_all_v2(["tests/a.py", "tests/b.py"])))
# ['tests/a.py::test_a', 'tests/a.py::test_b', 'tests/b.py::test_a', 'tests/b.py::test_b']

yield from sirf shortcut nahi hai — wo ek full delegation channel hai:

  1. Sub-generator ke saare yields aage bhejta hai.
  2. send() ko sub-generator tak pahunchata hai.
  3. throw() ko sub-generator tak pahunchata hai.
  4. Sub-generator ka return value ko yield from ka result banata hai.
  5. close() propagate karta hai.
def inner():
    x = yield 1
    print(f"  inner got {x}")
    y = yield 2
    print(f"  inner got {y}")
    return "inner done"                       # return value

def outer():
    result = yield from inner()               # inner ka return value yahan aata hai
    print(f"  outer got result: {result}")
    yield 3

g = outer()
print(next(g))          # 1
print(g.send("a"))      # inner got a -> 2
print(g.send("b"))      # inner got b -> outer got result: inner done -> 3

Recursive traversal — yield from ka best use:

def walk_test_tree(node: dict, prefix: str = ""):
    """Nested test suite structure ko flat mein badlo."""
    name = f"{prefix}{node['name']}"
    if "children" not in node:
        yield name                                          # leaf = actual test
    else:
        for child in node["children"]:
            yield from walk_test_tree(child, f"{name}::")    # recursive delegation

tree = {
    "name": "root",
    "children": [
        {"name": "auth", "children": [{"name": "test_login"}, {"name": "test_logout"}]},
        {"name": "cart", "children": [{"name": "test_add"}]},
    ],
}
print(list(walk_test_tree(tree)))
# ['root::auth::test_login', 'root::auth::test_logout', 'root::cart::test_add']
  1. yield from walk_test_tree(...) — bina iske aapko for x in walk_test_tree(...): yield x likhna padta, jo har recursion level par ek extra frame add karta.
  2. yield from internally optimised hai — ye recursion ke liye zaruri hai warna deep trees par O(depth) overhead per item hota hai.

docs.title: PEP 479 — StopIteration generator ke andar
docs.text:
def broken(items):
    it = iter(items)
    while True:
        yield next(it)                # items khatam hone par StopIteration

# Python 3.7+ mein:
# list(broken([1, 2]))
# RuntimeError: generator raised StopIteration
  1. Python 3.7 se pehle ye chupchaap generator ko khatam kar deta tha — jo bug chhupata tha.
  2. Ab wo RuntimeError mein badal jaata hai. Ye ek important safety change hai.
  3. Fix: try/except StopIteration: return ya seedha yield from items.

docs.title: Gotchas
docs.text:
Gotcha 1 — generator ek baar chalta hai.

gen = (x for x in range(3))
print(list(gen), list(gen))         # [0, 1, 2] []

Gotcha 2 — exception generator ke andar tab tak nahi aati jab tak wo consume na ho.

def risky():
    raise ValueError("boom")
    yield 1                          # unreachable, par 'yield' hone se ye generator hai

g = risky()                          # koi error NAHI
print("created fine")
# next(g)                            # ValueError: boom   <- ab aayi

Ye debugging mein confuse karta hai: error us line par dikhta hai jahan aapne consume kiya, jahan generator banaya wahan nahi.

Gotcha 3 — generator ke andar with aur early exit.

def read_lines(path):
    with open(path) as f:
        for line in f:
            yield line

g = read_lines("test.log")
print(next(g))                       # ek line li
del g                                # generator delete -> GeneratorExit -> 'with' ka __exit__ -> file band
  1. Agar aap generator ko half-consume karke chhod do, file tab band hoti hai jab generator garbage collect hota hai. CPython mein wo turant hota hai (refcounting), par PyPy mein nahi.
  2. Deterministic cleanup ke liye contextlib.closing ya explicit g.close().

Gotcha 4 — generator mein late binding.

funcs = []
for i in range(3):
    funcs.append(lambda: i)          # 4.5 wala bug
print([f() for f in funcs])          # [2, 2, 2]

gens = (i for i in range(3))         # ye theek hai -- genexp apna scope banati hai
print(list(gens))                    # [0, 1, 2]

# Par genexp ka PEHLA iterable turant evaluate hota hai:
data = [1, 2, 3]
g = (x for x in data)                # 'data' ABHI evaluate hua
data = [9, 9, 9]                      # rebind
print(list(g))                        # [1, 2, 3]   <- purana data

data2 = [1, 2, 3]
g2 = (x for x in data2)
data2.append(4)                       # MUTATION (rebind nahi)
print(list(g2))                       # [1, 2, 3, 4]   <- mutation dikha!

Ye ek nuanced but real gotcha hai: outermost iterable turant evaluate hota hai (rebinding se safe), par uska content lazily padha jaata hai (mutation dikhta hai).

Interview answer: "A generator function is any function containing yield. Calling it doesn't run the body — it returns a generator object, and the body only advances on each next(). Mechanically, the frame lives on the heap rather than the call stack, so when you hit yield the value goes to the caller and the entire frame is suspended with its locals and instruction pointer intact; the next next() resumes on the line after the yield. You can actually see it: while suspended, gen.gi_frame.f_locals still shows the live locals, which is impossible for a normal function.

The practical payoff is constant memory and early exit. Parsing a five-gigabyte log with a generator uses the same memory as a five-kilobyte one, and any(e.level == 'ERROR' for e in parse(path)) stops reading at the first match instead of parsing the whole file. yield from is more than a shortcut for a loop — it's a full delegation channel that forwards send, throw, and close, and makes the sub-generator's return value the expression's result, which is what makes recursive tree walks clean. The trap is that a generator is a one-shot iterator: consuming it twice silently gives you nothing the second time, with no error at all."

Cross-question — "What's the actual memory difference between a list comprehension and a generator expression, and when would the list still be the right choice?" "The generator object is a fixed size, around two hundred bytes, regardless of how many items it will produce, because it only holds the suspended frame. A list holds a pointer per element plus the elements themselves, so it's linear. For a hundred thousand floats that's roughly 800 kilobytes for the list versus 208 bytes for the generator. But the list is still right whenever you need more than one pass, len, indexing, or slicing — and it's actually faster when you're going to consume everything anyway, because each next() on a generator resumes a frame, which costs more than walking a contiguous array. So my rule is: generator when the data is large, when I'm building a pipeline, or when there's an early exit; list when the data is small and I need random access or multiple passes. And if I find myself calling list() on a generator immediately, I should have written the comprehension."

docs.title: 6.3 Lazy evaluation in practice — QA pipelines
Kya hai
docs.text:
Lazy evaluation = kaam tab karo jab result maanga jaaye, pehle nahi. Generators isko compose karne deti hain: chhote-chhote transform stages, jinme se data ek-ek item karke behta hai.

Analogy: factory assembly line vs batch processing. Batch mein: 1000 parts banao, phir sab paint karo, phir sab pack karo — teen baar 1000 parts ki jagah chahiye. Assembly line mein: ek part banao → paint → pack → agla. Ek waqt mein 3 parts line par hain.

docs.title: Poora pipeline example — 5 GB CI log
docs.text:
import re
from pathlib import Path
from collections import Counter
from typing import Iterator


LOG_PATTERN = re.compile(
    r"^(?P<ts>\d{4}-\d{2}-\d{2} \d{2}:\d{2}:\d{2}) "
    r"(?P<level>\w+) "
    r"\[(?P<test>[\w:./]+)\] "
    r"(?P<message>.*)$"
)


# ---------- STAGE 1: raw lines ----------
def read_lines(path: Path) -> Iterator[str]:
    """File se lines -- ek-ek karke, buffered."""
    with path.open(encoding="utf-8", errors="replace") as f:
        yield from f


# ---------- STAGE 2: parse ----------
def parse(lines: Iterator[str]) -> Iterator[dict]:
    """Har line ko structured dict mein badlo; jo match na ho, chhod do."""
    for line in lines:
        if match := LOG_PATTERN.match(line):
            yield match.groupdict()


# ---------- STAGE 3: filter ----------
def only_errors(entries: Iterator[dict]) -> Iterator[dict]:
    for e in entries:
        if e["level"] in ("ERROR", "CRITICAL"):
            yield e


# ---------- STAGE 4: enrich ----------
def add_error_type(entries: Iterator[dict]) -> Iterator[dict]:
    """Message se exception type nikaalo."""
    exc_re = re.compile(r"(\w+Error|\w+Exception)")
    for e in entries:
        m = exc_re.search(e["message"])
        yield {**e, "error_type": m.group(1) if m else "Unknown"}


# ---------- STAGE 5: dedupe ----------
def dedupe_by(entries: Iterator[dict], key: str) -> Iterator[dict]:
    """Har unique key ka pehla entry hi do."""
    seen = set()
    for e in entries:
        k = e[key]
        if k not in seen:
            seen.add(k)
            yield e


# ---------- COMPOSE ----------
def analyse_ci_log(path: Path):
    lines = read_lines(path)                # kuch nahi hua
    entries = parse(lines)                  # kuch nahi hua
    errors = only_errors(entries)           # kuch nahi hua
    enriched = add_error_type(errors)       # kuch nahi hua
    unique = dedupe_by(enriched, "test")    # kuch nahi hua
    return unique                           # abhi bhi kuch nahi hua!


# ---------- CONSUME (ab kaam hota hai) ----------
def summarise(path: Path, limit: int = 10):
    import itertools
    pipeline = analyse_ci_log(path)
    top = list(itertools.islice(pipeline, limit))       # SIRF 10 tak file padhi
    counts = Counter(e["error_type"] for e in top)
    return top, counts

Line-by-line walkthrough:

  1. LOG_PATTERN = re.compile(...) — module level par compile, ek baar. Named groups (?P<name>) se groupdict() seedha dict deta hai.
  2. errors="replace" — corrupt bytes ko � se replace karo, crash mat karo. CI logs mein ye zaruri hai — ek galat byte poori analysis nahi roknee chahiye (Part 11).
  3. yield from f — file object khud iterator hai. for line in f: yield line likhne ki zarurat nahi.
  4. if match := LOG_PATTERN.match(line): — walrus (2.5). Regex ek baar chalta hai.
