docs.text:
try:
    # A: wo code jo fail kar sakta hai
except SomeError as e:
    # B: sirf tab jab matching exception aaye
else:
    # C: sirf tab jab koi exception NA aaye
finally:
    # D: HAMESHA -- chahe kuch bhi ho

docs.title: Exact order — saare cases
docs.text:
def demo(scenario: str):
    print(f"\n--- {scenario} ---")
    try:
        print("1. try block start")
        if scenario == "raises":
            raise ValueError("boom")
        if scenario == "returns":
            return "from try"
        if scenario == "unhandled":
            raise TypeError("not caught here")
        print("2. try block end")
    except ValueError as e:
        print(f"3. except: caught {e}")
        if scenario == "return_in_except":
            return "from except"
    else:
        print("4. else: no exception happened")
        if scenario == "return_in_else":
            return "from else"
    finally:
        print("5. finally: always runs")
    print("6. after try block")
    return "normal end"


print("result:", demo("normal"))
print("result:", demo("raises"))
print("result:", demo("returns"))
try:
    demo("unhandled")
except TypeError:
    print("result: TypeError propagated")

Output:

--- normal ---
1. try block start
2. try block end
4. else: no exception happened
5. finally: always runs
6. after try block
result: normal end

--- raises ---
1. try block start
3. except: caught boom
5. finally: always runs
6. after try block
result: normal end

--- returns ---
1. try block start
5. finally: always runs
result: from try

--- unhandled ---
1. try block start
5. finally: always runs
result: TypeError propagated

Line-by-line walkthrough — key observations:

  1. else sirf tab chalta hai jab try bina exception ke poora ho. "normal" case mein else chala; "raises" mein nahi.
  2. else except ke baad likha hai par except ke ULTE case mein chalta hai. Ye naam confusing hai (loop-else ki tarah), par semantics saaf hai.
  3. return ke case mein bhi finally chalta hai — "returns" case mein 5. finally print hua return execute hone se pehle (technically return value compute ho chuki thi, par frame return se pehle finally chala).
  4. Unhandled exception mein bhi finally chalta hai, phir exception aage jaati hai.
  5. "returns" case mein else, 6., aur return "normal end" — kuch nahi chala. return ne poora block chhod diya (sirf finally chhod ke).

docs.title: else kyun use karo
docs.text:
# --- BINA else: try block bada hai ---
def load_config_bad(path):
    try:
        with open(path) as f:
            data = json.load(f)
        # ye lines try mein hain -- inki exceptions bhi pakdi jaayengi!
        validate(data)                            # agar ye ValueError de toh?
        return normalise(data)
    except (OSError, json.JSONDecodeError) as e:
        raise ConfigurationError(f"cannot load {path}") from e

# --- else ke SAATH: try mein sirf wo jo fail ho sakta hai ---
def load_config(path):
    try:
        with open(path) as f:
            data = json.load(f)                    # SIRF ye do lines risky hain
    except (OSError, json.JSONDecodeError) as e:
        raise ConfigurationError(f"cannot load {path}") from e
    else:
        validate(data)                             # inki exceptions ALAG rehti hain
        return normalise(data)

Line-by-line walkthrough:

  1. Pehle version mein validate(data) try ke andar hai. Agar wo json.JSONDecodeError raise kare (unlikely par possible) toh wo galti se "cannot load" ban jaayega.
  2. else block mein wo code hai jo try safal hone par chalna chahiye, par jiski exceptions pakdi nahi jaani chahiye.
  3. Rule: try block jitna chhota rakho, utna better. Ideally usme sirf wo ek call ho jiski exception aap expect kar rahe ho.

docs.title: finally ke gotchas
docs.text:
Gotcha 1 — finally mein return exception ko nigal jaata hai.

def dangerous():
    try:
        raise ValueError("important error")
    finally:
        return "swallowed"                # <- exception GAYAB ho gayi

print(dangerous())                        # 'swallowed'   -- koi exception nahi!
  1. finally mein return (ya break, ya continue) pending exception ko discard kar deta hai.
  2. Ye 8.2 ke return True jaisa hi paap hai. finally mein kabhi return mat likho.
  3. Python 3.8+ mein finally mein continue allowed hai; usse pehle SyntaxError tha — kyunki wo itna khatarnak tha.

Gotcha 2 — finally mein exception original ko replace kar deti hai.

def cleanup_fails():
    try:
        raise ValueError("original error")
    finally:
        raise RuntimeError("cleanup error")       # original ab __context__ mein hai

try:
    cleanup_fails()
except RuntimeError as e:
    print(f"got: {e}")                             # got: cleanup error
    print(f"context: {e.__context__}")             # context: original error
  1. Traceback mein dono dikhte hain ("During handling of the above exception, another exception occurred"), par top-level exception cleanup wali hai.
  2. Isliye cleanup code ko defensive banao: 
    try:
    do_work()
finally:
    try:
        risky_cleanup()
    except Exception as e:
        log.warning("cleanup failed: %s", e)    # log karo, raise mat karo

Gotcha 3 — finally return value ko override kar sakta hai.

def confusing():
    try:
        return "A"
    finally:
        print("finally ran")
        # return "B"          # agar ye uncomment karo toh "B" milega

print(confusing())            # finally ran -> A

return "A" ki value compute ho chuki hoti hai, phir finally chalta hai. Agar finally apna return na kare toh "A" hi milta hai.

docs.title: try ka cost
docs.text:
import timeit

setup = "d = {'a': 1}"

# Success path -- try/except lagbhag FREE hai
print(timeit.timeit("try:\n d['a']\nexcept KeyError:\n pass", setup=setup, number=1_000_000))
# ~0.05s
print(timeit.timeit("if 'a' in d:\n d['a']", setup=setup, number=1_000_000))
# ~0.06s

# Failure path -- exception raise karna MEHNGA hai
print(timeit.timeit("try:\n d['z']\nexcept KeyError:\n pass", setup=setup, number=1_000_000))
# ~0.35s   -- 7x dheema
  1. Python 3.11+ mein "zero-cost exceptions" hain: try block enter karne ka koi runtime cost nahi hai (pehle ek block setup hota tha). Cost sirf tab lagti hai jab exception actually raise ho.
  2. Isliye EAFP (Easier to Ask Forgiveness than Permission) Python mein idiomatic hai — jab tak exception rare ho.
  3. Agar exception common ho (50% cases), toh LBYL (if key in d) tez hai. Part 16 mein detail.

Interview answer: "The order is: try, then either except or else — never both — and finally always. else runs only when the try block completed without an exception, and it exists so the try block can stay minimal: I put only the call that might fail inside try, and everything that should follow success inside else, so an unrelated exception from the follow-up code doesn't get misattributed to the risky call. finally runs on every exit path — normal completion, handled exception, unhandled exception propagating, and return. Two dangerous behaviours there: a return inside finally discards a propagating exception entirely, which silently turns a failure into a success; and an exception raised inside finally replaces the original, which is why cleanup code that can fail — closing a dead browser, deleting a missing file — gets its own try/except that logs rather than raises. Since 3.11 exceptions are zero-cost on the happy path, so wrapping code in try costs nothing unless something is actually raised; raising is still roughly an order of magnitude more expensive than a check, so EAFP is right when the exception is rare and LBYL when it isn't."

docs.title: Kya hai
docs.text:
Jab ek exception handle karte hue doosri exception aati hai, Python dono ko jod kar rakhta hai. Do attributes hain:

  • __context__ — implicit chaining. Automatically set hota hai.
  • __cause__ — explicit chaining. raise X from Y se set hota hai.
  • __suppress_context__ — raise X from None se True hota hai.

docs.title: Teeno cases
docs.text:
def demo_implicit():
    """Bina 'from' -- implicit chaining."""
    try:
        1 / 0
    except ZeroDivisionError:
        raise ValueError("could not compute rate")


def demo_explicit():
    """'from exc' -- explicit cause."""
    try:
        1 / 0
    except ZeroDivisionError as e:
        raise ValueError("could not compute rate") from e


def demo_suppressed():
    """'from None' -- purani exception chhupa do."""
    try:
        1 / 0
    except ZeroDivisionError:
        raise ValueError("could not compute rate") from None


for fn in (demo_implicit, demo_explicit, demo_suppressed):
    try:
        fn()
    except ValueError as e:
        print(f"{fn.__name__}:")
        print(f"  __context__ = {e.__context__!r}")
        print(f"  __cause__   = {e.__cause__!r}")
        print(f"  suppress    = {e.__suppress_context__}")

Output:

demo_implicit:
  __context__ = ZeroDivisionError('division by zero')
  __cause__   = None
  suppress    = False
demo_explicit:
  __context__ = ZeroDivisionError('division by zero')
  __cause__   = ZeroDivisionError('division by zero')
  suppress    = False
demo_suppressed:
  __context__ = ZeroDivisionError('division by zero')
  __cause__   = None
  suppress    = True

Traceback mein kya dikhta hai:

# IMPLICIT (bina from):
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "x.py", line 3, in demo_implicit
    1 / 0
ZeroDivisionError: division by zero

During handling of the above exception, another exception occurred:
              ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^ "handling ke DAURAN kuch aur hua" -- shayad bug hai

Traceback (most recent call last):
  ...
ValueError: could not compute rate


# EXPLICIT (from e):
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "x.py", line 3, in demo_explicit
    1 / 0
ZeroDivisionError: division by zero

The above exception was the direct cause of the following exception:
              ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^ "ye deliberate translation thi"

Traceback (most recent call last):
  ...
ValueError: could not compute rate


# SUPPRESSED (from None):
Traceback (most recent call last):
  ...
ValueError: could not compute rate
              ^^^^ ZeroDivisionError bilkul nahi dikha

Line-by-line walkthrough:

  1. Implicit chaining automatic hai — Python except block ke andar raise hui har exception ka __context__ set kar deta hai.
  2. from e __cause__ set karta hai, aur message badal jaata hai: "During handling" (accident lagta hai) se "direct cause" (deliberate lagta hai).
  3. Ye sirf cosmetic nahi hai — jo bhi aapka traceback padhega (aap, 6 mahine baad), usko turant pata chalega ki ye translation intentional thi ya cleanup mein bug hai.
  4. from None — purani exception poori tarah chhupa deta hai. Use tab karo jab purani exception implementation detail ho aur user ke liye noise ho.

docs.title: Kab kaunsa — QA examples
docs.text:
from e — jab aap low-level ko domain-level mein badal rahe ho

class ConfigurationError(Exception):
    pass


def load_test_config(path: str) -> dict:
    import json
    try:
        with open(path, encoding="utf-8") as f:
            return json.load(f)
    except FileNotFoundError as e:
        raise ConfigurationError(
            f"config file not found: {path}. "
            f"Did you run 'cp config.example.json {path}'?"
        ) from e
    except json.JSONDecodeError as e:
        raise ConfigurationError(
            f"config file {path} is not valid JSON: {e.msg} at line {e.lineno}"
        ) from e
    except PermissionError as e:
        raise ConfigurationError(f"cannot read {path}: permission denied") from e
  1. Har except ek actionable message deta hai — user ko batata hai kya karna hai.
  2. from e se original traceback bhi rehta hai — agar message se kaam na chale toh full detail available hai.
  3. e.msg, e.lineno — JSONDecodeError ke structured attributes. String parse karne se behtar.

from None — jab original noise ho

LOCATORS = {"submit": "#submit", "username": "#username"}


def get_locator(name: str) -> str:
    try:
        return LOCATORS[name]
    except KeyError:
        raise ValueError(
            f"unknown locator {name!r}; available: {sorted(LOCATORS)}"
        ) from None
  1. Bina from None ke traceback mein KeyError: 'submitt' bhi dikhta — jo user ke liye redundant hai (message mein already hai).
  2. from None se ek clean, single error milta hai.
  3. Caveat: from None debugging info hata deta hai. Sirf tab use karo jab aap 100% sure ho ki original mein kuch naya nahi hai.

Bare raise — re-raise with original traceback

import logging

log = logging.getLogger(__name__)


def run_test_with_logging(test_fn):
    try:
        return test_fn()
    except Exception:
        log.exception("test %s failed", test_fn.__name__)     # traceback log kiya
        raise                                                  # ORIGINAL exception, ORIGINAL traceback
  1. raise bina argument — current exception ko exactly aage bhejta hai, poora traceback preserve.
  2. raise e likhna galat hai — wo ek naya raise point add karta hai: 
    except Exception as e:
    raise e          # traceback mein ye line bhi add ho jaati hai -- noise
    Technically Python 3 mein raise e original traceback preserve karta hai (e.__traceback__ se), par ek extra frame add hota hai. raise cleaner hai.
  3. log.exception(...) — ye log.error(..., exc_info=True) ka short form hai, sirf exception handler ke andar use karo.

docs.title: Exception ke saath data attach karna
docs.text:
class APIError(Exception):
    def __init__(self, method: str, url: str, status: int, body: str = "", request_id: str = ""):
        self.method = method
        self.url = url
        self.status = status
        self.body = body[:1000]
        self.request_id = request_id
        super().__init__(f"{method} {url} -> {status}"
                         + (f" (request_id={request_id})" if request_id else ""))

    @property
    def is_retryable(self) -> bool:
        """Kya ye error retry karne layak hai?"""
        return self.status in (408, 425, 429, 500, 502, 503, 504)


def call_api(method, url):
    # ... actual call ...
    raise APIError(method, url, 503, body="service unavailable", request_id="req-abc123")


try:
    call_api("POST", "/api/orders")
except APIError as e:
    print(f"error: {e}")
    print(f"retryable: {e.is_retryable}")
    print(f"request_id for support: {e.request_id}")
    # error: POST /api/orders -> 503 (request_id=req-abc123)
    # retryable: True
    # request_id for support: req-abc123
  1. Structured attributes exception par — caller ko string parse nahi karna padta.
  2. is_retryable property — decision logic exception ke saath, caller ke saath nahi. Ye DRY hai: har caller ko status codes ki list nahi likhni padti.
  3. request_id — production debugging ke liye. Ye backend logs se correlate karta hai.

docs.title: add_note() — Python 3.11+
docs.text:
def process_test_batch(tests: list[str]):
    for i, test in enumerate(tests):
        try:
            run_test(test)
        except Exception as e:
            e.add_note(f"while running test {i + 1}/{len(tests)}: {test!r}")
            e.add_note(f"batch started at 10:00:00, elapsed 45s")
            raise


# Traceback mein notes exception ke baad dikhte hain:
# ValueError: assertion failed
# while running test 3/10: 'test_checkout'
# batch started at 10:00:00, elapsed 45s
  1. add_note exception ko modify karta hai bina naya banaye. Isliye type wahi rehta hai aur upstream handlers abhi bhi kaam karte hain.
  2. Ye raise NewError(...) from e se behtar hai jab aap sirf context add karna chahte ho, type badalna nahi.
  3. Notes e.__notes__ list mein rehte hain.

docs.title: Gotchas
docs.text:
Gotcha 1 — except ... as e ke baad e gayab ho jaata hai. (4.2)

try:
    raise ValueError("x")
except ValueError as e:
    pass
# print(e)                     # NameError -- implicit 'del e'

Fix: doosre naam mein copy karo.

Gotcha 2 — exception object mein traceback hota hai, jo memory pakadta hai.

errors = []
for test in tests:
    try:
        run(test)
    except Exception as e:
        errors.append(e)         # e ka __traceback__ poora frame chain pakde hue hai!
# 1000 failures = 1000 frame chains = potentially GBs

Fix:

import traceback

errors = []
for test in tests:
    try:
        run(test)
    except Exception as e:
        errors.append({
            "test": test,
            "type": type(e).__name__,
            "message": str(e),
            "traceback": traceback.format_exc(),      # STRING -- frames free ho jaate hain
        })

Ye Part 14 (memory) se juda hua real issue hai.

Gotcha 3 — raise except block ke bahar.

# raise                         # RuntimeError: No active exception to re-raise

Gotcha 4 — exception class raise karna vs instance.

raise ValueError                # Python khud ValueError() bana deta hai
raise ValueError("message")     # instance -- preferred, message ke saath
# raise "error"                 # TypeError: exceptions must derive from BaseException

Interview answer: "When you raise inside an except block, Python automatically links the old exception as __context__, and the traceback says 'During handling of the above exception, another exception occurred' — which reads like something went wrong in your handler. raise X from Y sets __cause__ instead, and the traceback says 'The above exception was the direct cause', which tells the reader this translation was deliberate. That distinction is worth real debugging time six months later. So whenever I convert a low-level exception into a domain one — FileNotFoundError into ConfigurationError with an actionable message — I use from e, so the caller gets my message and the original stack. from None suppresses the context entirely, and I use it only when the original adds nothing, like a KeyError whose key is already in my message.

For re-raising unchanged, bare raise is correct — it preserves the original traceback exactly, whereas raise e adds an extra frame. Since 3.11 there's also add_note, which attaches context to an exception without changing its type, so upstream handlers still match. And I put structured attributes on custom exceptions — status code, selector, request id — plus properties like is_retryable, so callers branch on data rather than substring-matching the message."

docs.title: Kya hai
docs.text:
ExceptionGroup ek exception hai jo kai exceptions ko ek saath carry karti hai. except* syntax se aap unme se specific types handle kar sakte ho.

Kyu hai: parallel operations mein ek se zyada cheezein fail ho sakti hain. Purane model mein aap sirf ek exception raise kar sakte the — baaki gum ho jaati thi.

# --- PURANA: sirf pehla error dikhta hai ---
def validate_config_old(config: dict):
    if "base_url" not in config:
        raise ValueError("base_url missing")
    if "timeout" not in config:
        raise ValueError("timeout missing")           # kabhi nahi pahunchte agar upar wala fail ho
    if config.get("retries", 0) < 0:
        raise ValueError("retries must be >= 0")
# User ek error fix karta hai, dobara chalata hai, agla error milta hai. Frustrating.

# --- NAYA: saare errors ek saath ---
def validate_config(config: dict):
    errors = []

    if "base_url" not in config:
        errors.append(ValueError("base_url is required"))
    elif not config["base_url"].startswith("http"):
        errors.append(ValueError(f"base_url must be absolute: {config['base_url']!r}"))

    if "timeout" not in config:
        errors.append(ValueError("timeout is required"))
    elif not isinstance(config["timeout"], int):
        errors.append(TypeError(f"timeout must be int, got {type(config['timeout']).__name__}"))

    if config.get("retries", 0) < 0:
        errors.append(ValueError(f"retries must be >= 0, got {config['retries']}"))

    if errors:
        raise ExceptionGroup("configuration is invalid", errors)


try:
    validate_config({"base_url": "staging.example.com", "timeout": "30", "retries": -1})
except* ValueError as eg:
    print(f"ValueErrors ({len(eg.exceptions)}):")
    for e in eg.exceptions:
        print(f"  - {e}")
except* TypeError as eg:
    print(f"TypeErrors ({len(eg.exceptions)}):")
    for e in eg.exceptions:
        print(f"  - {e}")

Output:

ValueErrors (2):
  - base_url must be absolute: 'staging.example.com'
  - retries must be >= 0, got -1
TypeErrors (1):
  - timeout must be int, got str

Line-by-line walkthrough:

  1. errors = [] — errors collect kiye, raise nahi kiye. Ye "collect all errors" pattern hai jo validation ke liye bahut better UX deta hai.
  2. elif — base_url hai toh uski value check karo. if/if likhne se missing key par KeyError aata.
  3. raise ExceptionGroup("configuration is invalid", errors) — message aur exceptions ki list. List khaali nahi ho sakti — ValueError: second argument (exceptions) must be a non-empty sequence. Isliye if errors: guard zaruri hai.
  4. except* ValueError as eg: — star syntax. eg ek ExceptionGroup hai jismein sirf matching exceptions hain.
  5. except* ke saare matching blocks chalte hain, sirf pehla nahi — ye normal except se bilkul alag hai. Yahan dono ValueError aur TypeError blocks chale.
  6. eg.exceptions — actual exceptions ka tuple.

docs.title: Nested groups aur subgroup/split
docs.text:
group = ExceptionGroup(
    "test suite failures",
    [
        ValueError("bad config"),
        ExceptionGroup(
            "browser failures",
            [TimeoutError("page load"), ConnectionError("proxy down")],
        ),
        TimeoutError("api call"),
    ],
)

# subgroup: matching exceptions ka naya group (structure preserve karke)
timeouts = group.subgroup(TimeoutError)
print(timeouts)
# ExceptionGroup('test suite failures',
#   [ExceptionGroup('browser failures', [TimeoutError('page load')]),
#    TimeoutError('api call')])

# split: (matching, non-matching)
matched, rest = group.split(TimeoutError)
print(len(matched.exceptions), len(rest.exceptions))

# Predicate se bhi
retryable = group.subgroup(lambda e: isinstance(e, (TimeoutError, ConnectionError)))
  1. subgroup nesting structure preserve karta hai — aapko pata chalta hai ki error kahan se aaya.
  2. split do groups deta hai; koi match na ho toh None.
  3. Predicate function bhi de sakte ho — flexible filtering.

docs.title: QA use case — parallel test execution
docs.text:
from concurrent.futures import ThreadPoolExecutor, as_completed


def run_suite_parallel(tests: list, max_workers: int = 4):
    """Saare tests chalao, saare failures collect karo -- pehle par ruko mat."""
    failures = []
    results = {}

    with ThreadPoolExecutor(max_workers=max_workers) as pool:
        future_to_test = {pool.submit(run_test, t): t for t in tests}

        for future in as_completed(future_to_test):
            test = future_to_test[future]
            try:
                results[test] = future.result()
            except Exception as e:
                e.add_note(f"test: {test}")            # 3.11+ context add kiya
                failures.append(e)

    if failures:
        raise ExceptionGroup(
            f"{len(failures)} of {len(tests)} tests failed", failures
        )
    return results


# Caller:
# try:
#     run_suite_parallel(all_tests)
# except* AssertionError as eg:
#     print(f"{len(eg.exceptions)} assertion failures -- likely real bugs")
# except* TimeoutError as eg:
#     print(f"{len(eg.exceptions)} timeouts -- likely infra, will rerun")
# except* Exception as eg:
#     print(f"{len(eg.exceptions)} other failures")

Line-by-line walkthrough:

  1. future_to_test = {pool.submit(...): t for t in tests} — future se test naam wapas map karne ke liye. as_completed order random hai, toh ye mapping zaruri hai.
  2. future.result() — worker mein jo exception aayi thi wo yahan raise hoti hai. Ye concurrent.futures ka design hai (Part 13).
  3. e.add_note(f"test: {test}") — kaunsa test fail hua, exception ke saath attach kiya.
  4. raise ExceptionGroup(...) — saare failures ek saath.
  5. except* se caller failures ko category-wise handle kar sakta hai — assertion failures real bugs hain, timeouts shayad infra. Ye ek genuinely useful CI pattern hai: "3 real failures, 12 timeouts — rerun the timeouts".

docs.title: except* ke rules
docs.text:
# 1. except aur except* MIX nahi kar sakte
# try:
#     pass
# except ValueError:
#     pass
# except* TypeError:            # SyntaxError
#     pass

# 2. except* ke andar 'as' variable HAMESHA ek group hai
try:
    raise ExceptionGroup("g", [ValueError("a")])
except* ValueError as eg:
    print(type(eg))                    # <class 'ExceptionGroup'>
    print(type(eg.exceptions[0]))      # <class 'ValueError'>

# 3. except* ek NORMAL exception ko bhi pakad leta hai (wrap karke)
try:
    raise ValueError("plain")
except* ValueError as eg:
    print(eg.exceptions)               # (ValueError('plain'),)

# 4. except* mein 'break'/'continue'/'return' allowed NAHI hai
# 5. BaseExceptionGroup -- jab group mein BaseException ho
try:
    raise BaseExceptionGroup("g", [KeyboardInterrupt()])
except* KeyboardInterrupt as eg:
    print("interrupted")

docs.title: Kab use karein
docs.text:
Use ExceptionGroup Don't Parallel operations (threads, asyncio TaskGroup) Sequential code jahan pehla error hi rok deta hai Validation — saare errors collect karo Ek hi cheez fail ho sakti hai Batch processing — har item ka result chahiye Fail-fast desired hai Test suites — saare failures report karo Simple helper functions

Note: asyncio.TaskGroup (3.11+) automatically ExceptionGroup raise karta hai jab kai tasks fail hon — toh async code mein aapko ye milega chahe aap chaho ya na chaho.

Interview answer: "ExceptionGroup, added in 3.11, carries multiple exceptions at once, and except* lets you handle them by type — with all matching clauses running, not just the first, which is the opposite of normal except. It exists because concurrency broke the one-exception model: when five parallel tasks fail, the old design could only surface one and silently dropped the rest. asyncio.TaskGroup raises one automatically for exactly that reason.

Where I'd use it in test infrastructure is twofold. Config validation: instead of raising on the first missing key, I collect every problem and raise them together, so the user fixes all five at once rather than rerunning five times. And parallel suite execution: collect the failure from every worker, attach the test name with add_note, and raise one group. The caller can then do except* AssertionError for probable real bugs and except* TimeoutError for probable infrastructure, and decide to rerun only the second set — which is a genuinely useful CI triage step. The mechanical details to remember are that the as variable is always a group even when only one exception matched, that the exceptions list can't be empty, and that subgroup and split let you filter while preserving the nesting so you can still see where each failure came from."

docs.title: 9.5 Why except: pass is the worst line in a test framework
docs.text: Ye section is doc ka sabse important practical section hai. Ise dhyaan se padho.

docs.title: Aapka apna bug — jo actually hua
docs.text:
Aapke suite mein ek date-picker fill karne wala helper tha, jo kuch aisa dikhta tha:

def fill_booking_date(page, date_str: str):
    page.click("#date-input")
    try:
        page.fill("#date-input", date_str)
    except:                                   # <- YE ek line
        pass
    page.click("#search")

Kya hua:

  1. Ek release mein date-picker widget badla. Naya widget #date-input ko readonly bana deta hai — aap type nahi kar sakte, sirf calendar se select kar sakte ho.
  2. page.fill("#date-input", date_str) ne exception di: Error: Element is not editable.
  3. except: pass ne use nigal liya.
  4. page.click("#search") chala. Search chala — default date ke saath (aaj ki date).
  5. Search results aaye. Test ne assert kiya "results dikh rahe hain" — PASS.
  6. Test hafton tak green raha. Poora date-filter feature toota hua tha aur suite bilkul khush thi.
  7. Bug production mein customer ne report kiya.

Ye ek "false green" hai, aur ye no-test se bura hai — kyunki no-test ke case mein aapko pata hota hai ki coverage nahi hai; false green mein aapko galat confidence hota hai.

docs.title: except: pass exactly kya karta hai
docs.text:
try:
    do_something()
except:              # bare except -- BaseException pakadta hai
    pass             # aur kuch bhi nahi karta

Ye teen alag paap ek line mein karta hai:

Paap 1 — Bare except: BaseException pakadta hai

import time

def long_running_suite():
    for i in range(1000):
        try:
            time.sleep(1)
        except:                       # KeyboardInterrupt bhi pakda gaya
            pass
# Ctrl+C KAAM NAHI KAREGA. Aapko kill -9 karna padega.
# SystemExit bhi pakda jaayega -- sys.exit() kaam nahi karega.
# GeneratorExit bhi -- cleanup toot sakta hai.

Paap 2 — pass matlab "mujhe pata hi nahi chala"

Exception ka poora point ye hai ki wo aapko batati hai ki kuch galat hua. pass us information ko delete kar deta hai. Wo information kabhi wapas nahi aati — na log mein, na report mein, na metrics mein.

Paap 3 — Wo code ke intent ko chhupa deta hai

Padhne wala nahi jaan sakta: - Kaunsi exception expected thi? - Ignore karna deliberate tha ya "TODO: fix later"? - Kya ye ab bhi zaruri hai?

6 mahine baad koi (aap) is line ko dekh kar sochega "shayad zaruri hoga" aur chhod dega.

docs.title: Failure ka spectrum — kaunsa kitna bura
docs.text:
# LEVEL 0 -- WORST: silent, universal
try:
    page.fill("#date-input", value)
except:
    pass

# LEVEL 1 -- BURA: specific type par abhi bhi silent
try:
    page.fill("#date-input", value)
except Exception:
    pass

# LEVEL 2 -- THEEK-THAAK: at least visible hai
try:
    page.fill("#date-input", value)
except Exception as e:
    print(f"could not fill date: {e}")        # print CI logs mein kho jaata hai

# LEVEL 3 -- BEHTAR: logged, specific
try:
    page.fill("#date-input", value)
except PlaywrightError as e:
    log.warning("could not fill date input: %s", e)

# LEVEL 4 -- ACHHA: specific, logged, AUR fallback hai
try:
    page.fill("#date-input", value)
except PlaywrightError as e:
    log.info("direct fill failed (%s); using calendar widget", e)
    select_date_from_calendar(page, value)     # ALTERNATIVE path

# LEVEL 5 -- SABSE ACHHA: pehle check karo, exception ki zarurat hi na ho
if page.get_attribute("#date-input", "readonly") is None:
    page.fill("#date-input", value)
else:
    select_date_from_calendar(page, value)

Level 4 aur 5 mein ek critical property hai: agar dono raaste fail ho jaayein toh test FAIL hoga. Level 0-2 mein test pass ho jaata hai.

docs.title: Sahi fix — aapke date-picker case ke liye
docs.text:
import logging
from playwright.sync_api import Error as PlaywrightError, TimeoutError as PlaywrightTimeout

log = logging.getLogger(__name__)


class DateFillError(Exception):
    """Date input fill nahi ho paayi -- kisi bhi tareeke se."""


def fill_booking_date(page, date_str: str) -> None:
    """
    Date input bharo. Do strategies try karo. Dono fail hon toh RAISE karo.

    Verification bhi karo -- kyunki fill safal hone ka matlab hamesha
    "value set ho gayi" nahi hota (masked inputs, JS validation).
    """
    strategies = [
        ("direct fill", lambda: page.fill("#date-input", date_str)),
        ("calendar widget", lambda: _select_from_calendar(page, date_str)),
    ]

    errors: list[Exception] = []

    for name, strategy in strategies:
        try:
            strategy()
        except (PlaywrightError, PlaywrightTimeout) as e:
            log.info("date strategy %r failed: %s", name, e)
            errors.append(e)
            continue                                  # agli strategy try karo

        # Strategy ne exception nahi di -- par KYA VALUE ACTUALLY SET HUI?
        actual = page.input_value("#date-input")
        if actual == date_str:
            log.debug("date set via %s", name)
            return                                    # SAFAL
        log.info("strategy %r ran but value is %r, expected %r", name, actual, date_str)
        errors.append(ValueError(f"{name}: value not applied (got {actual!r})"))

    # SAARI strategies fail -- ab LOUDLY fail karo
    raise DateFillError(
        f"could not set date to {date_str!r} using any strategy. "
        f"Page: {page.url}. Attempts: {[str(e) for e in errors]}"
    ) from (errors[-1] if errors else None)


def _select_from_calendar(page, date_str: str) -> None:
    page.click("#date-input")                          # calendar kholo
    page.wait_for_selector(".calendar-popup", timeout=3000)
    page.click(f".calendar-day[data-date='{date_str}']")

Line-by-line walkthrough:

  1. class DateFillError(Exception): — apna exception. Caller isko specifically pakad sakta hai aur retry ya skip decide kar sakta hai.
  2. strategies = [("direct fill", lambda: ...), ...] — strategies ki list, naam ke saath. Naam log messages mein aata hai — debugging mein exactly pata chalta hai kaunsa raasta fail hua.
  3. except (PlaywrightError, PlaywrightTimeout) as e: — specific exception types. Agar AttributeError aaye (aapke code mein bug) toh wo pakdi nahi jaayegi aur turant surface karegi. Bare except isko bhi nigal leta.
  4. log.info(...) — visible, par test fail nahi karta abhi. Ye "expected fallback" hai.
  5. errors.append(e); continue — error record kiya, agli strategy par gaye.
  6. actual = page.input_value("#date-input") — ye sabse important line hai. page.fill() exception nahi deti ka matlab ye nahi hai ki value set ho gayi:
  7. Input masked ho sakta hai (__/__/____ format) aur aapki string reject ho jaaye.
  8. JS validation value ko clear kar sakti hai.
  9. React controlled input state se overwrite ho sakta hai. Aapka original bug isi verification ki kami se aur bhi bada tha.
  10. if actual == date_str: return — verified success.
  11. raise DateFillError(...) — saari strategies fail hone par LOUD failure. Message mein URL aur saare attempts hain — bug report ke liye ready.
  12. from (errors[-1] if errors else None) — aakhri underlying error ko cause banaya.

docs.title: Baaki except: pass ke pattern jo QA mein milte hain
docs.text:
Anti-pattern 1 — "optional element"

# BURA
try:
    page.click(".cookie-banner-accept")
except:
    pass

# SAHI -- explicitly "hai ya nahi" check karo
banner = page.locator(".cookie-banner-accept")
if banner.count() > 0:                          # exception ki zarurat hi nahi
    banner.click()

# Ya, agar count() reliable na ho:
try:
    page.click(".cookie-banner-accept", timeout=1000)     # SHORT timeout
except PlaywrightTimeout:                                  # SPECIFIC exception
    log.debug("no cookie banner on this page")             # VISIBLE
  1. Short timeout — 1 second, 30 nahi. Cookie banner turant dikhta hai ya bilkul nahi.
  2. except PlaywrightTimeout — specific. Agar selector syntax galat ho toh wo alag exception degi aur surface karegi.
  3. log.debug — visible par noisy nahi.

Anti-pattern 2 — "cleanup jo fail ho sakta hai"

# BURA
def teardown():
    try:
        browser.close()
        db.disconnect()
        os.remove(temp_file)
    except:
        pass                                     # teen alag failures, sab chhupe

# SAHI -- har cleanup independent, har failure logged
def teardown():
    for name, action in [
        ("browser", browser.close),
        ("database", db.disconnect),
        ("temp file", lambda: Path(temp_file).unlink(missing_ok=True)),
    ]:
        try:
            action()
        except Exception as e:
            log.warning("cleanup of %s failed: %s", name, e)     # visible
  1. Original mein agar browser.close() fail ho toh db.disconnect() aur file cleanup chalte hi nahi — connection leak.
  2. Naye mein har cleanup independent hai aur har failure visible hai.
  3. Yahan except Exception acceptable hai kyunki cleanup ka failure test ko fail nahi karna chahiye — par wo logged hona chahiye. Ye Level 3 hai, Level 0 nahi.

Anti-pattern 3 — "parse jo fail ho sakti hai"

# BURA
def get_duration(row):
    try:
        return float(row["duration"])
    except:
        return 0.0                               # KyuN 0? Missing aur 0 mein farak khatam

# SAHI
def get_duration(row) -> float | None:
    raw = row.get("duration")
    if raw is None or raw == "":
        return None                              # "missing" explicitly
    try:
        return float(raw)
    except ValueError:
        log.warning("unparseable duration %r in row %r", raw, row.get("name"))
        return None                              # "invalid" bhi None, par LOGGED
  1. 0.0 return karna data corrupt karta hai — aapke average duration calculations galat ho jaayenge aur aapko pata nahi chalega.
  2. None "koi value nahi" ko honestly represent karta hai, aur downstream code use handle karne ko majboor hota hai.

Anti-pattern 4 — "flaky assertion"

# BURA -- ye literally test ko disable kar deta hai
try:
    assert page.locator(".total").inner_text() == "Rs 1,299"
except:
    pass

# SAHI -- agar test flaky hai toh use mark karo, chhupao mat
@pytest.mark.flaky(reruns=2)
def test_cart_total(page):
    assert page.locator(".total").inner_text() == "Rs 1,299"

# Ya, agar wo genuinely broken hai:
@pytest.mark.xfail(reason="BUG-1234: total shows stale value after coupon", strict=True)
def test_cart_total(page):
    assert page.locator(".total").inner_text() == "Rs 1,299"
  1. @pytest.mark.xfail(strict=True) — test expected to fail hai. Agar wo pass ho jaaye toh suite fail hogi ("XPASS strict") — matlab aapko pata chalega ki bug fix ho gaya aur marker hata sakte ho.
  2. Ye try/except: pass se infinitely better hai: intent documented hai, bug ID linked hai, aur fix hone par aapko pata chalega.

docs.title: Review checklist — except dekhte hi ye poochho
docs.text: Sawaal Agar jawab "nahi" hai Kya exception type specific hai? except Exception/except: ko specific karo Kya failure kahin visible hai (log/metric/report)? Logging add karo Kya try block sirf ek risky operation ke around hai? Chhota karo Kya koi fallback hai, ya sirf ignore kar rahe ho? Fallback add karo ya raise karo Agar fallback bhi fail ho toh kya test fail hoga? raise add karo Kya ek comment hai jo bata raha hai kyun ignore karna sahi hai? Comment likho Kya ye contextlib.suppress(SpecificError) ho sakta hai? Use karo — intent clearer

docs.title: Ek except: pass ka legitimate case
docs.text:
Sach mein ek hai — jab aap already failing ho aur cleanup best-effort ho:

def emergency_artifact_capture(page, test_name: str):
    """Test already fail ho chuka hai. Jo mil jaaye capture kar lo. Yahan failure acceptable hai."""
    with contextlib.suppress(Exception):
        page.screenshot(path=f"artifacts/{test_name}.png")
    with contextlib.suppress(Exception):
        Path(f"artifacts/{test_name}.html").write_text(page.content())
    with contextlib.suppress(Exception):
        Path(f"artifacts/{test_name}.log").write_text("\n".join(page.console_messages))

Kyun ye theek hai:

  1. Test already fail ho chuka hai — asli failure record ho chuki hai.
  2. Har capture independent hai — ek fail ho toh baaki try hote hain.
  3. contextlib.suppress se intent explicit hai — "ye deliberately best-effort hai".
  4. Agar screenshot fail ho toh original failure replace nahi hoti (8.1 ka gotcha).
  5. Aur ek comment hai jo bata raha hai kyun.

Iske alawa, except: pass hamesha ek bug hai ya ek TODO jo kabhi nahi hua.

Interview answer: "except: pass is the line I look for hardest in review, and I have a concrete reason. We had a helper that filled a date input with a bare try/except: pass around it. A release made that input readonly, so fill started throwing 'element is not editable' — and the except swallowed it. The test then clicked search with the default date, got results, asserted that results appeared, and passed. The whole date-filter feature was broken for weeks with a green suite, and a customer found it. That's worse than having no test, because a missing test is a known gap while a false green is active misinformation.

Mechanically it does three bad things at once. A bare except catches BaseException, so KeyboardInterrupt and SystemExit are caught too — Ctrl+C stops working during a long run. pass destroys the only signal that something went wrong. And it hides intent, so nobody can tell later whether ignoring the error was deliberate.

The fix I wrote has four properties: catch specific exception types so a bug in my own code still surfaces, log every attempt so the fallback path is visible, try an alternative strategy, and — critically — raise a custom DateFillError if every strategy fails, so the test goes red. I also added a verification step: fill not throwing doesn't mean the value was applied, because a masked input or a React controlled component can silently reject it. So after each strategy I read input_value back and compare. The only place I accept swallowing is best-effort artifact capture after a failure has already been recorded, and there I use contextlib.suppress per capture so the intent is explicit."

Cross-question — "Your team has a hundred except: pass lines in a legacy suite. How do you clean that up without breaking everything?" "I wouldn't do it in one pass — flipping a hundred silent swallows into raises would turn a green suite red overnight and nobody would trust the result. I'd do it in three stages. First, make them visible without changing behaviour: replace every bare except: pass with except Exception as e: log.warning('suppressed at %s: %s', __name__, e) — a mechanical change, scriptable with a codemod or caught by ruff's S110 and E722 rules, and it changes nothing about pass/fail. Run the suite for a week and collect the counts. Second, triage what the logs show: the ones that never fire get deleted; the ones that fire constantly are the real bugs and get tickets; the ones that fire occasionally get a specific exception type and a fallback. Third, add ruff with E722 and S110 as errors in CI so no new ones appear, and fix the backlog against the triage. The important part is that stage one is zero-risk and produces the data — you can't prioritise a hundred of anything without knowing which ones actually fire."

docs.title: 10.1 Imports — Python naam kaise resolve karta hai
Kya hai
docs.text: Module = ek .py file. Package = ek directory jismein modules hain (aur usually __init__.py).

docs.title: Kaise kaam karta hai — import ka poora flow
docs.text:
Jab aap import mypackage.mymodule likhte ho:

1. sys.modules mein dekho  -- already imported hai?
      HAAN -> wahi object do. BAS. (isliye import idempotent hai)
      NAHI -> aage

2. FINDERS se module dhoondho (sys.meta_path):
      a. BuiltinImporter    -- sys, time, math (C mein compiled, interpreter ke andar)
      b. FrozenImporter     -- frozen modules (importlib ka bootstrap)
      c. PathFinder         -- sys.path ke har entry mein dekho

3. sys.path ka order:
      a. Script ki directory (ya '' = current dir agar -c/-m/REPL)
      b. PYTHONPATH environment variable ki entries
      c. Installation-dependent defaults (site-packages)

4. LOADER module ko load karta hai:
      a. .pyc cache valid hai? -> usse load karo
      b. Warna: source padho -> compile -> .pyc likho -> load

5. Naya module object banao, sys.modules mein DAALO (recursion se pehle!)
6. Module ka code TOP-TO-BOTTOM execute karo
7. Naam ko current namespace mein bind karo

Step 5 sabse important hai: module sys.modules mein execute hone se pehle daala jaata hai. Ye circular imports ko partially kaam karne deta hai (10.4).

import sys

print(len(sys.modules))                    # startup par ~70-100 modules already loaded
print(sys.path)                             # search path
print("json" in sys.modules)               # False (abhi import nahi kiya)
import json
print("json" in sys.modules)               # True

# Module object dekho
print(json.__name__)                        # 'json'
print(json.__file__)                        # /usr/lib/python3.11/json/__init__.py
print(json.__package__)                     # 'json'
print(type(json))                           # <class 'module'>

docs.title: Import ke saare forms
docs.text:
# 1. Poora module
import json
data = json.loads("{}")

# 2. Module with alias
import numpy as np                          # convention se short alias

# 3. Specific names
from json import loads, dumps
data = loads("{}")

# 4. Name with alias
from json import loads as parse_json

# 5. Submodule
import os.path                              # 'os' aur 'os.path' dono import hote hain
print(os.path.join("a", "b"))               # 'os' se access karna padta hai

from os import path                         # ab seedha 'path'
from os.path import join                    # ab seedha 'join'

# 6. Star import -- ZYADATAR MAT KARO
from os.path import *                       # sab kuch namespace mein ghusa diya

# 7. Relative (sirf packages ke andar)
# from . import sibling_module              # same package
# from .helpers import click                # same package ka module
# from .. import parent_module              # ek level upar
# from ..utils.selectors import BUTTON      # do level upar, phir neeche

# 8. Conditional / lazy import
def heavy_operation():
    import pandas as pd                     # sirf tab import jab ye function chale
    return pd.DataFrame()

# 9. Dynamic import
import importlib
mod = importlib.import_module("json")
cls = getattr(importlib.import_module("mypackage.pages"), "LoginPage", None)

Line-by-line walkthrough:

  1. import json — module object ko json naam se bind karta hai. Module poora execute hota hai (uski top-level statements chalti hain).
  2. import numpy as np — alias. Ye convention communities mein standardised hai (np, pd, plt) — apne aliases mat banao.
  3. from json import loads — module phir bhi poora import hota hai aur sys.modules mein jaata hai; sirf naam binding alag hai. Ye "sirf ek function import kiya, isliye tez hai" wali galatfehmi door karta hai.
  4. import os.path — dono os aur os.path sys.modules mein jaate hain, par local naam sirf os bind hota hai.
  5. from os.path import * — problems:
  6. Kaun sa naam kahan se aaya, pata nahi chalta.
  7. Existing names silently shadow ho sakte hain.
  8. Linters (F403, F405) unused/undefined detect nahi kar paate.
  9. Sirf tab acceptable jab module explicitly __all__ define karta ho aur wo DSL-style ho (jaise from tkinter import *).
  10. Relative imports — sirf package ke andar kaam karte hain. Script ko directly chalane par ImportError: attempted relative import with no known parent package.
  11. Lazy import — startup time bachaata hai. conftest.py mein heavy imports (pandas, selenium) ko function ke andar rakhna collection ko tez karta hai.
  12. importlib.import_module(name) — string se import. Plugin systems ke liye.

docs.title: sys.path — kaha se aata hai
docs.text:
import sys

for i, p in enumerate(sys.path):
    print(f"{i}: {p!r}")

Typical output:

0: '/Users/ritik/project/tests'          <- script ki directory (ya '' REPL mein)
1: '/Users/ritik/project'                <- PYTHONPATH se
2: '/usr/lib/python311.zip'
3: '/usr/lib/python3.11'
4: '/usr/lib/python3.11/lib-dynload'
5: '/Users/ritik/project/.venv/lib/python3.11/site-packages'   <- installed packages

Shadowing ka khatra:

# Aapke project mein ek file: tests/json.py
# Ab 'import json' aapki file import karega, stdlib wali nahi!

# Ye common shadow-collisions hain jo real bugs bante hain:
# json.py, types.py, string.py, random.py, time.py, email.py, test.py,
# select.py, code.py, token.py, queue.py, copy.py, logging.py

Diagnose karna:

import json
print(json.__file__)          # agar ye aapke project mein point kare toh shadow hua hai

docs.title: import idempotent hai — aur uske consequences
docs.text:
# module_a.py
print("module_a is being executed")
CONSTANT = 42

# main.py
import module_a               # "module_a is being executed" print hoga
import module_a               # kuch NAHI hoga -- sys.modules se aaya
import module_a as ma         # kuch nahi -- wahi object, naya naam
print(module_a is ma)         # True
  1. Module ka code sirf ek baar chalta hai per process.
  2. Isliye module-level code (connections, config loading) sirf ek baar hota hai — ye faayda bhi hai aur khatra bhi.
  3. Reload karna: 
    import importlib
importlib.reload(module_a)          # code dobara chalta hai
    Par ye purane objects ko update nahi karta — jo instances pehle bane the wo purani class ke hain. Testing mein reload par bharosa mat karo.

docs.title: Gotchas
docs.text:
Gotcha 1 — from X import Y circular imports mein zyada tootta hai. (10.4)

Gotcha 2 — mutable module-level state shared hai.

# config.py
SETTINGS = {"env": "staging"}

# test_a.py
from config import SETTINGS
SETTINGS["env"] = "prod"           # POORE process ke liye badal gaya

# test_b.py
from config import SETTINGS
print(SETTINGS["env"])              # 'prod'  <- test_a ne badla tha

Ye 1.2 ka name-tag bug, module scale par. Fix: config ko immutable rakho ya factory se do.

Gotcha 3 — from module import name binding ka snapshot leta hai.

# counter.py
count = 0
def increment():
    global count
    count += 1

# main.py
from counter import count, increment
increment()
print(count)                        # 0  <- purana snapshot!

import counter
counter.increment()
print(counter.count)                # 2  <- module se padha, sahi value
  1. from counter import count — us waqt ki value ko count naam se bind kiya. Baad mein module mein count badla toh aapka local naam nahi badla.
  2. Rule: mutable/changing module state ke liye import module use karo, from module import name nahi.

Interview answer: "Import first checks sys.modules — that cache is what makes imports idempotent, so a module's top-level code runs exactly once per process no matter how many times it's imported. If it's not cached, finders search sys.path, whose first entry is the script's directory, then PYTHONPATH, then site-packages. That ordering is why a file called json.py in your test directory shadows the standard library — I've debugged that, and the diagnostic is printing json.__file__. A detail that matters for circular imports is that the module object is put into sys.modules before its body executes, which is why a partially-initialised module can be observed. And from module import name binds the value at import time, so if the module rebinds that name later your copy doesn't see it — for anything that changes I import the module and access through it."

docs.title: __init__.py
docs.text:
Kya hai: wo file jo ek directory ko package banati hai (aur jo package import hone par chalti hai).

tests/
  __init__.py           <- 'tests' ab ek package hai
  conftest.py
  pages/
    __init__.py         <- 'tests.pages' ek subpackage hai
    base_page.py
    login_page.py

Chaar kaam jo __init__.py karta hai:

1. Directory ko package banana (Python 3.3+ mein optional)

# Python 3.3+ mein "namespace packages" hain -- __init__.py ke bina bhi import ho jaata hai
# PAR:
#   - Namespace packages dheeme hain (har import par filesystem scan)
#   - Tools (mypy, pytest, setuptools) unhe alag treat karte hain
#   - pytest ko rootdir/test discovery mein confusion hoti hai
# RULE: apne packages mein hamesha __init__.py rakho (chahe khaali ho)

2. Public API define karna

# tests/pages/__init__.py
"""Page objects for the application under test."""

from .base_page import BasePage
from .login_page import LoginPage
from .cart_page import CartPage
from .checkout_page import CheckoutPage

__all__ = ["BasePage", "LoginPage", "CartPage", "CheckoutPage"]
__version__ = "1.2.0"

# Ab user ko ye likhna padta hai:
from tests.pages import LoginPage                    # saaf

# ...na ki ye:
from tests.pages.login_page import LoginPage         # internal structure expose
  1. from .base_page import BasePage — relative import. Dot matlab "isi package se".
  2. __all__ — do kaam karta hai: from package import * ka scope define karta hai, aur documentation tools aur linters ko batata hai ki public API kya hai.
  3. Faayda: aap login_page.py ko login.py rename kar sakte ho aur sirf __init__.py badalna padega — koi user code nahi tootega.
  4. Trade-off: import tests.pages ab saare page modules import karega, chahe aapko ek hi chahiye. Bade packages mein ye startup slow karta hai.

3. Package-level initialisation

# tests/__init__.py
import logging
import os
from pathlib import Path

# Package-level constants
ROOT_DIR = Path(__file__).parent.parent
ARTIFACTS_DIR = ROOT_DIR / "artifacts"
ARTIFACTS_DIR.mkdir(exist_ok=True)

# Logging setup -- ek baar
logging.getLogger(__name__).addHandler(logging.NullHandler())
  1. Path(__file__).parent.parent — file ki location se project root. Ye os.getcwd() se behtar hai — CWD depends on kahan se aapne command chalayi, __file__ nahi.
  2. logging.NullHandler() — library code ka best practice. Ye "no handler" warnings rokta hai bina user ki logging config ko override kiye (Part 12).
  3. Caution: __init__.py mein heavy kaam (DB connections, file I/O) mat karo — wo har import par chalega aur startup slow karega.

4. Lazy imports (Python 3.7+)

# tests/pages/__init__.py -- heavy submodules ko lazy banao
from typing import TYPE_CHECKING

if TYPE_CHECKING:                                    # sirf type checker ke liye
    from .heavy_page import HeavyPage

__all__ = ["LoginPage", "HeavyPage"]


def __getattr__(name: str):
    """Module-level __getattr__ (PEP 562) -- lazy attribute access."""
    if name == "HeavyPage":
        from .heavy_page import HeavyPage
        return HeavyPage
    raise AttributeError(f"module {__name__!r} has no attribute {name!r}")
  1. def __getattr__(name) module level par — PEP 562, Python 3.7+. Jab bhi package par koi missing attribute access ho toh ye chalta hai.
  2. if TYPE_CHECKING: — ye block runtime par kabhi nahi chalta (TYPE_CHECKING runtime par False hai), par mypy use padhta hai. Isse type hints milte hain bina import cost ke.
  3. Ye pattern bade libraries (numpy, scipy) use karte hain.

docs.title: if __name__ == "__main__":
docs.text:
# tools/generate_report.py
"""Generate an HTML report from test results JSON."""

import json
import sys
from pathlib import Path


def load_results(path: Path) -> list[dict]:
    """Ye function import bhi ho sakta hai."""
    return json.loads(path.read_text(encoding="utf-8"))


def render_html(results: list[dict]) -> str:
    rows = "\n".join(
        f"<tr><td>{r['name']}</td><td>{r['status']}</td><td>{r['duration']:.2f}s</td></tr>"
        for r in results
    )
    return f"<table>{rows}</table>"


def main(argv: list[str] | None = None) -> int:
    """Entry point -- int return karta hai (exit code)."""
    argv = argv if argv is not None else sys.argv[1:]
    if not argv:
        print("usage: generate_report.py RESULTS.json", file=sys.stderr)
        return 2                                       # 2 = usage error (convention)

    path = Path(argv[0])
    if not path.exists():
        print(f"error: {path} not found", file=sys.stderr)
        return 1

    results = load_results(path)
    Path("report.html").write_text(render_html(results), encoding="utf-8")
    print(f"wrote report.html ({len(results)} results)")
    return 0                                           # 0 = success


if __name__ == "__main__":
    sys.exit(main())

Line-by-line walkthrough:

  1. if __name__ == "__main__": — __name__ ek automatic module attribute hai:
  2. Directly chalaya (python script.py) → __name__ == "__main__".
  3. Import kiya (import script) → __name__ == "script". Toh ye block sirf directly chalane par chalta hai.
  4. Kyun zaruri hai:
  5. File ko import kar ke uske functions test kar sakte ho, bina main logic chale.
  6. multiprocessing Windows par ise mandatory karta hai — bina iske infinite process spawning hoti hai (Part 13).
  7. pytest aapke test modules ko import karta hai — agar top-level par side effects hon toh collection ke waqt hi wo chal jaate hain.
  8. def main(argv=None) -> int: — argv parameter se main ko test kar sakte ho: 
    def test_main_with_missing_file():
    assert main(["nonexistent.json"]) == 1
    sys.argv ko directly padhna testing mushkil banata hai.
  9. sys.exit(main()) — main ka return value exit code banta hai. Exit code conventions: 0 = success, 1 = general error, 2 = usage/CLI error. CI pipelines exit code par depend karte hain.
  10. print(..., file=sys.stderr) — errors stderr par, output stdout par. Ye Unix convention hai aur piping ke liye zaruri hai.

docs.title: __main__.py — package ko executable banana
docs.text:
tools/
  __init__.py
  __main__.py           <- 'python -m tools' isko chalata hai
  report.py

# tools/__main__.py
from .report import main
import sys

if __name__ == "__main__":
    sys.exit(main())

python -m tools results.json         # tools/__main__.py chalega
  1. python -m package — package ke __main__.py ko chalata hai. pytest, pip, venv, http.server — sab aise chalte hain.
  2. python -m pytest vs pytest: python -m pytest current directory ko sys.path mein daalta hai, plain pytest nahi. Isliye import errors mein python -m pytest try karna pehla debugging step hai.

│   │

│   │   ├── test_orders.py

│   │

│       ├── test_retry.py
│       └── test_factories.py
│

Design decisions ka explanation:

  1. src/ layout — framework code src/ ke andar hai. Faayda: aap tests ko installed package ke against chalate ho, working directory ke against nahi. Isse "mere machine par chalta hai" wale bugs pakde jaate hain (missing __init__.py, missing package data).
  2. tests/ src/ se bahar — tests package ka hissa nahi hain, toh wo distribute nahi hote.
  3. Nested conftest.py — fixtures scope-wise. tests/ui/conftest.py ki fixtures sirf UI tests ko milti hain (10.5, Part 15).
  4. tests/unit/ — aapke framework ke apne tests. Ye ek senior signal hai: test code bhi code hai, aur uska bhi test hona chahiye. retry decorator ka unit test likhna trivial hai aur bahut value deta hai.
  5. exceptions.py alag — custom exception hierarchy ek jagah, taaki circular imports na hon (exceptions kisi par depend nahi karte).
  6. components/ — page objects ke andar reusable components. Composition (5.11).

docs.title: Gotchas
docs.text:
Gotcha 1 — tests/ mein __init__.py chahiye ya nahi?

Bina __init__.py:
  - pytest "rootdir-based" import mode use karta hai
  - Do alag directories mein same naam ki file (tests/ui/test_login.py aur
    tests/api/test_login.py) CLASH karti hain:
    "import file mismatch" error
  - Fix: __init__.py add karo, ya pytest ka importmode=importlib use karo

Ke saath __init__.py:
  - Test modules unique package paths mein hote hain -- koi clash nahi
  - Par: tests ab ek package hain, toh relative imports kaam karte hain

Recommendation: tests/ aur uski subdirectories mein __init__.py rakho, ya pyproject.toml mein:

[tool.pytest.ini_options]
addopts = "--import-mode=importlib"

Gotcha 2 — conftest.py mein __init__.py nahi hota.

conftest.py pytest ka special file hai — wo automatically discover hota hai, import statement ki zarurat nahi.

Gotcha 3 — script ko module ki tarah chalane par relative imports.

python src/qa_framework/pages/login_page.py      # ImportError: attempted relative import
python -m qa_framework.pages.login_page          # kaam karega

Interview answer: "__init__.py marks a directory as a package and runs on import. I use it for three things: re-exporting the public API with from .login_page import LoginPage plus an __all__, so callers write from pages import LoginPage and I can rename internal modules freely; defining package-level constants derived from __file__ rather than os.getcwd(), because the working directory depends on where the command was run; and adding a NullHandler to the package logger so library code doesn't hijack the application's logging config. Since 3.3 it's technically optional because of namespace packages, but I always include it — namespace packages are slower and confuse pytest's test discovery.

if __name__ == '__main__' works because __name__ is '__main__' only when the file is run directly, and the module's own name when imported. It lets me import a script's functions for testing without triggering its side effects — and on Windows it's mandatory for multiprocessing, otherwise child processes re-import the module and spawn infinitely. I put the actual logic in a main(argv=None) that returns an exit code, so I can unit-test the CLI without touching sys.argv.

For layout I use src/ for the framework and a separate tests/ tree with per-directory conftest.py files, plus a tests/unit/ directory testing the framework itself — the retry decorator and the data factories have their own tests, because test code is still code."

docs.title: Kya hai
docs.text:
# ABSOLUTE -- poora path root package se
from qa_framework.pages.login_page import LoginPage
from qa_framework.utils.retry import retry

# RELATIVE -- current module ki position se
from .login_page import LoginPage          # same package
from ..utils.retry import retry            # ek level upar, phir neeche
from . import base_page                    # same package ka module

docs.title: Dot ka matlab
docs.text:
qa_framework/
  __init__.py
  utils/
    __init__.py
    retry.py
  pages/
    __init__.py
    base_page.py
    login_page.py          <- hum yahan hain
    components/
      __init__.py
      navbar.py

login_page.py se:
  from . import base_page                   -> qa_framework.pages.base_page
  from .components import NavBar            -> qa_framework.pages.components.NavBar
  from .. import config                     -> qa_framework.config
  from ..utils.retry import retry           -> qa_framework.utils.retry
  from ... import something                 -> ERROR (qa_framework se upar kuch nahi)

Ek dot = current package, do dots = parent, teen = grandparent.

docs.title: Comparison
docs.text: Absolute Relative Readability Poora path dikhta hai Chhota, par context chahiye Package rename Har import badalna padta hai Internal imports safe Move a module Uske imports safe (agar package same ho) Depth badle toh dots badalne padte hain Script directly chalana Kaam karta hai ImportError Circular import risk Same Same PEP 8 recommendation Preferred Acceptable for intra-package Copy-paste between files Safe Depth par depend karta hai

docs.title: PEP 8 kya kehta hai
docs.text:
"Absolute imports are recommended, as they are usually more readable and tend to be better behaved. [...] However, explicit relative imports are an acceptable alternative to absolute imports, especially when dealing with complex package layouts where using absolute imports would be unnecessarily verbose."

Practical rule jo main use karta hoon:

Situation Use Package ke andar, sibling module Relative (from .base_page import BasePage) Package ke andar, doosre subpackage se Absolute (from qa_framework.utils import retry) Tests se framework import Absolute (from qa_framework.pages import LoginPage) Third-party libraries Absolute (koi choice nahi)

Kyun: relative imports package ko relocatable banate hain — agar aap qa_framework ko my_company.qa mein move karo toh internal imports nahi tootenge. Par do level se zyada dots (from ...utils import x) readability kill kar dete hain — wahan absolute better hai.

docs.title: Relative imports kab fail hote hain
docs.text:
# qa_framework/pages/login_page.py
from .base_page import BasePage

class LoginPage(BasePage):
    pass

if __name__ == "__main__":
    print(LoginPage())

python qa_framework/pages/login_page.py
# ImportError: attempted relative import with no known parent package

Kyun: jab aap file directly chalate ho toh uska __name__ "__main__" hota hai aur __package__ "" (khaali). Relative import ko resolve karne ke liye Python ko __package__ chahiye — wo nahi hai, toh fail.

Fix:

# Module ki tarah chalao
python -m qa_framework.pages.login_page

# Ya, agar src layout hai:
pip install -e .                     # package install karo (editable)
python -m qa_framework.pages.login_page

docs.title: Circular import mein relative vs absolute
docs.text: Dono equally affected hain — dots ka koi jaadu nahi. Par from X import Y (chahe relative ho ya absolute) import X se zyada tootta hai (10.4).

docs.title: Import ordering — PEP 8 + isort
docs.text:
"""Login page object."""

# 1. FUTURE imports (sabse pehle)
from __future__ import annotations

# 2. STANDARD LIBRARY
import logging
import os
import re
from dataclasses import dataclass
from pathlib import Path
from typing import TYPE_CHECKING

# 3. THIRD PARTY
import pytest
from playwright.sync_api import Page, expect

# 4. FIRST PARTY (aapka apna package)
from qa_framework.config import settings
from qa_framework.utils.retry import retry

# 5. LOCAL / RELATIVE
from .base_page import BasePage
from .components.navbar import NavBar

# 6. TYPE_CHECKING-only imports (runtime par nahi chalte)
if TYPE_CHECKING:
    from qa_framework.api.client import ApiClient

log = logging.getLogger(__name__)
  1. Har group ke beech ek blank line.
  2. Har group ke andar alphabetical order.
  3. import X from X import Y se pehle (har group ke andar).
  4. isort ya ruff --select I ye automatically karta hai — manually mat karo.
# pyproject.toml
[tool.ruff.lint]
select = ["E", "F", "I", "UP", "B", "SIM"]     # I = isort rules

[tool.ruff.lint.isort]
known-first-party = ["qa_framework"]

docs.title: TYPE_CHECKING — circular imports ka legitimate hal
docs.text:
from __future__ import annotations           # annotations ko strings banao
from typing import TYPE_CHECKING

if TYPE_CHECKING:
    from qa_framework.api.client import ApiClient      # sirf mypy ke liye


class LoginPage:
    def __init__(self, page, api: ApiClient):          # annotation string hai
        self.page = page
        self.api = api
  1. TYPE_CHECKING runtime par False hai, toh wo import kabhi nahi hota — koi circular import problem nahi.
  2. mypy TYPE_CHECKING ko True maanta hai, toh use type mil jaata hai.
  3. from __future__ import annotations — annotations evaluate nahi hoti (strings ban jaati hain), toh ApiClient ka runtime par exist karna zaruri nahi.
  4. Ye pattern circular type-only dependencies ka standard solution hai.

Interview answer: "Absolute imports spell the full path from the root package; relative imports use dots for position — one dot for the current package, two for the parent. PEP 8 prefers absolute because the path is explicit and it survives copy-paste, but explicitly allows relative for intra-package imports. My rule is relative for siblings inside the same subpackage, because that keeps the package relocatable — I can move qa_framework under a company namespace and nothing internal breaks — and absolute for anything crossing subpackages or coming from tests, because two or more dots gets unreadable fast. The gotcha is that relative imports fail when you run a file directly, because __package__ is empty; the fix is python -m package.module, or installing the project with pip install -e .. For import ordering I don't do it by hand — ruff with the isort rules enforces future, stdlib, third-party, first-party, local, with a blank line between groups."

docs.title: 10.4 Circular imports — kaise tootte hain aur kaise thik karo
Kya hai
docs.text:
Do (ya zyada) modules ek doosre ko import karte hain.

# page.py
from api import ApiClient                   # api ko import kiya

class Page:
    def __init__(self):
        self.api = ApiClient()


# api.py
from page import Page                       # page ko import kiya -- CIRCULAR

class ApiClient:
    def get_page(self) -> Page:
        return Page()

python -c "import page"
# ImportError: cannot import name 'ApiClient' from partially initialized module 'api'
#              (most likely due to a circular import)

docs.title: Kaise kaam karta hai — exact trace
docs.text:
1. python -c "import page"
2. sys.modules["page"] = <empty module object>          <- pehle daala, phir execute
3. page.py chalna shuru
4. Line 1: from api import ApiClient
5.   sys.modules mein "api" nahi hai -> import karo
6.   sys.modules["api"] = <empty module object>
7.   api.py chalna shuru
8.   Line 1: from page import Page
9.     sys.modules mein "page" HAI (step 2 se) -> use return karo
10.    PAR wo module abhi KHAALI hai -- class Page abhi define nahi hui!
11.    -> ImportError: cannot import name 'Page' from partially initialized module 'page'

Key insight: module sys.modules mein execute hone se pehle daala jaata hai, aur from X import Y ko Y abhi chahiye. Ye timing hi problem hai.

docs.title: Fix 1 — import module use karo, from module import name nahi
docs.text:
# page.py
import api                                  # module object le liya, attribute abhi nahi

class Page:
    def __init__(self):
        self.client = api.ApiClient()       # attribute RUNTIME par resolve hoga


# api.py
import page

class ApiClient:
    def get_page(self):
        return page.Page()                  # runtime par resolve

Kyun kaam karta hai:

  1. import api sirf module object maangta hai, uska koi attribute nahi. Wo object step 6 mein already bana tha (khaali hi sahi).
  2. api.ApiClient() jab call hoga tab attribute lookup hoga — us waqt tak dono modules poore load ho chuke honge.
  3. Ye sabse simple fix hai aur aksar kaam kar jaata hai.
  4. Limitation: agar aap module-level par api.ApiClient use karo (class body mein, ya default argument mein) toh phir bhi fail hoga.

docs.title: Fix 2 — Import ko function ke andar move karo (deferred import)
docs.text:
# page.py
class Page:
    def __init__(self):
        from api import ApiClient           # import CALL time par hota hai
        self.client = ApiClient()
  1. Import tab hota hai jab function chalta hai — module load ke baad.
  2. Cost: har call par sys.modules lookup (chhota, par non-zero). Hot loops mein noticeable ho sakta hai.
  3. Downside: import errors ab runtime par milte hain, import time par nahi — jo late feedback hai. Aur code padhne wale ko upar imports mein wo dependency nahi dikhti.
  4. Kab theek hai: genuinely optional/heavy dependencies, ya circular ko todne ka last resort.

docs.title: Fix 3 — TYPE_CHECKING (agar sirf type hint ke liye chahiye)
docs.text:
# page.py
from __future__ import annotations
from typing import TYPE_CHECKING

if TYPE_CHECKING:
    from api import ApiClient               # runtime par NAHI hota

class Page:
    def __init__(self, client: ApiClient):  # annotation ek string hai
        self.client = client
  1. Sabse clean fix jab dependency sirf typing ke liye ho.
  2. Zero runtime cost.
  3. mypy ko poora type info milta hai.

docs.title: Fix 4 — Dependency inversion (SABSE ACHHA)
docs.text:
Circular import aksar ek design smell hai — do modules ek doosre ko jaante hain, matlab unki responsibilities theek se separate nahi hain.

# --- BEFORE: page <-> api circular ---

# --- AFTER: dono ek third module par depend karte hain ---

# protocols.py (koi dependency nahi)
from typing import Protocol

class ApiClientProtocol(Protocol):
    def get(self, path: str) -> dict: ...
    def post(self, path: str, data: dict) -> dict: ...


# page.py
from protocols import ApiClientProtocol

class Page:
    def __init__(self, client: ApiClientProtocol):     # INJECTED, imported nahi
        self.client = client


# api.py
from protocols import ApiClientProtocol

class ApiClient:                                        # Protocol se inherit nahi kiya
    def get(self, path: str) -> dict: ...
    def post(self, path: str, data: dict) -> dict: ...


# main.py / conftest.py -- wiring ek jagah
from api import ApiClient
from page import Page

page = Page(client=ApiClient())

Kyun ye sabse achha hai:

  1. protocols.py ki koi dependency nahi hai, toh wo cycle mein aa hi nahi sakta.
  2. Page ko ApiClient ka concrete class nahi chahiye — sirf uska interface chahiye.
  3. Testing mein aap fake client inject kar sakte ho — koi mocking library nahi chahiye (5.11).
  4. Ye Dependency Inversion Principle hai: "depend on abstractions, not concretions".
  5. Wiring ek jagah (conftest.py, main.py) — jahan cycles ho hi nahi sakti.

docs.title: Fix 5 — Modules ko merge ya split karo
docs.text:
Agar A aur B itne coupled hain ki cycle ban rahi hai, toh do options:

1. MERGE: shayad wo ek hi module hone chahiye (dono ek concept ke do parts hain)

2. SPLIT: shayad ek common part hai jo teesre module mein jaana chahiye
   A -> C <- B    (C mein wo cheez jo dono ko chahiye)

QA framework mein practical example:

BEFORE (circular):
  pages/base_page.py    ---imports--> utils/waits.py
  utils/waits.py        ---imports--> pages/base_page.py   (BasePage type hint ke liye)

AFTER (split):
  protocols.py          (koi dependency nahi -- PageProtocol define karta hai)
  pages/base_page.py    ---imports--> protocols.py, utils/waits.py
  utils/waits.py        ---imports--> protocols.py

docs.title: Detect karna
docs.text:
# 1. Simple: import karke dekho
# python -c "import qa_framework.pages.login_page"

# 2. Import graph banao
# pip install pydeps
# pydeps qa_framework --max-bacon=2 --cluster

# 3. Import time verbose
# python -X importtime -c "import qa_framework" 2>&1 | sort -k2 -rn | head -20

# 4. Ruff / flake8 se
# ruff check --select TID  (tidy imports)

docs.title: Ek partial-import gotcha jo pakadna mushkil hai
docs.text:
# a.py
import b

X = "from a"

def get_x():
    return X


# b.py
import a

print(a.X)               # AttributeError: partially initialized module 'a' has no attribute 'X'
  1. Yahan import a safal ho gaya (module object mil gaya), par a.X abhi define nahi hua.
  2. Ye from a import X se bhi bura hai — kyunki error message thoda alag hai aur log confuse ho jaate hain.
  3. Sabak: circular imports mein module-level code kabhi doosre module ke attributes use na kare. Sirf function bodies mein.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
Fix Kab Trade-off import module instead of from module import name Quick fix, dono runtime par use hote hain Module-level use par phir bhi fail Function ke andar import Optional/heavy dependency Late errors, hidden dependency TYPE_CHECKING Sirf type hints ke liye chahiye Kuch nahi — best for this case Protocol + injection Design theek karna hai Ek extra module, thoda upfront kaam Merge/split modules Structural problem hai Refactor effort

Interview answer: "A circular import fails because the module object goes into sys.modules before its body runs, so when the cycle comes back around it finds a partially initialised module. from X import Y needs Y to exist right now, so it fails; plain import X only needs the module object, and attribute lookup happens at call time — which is why swapping to import module plus module.Name() is the quickest fix. Moving the import inside a function also works but defers the error to runtime and hides the dependency from anyone reading the file.

When the dependency is only for a type annotation — which is most of the cases I've hit — the clean fix is if TYPE_CHECKING: with from __future__ import annotations, since that import never runs but mypy still sees it. But my actual preference is to treat the cycle as a design signal. In our framework, base_page and waits imported each other. Rather than patching it, I extracted a protocols.py with a PageProtocol that has no dependencies at all, and had both import that. Now the page takes its collaborators by injection instead of importing them, which broke the cycle and also made the pages testable with a plain fake instead of patching."

docs.title: Kyu virtual environments
docs.text:
BINA venv (system Python):
  Project A ko playwright==1.40 chahiye
  Project B ko playwright==1.30 chahiye
  -> Dono ek hi site-packages mein -> CONFLICT
  -> pip install ek ko todta hai

  Aur:
  - sudo pip install system Python ko corrupt kar sakta hai (OS tools use karte hain)
  - "mere machine par chalta hai" -- kyunki aapke paas 40 extra packages hain
  - CI par alag versions -> alag behaviour -> flaky/failing tests

venv ke SAATH:
  project-a/.venv/lib/python3.11/site-packages/  <- playwright 1.40
  project-b/.venv/lib/python3.11/site-packages/  <- playwright 1.30
  System Python -- untouched

docs.title: Kaise kaam karta hai
docs.text:
python3 -m venv .venv

Ye banata hai:

.venv/
├── bin/                        # (Windows par Scripts/)
│   ├── python -> /usr/bin/python3.11    # SYMLINK system Python par
│   ├── pip
│   └── activate
├── lib/
│   └── python3.11/
│       └── site-packages/      # yahan packages install hote hain
└── pyvenv.cfg                  # config: home = /usr/bin, include-system-site-packages = false

Mechanism:

  1. .venv/bin/python system Python ka symlink hai (copy nahi) — toh venv chhota hota hai (~5 MB, poora Python nahi).
  2. Jab .venv/bin/python chalta hai, wo pyvenv.cfg dekh kar apna sys.prefix set karta hai.
  3. sys.prefix badalne se site-packages ka path badal jaata hai.
  4. activate script sirf PATH mein .venv/bin ko aage daalti hai — kuch magic nahi.
source .venv/bin/activate

# Verify karo
which python                    # /path/to/project/.venv/bin/python
python -c "import sys; print(sys.prefix)"        # /path/to/project/.venv
python -c "import sys; print(sys.base_prefix)"   # /usr  (system Python)

deactivate                      # PATH restore

Activation optional hai:

.venv/bin/python -m pytest      # activate kiye bina bhi kaam karta hai

CI scripts mein ye behtar hai — koi shell state par depend nahi.

docs.title: venv alternatives
docs.text:
Tool Kya karta hai Kab venv (stdlib) Basic isolation Default, koi extra install nahi virtualenv Tez, purane Python versions support Legacy projects pyenv Python versions manage karta hai Multiple Python versions chahiye poetry venv + dependency resolution + publishing Libraries, complex deps pdm poetry jaisa, PEP 582 support Modern alternative uv Rust mein, bahut tez pip+venv replacement 2024+, tezi se popular conda Python + non-Python deps (C libs) Data science, scientific

QA context mein: venv + pip kaafi hai. uv try karne layak hai — wo 10-100x tez hai aur CI time bachaata hai.

docs.title: pip — practical commands
docs.text:
# Install
pip install playwright                      # latest
pip install "playwright==1.40.0"            # exact
pip install "playwright>=1.40,<2.0"         # range
pip install "playwright~=1.40.0"            # compatible: >=1.40.0, <1.41.0
pip install -e .                            # editable/development install (current project)
pip install -e ".[dev]"                     # extras ke saath
pip install -r requirements.txt             # file se
pip install --upgrade playwright
pip install --no-deps playwright            # dependencies mat install karo

# Inspect
pip list                                    # sab installed
pip list --outdated                         # kaunse purane hain
pip show playwright                         # ek package ki detail
pip show -f playwright                      # + files
pip freeze                                  # requirements.txt format mein exact versions

# Debug
pip check                                   # dependency conflicts dhoondho
pip download playwright -d ./wheels         # download without install
pip install --dry-run playwright            # kya hoga, batao (pip 22.2+)

# Uninstall
pip uninstall playwright

docs.title: requirements.txt — do file ka pattern
docs.text:
# requirements.in  -- INSAAN likhta hai: direct dependencies, loose versions
playwright>=1.40,<2.0
pytest>=7.4
pytest-xdist>=3.5
pytest-html>=4.1
requests>=2.31
pyyaml>=6.0

# requirements.txt -- TOOL generate karta hai: exact versions, transitive deps, hashes
#
#    pip-compile requirements.in
#
attrs==23.2.0
    # via pytest
certifi==2024.2.2
    # via requests
charset-normalizer==3.3.2
    # via requests
execnet==2.0.2
    # via pytest-xdist
greenlet==3.0.3
    # via playwright
idna==3.6
    # via requests
