# qa_framework/__init__.py
import logging

logging.getLogger(__name__).addHandler(logging.NullHandler())

Kyun:

  1. Agar library ka logger ke paas koi handler na ho aur user ne logging configure na ki ho, toh Python "No handlers could be found for logger X" warning deta hai (Python 2) ya "last resort" handler use karta hai jo WARNING+ ko stderr par bhejta hai (Python 3).
  2. NullHandler ye rok deta hai — library chup rehti hai jab tak user configure na kare.
  3. Library kabhi basicConfig ya setLevel na kare — wo application ka kaam hai. Library sirf logger banaye aur log kare.

# conftest.py
import logging
import os
from pathlib import Path
import pytest


def pytest_configure(config):
    """pytest startup par logging setup karo."""
    worker_id = os.environ.get("PYTEST_XDIST_WORKER", "master")
    log_dir = Path("artifacts/logs")
    setup_logging(
        level=config.getoption("--log-level") or "INFO",
        log_file=log_dir / f"test_{worker_id}.log",
        worker_id=worker_id,
    )


@pytest.fixture(autouse=True)
def log_test_boundaries(request):
    """Har test ke start aur end par ek marker log karo."""
    log = logging.getLogger("qa_framework.test")
    log.info("=" * 70)
    log.info("START %s", request.node.nodeid)
    yield
    outcome = "PASSED"
    if hasattr(request.node, "rep_call") and request.node.rep_call.failed:
        outcome = "FAILED"
    log.info("END   %s -> %s", request.node.nodeid, outcome)


@pytest.hookimpl(hookwrapper=True)
def pytest_runtest_makereport(item, call):
    """Test outcome ko item par attach karo taaki fixtures use padh saken."""
    outcome = yield
    report = outcome.get_result()
    setattr(item, f"rep_{report.when}", report)

Line-by-line walkthrough:

  1. PYTEST_XDIST_WORKER — xdist ye env var set karta hai (gw0, gw1, ...). Master process mein nahi hota, toh default "master".
  2. Per-worker log file — parallel runs mein ye zaruri hai, warna sab ek file mein likhte hain aur output interleave ho jaata hai.
  3. @pytest.fixture(autouse=True) — har test par automatically. Test boundaries se log file navigate karna aasan ho jaata hai.
  4. request.node.nodeid — full test ID (tests/test_login.py::test_valid[chromium]).
  5. pytest_runtest_makereport hook — test ka result fixture tak pahunchane ka standard tareeka. rep_setup, rep_call, rep_teardown attributes set hote hain.

pytest ke built-in logging options:

# pyproject.toml
[tool.pytest.ini_options]
log_cli = true                                   # live logs during run
log_cli_level = "INFO"
log_cli_format = "%(asctime)s %(levelname)-8s %(name)s %(message)s"
log_cli_date_format = "%H:%M:%S"

log_file = "artifacts/pytest.log"                # file mein bhi
log_file_level = "DEBUG"
log_file_format = "%(asctime)s %(levelname)-8s %(name)s:%(lineno)d %(message)s"

# caplog fixture -- logs par assert karo
def test_retry_logs_warning(caplog):
    with caplog.at_level(logging.WARNING):
        flaky_operation()

    assert "retrying" in caplog.text
    warnings = [r for r in caplog.records if r.levelno == logging.WARNING]
    assert len(warnings) == 2
    assert warnings[0].name == "qa_framework.utils.retry"
  1. caplog.text — poora captured output.
  2. caplog.records — LogRecord objects, jinme structured access hai.
  3. caplog.at_level(...) — temporarily level badlo.

import json
import logging
from datetime import datetime, timezone


class JsonFormatter(logging.Formatter):
    """Structured JSON logs -- log aggregators (ELK, Datadog) ke liye."""

    RESERVED = {
        "name", "msg", "args", "levelname", "levelno", "pathname", "filename",
        "module", "exc_info", "exc_text", "stack_info", "lineno", "funcName",
        "created", "msecs", "relativeCreated", "thread", "threadName",
        "processName", "process", "message", "asctime", "taskName",
    }

    def format(self, record: logging.LogRecord) -> str:
        payload = {
            "timestamp": datetime.fromtimestamp(record.created, timezone.utc).isoformat(),
            "level": record.levelname,
            "logger": record.name,
            "message": record.getMessage(),               # args apply karta hai
            "module": record.module,
            "function": record.funcName,
            "line": record.lineno,
        }

        if record.exc_info:
            payload["exception"] = self.formatException(record.exc_info)

        # extra= se aaye custom fields
        for key, value in record.__dict__.items():
            if key not in self.RESERVED and not key.startswith("_"):
                payload[key] = value

        return json.dumps(payload, default=str)           # default=str -- non-serialisable safe

Line-by-line walkthrough:

  1. record.getMessage() — record.msg % record.args apply karta hai. record.msg directly use mat karo — usme %s placeholders reh jaayenge.
  2. RESERVED set — built-in LogRecord attributes. Baaki sab extra= se aaye hain.
  3. default=str in json.dumps — agar extra mein koi non-serialisable object ho toh str() se convert ho jaayega, crash nahi hoga. Logging kabhi crash nahi karni chahiye.
  4. ISO timestamp with UTC — log aggregators ke liye standard.

docs.title: Gotchas
docs.text:
Gotcha 1 — basicConfig sirf ek baar kaam karta hai.

import logging
logging.basicConfig(level=logging.INFO)
logging.basicConfig(level=logging.DEBUG)          # IGNORE ho gaya!
print(logging.getLogger().level)                  # 20 (INFO)

logging.basicConfig(level=logging.DEBUG, force=True)   # 3.8+: force se reconfigure
print(logging.getLogger().level)                  # 10 (DEBUG)

basicConfig root logger par handler add karta hai agar wahan pehle se handler na ho.

Gotcha 2 — duplicate log lines.

import logging
log = logging.getLogger("myapp")
log.addHandler(logging.StreamHandler())
logging.basicConfig()                              # root par bhi handler laga
log.warning("test")                                # DO baar print hoga (propagation se)

# Fix: log.propagate = False   ya  root par handler mat lagao

Gotcha 3 — logger ke bajaye module-level logging.info().

import logging
logging.info("message")            # ROOT logger use karta hai -- naam nahi, filter nahi kar sakte
log = logging.getLogger(__name__)
log.info("message")                # SAHI

Gotcha 4 — f-string in logging.

import logging
log = logging.getLogger(__name__)
# log.debug(f"payload: {build_huge_payload()}")    # ALWAYS evaluates
log.debug("payload: %s", lazy_payload_object)      # sirf tab jab emit ho

Gotcha 5 — extra keys ka clash.

import logging
log = logging.getLogger(__name__)
# log.info("test", extra={"message": "x"})     # KeyError: "Attempt to overwrite 'message'"
log.info("test", extra={"custom_message": "x"})  # sahi

Interview answer: "Logging beats print because you get levels you can filter at runtime, a logger name that maps to the module hierarchy, and pluggable handlers so the same call can go to the console, a file, and a log aggregator with different levels and formats. In every module I write log = logging.getLogger(__name__), which makes the logger name the dotted module path — so I can turn on DEBUG for one page object without drowning in Playwright's internals.

Configuration lives in one place, dictConfig at the entry point, and I always set disable_existing_loggers: False, because the default silently kills every logger created before the config runs — which is most third-party libraries. Console gets INFO with a compact format; the file handler gets DEBUG with function name and line number, and it's a RotatingFileHandler so a long suite doesn't fill the disk.

Two rules on call sites. Always %s-style arguments, never f-strings, so the message is only formatted if the record is actually emitted — ruff's G004 enforces that. And log.exception inside an except block, because it attaches the traceback automatically. For parallel runs I add a logging Filter that stamps the PYTEST_XDIST_WORKER id onto every record and writes a per-worker file — without that, interleaved output from eight workers is unusable. And in tests, caplog lets me assert on log records, which is how I verify that the retry decorator actually warned rather than silently retrying."

docs.title: subprocess.run — modern API
docs.text:
import subprocess
from pathlib import Path

result = subprocess.run(
    ["pytest", "tests/", "-v", "--tb=short"],       # LIST, string nahi
    capture_output=True,                             # stdout aur stderr capture karo
    text=True,                                       # bytes ki jagah str do
    timeout=600,                                     # 10 minute -- HAMESHA timeout do
    cwd=Path("/path/to/project"),                    # working directory
    env={**os.environ, "TEST_ENV": "staging"},       # environment
    check=False,                                     # non-zero exit par raise mat karo
)

print(result.returncode)          # 0 = success, non-zero = failure
print(result.stdout)              # captured stdout
print(result.stderr)              # captured stderr
print(result.args)                # jo command chalayi thi

Line-by-line walkthrough:

  1. ["pytest", "tests/", ...] — list of arguments, string nahi. Ye sabse important security rule hai (neeche detail).
  2. capture_output=True — stdout=PIPE, stderr=PIPE ka short form. Bina iske output parent ke stdout par jaata hai.
  3. text=True — bytes ki jagah str deta hai, locale encoding se decode karke. encoding="utf-8" explicitly dena behtar hai: 
    subprocess.run([...], capture_output=True, encoding="utf-8", errors="replace")
  4. timeout=600 — HAMESHA do. Bina timeout ke ek hung process aapki poori CI job ko block kar dega jab tak CI ka apna timeout na aaye (aksar 60 minutes).
  5. cwd=... — working directory. os.chdir() se better (jo global state hai aur parallel tests mein disaster).
  6. env={**os.environ, "TEST_ENV": "staging"} — os.environ ko spread karna zaruri hai. env={"TEST_ENV": "staging"} likhne se PATH bhi gayab ho jaayega aur command hi nahi milegi.
  7. check=False (default) — non-zero exit code par exception nahi. check=True se CalledProcessError.

docs.title: Shell injection — sabse bada khatra
docs.text:
import subprocess

test_filter = input("Enter test name: ")           # user input

# --- KHATARNAK ---
# subprocess.run(f"pytest -k {test_filter}", shell=True)
# User type kare: "test_login; rm -rf /"
# -> Command banti hai: pytest -k test_login; rm -rf /
# -> DONO chalti hain

# --- SAFE ---
subprocess.run(["pytest", "-k", test_filter])      # shell involved hi nahi
# 'test_login; rm -rf /' ek SINGLE argument hai, ek command nahi

shell=True kab zaruri hai:

import subprocess
import shlex

# 1. Shell features chahiye: pipes, redirection, globs, variable expansion
subprocess.run("pytest tests/ | tee output.log", shell=True)          # pipe
subprocess.run("pytest tests/*.py", shell=True)                        # glob

# 2. Par ye BINA shell ke bhi ho sakta hai:
from pathlib import Path
files = [str(p) for p in Path("tests").glob("*.py")]                   # Python mein glob
subprocess.run(["pytest", *files])

# 3. Agar shell=True zaruri hi ho toh quote karo
user_input = "test_login; rm -rf /"
safe_cmd = f"pytest -k {shlex.quote(user_input)}"
print(safe_cmd)
# pytest -k 'test_login; rm -rf /'      <- quoted, ek argument
  1. shlex.quote() — string ko shell-safe banata hai.
  2. Par best answer ye hai: shell=True avoid karo. 95% cases mein list form kaam karta hai.
  3. shlex.split() — ulta kaam: shell-style string ko list mein todta hai: 
    import shlex
print(shlex.split('pytest -k "test login" --tb=short'))
# ['pytest', '-k', 'test login', '--tb=short']

docs.title: Error handling
docs.text:
import subprocess


def run_tests(paths: list[str], *, timeout: int = 600) -> tuple[int, str, str]:
    """Tests chalao, structured result do."""
    try:
        result = subprocess.run(
            ["pytest", *paths, "--tb=short", "-q"],
            capture_output=True,
            encoding="utf-8",
            errors="replace",
            timeout=timeout,
            check=False,
        )
        return result.returncode, result.stdout, result.stderr

    except FileNotFoundError as e:
        raise RuntimeError(
            "pytest not found on PATH. Is the virtualenv activated?"
        ) from e

    except subprocess.TimeoutExpired as e:
        # TimeoutExpired mein partial output hota hai!
        partial_out = (e.stdout or b"").decode("utf-8", errors="replace") if isinstance(e.stdout, bytes) else (e.stdout or "")
        raise TimeoutError(
            f"pytest timed out after {timeout}s.\n"
            f"Last output:\n{partial_out[-2000:]}"
        ) from e

    except subprocess.CalledProcessError as e:                  # check=True hone par
        raise RuntimeError(f"pytest failed with exit code {e.returncode}") from e


# pytest ke exit codes -- ye jaanna interview mein achha point hai
PYTEST_EXIT_CODES = {
    0: "all tests passed",
    1: "some tests failed",
    2: "interrupted by user (Ctrl+C)",
    3: "internal error",
    4: "command line usage error",
    5: "no tests collected",              # <- ye CI mein aksar galat pass ban jaata hai!
}

code, out, err = run_tests(["tests/smoke"])
print(f"{code}: {PYTEST_EXIT_CODES.get(code, 'unknown')}")

Line-by-line walkthrough:

  1. FileNotFoundError — command hi nahi mili. Actionable message zaruri hai.
  2. subprocess.TimeoutExpired — e.stdout aur e.stderr mein timeout tak ka output hota hai. Ye debugging ke liye critical hai — "process hang kahan hua".
  3. partial_out[-2000:] — aakhri 2000 characters. Poora output error message mein daalna unusable hai.
  4. PYTEST_EXIT_CODES — exit code 5 ("no tests collected") sabse khatarnak hai. Agar aapki CI sirf if returncode == 0 check kare toh 5 fail dikhega (theek), par agar aap returncode != 1 check karo toh 5 pass ban jaayega — aur aapke tests chale hi nahi.

docs.title: Streaming output — long-running processes
docs.text:
import subprocess
import sys
from typing import Iterator


def run_streaming(cmd: list[str], *, timeout: int | None = None) -> Iterator[str]:
    """
    Output ko live stream karo, poore process ke khatam hone ka wait kiye bina.
    Long-running test suites ke liye zaruri hai -- warna CI 30 minute tak kuch nahi dikhata.
    """
    process = subprocess.Popen(
        cmd,
        stdout=subprocess.PIPE,
        stderr=subprocess.STDOUT,                  # stderr ko stdout mein merge karo
        encoding="utf-8",
        errors="replace",
        bufsize=1,                                 # line buffered
    )
    try:
        assert process.stdout is not None
        for line in process.stdout:                # blocking read, line by line
            yield line.rstrip("\n")
        process.wait(timeout=timeout)
    except BaseException:
        process.kill()                             # generator abort hua -> process maar do
        process.wait()
        raise
    finally:
        if process.stdout:
            process.stdout.close()

    if process.returncode != 0:
        raise subprocess.CalledProcessError(process.returncode, cmd)


# Use:
# for line in run_streaming(["pytest", "tests/", "-v"]):
#     print(line)
#     if "FAILED" in line:
#         send_slack_alert(line)                   # REAL TIME reaction

Line-by-line walkthrough:

  1. subprocess.Popen — run se low-level. run internally Popen use karta hai aur wait karta hai. Streaming ke liye Popen chahiye.
  2. stderr=subprocess.STDOUT — dono streams merge. Ye ordering preserve karta hai (alag pipes mein interleaving lost ho jaati hai).
  3. bufsize=1 — line buffered. Bina iske output chunks mein aata hai aur "live" nahi lagta.
  4. for line in process.stdout: — file object iterator (Part 6). Blocking hai — agli line ka wait karta hai.
  5. except BaseException: process.kill() — ye critical hai. Agar consumer generator ko abandon kar de (break ya exception), toh child process zombie ban jaayega. kill() + wait() usko clean karta hai.
  6. process.wait() after kill() — zombie process reap karne ke liye zaruri hai.

docs.title: Deadlock — classic Popen bug
docs.text:
import subprocess

# --- DEADLOCK ---
# process = subprocess.Popen(cmd, stdout=subprocess.PIPE, stderr=subprocess.PIPE)
# process.wait()                    # child ke khatam hone ka wait
# out = process.stdout.read()       # yahan kabhi nahi pahunchte
#
# Kyun: OS pipe buffer limited hai (~64 KB). Child usse zyada likhta hai ->
# pipe bhar jaati hai -> child BLOCK ho jaata hai -> kabhi exit nahi karta ->
# parent ka wait() kabhi return nahi karta -> DEADLOCK

# --- SAFE: communicate() ---
process = subprocess.Popen(["echo", "hello"], stdout=subprocess.PIPE, stderr=subprocess.PIPE, text=True)
out, err = process.communicate(timeout=60)      # dono pipes ko CONCURRENTLY drain karta hai
print(out.strip())

# --- Ya bas subprocess.run use karo ---
result = subprocess.run(["echo", "hello"], capture_output=True, text=True)
print(result.stdout.strip())

communicate() internally threads ya select use karke dono pipes ek saath padhta hai. Isliye deadlock nahi hota. subprocess.run hi use karo jab tak streaming na chahiye.

docs.title: Input dena
docs.text:
import subprocess

# stdin par data bhejo
result = subprocess.run(
    ["grep", "FAILED"],
    input="test_a PASSED\ntest_b FAILED\ntest_c FAILED\n",
    capture_output=True,
    text=True,
)
print(result.stdout)               # test_b FAILED / test_c FAILED

# Pipeline (do processes)
p1 = subprocess.Popen(["cat", "results.log"], stdout=subprocess.PIPE)
p2 = subprocess.Popen(["grep", "ERROR"], stdin=p1.stdout, stdout=subprocess.PIPE, text=True)
p1.stdout.close()                  # p1 ko SIGPIPE milega agar p2 pehle exit kare
out, _ = p2.communicate()
  1. input=... — stdin par data. text=True ke saath string, warna bytes.
  2. p1.stdout.close() parent mein — zaruri hai, warna p2 exit hone par p1 ko SIGPIPE nahi milega aur wo hang kar sakta hai.
  3. Realistically: Python mein pipeline banane se better hai ki aap p1 ka output Python mein padho aur filter karo — clearer aur debuggable.

docs.title: QA use cases
docs.text:
import subprocess
import json
import re
from pathlib import Path


def get_git_info() -> dict:
    """Test report mein git context add karo."""
    def git(*args) -> str:
        return subprocess.run(
            ["git", *args], capture_output=True, text=True, check=True, timeout=10
        ).stdout.strip()

    try:
        return {
            "commit": git("rev-parse", "HEAD"),
            "short_commit": git("rev-parse", "--short", "HEAD"),
            "branch": git("rev-parse", "--abbrev-ref", "HEAD"),
            "author": git("log", "-1", "--pretty=%an"),
            "message": git("log", "-1", "--pretty=%s"),
            "dirty": bool(git("status", "--porcelain")),
        }
    except (subprocess.CalledProcessError, FileNotFoundError):
        return {"commit": "unknown", "branch": "unknown", "dirty": False}


def install_playwright_browsers(browsers: list[str] | None = None) -> None:
    """CI setup: browsers install karo."""
    cmd = ["playwright", "install", "--with-deps"]
    if browsers:
        cmd.extend(browsers)
    result = subprocess.run(cmd, timeout=600, capture_output=True, text=True)
    if result.returncode != 0:
        raise RuntimeError(
            f"playwright install failed (exit {result.returncode}):\n{result.stderr[-2000:]}"
        )


def run_and_parse_pytest(paths: list[str]) -> dict:
    """pytest chalao aur JSON report parse karo."""
    report_path = Path("artifacts/report.json")
    report_path.parent.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)

    result = subprocess.run(
        ["pytest", *paths, "--json-report", f"--json-report-file={report_path}", "-q"],
        capture_output=True,
        text=True,
        timeout=1800,
    )

    summary = {"exit_code": result.returncode, "stdout_tail": result.stdout[-1000:]}

    if report_path.exists():
        data = json.loads(report_path.read_text(encoding="utf-8"))
        summary.update({
            "total": data["summary"].get("total", 0),
            "passed": data["summary"].get("passed", 0),
            "failed": data["summary"].get("failed", 0),
            "duration": data.get("duration", 0),
        })
    else:
        # Fallback: stdout se parse karo
        m = re.search(r"(\d+) passed", result.stdout)
        summary["passed"] = int(m.group(1)) if m else 0

    return summary

Line-by-line walkthrough:

  1. def git(*args) — nested helper. check=True se non-zero exit exception deta hai — git commands ke liye ye theek hai (agar git fail ho toh humein pata hona chahiye).
  2. git("status", "--porcelain") — porcelain format machine-parseable hai. Khaali output = clean working tree.
  3. except (CalledProcessError, FileNotFoundError): return {...} — graceful degradation. Git info nahi mili toh test run nahi rukna chahiye.
  4. timeout=600 playwright install ke liye — browser downloads bade hain.
  5. result.stderr[-2000:] — truncated error. Poora stderr megabytes ka ho sakta hai.
  6. JSON report parse karna stdout parse karne se better hai — stdout format pytest versions ke saath badalta hai. Fallback rakha hai par primary structured data hai.

docs.title: shutil.which — command exist karti hai?
docs.text:
import shutil
import subprocess


def ensure_command(name: str, install_hint: str = "") -> str:
    """Command PATH par hai ya nahi, check karo -- CHALANE se pehle."""
    path = shutil.which(name)
    if path is None:
        msg = f"{name!r} not found on PATH"
        if install_hint:
            msg += f". {install_hint}"
        raise FileNotFoundError(msg)
    return path


ensure_command("pytest", "Run: pip install pytest")
ensure_command("git", "Install git from https://git-scm.com")

shutil.which PATH search karta hai aur full path deta hai. Ye pehle check karna better error deta hai than a raw FileNotFoundError from subprocess.

docs.title: Gotchas
docs.text:
Gotcha 1 — string vs list.

import subprocess
# subprocess.run("ls -la")                    # FileNotFoundError: 'ls -la' -- ek file naam samjha
subprocess.run(["ls", "-la"])                 # sahi
subprocess.run("ls -la", shell=True)          # kaam karta hai par shell involve hai

Gotcha 2 — env replace karta hai, merge nahi.

import os, subprocess
# subprocess.run(["python", "-c", "print(1)"], env={"MY_VAR": "x"})
# FileNotFoundError -- PATH gayab hai!
subprocess.run(["python", "-c", "print(1)"], env={**os.environ, "MY_VAR": "x"})    # sahi

Gotcha 3 — timeout na dena.

import subprocess
# subprocess.run(["some_hanging_command"])          # FOREVER
subprocess.run(["echo", "ok"], timeout=30)          # bounded

Gotcha 4 — exit code aur output ka confusion.

import subprocess
result = subprocess.run(["pytest", "tests/"], capture_output=True, text=True)
# if "passed" in result.stdout:               # FRAGILE -- "0 passed" bhi match karta hai
if result.returncode == 0:                    # ROBUST
    print("all passed")

Gotcha 5 — Windows par shell=True ke bina batch files.

import subprocess
# Windows par .bat/.cmd files ko shell chahiye
# subprocess.run(["setup.bat"])               # FileNotFoundError on Windows
# subprocess.run(["setup.bat"], shell=True)   # kaam karta hai

Interview answer: "subprocess.run is the modern API — os.system and os.popen are legacy. I always pass a list of arguments rather than a string, because that avoids the shell entirely: with shell=True and interpolated input, test_login; rm -rf / is two commands, whereas in list form it's one harmless argument. If I genuinely need a pipe or a glob I do it in Python instead, and only fall back to shell=True with shlex.quote when there's no alternative.

Three things I always set: timeout, because a hung child otherwise blocks the whole CI job until the job-level timeout; encoding='utf-8', errors='replace' rather than bare text=True, so mixed-encoding output doesn't crash the parser; and when passing env, I spread os.environ into it, because env replaces rather than merges and dropping PATH means the command isn't even found.

For long-running suites I use Popen with line buffering and yield lines as they arrive, so CI shows progress instead of thirty silent minutes — but with a kill() in the exception path, otherwise abandoning the generator leaves a zombie. The classic bug I'd point out is deadlocking on Popen by calling wait() before reading the pipes: the OS pipe buffer is about 64 kilobytes, the child blocks when it fills, and neither side ever finishes. communicate() drains both pipes concurrently, which is why run is safe."

docs.title: Kya hai
docs.text:
CLI arguments parse karne ka stdlib tool. sys.argv ko manually parse karna galat hai.

import argparse
import sys
from pathlib import Path


def build_parser() -> argparse.ArgumentParser:
    parser = argparse.ArgumentParser(
        prog="qa-runner",
        description="Run the QA automation suite",
        epilog="Example: qa-runner --env staging --browser chromium -m smoke",
        formatter_class=argparse.ArgumentDefaultsHelpFormatter,     # defaults help mein dikhao
    )

    # --- POSITIONAL ---
    parser.add_argument(
        "paths",
        nargs="*",                                   # 0 ya zyada
        default=["tests/"],
        help="test paths to run",
    )

    # --- OPTIONAL with choices ---
    parser.add_argument(
        "-e", "--env",
        choices=["local", "dev", "staging", "prod"],
        default="staging",
        help="target environment",
    )

    # --- MULTIPLE values ---
    parser.add_argument(
        "-b", "--browser",
        action="append",                             # -b chromium -b firefox
        choices=["chromium", "firefox", "webkit"],
        dest="browsers",
        help="browser to run against (repeatable)",
    )

    # --- BOOLEAN flags ---
    parser.add_argument("--headless", action="store_true", help="run headless")
    parser.add_argument("--no-headless", dest="headless", action="store_false")
    parser.set_defaults(headless=True)

    # Python 3.9+: BooleanOptionalAction se --flag / --no-flag automatic
    parser.add_argument(
        "--trace",
        action=argparse.BooleanOptionalAction,       # --trace / --no-trace
        default=False,
        help="record Playwright traces",
    )

    # --- TYPED arguments ---
    parser.add_argument("-w", "--workers", type=int, default=4, help="parallel workers")
    parser.add_argument("-t", "--timeout", type=float, default=30.0, help="timeout in seconds")
    parser.add_argument("--config", type=Path, default=Path("config.yaml"), help="config file")

    # --- CUSTOM type/validation ---
    def positive_int(value: str) -> int:
        n = int(value)
        if n < 1:
            raise argparse.ArgumentTypeError(f"must be >= 1, got {n}")
        return n

    parser.add_argument("--retries", type=positive_int, default=1)

    # --- COUNT (verbosity) ---
    parser.add_argument("-v", "--verbose", action="count", default=0,
                        help="increase verbosity (-v, -vv, -vvv)")

    # --- MUTUALLY EXCLUSIVE ---
    group = parser.add_mutually_exclusive_group()
    group.add_argument("--only-failed", action="store_true", help="rerun last failures")
    group.add_argument("--only-new", action="store_true", help="run only new tests")

    # --- VERSION ---
    parser.add_argument("--version", action="version", version="%(prog)s 1.2.0")

    return parser


def main(argv: list[str] | None = None) -> int:
    parser = build_parser()
    args = parser.parse_args(argv)                   # None -> sys.argv[1:]

    # Post-parse validation
    if not args.browsers:
        args.browsers = ["chromium"]
    if args.env == "prod" and not args.headless:
        parser.error("--no-headless is not allowed against prod")     # exit code 2
    if not args.config.exists():
        parser.error(f"config file not found: {args.config}")

    log_level = ["WARNING", "INFO", "DEBUG"][min(args.verbose, 2)]

    print(f"env={args.env} browsers={args.browsers} workers={args.workers}")
    print(f"headless={args.headless} trace={args.trace} log_level={log_level}")
    print(f"paths={args.paths}")
    return 0


if __name__ == "__main__":
    sys.exit(main())

Line-by-line walkthrough:

  1. formatter_class=ArgumentDefaultsHelpFormatter — --help mein har option ka default dikhata hai. Ye default hona chahiye tha — bina iske users guess karte hain.
  2. nargs="*" — 0 ya zyada positional. Options: "?" (0 ya 1), "+" (1 ya zyada), N (exactly N), argparse.REMAINDER (baaki sab).
  3. action="append" — -b chromium -b firefox → ["chromium", "firefox"]. default=[] mat do — argparse ka known bug hai ki default list mein append hota hai (1.4 wala bug). default=None rakho aur baad mein handle karo (jo maine kiya).
  4. dest="browsers" — attribute ka naam. Bina iske args.browser hota (singular).
  5. --headless / --no-headless + set_defaults — purana pattern. 3.9+ mein BooleanOptionalAction better hai — ek line mein dono flags.
  6. type=int — argparse conversion karta hai aur fail hone par clean error deta hai. type=Path bhi kaam karta hai (Path callable hai).
  7. def positive_int(value) — custom type function. ArgumentTypeError raise karo — argparse use clean CLI error mein badal deta hai (traceback nahi).
  8. action="count" — -vvv → 3. Verbosity ka standard pattern.
  9. add_mutually_exclusive_group() — dono ek saath dene par error.
  10. parser.parse_args(argv) — argv parameter se testable: 
    def test_prod_requires_headless():
    with pytest.raises(SystemExit) as exc:
        main(["--env", "prod", "--no-headless"])
    assert exc.value.code == 2
  11. parser.error(msg) — usage message print karke sys.exit(2) karta hai. Manual print + sys.exit se better — consistent format.

docs.text:
import argparse


def build_parser() -> argparse.ArgumentParser:
    parser = argparse.ArgumentParser(prog="qa")
    subparsers = parser.add_subparsers(dest="command", required=True, help="sub-command")

    # qa run ...
    run_p = subparsers.add_parser("run", help="run tests")
    run_p.add_argument("paths", nargs="*", default=["tests/"])
    run_p.add_argument("-e", "--env", default="staging")
    run_p.set_defaults(func=cmd_run)

    # qa report ...
    report_p = subparsers.add_parser("report", help="generate report")
    report_p.add_argument("results", type=str)
    report_p.add_argument("-f", "--format", choices=["html", "json", "md"], default="html")
    report_p.set_defaults(func=cmd_report)

    # qa clean ...
    clean_p = subparsers.add_parser("clean", help="remove artifacts")
    clean_p.add_argument("--older-than", type=int, default=7, metavar="DAYS")
    clean_p.set_defaults(func=cmd_clean)

    return parser


def cmd_run(args) -> int:
    print(f"running {args.paths} on {args.env}")
    return 0

def cmd_report(args) -> int:
    print(f"generating {args.format} report from {args.results}")
    return 0

def cmd_clean(args) -> int:
    print(f"cleaning artifacts older than {args.older_than} days")
    return 0


def main(argv=None) -> int:
    args = build_parser().parse_args(argv)
    return args.func(args)                           # dispatch


# main(["run", "tests/smoke", "-e", "prod"])
# main(["report", "results.json", "-f", "md"])
  1. subparsers.add_parser("run") — har subcommand ka apna parser aur apne arguments.
  2. set_defaults(func=cmd_run) — dispatch ka clean pattern. args.func(args) se sahi handler chal jaata hai — koi if/elif chain nahi.
  3. required=True — subcommand mandatory. Python 3.7+ mein ye explicitly dena padta hai.
  4. metavar="DAYS" — help mein --older-than DAYS dikhta hai, --older-than OLDER_THAN nahi.

docs.title: Config file + env vars + CLI — precedence
docs.text:
import argparse
import os
from pathlib import Path
import yaml


def load_config(cli_args: list[str] | None = None) -> dict:
    """
    Precedence (highest first): CLI > env vars > config file > defaults
    """
    DEFAULTS = {"env": "staging", "browsers": ["chromium"], "workers": 4, "headless": True}

    # 1. Config file
    file_config = {}
    config_path = Path(os.environ.get("QA_CONFIG", "qa.yaml"))
    if config_path.exists():
        file_config = yaml.safe_load(config_path.read_text(encoding="utf-8")) or {}

    # 2. Environment variables (QA_ prefix)
    env_config = {}
    for key, value in os.environ.items():
        if not key.startswith("QA_") or key == "QA_CONFIG":
            continue
        name = key[3:].lower()
        if name in ("workers",):
            env_config[name] = int(value)
        elif name in ("headless",):
            env_config[name] = value.lower() in ("1", "true", "yes")
        elif name in ("browsers",):
            env_config[name] = value.split(",")
        else:
            env_config[name] = value

    # 3. CLI (sirf jo EXPLICITLY diye gaye)
    parser = argparse.ArgumentParser()
    parser.add_argument("-e", "--env")
    parser.add_argument("-w", "--workers", type=int)
    parser.add_argument("--headless", action=argparse.BooleanOptionalAction, default=None)
    parser.add_argument("-b", "--browser", action="append", dest="browsers")
    args = parser.parse_args(cli_args)

    cli_config = {k: v for k, v in vars(args).items() if v is not None}   # None = "diya hi nahi"

    return {**DEFAULTS, **file_config, **env_config, **cli_config}

Line-by-line walkthrough:

  1. default=None har CLI argument par — ye critical hai. Agar aap argparse mein default do toh aap distinguish nahi kar paoge ki user ne value di ya default hai, aur CLI default config file ko override kar dega.
  2. {k: v for k, v in vars(args).items() if v is not None} — sirf explicitly diye gaye arguments.
  3. {**DEFAULTS, **file_config, **env_config, **cli_config} — dict merge, right wins (3.4). Precedence order visible hai.
  4. Env var type conversion manual — env vars hamesha strings hoti hain.
  5. Alternative: ChainMap (3.6.6) — same precedence, par layers alag rehti hain aur aap debug kar sakte ho ki value kahan se aayi.

docs.title: Gotchas
docs.text:
Gotcha 1 — action="append" with default=[].

import argparse
p = argparse.ArgumentParser()
p.add_argument("-b", action="append", default=["chromium"])
print(p.parse_args(["-b", "firefox"]))
# Namespace(b=['chromium', 'firefox'])     <- default ke UPAR append hua!

Default None rakho aur baad mein handle karo.

Gotcha 2 — hyphen dest mein underscore ban jaata hai.

import argparse
p = argparse.ArgumentParser()
p.add_argument("--log-level")
args = p.parse_args(["--log-level", "DEBUG"])
print(args.log_level)              # 'log_level', 'log-level' nahi

Gotcha 3 — type=bool kaam nahi karta.

import argparse
p = argparse.ArgumentParser()
p.add_argument("--flag", type=bool)
print(p.parse_args(["--flag", "False"]))
# Namespace(flag=True)    <- bool("False") == True !
# Fix: action="store_true" ya BooleanOptionalAction use karo

Gotcha 4 — nargs="+" aur positional ka clash.

import argparse
p = argparse.ArgumentParser()
p.add_argument("-b", nargs="+")
p.add_argument("paths", nargs="*")
# p.parse_args(["-b", "chromium", "tests/"])
# 'tests/' bhi -b mein chala jaata hai! nargs="+" greedy hai
# Fix: -- separator use karo: ["-b", "chromium", "--", "tests/"]

Interview answer: "argparse handles parsing, type conversion, validation, and --help generation. The details that make a CLI good: ArgumentDefaultsHelpFormatter so --help shows defaults; choices=[...] so invalid values fail at parse time with a clear message rather than deep in the code; custom type functions raising ArgumentTypeError for domain validation; and parser.error() for cross-argument rules, because it prints the usage line and exits with code 2, which is the conventional CLI usage-error code.

The structural thing I do is put everything in a main(argv=None) that returns an exit code and call parser.parse_args(argv). That makes the whole CLI unit-testable — I can assert that main(['--env', 'prod', '--no-headless']) exits with 2 without touching sys.argv. For subcommands, set_defaults(func=handler) on each subparser gives a clean dispatch with args.func(args) instead of an if-chain.

The one detail people get wrong is layered configuration. If you give argparse defaults, you can't tell whether a value came from the user or the default, so the CLI default silently overrides the config file. I set every CLI default to None, filter those out, and then merge defaults, then config file, then environment, then CLI — or use a ChainMap so I can still tell which layer a value came from."

docs.title: random
docs.text:
import random

# --- SEEDING -- reproducibility ke liye ---
random.seed(42)                             # global generator seed karo
print([random.randint(1, 100) for _ in range(5)])     # hamesha same

# --- Better: apna Random instance ---
rng = random.Random(42)                     # global state se independent
print([rng.randint(1, 100) for _ in range(5)])

# --- Integers ---
print(random.randint(1, 10))                # 1 se 10 INCLUSIVE
print(random.randrange(1, 10))              # 1 se 9 (stop exclusive, range jaisa)
print(random.randrange(0, 100, 5))          # 0, 5, 10, ... 95

# --- Floats ---
print(random.random())                       # 0.0 <= x < 1.0
print(random.uniform(1.0, 5.0))              # 1.0 <= x <= 5.0
print(random.gauss(mu=100, sigma=15))        # normal distribution
print(random.expovariate(lambd=1.0))         # exponential -- realistic wait times

# --- Sequences ---
items = ["chromium", "firefox", "webkit"]
print(random.choice(items))                  # ek item
print(random.choices(items, k=5))            # k items WITH replacement
print(random.choices(items, weights=[70, 20, 10], k=5))    # weighted
print(random.sample(items, k=2))             # k items WITHOUT replacement
shuffled = items.copy()
random.shuffle(shuffled)                     # IN-PLACE shuffle
print(shuffled, items)                       # original safe kyunki copy ki thi

Line-by-line walkthrough:

  1. random.seed(42) — global generator seed karta hai. Problem: koi doosri library bhi global generator use kar sakti hai aur aapki reproducibility tod sakti hai.
  2. random.Random(42) — apna instance. Ye isolated hai. Test data generation ke liye ye use karo.
  3. randint(1, 10) inclusive hai dono taraf — range se alag. Ye off-by-one ka source hai.
  4. choices (with replacement, k items) vs choice (ek item) vs sample (without replacement). Naam mila-jula hai, dhyaan rakho.
  5. weights=[70, 20, 10] — realistic distributions. Browser market share simulate karne ke liye.
  6. random.shuffle in-place hai aur None deta hai. random.sample(items, len(items)) naya shuffled list deta hai.

Test data generation:

import random
import string
from datetime import date, timedelta


class TestDataGenerator:
    """Reproducible test data -- seed do toh same data milta hai."""

    def __init__(self, seed: int | None = None):
        self.rng = random.Random(seed)

    def email(self, domain: str = "test.example.com") -> str:
        user = "".join(self.rng.choices(string.ascii_lowercase, k=8))
        return f"{user}@{domain}"

    def password(self, length: int = 12) -> str:
        """Valid password: upper, lower, digit, special -- har ek at least ek."""
        chars = [
            self.rng.choice(string.ascii_uppercase),
            self.rng.choice(string.ascii_lowercase),
            self.rng.choice(string.digits),
            self.rng.choice("!@#$%^&*"),
        ]
        pool = string.ascii_letters + string.digits + "!@#$%^&*"
        chars += self.rng.choices(pool, k=length - 4)
        self.rng.shuffle(chars)                       # positions randomise karo
        return "".join(chars)

    def phone_in(self) -> str:
        """Valid Indian mobile: 6-9 se shuru, 10 digits."""
        return f"{self.rng.choice('6789')}{''.join(self.rng.choices(string.digits, k=9))}"

    def pincode(self) -> str:
        return f"{self.rng.randint(1, 9)}{''.join(self.rng.choices(string.digits, k=5))}"

    def amount(self, min_val: float = 1, max_val: float = 100000) -> str:
        """Realistic amount -- log distribution (chhote amounts zyada common)."""
        import math
        log_val = self.rng.uniform(math.log(min_val), math.log(max_val))
        return f"{math.exp(log_val):.2f}"

    def future_date(self, min_days: int = 1, max_days: int = 90) -> date:
        return date.today() + timedelta(days=self.rng.randint(min_days, max_days))


gen = TestDataGenerator(seed=42)
print(gen.email(), gen.password(), gen.phone_in(), gen.pincode(), gen.amount())

gen2 = TestDataGenerator(seed=42)
print(gen2.email())                            # WAHI email -- reproducible

Line-by-line walkthrough:

  1. self.rng = random.Random(seed) — instance-level generator. seed=None par system entropy.
  2. password mein pehle 4 characters guarantee kiye, phir shuffle — ye zaruri hai kyunki pure random string password policy fail kar sakti hai (koi digit na ho).
  3. self.rng.shuffle(chars) — positions randomise, warna hamesha pehla character uppercase hota.
  4. amount mein log distribution — realistic test data. Uniform distribution mein 50% amounts 50,000 se upar honge, jo real e-commerce data nahi hai.
  5. Reproducibility ka faayda: flaky test debug karte waqt aap seed ko log kar sakte ho aur exact same data se test dobara chala sakte ho: 
    @pytest.fixture
def data_gen(request):
    seed = request.config.getoption("--data-seed") or random.randint(0, 2**32)
    print(f"test data seed: {seed}")          # failure par ye log mein dikhega
    return TestDataGenerator(seed=seed)

token = secrets.token_hex(32)                  # 64 hex characters

Kab kya:

Use random Use secrets Test data generation API tokens, session IDs Shuffling test order Passwords (real ones) Simulations, sampling Cryptographic keys Jitter in retry delays Anything security-relevant

Kyun: random Mersenne Twister use karta hai jo deterministic hai. 624 consecutive outputs dekh kar poora internal state reconstruct kiya ja sakta hai. Isliye security ke liye kabhi nahi.

import hashlib
from pathlib import Path

# --- String hashing ---
data = "test_login_result"
print(hashlib.sha256(data.encode("utf-8")).hexdigest())
print(hashlib.md5(data.encode("utf-8")).hexdigest())            # FAST par CRYPTOGRAPHICALLY BROKEN
print(hashlib.blake2b(data.encode("utf-8"), digest_size=16).hexdigest())    # modern, fast

# --- File hashing (chunked -- bade files ke liye) ---
def file_hash(path: Path, algorithm: str = "sha256", chunk_size: int = 65536) -> str:
    h = hashlib.new(algorithm)
    with path.open("rb") as f:
        while chunk := f.read(chunk_size):
            h.update(chunk)
    return h.hexdigest()

# Python 3.11+: file_digest helper
# with open("file.bin", "rb") as f:
#     print(hashlib.file_digest(f, "sha256").hexdigest())

# --- Available algorithms ---
print(sorted(hashlib.algorithms_guaranteed))
# ['blake2b', 'blake2s', 'md5', 'sha1', 'sha224', 'sha256', 'sha384', 'sha3_224',
#  'sha3_256', 'sha3_384', 'sha3_512', 'sha512', 'shake_128', 'shake_256']

# --- Password hashing -- sha256 NAHI, PBKDF2/scrypt/argon2 ---
salt = b"random_salt_16_bytes"
key = hashlib.pbkdf2_hmac("sha256", b"password", salt, iterations=600_000)
print(key.hex()[:32])

QA use cases:

import hashlib
import json
from pathlib import Path


def stable_test_id(test_name: str, params: dict) -> str:
    """Parametrised test ka stable, short ID."""
    payload = json.dumps({"name": test_name, "params": params}, sort_keys=True)
    return hashlib.sha256(payload.encode("utf-8")).hexdigest()[:12]


def content_hash(text: str) -> str:
    """Normalised content ka hash -- snapshot testing ke liye."""
    normalised = " ".join(text.split())                    # whitespace normalise
    return hashlib.sha256(normalised.encode("utf-8")).hexdigest()


def cache_key(*parts) -> str:
    """Cache key from arbitrary parts."""
    payload = "|".join(str(p) for p in parts)
    return hashlib.blake2b(payload.encode("utf-8"), digest_size=16).hexdigest()


print(stable_test_id("test_login", {"browser": "chromium", "env": "staging"}))
print(cache_key("test_login", "chromium", "staging"))
  1. sort_keys=True — deterministic JSON. Bina iske same data ka alag hash aa sakta hai.
  2. [:12] — truncated hash. 12 hex chars = 48 bits = ~281 trillion values. Test IDs ke liye kaafi (birthday paradox se ~16 million tests par collision ka 50% chance).
  3. blake2b(digest_size=16) — sha256 se tez hai aur configurable output size. Non-security use cases ke liye ideal.

print(uuid.uuid1())                     # timestamp + MAC address (PRIVACY LEAK)
print(uuid.uuid3(uuid.NAMESPACE_DNS, "example.com"))     # MD5 of namespace+name
print(uuid.uuid4())                     # RANDOM -- ye 99% cases mein use karo

Version comparison:

Version Based on Deterministic Kab uuid1 timestamp + MAC Nahi Avoid — MAC address leak karta hai uuid3 MD5(namespace + name) Haan Legacy — uuid5 use karo uuid4 Random (122 bits) Nahi Default choice uuid5 SHA1(namespace + name) Haan Same input se same UUID chahiye

QA use cases:

import uuid


def unique_test_email(prefix: str = "test") -> str:
    """Har run mein unique email -- database constraint conflicts se bachne ke liye."""
    return f"{prefix}_{uuid.uuid4().hex[:12]}@test.example.com"


def deterministic_test_user(test_name: str) -> str:
    """Ek test ka HAMESHA same user -- cleanup aur debugging aasan."""
    namespace = uuid.UUID("6ba7b810-9dad-11d1-80b4-00c04fd430c8")     # NAMESPACE_DNS
    return f"user_{uuid.uuid5(namespace, test_name).hex[:12]}@test.example.com"


def correlation_id() -> str:
    """Request tracing ke liye -- test se backend logs tak correlate karo."""
    return str(uuid.uuid4())


print(unique_test_email())                              # har baar alag
print(deterministic_test_user("test_login"))            # HAMESHA same
print(deterministic_test_user("test_login"))            # wahi

Line-by-line walkthrough:

  1. uuid4().hex[:12] — 12 hex chars = 48 bits. Emails ke liye kaafi unique hai aur padhne mein manageable.
  2. uuid5(namespace, name) — deterministic. Same test name se hamesha same UUID. Ye QA mein bahut useful hai: har test ka apna dedicated test user, jo debugging aur cleanup ko trivial banata hai — aap DB mein exactly wo user dhoondh sakte ho.
  3. correlation_id() — har test request mein header ke roop mein bhejo: 
    headers = {"X-Correlation-ID": correlation_id()}
    Phir backend logs mein us ID se poora request trace mil jaata hai. Ye ek strong senior QA practice hai.

docs.title: Gotchas
docs.text:
Gotcha 1 — random.seed() global hai.

import random
random.seed(42)
# ...koi third-party library bhi random use karti hai...
# ...aapki reproducibility TOOT gayi
rng = random.Random(42)         # isolated -- ye use karo

Gotcha 2 — random security ke liye nahi.

import random, secrets
# token = "".join(random.choices("abcdef0123456789", k=32))     # PREDICTABLE
token = secrets.token_hex(16)                                    # secure

Gotcha 3 — MD5/SHA1 security ke liye nahi.

import hashlib
# MD5 aur SHA1 collision attacks ke liye broken hain
# Par NON-security use (cache keys, dedup) ke liye theek hain -- aur tez hain
h = hashlib.md5(b"data", usedforsecurity=False).hexdigest()      # 3.9+: intent explicit

usedforsecurity=False FIPS mode mein zaruri hai, aur code review mein intent clear karta hai.

Gotcha 4 — hash consistency across runs.

# hash() built-in strings ke liye RANDOMISED hai (PYTHONHASHSEED)
print(hash("test"))            # har run mein alag!

import hashlib
print(hashlib.sha256(b"test").hexdigest())    # HAMESHA same

Persistent IDs ke liye hashlib use karo, hash() nahi.

Interview answer: "random is a deterministic PRNG — Mersenne Twister — so I use it for test data and never for anything security-relevant, where secrets uses the OS entropy source instead. The key practice with random is to create my own random.Random(seed) instance rather than seeding the global one, because a third-party library sharing the global generator breaks reproducibility. I log the seed at the start of each run, so when a data-driven test fails I can replay it with the exact same data — that turns 'flaky, can't reproduce' into a one-command repro.

hashlib I use for stable identifiers: hashing a sorted-JSON of the test name and parameters gives a short deterministic ID, and chunked hashing gives me file checksums for artifact deduplication in constant memory. Note that the builtin hash() is randomised per process, so anything persistent has to use hashlib.

For uuid the distinction that matters is uuid4 versus uuid5. uuid4 is random, which I use for correlation IDs sent as a request header so I can trace a test through the backend logs. uuid5 is deterministic from a namespace and a name, so uuid5(ns, test_name) gives each test a permanent dedicated user — same across every run, which makes cleanup and debugging in the database straightforward. And I avoid uuid1 entirely, because it embeds the MAC address."

from enum import Enum, IntEnum, StrEnum, Flag, IntFlag, auto, unique


# --- 1. Enum: basic ---
@unique                                          # duplicate values ban karo
class Status(Enum):
    PASSED = "passed"
    FAILED = "failed"
    SKIPPED = "skipped"

print(Status.PASSED)                              # Status.PASSED
print(Status.PASSED.name)                         # 'PASSED'
print(Status.PASSED.value)                        # 'passed'
print(Status("passed"))                           # Status.PASSED   -- value se lookup
print(Status["PASSED"])                           # Status.PASSED   -- name se lookup
print(list(Status))                               # [Status.PASSED, ...]  -- iterable
print(Status.PASSED == Status.PASSED)             # True
print(Status.PASSED == "passed")                  # FALSE!  -- Enum string ke barabar nahi
print(Status.PASSED is Status.PASSED)             # True -- singletons hain


# --- 2. IntEnum: int ki tarah behave karta hai ---
class Priority(IntEnum):
    LOW = 1
    MEDIUM = 2
    HIGH = 3
    CRITICAL = 4

print(Priority.HIGH > Priority.LOW)               # True -- COMPARE ho sakte hain
print(Priority.HIGH + 1)                          # 4    -- arithmetic
print(Priority.HIGH == 3)                         # True -- int ke barabar
print(sorted(Priority, reverse=True))             # sortable


# --- 3. StrEnum (3.11+): str ki tarah ---
class Browser(StrEnum):
    CHROMIUM = "chromium"
    FIREFOX = "firefox"
    WEBKIT = "webkit"

print(Browser.CHROMIUM == "chromium")             # True!
print(f"running on {Browser.CHROMIUM}")           # running on chromium
print("chromium" in [b for b in Browser])         # True
# 3.11 se pehle: class Browser(str, Enum): ...


# --- 4. auto(): values automatically ---
class Phase(Enum):
    SETUP = auto()                                # 1
    CALL = auto()                                 # 2
    TEARDOWN = auto()                             # 3

print([f"{p.name}={p.value}" for p in Phase])


# --- 5. Flag: bitwise combinations ---
class TestTag(Flag):
    NONE = 0
    SMOKE = auto()                                # 1
    REGRESSION = auto()                           # 2
    SLOW = auto()                                 # 4
    FLAKY = auto()                                # 8
    CRITICAL_PATH = SMOKE | REGRESSION            # 3 -- composite

tags = TestTag.SMOKE | TestTag.SLOW
print(tags)                                        # TestTag.SMOKE|SLOW
print(TestTag.SMOKE in tags)                       # True
print(TestTag.FLAKY in tags)                       # False
print(tags & TestTag.SLOW)                         # TestTag.SLOW
print(tags | TestTag.FLAKY)                        # TestTag.SMOKE|SLOW|FLAKY
print(~TestTag.SMOKE)                              # baaki sab
print(list(tags))                                  # [TestTag.SMOKE, TestTag.SLOW]  (3.11+)

Line-by-line walkthrough:

  1. @unique — duplicate values par ValueError at class creation. Bina iske duplicate value wala member ek alias ban jaata hai: 
    class Bad(Enum):
    A = 1
    B = 1              # B ab A ka alias hai
print(Bad.B is Bad.A)  # True
print(list(Bad))       # [Bad.A]  -- B list mein nahi hai!
  2. Status.PASSED == "passed" → False. Plain Enum apni value ke barabar nahi hota. Ye deliberate type safety hai. Agar aapko string comparison chahiye toh StrEnum use karo.
  3. Status("passed") — value se member. Invalid value par ValueError.
  4. IntEnum — int se inherit karta hai, toh comparison, arithmetic, aur JSON serialisation sab kaam karte hain. HTTP status codes ke liye perfect (http.HTTPStatus yahi hai).
  5. StrEnum (3.11+) — str se inherit. f-strings mein natural, JSON mein seedha jaata hai, aur existing string-based code ke saath compatible hai.
  6. auto() — sequential values. Jab value ki actual importance na ho.
  7. Flag — bitwise combinations. Har member power of 2 hona chahiye (auto() ye handle karta hai). Test tags, permissions, feature flags ke liye.

docs.title: Methods aur properties enums par
docs.text:
from enum import Enum
from functools import total_ordering


class Status(Enum):
    PASSED = "passed"
    FAILED = "failed"
    SKIPPED = "skipped"
    ERROR = "error"
    XFAILED = "xfailed"
    XPASSED = "xpassed"

    @property
    def is_failure(self) -> bool:
        return self in (Status.FAILED, Status.ERROR, Status.XPASSED)

    @property
    def is_success(self) -> bool:
        return self in (Status.PASSED, Status.XFAILED)

    @property
    def symbol(self) -> str:
        return {
            Status.PASSED: ".",
            Status.FAILED: "F",
            Status.SKIPPED: "s",
            Status.ERROR: "E",
            Status.XFAILED: "x",
            Status.XPASSED: "X",
        }[self]

    @property
    def colour(self) -> str:
        if self.is_failure:
            return "\033[31m"                     # red
        if self is Status.SKIPPED:
            return "\033[33m"                     # yellow
        return "\033[32m"                         # green

    @classmethod
    def from_pytest(cls, outcome: str, *, xfail: bool = False) -> "Status":
        """pytest ke outcome strings se mapping."""
        mapping = {
            "passed": cls.XPASSED if xfail else cls.PASSED,
            "failed": cls.XFAILED if xfail else cls.FAILED,
            "skipped": cls.SKIPPED,
            "error": cls.ERROR,
        }
        try:
            return mapping[outcome.lower()]
        except KeyError:
            raise ValueError(
                f"unknown pytest outcome {outcome!r}; expected {sorted(mapping)}"
            ) from None

    def __str__(self) -> str:
        return self.value


for s in Status:
    print(f"{s.symbol} {s.name:<8} failure={s.is_failure}")

print(Status.from_pytest("passed"))                # Status.PASSED
print(Status.from_pytest("passed", xfail=True))    # Status.XPASSED
  1. @property enum members par kaam karta hai — ye normal class hi hai.
  2. @classmethod from_pytest — alternative constructor (5.3). External representation se internal enum tak mapping ek jagah.
  3. __str__ override — print(status) par Status.PASSED ki jagah passed dikhega.
  4. Ye pattern bahut powerful hai: saara status-related logic ek jagah, magic strings kahin nahi.

docs.title: Custom _missing_ — flexible lookup
docs.text:
from enum import Enum


class Browser(Enum):
    CHROMIUM = "chromium"
    FIREFOX = "firefox"
    WEBKIT = "webkit"

    @classmethod
    def _missing_(cls, value):
        """Jab normal lookup fail ho toh ye call hota hai."""
        if not isinstance(value, str):
            return None
        normalised = value.strip().lower()

        # Aliases
        aliases = {
            "chrome": cls.CHROMIUM,
            "google-chrome": cls.CHROMIUM,
            "ff": cls.FIREFOX,
            "safari": cls.WEBKIT,
            "edge": cls.CHROMIUM,
        }
        if normalised in aliases:
            return aliases[normalised]

        # Case-insensitive exact match
        for member in cls:
            if member.value == normalised:
                return member
        return None                               # None -> ValueError raise hoga


print(Browser("CHROMIUM"))          # Browser.CHROMIUM   (case-insensitive)
print(Browser("chrome"))            # Browser.CHROMIUM   (alias)
print(Browser("  Safari  "))        # Browser.WEBKIT     (alias + strip)
# print(Browser("netscape"))        # ValueError: 'netscape' is not a valid Browser
  1. _missing_ — enum ka hook jab value lookup fail ho. None return karne se normal ValueError aata hai.
  2. Ye config parsing ke liye bahut useful hai — users chrome, Chrome, chromium kuch bhi likh sakte hain aur sab kaam karta hai.

docs.title: JSON serialisation
docs.text:
import json
from enum import Enum, StrEnum


class Status(Enum):
    PASSED = "passed"
    FAILED = "failed"


class Browser(StrEnum):
    CHROMIUM = "chromium"


# Plain Enum -- serialise nahi hota
# json.dumps({"status": Status.PASSED})       # TypeError: Object of type Status is not JSON serializable

# Options:
# 1. .value use karo
print(json.dumps({"status": Status.PASSED.value}))

# 2. default function
print(json.dumps({"status": Status.PASSED}, default=lambda o: o.value if isinstance(o, Enum) else str(o)))

# 3. StrEnum / IntEnum -- automatically serialise hote hain
print(json.dumps({"browser": Browser.CHROMIUM}))          # {"browser": "chromium"}

StrEnum/IntEnum ka bada practical faayda yahi hai — wo JSON, database, aur string APIs ke saath transparently kaam karte hain.

docs.title: QA use cases
docs.text:
from enum import Enum, IntEnum, StrEnum, Flag, auto


class TestEnvironment(StrEnum):
    LOCAL = "local"
    DEV = "dev"
    STAGING = "staging"
    PROD = "prod"

    @property
    def is_production(self) -> bool:
        return self is TestEnvironment.PROD

    @property
    def allows_destructive_tests(self) -> bool:
        return self in (TestEnvironment.LOCAL, TestEnvironment.DEV)

    @property
    def base_url(self) -> str:
        return {
            TestEnvironment.LOCAL: "http://localhost:3000",
            TestEnvironment.DEV: "https://dev.example.com",
            TestEnvironment.STAGING: "https://staging.example.com",
            TestEnvironment.PROD: "https://www.example.com",
        }[self]


class Severity(IntEnum):
    """Bug severity -- comparable hona chahiye."""
    TRIVIAL = 1
    MINOR = 2
    MAJOR = 3
    CRITICAL = 4
    BLOCKER = 5

    @property
    def sla_hours(self) -> int:
        return {1: 720, 2: 168, 3: 72, 4: 24, 5: 4}[self.value]


class TestCapability(Flag):
    """Test kya-kya kar sakta hai."""
    NONE = 0
    NETWORK = auto()
    DATABASE = auto()
    FILESYSTEM = auto()
    BROWSER = auto()
    EMAIL = auto()

    UNIT = NONE
    INTEGRATION = NETWORK | DATABASE
    E2E = NETWORK | DATABASE | BROWSER | EMAIL


# Use
env = TestEnvironment("staging")
print(env.base_url, env.allows_destructive_tests)

bug = Severity.CRITICAL
print(bug >= Severity.MAJOR, f"SLA: {bug.sla_hours}h")     # True SLA: 24h

caps = TestCapability.E2E
print(TestCapability.BROWSER in caps)                       # True
print(TestCapability.FILESYSTEM in caps)                    # False


def can_run_in_ci(caps: TestCapability) -> bool:
    """CI mein email aur filesystem access nahi hai."""
    forbidden = TestCapability.EMAIL | TestCapability.FILESYSTEM
    return not (caps & forbidden)

print(can_run_in_ci(TestCapability.INTEGRATION))            # True
print(can_run_in_ci(TestCapability.E2E))                    # False (EMAIL chahiye)

Line-by-line walkthrough:

  1. TestEnvironment(StrEnum) — config se string aati hai, seedha enum ban jaati hai. Aur f-strings mein natural.
  2. env.allows_destructive_tests — business logic enum par. Ye har jagah if env in ("local", "dev") likhne se better hai.
  3. Severity(IntEnum) — comparison natural hai (bug >= Severity.MAJOR). Ordering semantically meaningful hai.
  4. TestCapability(Flag) — composite values (INTEGRATION = NETWORK | DATABASE). Ye requirements express karne ka clean tareeka hai.
  5. not (caps & forbidden) — bitwise intersection. Agar koi common bit ho toh truthy.

docs.title: Gotchas
docs.text:
Gotcha 1 — plain Enum string ke barabar nahi.

from enum import Enum
class Status(Enum):
    PASSED = "passed"

print(Status.PASSED == "passed")           # False
print(Status.PASSED.value == "passed")     # True
# Fix: StrEnum use karo agar string comparison chahiye

Gotcha 2 — duplicate values alias bante hain.

from enum import Enum
class Bad(Enum):
    A = 1
    B = 1
print(list(Bad), Bad.B is Bad.A)           # [<Bad.A: 1>] True
# Fix: @unique decorator

Gotcha 3 — mutable default enum members.

from enum import Enum
# class Bad(Enum):
#     A = []          # ValueError-ish behaviour; list unhashable, enum ko value hashable chahiye

Gotcha 4 — enum ko subclass nahi kar sakte (agar usme members hon).

from enum import Enum
class Base(Enum):
    A = 1
# class Child(Base):        # TypeError: Base: cannot extend enumeration
#     B = 2

# Par MEMBER-LESS enum extend ho sakti hai (mixin pattern):
class Mixin(Enum):
    @property
    def described(self): return f"{self.name}={self.value}"

class Real(Mixin):
    A = 1
print(Real.A.described)                     # A=1

Gotcha 5 — IntEnum accidentally int ki tarah use ho jaata hai.

from enum import IntEnum
class Priority(IntEnum):
    LOW = 1

print(Priority.LOW + 100)              # 101 -- int ban gaya, enum nahi
print(type(Priority.LOW + 100))        # <class 'int'>

Ye faayda bhi hai aur khatra bhi. Agar aap type safety chahte ho toh plain Enum use karo.

Interview answer: "An enum is a set of named constants that are singletons, so you compare with is and typos fail at import time as an AttributeError rather than silently flowing through as a magic string. The variants matter: plain Enum is not equal to its value, which is deliberate type safety; IntEnum inherits from int so it compares, sorts, does arithmetic, and serialises — that's what http.HTTPStatus is, and it's right for anything with a natural ordering like bug severity; StrEnum in 3.11 does the same for strings, which is what I use for environment names and browsers because it drops straight into f-strings, JSON, and existing string-based APIs.

What makes enums more than constants is that they're classes, so behaviour lives with the value. My TestEnvironment enum has base_url and allows_destructive_tests as properties, which replaces if env in ('local', 'dev') scattered across the codebase. _missing_ is another hook I use for config parsing — it lets Browser('Chrome') and Browser(' safari ') resolve to the right member through aliases and normalisation, instead of forcing users to type the exact value. And Flag gives bitwise composition, which I use to express what capabilities a test needs — network, database, browser — so CI can skip anything requiring something the environment doesn't have."

docs.title: 12.9 unittest.mock
docs.text: (Poora mocking treatment Part 15 mein hai — yahan module ka tour.)

docs.title: Mock vs MagicMock vs patch
docs.text:
from unittest.mock import Mock, MagicMock, patch, call, ANY, sentinel, PropertyMock

# --- Mock: koi bhi attribute/method auto-create hota hai ---
m = Mock()
m.anything.at.all()                              # koi error nahi
print(m.some_attribute)                          # <Mock name='mock.some_attribute' id='...'>
print(m.some_method(1, 2))                        # <Mock name='mock.some_method()' id='...'>

# --- Return values ---
m.get_status.return_value = "passed"
print(m.get_status())                             # 'passed'
print(m.get_status(1, 2, 3))                      # 'passed'  -- arguments ignore

# --- side_effect: function, exception, ya iterable ---
m.fetch.side_effect = ConnectionError("network down")
try:
    m.fetch()
except ConnectionError as e:
    print(f"raised: {e}")

m.get_page.side_effect = ["page1", "page2", "page3"]
print(m.get_page(), m.get_page(), m.get_page())   # page1 page2 page3
# m.get_page()                                     # StopIteration

m.compute.side_effect = lambda x: x * 2
print(m.compute(21))                              # 42

# --- Assertions ---
m2 = Mock()
m2.click("#submit", timeout=5000)
m2.click("#cancel")

m2.click.assert_called()                          # kabhi bhi call hua?
m2.click.assert_called_once()                     # EXACTLY ek baar? -> AssertionError (2 baar)
m2.click.assert_called_with("#cancel")            # LAST call se match
m2.click.assert_any_call("#submit", timeout=5000) # KISI bhi call se match
m2.click.assert_has_calls([call("#submit", timeout=5000), call("#cancel")])
print(m2.click.call_count)                        # 2
print(m2.click.call_args)                         # call('#cancel')  -- last
print(m2.click.call_args_list)                    # saare calls
print(m2.click.call_args.args, m2.click.call_args.kwargs)

m2.nonexistent.assert_not_called()                # True

# --- MagicMock: dunder methods bhi support karta hai ---
mm = MagicMock()
print(len(mm))                                    # 0    (Mock par TypeError)
print(list(mm))                                   # []
print(mm[0])                                      # <MagicMock ...>
print(bool(mm))                                   # True
with mm:                                          # context manager bhi
    pass
mm.__len__.return_value = 5
print(len(mm))                                    # 5

Mock vs MagicMock:

Mock MagicMock Attributes/methods auto-create auto-create Dunder methods (__len__, __iter__, __enter__) Nahi Haan Speed thoda tez thoda dheema Kab simple objects containers, context managers, iterables

Default: MagicMock (aur patch bhi default MagicMock use karta hai).

docs.title: patch — kahan patch karna hai (THE key concept)
docs.text:
# --- module structure ---
# myapp/api.py
#     import requests
#     def fetch_status(url):
#         return requests.get(url).json()
#
# myapp/service.py
#     from myapp.api import fetch_status
#     def check_health():
#         return fetch_status("https://api.example.com/health")


# --- GALAT ---
# with patch("myapp.api.fetch_status"):           # api module mein patch kiya
#     check_health()                               # ...par service ne pehle hi import kar liya tha
# -> Original function chalega, patch bekaar

# --- SAHI ---
# with patch("myapp.service.fetch_status") as mock_fetch:   # JAHAN USE HO RAHA HAI
#     mock_fetch.return_value = {"status": "ok"}
#     result = check_health()
# -> Mock chalega

Rule: "Patch where it's LOOKED UP, not where it's DEFINED."

Kyun: from myapp.api import fetch_status service module ke namespace mein ek naya naam binding banata hai jo us waqt ke function object par point karta hai. Baad mein api module mein us naam ko rebind karne se service ka binding nahi badalta (10.1 ka from module import name gotcha).

Ek exception:

# Agar service.py aisa likha ho:
# import myapp.api
# def check_health():
#     return myapp.api.fetch_status(...)          # RUNTIME par lookup
#
# Toh patch("myapp.api.fetch_status") KAAM KAREGA

Isliye import module + module.function() pattern testing-friendly hai.

docs.title: patch ke forms
docs.text:
from unittest.mock import patch, MagicMock

# 1. Decorator
# @patch("myapp.service.fetch_status")
# def test_health(mock_fetch):                     # mock argument mein aata hai
#     mock_fetch.return_value = {"status": "ok"}
#     assert check_health()["status"] == "ok"

# 2. Multiple decorators -- BOTTOM-UP order
# @patch("myapp.service.send_email")               # ye TEESRA argument
# @patch("myapp.service.save_to_db")               # ye DOOSRA argument
# @patch("myapp.service.fetch_status")             # ye PEHLA argument
# def test_flow(mock_fetch, mock_save, mock_email):
#     ...

# 3. Context manager
# with patch("myapp.service.fetch_status") as mock_fetch:
#     mock_fetch.return_value = {"status": "ok"}
#     ...

# 4. Manual start/stop
# patcher = patch("myapp.service.fetch_status")
# mock_fetch = patcher.start()
# ...
# patcher.stop()

# 5. patch.object -- attribute ko patch karo
# with patch.object(SomeClass, "method_name") as mock_method:
#     ...

# 6. patch.dict -- dict ko temporarily modify karo
import os
with patch.dict(os.environ, {"TEST_ENV": "staging"}, clear=False):
    print(os.environ["TEST_ENV"])                  # staging
# restore ho gaya

# 7. patch multiple with new=
with patch("os.getcwd", new=lambda: "/fake/path"):
    print(os.getcwd())                             # /fake/path

Decorator order: decorators bottom-up apply hote hain, toh sabse neeche wala patch sabse pehla argument banta hai. Ye counterintuitive hai aur common bug source.

docs.title: autospec — signature enforcement
docs.text:
from unittest.mock import patch, create_autospec


class ApiClient:
    def get(self, path: str, timeout: int = 10) -> dict:
        return {}


# --- Bina autospec: koi bhi call chal jaati hai ---
# with patch("__main__.ApiClient") as MockClient:
#     MockClient().get()                            # arguments missing -- par mock khush hai
#     MockClient().nonexistent_method()             # method exist hi nahi karta -- par chal gaya

# --- autospec ke saath: signature enforce hoti hai ---
mock_client = create_autospec(ApiClient, instance=True)
mock_client.get("/health")                          # theek
# mock_client.get()                                 # TypeError: missing required argument: 'path'
# mock_client.nonexistent()                         # AttributeError

# patch mein:
# with patch("myapp.service.ApiClient", autospec=True) as MockClient:
#     ...
  1. autospec=True — mock ko real object ka signature milta hai. Galat call turant fail hoti hai.
  2. Bina autospec ke, mock aapke refactors ke saath rot jaate hain: aapne method rename kiya, real code toot gaya, par test abhi bhi pass ho raha hai kyunki mock kuch bhi accept karta hai.
  3. autospec=True default hona chahiye. Slight performance cost hai (introspection) par correctness ke liye worth it.

docs.title: ANY, sentinel, PropertyMock
docs.text:
from unittest.mock import Mock, ANY, sentinel, PropertyMock, patch

# --- ANY: "is argument ki parwah nahi" ---
m = Mock()
m.log("test_login", timestamp=1234567890.123, level="INFO")
m.log.assert_called_with("test_login", timestamp=ANY, level="INFO")     # timestamp ignore

# --- sentinel: unique placeholder objects ---
def process(data):
    return data

result = process(sentinel.input_data)
print(result is sentinel.input_data)               # True
print(sentinel.input_data)                          # sentinel.input_data  (readable repr)
# Faayda: agar test fail ho toh 'sentinel.input_data' dikhta hai, '<Mock id=...>' nahi

# --- PropertyMock: properties ko mock karo ---
class Page:
    @property
    def url(self) -> str:
        return "https://real.example.com"

with patch.object(Page, "url", new_callable=PropertyMock) as mock_url:
    mock_url.return_value = "https://fake.example.com"
    p = Page()
    print(p.url)                                    # https://fake.example.com
    mock_url.assert_called_once()
  1. ANY — __eq__ hamesha True deta hai. Timestamps, UUIDs, aur doosre non-deterministic arguments ke liye.
  2. sentinel.X — unique object jiska readable repr hai. Ye object() se better hai debugging mein.
  3. PropertyMock — properties class par patch karni padti hain (5.4: data descriptors instance dict se jeette hain). new_callable=PropertyMock zaruri hai.

docs.title: mock_open — file operations
docs.text:
from unittest.mock import mock_open, patch

# Read
with patch("builtins.open", mock_open(read_data="line1\nline2\n")) as m:
    with open("any_file.txt") as f:
        content = f.read()
    print(content)                                  # line1\nline2\n
    m.assert_called_once_with("any_file.txt")

# Write
m = mock_open()
with patch("builtins.open", m):
    with open("output.txt", "w") as f:
        f.write("test data")
m().write.assert_called_once_with("test data")

# NOTE: mock_open ka readline/iteration support 3.6+ mein hai par thoda limited hai.
# Real files ke liye tmp_path fixture better hai.

Practical advice: mock_open se better hai tmp_path fixture use karke real file likhna — kam magic, zyada realistic.

docs.title: Kab mock karo, kab nahi
docs.text:
Mock karo Mat karo External APIs (network) Aapka apna code jo aap test kar rahe ho Database (unit tests mein) Simple data structures (dict, list) Time (datetime.now) Pure functions Randomness Standard library ka behaviour File system (kabhi-kabhi) Jo cheez integration test se better cover hoti hai Slow operations Sab kuch (over-mocking = tests jo kuch test nahi karte)

Over-mocking ka symptom: aap refactor karte ho, real code toot jaata hai, par saare tests pass hote hain. Tab aapke tests implementation ko test kar rahe hain, behaviour ko nahi.

Interview answer: "Mock auto-creates any attribute you touch; MagicMock adds the dunder methods, so it works as a container, iterable, or context manager — that's why patch uses it by default. You configure behaviour with return_value or side_effect, where side_effect can be an exception, a callable, or an iterable that yields a different value per call — that last one is how I simulate a flaky endpoint that fails twice then succeeds.

The thing everyone gets wrong is where to patch: you patch where the name is looked up, not where it's defined. If service.py does from api import fetch, then patching api.fetch does nothing, because service already holds its own binding to the original object — you have to patch service.fetch. The exception is if the code does import api and calls api.fetch(), because that resolves at call time. That's actually an argument for writing import module rather than from module import name in code you'll need to test.

And I always pass autospec=True. Without it a mock accepts any call at all, so after you rename a method or change its signature the production code breaks while the test still passes — the mock has silently rotted. With autospec the mock takes the real signature and wrong calls raise immediately."

docs.title: 12.10 typing and dataclasses — quick cross-reference
docs.text:
Ye dono modules poori detail mein pehle cover ho chuke hain, kyunki wo language-level concepts hain:

Topic Section typing — Optional, Union, generics, TypeVar, Protocol, TypedDict, Callable, Literal Part 4.7 dataclasses — @dataclass, field, frozen, slots, kw_only, __post_init__, asdict, replace Part 5.8 enum 12.8 (upar)

Ek quick reminder table jo interview mein kaam aata hai:

Chahiye Use Mutable record with methods @dataclass Immutable hashable record @dataclass(frozen=True) ya typing.NamedTuple Tuple compatibility + unpacking typing.NamedTuple Dict ka shape describe karna (JSON) typing.TypedDict Runtime validation (API boundary) pydantic.BaseModel "Koi bhi cheez jisme ye methods hon" typing.Protocol Named constants with behaviour enum.Enum / StrEnum / IntEnum Fixed set of allowed string values typing.Literal["a", "b"]

docs.title: Kya hai
docs.text:
GIL (Global Interpreter Lock) ek mutex hai jo guarantee karta hai ki ek CPython process mein ek waqt par sirf ek thread Python bytecode execute kar sakta hai.

Analogy: ek office mein 8 employees (threads) hain par sirf ek keyboard (GIL) hai. Sirf jiske paas keyboard hai wo type kar sakta hai. Baaki wait karte hain — ya phir wo kaam karte hain jismein keyboard ki zarurat nahi (phone call = I/O). Jab koi phone par hai, wo keyboard chhod deta hai taaki koi aur type kar sake.

docs.title: Kyu hai
docs.text:
CPython reference counting se memory manage karta hai (Part 14). Har object mein ek counter hai jo badhta-ghatta rehta hai:

// Simplified CPython internals
Py_INCREF(obj);     // obj->ob_refcnt++
Py_DECREF(obj);     // obj->ob_refcnt--; if (obj->ob_refcnt == 0) free(obj);

ob_refcnt++ atomic nahi hai — wo teen machine instructions hai (read, add, write). Do threads ek saath karein toh:

Thread A: read refcnt (= 2)
Thread B: read refcnt (= 2)
Thread A: add 1        (= 3)
Thread B: add 1        (= 3)
Thread A: write 3
Thread B: write 3

Actual refcount: 3.  Sahi hona chahiye tha: 4.
-> Ek reference "kho" gaya -> object jaldi free ho jaayega -> USE AFTER FREE -> crash/corruption

Options the:

  1. Har object par ek lock — bahut zyada overhead (har INCREF par lock acquire).
  2. Atomic operations — dheeme hain aur portability issues.
  3. Ek global lock — simple, single-threaded code ko fast rakhta hai. CPython ne ye chuna.

GIL ka faayda: single-threaded code (jo 95% Python code hai) fast rehta hai, aur C extensions likhna simple hai. Nuksan: CPU-bound multithreading kaam nahi karta.

docs.title: GIL kya BLOCK karta hai aur kya NAHI
docs.text:
GIL BLOCK karta hai:
  - CPU-bound pure Python code ka parallel execution
    (do threads ek saath loops nahi chala sakte)

GIL NAHI block karta:
  - I/O operations (file read/write, network, socket, subprocess)
    -> Python I/O call ke doraan GIL RELEASE kar deta hai
  - time.sleep()
    -> GIL release
  - Kai C extensions: NumPy, Pillow, hashlib, zlib, lxml, cryptography
    -> Wo apni heavy computation ke doraan GIL release karte hain
  - Multiprocessing
    -> Har process ka apna interpreter aur apna GIL
  - Subprocess
    -> Bilkul alag process

Proof — CPU-bound:

import time
import threading
import multiprocessing


def cpu_work(n: int = 15_000_000) -> int:
    """Pure Python CPU-bound work."""
    total = 0
    for i in range(n):
        total += i * i
    return total


def measure(label: str, fn) -> float:
    start = time.perf_counter()
    fn()
    elapsed = time.perf_counter() - start
    print(f"{label:<28} {elapsed:.2f}s")
    return elapsed


if __name__ == "__main__":
    # Sequential
    t_seq = measure("sequential (2x)", lambda: [cpu_work(), cpu_work()])

    # Threads
    def run_threads():
        ts = [threading.Thread(target=cpu_work) for _ in range(2)]
        for t in ts: t.start()
        for t in ts: t.join()
    t_thr = measure("2 threads", run_threads)

    # Processes
    def run_processes():
        ps = [multiprocessing.Process(target=cpu_work) for _ in range(2)]
        for p in ps: p.start()
        for p in ps: p.join()
    t_proc = measure("2 processes", run_processes)

    print(f"\nthreads speedup:   {t_seq / t_thr:.2f}x")
    print(f"processes speedup: {t_seq / t_proc:.2f}x")

Typical output (multi-core machine):

sequential (2x)              2.84s
2 threads                    2.91s        <- KOI faayda nahi (thoda dheema, overhead se)
2 processes                  1.48s        <- ~2x faster

threads speedup:   0.98x
processes speedup: 1.92x

Proof — I/O-bound:

import time
import threading
import urllib.request
from concurrent.futures import ThreadPoolExecutor


def io_work(delay: float = 0.5):
    """I/O simulate karo -- sleep GIL release karta hai."""
    time.sleep(delay)


def measure(label, fn):
    start = time.perf_counter()
    fn()
    print(f"{label:<28} {time.perf_counter() - start:.2f}s")


measure("sequential (8x)", lambda: [io_work() for _ in range(8)])

def run_threads():
    ts = [threading.Thread(target=io_work) for _ in range(8)]
    for t in ts: t.start()
    for t in ts: t.join()
measure("8 threads", run_threads)

Output:

sequential (8x)              4.02s
8 threads                    0.51s        <- ~8x faster!

Yahi poori kahani hai: GIL sirf Python bytecode execution ko serialise karta hai. I/O wait ke doraan GIL release ho jaata hai, toh threads genuinely parallel wait karte hain.

docs.title: GIL kab release hota hai
docs.text:
1. I/O operations (file, socket, pipe)
2. time.sleep()
3. Har ~5ms (sys.getswitchinterval()) -- CPU-bound threads ke beech switching ke liye
4. C extensions jo explicitly Py_BEGIN_ALLOW_THREADS / Py_END_ALLOW_THREADS use karti hain
